stem: You are called to the Emergency Department to see a 25-year-old man who experienced a sudden-onset, severe posterior headache 5 hours previously. He has vomited once and has minimal neck stiffness. He is apyrexial and the neurological examination is entirely normal. There is a family history of a ‘burst blood vessel’. An emergency plain CT scan (at 6½ hours after the onset of symptoms) is normal. Which one of the following is the most practical next step to reach a diagnosis?
options: Computed venography followed by CSF examination for xanthochromia
Cranial MRI with gadolinium contrast enhancement
CSF examination with spectrophotometry for haemoglobin breakdown products in 12 hours’ after
CSF examination for xanthochromia within the next 2 hours
explanation:
CSF examination with spectrophotometry for haemoglobin breakdown products in 12 hours’ after
CSF examination with spectrophotometry for haemoglobin breakdown products in 12 hours’ after the onset of headache The clinical presentation suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH): typical sudden posterior headache, meningism, vomiting and possible positive family history. As CT performed outside the six-hour window is normal, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination must be performed. The most sensitive and specific test is spectrophotometry for haemoglobin breakdown products, particularly CSF bilirubin, which proves the presence of prior recent bleeding. This is now recommended instead of measuring the CSF red cell count or xanthochromia, as the procedure of lumbar puncture itself can introduce red cells into the CSF sample and thus give an uninterpretable result. CSF examination 12 hours after the onset of headache absolutely excludes SAH, but most units now accept that an examination 12 hours after headache is sufficient to rule out the vast majority of SAHs. This test has the important advantage of being able to exclude SAH in patients with a delayed presentation to medical services (spectrophotometry remains positive for 2 weeks with 100% sensitivity, sensitivity drops thereafter). The CSF sample must be centrifuged as soon as possible after the lumbar puncture (LP) (ie if LP is performed outside normal hours, the CSF sample must be centrifuged overnight to remove red cells introduced during LP, and it can then be processed the next morning).

4-Vessel intracerebral angiography
4-Vessel intracerebral angiography is incorrect. 4-vessel intracerebral angiography is only recommended for the detection of aneurysms when a proven SAH has occurred, or when adequate exclusion of a SAH is impossible in a highly suggestive case (eg inconclusive LP because spectrophotometry not used).

Computed venography followed by CSF examination for xanthochromia
Computed venography followed by CSF examination for xanthochromia is incorrect. Computed venography is a test for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis which seems less clinically likely here and therefore is not the correct answer.

Cranial MRI with gadolinium contrast enhancement
Cranial MRI with gadolinium contrast enhancement is incorrect. Cranial MRI with gadolinium contrast is not thought to be more sensitive to SAH than a prompt CT scan, so does not add anything to the diagnosis. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

CSF examination for xanthochromia within the next 2 hours
CSF examination for xanthochromia within the next 2 hours is incorrect. As outlined CSF sampling and spectrophotometry must be performed 12 hours or more after the onset of the suspected bleed.

stem: A 30-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic with a 3-month history of deteriorating physical performance at work, associated with dysarthria and clumsiness. He also complains of becoming more forgetful about simple tasks. There is no past medical history of note and he consumes 10 units of alcohol per week. He reports that his father died from a ‘psychiatric illness’ in his early 40s. On examination, his heart rate is 77 bpm and his blood pressure is 127/79 mmHg. He appears fidgety, with involuntary movements of his arms and legs. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. There is visible asterixis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive condition associated with excessive copper deposits within tissues. It can present in childhood, adolescence or early adulthood. Symptoms and signs may be clinically undetectable under five years of age and few present after the age of 35 years, although diagnosis at age over 55 years has been reported. In 90% of patients, the disease presents with either juvenile hepatic disease or neurological/psychiatric manifestations. In large studies of patients with Wilson’s disease, initial manifestations were: hepatic (40%), neurological (30%), psychiatric (10%), haematological (12%) and renal (1%). Around 25% of patients have two or more organs involved at initial assessment (usually the liver and brain). This patient has evidence of chorea and asterixis, suggesting both neurological and hepatic involvement.

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease secondary to the presence of prion proteins. Symptoms of CJD include rapid onset of dementia, behavioural change and myoclonus. Most cases of CJD are sporadic, although some are familial. It does not, however, explain this patient’s chorea or asterixis.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease is a neurodegenerative disease that targets the gamma aminobutyric acid-ergic cells in the corpus striatum of the basal ganglia. Symptoms of Huntington’s disease typically occur between 30–50 years of age, although, through anticipation, subsequent generations can have an earlier onset of the disease. The most classical symptom is chorea, uncontrolled and uncoordinated movements of the body and dementia is seen in the later stages of Huntington’s disease. Although these features are seen in this patient, the presence of asterixis points towards an alternative diagnosis of Wilson’s disease.

Motor neurone disease
Patients with motor neurone disease can present with a combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs. Initial presenting symptoms may include extreme unintentional weight loss and muscle atrophy. This diagnosis is unlikely here, as the patient also has features of liver failure not explained by motor neurone disease.

Wernicke’s encephalopathy
Alcohol excess can cause acute liver failure and, in the long term, can lead to liver cirrhosis and neurological manifestations such as Wernicke’s encephalopathy, characterised by bilateral cerebellar signs, nystagmus and confusion. This patient is, however, very young to be presenting with Wernicke’s encephalopathy and 10 units of alcohol per week is not a large enough quantity to cause the disease. Wilson’s.

stem: A 17-year-old woman presents to the clinic with worsening headache and neck pain, exacerbated by coughing. She also complains of muscle weakness and problems with unsteadiness. On examination her BP is 112/72 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. There is downbeat nystagmus, with cerebellar signs, distal weakness of the upper limb affecting the hands, and dissociated sensory loss leading to cape anaesthesia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chiari Type 1 malformation
Chiari Type 1 malformation is characterized by the descent of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal. This condition often presents with headaches exacerbated by activities that increase intracranial pressure, such as coughing. Neurological symptoms can include muscle weakness, problems with balance and coordination, and sensory abnormalities such as cape anaesthesia. Downbeat nystagmus is also commonly associated with Chiari Type 1 malformation due to compression of the cerebellum and brainstem. The combination of these symptoms aligns well with the patient's clinical presentation, making Chiari Type 1 malformation the most likely diagnosis.

Cervical spondylosis
Cervical spondylosis is a degenerative condition of the cervical spine caused by the wear and tear of the intervertebral discs and facet joints. It typically presents in older adults, usually over the age of 50, and is characterized by neck pain, stiffness, and possible radicular pain due to nerve compression. While it can occasionally cause some neurological symptoms, these are usually limited to the areas directly affected by nerve impingement, not system-wide symptoms like those described. The patient's age and extensive neurological signs, such as downbeat nystagmus and cerebellar involvement, make cervical spondylosis an unlikely diagnosis in this case.

Chiari Type 2 malformation
Chiari Type 2 malformation, also known as Arnold-Chiari malformation, usually presents in infancy or early childhood. It involves herniation of both the cerebellar tonsils and vermis, often associated with myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus. Symptoms typically include more severe brainstem dysfunction, developmental delays, and feeding difficulties rather than isolated headaches and neck pain in a teenager. The patient’s age, the nature of her symptoms, and the absence of associated congenital spinal abnormalities argue strongly against Chiari Type 2 malformation as the diagnosis.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune condition that typically presents with relapsing-remitting neurological deficits, including patchy motor and sensory loss, visual disturbances, and abnormal gait. Multiple sclerosis tends to have asymmetrical presentations rather than symmetrical neurological signs. The disease is marked by the formation of plaques in the central nervous system, leading to varying symptoms but not generally continuous headaches exacerbated by coughing or neck pain. The patient's specific neurological signs, such as downbeat nystagmus and cape anaesthesia, are more indicative of a structural abnormality like Chiari Type 1 malformation rather than multiple sclerosis. Cerebellum NeuroanatomySpondylolysthesis
Spondylolisthesis refers to the displacement of a vertebra relative to the one below it, commonly occurring in the lumbar region rather than the cervical spine. This condition leads to back pain and sometimes radicular symptoms if there is compression of spinal nerves, but it does not typically cause widespread neurological symptoms or cranial nerve involvement. The presentation in a 17-year-old with negative systemic neurological signs associated with balance and coordination issues, as well as specific cervical and brainstem involvement, is inconsistent with spondylolisthesis. Therefore, this diagnosis does not match the patient's profile as well as Chiari Type 1 malformation does.

stem: A patient with a history of left optic neuritis 1 year ago, and transient spastic paraplegia (lasting 6 weeks) 6 months ago is seen in clinic. His T2-weighted MRI scan shows multiple periventricular hyperintensities and three similar lesions in the posterior fossa, with one lesion in the corpus callosum. Lumbar puncture shows oligoclonal bands. Only a relative afferent pupillary defect on the left is evident on examination. So far, he has not been treated for his problems. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Beta-interferon
This patient has multiple sclerosis as evidenced by two separated episodes of neurological dysfunction, a typical MRI appearance and characteristic immunological changes in the cerebrospinal fluid. This patient fulfils the currently accepted UK criteria for the prescription of β-interferon. Randomised evidence now exists that interferon given after the first attack reduces the likelihood of a second attack within 2 years, and numerous randomised trials have shown a reduction of the relapse rate (by one-third to one-half) in patients with definite multiple sclerosis (such as this patient). Other treatments for MS are now available, although β-interferon remains widely used.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is incorrect. Azathioprine is not a widely accepted treatment for MS, although some trialAIdata Tutordo exist that suggest it might be useful.

Intravenous methylprednisolone
Intravenous methylprednisolone is incorrect. Intravenous methylprednisolone shortens the relapse duration, but is not used to prevent relapse.

Oral methylprednisolone
Oral methylprednisolone is incorrect. Oral methylprednisolone shortens the relapse duration, but is not used to prevent relapse.

Plasmapheresis
Plasmapheresis is incorrect. Plasmapheresis is used as a rescue therapy if steroids fail to help in cases of severe relapse.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a decreased level of consciousness. She had a severe headache before being found unconscious by her friend. She has been complaining of generalised headaches, forgetfulness and dizziness for the last few days. Her heart rate is 98 bpm, blood pressure 99/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and her oxygen saturation is 100% on 15 litres via a nonrebreathe mask. Examination of her retinas demonstrates Roth spots. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Roth spots appear as white-centred haemorrhages, consisting of perivascular collections of lymphocytes. Their appearance can be due to a variety of causes, including carbon monoxide poisoning, as in this case here. Other causes of Roth spots include myeloma, trauma, hypoxia, anaesthesia, pre-eclampsia and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) retinopathy. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas. Accumulation can occur in a non-vented room with a gas source such as an old fire. This can lead to headaches, memory loss and dizziness. As carbon monoxide accumulates, producing carboxyhaemoglobin, the skin can show a red, flushed colour. Severe poisoning can lead to cardiac arrhythmia, confusion, seizures, decreased conscious level, respiratory depression and death.

Glioblastoma
Glioblastoma presents subacutely over days to weeks with headache, seizures and focal neurological deficit such as memory loss and motor or sensory symptoms. While the presentation with the reduced conscious state could indicate a post-ictal state, the age of the patient (median age of glioblastoma is 65 years) and the presence of Roth spots make glioblastoma less likely.

Herpes simplex encephalitis
Herpes simplex encephalitis is not associated with Roth spots and the oxygen requirement would be unexplained.

Subacute bacterial endocarditis
Although subacute bacterial endocarditis can cause Roth spots (white, centred retinal haemorrhages), they are not exclusive to this condition. Carbon monoxide poisoning is much more likely in this case and can also cause Roth spots due to a build-up of carboxyhaemoglobin on the skin.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is not typically associated with Roth Spots, but is more often associated with a sudden and severe onset of headaches, although a milder headache is possible with sentinel bleeds.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of a tremor. She tells you it began in her right arm, but her left arm and head are also involved, causing her to have an annoying head nodding tremor. She says the tremor is worse when she gets emotional and her husband tells you that she does not appear to have it when she is asleep. She tells you that her father had the same problem when he approached a similar age. On examination her gait and balance appear normal, as are her tone and reflexes. A sample of handwriting also appears normal, although the patient preferred to use capital letters. Which one of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her tremor?
explanation:
Propranolol
This patient has essential tremor for which propranolol or topiramate are the usual first-line therapies. Primidone can also be used, but often causes drowsiness. More difficult tremors can be treated with botulin toxin injections or even deep brain stimulation. Essential tremor is characterised by upper limb postural and action tremor without rest tremor. Parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia or rigidity are absent. The neck and voice (due to involvement of the larynx) can also become tremulous. There is a positive family history in over 50% of cases and the tremor classically improves after the consumption of alcohol.

Levodopa
Levodopa is incorrect. Levodopa is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease.

Metoprolol
Metoprolol is incorrect. Metoprolol is a β-blocker, but is not usually used for the treatment of essential tremor as it is relatively cardioselective.

Pramipexole
Pramipexole is incorrect. Pramipexole is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease.

Selegiline
Selegiline is incorrect. Selegiline is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s.

stem: A 45-year-old lady has been complaining of unsteady gait, tinnitus and nausea. After investigation a vestibular schwannoma was diagnosed. What additional sign would you be most likely to find on examination?
explanation:
Loss of corneal sensation
Vestibular schwannomas are intracranial extra-axial tumours that arise from the Schwann cell sheath investing either the vestibular or cochlear nerve. As they increase in size, they eventually occupy a large portion of the cerebellopontine angle. Unilateral hearing loss is overwhelmingly the most common symptom present at the time of diagnosis and is generally the symptom that leads to diagnosis. Patients may also have ipsilateral ataxia, facial weakness and trigeminal sensory loss – absent corneal sensation is an early sign of trigeminal involvement.

Dysphagia
Dysphagia is incorrect. Dysphagia does not occur as the lower cranial nerves are spared.

Muscle atrophy
Muscle atrophy is incorrect. Facial weakness may be seen but it is not usual to see atrophy.

Ophthalmoplegia
Ophthalmoplegia is incorrect. Ophthalmoplegia does not occur with these tumours as cranial nerves III, IV and VI are not affected. Acoustic Neuroma

Ptosis
Ptosis is incorrect. Ptosis is not seen, as autonomic fibres are not compromised.

stem: A 28-year-old-female is admitted with recurrent epileptic fits. She is known to have epilepsy and has been taking phenytoin for five years, but her fits are not controlled. During her stay, the resident doctor was able to make the patient respond to verbal commands during the fit and he thought that the fits he witnessed were probably psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (pseudoseizures). In this patient the presence of which one of the following features would be most helpful in establishing the diagnosis of genuine epileptic fits?
options: History of two previous admissions with status epilepticus
explanation:
Lateral tongue biting
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (pseudoseizures) have been linked to stress, anxiety and possible dissociative tendencies. Differentiating pseudoseizures from true epilepsy is difficult. This often results in a misdiagnosis and unnecessary and ineffective treatment. Although incontinence may be seen in pseudoepilepsy, tongue biting is virtually never seen. Prolonged EEG/video recording is the most sensitive tool for differentiating pseudoseizures from epilepsy but is costly and therefore limited in availability. Measurement of serum prolactin levels may also help to discriminate between organic and psychogenic seizures, since most generalised seizures and many complex-partial seizures are accompanied by rises in serum prolactin (during the immediate 30-min postictal period), whereas psychogenic seizures are not.

Urinary incontinence
Urinary incontinence is incorrect. Urinary incontinence may be seen in association with pseudoseizures and is not as useful a discriminator as tongue biting.

Pelvic thrusting
Pelvic thrusting is incorrect. Certain behaviour, such as side-to-side turning of the head, asymmetric and large amplitude shaking movements of the limbs, twitching of all four extremities without loss of consciousness, pelvic thrusting, and screaming or talking during the event, are more commonly associated with psychogenic than with epileptic seizures.

History of two previous admissions with status epilepticus
History of two previous admissions with status epilepticus is incorrect. Pseudoseizures may co-exist with bone fide epilepsy, and previous status epilepticus may indeed have been a mis-diagnosis. Non-epileptic Attack DisorderA 35-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia. During the next 24 hours he developed a dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, breathlessness and progressive weakness of his upper and lower limbs, initially affecting the proximal muscles. On examination, he has fixed dilated pupils, generalised ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria and pharyngeal weakness. His cough is weak. He has a global weakness of his upper and lower limbs. Tone is reduced, reflexes depressed and plantar responses flexor. Sensation is normal. General medical examination is normal.

Family history of epilepsy (sister)
Family history of epilepsy (sister) is incorrect. Approximately 90% of patients are females, and a ‘role model’ (a family history of epilepsy or experience of epilepsy in a paramedical occupation) is often present.

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of increasing deafness and tinnitus in her right ear. Her right corneal reflex is absent, there is hearing loss in her right ear with air conduction greater than bone conduction, and Weber’s test lateralises to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vestibular schwannoma
The examination findings describe sensorineural deafness and loss of the corneal reflex on the right. This suggests a right cerebello-pontine angle lesion involving the right vestibulocochlear and right trigeminal nerve. The most common lesion at this site affecting the vestibulocochlear nerve is a vestibular schwannoma. It usually presents in middle age and is most common in women. As the tumour enlarges it may involve the facial, abducens and bulbar cranial nerves. In addition, during the late stages it may compress the brainstem (causing hydrocephalus) or the cerebellum (causing ataxia and nystagmus).

Basilar artery aneurysm
Basilar artery aneurysm is incorrect. Basilar artery aneurysm usually produces eye movement abnormalities, diplopia and longtract signs. The vestibulocochlear nerve is rarely affected.

Ménière’s disease
Ménière’s disease is incorrect. Ménière’s disease is a disorder causing recurrent episodes of severe vertigo associated with sensorineural deafness and tinnitus; it does not cause loss of the corneal reflex.

Meningioma
Meningioma is incorrect. Meningioma is a possibility, but cerebellopontine angle meningiomas are not common. Acoustic Neuroma

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is incorrect. MS is multifocal and is typically associated with longtract and cerebellar signs. Deafness is an uncommon symptom in MS.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents complaining of a 3-month history of diplopia and blurred vision in her left eye. She denies having any pain in the eye apart from a dull ache in the left frontal region on occasion, or other neurological symptoms. Her previous medical history is unremarkable. She smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks alcohol in moderation. Her general medical examination is normal. Her visual acuity on the right is 6/6 and on the left 6/36. There is left partial ptosis and mild proptosis with conjunctival injection. The left pupil is smaller than the right but reacts normally to light. There is some limitation of abduction of the left eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale left optic disk. The left corneal reflex is reduced. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Where is the most likely site for the cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Orbital apex
The combination of optic neuropathy, proptosis, chemosis, Horner syndrome, ophthalmoplegia (in this case due to CN VI nerve palsy) and involvement of the first branch of the trigeminal nerve is typical of orbital apex syndrome. The presence of proptosis, with swelling of eyelids and chemosis (swelling of the ocular surface membranes) indicates significant mass extension within the orbit.

Brainstem
Brainstem is incorrect. A brainstem lesion will not cause ptosis and proptosis with conjunctival Chatinjection. with Cavernous sinus
Cavernous sinus is incorrect. Cavernous sinus syndrome is defined as involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, and periarterial sympathetic plexus. Cavernous sinus lesions do not involve the cranial nerve II. Further, cavernous sinus lesions may be bilateral depending on the underlying cause. A potential differentiator is the duration of onset. Cavernous sinus lesions would be unlikely to present after 3 months. The patient would seek medical attention much earlier.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm is incorrect. Optic chiasm lesion causes bi-temporal hemianopia. A pale optic disc (optic atrophy) can occur due to compression secondary to a mass lesion.

Superior orbital fissure
Superior orbital fissure is incorrect. In superior orbital fissure syndrome, there is involvement of cranial nerves III, IV and VI. Sensory deficits in the frontal branch of the trigeminal nerve and involvement of the orbital sympathetic innervation are seen. However, there is no loss of vision.

stem: A 69-year-old patient with no previous medical history has been diagnosed with a right-sided lacunar stroke. You are now seeing him in the follow-up clinic at 6 weeks, and his hemiplegia is improving. His total cholesterol is 5.5 mmol/l and his blood pressure is 136/78 mmHg. He is in sinus rhythm. His blood glucose level is normal. He is treated with perindopril for hypertension and aspirin (which he had already been taking prior to the recent stroke) but is on no other medication. What secondary preventive medications should he be taking, on the basis of current evidence?
explanation:
Clopidogrel and statin
Current UK guidelines recommend aspirin 300 mg daily for acute ischaemic stroke (given after CT brain has excluded a bleed and preferably before 24 hours post symptom onset). The current rcommendation on longer term antiplatelet therapy is that patients should receive clopidogrel 75 mg daily. It is generally accepted that the aspirin is given for 2 weeks and then switched to clopidogrel. NICE guidance also suggests statins are given to patients after an acute stroke so clopidogrel and statin is the best choice here.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin, in combination with modified release dipyridamole, should be used for those who are intolerant of, or have a contraindication to clopidogrel ruling this choice out here.

Aspirin and β-blocker
Aspirin and β-blocker is incorrect. Aspirin, in combination with modified release dipyridamole, should be used for those who are intolerant of, or have a contraindication to clopidogrel ruling this choice out here.

Aspirin and statin
Aspirin and statin is incorrect. Aspirin, in combination with modified release dipyridamole, should be used for those who are intolerant of, or have a contraindication to clopidogrel ruling this choice out here. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Aspirin, statin and diuretic
Aspirin, statin and diuretic is incorrect. Aspirin, in combination with modified release dipyridamole, should be used for those who are intolerant of, or have a contraindication to clopidogrel ruling this choice out here.

stem: A 62-year-old builder is admitted with a history of collapsing while lifting heavy building blocks. In the Emergency Department he is unable to give a clear history, but his wife says he was previously well. He has smoked all his life and regularly drinks 8–10 pints of beer on a Friday or Saturday night. On examination in the Emergency Department, he was noted to be talking incomprehensibly and to have moderate weakness of his right side. Computed tomography head confirms a left hemisphere infarction. Two days later he suddenly deteriorates. He appears awake but is no longer talking at all and responds only to some, but not all, commands. His head and eyes look towards the left. He moves his left arm and leg spontaneously, but even pinching the skin elicits no movement of his right arm or leg. There is no obvious difference in the tone or reflexes in his limbs, but the right plantar response is extensor. On general physical examination, you note he is overweight and his blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg. The remainder of your examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Continuing emboli from internal carotid artery stenosis
Left hemisphere infarction with subsequent seizures
Right internal carotid artery occlusion and cerebral infarction
Posterior fossa haemorrhage with rapid-onset hydrocephalus
explanation:
Left hemisphere intracranial haemorrhage transformation
This man has had some form of stroke followed by rapid deterioration. He has clearly suffered from a left hemisphere stroke, and the deterioration is in the same territory, not a different one. The rapid clinical deterioration suggests haemorrhagic transformation as the diagnosis, but cerebral infarction from left middle cerebral or internal carotid artery occlusion causes a similar syndrome.

Continuing emboli from internal carotid artery stenosis
Continuing emboli from internal carotid artery stenosis is incorrect. Continuing emboli from carotid stenosis would present with multiple stroke-like events, not a general deterioration as seen here.

Left hemisphere infarction with subsequent seizures
Left hemisphere infarction with subsequent seizures is incorrect. Left hemisphere infarction followed by seizures is unlikely as the seizures would usually be clinically evident, with either focal clonic jerking or generalised tonic–clonic activity noted.

Right internal carotid artery occlusion and cerebral infarction
Right internal carotid artery occlusion and cerebral infarction is incorrect. Cerebral infarction from left middle cerebral or internal carotid artery occlusion causes a similar syndrome, however, it would be left not right sided occlusion / infarction based on examination findings.

Posterior fossa haemorrhage with rapid-onset hydrocephalus
Posterior fossa haemorrhage with rapid-onset hydrocephalus is incorrect. Posterior fossa haemorrhage with hydrocephalus is unlikely as the signs are of left hemispheric dysfunction, not brainstem compromise.

stem: Which one of the following is most suggestive of a lesion of the sciatic nerve?
options: Decreased sensation on anterior thigh and medial leg
Intervertebral disc prolapse at L2/L3 levels
explanation:
Foot drop
The sciatic nerve originates in the sacral plexus, mainly from the spinal segment L5 to S2. It divides into two major branches, the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve, which are responsible for all foot movements; therefore, of the options given, foot drop is the most suggestive of a lesion to the sciatic nerve.

Absent knee tendon jerk
Absent knee tendon jerk is incorrect. The sciatic nerve is not involved in the reflex arc tested when performing the knee jerk (L3 nerve root and femoral nerve).

Decreased sensation on anterior thigh and medial leg
Decreased sensation on anterior thigh and medial leg is incorrect. Anterior thigh and medial leg sensory loss is typical of femoral nerve lesion.

Inability to flex the hip
Inability to flex the hip is incorrect. The femoral nerve mediates flexion of the hip. Mononeuropathies

Intervertebral disc prolapse at L2/L3 levels
Intervertebral disc prolapse at L2/L3 levels is incorrect. A disc prolapse at this level will compress the L3 nerve root, causing pain over the anterior thigh and knee along with weakness of thigh adduction (obturator nerve) and knee extension (femoral nerve).

stem: Which one of the following is the first line treatment used to prevent further attacks?
explanation:
Carbamazepine
This patient has a typical history for trigeminal neuralgia (TN). Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant with sodium channel blocking properties. Other anticonvulsants (especially lamotrigine or phenytoin) and baclofen may Tutor also be effective for symptomatic management in TN, although there is less trial evidence for their use.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant that can be used for neuropathic pain, but is generally unhelpful in TN.

Baclofen
Baclofen may have additive effects when combined with carbamazepine, and is used in combination by some pain physicians.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Benzodiazepines are not effective in the treatment of TN.

Sertraline
Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and is not used to treat TN. Trigeminal neuralgiaA 45-year-old woman with an established diagnosis of multiple sclerosis presents with new weakness in the left leg. Intercurrent infection is excluded and there is no suggestion that the presentation marks disease progression. Two days have elapsed since her symptoms began; she has no history of psychological conditions.

stem: A 43-year-old woman who fractured the head of her right radius 6 weeks ago presents with weakness of extension of her right hand fingers. She has experienced no sensory loss. On examination there is weakness of fingers and at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Although able to extend her wrist, she performs this action with radial deviation. Other motor and sensory functions are intact. Reflexes are all present and symmetrical. Plantar responses are flexor. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Right posterior interosseous nerve
The right posterior interosseous nerve is correct.The posterior interosseous nerve (or dorsal interosseous nerve) is a nerve in the forearm. It is the continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve. Posterior interosseous neuropathy is purely a motor syndrome resulting in finger drop, and radial wrist deviation on extension.

Right anterior interosseous nerve
The right anterior interosseous nerve is incorrect. Anterior interosseous syndrome or Kiloh-Nevin syndrome causes pain in the forearm and a characteristic weakness of the pincer movement of the thumb and index finger.

Right axillary nerve
The right axillary nerve is incorrect. The axillary nerve or the circumflex nerve originates from the brachial plexus (upper trunk, posterior division, and posterior cord) at the level of the axilla (armpit) and carries nerve fibres from C5 and C6.Injury to the nerve results in paralysis of the teres minor muscle and deltoid muscle, resulting in loss of abduction of the arm (from 15 to 90°) and loss of sensation in the skin over a small part of the lateral upper arm (an area known as the regimental badge/patch).

Right brachial plexopathy
The right brachial plexopathy is incorrect. Injury to the brachial plexus would cause more proximal weakness and there would be reflex loss.

Right ulnar neuropathy.

stem: A 69-year-old man with recently diagnosed coeliac disease presents with paraesthesias in the feet and gait disturbance. On lower limb examination he has increased tone and weakness predominantly affecting the flexor muscle groups. Knee jerks are brisk and ankle jerks are absent. Both plantar responses are absent. He has loss of vibration sense to the costal margins and impaired joint-position sense at the toes, although pin-prick and temperature sensations are normal. He has a macrocytic anaemia and his vitamin B12 level is confirmed to be very low. What imaging abnormalities are likely to be seen on spinal MRI?
options: Diffuse patchy white-matter lesions on T2-weighted imaging
Evidence of microhaemorrhages in the posterior columns
Evidence of microhaemorrhages in the pyramidal tracts
Increased T1-weighted signal in the pyramidal tracts
Increased T2-weighted signal in the posterior columns
explanation:
Increased T2-weighted signal in the posterior columns
This patient has subacute combined degeneration of the cord due to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. This causes the classic combination of an evolving spastic paraparesis (long tract signs), peripheral neuropathy (absent ankle jerks) and a posterior column pattern of sensory loss (vibration and joint-position sense). The MRI typically shows increased signal on T2-weighted imaging, predominantly in the dorsal columns.

Diffuse patchy white-matter lesions on T2-weighted imaging
Diffuse patchy white-matter lesions on T2-weighted imaging is incorrect. Diffuse patchy white-matter lesions would be more consistent with CNS demyelination (as seen in multiple sclerosis).

Evidence of microhaemorrhages in the posterior columns
Evidence of microhaemorrhages in the posterior columns is incorrect. Microhaemorrhages are not seen in B12 deficiency or CNS demyelination.

Evidence of microhaemorrhages in the pyramidal tracts
Evidence of microhaemorrhages in the pyramidal tracts is incorrect. Microhaemorrhages are not seen in B12 deficiency or CNS demyelination. MyelopathyFlashcards A 48-year-old man, with a history of chronic injectiondrug use, presents with sequential footdrop and then wrist drop associated with pain and occurring over a 3-week period. Nerve conduction studies show evidence of a multifocal axonal neuropathy. He is also noted to have nailfold infarcts in his hands and feet, purpura and hepatomegaly. Which one of the following diagnoses is the most likely?

Increased T1-weighted signal in the pyramidal tracts
Increased T1-weighted signal in the pyramidal tracts is incorrect. Increased T1-weighted signal is an unusual finding in spinal imaging and does not have a specific disease correlation.

stem: A 66-year-old previously fit and well man attends with difficulty walking, a mild dementia (most notably a loss of interest in daily activities) and loss of bladder control. A diagnosis of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is made after a computed tomography (CT) scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Which of the following treatment options is the most appropriate?
explanation:
Shunt surgery
NPH is one of the few causes of dementia that can be controlled or reversed with treatment. The lumboperitoneal shunt surgery for idiopathic NPH (SINPHONI-2) trial results, published in the June 2015 issue of Lancet, found that people with NPH may benefit from lumbo-peritoneal shunting; available data suggest that difficulty walking is the symptom most likely to . None of the other options have the same evidence base as this option; this option should be considered especially when the physiological status of the patient is good.

Furosemide
Drugs that remove excess fluid throughout the body, such as diuretics, do not appear to symptoms of NPH.

Acetazolamide
A number of case-series have suggested that acetazolamide may symptoms in normal pressure hydrocephalus. However, a randomised clinical trial looking to study the effect of acetazolamide in NPH had to be terminated due to difficulty in recruiting participants to the study. In patients who are poor candidates for shunt surgery, repeated lumbar punctures in combination with acetazolamide may be considered as an option.

Levodopa
No definitive evidence exists that medication can successfully treat NPH. While levodopa/carbidopa has been reported to be of benefit in anecdotal reports, these patients with NPH may represent misdiagnosed cases of parkinsonism. Currently, no definitive evidence exists that levodopa/carbidopa is an effective treatment for NPH.

Mycophenolate
There is no definitive role for immunosuppressives in the treatment of NPH.

stem: A 28-year-old woman began to stumble when walking. Her right leg was slightly stiff and weak, especially after exercise and hot showers. These symptoms developed over 3 days and gradually disappeared over 4 weeks. She was on the college swimming team before these symptoms arose. There, she developed a unique and extreme type of fatigue that was different from the usual fatigue she experienced when swimming. This disappeared after several weeks, but had reappeared again 6 months before her current presentation. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis
The description is of relapsing–remitting neurological symptoms in a young woman and the most likely explanation is multiple sclerosis. Patients with multiple sclerosis commonly complain that their symptoms are worse with exercise and heat. They also experience profound fatigue.

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is incorrect. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a monophasic acute syndrome of CNS demyelination so cannot account for this history.

Chronic fatigue syndrome
Chronic fatigue syndrome is incorrect. The focal neurological syndrome described in the initial paragraph is inconsistent with chronic fatigue syndrome.

Diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy
Diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy is incorrect. Diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy causes a symmetrical distal pattern of sensory loss typically affecting the legs more than the arms and comes on chronically in the context of a patient with diabetes, so seems unlikely here. Multiple Sclerosis

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an acute monophasic illness characterised by ascending weakness and sensory loss, so cannot account for this history.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a drop foot following a sports injury. On examination there is weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, and weakness of extension of the greattoe. He has some sensory loss restricted to the dorsum of his foot. The ankle jerk is present and other examination is within normal limits. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Common peroneal nerve at the ankle
Common peroneal nerve at the head of the fibula
Sciatic nerve at the sciatic notch
Tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa
explanation:
Common peroneal nerve at the head of the fibula
The fibular head is a common site for a compression neuropathy affecting the common peroneal nerve (CPN). The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is formed from the L5 and S1 nerve roots. The CPN supplies the ankle dorsiflexors, toe extensors, ankle everters and sensation of the skin over the upper lateral and lower posterolateral leg. Also supplies (via branches) cutaneous innervation to the skin of the anterolateral leg, and the dorsum of the foot.

Common peroneal nerve at the ankle
Common peroneal nerve at the ankle is incorrect. The common peroneal nerve divides into deep and superficial branches soon after looping around the head of the fibula. Therefore, common peroneal nerve at the ankle is wrong.

L5 nerve root
L5 nerve root is incorrect. A lesion affecting the L5 nerve root lesion can be difficult to distinguish from a CPN palsy, especially given the similar distribution of sensory disturbance. However, L5 nerve root lesions will usually affect fibres of the tibial nerve as well those of the CPN. In particular, ankle inversion is supplied by the L5 portion of the tibial nerve and weakness here will therefore indicate a lesion outside the CPN. L5 nerve root is therefore wrong. This scenario indicates the importance of focused clinical examination in this scenario.

Sciatic nerve at the sciatic notch
Sciatic nerve at the sciatic notch is incorrect. A lesion affecting the sciatic nerve is likely to cause signs and symptoms in areas innervated by both the sciatic and tibial nerves as well as an absent ankle jerk. Sciatic nerve at the sciatic notch is therefore wrong. Mononeuropathies A 45-year-old woman with a history of multiple sclerosis presents to the clinic with left foot drop. There is no obvious wasting or fasciculations on examination, and testing power in the lower left limb demonstrates ankle dorsiflexion 2/5 (MRC grading), ankle eversion 2/5, ankle inversion 5/5 and ankle plantar flexion 5/5. Reflexes are normal throughout the legs. Where would you expect the patient to experience loss of sensation?

Tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa
Tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa is incorrect. Lesions affecting the tibial nerve will not cause a footdrop (the tibial nerve does not supply ankle dorsiflexors). Tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa is therefore wrong.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of untreated hypertension and diet-controlled diabetes presents with acute, painless, binocular horizontal diplopia, worse on looking to the left. On examination, his BP is 170/96 mmHg and his random blood glucose level is 13.4 mmol/l. The left eye is slightly adducted when looking straight ahead. On testing eye movements, he is unable to abduct the left eye, and sees two images side by side when asked to look to the left. The outer, fainter image disappears when the left eye is covered. The remainder of the cranial nerve tests, ophthalmological and general examination are normal. What course of action would you recommend?
options: Aspirin, metformin and an ACE inhibitor, with review at 4 weeks
MRI scan of the cavernous sinus
explanation:
Aspirin, metformin and an ACE inhibitor, with review at 4 weeks
This patient has an acute left sixth nerve palsy, likely caused by microvascular ischemia due to his untreated hypertension and diabetes. This condition usually has a benign prognosis with most patients recovering fully over time. The use of aspirin helps reduce the risk of further vascular events by preventing platelet aggregation. Metformin helps control elevated blood glucose levels, thereby addressing the patient's diabetes, while an ACE inhibitor helps manage high blood pressure and offers renal protection. A follow-up in 4 weeks is essential to monitor his progress, assess whether the nerve palsy is improving, and check for any new symptoms or signs that may require further investigation.

Cerebral angiogram
A cerebral angiogram is an invasive test used to visualize the blood vessels in the brain, typically considered when there is a suspicion of vascular abnormalities such as aneurysms or arteriovenous malformations. In the case of an isolated sixth nerve palsy without other neurological deficits, there is no indication for such an extensive investigation. The patient's symptoms are most likely due to microvascular ischemia rather than a vascular anomaly that would require angiography. Therefore, subjecting the patient to an angiogram would be unnecessary and could expose him to undue risk without clear benefit.

Dipyridamole and a ß-blocker
Dipyridamole is occasionally used in the secondary prevention of stroke but lacks robust evidence for efficacy in managing ischaemic heart disease. Additionally, ß-blockers are not the first-line treatment for hypertension in diabetic patients as they can interfere with glucose metabolism and mask hypoglycaemia symptoms. Their use in this context could lead to adverse outcomes, given the patient's elevated blood glucose levels. Thus, dipyridamole and a ß-blocker would not address the root causes of the patient's sixth nerve palsy and related vascular risk factors effectively.

MRI scan of the brainstem
An MRI scan of the brainstem is a diagnostic tool useful in cases where there are complex neurological symptoms suggestive of central nervous system pathology, such as tumours or multiple sclerosis. In this instance, the patient's presentation is consistent with an isolated sixth nerve palsy, commonly resulting from microvascular ischemia. MRI brainstem imaging would be excessive since the likely diagnosis can be managed conservatively with close monitoring. Imaging should be reserved for cases with additional symptoms or if the patient's condition fails to with initial treatment. Eye Movements and StrabismusMRI scan of the cavernous sinus
An MRI scan of the cavernous sinus might be indicated if there were signs of other cranial nerve involvement, suggesting a more extensive pathology, like a cavernous sinus syndrome. Because this patient has isolated sixth nerve palsy without involvement of other cranial nerves, cavernous sinus imaging is not warranted. Microvascular issues related to his hypertension and diabetes are the probable cause, which usually resolves without the need for extensive imaging. Pursuing this investigation would be unnecessary given the presenting symptoms and the likely benign course of microvascular nerve palsy.

stem: A 52-year-old chef comes to the Neurology Clinic. He has been having problems with dropping pans and clumsiness at work and has had to take frequent breaks to sit down in the kitchen because he feels like his legs are weaker than they should be. His only past medical history is type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is complicated by pre-proliferative retinopathy and proteinuria. His BP is 146/72 mmHg, with pulse 75/min and regular. On examination there is weakness of both lower limbs, more marked on the left than the right, and diminished lower limb reflexes. You notice fasciculations in the left calf muscle. There is weakness of both hands, with an accentuated biceps reflex bilaterally. He has loss of vibration sense from the toes to the knees bilaterally, and loss of pinprick sensation from the toes to the mid-shin bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is the most common subtype of motor neurone disease. This patient presents with a mixture of lower motor neurone (fasciculations, diminished lower limb reflexes) and upper motor neurone signs (brisk biceps reflex). Many candidates will assume that the sensory signs negate a diagnosis of motor neurone disease. However, these sensory findings are consistent with diabetic neuropathy; this patient has type 2 diabetes with significant microvascular involvement (retinopathy and renal impairment), and therefore it is highly likely that he has concomitant diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Needle electromyography, coupled with nerve conduction studies, is the diagnostic modality of choice for motor neurone disease. Imaging may be performed to rule out other conditions that may account for motor lesions.

Becker’s muscular dystrophy
Becker’s muscular dystrophy is incorrect. This is an X-linked progressive proximal muscle weakness. It would be unusual for Becker’s muscular dystrophy to present in a patient in his 50s; usually patients present between late childhood and early 20s. Furthermore, you would not expect to find upper motor neurone signs and there would likely be marked proximal muscle wasting, possibly with hypertrophy of the calf muscles.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, or hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy, is incorrect. This is a heterogeneous group of disorders that are heritable (usually autosomal dominant), and can present with a variety of purely sensory, purely motor or mixed neuropathy. It usually presents in childhood or early 20s (rather than in middle age), and it affects distal sensory and motor functions, rather than proximal. It can affect both the upper and lower limbs. However, you would not expect to find any upper motor neurone signs in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, or CIDP, is incorrect. CIDP is related to Guillain-Barré syndrome, but has a more chronic course and may relapse. As it involves demyelination and inflammation in the it peripheral nerves, you would only expect lower motor neurone signs on clinical examination. In particular, would be highly unusual to find a brisk reflex in CIDP.

Guillain-Barré syndrome
Guillain-Barré syndrome is incorrect. This typically presents as ascending sensory and motor disturbance with some autonomic involvement. Specifically, you would not expect to find upper motor neurone signs in GuillainBarré syndrome, especially brisk reflexes, as Guillain-Barré is an inflammatory process affecting peripheral nerves.

stem: A 45-year-old alcoholic man who has previously presented with confusion and walking difficulties was given a diagnosis of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. This was treated with thiamine replacement, and over time he made a good recovery. He reattends the Emergency Department with his partner. He has apparently started drinking again and stopped taking his vitamin supplements. Which of the following would you most expect to find?
explanation:
Nystagmus
Nystagmus is the commonest presenting eye sign, although lateral rectus palsies and ophthalmoplegia are also seen. Wernicke’s encephalopathy is classically defined by a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion, although not all three need to be present to be Wernicke’s encephalopathy. It is due to thiamine deficiency, commonly seen in those with alcohol dependence or malnutrition. In patients such as these, intravenous (IV) Pabrinex® is commenced at 2–3 pairs for 3–5 days, before reducing to one pair a day for a further 3–5 days. Treatment of thiamine/B vitamin deficiency can reverse the neurological signs caused in Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Thiamine works in the brain through metabolism of glucose and production of neurotransmitters and lipids essential for myelin. Untreated, Wernicke’s encephalopathy can lead to a permanent state of memory dysfunction termed Korsakoff syndrome.

Coma
Coma is incorrect. While drowsiness and coma can be seen in patients with Wernicke’s encephalopathy, agitation is actually seen more frequently. A decrease in a patient’s GCS score may be seen in alcohol intoxication but warrants further examination and investigation. Individuals with alcohol dependence and possible recurrent falls are at risk of a subdural haematoma that may present with reduced GCS scores.

Drowsiness
Drowsiness is incorrect. Agitation is actually seen more frequently than drowsiness. Drowsiness again may be due to toxins or an alternative diagnosis. A careful collateral history and examination, with additional investigations, is warranted. It is, however, unlikely to be seen in a primary presentation of Wernicke’s encephalopathy.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. Beriberi syndrome is an overarching term for severe and chronic thiamine deficiency. It can be subclassified as dry and wet. Dry beriberi syndrome includes Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Wet beriberi syndrome can present as high-output cardiac failure, with hypotension rather than hypertension. NystagmusSeizures
Seizures are incorrect. Seizures are not a common feature of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, or Korsakoff syndrome, but may be seen in acute alcohol withdrawal where benzodiazepines, such as chlordiazepoxide, are used to reduce symptoms of withdrawal. Anyone presenting with a history of acute alcohol intake and dependence should be monitored for alcohol withdrawal symptoms.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department. His school teacher gives a history of a fall during a rugby match, and a blow to the right-hand side of the head. Apparently, there was a brief loss of consciousness but he recovered quickly. After sitting out the rest of the game he became confused and aggressive, then drowsy during the journey home from their away game. By the time you see him he is unconscious, his BP is 155/90 mmHg, his pulse is 55 beats/min. His pupils are only sluggishly reactive. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Extradural haemorrhage
This is the classical history for extradural haemorrhage, which usually occurs after sustaining a head injury that ruptures the middle meningeal artery. However, it is worth noting that only around one-third of patients present with the classical history of a brief loss of consciousness then delayed deterioration. The period between these two phases is known as the ‘lucid interval’. Initial management should include a basic airways, breathing, circulation (ABC) assessment and involvement of Anaesthetists and the trauma team as necessary. CT scanning of the head is the initial investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis. Given the speed of deterioration optimal management of this patient would involve an early referral for neurosurgical intervention.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. This is not the typical history for a subarachnoid haemorrhage, which would usually present with a thunderclap headache.

Subdural haemorrhage
Subdural haemorrhage is incorrect. Subdural haemorrhages are more common in the elderly, and can occur after even relatively mild trauma. The source of bleeding in subdural haemorrhages is venous and as such the haematoma expands much more slowly, and in some cases neurological symptoms and signs may take many days, or even weeks, to develop.

Concussion
Concussion is incorrect. The neurological symptoms and signs here (low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), hypertension, bradycardia and abnormal pupillary reflexes) are suggestive of a neurological emergency and not those that would be expected in patients with concussion.

Cerebral oedema
Cerebral oedema is incorrect. The neurological deterioration here is caused by increased intracranial pressure because of the expanding haematoma, rather than because of cerebral oedema.

stem: A 19-year-old college student is noted by her flatmate to seem confused. She has been complaining of a diffuse headache and general malaise for the past 24 hours. On examination she has a temperature of 38 °C. She is restless and mildly dysphasic. The remainder of the general and neurological examination is normal. CT brain scan shows hypodensity in both temporal lobes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination shows a white cell count of 16/mm 3 (lymphocytes), a slightly raised protein concentration of 0.75 g/l and a normal CSF/blood glucose ratio. Which of the following is likely to be the most effective early treatment?
options: Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and prophylactic anticonvulsants
explanation:
Intravenous fluids and aciclovir
The short history and presence of dysphasia are both characteristic of herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE), which is caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV): HSV-1 in 90% of cases, and in the remainder HSV-2, mainly neonates and immunocompromised patients. The presence of temporal lobe changes (focal oedema) on neuroimaging is typical of HSV (although note that CT may be normal in the early stages – MRI is much more sensitive). Diagnosis may be confirmed by CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for HSV (specificity > 95%; sensitivity should be 95% in an experienced laboratory, although there may be false-negatives very early or very late) Infective encephalitis must be distinguished from other causes of encephalopathy (eg metabolic, ischaemic, toxic). Many other viruses cause encephalitis (eg varicella, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), influenza). However, HSE is the most important to consider because of the existence of an effective antiviral treatment. Intravenous aciclovir treatment should always be given in adequate doses for any possible case, and continued until CSF PCR is negative, or for at least 14 days. Intravenous fluids and aciclovir is the best option here.

Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and broad-spectrum antibiotics is incorrect. The question asks which treatment is likely to be most effective. Given that the CSF findings (and whole clinical presentation) are in keeping with viral encephalitis, the addition of antibiotics to the regimen will not increase its effectiveness.

Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and corticosteroids
Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and corticosteroids is incorrect. Routine use of corticosteroids in viral encephalitis is not currently recommended although it is the subject of a forthcoming clinical trial.

Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and prophylactic anticonvulsants
Intravenous fluids, aciclovir and prophylactic anticonvulsants is incorrect. Anticonvulsants are not routinely given prophylactically in this setting ruling this option out.

Intravenous fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Intravenous fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics is incorrect. This is not the best choiceas antivirals have been omitted from the treatment regimen. It should also be noted that it is of paramount importance to perform lumbar puncture as soon as it is safe to do so. This presentation is not typical of a bacterial illness, in particular the CSF findings are not in keeping with this.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of a headache and blurring of vision in his right eye lasting for 5 minutes. Two days later he developed sudden-onset weakness affecting both the left upper and lower limb, and lasting for 30 minutes. His past medical history includes mild hypertension. He is a non-smoker. There are no neurological abnormalities. His blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm. There is a quiet right sided carotid bruit. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transient ischaemic attack secondary to cardioembolism
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to carotid artery disease
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to giant-cell arteritis
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to small-vessel disease
explanation:
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to carotid artery disease
The transient monocular visual disturbance is consistent with the description of amaurosis fugax. Characteristically, patients describe a ‘curtain coming down’ over their vision, but are just as likely to describe blurring or greying The subsequent left-sided weakness is suggestive of a right cerebral hemisphere transient ischaemic attack. The combination of these two strongly points towards a right internal carotid artery stenosis as the source of platelet emboli, although other sources of emboli should be considered.

Migraine aura
Migraine aura is incorrect. Migraine aura can provide diagnostic difficulties, but there is no suggestion of the characteristic slow spread of symptoms in this patient and there is no previous history of migraine either. Genuine hemiparesis in migraine is very rare.

Transient ischaemic attack secondary to cardioembolism
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to cardioembolism is incorrect. Cardioembolism is unlikely in the absence of either atrial fibrillation (AF) or previous cardiac symptoms (of either cardiac ischaemia or cardiac failure). Paroxysmal AF should be considered if carotid artery investigations were negative.

Transient ischaemic attack secondary to giant-cell arteritis
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to giant-cell arteritis is incorrect. Giant-cell arteritis should always be considered in patients over 60 years of age, but there are no specific features (such such as jaw or tongue claudication) to support the diagnosis, although it is always worthwhile checking the ESR and CRP. In addition, anterior circulation strokes/TIAs are not common in giant-cell arteritis. Transient Ischaemic Attack A wheelchair-bound 19-year-old woman complains that she has difficulty reading. She describes the words jumping as she tries to follow the text. She is known to have an Arnold–Chiari malformation. What findings are you most likely to find on oculomotor examination?

Transient ischaemic attack secondary to small-vessel disease
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to small-vessel disease is incorrect. Transient occlusion of a small penetrating vessel (small-vessel disease) could cause the hemiparesis, but not the amaurosis fugax.

stem: Which one of the following drugs commonly exacerbates weakness in myasthenia gravis?
explanation:
Procainamide
Drugs that commonly cause deterioration in myasthenia gravis include: D-penicillamine Neuromuscular blocking agents, eg succinylcholine Aminoglycoside and fluoroquinolone antibiotics Antiarrhythmics, eg quinidine, procainamide β-blockers, eg propranolol This is not an exhaustive list and you should review a suitable web resource before prescribing in MG.

Amphotericin
Amphotericin is incorrect. Amphotericin is not known to worsen myasthenic weakness.

Cefotaxime
Cefotaxime is incorrect. Cefotaxime is not known to worsen myasthenic weakness.

Ciclosporin
Ciclosporin is incorrect. Ciclosporin is not known to worsen myasthnic weakness and this drug can be used to treat myasthenia as an immunosuppressant. Myasthenia Gravis

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. Sodium valproate is not known to worsen myasthenic weakness.

stem: A 20-year-old medical student presents with a 6-day history of blurred vision in her right eye and pain on eye movement. On examination she has a reduced acuity of 6/36, impaired colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect and a swollen pale optic disc. A diagnosis of optic neuritis is made. She has heard about an association between optic neuritis and multiple sclerosis and asks whether further tests could help to determine her chances of developing this. Which one of the following is correct?
options: Cranial MRI findings do not help to predict the risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis
If a cranial MRI is normal, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around
If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently
If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently
The presence of unpaired oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid does not help to predict the
explanation:
If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently
If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around 50% Following a first episode of optic neuritis (or another ‘clinically isolated syndrome’(CIS)), various factors can, to some extent, predict the likelihood of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis (MS), one of these is the presence of up to three white matter lesions on MRI, where the risk of developing MS is around 50%. The risk is increased in women and those with positive oligoclonal bands on CSF examination. Option E is therefore incorrect. However, the strongest predictor of risk of conversion from CIS to MS is MRI. Option A is therefore incorrect. Various studies have shown that the presence of asymptomatic white-matter lesions visible on T2-weighted imaging indicates an increased risk, of the order of 50% over those with a normal scan. Options B and D are therefore incorrect. Even if MS does develop, the prognosis for disability is relatively good, as onset with optic neuritis is associated with a more benign course of the disease in population studies. Therefore, brain imaging and lumbar puncture do allow prognostic information to be given to the patient if wished.

Cranial MRI findings do not help to predict the risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis
Cranial MRI findings do not help to predict the risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is incorrect. As outlined the strongest predictor of risk of conversion of CIS to MS is MRI.

If a cranial MRI is normal, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around
If a cranial MRI is normal, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around 50% If a cranial MRI is normal, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around 50% is incorrect. Various studies have shown that the presence of asymptomatic white-matter lesions visible on T2weighted imaging indicates an increased risk, of the order of 50% over those with a normal scan.

If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently
If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around 95% If a cranial MRI shows more than three white-matter lesions, the 5-year risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is around 95% is incorrect. Various studies have shown that the presence of asymptomatic white-matter lesions visible on T2-weighted imaging indicates an increased risk, of the order of 50% over those with a normal scan.

The presence of unpaired oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid does not help to predict the
The presence of unpaired oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid does not help to predict the risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis The presence of unpaired oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid does not help to predict the risk of subsequently developing multiple sclerosis is incorrect. As described the risk is increased in women and those with positive oligoclonal bands on CSF examination.

stem: A 31-year-old man, who has a history of epilepsy controlled with phenytoin, is admitted to the Emergency Department following three breakthrough seizures over the course of four months. He had been fit free before this period for the past 3 years. He usually takes 300 mg/day and his weight has increased to 100 kg over the past few years. A decision is therefore taken to increase his total daily dose to 500 mg. How soon after this time should a phenytoin level be checked?
explanation:
2 weeks
Phenytoin has an average half-life of 22 h, and reaching the steady state may take up to 5-14 days according to the Summaries of Product Characteristics (SPC). As such, it is sensible to wait for up to two weeks before checking a phenytoin level. A clinically effective dose of phenytoin is usually considered to be between 3 and 4 mg/kg initially, titrated up to a dose of 500 mg/day if required. With respect to therapeutic drug monitoring, a clinically effective level is usually considered to be between 10 and 20 mg/l. With respect to monitoring of phenytoin levels, it is worth remembering that therapeutic drug monitoring measures free and bound phenytoin; in certain situations, this may mean that there is drug toxicity in terms of side effects at an apparently therapeutic plasma level.

24 hours
24 hours is incorrect. This is too soon to check the phenytoin level as it has a half-life of 22 h and takes 5-14 days to reach steady state.

3 days
3 days is incorrect. This is too soon to check the phenytoin level as it takes 5-14 days to reach steady state. Tutor

5 days
5 days is incorrect. This is too soon to check the phenytoin level as takes 5-14 days to reach steady state. Checking it at 5 days may give false reassurance that the level is in the correct range.

1 month.

stem: Which one of these diseases has a polygenic inheritance?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis
Many disorders demonstrate familial clustering that does not conform to any recognised pattern of Mendelian inheritance. Multiple sclerosis is an example of one such disorder.

Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder.

Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is incorrect. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder.

Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is incorrect. Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease is incorrect. Huntington’s disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder. Multiple Sclerosis An 80-year-old lady with a history of hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus and a 50-pack-per-year smoking history presents to her GP complaining of ‘bumping into things’ all the time. On examination her gait is normal, there are no cerebellar signs and her eye movements are normal. However, an assessment of her visual fields reveals a left-sided homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing.

stem: Which one of the following is a good first-choice oral treatment for primary generalised epilepsy in a 20year-old man?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is a well-tolerated agent with the main side effect being the risk of Steven Johnson syndrome, in rare cases. For this reason, patients uptitrate lamotrigine slowly, in steps of 50mg daily increments every two weeks with information to consult a medical progressional if a rash occurs.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Carbamazepine is often avoided in primary generalised epilepsy as it can worsen myoclonus, which is a feature of some PGEs.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is incorrect. Phenytoin is a useful drug acutely, but has troublesome problems associated with longer term use, and would generally be avoided in this age group.

Topiramate
Topiramate is incorrect. There is insufficient evidence to support the use of first-line treatment with topiramate for any seizure type – it is used as a second line or adjunctive treatment. Epilepsy and Seizures

Valproate
Whilst traditional first-choice treatments for primary generalised epilepsy (PGE) are lamotrigine and valproate, MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate, unless two consultants agree that there is no suitable alternative treatment. In women of childbearing age, valproate is avoided due to the high risk of foetal abnormalities.

stem: A 62-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of an asymmetrical akinetic rigid syndrome. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and treated with ropinirole for 6 months with no improvement, therefore the diagnosis was questioned. Which clinical feature would most strongly suggest idiopathic Parkinson's disease as the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Persistence of asymmetry
Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease is associated with asymmetrical disease, tremor and rigidity usually being worse on one side of the body than the other, whereas symptoms associated with other causes of parkinsonism tend to be bilateral.

Axial rigidity
Axial rigidity is incorrect. Axial rigidity is a more prominent feature of PSP than idiopathic Parkinson’s disease.

Falling backwards
Falling backwards is incorrect. Both Parkinson’s and patients with progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) suffer from a tendency to fall, although falling backwards is commoner in PSP.

Rapid progression
Rapid progression is incorrect. Symptoms of Parkinson’s disease occur over several years, rapid progression suggesting an alternative cause.

Turning en bloc.

stem: A 50-year-old hypertensive man presents with difficulty in using his right arm, slow walking and occasional loss of balance. He has developed symptoms of urinary urgency. On examination he has a broad-based gait, there is cogwheel rigidity and intention tremor of his right arm. His blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg sitting and 100/60 mmHg standing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple system atrophy
This patient presents in middle age with a combination of extrapyramidal, cerebellar and autonomic features. There is no typical parkinsonian rest tremor. This makes multiple system atrophy the most likely diagnosis. The condition is characterised by combinations of parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, dysautonomia and sometimes pyramidal signs. It is a neurodegenerative disease associated with alpha synuclein neuropathology. The condition is poorly responsive to Levodopa, unlike idiopathic Parkinson’s disease.

Corticobasal degeneration
Corticobasal syndrome is incorrect. Corticobasal syndrome is a rare condition characterised by asymmetrical limb rigidity and apraxia. Alien limb phenomena may be observed (where the affected limb seems to ‘have a mind of its own’). Patients often have speech disturbance with dysphasia or apraxia of speech.

Drug-induced parkinsonism
Drug-induced parkinsonism is incorrect. As indicated the clinical presentation and lack of typical parkinsonian rest tremor makes multisystem atrophy a more likely diagnosis.

Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease
Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease is incorrect. Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease presents with asymmetric upper limb onset of rest tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia. Autonomic symptoms are usually mild at presentation. Ataxia is not part of the syndrome.

Progressive supranuclear palsy
Progressive supranuclear palsy is incorrect. Progressive supranuclear palsy is characterised by early falls, symmetrical parkinsonism and supranuclear gaze palsy. Dysarthria and subcortical dementia may be seen. Only a minority of patients respond to levodopa. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s Disease A 24-year-old male, injecting heroin addict presented with rapidly progressive, mild, generalised limb weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia and a dry mouth. Some 12 hours after admission he suddenly deteriorated resulting in a respiratory arrest, following which he required ventilation. On examination in the Intensive Therapy Unit he was alert and orientated. He had bilateral ptosis, dilated unreactive pupils, diplopia on both horizontal and vertical gaze, with restriction of eye movements in all directions and profound bilateral facial weakness. He now has marked weakness in all four limbs with depressed reflexes. Both plantar responses are flexor. Sensory testing is normal. He had recently been prescribed antibiotics by his GP for an infected injection site in his groin.

stem: A 78-year-old patient presents with a 3-month history of progressive loss of vision predominantly affecting the frontal region and causing discomfort behind his left eye. Clinically, there is a superior arcuate visual loss of the left eye. Fundoscopy shows cupping of the optic nerve of the left eye. What is the next investigation that would yield the diagnosis?
options: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)
explanation:
Intraocular pressures
This patient presents with progressive visual loss, superior arcuate visual field loss, and cupping of the optic nerve. These findings are indicative of chronic open-angle glaucoma (POAG). The best way to diagnose POAG is by measuring intraocular pressures, although normal tension glaucoma can occur with normal pressures. POAG typically causes slow, progressive vision loss and is often asymptomatic until significant vision loss has occurred, hence the recommendation for regular optician visits for the elderly. In contrast, acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with a rapid onset of symptoms, including headache, nausea, vomiting, and retro-orbital pain, and requires prompt medical attention.

Carotid ultrasound
Carotid ultrasound is incorrect. In a patient with amourosis fugax these investigations might be performed. However, the history given in this case is not at all in keeping with the hyperacute, but brief,Chat visual seen in withloss amourosis fugax.

Echocardiogram
Echocardiogram is incorrect. In a patient with amourosis fugax these investigations might be performed. However, the history given in this case is not at all in keeping with the hyperacute, but brief, visual loss seen in amourosis fugax.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) is incorrect. ESR and CRP should be requested if one suspects temporal arteritis. The patient in this case is certainly in the ‘at risk’ age group (over 50 years) for temporal arteritis but the history otherwise is not in keeping when you consider the absence of temporal headache or jaw claudication. Glaucoma

Fluorescein retinal arteriography
Fluorescein retinal arteriography is incorrect. Retinal arteriography would be performed if one were suspecting a retinal artery occlusion and can be performed in the work-up of a patient with amourosis fugax or temporal arteritis.
