Again, the history in this case is not typical of these conditions and, as such, this answer is incorrect.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of blurred vision, bilateral shoulder pain and shoulder girdle weakness over a week or so. In particular, he finds it difficult to lift his arms above his head or to pull objects towards him. On examination, his BP is 110/72 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. There is bilateral diplopia and nystagmus, he finds it difficult to maintain lateral gaze. You can also demonstrate bilateral weakness of the shoulder girdle. Deep tendon reflexes are reduced throughout. He has an ataxic gait. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Miller Fisher syndrome
This rare variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome begins with proximal muscle weakness, affecting the eye muscles and then spreading distally. This is in contrast to normal Guillain-Barré syndrome, which begins peripherally in the lower limbs.

Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy is incorrect. Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal-dominant chronic genetic disorder, which presents with slowly progressive muscle wasting and weakness. Patients often mention impaired relaxation of handgrip as an early sign.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease presents with muscle weakness, speech or swallowing problems, or breathing difficulties, depending on the type of motor neurons affected. It often presents with a combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs, including brisk reflexes, fasciculations and muscle weakness.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis is more usually associated with focal neurological signs, associated with focal areas of demyelination, and predominantly upper motor neuron signs on examination. Guillain-Barré Syndrome A 18-year-old man presented with recurrent convulsions. The convulsions usually occur at night and are confirmed by an eyewitness. Clinical examination revealed three café-au-lait spots (15 mm in diameter) on the lower limbs, and four on his back. Which one of the following would be most helpful in confirming the suspected underlying diagnosis?

Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN)
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN) is incorrect. HMSN is associated with gradual onset of muscle weakness, combined with sensory symptoms.

stem: Which one of the following is a characteristic finding in the CSF of patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome?
options: Low glucose in relation to blood glucose
explanation:
Raised CSF protein
In Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), the CSF classically shows albuminocytological dissociation, ie an acellular CSF with markedly elevated protein. However, the CSF may be entirely normal, especially in the early stages.

Atypical lymphocytes on cytology
Atypical lymphocytes on cytology is incorrect. Atypical lymphocytes on cytology would suggest the need to look for a haematological malignancy such as lymphoma, which can rarely present with a GBS like illness.

Low glucose in relation to blood glucose
Low glucose in relation to blood glucose is incorrect. Low glucose in relation to blood glucose could be seen in bacterial infection or malignancy.

Oligoclonal bands, unmatched in serum
Oligoclonal bands, unmatched in serum is incorrect. Oligoclonal bands, unmatched in serum are seen in multiple sclerosis. Guillain-Barré Syndrome A 69-year-old man with recently diagnosed coeliac disease presents with paraesthesias in the feet and gait disturbance. On lower limb examination he has increased tone and weakness predominantly affecting the flexor muscle groups. Knee jerks are brisk and ankle jerks are absent. Both plantar responses are absent. He has loss of vibration sense to the costal margins and impaired joint-position sense at the toes, although pin-prick and temperature sensations are normal. He has a macrocytic anaemia and his vitamin B12 level is confirmed to be very low. What imaging abnormalities are likely to be seen on spinal MRI?

Raised lactate
Raised lactate is incorrect. Raised lactate in the CSF may be seen in mitochondrial cytopathies such as MELAS (mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes).

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with a first generalised tonic–clonic seizure (GTCS). He has been complaining about headaches for the preceding 2 weeks, although he has been able to carry on in his job as a baker as normal. On examination he has mild left hemiparesis and bilateral extensor plantar responses. General examination is otherwise unremarkable. An urgent CT brain scan shows a 5-cm multicentric mass lesion in the right frontal lobe with surrounding vasogenic oedema and some hemisphere shift. What is the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
Glioblastoma
Glioblastoma multiforme (or anaplastic astrocytoma) is the highest grade (most malignant) form of astrocytoma, and accounts for about 20% of all cerebral tumours. These often remain clinically silent until they have reached a large size. About half occupy more than one hemisphere at presentation, and some are multicentric. For the presentation described gliobastoma is the best option here.

Ependymoma
Ependymoma is incorrect. Ependymomas develop from cells that line the ventricles and grow into the ventricles when they arise in the brain. Thus the lesion location in this case is not consistent with this type of tumour.

Meningioma
Meningioma is incorrect. Meningiomas are generally slow growing and arise directly from the meninges; this can be seen on cranial imaging. The lesion described here sounds parenchymal and rapidly growing (based on the presence of surrounding oedema).

Metastatic melanoma
Metastatic melanoma is incorrect. Metastatic melanoma is a cause of CNS lesions, but multiple lesions are usually present.

Oligodendroglioma
Oligodendroglioma is incorrect. Oligodendrogliomas tend to have a more indolent course than is suggested by this history. They are rarely multicentric. CNS Tumours A 39-year-old keen camper presents with a 2-week history of headaches, a ‘droopy face’, joint pains and a lowgrade temperature. He had returned from a camping holiday 1 month earlier. The only abnormality on neurological examination is left facial weakness. A lumbar puncture was carried out and the results of the CSF analysis are as follows: 250 cells/μl, over 90% lymphocytes, protein 2.1 g/l, glucose 4.0 mmol/l (serum glucose 8.0 mmol/l).

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of multiple sclerosis presents to the clinic with left foot drop. There is no obvious wasting or fasciculations on examination, and testing power in the lower left limb demonstrates ankle dorsiflexion 2/5 (MRC grading), ankle eversion 2/5, ankle inversion 5/5 and ankle plantar flexion 5/5. Reflexes are normal throughout the legs. Where would you expect the patient to experience loss of sensation?
explanation:
Dorsum of the foot
This patient has a common peroneal nerve palsy. It is common to mistake this clinical presentation for an L5 radiculopathy; however, in an L5 radiculopathy, you would expect weakness of ankle inversion in addition to dorsiflexion and eversion. Weakness of ankle inversion is not found in common peroneal palsy, as the posterior tibialis muscle (an invertor) is supplied by the tibial nerve, not the common peroneal nerve. The common peroneal nerve wraps around the head of the fibula (where it is relatively exposed, passing close to the surface) and then branches to form the superficial and the deep peroneal nerves. For most patients with common peroneal nerve palsy, their major concern is the resultant foot drop (due to paralysis of the tibialis anterior, supplied by the deep peroneal nerve). However, sensory involvement is also common due to involvement of the superficial peroneal nerve, which supplies sensation to the dorsum of the foot.

Inner thigh
The inner thigh is incorrect. This area is supplied by the genitofemoral nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh. This is above the level of the common peroneal nerve, which originates from the sciatic nerve in the popliteal fossa.

Medial lower leg
The medial lower leg is incorrect. The saphenous nerve provides sensory innervation to this area. The saphenous nerve is easily damaged during knee arthroscopy or vein harvest for cardiac bypass surgery.

Posterior calf
The posterior calf is incorrect. This area is supplied by the saphenous and sural nerves. However, sensation to the anterolateral area of the lower leg is supplied by the common peroneal.

Sole of the foot
The sole of the foot is incorrect. Several nerves provide sensation to this area. The major portion of the sensory innervations of the sole of the foot comes from the medial and lateral plantar nerves. The remainder is provided by the tibial and sural nerves, with a minimal portion supplied by the saphenous nerve. None of these are derivatives of the common peroneal nerve. Mononeuropathies A 59-year-old patient who is a known hypertensive presents with confusion, blurred vision, vomiting and a severe headache. You understand from his wife that he fell in the shower at the weekend and knocked his head. On examination he is conscious although confused; there are no focal cranial nerve deficits and no peripheral sensory or motor deficits. His BP is markedly elevated at 195/115 mmHg. He looks short of breath and there are bibasal crackles consistent with heart failure on auscultation of the chest. Investigations.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with difficulty fastening up the buttons on his coat when using his right hand. He tells you he had a car crash involving a rear shunt around 1 year earlier. On examination he has sensory loss affecting the medial aspect of his right arm around the elbow but the sensory supply to the hand appears intact. The intrinsic hand muscles are wasted on the right side. Where is the most likely lesion?
explanation:
Thoracic nerve root T1
The T1 nerve root supplies the small muscles of the hands and sensation on the medial aspect of the upper arm to an area just below the elbow. It is likely that this patient’s road accident led to a brachial plexus injury and his eventual presentation.

Median nerve
Median nerve is incorrect. The area of sensory abnormality here is clearly outside of the area innervated by the median nerve (the lateral aspect of the hand as well as the thumb, index, middle and medial aspect of the ring finger). The median nerve supplies the muscles of the thenar eminence and the lateral two lumbricals. A lesion would not cause the widespread wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the hand described here.

Cervical nerve root C7
Cervical nerve root C7 is incorrect. The C7 sensory supply is to the central aspect of the forearm and hand (around the middle finger). It primarily supplies motor innervation to the triceps (elbow extension), although via the posterior interosseous nerve it also contributes to muscles actioning wrist, thumb and finger extension.

Radial nerve
Radial nerve is incorrect. Lesions of the radial nerve would cause some sensory abnormality over the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the hand (primarily in the “anatomical snuffbox” area), as well as over the lateral aspect of the arm and forearm (depending on the level of the radial nerve lesion). Weakness of elbow and wrist extension are the primary motor deficits expected for a radial nerve lesion (as seen in the “Saturday night palsy”).

Ulnar nerve
Ulnar nerve is incorrect. Although this is the key differential here given that the ulnar nerve supplies most intrinsic hand muscles. However, ulnar nerve lesions generally cause sensory abnormalities in the medial aspect of the hand, the little finger and medial aspect of the ring finger. The exception to this is a lesion solely of the deep motor branch as it passes through Guyon’s canal. However, whilst this causes weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hand, it would not produce the sensory abnormalities described in this case.

stem: A wheelchair-bound 19-year-old woman complains that she has difficulty reading. She describes the words jumping as she tries to follow the text. She is known to have an Arnold–Chiari malformation. What findings are you most likely to find on oculomotor examination?
explanation:
Downbeat nystagmus
Downbeat nystagmus is classically associated with lesions at the foramen magnum, although it may have other causes. Arnold–Chiari malformations consist of specific abnormalities in the formation of the brainstem, with elongation of the cerebellar tonsils and sometimes a syrinx in the cervical spinal cord; the tonsils protrude through the foramen magnum. Hydrocephalus may result from blockage of the fourth ventricular outlets or an associated aqueductal stenosis. This patient describes oscillopsia on looking down because the downward gaze accentuates the nystagmus.

Brun’s nystagmus
Brun’s nystagmus is incorrect. Brun’s nystagmus is defined by mild horizontal nystagmus in one direction of gaze and coarse horizontal nystagmus in the opposite direction of gaze. It occurs with brainstem compression, usually due to cerebellopontine angle lesions.

Convergence retraction nystagmus
Convergence retraction nystagmus is incorrect. Convergence retraction nystagmus occurs in Parinaud syndrome due to dorsal midbrain lesions.

Pendular nystagmus
Pendular nystagmus is incorrect. Pendular nystagmus is defined as nystagmus with the speed of eye movement the same in both directions. The most common acquired cause is multiple sclerosis, but it may also be congential (in which case the patient does not describe symptoms of oscillopsia).

Upbeat nystagmus.

stem: A 35-year-old South Indian woman presents with a small, hard, palpable nodule over her left thigh. While awaiting surgical referral she has an epileptic seizure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cysticercosis
Cysticercosis is caused by the larvae of the pork tapeworm (Taenia solium). In endemic areas it is a common cause of adult-onset focal epilepsy. Cysticercosis is contracted by the ingestion of tapeworm eggs, usually from contact with the faeces of a human tapeworm carrier. Once in the bowel the eggs hatch and invasion into the blood stream can occur with subsequent haematogenous spread to brain, muscle, liver and, more rarely, other organs. Cysts form within these tissues and when this occurs in the brain the condition is termed neurocysticercosis. The cysts in the muscle can be palpated and also show up as radio-opaque on plain X-ray.

Hydatid disease
Hydatid disease is incorrect. Hydatid disease is caused by Echinococcus granulosus and is found in sheepraising areas, and usually presents with liver and lung cysts. It does not typically cause palpable lesions and only rarely causes CNS disease.

Idiopathic generalised epilepsy
Idiopathic generalised epilepsy (IGE) is incorrect. Although this patient may have IGE, there is no way to link the palpable nodule and 35 is an older age of onset than would be typical; most patients with IGE present in childhood or adolescence.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is incorrect. NF1 is unlikely to present with a single nodule and patients typically have numerous neurofibromata, as well as café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling and Lisch nodules. Only 4–6% of NF1 patients have epilepsy.

Toxoplasmosis
Toxoplasmosis is incorrect. Toxoplasmosis is not associated with subcutaneous nodules.

stem: An 83-year-old man is admitted complaining of a rapidly progressive weakness in both legs. He has also had back pain for the previous 2 months. On the day of admission he has developed urinary urgency. On examination he is cachectic and pale. Blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg, pulse 66 and regular. He is apyrexial. Cranial nerve examination is normal. Tone and power in his arms appear normal. His biceps and supinator jerks are present only with reinforcement, but the triceps jerks are brisk. His hip and knee flexors are moderately weak. He has a sensory level between the umbilicus and sternum. His lower limb reflexes are brisk with extensor plantar reflexes. He has an abdominal fullness consistent with an enlarged bladder. Rectal tone is normal. Which one of the following would be the most useful investigation?
explanation:
MRI whole spine
This man has cord compression and therefore needs urgent imaging of his spine. Despite the sensory level, he has brisk triceps reflexes, suggesting that the cervical cord above C7 is compressed. Sensory levels can be misleading, and in the face of upper motor neurone signs in the arms, the site of compression is likely to be higher than you think, ie in the cervical cord – therefore MRI whole spine to include the cervical region is the best option.

MRI head
MRI head is incorrect. The signs suggest a cord syndrome so MRI head is unhelpful here.

MRI lumbosacral spine
MRI lumbosacral spine is incorrect. This man has clear upper motor neurone signs. The spinal cord ends at vertebral level L1 so an MRI scan of the lumbosacral spine is inappropriate.

Radioisotope bone scan
Radioisotope bone scan is incorrect. The clinical syndrome is cord compression and a radioisotope bone scan is not designed to investigate the causes of this – common pathologies such as herniated discs would be missed. Which one of the following features is most typical of cavernous sinus thrombosis?

Radiograph thoracolumbar spine
Radiograph thoracolumbar spine is incorrect. Radiography is insufficiently sensitive to detect spinal cord compression and the thoracolumbar spine is the wrong area to X-ray based on his signs.

stem: A 42-year-old man has been taking antiepileptic medication for a number of years. He has been managed in primary care as he has suffered no further fits, but is concerned about a number of other symptoms that have appeared over the past few years. He says that a number of ‘lumps and bumps’ have appeared around his neck, jaw line and axillae, and he also has started to develop unpleasant contractures of his little fingers. Finally, the last straw has been pins and needles in both feet. On examination he has bilateral Dupuytren’s contractures, more marked on the left than the right. There is lymphadenopathy of the neck and axillae. You can also demonstrate a stocking neuropathy with numbness over both feet. Which one of the following medications is he most likely to be taking?
explanation:
Phenytoin
Side-effects of phenytoin include dyscrasias, morbiliform rash, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, hepatitis, gingival hyperplasia, acne, coarse features and hirsutism, nystagmus, increased seizure frequency (overdose), movement disorders, folate deficiency and anaemia, premature osteoporosis, osteomalacia, cerebellar atrophy, mild peripheral neuropathy, phlebitis (intravenous) and conduction abnormalities. Long-term phenytoin is associated with the development, in some cases, of marked lymphadenopathy, which has been referred to as ‘pseudo lymphoma’ and, when it is severe, Dupuytren’s contracture.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. The side-effects described are not characteristic of carbamazepine. The major adverse effects of carbamazepine include dose-related side-effects: dizziness, diplopia, nausea, sedation, mild leucopenia, hyponatraemia, bradyarrhythmias. Idiosyncratic side-effects include Stevens–Johnson syndrome, agranulocytosis, hepatic failure, pancreatitis, lupus-like syndrome. Chronic side-effects include osteopenia.

Clonazepam
Clonazepam is incorrect. The side-effects include mainly sedation and slowed cognition.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect. Adverse effects include dizziness, ataxia and drowsiness (which are all dose related) and rash and hypersensitivity syndrome, which are idiosyncratic. Epilepsy and Seizures A patient with atrial fibrillation, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia presents with sudden-onset rightsided weakness, hemianopia and aphasia. This occurred an hour previously while he was eating his breakfast. He is taking aspirin, simvastatin, ramipril and digoxin. What action would you recommend?

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. Major adverse effects include GI upset, anorexia, tremor, thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis, hepatic failure, stupor, coma, depression, rash, hyperammonaemia, thrombocytopenia, weight gain, hair loss or change in texture, and polycystic ovarian syndrome.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents after collapsing at home. She has diplopia on right gaze, right-sided facial weakness and left flaccid hemiparesis. What is the most likely site for her lesion?
explanation:
Right pons
This lady has crossed neurological signs (right face, left arm and leg), which immediately localise to the brainstem (midbrain, pons or medulla). Diplopia on right gaze is suggestive of a right abducens nerve palsy and right facial weakness suggests a right facial nerve palsy. Both of these cranial nerve nuclei are located in the pons and indicate a lesion on the right side. The left-sided (contralateral) limb weakness is a consequence of disruption of the descending (and as yet uncrossed) corticospinal tract, and it is flaccid because she presents soon after the event.

Left mid-brain
Left mid-brain is incorrect. Midbrain syndromes would not involve the abducens or facial nerve nuclei, but more usually involve dysfunction of the oculomotor nerve.

Left pons
Left pons is incorrect. A lesion in the left pons would cause a left-sided abducens and facial palsy and rightsided limb weakness.

Right cerebral hemisphere
Right cerebral hemisphere is incorrect. A lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere would not cause crossed signs.

Right mid-brain
Right mid-brain is incorrect. Midbrain syndromes would not involve the abducens or facial nerve nuclei, but more usually involve dysfunction of the oculomotor nerve.

stem: A 41-year-old man presents to the clinic with a tremor. He tells you that his father also suffered from a tremor and problems with head nodding. On examination, you notice a low-amplitude tremor with a frequency of 8-10 Hz in the patient’s right arm. There is no evidence of bradykinesia or increased rigidity. He says that the degree of tremor seems to increase if he is under stress at work. Reflexes, speech and eye movements are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Essential tremor
The family history and absence of parkinsonian features (see below) both favour essential tremor as the most likely diagnosis. Propranolol and primidone are both effective in managing essential tremor, but once patients are reassured that there is nothing more serious going on, they may elect not to commence pharmacotherapy.

Cerebellar tumour
Cerebellar tumour is incorrect. You would expect a cerebellar tumour to cause cerebellar signs , such as ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria or dysdiadochokinesis: this patient has normal eye movements and speech, and there is it no mention of ataxia in the clinical information. The tremor seen in cerebellar disease is an intention tremor: worsens as the patient tries to reach for a target. The tremor described in the clinical information is a resting tremor.

Epilepsy
Epilepsy is incorrect. Epilepsy itself is not associated with tremor. There may be syndromes or disease states that lead to both tremor and seizures (these are beyond the scope of knowledge required for MRCP Part 1), but epilepsy is the wrong answer because on its own, it does not explain the patient’s symptoms and signs.

Lewy body disease
Lewy body disease is incorrect. Lewy body disease is dementia with parkinsonian features: besides the tremor itself, there are no parkinsonian features in this patient, and the clinical information makes no mention of any features of dementia. Essential TremorParkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease is incorrect. Essential tremor and Parkinson’s disease can be difficult to distinguish in clinical practice. Here, the patient’s age makes Parkinson’s disease less likely (although not impossible, as patients can develop early-onset Parkinson’s in their 40s). The key point is the absence of either bradykinesia or rigidity; this makes Parkinson’s disease much less likely.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely artery to have been occluded?
explanation:
Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery
This patient has the lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. This ischaemic stroke syndrome leads to ipsilateral pain and numbness on the face, contralateral pain and temperature sensory loss, nystagmus and ipsilateral Horner syndrome. There is also vertigo and severe vomiting as seen here, with poor co-ordination and a tendency to fall towards the side of the lesion. MRI is the imaging investigation of choice for posterior fossa lesions. Management involves intensification of measures to reduce vascular risk.

Left middle cerebral artery
The left middle cerebral artery is part of the anterior circulation and supplies a different region of the brain. Occlusion of this artery typically results in symptoms like aphasia, hemiparesis, and hemisensory loss, predominantly affecting the face and arm on the contralateral side. These patients do not usually present with vertigo, vomiting, or the combination of ipsilateral facial and contralateral body sensory loss seen in lateral medullary syndrome. Therefore, the symptoms described do not align with an occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery.

Right anterior inferior cerebellar artery
The right anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplies the lateral pons and the inner ear structures. Occlusion of this artery can cause lateral pontine syndrome, which presents with ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss, and vertigo. However, AICA strokes do not typically cause the combination of ipsilateral facial sensory loss and contralateral body sensory loss seen in lateral medullary syndrome. Therefore, the symptoms described are inconsistent with an occlusion of the right anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
The right posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) occlusion would present with lateral medullary syndrome symptoms, but on the opposite side. This would include ipsilateral facial sensory loss, contralateral body sensory loss, and ipsilateral Horner syndrome, but all these symptoms would be on the right side. Since the patient’s symptoms are on the left side of the face and the right side of the body, a right PICA occlusion is not the correct diagnosis. The symptoms described are consistent with a left PICA occlusion.

Right middle cerebral artery
The right middle cerebral artery, like the left middle cerebral artery, is part of the anterior circulation. Occlusion of this artery typically results in contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss, predominantly affecting the face and arm, and possibly neglect if the non-dominant hemisphere is involved. These symptoms do not match the combination of vertigo, vomiting, ipsilateral facial sensory loss, and contralateral body sensory loss seen in lateral medullary syndrome. Therefore, the symptoms described are not consistent with an occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke A 27-year-old female who delivered a healthy baby 36 hours ago under epidural anaesthesia complains of worsening headaches. Shortly afterwards she has two fits. She has a temperature of 37.8°C and the full blood count reveals a mild neutrophilia. Neurological examination shows a left hemiplegia and bilateral upgoing plantar reflexes. There is no meningism. The optic discs appear mildly swollen.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents with malaise, headache, diarrhoea and neck stiffness. On examination she has a temperature of 38.2 °C and mild meningism. Her general practitioner had prescribed oral antibiotics earlier that day but she attended the Emergency Department later in the day. A CT brain scan was requested by a nurse practitioner in the Emergency Department. This was normal. The medical team then performed a lumbar puncture. The opening pressure was 14 cm of CSF. The CSF analysis was a slightly elevated protein of 0.45 g/l, a white cell count of 200/mm 3 (90% lymphocytes), CSF glucose level of 3.3 mmol/l and blood glucose of 4 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Viral meningitis due to echovirus
Viral meningitis due to echovirus is most likely because: The pattern of slightly elevated protein, lymphocytosis and normal CSF/blood glucose ratio is most suggestive of viral meningitis. The other aetiologies typically cause a low (bacterial) or very low (tuberculous, fungal) CSF/blood glucose ratio (ie CSF glucose < 40% of blood glucose). Enteroviruses (including echovirus and coxsackie) are the most common cause of viral meningitis in the UK.

Cryptococcal meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis is incorrect. The CSF pressure should be raised and the CSF glucose should be very low in crytpococcal meningitis. It is also rare in those that are not immunocompromised.

Listeria meningitis
Listeria meningitis is a possibility given that listeria is more common in pregnant women, the CSF in this setting often shows a predominance of lymphocytes and a low CSF to serum glucose ratio.

Partially treated streptococcal meningitis
Partially treated streptococcal meningitis is incorrect. Although partial treatment of bacterial meningitis may give a lymphocytic rather than a polymorph predominant CSF, the CSF/blood glucose ratio is not in keeping with a bacterial infection. Furthermore, although pregnant women are more at risk of developing streptococcal meningitis than the general population, it remains rare in adults.

Tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculous meningitis is incorrect. With TB meningitis one would expect the CSF glucose to be very low.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with weakness of his right upper limb. On examination, there is weakness of the right triceps, brachioradialis and extensor digitorum. Sensation is normal. The right triceps jerk is absent. There is some wasting of the dorsum of the forearm. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Right radial nerve
The radial nerve supplies the triceps, brachioradialis and extensor digitorum profundus. Sensory loss in patients with radial nerve palsy is variable and should not be relied upon to localise the lesion. However, the commonest site of sensory loss is at the anatomical snuffbox.

C6 radiculopathy
C6 radiculopathy is incorrect. The myotome of the triceps and extensor digitorum is C7, but that of the brachioradialis is C6. Therefore, either in isolation would not cause the constellation of signs seen in this case. Radiculopathies are also usually associated with radicular pain.

C7 radiculopathy
C7 radiculopathy is incorrect. The myotome of the triceps and extensor digitorum is C7, but that of the brachioradialis is C6. Therefore, either in isolation would not cause the constellation of signs seen in this case. Radiculopathies are also usually associated with radicular pain.

Right brachial plexus
Right brachial plexus is incorrect. Brachial plexus lesions cause a mixture of motor and sensory signs across multiple nerve territories. Furthermore, proximal involvement is common. For example, it might be possible to identify weakness of supraspinatus (supplied by the suprascapular nerve) and winging of the scapula (due to a lesion of the long thoracic nerve of Bell, which supplies serratus anterior).In this case, all signs can be attributed to a lesion of a single peripheral nerve, therefore making right brachial plexus unlikely. Mononeuropathies A 62-year-old woman with a history of hypertension is brought to the Emergency Department with sudden onset severe occipital headache and left sided weakness. On examination, her GCS is 13. Her BP is 190/100 mmHg. She has a left-sided hemiplegia. An urgent scan confirms a large right-sided subarachnoid haemorrhage. Over the course of the next 30 minutes, she becomes increasingly drowsy and begins to vomit.

Right posterior interosseous nerve
Right posterior interosseous nerve is incorrect. The posterior interosseous nerve is a pure motor branch of the radial nerve which supplies muscles of finger extension and extensor carpi ulnaris. Hence a posterior interosseous nerve palsy causes a finger drop and radial diversion of the wrists (due to intact extensor carpi radialis) on attempted wrist extension.

stem: Fundoscopy shows severe hypertensive retinopathy with haemorrhages and papilloedema. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Hypertensive encephalopathy
This man is suffering from malignant hypertension; he has encephalopathy, severe hypertensive retinopathy and papilloedema. He also has evidence of hypertensive heart failure. In this situation where there isAIsevere Tutor compromise, the most appropriate management would be IV blood pressure control with an agent such as sodium nitroprusside or labetalol.

Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. It is unclear as to how diabetic retinopathy would cause the other features described in this case.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with thunderclap headache and cannot fully explain the range of features seen here. Some patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage have papilloedema, retinal haemorrhage or subhyaloid haemorrhage, but not all the features of hypertensive retinopathy.

Subdural haematoma
Subdural haematoma is incorrect. Subdural haematoma may cause confusion but will also likely cause some focal neurological signs and cannot explain the retinal and systemic findings.

Viral encephalitis
Viral encephalitis is incorrect. This should be considered and could present in a similar way. However, the findings on fundoscopy and the evidence of heart failure make this option less likely in this case.

stem: A 33-year-old-female teacher presents with a subacute onset of weakness, numbness and paraesthesia in the right leg. She says this previously happened to a lesser extent on the left-hand side and resolved after a few months. She has light headedness and an electric-shock-like feeling from the neck down the spine whenever she bends her head forward. She denies any history of fits but her brother who is 16 years old suffers with epilepsy. On examination there is evidence of profound weakness and reduced pinprick sensation in the right leg. Horizontal nystagmus on looking to the right is evident. Apart from MRI scanning, which of the following is a potentially helpful test?
explanation:
Visual evoked potentials
Although current diagnostic criteria for MS rely on brain MRI findings, visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and lumbar puncture may be performed in addition. VEPs are averaged cerebral potentials evoked by visual stimuli (a flash or black-and-white checkerboard pattern) and detected by scalp electrodes placed over the occiput. The method is sensitive for detecting demyelination of the optic nerve and central visual pathways. In the context of a typically abnormal MRI scan it is now unusual to have to perform VEPs.

Electroencephalograph
Electroencephalograph (EEG) is incorrect. EEG is used to assist epilepsy syndrome classification.

Electromyography
Electromyography (EMG) is incorrect. This presentation is typical of MS which purely affects the central nervous system. EMG is therefore not helpful in securing the diagnosis.

Nerve conduction study
Nerve conduction study (NCS) is incorrect. This presentation is typical of MS which purely affects the central nervous system. NCS is therefore not helpful in securing the diagnosis.

Polysomnography
Polysomnography is incorrect. Polysomnography might be used to secure a diagnosis of sleep apnoea but is not useful in this scenario.

stem: Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the strongest indicator of prognosis?
explanation:
Vital capacity
The history of facial, proximal limb and abdominal muscle weakness, in association with winged scapulae, footdrop and elevated CK, is suggestive of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD). As with other chronic muscle and nerve diseases, respiratory muscle weakness and consequent respiratory failure is the major cause of morbidity and mortality.

12-lead ECG
12-lead ECG is incorrect. It would be prudent to perform a baseline ECG in those with FSHD, but cardiac involvement in this condition is exceedingly rare.

FEV1
FEV 1 is incorrect. FEV 1 is a less accurate measure of respiratory function in this setting where we are interested in detecting subtle respiratory muscle weakness that might cause type 2 respiratory failure. FEV 1 is more useful when concerned about obstructive respiratory problems such as asthma that can cause type 1 respiratory failure.

Level of CK
Level of CK is incorrect. CK should not be used to guide prognosis in this setting. Furthermore, CK can be normal in those with muscular dystrophies.

Response to corticosteroid therapy
Response to corticosteroid therapy is incorrect. Steroids have no role in the treatment of FSHD.

stem: Multifocal motor neuropathy is most commonly associated with which one of the following?
explanation:
Anti-GM1 antibodies
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block initially causes progressive, asymmetrical and usually distal upper limb weakness in the majority of cases. High titres of IgM antibody to the ganglioside GM1 are found in 80% of affected patients, but they are not specific for the disease; anti-GM1 antibodies may also be seen in axonal Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Anti-GQ1b antibodies
Anti-GQ1b antibodies is incorrect. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are associated with Miller Fisher syndrome.

Anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies
Anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies is incorrect. Anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) antibodies are seen in association with immune mediated sensory ataxic neuropathy, often with a prominent tremor.

Antineuronal antibodies
Antineuronal antibodies is incorrect. Antineuronal antibodies are also known as ‘paraneoplastic’ antibodies and are seen in conjunction with numerous cancers and neurological syndromes (for example: anti-Hu antibodies associated with small-cell lung cancer and sensory neuronopathy).

Antinuclear antibodies
Antinuclear antibodies is incorrect. Antinuclear antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosis (SLE).

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate way to monitor her respiratory function?
options: CO 2 on arterial blood gas measurement
explanation:
Forced vital capacity
Mortality from respiratory failure is the most important cause of death associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome, the most likely diagnosis here. Epstein Barr, the most likely pre-disposing illness here, is a well recognised cause, as are cytomegalovirus, mycoplasma and campylobacter infections. Both secondary infection related to hypoventilation and increased risk of pulmonary embolism related to inactivity are known complications of the disease, with mortality approaching 10%. Around 20% of patients have a degree of residual weakness or sensory loss after the acute illness. Forced vital capacity is the major determinant of the need for intubation and ITU admission.

PEFR
PEFR is incorrect. Each of these methods can give falsely reassuring results in those with the early stages of respiratory muscle weakness.

FEV 1
FEV1 is incorrect. Each of these methods can give falsely reassuring results in those with the early stages of respiratory muscle weakness.

Oxygen saturation
Oxygen saturation is incorrect. Each of these methods can give falsely reassuring results in those with the early stages of respiratory muscle weakness.

CO 2 on arterial blood gas measurement
CO2 on arterial blood gas measurement is incorrect. A rise in CO2 would indicate that type 2 respiratory failure (and thus significant respiratory muscle weakness) has already occurred. The aim here is to identify impending respiratory muscle weakness. Guillain-Barré.

stem: Six hours post stroke you are considering anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy. Which one of the following would be most appropriate for acute treatment?
options: Low molecular weight heparin and commence warfarin treatment
explanation:
Aspirin
The clinical scenario is of a 54 years old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation who presents with stroke (left face and arm weakness). Her B.P is high (162/82 mmHg) and her pulse has a normal rate with atrial fibrillation (85 bpm, irregular). Her blood investigations are normal and her CT head shows no evidence of intracerebral haemorrhage. According to the NICE Guidelines [CG68; July 2008] and NICE Pathways for Chat Acutewith Stroke (last st updated 21 June 2016) – “all people presenting with acute stroke who have had a diagnosis of primary intracerebral haemorrhage excluded by brain imaging should, as soon as possible but certainly within 24 hours, be given aspirin 300 mg orally if they are not dysphagic or aspirin 300 mg rectally or by enteral tube if they are dysphagic”.

Full iv heparinisation
Full IV heparinisation is incorrect. There is little or no therapeutic benefit from IV heparinisation, and significant risk of haemorrhagic transformation. As such heparin should not be used.

Low molecular weight heparin and commence warfarin treatment
Low molecular weight heparin and commence warfarin treatment is incorrect. Like full IV heparinisation, low molecular weight heparin has no value in the treatment of acute stroke.

Alteplase
Alteplase is incorrect. This patient is outside the recommended window, (4.5 hours) for thrombolysis.

Streptokinase
Streptokinase is incorrect. This patient is outside the recommended window for thrombolysis, and rTPA rather than streptokinase is the preferred agent.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with paroxysmal episodes of severe right periocular pain lasting 15–40 min associated with redness of the right eye, lacrimation and nasal congestion. The episodes seem to be very stereotyped and occur around 0100 hours. The attacks occur over a period of 6–8 weeks and then seem to remit, only to occur again after 6–8 months. What is the prophylactic treatment of choice?
explanation:
Verapamil
The clinical features and history of the episodes are typical of cluster headache. The pharmacological treatment of choice for prophylaxis in cluster headache is verapamil. Other options include lithium, sodium valproate and gabapentin.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline is used for neuropathic pain and as prophylactic medication for migraine and tension headache.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin is used in the acute management of migraine and tension headache.

Propranolol
Propranolol is inorrect. Propranolol is used as prophylaxis for migraine. 692 Cluster Headache A 70-year-old female with a 2-month history of proximal upper limb pain and right-sided headaches develops sudden-onset right-sided visual blurring. On examination there is an altitudinal field defect in the right eye.

Sumatriptan
Sumatriptan is incorrect. Subcutaneous sumatriptan is used for the acute management of cluster headache. Sumatriptan is also used in the acute treatment of migraine.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has long-standing multiple sclerosis (MS). She comes to the clinic complaining of urinary frequency, urgency and occasional urge incontinence, present for the past 6 months. She has signs of a chronic spastic paraparesis and mild cerebellar ataxia. What would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Exclude infection and measure post-micturition residual volume
Low-dose trimethoprim as a long-term prophylaxis
explanation:
Exclude infection and measure post-micturition residual volume
This patient’s symptoms are likely related to neurogenic detrusor overactivity, due to her spinal disease. The result is a small-capacity bladder prone to uncontrollable contractions. Estimation of the post-micturition residual volume (with or without cystometry) is an essential step in management. Nowadays, this can often be readily performed via a nurse-led incontinence advice service.

Intradetrusor injections with botulinum
Intradetrusor injections with botulinum is incorrect. Botulinum injections are a second-line therapy.

Low-dose trimethoprim as a long-term prophylaxis
Low-dose trimethoprim as a long-term prophylaxis is incorrect. Long-term antibiotics may be required in some cases, but the aim would be to manage the bladder symptoms sufficiently well so as to minimise the occurrence of frequent UTIs.

Teach intermittent self-catheterisation
Teach intermittent self-catheterisation is incorrect. Exclusion of infection and residual volume measurement must happen first. If the residual volume is more than 100 ml, intermittent self-catheterisation is a more appropriate management. Multiple Sclerosis

Treat with oxybutynin (anticholinergic)
Treat with oxybutynin (anticholinergic) is incorrect. If the volume is less than 100 ml, anticholinergic treatment is advised, but the exclusion of infection and residual volume measurement must occur first.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Neurology Clinic complaining of weakness and loss of pain in her upper arms. Her GP is worried that she may have syringomyelia. Which of the following signs would best support the diagnosis?
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensation over upper limbs
Loss of pain sensation in the lower limbs
Loss of proprioception over upper limbs
Loss of vibration sense in the upper limbs
explanation:
Loss of pain and temperature sensation over upper limbs
First signs are involvement of the anterior commissure of the spinal cord and crossing spinothalamic fibres, resulting in segmental distribution of ‘dissociated’, selective sensory loss of pain and temperature (cape-like distribution if it occurs in the cervical spinal cord). Anterior horn cell damage leads to muscle weakness, which begins in the hands and then affects forearms and shoulders and may involve respiratory musculature. Owing to the way that the syrinx extends, pain and temperature sensation is lost first over the upper limbs, with fine touch, vibration sense and proprioception lost later in the lower limbs. Tendon reflexes are lost and claw hand may result. Various surgical procedures including stenting may result in a delay of progression of symptoms. Involvement of sympathetic pathways in the cervical cord results in Horner syndrome.

Loss of pain sensation in the lower limbs
Loss of pain and sensation in the lower limbs is incorrect. With further expansion, the lateral spinothalamic tracts are involved. This results in loss of sensation in the lower limbs. The sacral fibres lie peripherally and are often spared until late during the expansion (sacral sparing). Loss of pain and sensation in the lower limbs will occur late in the progression of the disease where other signs would also be present.

Loss of proprioception over upper limbs
Loss of proprioception over upper limbs is incorrect. Posterior columns are relatively spared.

Loss of vibration sense in the upper limbs
Loss of vibration sense in the upper limbs is incorrect. Posterior columns are relatively spared.

Upper-limb fasciculation
Upper limb fasciculation is incorrect. Fasciculation can be caused by certain motor neurone pathologies, however most cases are benign. If the patient has a normal neurological exam and EMG the fasciculation can be diagnosed as benign fasciculation syndrome. Fasciculation can occur in the upper limbs as part of syringomyelia, however it is not a common sign and loss of pain and temperature sensation over the upper limbs is usually the predominant sign which would support diagnosis. A patient with a history of left optic neuritis 1 year ago, and transient spastic paraplegia (lasting 6 weeks) 6 months ago is seen in clinic. His T2-weighted MRI scan shows multiple periventricular hyperintensities and three similar lesions in the posterior fossa, with one lesion in the corpus callosum. Lumbar puncture shows oligoclonal bands. Only a relative afferent pupillary defect on the left is evident on examination. So far, he has not been treated for his problems.

stem: A 56-year-old right-handed man has an ischaemic stroke following right carotid artery thrombotic occlusion, and has clinical signs of a right total anterior cerebral artery stroke. As well as left hemiparesis and left homonymous hemianopia, which clinical sign of parietal lobe dysfunction would you most expect to find?
options: Inability to copy a drawing of a clock-face
explanation:
Inability to copy a drawing of a clock-face
Parietal lesions are associated with several characteristic signs; some are specific to whether the lesion is dominant (left), non-dominant (right) or bilateral. Unilateral lesions (either right or left) may cause: contralateral hemisensory loss and sensory inattention homonymous hemianopia/quadrantanopia mild hemiparesis abolition of optokineticnystagmus Unilateral dominant (usually left) parietal lesions can produce: disorders of language, especially alexia agnosia ideomotor and ideational apraxia Gerstmann syndrome (right–left confusion, acalculia, agraphia and finger agnosia) Unilateral non-dominant (usually right) parietal lesions may cause: predominantly visuospatial dysfunction constructional apraxia anosognosia and dressing apraxia The correct answer is therefore inability to copy a drawing, as this is an example of constructional apraxia.

Acalculia
Acalculia is incorrect. Acalculia is a component of Gerstmann syndrome and indicates left (dominant) inferior parietal lobe dysfunction.

Agraphia
Agraphia is incorrect. Agraphia is a component of Gerstmann syndrome and indicates left (dominant) inferior parietal lobe dysfunction.

Receptive dysphasia
Receptive dysphasia is incorrect. Receptive dysphasia is caused by dominant temporal lobe dysfunction.

Right–left confusion
Right–left confusion is incorrect. Right–left confusion is a component of Gerstmann syndrome and indicates left (dominant) inferior parietal lobe dysfunction.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with a subacute history of intermittent difficulty in walking, dry mouth and variable slurring of speech. When the latter is severe he also has difficulty in swallowing. He mentions that he notices a temporary improvement in strength when he first starts walking or exercising, but this is followed by progressive worsening with sustained effort. He has lost 3 kg in weight in the last 2 months. On examination he has bilateral mild ptosis, dysarthria and proximal weakness of the upper and lower limbs and is areflexic. The degree of weakness is variable. Nerve conduction studies confirm the clinical suspicion of a neuromuscular junction disorder. Which one of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be identified in his blood?
options: Anti voltage gated calcium channel antibody
explanation:
Anti voltage gated calcium channel antibody
The clinical picture is highly suggestive of the Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). This is associated with antibodies directed against the presynaptic calcium channels on the motor end plate at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), so anti voltage gated calcium channel antibody is correct. The disorder most often occurs as a paraneoplastic phenomenon, and has a particular association with smallcell lung cancer, although the neurological presentation often occurs at a time when the cancer is ‘subclinical’. The absence of reflexes is characteristic, in contrast to myasthenia gravis where the reflexes are unaffected. It may be useful to think of LEMS as the most distal of peripheral neuropathies to help understand why this occurs. Autonomic features (such as dry mouth in this case) are common in patients with LEMS. The variability (fatigability) of symptoms is characteristic but, in contrast to myasthenia, there may be a temporary increase in muscle power following exercise. This clinical feature can be elicited at the bedside as the post-tetanic potentiation of deep tendon reflexes and also by demonstrating increment on neurophysiological testing. Treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine (DAP), intravenous immunoglobulins and/or plasma exchange. Treatment of the underlying cancer, if detected, may symptoms, and determines prognosis.

Acetylcholine receptor antibody
Acetylcholine receptor antibody is incorrect. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are associated with myasthenia gravis (MG). MG can be differentiated from LEMS in this case as: Areflexia is not a typical feature of MG Autonomic symptoms are uncommon in MG The majority of patients with MG have a degree of oculoparesis, not just mild ptosis

Antiganglioside antibody GM1
Antiganglioside antibody GM1 is incorrect. GM1 antibodies are found in around half of patients with multifocal motor neuropathy. This is an inflammatory peripheral motor neuropathy whichmay mimic motor neurone disease. The clinical presentation does not include variability/fatigability and the neurophysiology would not show evidence of NMJ dysfunction. GM1 antibodies may also be seen in some patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Antiganglioside antibody GQ1B
Antiganglioside antibody GQ1B is incorrect. GQ1B antibodies are seen in the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain– Barré syndrome (GBS). The ophthalmoplegia seen in this condition can sometimes lead to confusion with a NMJ disorder, but the characteristic association with ataxia and areflexia and the subacute progressive course in the Miller Fisher syndrome will allow clinical differentiation in most cases. Additionally, fatigability is only seen in NMJ disorders. These clinical differences and the fact that neurophysiology in this case shows evidence of a NMJ disorder mean that Antiganglioside antibody GQ1B is wrong.

Anti-Hu paraneoplastic antibody
Anti-Hu paraneoplastic antibody is incorrect. Anti-Hu antibodies are usually associated with small-cell lung cancer. The paraneoplastic neurological syndrome in this case is usually an encephalomyelitis and sensory neuronopathy (also called ‘dorsal root ganglionopathy’), although paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration and other syndromes are also seen. Although autonomic dysfunction can occur in the paraneoplastic neuropathy syndromes, the clinical presentation here is otherwise not in keeping. In addition, the neurophysiology would not show evidence of an NMJ disorder. Lambert-Eaton.

stem: The paralysis associated with myasthenia gravis is thought to result from the influence of autoimmune antibodies that bind to the ligand-gated ion channel known as:
explanation:
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
The fundamental disorder in myasthenia gravis is loss of functional (post-synaptic) nicotinic acetylcholine receptors upon binding of anti-acetylcholine receptor (anti-AChR) antibodies. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) class antibodies can be detected, by the standard assay used for diagnostic purposes, in 85% of patients with generalised myasthenia, and about one-half of those with purely ocular myasthenia.

Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor is incorrect. Muscarinic ACh receptors are only found in the autonomic nervous system and are not affected in myasthenia gravis.

Muscle specific kinase (MuSK)
Muscle specific kinase (MuSK) is incorrect. MuSK is a receptor tyrosine kinase and not a ligand-gated ion channel. However, some patients with myasthenia gravis previously thought to be seronegative have been found to have anti-MuSK antibodies.

Voltage gated calcium channel
Voltage gated calcium channel is incorrect. Antibodies against these presynaptic channels are pathogenic in the Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Myasthenia Gravis

Voltage gated potassium channel (VGKC)
Voltage gated potassium channel (VGKC) is incorrect. Anti-VGKC antibodies have been found in a myriad of neurological conditions, particularly limbic encephalitis, but not myasthenia gravis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred with a 2-week history of blurred vision, unsteady gait and numbness in the right hand. She has experienced similar short-lived attacks in the past. One year ago, she abruptly lost function in the left hand, which returned to normal after 5 days. On examination she has bilateral horizontal nystagmus and generalised hyperreflexia. There is reduced vibration sense in the limbs and central scotoma. The brain MRI scan showed multiple lesions in the white matter with no surrounding oedema at the periventricular area and cerebellum. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis
This patient has neurological symptoms which are ‘disseminated in time and space’. The MRI revealed evidence of discrete white matter lesions. The whole picture is highly suggestive of multiple sclerosis.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is incorrect. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is not associated with the brain abnormalities on MRI described in this case. Occasionally abnormalities of the deep motor tracts can be seen in those with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Metastatic tumour to brain
Metastatic tumour to brain is incorrect. Brain metastases are usually associated with multiple lesions, but often there is prominent interstitial oedema surrounding the lesions with or without tissue or midline shift. The relapsing–remitting history is also not in keeping with cerebral metastases.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is incorrect. Syringomyelia is not associated with the brain abnormalities on MRI scan described in this case. However, syringomyelia is often associated with an Arnold–Chiari malformation. Multiple Sclerosis

Thrombophilia with multiple cerebral infarcts
Thrombophilia with multiple cerebral infarcts is incorrect. Occasionally Hughes thrombophilia syndrome (antiphospholipid syndrome) can mimic MS. However, cerebral infarcts should involve the cortex (grey matter) on MRI scanning of the brain.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic for review. She has suffered from a second episode of optic neuritis in the last 9 months, and poor co-ordination affecting her right hand. A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis is suspected and a decision is made to start fingolimod. Which of the following is the mode of action of fingolimod?
explanation:
Sphingosine 1-phosphate receptor modulator
Fingolimod binds to the S1P receptor on lymphocytes, and on neural cells. By doing this it modulates the egress of lymphocytes from lymph nodes.

Anti-CD52
Anti-CD52 is incorrect. Alemtuzumab is an anti-CD52 antibody used in the treatment of MS.

Interferon beta
Interferon beta is incorrect. Interferon beta modulates inflammation and may be of value in treating some patients with relapsing remitting MS.

Myelin analogue
Myelin analogue is incorrect. Glatiramer is a polymer which is thought to act as an alternative target to myelin for lymphocyte mediated immune attack.

Nicotinic receptor agonist.

stem: An 80-year-old lady with a history of hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus and a 50-pack-per-year smoking history presents to her GP complaining of ‘bumping into things’ all the time. On examination her gait is normal, there are no cerebellar signs and her eye movements are normal. However, an assessment of her visual fields reveals a left-sided homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Occipital cortex lesion
Homonymous hemianopia occurs as a result of a lesion involving the occipital cortex, typically caused by a stroke or a space-occupying lesion.

Temporal lobe tumour
Temporal lobe tumour is incorrect. A lesion here might present with a partial hemianopia or a superior quadrantanopia.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. In the aura stage this can present with complex visual phenomena such as lines, spots, dots, zigzags or a hemianopia, but this is a less likely cause of hemianopia that an occipital lobe lesion.

Optic chiasm lesion
Optic chiasm lesion is incorrect. This would result in bitemporal hemianopia. Visual Field Defects A 25-year-old woman weighing 90 kg and 162 cm tall presents with visual loss and headaches. On examination she has a sixth nerve palsy and swelling of the optic disc. MRI of the brain is normal.

Optic nerve lesion
Optic nerve lesion is incorrect. This would usually present as monocular visual loss.

stem: A 25-year-old woman visits her GP with a 6-month history of intermittent headaches. These last for 2 hours and are associated with visual blurring and nausea. The GP feels that this is migraine, but examination reveals that her left pupil is smaller than the right and her upper and lower limb reflexes are all diminished. Her eye movements are normal and there is no ptosis. The right pupil does not appear to react to light and reacts poorly to accommodation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Argyll Robertson pupil on the left
Right third cranial nerve palsy caused by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
explanation:
Holmes–Adie syndrome
The first step is to decide which, if any, is the abnormal pupil. This may be done by altering the lighting intensities. Normal physiological anisocoria will not be altered (so option A is incorrect). However, in the dark, an abnormally small pupil will fail to dilate, and in very bright light an abnormally large pupil will fail to constrict. Holmes–Adie syndrome consists of a ‘tonic’ pupil that is usually larger, and fails to react to light, with a sluggish reaction to accommodation. Diminished reflexes (or areflexia) complete the syndrome. It is a benign condition.

Argyll Robertson pupil on the left
Argyll Robertson pupil on the left is incorrect. Argyll Robertson pupils are small, usually bilateral (although often asymmetrically) and react to accommodation, but not to direct light.

Left-sided Horner syndrome
Left-sided Horner syndrome is incorrect. There is no ptosis to suggest Horner syndrome and, in addition, the right pupil is the abnormal one on examination.

Physiological anisocoria
Physiological anisocoria is incorrect. As described normal physiological aniscoria will not be altered. Holmes–Adie SyndromeRight third cranial nerve palsy caused by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Right third cranial nerve palsy caused by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm is incorrect. There are no additional features (such as oculoparesis and ptosis of the affected eye) to suggest a third cranial nerve palsy, so this is unlikely.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with a 6-day history of poor balance, worsening double vision and slurred speech. The symptoms began after a flu-like illness. On examination he has impaired eye movements in all directions of gaze, mild dysarthria and bilateral ataxia. None of his tendon reflexes can be elicited and the plantar responses are flexor. Which one of the following best describes the diagnosis?
explanation:
Miller Fisher syndrome
This clinical picture is typical of the Miller Fisher syndrome, which classically consists of a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia It is a variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) and affects the brainstem, cranial nerves and peripheral nerves Like GBS it often follows an infective illness Typically, cerebrospinal fluid protein is high and there is no cellular response (cytoalbuminologic dissociation) There is an association with the antiganglioside antibody GQ1B Treatment is with immunoglobulins and plasma exchange for those with more severe disease (ie those who are non-ambulant). Steroids are not a treatment for GBS or the Miller Fisher syndrome

Cytomegalovirus polyradiculoneuropathy
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polyradiculoneuropathy is incorrect. CMV infection is a rare cause of a polyradiculopathy. Neurological manifestations of this infection more commonly involve retinitis and encephalitis occurring in the immunosuppressed patient (eg HIV infection). The case presented here is not at all typical of CMV infection.

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) is a type of Guillain-Barre syndrome which is characterised solely by demyelination within the peripheral nervous system. It would not account for ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria or ataxia observed in the vignette. More broadly, it can be useful to think of GBS as a spectrum of illnesses with central (CNS) and peripheral (PNS) involvement. Pure CNS involvement occurs in Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis. Miller Fisher syndrome straddles both the CNS and PNS. PNS variants of GBS include acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP, ‘classic GBS’), acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) and acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN).

Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
The Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is incorrect. LEMS and myasthenia gravis (MG) can be confused with Miller Fisher syndrome clinically. Overlap includes the areflexia of LEMS and the ophthalmoplegia of MG. However, neither should cause true ataxia and one should be able to demonstrate fatigable muscle weakness in LEMS and MG, which are disorders of the neuromuscular junction. Additionally, in LEMS an eye movement abnormality should not be seen and in MG the reflexes should not be absent. Guillain-Barré Syndrome A 62-year-old woman with a history of obesity, type II diabetes and long-standing back pain comes to the Emergency Department for review. Her symptoms have worsened over the past 4-6 weeks and she now claims to be unable to mobilise this morning, corresponding with a worsening in her back pain. She has been faecally incontinent which has never happened to her before Her BP is 155/72 mmHg, heart rate is 82 bpm and regular. She has 3/5 power weakness affecting both lower limbs, more marked distally versus proximal muscle groups, peri-anal anaesthesia, knee jerks preserved but absent ankle jerks. Investigations:

Paraneoplastic neuropathy
Paraneoplastic neuropathy is incorrect. There is no suggestion of underlying malignancy and the presentation is rather acute. Apart from this, the most common paraneoplastic neuropathy is a sensory neuronopathy (also called ‘dorsal root ganglionopathy’) in which sensory ataxia occurs but without the eye movement disorder described here. The preceding flu-like illness is also more in keeping with Miller Fisher syndrome.

stem: Which of the following would be most suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of Korsakoff’s psychosis?
options: Loss of memory of distant events
explanation:
Inability to form new memories
Korsakoff’s psychosis is a form of Wernicke’s encephalopathy that is caused by chronic thiamine deficiency, usually seen in long-term abusers of alcohol. Classically patients have anterograde amnesia (they are unable to form new memories) associated with confabulation, where memories are invented to cover the gaps caused by the anterograde amnesia.

Auditory hallucinations
Auditory hallucinations are not a feature of Korsakoff’s psychosis. They can be a feature of delirium tremens, which is delirium precipitated by the acute withdrawal of alcohol. Here the patient stopped drinking alcohol two months ago, and has completed a reducing course of chlordiazepoxide, and therefore there is no acute withdrawal of alcohol.

Loss of memory of distant events
Loss of memory of distant events is incorrect. Although patients with Korsakoff’s psychosis can have profound memory loss, often memory of distant events is relatively well preserved. Characteristically in Korsakoff’s there is ‘telescoping’ of memory, where distant events are thought to have occurred recently.

Tactile hallucinations
Tactile hallucinations is incorrect. Tactile hallucinations are not a feature of Korsakoff’s psychosis. These are a common feature of delirium tremens, which is acute confusion caused by the withdrawal of alcohol. This patient stopped drinking two months ago and has been managed on a reducing dose of chlordiazepoxide, and therefore is very unlikely to be suffering from delirium tremens.

Visual hallucinations
Visual hallucinations is incorrect. Visual hallucinations are not seen in Korsakoff’s psychosis and therefore would not be suggestive of this disorder. They may be seen in delirium tremens, which is an acute confusional state caused by the sudden withdrawal of alcohol in an alcohol-dependent patient. This patient stopped drinking two months ago and has had a reducing course of chlordiazepoxide, and therefore it is highly unlikely that his confusion could be explained by delirium tremens.

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with severe confusion and ataxia. On examination, he has difficulty abducting both eyes and gait ataxia. He is disoriented in time and place. A full blood count shows an MCV of 110 fl. What immediate treatment should be administered?
explanation:
Intravenous thiamine
This presentation is typical of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Therefore the answer is intravenous thiamine. The combination of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia are typical features found on examination. Other less common features include autonomic dysfunction and hypothermia. In this case, another clue is that the high MCV is most likely to be consistent with chronic alcohol abuse. Other causes of Wernicke’s encephalopathy include persistent vomiting. Immediate intravenous thiamine is the treatment of choice and avoids permanent damage to the brain (ie conversion to Korsakoff’s syndrome).

Intravenous aciclovir
Intravenous aciclovir is incorrect. This would imply the thinking was that the patient had a viral infection causing the presentation. The lack of fever is obviously against this and the raised mean corpuscular volume (MCV) would also remain unexplained.

Intravenous cefuroxime
Intravenous cefuroxime is incorrect. This would imply that one thought the patient had a bacterial infection causing the presentation. The lack of fever is obviously against this and the raised MCV would also remain unexplained.

Intravenous dexamethasone
Intravenous dexamethasone is incorrect. Dexamethasone may have a role in the treatment of some forms of meningitis. However, the presentation here is not in keeping with a meningitic illness (classically presenting with fever, neck stiffness and photophobia).

Intravenous diazepam
Intravenous diazepam is incorrect. IV diazepam is a useful treatment for seizures, but would not be recommended in this setting.

stem: An 80-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with difficulty with his speech. He appears to understand what is being said to him and can follow commands, but he has difficulty speaking to staff and becomes frustrated trying to form sentences. His past medical history includes hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which of the following arterial territories is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
Left middle cerebral artery
This describes the inability to, or difficulty with, producing language or putting words together to make meaningful language. It is also known as Broca’s aphasia and occurs as a result of a lesion or damage to Broca’s area in the brain (located in the dominant frontal lobe). This area of the brain is supplied by the middle cerebral artery. Since the majority of patients are left hemisphere-dominant, the most likely arterial territory affected is the left middle cerebral artery.

Left anterior cerebral artery
Involvement of the left anterior cerebral artery would cause contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss, predominantly affecting the lower extremities.

Left internal carotid artery
The left internal carotid artery gives rise to the left middle cerebral artery. Its involvement, however, would also cause motor and sensory weakness, which is not seen here.

Right internal carotid artery
Given that most patients are left hemisphere-dominant and this patient has no sensory or motor dysfunction, it is very unlikely that the right internal carotid artery has been affected.

Right middle cerebral artery
A much smaller number of people are right hemisphere-dominant, making involvement of the right middle cerebral artery less likely.

stem: A 73-year-old man with advanced Parkinson’s disease is being treated on the ward for a urinary tract infection (UTI). His regular medication includes co-careldopa, entacapone, cabergoline, and sc apomorphine injections p.r.n. His wife tells you that for the last month his behaviour has changed and he has become agitated, disinhibited and he keeps asking her for money. His dyskinesia has also become more pronounced over this period. On examination he is distractible. He denies having hallucinations and, after probing questioning, you can find no evidence of delusional thought. Mood assessment shows him to be cheerful and there are no cognitive or biological features of depression. What is the likely physiological cause of the behavioural change?
explanation:
Direct effect of dopamine agonism
Impulse control disorders are a recognised side-effect in PD patients taking dopamine agonists. This can lead to pathological gambling, compulsive shopping or hypersexuality. This can occur together with dopaminergic dysregulation syndrome (DDS), where patients take increasing quantities of dopaminergic drugs despite increasingly severe drug-induced dyskinesia. DDS can be associated with mood disorders such as hypomania or psychosis. Other common neuropsychiatric complications in PD include: Depression (50%, associated with a younger onset, female gender) Anxiety (40%) Sleep disorders (70%) Psychosis (40%, visual hallucinations and persecutory delusions, often drug-related) Dementia – exists on a continuum of severity and can be of several different types: Mild cognitive impairment is increasingly recognised as a common feature of PD; more frank dementia is known as PD dementia; and dementia with Lewy bodies is also associated with PD, which is diagnosed when the Tutor patient develops the symptoms of dementia either before or at the same time that they develop PD. Whether these are distinct entities or different spectrums of the same disease is under debate. In addition PD can coexist with other common causes of dementia, such as Alzheimer’s or vascular dementia.

Change in sensitivity to dopamine
Change in sensitivity to dopamine is incorrect. It would not explain the symptoms. Over time PD patients tend to become less sensitive to the dopamine, which means dopamine agonists become less effective and sideeffects, particularly dyskinesias, increase.

Coexisting dementia
Coexisting dementia is incorrect. Although cognitive dysfunction is common in PD, it would not explain his specific symptoms.

Delirium due to urosepsis
Delirium due to urosepsis is incorrect. His symptoms have been ongoing for a month. Although infections such as a UTI can cause delirium in any elderly patient, the specific features described are much more typical of an impulse control disorder.

Reduced breakdown of dopamine.

stem: A 35-year-old man has been suffering from increasingly frequent headaches for the last 3 months. They start from his neck and reach over the occipital area, radiating then to his right temporal area. He gets a feeling of pressure behind the right eye. Sometimes he vomits with his headache and he often needs to rest in bed. The whole thing can last several hours, or even a whole day. He has not suffered headaches since a spell of severe headaches in his teenage years around the time of exams. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Migraine
The features of this headache suggest it will be due to migraine. The pain is one sided and retro-orbital. There is associated vomiting and he needs to rest. The duration is several hours. There is a previous history of episodic headaches as a teenager.

Brain tumour
Brain tumour is incorrect. A brain tumour is unlikely given the episodic nature of the headache and classical migraine symptomatology described.

Cluster headache
Cluster headache is incorrect. Cluster headache is usually diurnal, with attacks occurring in the night-time. The pain is often excruciating and patients tend to pace around rather that rest. Autonomic symptoms such as running nose, watery eye and ptosis are common.

Giant cell arteritis
Giant cell arteritis is incorrect. Giant cell arteritis does not occur in people younger than 50. Migraine A 44-year-old man with an unremarkable past medical history developed dizziness, tinnitus and mild left-sided hearing loss. The symptoms presented over several months and were slowly progressive, with tinnitus being continuous over the past 2 months. The initial evaluation by his GP was unremarkable with a normal neurological examination and normal otoscopy. Audiometry revealed a mild degree of sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. What would be your next course of action?

Tension headache
Tension headache is incorrect. Tension headache is a featureless dull pain with no associated features and typically bilateral, so does not match this description.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Neurology Clinic for review with a diagnosis of focal epilepsy. She has had intolerable side-effects previously with carbamazepine and levetiracetam and may wish to start a family with her new partner. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next option for her?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
The clinical trial evidence base for use of antiepileptics in pregnancy is small/non-existent, as no randomised controlled trials have been conducted. All pharmaceutical companies keep a register of pregnant patients who are on antiepileptic medication, and countries including the UK keep amalgamated pregnancy registers, the data being available for analysis. Lamotrigine works by inhibiting glutamate release and voltage-gated sodium channels and appears to be the safest choice in this scenario.

Gabapentin
Gabapentin is incorrect. Although gabapentin can potentially be used during pregnancy, in the SANAD study, gabapentin was shown to perform poorly in terms of seizure control when compared against lamotrigine.

Phenobarbitone
Phenobarbitone is incorrect. Phenobarbitone is now rarely used due to its unfavourable adverse effect profile.

Topiramate
Topiramate is incorrect. Very high rates of malformation have been seen with relatively little data for topiramate and this is not recommended for use in pregnancy.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with clinical features consistent with Parkinson’s disease. Which of the following neurotransmitters, if reduced, is most likely to cause Parkinson’s disease?
explanation:
Dopamine
Dopamine is a neurotransmitter secreted by the neurons of the substantia nigra. Its effects are both excitatory and inhibitory. It inhibits unnecessary movements, inhibits the release of prolactin, and stimulates the secretion of growth hormone. Dopamine deficiency related to the destruction of the substantia nigra leads to Parkinson’s disease.

Serotonin
Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that is intimately involved in emotion and mood. It is secreted by the neurons of the brainstem and by neurons that innervate the gastrointestinal tract (enteric nervous system). In addition, serotonin is found in platelets (thrombocytes) which release it during coagulation (haemostasis). Serotonin deficiency may result in decreased immune system function, as well as depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and deliberate self-harm.

Glutamate
