Glutamate is the most powerful excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system; it is integral to learning and memory. Thus, inappropriate glutamate neurotransmission contributes to epilepsy, cognitive and affective disorders.

Acetylcholine
Acetylcholine is an excitatory neurotransmitter secreted by motor neurons that innervate muscle cells, basal ganglia, preganglionic neurons of the autonomic nervous system, and postganglionic neurons of the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems. Its main function is to stimulate muscle contraction. However, the only exception to this, where acetylcholine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, is at the parasympathetic endings of the vagus nerve. These inhibit the heart muscle through the cardiac plexus.

Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).

stem: A 38-year-old woman was assessed for new-onset facial weakness. She had been in excellent health until the summer when, after a walking holiday, she noted an expanding erythematous rash on her abdomen, ultimately about 8 inches in diameter, and lasting about 3 weeks. This improved following treatment with an oral cephalosporin, but she developed 6 weeks of diffuse arthralgias and headaches. She has developed acute right facial paralysis, evolving over 24 hours, with retroauricular pain, hyperacusis and a decreased sense of taste. Past medical history is otherwise unremarkable, and examination is notable only for a complete, right lower motor neurone, seventh nerve palsy. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Lyme disease
Although there is no specific history of tick bite, the rest of the story fits well with Lyme disease, a common neurological manifestation of which is facial paralysis. The rash could be consistent with erythema migrans, and the history of arthralgias is very suggestive.

Bell’s palsy
Bell’s palsy is incorrect. Bell’s palsy is possible if only the facial weakness history is counted, but would not explain the rest of the story.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis can cause a facial weakness but one might reasonably expect other associated brainstem symptoms and signs. In addition, it would not explain the other features of the history such as the rash and arthralgia.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Ramsay Hunt syndrome is incorrect. Ramsay Hunt syndrome would cause pain and a vesicular eruption in and around the ear.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is another possibility, although it fits less well with the story and, in particular, the rash.

stem: A 60-year-old man attends the Neurology Clinic with his wife. He has become increasingly confused and forgetful over the past few months and is drinking heavily, to the extent that now he is unable to carry out his usual activities. He has had a number of falls in the last two weeks and seems unbalanced on his feet. He has a past medical history of hypertension, for which he takes ramipril and amlodipine daily. On examination, his BP is 111/70 mmHg and his pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable. Neurology examination is unremarkable, except for horizontal nystagmus. His Mini-Mental State Examination score is 20/30 and he confabulates during the assessment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome is due to chronic thiamine deficiency (in this case as a result of alcoholism). Horizontal nystagmus persists in around 60% of cases and recovery from ataxia occurs in around 40%. However, memory recovers in only 20% after thiamine treatment.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is not commonly associated with ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus. Confabulation would be unusual in Alzheimer’s disease where problems with declarative episodic memory would be expected. Furthermore, the alcohol history means that Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome should be excluded first. Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is most commonly associated with behavioural changes, such as gaining a sweet tooth and difficulties with respect to socialisation. Episodic memory is usually preserved early in the disease course. Ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus and instability would be unusual in FTD and make it less likely.

Multi-infarct disease
Multi-infarct dementia is most common in patients with pre-existing vascular risk factors. Cognitive impairment is due to a series of strokes, some of which could be ‘silent’, although it would be expected that the history would encompass several stroke episodes and hence a stepwise neurological deterioration, rather than the gradual deterioration here. Wernickes Encephalopathy A 50-year-old hypertensive man presents with difficulty in using his right arm, slow walking and occasional loss of balance. He has developed symptoms of urinary urgency. On examination he has a broad-based gait, there is cogwheel rigidity and intention tremor of his right arm. His blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg sitting and 100/60 mmHg standing.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents as a triad of symptoms which develop over several months, including dementia, gait disturbance and urinary incontinence. It is a reasonable differential diagnosis for this patient.

stem: A 26-year-old develops foot drop after a motorcycle accident. You find weakness of foot dorsiflexion and eversion. Which structure is most likely to have been damaged?
explanation:
Common peroneal nerve
The common peroneal nerve is the motor supply to the peronei and anterior tibial muscles, so lesions result in paralysis of dorsiflexion (leading to foot drop) and inability to evert the foot. A lesion above the lateral cutaneous branch results in anaesthesia over the anterolateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot.

Lumbar nerve roots
Lumbar nerve roots is incorrect. Lumbar nerve root lesions such as L5 radiculopathy could produce a foot drop. However, given the recent history of a motorcycle accident the most likely answer is a common peroneal nerve lesion; that nerve is superficially positioned around the head of fibula and is prone to damage in such events.

Lumbosacral plexus
Lumbosacral plexus is incorrect. A lumbosacral plexus lesion would produce more diffuse weakness and sensory loss than described in this case.

Sciatic nerve
Sciatic nerve is incorrect. The sciatic nerve gives rise to the peroneal and tibial nerves so a lesion here produces a ‘flail ankle’ with weakness of all movements around that joint. Mononeuropathies

Tibial nerve
Tibial nerve is incorrect. The tibial (medial popliteal) nerve mediates the ankle reflex and supplies the muscles of the calf – lesions of this nerve produce weakness in plantar flexion and loss of the ankle reflex.

stem: A 60-year-old engineer who was previously well was found collapsed on the floor. When he was admitted, examination revealed weakness of the right side of his body, with his arm and face more severely affected than his leg, and severe aphasia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A tumour of the left cerebral hemisphere
A tumour of the left thalamus
An occlusion of the left anterior cerebral artery
An occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery
An occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery
explanation:
An occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery
The sudden onset of symptoms and signs suggests a vascular cause. Depending on the site of involvement, several clinical syndromes of middle cerebral artery occlusion can occur: Superior division Occlusion of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery results in: If the dominant hemisphere is involved, there is also expressive aphasia Contralateral hemiparesis that affects the face, hand and arm, but with relative sparing of the leg Contralateral hemisensory deficit in the same distribution No homonymous hemianopia Inferior division Occlusion of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery results in: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia Marked impairment of cortical sensory functions, such as agraphaesthesia and astereognosis on the contralateral side of the body Disorders of higher cortical function, including: A lack of awareness that a deficit exists (anosognosia) Neglect of and failure to recognise the contralateral limbs Neglect of the contralateral side of external space Dressing apraxia Constructional apraxia Involvement of the dominant hemisphere also causes receptive aphasia An acute confusional state may occur if the non-dominant hemisphere is affected

A tumour of the left cerebral hemisphere
A tumour of the left cerebral hemisphere is incorrect. Tumours grow slowly and unless presenting with a seizure, the evolution of symptoms occurs in a similarly slow way.

A tumour of the left thalamus
A tumour of the left thalamus is incorrect. Tumours grow slowly and unless presenting with a seizure, the evolution of symptoms occurs in a similarly slow way.

An occlusion of the left anterior cerebral artery
An occlusion of the left anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Strokes affecting the anterior cerebral artery territory typically present with leg weakness on the contralateral side. Here, the predominant weakness is arm and face.

An occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery
An occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Strokes affecting the anterior cerebral artery territory typically present with contralateral leg weakness. 254 Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke A 49-year-old man hit his forehead getting into his car. A few hours later he developed diplopia, vomiting and severe headache. On examination he is slightly drowsy, and has dilated right pupil, partial right ptosis, little movement in any direction of gaze in his right eye, with reduced sensation over the right forehead. He had a postural systolic BP drop of 20 mmHg.

stem: A 72-year-old hypertensive male with a history of coronary artery bypass developed slurring of speech and mild dysphagia over a period of 2 weeks. He was diagnosed with an upper respiratory infection and treated with antibiotic therapy without further diagnostic testing. He gradually improved a little over the next 1–2 months, but his symptoms returned subacutely after 4 months. In addition to dysarthria and dysphagia, he then experienced diplopia and mild ptosis for the first time. Examination reveals bilateral ptosis and a slurred voice towards the end of the consultation, but is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis
The history is most suggestive of myasthenia gravis, affecting the bulbar and ocular muscles.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is incorrect. Guillain–Barré syndrome can occasionaly present with cranial nerve symptoms and signs before limb involvement, but this is rare. In addition the history here suggests a waxing and waning disease course that is not seen with GBS, which is monophasic.

Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome is incorrect. Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome tends to present with limb symptoms (classically lower limb weakness) and oculo-bulbar symptoms are rarer. In addition, patients usually have autonomic dysfunction, which is not mentioned here.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease is an important consideration, but is unlikely to present at this stage without supportive clinical signs (fasciculation, upper motor neurone features), and would not cause ptosis.

Small-vessel cerebral ischaemia
Small-vessel cerebral ischaemia is incorrect. Small-vessel cerebral ischaemia can lead to pseudobulbar palsy, but would not cause ptosis. Fatigability in the neurological features would not be expected.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with a 4-week history of headache and fever. He has asymmetrical upper cranial nerve palsies. CSF examination reveals: opening pressure 30 cm; 200 white cells/dl (lymphocytic predominance); protein 2.0 g/l; glucose (CSF/plasma) 0.8/6.3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberculous meningitis
The patient has a subacute–chronic lymphocytic meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies. The CSF glucose is low and the opening pressure is moderately high. This is a typical picture for tuberculous meningitis. The CSF should be examined with auramine or Ziehl–Neelsen stain to look for myocobacteria.

Brain abscess
Brain abscess is incorrect. Brain abscess is more likely to present with seizures and focal cortical signs than multiple cranial neuropathies.

Cryptococcal meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis is incorrect. Cryptococcal meningitis also causes a subacute lymphocytic meningitis; it typically occurs in immunosuppressed individuals. The CSF opening pressure is often very high (>40 cm) and, although sixth nerve palsies may occur as a false localising sign of raised pressure, multiple cranial neuropathies are not typical.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. Guillain–Barré syndrome may rarely present with cranial neuropathies, but the CSF picture does not fit, as GBS is associated with normal cells and high protein. Tuberculosis Meningitis A 25-year-old woman visits her GP with a 6-month history of intermittent headaches. These last for 2 hours and are associated with visual blurring and nausea. The GP feels that this is migraine, but examination reveals that her left pupil is smaller than the right and her upper and lower limb reflexes are all diminished. Her eye movements are normal and there is no ptosis. The right pupil does not appear to react to light and reacts poorly to accommodation.

Herpes zoster meningitis
Herpes zoster meningitis is incorrect. Herpes zoster meningitis may produce a lymphocytoc CSF, but one would not expect low CSF glucose or a high opening pressure. In addition the multiple cranial neuropathies would be unusual.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with no relevant past medical history has presented with acute, binocular horizontal diplopia and severe headache. On examination there is a partial ptosis on the left and a dilated and unreactive left pupil. The left eye is abducted when looking straight ahead. Eye movement testing reveals moderate underaction of adduction, elevation and depression of the left eye. The right eye moves normally. There is intorsion of the left eye in downgaze. The rest of the neurological examination, including fundal examination, is normal. Blood pressure and blood glucose testing were normal in the Emergency Department. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm
The physical signs are those of an oculomotor palsy. In the context of pain and pupil involvement an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm is most likely.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis is incorrect. The fact that these very distinct signs are present in isolation (discrete third nerve palsy) is important: lesions in the cavernous sinus would affect other structures and so cause other signs than those described.

Ischaemic oculomotor palsy
Ischaemic oculomotor palsy is incorrect. Microvascular/ischaemic oculomotor palsy normally spares the pupil and is less likely to be painful.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis and eye muscle weakness but one would not see pupil involvement and pain would not be a feature.

Pontine infarct
Pontine infarct is incorrect. The fact that these very distinct signs are present in isolation (discrete third nerve palsy) is important: posterior circulation stroke (pontine infarct) would affect other structures and so cause other signs.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with cerebellar ataxia. Her MRI shows a large, left-sided cerebellar cyst with nodular enhancement in one wall. The radiologist suggests the possible diagnosis of von Hippel–Lindau syndrome. What serious pathology might she have most increased risk for in other organ systems?
explanation:
Renal-cell carcinoma
The von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome is autosomal dominant and is characterised by cerebellar haemangioma, which may present as cerebellar ataxia or with signs of increased intracranial pressure due to compression of the IVth ventricle. Excision of the brain cyst may be curative, but there is a high risk of recurrence if the nodule is not fully excised. There may be associated retinal angioma, pancreatic and/or hepatic cysts, and there is a risk of developing malignant adrenal and renal tumours in later life. Screening for these must therefore be carried out.

Cutaneous neurofibroma
Cutaneous neurofibroma is incorrect. Cutaneous neurofibromas occur in neurofibromatosis, not VHL.

Pancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. Pancreatic carcinoma is not seen in VHL, whereas pancreatic cysts may be seen.

Pulmonary fibrosis
Pulmonary fibrosis is incorrect. Pulmonary fibrosis is not part of the VHL syndrome. Von Hippel–Lindau DiseaseRetinoblastoma
Retinoblastoma is incorrect. Retinal angiomas may be seen in VHL but not retinoblastomas.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of a clumsy right hand and difficulty speaking. His symptoms came on that morning, and were still present 8 hours later. His past medical history includes hypertension and migraines as a young man. He smokes ten cigarettes per day. On examination he was found to have some weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles on his right only. Speech was mildly slurred. Visual fields and sensation were normal. Blood pressure was 180/100 mmHg. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Left, middle cerebral artery territory, cardioembolic stroke
explanation:
Left hemisphere lacunar stroke
Lacunar infarcts are small deep infarcts with a maximum diameter of 1.5 cm and a volume of 0.2–3.4 cm3. Lacunar infarcts mainly occur in the basal ganglia, lenticular nucleus and especially the putamen, thalamus and white matter of the internal capsule, pons and centrum semiovale. The five classic lacunar syndromes, described in neuropathological studies in the 1960s and 1970s are: pure motor hemiparesis, pure sensory stroke, sensorimotor stroke, ataxic hemiparesis and clumsy-hand dysarthria. However, in the modern imaging era many more syndromes have been described.

Left, middle cerebral artery territory, cardioembolic stroke
Left, middle cerebral artery territory, cardioembolic stroke is incorrect. Left middle cerebral artery stroke would be expected to cause more extensive right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia.

Left pontine microhaemorrhage
Left pontine microhaemorrhage is incorrect. The usual site of damage in the dysarthria–clumsy-hand syndrome is in the internal capsule or pons. Microhaemorrhage in the pons is therefore a possible cause for this syndrome, but ischaemia is more common than haemorrhage making this option less likely.

Migraine equivalent
Migraine equivalent is incorrect. Migraine equivalents (aura-like symptoms without headache) can provide diagnostic difficulties and should always be considered in those with a previous history of migraine, but there is no suggestion of the characteristic slow spread of symptoms in this patient, so this is not the best option. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke Which one of the following is most suggestive of a lesion of the sciatic nerve?

Neck–tongue syndrome
Neck–tongue syndrome is incorrect. The neck–tongue syndrome consists of pain and paraesthesias in one half of the tongue precipitated by neck movement.

stem: A patient presents with eye pain and diplopia of 2 days’ duration. On examination there is no proptosis, but a left-sided VIth nerve palsy, a partial left IIIrd nerve palsy, and left Vth nerve sensory changes over the maxilla are present. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Cavernous sinus
The cavernous sinuses are paired venous structures on either side of the sella turcica. The cavernous sinus contains the carotid artery and the accompanying sympathetic plexus, with the IIIrd, IVth and VIth cranial nerves and the ophthalmic and sometime maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve (NV). Causes of pressure within the carotid sinus include tumours, aneurysms, carotid-cavernous fistulas and cavernous sinus thrombosis. MRI/MR venography is the investigation of choice in these patients.

Anterior cerebral artery
Anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Predominantly, the anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal lobes. A stroke in this area can present with contralateral leg weakness. Cranial nerve lesions are not a feature.

Cerebellopontine angle
Cerebellopontine angle is incorrect. A lesion at the cerebellopontine angle can cause trigeminal nerve dysfunction, but this would be accompanied by lesions of the facial (NVII) and vestibulocochlear (NVIII) nerves, rather than the nerve lesions seen in this case.

Middle cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery is incorrect. The middle cerebral artery supplies many areas of the lateral cerebral cortex. A typical ‘MCA-stroke’ presents with contralateral face and arm weakness. Cranial nerve lesions are not a feature.

Vertebral artery
Vertebral artery is incorrect. Pathology affecting the vertebral artery (eg dissection) can cause brain stem signs, but these usually affect the medulla (eg the lateral medullary syndrome). The cranial nerves affected in this case are located in the midbrain/pons.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presented at the age of 3 years with progressive ataxia. She is now wheelchair-bound. On examination, she is now dysarthric, with bilateral Optic atrophy. There is ataxia in both upper limbs. Reflexes in her lower limbs are absent with bilateral extensor plantar response. She has absent vibration and impaired joint position in both feet. Bilateral pes cavus is apparent. ECG shows inverted T waves. Echocardiogram reveals left ventricular hypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is considered the most common hereditary ataxia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder with variable phenotype. Onset is usually in early life and life expectancy is generally about 35 years. There is a degeneration of the cerebellum, certain spinal cord tracts and peripheral nerves. Associated clinical features include ataxia, dysarthria, optic atrophy, hearing impairment, learning difficulties, sensory neuropathy, extensor plantar responses, diabetes and cardiomyopathy. Pes cavus and kyphoscoliosis are also common features. Given the clinical information in the question, Friedreich’s ataxia is the best answer.

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease
Charcot–Marie–Tooth (CMT) disease is incorrect. CMT describes a range of genetic neuropathies with a variable age of presentation (from infancy to old age) and a wide range of phenotypes. Most forms of CMT do not involve the central nervous system, so optic atrophy and upgoing plantars would not be expected.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease is incorrect. Huntington’s disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder characterised by a progressive movement disorder (usually chorea or parkinsonism) with cognitive deterioration and affective disturbance. Thus the picture here does not fit with this diagnosis.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis rarely presents in early childhood and peripheral nervous system signs such as areflexia are not seen. The cardiac problems described here are not seen in MS. Friedreich’s AtaxiaVitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause subacute combined degeneration of the cord, which as the name suggests is an illness that evolves over weeks to months – not the chronic progressive course described in this question. The combination of spinal tract degeneration (corticospinal tract and posterior column) together with co-existing sensory neuropathy is seen in subacute combined degeneration, so some of the clinical signs may be similar.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with paroxysmal episodes of vertigo, vomiting and impaired hearing on the right side lasting for 1–4 hours. She has experienced eight such episodes over the last 12 months. Neurological examination shows evidence of right sensorineural deafness. An audiogram confirms the presence of right lowfrequency sensorineural deafness. Computed tomography (CT) brain is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ménière’s disease
Ménière’s disease presents as paroxysmal episodes of vertigo, nausea/vomiting and deafness lasting for hours. An audiogram shows a unilateral low frequency sensorineural deafness. Prochlorperazine and cyclizine are commonly used for acute attacks; betahistine and or diuretics and a low-salt diet are used for prophylaxis.

Acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma is incorrect. Acoustic neuroma can result in hearing loss and vertigo; however, these will be persistent. The episodic pattern does not suggest an acoustic neuroma. Further CT brain may show abnormalities.

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is incorrect. The episodes last a few seconds and are associated with positional change. Tinnitus is associated with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, but not impaired hearing with sensorineural deafness.

Labyrinthitis
Labyrinthitis is incorrect. It results from inflammation of the vestibular nerve. Symptoms are relieved within 1–3 weeks and recover fully in 1 or 2 months. Hearing loss is uncommon.

Vertebrobasilar insufficiency
Vertebrobasilar insufficiency is incorrect. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency usually affects older patients and the duration of symptoms is shorter, lasting only few minutes.

stem: A 19-year-old patient originally from Finland presents to the Ophthalmology Clinic for review. He has gradually worsening myopia, decreased night vision and peripheral visual field loss. On examination there is atrophy of the retinae. What enzyme deficiency is this patient most likely to have?
explanation:
Ornithine aminotransferase
Deficiency of ornithine-δ-aminotransferase causes atrophy of the choroid and retina, beginning as a small yellowish spot and increasing to a circular lesion edged with pigment. Children present with myopia and decreased night vision, which progresses from tunnel vision to blindness in middle life. Cataracts also develop but the optic discs, cornea and iris remain normal. A few patients develop mild proximal muscle weakness. Microscopic abnormalities of skeletal muscle fibres and MRI changes in the CNS are seen, but the longer term clinical implications are unclear, as is the exact pathology which drives retinal atrophy. Deficiency of the enzyme results in a massive rise in plasma ornithine, with particularly high concentrations in the CSF and aqueous humour.

Acetyl-coenzyme A acetyltransferase
Acetyl-coenzyme A acetyltransferase is incorrect. Acetyl-coenzyme A acetyltransferase deficiency results in neurological deterioration with recurrent attacks of ketoacidosis and convulsions.

Argininosuccinic acid synthetase
Argininosuccinic acid synthetase is incorrect. Argininosuccinic acid synthetase deficiency mostly presents in childhood with severe symptoms associated with high levels of ammonia. The adult form of the disease is seen almost exclusively in Japanese. Papilloedema may be seen if there is cerebral oedema.

Glutathione synthetase
Glutathione synthetase is incorrect. Glutathione synthetase deficiency presents with marked neurological deterioration and peripheral retinal pigmentation abnormalities. Visual Field Defects

Lipoprotein lipase
Lipoprotein lipase is incorrect. Retinal changes are seen in familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency; lipaemia retinalis is seen, but this does not affect visual fields or acuity.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents complaining of slowly progressive weakness of his legs, which he says has occurred over the last 10 years. He also experiences difficulty with fine tasks involving his hands, including difficulty holding a cup. Over the last 2 years he has also noticed occasional difficulty in swallowing. He denies any sensory symptoms or bladder disturbances. He is on no drugs. He does not smoke or drink alcohol excessively. There is no relevant family history. On examination there is marked wasting of the quadriceps and forearm muscles. There is finger flexion and knee extension weakness. Sensation and reflexes are normal. Plantar response is flexor bilaterally. Cranial nerves are intact. EMG shows increased insertional and spontaneous activity, and small-amplitude, short-duration polyphasic units of both the quadriceps and forearm flexor muscles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inclusion body myositis
Inclusion body myositis (IBM) typically presents with slowly progressive weakness and wasting of the finger flexors and quadriceps. The slow, relentless progression of muscle weakness in IBM leads to walking difficulty, frequent falls and eventual need for mobility aids. Dysphagia is a common manifestation of the disease. Creatinine kinase (CK) is either normal or up to fivefold the upper range of normal. EMG shows inflammatory myopathic changes: increased insertional and spontaneous activity as well as small-amplitude, short-duration polyphasic unit. There is no available treatment.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyosistis is incorrect. The onset is in childhood or adulthood. There is a myopathic (proximal) distribution of weakness. Characteristic heliotropic rash of dermatomyositis is present. One-third of patients complain of muscle pain and tenderness. There is spontaneous activity on needle EMG. Serum CK is markedly elevated. Muscle biopsy shows evidence of perivascular and perimysial inflammatory infiltrates with perifascicular atrophy and provides a definitive diagnosis.

Limb-girdle muscular atrophy
Limb-girdle muscular atrophy is incorrect. There is a positive family history with an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. The onset is evident with onset of weakness and wasting in pelvic or shoulder girdle muscles. Serum CK is elevated in autosomal recessive cases. Muscle biopsy shows lack of staining for the proteins sarcoglycan, calpain, dysferlin or caveolin. Genetic testing provides a definitive diagnosis.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. In motor neurone disease there will be muscle weakness and atrophy. Overt cognitive changes and sensory changes are not present. Tendon reflexes will be hyperactive if upper motor neurones are affected, or hypoactive if lower motor neurones are affected. Babinski sign will be positive if upper motor neurones are involved. There are different subtypes of motor neurone disease. In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis there is a mixed upper motor and lower motor neurone presentation. In primary lateral sclerosis the signs are of upper motor neurone involvement.

stem: A 46-year-old woman has, over the past 14 hours, developed weakness and numbness in her legs. She has no previous medical history of note, apart from treated hypertension. She smokes cigarettes ‘occasionally’. Her mother died of a ‘heart problem’ in her early forties. On examination, the cranial nerves and upper limbs are normal to examination. Power is reduced to 3/5 in all modalities below the hips and reflexes are absent. Pain and temperature sensation are lost to the waist. Vibration and joint-position sense are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
A lesion at the conus medullaris
explanation:
Anterior spinal artery thrombosis
This affects the descending corticospinal tracts and ascending spinothalamic tracts, both of which are anteriorly located within the topographic arrangement of the spinal cord. Posterior columns are spared, thus vibration and joint-position sense are retained. In the acute stage reflexes are diminished, in keeping with "spinal shock", this may last for several days.

Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is incorrect. This genetic disorder does not develop suddenly and the clinical picture usually involves a combination of upgoing plantars with absent ankle jerks.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Again, the presentation is too sudden here. Additionally, motor neurone disease does not affect the sensory nerves and hence sensation would be unaffected.

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is incorrect. Again the presentation is too sudden here. Additionally, subacute combined degeneration of the cord is characterized by dysfunction of dorsal column sensation, which is specifically preserved in this case.

A lesion at the conus medullaris
A lesion at the conus medullaris is incorrect. A structural lesion causing compression of the level of the conus medullaris should be considered in patients with acute leg weakness. However, sphincter disturbance would be prominent and the discrete pattern of sensory abnormality seen in this case (i.e. spinothalamic affected, dorsal column spared) would not be seen.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a disabling headache syndrome consisting of recurrent, severe, unilateral (either right or left) headaches twice a week lasting for 8 hours each. The pain is constant, throbbing and associated with nausea and phonophobia. It has not responded to ibuprofen or paracetamol. The headaches are more common after physical exercise. She has identified no dietary triggers, and there is no family history of migraine. She is very worried about her increasing weight. Which one of the following is a sensible treatment course?
options: Methysergide (for prophylaxis) and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for the acute
Pizotifen (for prophylaxis) and ergotamine (for the acute attacks)
Regular daily co-proxamol (for prophylaxis), increased during the acute attacks
Regular daily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for prophylaxis), increased during the
Topiramate (for prophylaxis) and a triptan (for the acute attacks)
explanation:
Topiramate (for prophylaxis) and a triptan (for the acute attacks)
The history is most consistent with common migraine (migraine without aura). The frequency of the attacks justifies prophylaxis. Topiramate is an effective migraine prophylactic and would be a good choice here. It is recommended in NICE guidelines. It does not cause weight gain, and indeed many patients describe reduced appetite and weight loss with this drug. Triptans could be used to treat acute attacks. Thus this option is the best choice.

Methysergide (for prophylaxis) and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for the acute
Methysergide (for prophylaxis) and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for the acute attacks) Methysergide (for prophylaxis) and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for the acute attacks) is incorrect. Methysergide is associated with pleural and retroperitoneal fibrosis, and is avoided in all but the most intractable cases.

Pizotifen (for prophylaxis) and ergotamine (for the acute attacks)
Pizotifen (for prophylaxis) and ergotamine (for the acute attacks) is incorrect. Pizotifen is an alternative prophylactic, but she is worried about her weight (pizotifen is associated with weight gain); and ergotamine is not commonly used for acute treatment nowadays, ruling this option out.

Regular daily co-proxamol (for prophylaxis), increased during the acute attacks
Regular daily co-proxamol (for prophylaxis), increased during the acute attacks is incorrect. Regular analgesics predispose patients to the development of chronic daily headache (medication overuse headache), particularly those that contain opiates (such as co-proxamol); this is very much the danger in the situation described, because her headaches are frequent, disabling and could lead to the use of large amounts of analgesia. Migraine

Regular daily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for prophylaxis), increased during the
Regular daily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for prophylaxis), increased during the acute attacks Regular daily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (for prophylaxis), increased during the acute attacks is incorrect. Regular analgesics predispose patients to the development of chronic daily headache (medication overuse headache), particularly those that contain opiates (such as co-proxamol); this is very much the danger in the situation described, because her headaches are frequent, disabling and could lead to the use of large amounts of analgesia.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 12-hour history of vomiting and headache. She has recently received a prescription from her GP for sinusitis. Examination of her cerebrospinal fluid demonstrates a lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein, slightly reduced glucose and negative for Gram staining (not stained with either dye). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Partially treated bacterial meningitis
Although untreated bacterial meningitis generally produces a very elevated polymorph cell count in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (> 1000/mm3), a partially treated bacterial meningitis may more closely resemble the ‘aseptic’ picture of CSF findings also seen with viral meningitis, such as is described here (moderate numbers of lymphocytes, pleocytosis).

Cryptococcal meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis is incorrect. Cryptococcal meningitis could potentially produce this CSF picture; however, it classically reduces CSF glucose levels. The recently prescribed antibiotics and lack of any suggestion that the patient may be immunosuppressed make this option less likely.

Meningeal carcinomatosis
Meningeal carcinomatosis is incorrect. Meningeal carcinomatosis could potentially produce this CSF picture; however, it classically reduces CSF glucose levels. The recently prescribed antibiotics and lack of any suggestion that the patient may be immunosuppressed make this option less likely.

Syphilitic meningitis
Syphilitic meningitis is incorrect. Syphilitic meningitis could potentially produce this CSF picture; however, it classically reduces CSF glucose levels. The recently prescribed antibiotics and lack of any suggestion that the patient may be immunosuppressed make this option less likely.

Tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculous meningitis is incorrect. Tuberculous meningitis could potentially produce this CSF picture; however, it classically reduces CSF glucose levels. The recently prescribed antibiotics and lack of any suggestion that the patient may be immunosuppressed make this option less likely.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with a 5-year history of progressive weakness, worse on the right and affecting the arms more than the legs. In addition, he describes intermittent cramps and muscle twitching. On examination you find distal weakness with wasting and fasciculations, predominantly affecting the right arm. There are no other neurological abnormalities. Electromyography/nerve conduction study reveals features of demyelination and conduction block limited to motor neurones. What is the most appropriate next investigation to perform?
explanation:
Anti-GM1 antibodies
Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) with conduction block (MMN) is closely related to chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP). Anti-GM1 antibodies are present in up to 80% of sufferers. It presents with asymmetrical motor neuropathies, usually in the upper limb. Reflexes may be preserved (or slightly elevated) at the onset of the disease, causing frequent misidentification with motor neurone disease. It is vital to make this distinction as MMN is treatable with immunomodulation. Motor conduction block (MCB) is considered the electro-diagnostic hallmark of multifocal motor neuropathy. MCB is the failure of a nerve action potential to propagate across a segment of intact myelinated nerve fibre. MCB leads to reduction of the amplitude and the area of a compound muscle action potential (CMAP) after stimulation of the nerve proximal to the affected segment. The compound muscle action potential is normal distal to the affected segment. In multifocal motor neuropathy, MCB occurs most frequently in the ulnar and median nerves. MCB is, however, not specific for multifocal motor neuropathy, as it occurs also in acute and chronic compressive neuropathies, Guillain–Barré syndrome and chronic inflammatory demyelination polyneuropathy.

Anti-GQ1b antibodies
Anti-GQ1b antibodies is incorrect. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are associated with Miller Fisher syndrome. This presents with the classical triad of ataxia, areflexia and ophthalmoplegia.

CSF for anti-Hu antibodies
CSF for anti-Hu antibodies is incorrect. Anti-Hu antibodies are associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration and are usually identified in the serum (rather than the CSF).

MRI of cervical cord
MRI of cervical cord is incorrect. Cervical radiculopathies might superficially mimic MMN (or in some cases, even motor neurone disease) but would not cause the neurophysiological abnormalities identified here.

Sural nerve biopsy
Sural nerve biopsy is incorrect. This investigation might be performed if a vasculitic neuropathy was suspected, which is not the case here.

stem: A 56-year-old man has a right hemisphere stroke due to thromboembolic occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery. He does not have a visual field deficit on confrontation testing, and makes a good neurological recovery within 5 days, being able to walk unaided. He is left with a mild degree of left-sided sensory loss and minimal weakness of left-hand grip (4+/5), but feels very well and has resumed all other activities including gardening. What advice is he likely to be given by the Driving and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA)?
options: Must not drive a Group 2 vehicle (eg heavy goods lorry) for at least 2 years
Must not drive until neurological signs fully resolved
explanation:
Must not drive for 1 month
Strokes and transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) generally have a driving restriction of 1 month from the date of the attack. Patients should be advised to contact the DVLA. If after this time significant neurological deficits that may interfere with the ability to drive persist (particularly visual field defects, cognitive defects or impaired limb function) then the restriction is likely to be prolonged. Very minor weakness that does not interfere with limb function is not considered a problem. Restriction on driving for 1 month is therefore correct as the residual deficit in this case is mild. In cases of doubt, driving assessments may be carried out at specialist rehabilitation centres.

Must not drive a Group 2 vehicle (eg heavy goods lorry) for at least 2 years
Must not drive a Group 2 vehicle (eg heavy goods lorry) for at least 2 years is incorrect. After a stroke, Group 2 entitlement is usually restricted for at least 1 year, so this is incorrect.

Must not drive for 3 months
Must not drive for 3 months is incorrect based on current DVLA advice.

Must not drive until neurological signs fully resolved
Must not drive until neurological signs fully resolved is incorrect based on current DVLA advice.

No driving restriction necessary.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department by ambulance with ongoing tonic–clonic seizures. She initially suffered a seizure 25 minutes before arrival, which responded to rectal diazepam. She remained confused and drowsy before exhibiting further tonic–clonic activity for the last two minutes. Intravenous lorazepam 4 mg and a loading dose of levetiracetam is given. Tonic–clonic seizures stop, but she remains only responsive to pain (withdraws from painful stimulus) and without eye opening and no vocal sounds. Her epilepsy is usually controlled with lamotrigine. Her heart rate is 99 bpm, blood pressure 110/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute, oxygen saturations 100% on 15 litres via a non-rebreather mask and her temperature 37.5 °C. What is the next step in this patient’s management?
explanation:
Intubation and ventilation
The patient has been treated for status epilepticus and now has a decreased conscious level. Being responsive to pain only is roughly equivalent to a Glasgow Coma Scale score of < 8. The patient should have a rapid sequence induction, followed by a propofol infusion, to protect her airway and prevent aspiration of gastric contents.

Intravenous sodium valporate
Intravenous sodium valproate is an alternative to levetiracetam for initial emergency management of status epilepticus. The next step in the patient’s management is to secure her airway before any further anticonvulsant therapy is considered.

Intravenous benzodiazepine infusion
The patient was treated for status epilepticus and her airway is now currently at risk. Her airway should be secured first before considering additional therapy. Given there is currently seizure control, further benzodiazepines are not indicated at this stage.

Intravenous phenytoin infusion
The patient has received intravenous levetiracetam. Given there is currently seizure control, phenytoin is not indicated.

Intravenous phenobarbital infusion.

stem: A 47-year-old, previously well, male dentist presents with a four-month history of numbness and paraesthesia in both legs distally. He also complains of mild unsteadiness on walking. He has no urinary symptoms. Examination reveals: mild weakness of the lower limbs; brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks; and upgoing plantars. Pinprick sensation is reduced to mid-shin bilaterally, and vibration sense is impaired to the iliac crests. MRI of the brain and spine, cerebrospinal fluid examination, HTLV-1, HIV and syphilis serology are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Nitrous oxide toxicity
Excessive exposure to the anaesthetic agent nitrous oxide results in a predominantly sensory neuropathy and associated myelopathy (leg weakness, combination of increased and decreased reflexes and sensory neuropathic signs). The clinical syndrome that develops may be indistinguishable from that of vitamin B 12 deficiency. Nitrous oxide interacts with vitamin B12 causing selective inhibition of methionine synthase. Prolonged exposure to nitrous oxide is usually needed to produce neurological symptoms in normal individuals, but patients who are already vitamin B 12 deficient (eg vegans) may experience neurological deficits after brief exposures to nitrous oxide during anaesthetic procedures. Traditionally the syndrome was seen in those individuals with access to medical nitrous oxide (Eg Dentists) but it is now widely used as a recreational drug and cases such as this have been on the increase.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is incorrect. The sensory symptoms here would be very unusual in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease of the motor neurons.

Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is incorrect. The presentation here is too rapid for Friedreich’s ataxia.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. This should be considered in any patient with subacute progressive flaccid paralysis. However, the history is too long in this case (by definition, patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome should not progressively worsen beyond 4 weeks of onset) and the brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars and normal cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) would be against this.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis might be considered, although the reduced ankle jerks, normal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and CSF would be against it.

stem: A 43-year-old man complains of something wrong with his right arm and hand, although he finds it difficult to be clear exactly what. He is left-handed and so is not unduly bothered by his symptoms. On examination he has a variable reduction in light-touch sensation in his right hand extending to above his elbow. Joint position sense appears intact. He has difficulty distinguishing his cigarette lighter from a pen when using his right hand (with his eyes closed), but has no problems with the left. His two-point discrimination on the right is 11 mm compared with 2 mm on the left. There are no other significant CNS signs. Which of the following investigations would be most useful in helping to make the diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI head
The sensory signs described here are cortical sensory signs, and are indicative of a lesion of the anterior parietal cortex, particularly of the mid-postcentral gyrus. The anterior parietal cortex contains neurons responsive to shape, size, and orientation of objects to be grasped as well as for manipulation of the hands themselves, both to viewed and remembered stimuli. MRI is used in the investigation of cortical sensory lesions.

Chest radiograph
Chest radiograph is incorrect. Chest radiography may be part of the work-up for patients with suspected brachial plexus lesions (eg due to Pancoast’s tumour).

Electromyogram and nerve conduction studies
Electromyogram (EMG) and nerve conduction studies is incorrect. EMG and nerve conduction studies are used to investigate peripheral nerve or muscle problems. In this patient these tests will be normal.

MRI cervical spine
MRI cervical spine is incorrect. MRI cervical spine can be used to investigate myelopathic or radiculopathic symptoms, but that is not what is described in this case.

Vitamin B12 levels
Vitamin B12 levels is incorrect. B12 levels can be checked in patients with suspected subacute combined degeneration of the cord or peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with left arm weakness and collapse. After 24 h he is left with minor weakness affecting his left hand and has a carotid ultrasound scan. This reveals a 49% stenosis affecting the right internal carotid artery and a 55% stenosis affecting the left internal carotid artery. This is the second event with leftsided symptoms to have occurred within the past 3 months, the first event left him with permanently impaired coordination on his left side. Other risk factors of note include smoking 30 cigarettes per day, which he refuses to stop, and hypertension. Pre-existing medication includes aspirin 75 mg, ramipril and atorvastatin 10 mg. Blood pressure in the clinic is 145/80 mmHg, he is in sinus rhythm and cholesterol is 5.1 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management to reduce risk of a further stroke affecting the same territory?
explanation:
Clopidogrel therapy
NICE guidance recommends the use of clopidogrel in this situation.

High-dose aspirin therapy
High-dose aspirin therapy is incorrect. Although aspirin alone reduces stroke risk, clopidogrel is recommended by NICE guidance, so clopidogrel therapy is more correct than high-dose aspirin therapy.

Increase statin therapy
Increase statin therapy is incorrect. Lowering total cholesterol further from this level is unlikely to have an impact on stroke risk to the same extent as optimised antiplatelet therapy.

Left carotid endarterectomy
Left carotid endarterectomy is incorrect. The symptoms are not suggestive of left internal carotid artery stroke; carotid endarterectomy is therefore excluded as an option.

Right carotid endarterectomy
Right carotid endarterectomy is incorrect. The right carotid artery stenosis is not severe enough to justify surgical intervention; carotid endarterectomy is therefore excluded as an option. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke A 72-year-old hypertensive male with a history of coronary artery bypass developed slurring of speech and mild dysphagia over a period of 2 weeks. He was diagnosed with an upper respiratory infection and treated with antibiotic therapy without further diagnostic testing. He gradually improved a little over the next 1–2 months, but his symptoms returned subacutely after 4 months. In addition to dysarthria and dysphagia, he then experienced diplopia and mild ptosis for the first time. Examination reveals bilateral ptosis and a slurred voice towards the end of the consultation, but is otherwise normal.

stem: A pregnant woman, who is 21 weeks’ gestation, presents to A&E with excessive vomiting for several weeks. This was then followed by progressive weakness of her lower limbs, a wide-based gait along with altered senses and double vision. On arrival she has a reduced GCS (8/15). This is due to a deficiency of which vitamin?
explanation:
Thiamine
Wernicke’s encephalopathy is directly caused by thiamine deficiency, which results from a combination of inadequate dietary intake, reduced gastrointestinal absorption, decreased hepatic storage and impaired utilization.

Folic acid
Folic acid is incorrect. Folic acid deficiency can cause fatigue, lethargy and breathlessness due to macrocytic anaemia. Folic acid is cinically similar to Vitamin B 12, except that it is more rapid as stores are smaller and CNS symptoms are rare. It has also been associated with plapitations and tinnitus.

Nicotinic acid
Nitcotinic acid is incorrect. Nicotinic acid deficiency (pellagra) may cause periods of disorientation and confusion in patients. It is classically characterized by the four Ds (photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia and death).

Vitamin B 12
Vitamin B 12 is incorrect. Vitamin B 12 deficiency (hypocobalaminaemia) may cause a progressive dementia, as well as increased infections, bleeding disorders, angular chelitis and infertility. Wernickes Encephalopathy

Vitamin D
Vitamin D is incorrect. Vitamin D deficiency can lead to a secondary hyperparathyroidism (due to lowered levels of circulating calcium and phosphate), producing poor bone mineralization.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with severe stabbing pain over the left maxillary region of the face over the past few months. No obvious illness preceded the onset of the problem. The pain occurs several times per day and lasts anything from a few seconds to 1–2 min. It can be brought on simply by touching the area. Sometimes the pain is accompanied by brief muscle spasms. Neurological examination is entirely normal. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Trigeminal neuralgia
This patient has a history typical of trigeminal neuralgia, which most commonly begins in the sixth decade and is slightly more common in women. Physical examination is usually normal, although if abnormal, or if trigeminal neuralgia occurs in an atypical setting (for example a young patient) secondary causes should be sought (such as multiple sclerosis). Anti-convulsants are the main-stay of therapy, particularly carbamazepine.

Atypical migraine
Atypical migraine is incorrect. The patient does not have symptoms of migraine, atypical or otherwise. If considering any ‘atypical’ diagnosis, one must be sure that a better explanation for the patient’s symptoms cannot be found.

Cluster headache
Cluster headache is incorrect. Cluster headaches are rare in women and produce a severe head pain that usually lasts up to 90 min and is associated with autonomic features (redness of the eye, stuffiness of the nose etc). This is not the description given in this case.

Post-herpetic neuralgia
Post-herpetic neuralgia is incorrect. Obviously the case description is lacking a preceding history of shingles. Furthermore the pain in post-herpetic neuralgia is usually described as burning and continuous, rather than the short stabs of pain seen here. Trigeminal neuralgiaAn 18-year-old man who is visiting relatives in the United Kingdom from Afghanistan is brought to the Emergency Department. He was unwell ten days ago with myalgia, fatigue and sore throat. This subsided over three days with symptomatic support by the Community Pharmacist. He now describes severe back and neck spasms and pain, which started 12 hours ago. On examination, his blood pressure is 149/80 mmHg, heart rate is 80 bpm and regular, oxygen saturations 100% on room air and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. There is decreased tone and power, particularly proximally, in the right lower limb with severe pain on neck flexion. Investigations:

Temporomandibular joint dysfunction
Temporomandibular joint dysfunction is incorrect. Temporomandibular joint dysfunction is occasionally the explanation in patients with otherwise unexplained facial pain. However, the short stabs of pain described in this case, often occurring after a stimulus (touching the area, but also brushing teeth, wind against the face etc) is typical of trigeminal neuralgia.

stem: A 50-year-old man is known to have a chronic polyneuropathy. On his most recent clinic visit, he mentions that he has started having diarrhoea, especially at night. He has also noticed that he feels dizzy when he stands up and indeed collapsed while standing at a bus stop a few days ago. On further questioning he admits to having had erectile problems for quite some time. His BP is 160/88 mmHg lying, and 136/60 mmHg standing. His signs of reduced knee jerks, absent ankle jerks and reduced pinprick and vibration sense to the knees are unchanged from his last clinic visit. Given the development of these recent symptoms, what underlying cause is most likely for his neuropathy?
explanation:
Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis associated neuropathy is classically associated with an autonomic neuropathy, which this patient describes symptoms of.

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease
Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease is incorrect. Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease is not usually associated with prominent autonomic symptoms.

Paraneoplastic neuropathy
Paraneoplastic neuropathy is incorrect. Autonomic involvement is not typically a prominent feature in paraneoplastic neuropathy.

Vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord with a peripheral neuropathy, but autonomic features are not prominent in that syndrome.

Vitamin E deficiency
Vitamin E deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin E deficiency produces an ataxic syndrome. Amyloidosis An 18-year-old woman presented at the age of 3 years with progressive ataxia. She is now wheelchair-bound. On examination, she is now dysarthric, with bilateral Optic atrophy. There is ataxia in both upper limbs. Reflexes in her lower limbs are absent with bilateral extensor plantar response. She has absent vibration and impaired joint position in both feet. Bilateral pes cavus is apparent. ECG shows inverted T waves. Echocardiogram reveals left ventricular hypertrophy.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with sudden onset of the loss of sensation of pain and temperature over his left face and right side of the body. In addition to these sensory abnormalities, there is a left-sided Horner syndrome. Which blood vessel is most likely to be involved?
explanation:
Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery
This man has a left lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), which is usually caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) secondary to vertebral artery dissection. Recent trauma or activities involving unusually prolonged or excessive neck extension are risk factors for vertebral artery dissection. The key feature here is the crossed nature of the signs (ie left side of face, right side of body), which localises the lesion to the brainstem. The PICA supplies the posteroinferior cerebellar hemisphere as well as the lateral portion of the medulla, where structures damaged include the: Vestibular nucleus (causing nystagmus and vomiting) Inferior cerebellar peduncle (causing ipsilateral limb ataxia) Spinothalamic tract (causing contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the limbs and torso) Spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve (causing ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face) Nucleus ambiguus (causing ipsilateral laryngeal, pharyngeal and palatal paralysis by disruption of projections to the vagus nerve; allows the uvula to be pulled away from the side of the lesion) Descending sympathetic fibres (causing an ipsilateral Horner syndrome).

Basilar artery
Basilar artery is incorrect. Basilar artery occlusion usually presents with reduced consciousness and tetraplegia.

Left anterior cerebral artery
Left anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Left anterior cerebral artery would not cause crossed sensory signs as described in this case and would likely cause a hemispheric stroke syndrome.

Left middle cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery is incorrect. Left middle cerebral artery would not cause crossed sensory signs as described in this case and would likely cause a hemispheric stroke syndrome.

Left posterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Left posterior cerebral artery would not cause crossed sensory signs as described in this case and would likely cause a hemispheric stroke syndrome. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke A 47-year-old, previously well, male dentist presents with a four-month history of numbness and paraesthesia in both legs distally. He also complains of mild unsteadiness on walking. He has no urinary symptoms. Examination reveals: mild weakness of the lower limbs; brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks; and upgoing plantars. Pinprick sensation is reduced to mid-shin bilaterally, and vibration sense is impaired to the iliac crests. MRI of the brain and spine, cerebrospinal fluid examination, HTLV-1, HIV and syphilis serology are all normal.

stem: A 30-year-old man with known epilepsy presents in the Emergency Department complaining of severe loin pain. Ultrasound scan of the renal tract shows bilateral renal stones. He also admits to having lost 6.4 kg (1 stone) over the last 3 months despite a good appetite. He was started on a new antiepileptic drug 6 months ago. Which antiepileptic drug is most likely to have caused these side-effects?
explanation:
Topiramate
The side effects of topiramate include weight loss, renal stones and cognitive and behaviour changes.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Side effects of carbamazepine include skin rash, ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect. Lamotrigine is commonly associated with a skin rash and, rarely, with the Stevens– Johnson syndrome.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is incorrect. Phenytoin is associated with ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, osteomalacia, gum hypertrophy and hirsutism. Epilepsy and Seizures A 58-year-old man with a history of chronic back pain presents for review. He is aware of a dragging feeling affecting his left foot when he tries to walk. This has developed since a minor injury to his left knee. On examination he has weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot. The right is unaffected and plantar flexion and inversion are normal on the left. MRI of the spinal cord shows degenerative disc changes at multiple levels but no evidence of cord or nerve root impingement. Nerve conduction studies and EMG are awaited. What sensory loss would you expect to find in association with this motor defect?

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. Side effects of sodium valproate include weight gain, teratogenicity and tremor.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has developed gradually increasing breathlessness on minimal exertion and double vision over 2 months. Her vital capacity is 3 l when sitting and 1.4 l when lying. Physical examination reveals a mild bilateral ptosis and she develops double vision intermittently when testing eye movements. There are no other abnormal neurological findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis
The presentation with ptosis, diplopia and respiratory muscle weakness is typical of myasthenia gravis (MG). This is a disorder of neuromuscular transmission which becomes disrupted by the binding of pathological autoantibodies (usually acetylcholine receptor antibodies) at the neuromuscular junction. Typically, the symptoms and signs exhibit fatigue. For example, ptosis may not be present on initial testing, but may become evident after a period of sustained upgaze.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is incorrect. GBS can cause ptosis and respiratory muscle weakness but not usually an eye movement disorder (apart from in the Miller Fisher variant). Furthermore, by definition, the deficits in GBS should not develop over more than 4 weeks.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. The age of the patient (too young), rapidity of onset (relatively speaking) and involvement of extra-ocular muscles all make this very unlikely. In addition there is no evidence of the mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs required to make this diagnosis.

Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy is incorrect. This is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder which can feature ptosis and occasionally respiratory muscle weakness. However, it should not involve extra-ocular muscles and would be unusual to present in this (sub)acute way. Most patients have evidence of distal limb weakness and myotonia (eg elicited by percussion of the thenar eminence) on examination. Myasthenia Gravis

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis should not present with ptosis or an eye movement disorder. More typically, the patient would have painless proximal (upper and lower limb) muscle weakness and constitutional upset (fatigue, fever, weight loss etc).

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with falls. On further questioning he complains of difficulty walking up stairs, worsening over the past year or so. His falls, he feels, have been precipitated by weak legs, rather than blackouts. He has never had an episode of loss of consciousness. He is hypertensive, and has suffered chronic back pain for many years. He has smoked for many years and has a chronic ‘smoker’s cough’. On examination he has weakness of hip flexion, and particularly of knee extension. He is unable to keep his fingers flexed against force, the right being weaker than the left. There are no sensory abnormalities and reflexes are preserved. Serum CK is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inclusion body myositis
The pattern of muscle weakness (quadriceps and long-finger flexors), the asymmetry of signs and presentation with falls, is characteristic of inclusion body myositis (IBM), an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. Importantly, serum CK can be normal in IBM. IBM is the most common acquired myopathy in those aged over 50 years and is more common in men.

Cervical cord compression
Cervical cord compression is incorrect. The signs are not consistent with upper cord compression, which would be sensory signs (ie a sensory level), reflex changes and sphincter symptoms.

Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is incorrect. The limb-girdle syndromes usually present with slowly progressive proximal arm and/or leg weakness. The distal involvement in this case, as well as the normal CK, and the fact that most limb-girdle syndromes are very rare, suggest that inclusion body myositis is more likely.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease is an important differential diagnosis in this clinical scenario, but there are no upper motor neurone or bulbar features to support this diagnosis, making it less likely in this case.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect as polymyositis is likely to cause a predominantly proximal weakness, sometimes associated with muscle pain.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sensory changes and lower leg weakness. She says that the symptoms have worsened rapidly over the past few weeks and she is now unable to stand. There is no past medical history of note and she takes no regular medication. Her BP is 144/82 mmHg, pulse is 78/min and regular. There is spastic paresis of the right lower limb, with reduced vibration and position sense on the right. There is loss of pain and temperature sensation affecting the left side below the level of T10. Routine bloods including white count and inflammatory markers are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Spinal meningioma
The clinical picture described here is consistent with Brown Séquard syndrome. This is due to damage to one half of the spinal cord resulting in paralysis and loss of proprioception ipsilaterally to the injury, and loss of pain and temperature sensation contralaterally. A number of causes exist, but the absence of other co-morbidities, and the progressive symptoms, fit best with a diagnosis of spinal meningioma.

Thoracic spine discitis
Discitis normally presents with rapidly worsening back pain coupled with systemic signs of infection and raised inflammatory markers, none of which are seen here.

Spinal stenosis
Lumbar spinal stenosis is most common, and leads to bilateral motor and sensory symptoms.

Spinal tuberculosis
Spinal tuberculosis can also present with Brown Séquard, although the absence of symptoms and signs of infection does not support a diagnosis of tuberculosis.

Spondylosis
Spondylosis is more common in the cervical region and presents with back pain.

stem: A 35-year-old man complains of paroxysmal stereotyped episodes consisting of a rising epigastric sensory feeling, and fear. The episodes last up to a minute and are followed by confusion lasting up to an hour. During the episodes his wife has seen him performing lip-smacking, chewing and swallowing movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Temporal lobe epilepsy
Clinical manifestations of temporal lobe epilepsy consist of ascending epigastric aura, olfactory and gustatory hallucinations, ictal fear, oroalimentary automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing and swallowing) and limb automatism (fiddling, picking, tapping). The commonest cause of temporal lobe epilepsy is hippocampal sclerosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain is diagnostic. Surgical treatment has a complete success rate in up to 70% of cases.

Frontal lobe epilepsy
Frontal lobe epilepsy is incorrect. These seizures usually occur between 0200 h and noon, have a stereotyped semiology, and are of a brief duration with rapid secondary generalisation. There are prominent motor manifestations and complex automatism.

Idiopathic generalised epilepsy
Idiopathic generalised epilepsy is incorrect. These seizures manifest as typical absences, myoclonic jerks and generalised tonic–clonic seizures. These can occur in varying combinations and severity.

Occipital lobe epilepsy
Occipital lobe epilepsy is incorrect. These seizures mainly present with visual or oculomotor symptoms. Visual symptoms include elementary or complex visual hallucinations, blindness and visual illusions. The oculomotor symptoms include tonic deviation of the eye, nystagmus and repetitive eyelid closure or eyelid fluttering. 697 Epilepsy and Seizures

Parietal lobe epilepsy
Parietal lobe epilepsy is incorrect. These seizures present as subjective somatosensory symptoms, disturbances of body image (somatic illusions), vertigo, visual illusions or complex formed visual hallucinations.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents with right-sided orbital headache. He has five attacks of stabbing sharp pains behind the right orbit per day, each lasting 10–20 min. During attacks he also experiences rhinorrhea and ptosis. He has been taking codeine and paracetamol for the last three months, with minimal improvement. On examination, his BP is 122/72 mmHg, with heart rate 70 bpm and regular. Neurological examination is entirely normal. Haematology and biochemistry are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paroxysmal hemicrania
Paroxysmal hemicrania is a type of trigeminal autonomic cephalgia, a group of primary headache disorders characterised by trigeminal distribution of pain with cranial autonomic features. Indomethacin is the drug of choice for the treatment although salicylates, NSAIDs and prednisolone may help.

Tension headache
Tension headache is incorrect. The pathophysiology of tension headaches is poorly understood, but may relate to heightened nociceptor sensitivity. Headaches are commonly described as a tight band across the forehead.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. Migraines are poorly understood in terms of pathophysiology, but are suggested to be a primary neuronal dysfunction. Clinically there are episodic attacks of severe headaches with nausea and commonly light and sound sensitivity. The lack of an aura makes this unlikely to be migraine; tension headache tends to be frontal in nature and significant stress/anxiety isn’t a feature of the scenario.

Analgesia-induced headache
Analgesia-induced headache is incorrect. It would be unusual for analgesia-induced (also known as rebound) headache to be episodic and confined to one specific area of the face only.

Primary stabbing headache.

stem: A 64-year-old librarian is referred to you, complaining of a burning sensation on the anterolateral aspect of her right thigh. She is diabetic and has not attended the Diabetic Follow-up Clinic for a year. Some 7 months ago she had a mild stroke affecting her right side and was found to be in atrial fibrillation, for which she was prescribed warfarin. In addition, her GP recently prescribed her an antibiotic for a chest infection. Examination reveals normal muscle power. Tone is slightly increased on the right, with the right-sided reflexes a little brisker than those on the left. Pinprick was reduced over the anterolateral aspect of her right thigh. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Iliopsoas haematoma from warfarin causing a femoral neuropathy
Thalamic pain secondary to previous stroke
explanation:
Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
This is meralgia paraesthetica, which is caused by entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh, and which then results in pain and sensory abnormalities in the anterolateral thigh. The reflexes and tone are increased slightly on the right as a consequence of the stroke she suffered 7 months previously. It is important to note that diabetes increases the susceptibility of any peripheral nerve to damage/compression.

Antibiotic-induced neuropathy
Antibiotic-induced neuropathy is incorrect. Antibiotic-induced neuropathy is typically a distal, symmetrical sensory neuropathy, not a focal mononeuropathy as described here.

Diabetic femoral amyotrophy
Diabetic femoral amyotrophy is incorrect. Diabetic amyotrophy causes pain, wasting and weakness, which are not features in this woman.

Iliopsoas haematoma from warfarin causing a femoral neuropathy
Iliopsoas haematoma from warfarin causing a femoral neuropathy is incorrect. Involvement of the femoral nerve from any cause will result in weakness of the quadriceps muscle (ie weak hip flexion and knee extension), reduced knee reflex and sensory disturbances over the anterior and medial aspects of the thigh and medial aspect of the lower leg.

Thalamic pain secondary to previous stroke
Thalamic pain secondary to previous stroke is incorrect. Thalamic pain from a previous cerebral infarction is not normally localised so well.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with weakness on the left side of their face. You suspect that he may have Bell’s palsy. Which of the following features would be most consistent with a diagnosis of Bell’s palsy?
explanation:
Hyperacusis
Bell’s palsy is the most common cause of unilateral facial paralysis and is due to a problem with the 7 th cranial nerve. It may be associated with hyperacusis and loss of lacrimation when the lesion occurs before the geniculate ganglion. High-dose prednisolone (25 mg) is the mainstay of therapy and should be given to all patients over the age of 16 years who present within the first 72 h.

Enhanced taste
Enhanced taste is incorrect. Bell’s palsy is associated with loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue in severe cases.

Hyperlacrimation
Hyperlacrimation is incorrect. Hypolacrimation (loss of) is seen in Bell’s palsy.

Loss of sensation
Loss of sensation is incorrect. Sensation is spared in Bell’s palsy. Bell’s PalsyA patient with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy – Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) – who was admitted with only mild sensory symptoms, is deteriorating in hospital. He has become progressively weaker over the last 12 hours, and is finding it harder to breathe. Which of the following interventions would NOT be considered?

Preserved ability to wrinkle forehead
Preserved ability to wrinkle forehead is incorrect. Preserved ability to wrinkle the forehead is seen in patients with an upper motor neurone lesion, whereas both upper and lower facial muscles are weak when the lesion is a lower motor neurone lesion as in Bell’s.

stem: A 68-year-old woman complains of a 6-month history of dysphagia and nasal regurgitation, which is worse during the evening. She also reports intermittent drooping of her left eyelid and diplopia when she gets tired. She has lost 3 kg over the last 3 months. Neurological examination reveals a partial left ptosis, diplopia but no ophthalmoplegia. She has a weak cough. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies
The findings of nasal regurgitations and weak cough point towards a diagnosis of bulbar dysphagia. Partial ptosis and diplopia, which is worse when a patient gets tired, is a common presentation of myasthenia gravis.This is an autoimmune disease with positive antibodies against the acetylcholine receptors; the presence of such antibodies is diagnostic of myasthenia gravis. They are present in 85–90% of generalised myasthenia and in 50% of ocular myasthenia.

Barium swallow
Barium swallow is incorrect. Barium swallow may be performed to diagnose structural or functional abnormalities of the pharynx and oesophagus. This procedure may help to identify the underlying cause of dysphagia, however, this will not throw any light on the ocular symptoms.

CT brain
CT brain is incorrect. The symptoms of dysphagia and diplopia are caused by lesions in the posterior fossa of the brain and CT brain is not an ideal imaging modality for visualising the posterior fossa structures.The history is of fluctuating symptoms and is against a structural abnormality in the brain.

Gastroscopy
Gastroscopy is incorrect. Gastroscopy will only identify gastrointestinal (structural) causes of dysphagia. The history is of fluctuating symptoms and is against a structural cause of dysphagia. Myasthenia Gravis

Tumour markers
A tumour marker is incorrect. The history of fluctuating dysphagia and diplopia is against a malignant condition, as these conditions tend to be progressive. The weight loss here is due to bulbar dysphagia.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of slurred speech as well as difficulty in chewing and swallowing, to the point where he is no longer eating solid food. On examination he has weakness of jaw closure and difficulty in protruding his tongue. There is some wasting and fasciculation involving both sides of the tongue. He has lost a few kilos in weight over this time. Apart from a generally thin appearance, the rest of the neurological and general examination appears to be normal. In particular, the tendon reflexes are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lower cranial nerve palsies secondary to skull base metastases
explanation:
Motor neurone disease
