This patient is most likely to have the progressive bulbar palsy form of motor neurone disease (MND). The age of onset, progressive nature and wasting and fasciculation of the tongue are in keeping with this. Weight loss is almost ubiquitous in those with MND.

Lower cranial nerve palsies secondary to skull base metastases
Lower cranial nerve palsies secondary to skull base metastases is incorrect. This diagnosis should be considered but it is rarer than MND and would be unusual to present with painless symmetrical signs.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Although jaw closure weakness can occur in myasthenia, it will not cause wasting and fasciculation of the tongue.

Syringobulbia
Syringobulbia is incorrect. Syringobulbia can cause lower cranial nerve palsies as well as disruption of the trigeminal nucleus which extends throughout the brainstem. Horner’s syndrome and upper motor neuron signs in the limbs can also be seen. The involvement of essentially only a single cranial nerve (NXII) in this case and the lack of sensory findings make this answer incorrect. Motor Neurone Disease A right-handed 70-year-old male patient presents with sudden weakness in the right arm and right leg with right hemisensory loss and aphasia. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg and he smokes 20 cigarettes per day.

X-linked spinobulbar atrophy
X-linked spinobulbar atrophy is incorrect. X-linked spinobulbar atrophy (Kennedy’s disease) can mimic this scenario but is rare and usually presents at around age 30. Bulbar dysfunction and associated perioral fasciculations are common. Gynaecomastia, infertility and diabetes are other features which often act as clues to the diagnosis.

stem: A 28-year-old comes to the Neurology Clinic for review. She has been seizure-free for more than one year on a combination of Phenytoin and Lamotrigine and would like to start a family having recently got married. She wants to know what to do with respect to her anti-epileptic medication. What would you advise?
explanation:
Slowly withdraw phenytoin
It is important to continue anti-epileptic medications where possible during pregnancy, as seizures can result in fetal death. However, dual anti-epileptic treatment is known to be associated with significantly greater risk of teratogenicity versus monotherapy; therefore one of the two medications should be discontinued. Phenytoin is known to interfere with folate metabolism (essential to normal fetal development) and should be discontinued, although this should occur gradually to reduce the risk of rebound seizures. Lamotrigine has been shown to be the safest anti-epileptic to use in pregnancy.

Change lamotrigine for levetiracetam
Change lamotrigine for levetiracetam is incorrect. Although there are no randomised controlled trials in antiepileptics in pregnancy, both lamotrigine and levetiracetam are felt to be some of the safestChat anti-epileptics with in pregnancy and equally safe. It therefore would be inappropriate to risk further seizures during a switch without any additional benefit.

Keep medication unchanged
Keep medication unchanged is incorrect. Treating with more than one anti-epileptic in pregnancy significantly increases the risk of teratogenicity, therefore one of the patient’s anti-epileptic medications should be withdrawn.

Slowly withdraw lamotrigine
Slowly withdraw lamotrigine is incorrect. Although it is appropriate to withdraw one of the patient’s medications to reduce the risk of teratogenicity, phenytoin would be the more appropriate choice. Lamotrigine is one of the safest anti-epileptics in pregnancy, whereas phenytoin is associated with a much greater risk of teratogenicity due to its interference with folate metabolism. Useful external weblinks: Tomson, T. et al. 2011. Dose-dependent risk of malformations with anti-epileptic drugs: an analysis of data from the EURAP epilepsy and pregnancy registry. The Lancet Neurology, 10(7), 609?617. Available at: Dose-dependent risk of malformations ( Epilepsy and Pregnancy

Slowly withdraw both medications
Slowly withdraw both medications is incorrect. Although anti-epileptic medications do carry a risk of teratogenicity, the risk of fetal harm or death in seizure is greater than the risk of teratogenicity. Consequently specialists recommend that patients should continue anti-epileptic medications in pregnancy, though ideally this should be monotherapy to minimise the risk of harm to the fetus.

stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of multiple sclerosis presents with horizontal diplopia. Clinically, the diplopia is most apparent while looking to the left. The outer image disappears when the right eye is occluded. On examination he has weakness of adduction of the right eye and nystagmus on attempted lateral gaze to either side, worse on looking to the left. What is the most likely explanation of these clinical signs?
explanation:
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is caused by a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which connects the sixth nerve nuclei (supplying the lateral rectus muscle, which controls abduction) to the contralateral third nerve nucleus (supplying medial rectus, which controls adduction). In unilateral INO this results in loss of adduction of the ipsilateral medial rectus on attempted conjugate gaze. There is abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye. This case therefore presents a right-sided INO (the laterality of an INO corresponds to the side with failure of adduction). Commonest causes of INO include multiple sclerosis and cerebrovascular disease. Bilateral INO is very strongly associated with multiple sclerosis.

Fourth nerve (NIV) palsy
Fourth nerve (NIV) palsy is incorrect. NIV palsies are often subtle and present with diplopia and an associated compensatory head tilt.

Parinaud’s syndrome
Parinaud’s syndrome is incorrect. Parinaud’s syndrome is caused by a lesion in the midbrain and is associated with a vertical (not horizontal) gaze paresis.

Sixth nerve (NVI) palsy
Sixth nerve (NVI) palsy is incorrect. In a NVI palsy, there would be failure of abduction of the affected eye. In the primary position of gaze, the affected eye is also usually slightly adducted due to weakness of lateral rectus. Eye Movements and StrabismusWhich one of the following drugs commonly exacerbates weakness in myasthenia gravis?

Third nerve (NIII) palsy
Third nerve (NIII) palsy is incorrect. In a NIII palsy, the affected eye is mydriatic (apart from in the ‘pupil sparing’ or ‘medical’ NIII palsy), hypotropic (downwards deviation primarily due to weakness of superior rectus) and exotropic (outwards deviation due to weakness of medial rectus).

stem: Her neurological symptoms resolve overnight and CT head is unremarkable. How would you elucidate the underlying aetiology of her neurological presentation?
explanation:
Echocardiogram
The underlying aetiology of this patient's neurological presentation can be elucidated using an echocardiogram. The combination of raised D-dimer levels, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia and a swollen right calf suggests the possibility of a pulmonary embolism, likely due to prolonged immobility during the flight from Australia. Neurological symptoms such as right facial palsy and arm weakness are unusual in the context of a venous embolism. This raises the possibility of a paradoxical embolism where a clot from a deep vein thrombosis passes into the arterial circulation through a patent foramen ovale. An echocardiogram can help identify a patent foramen ovale or other intracardiac shunts that could allow a venous clot to cross into the arterial system and cause a stroke.

Brain PET scan
A brain PET scan is incorrect because, although it may confirm an area of cerebral ischaemia, it will not elucidate the underlying cause of the embolism. PET scans are primarily used for metabolic and functional imaging rather than structural abnormalities. They do not provide information regarding the source of emboli or the presence of a patent foramen ovale. Therefore, a brain PET scan would not be helpful in identifying the pathway through which the embolus travelled.

Carotid duplex
A carotid duplex is incorrect because significant carotid disease leading to a stroke is very unlikely in a young patient without a history of atherosclerosis. Carotid duplex scans are used to evaluate the blood flow and detect stenosis or blockages in the carotid arteries. This patient’s presentation and history do not suggest carotid artery disease as the source of her embolism. Additionally, a carotid duplex would not link the pulmonary embolism to the neurological symptoms experienced.

MRI brain
An MRI brain is incorrect because, although it may indicate an acute stroke, it will not provide information regarding the source of any embolus. MRI scans are effective at visualising brain tissue and detecting areas of infarction or haemorrhage. However, they do not reveal the pathway or origin of embolic events. Therefore, while an MRI brain might show the effect of the embolus, it does not elucidate the underlying cause or mechanism. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Thrombophilia screen
A thrombophilia screen is incorrect because, although it may identify a predisposition to clot formation, it does not indicate whether the embolus came from a lower limb deep vein thrombosis. Thrombophilia screens test for inherited or acquired conditions that increase the risk of thrombosis. However, they do not provide information about the presence of a patent foramen ovale or other cardiac abnormalities that could explain a paradoxical embolism. Therefore, a thrombophilia screen would not help in understanding how the embolus led to neurological symptoms.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with symptoms of oscillopsia. On examination he is found to have a nystagmus in which the direction of the fast and slow component alternates every 2 minutes. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Cerebellum
Oscillopsia is a periodic alternating nystagmus (jerk nystagmus) where the direction of the fast and slow components changes about every 2 minutes. The typical site of the lesion is the cerebellum (flocculus and nodulus).

Medulla
Medulla is incorrect. Lesions in the medulla (craniocervical junction) cause a down beating nystagmus.

Mid-brain
Mid-brain is incorrect. Lesions in the dorsal mid-brain cause a convergence-retraction nystagmus.

Optic chiasma
Optic chiasma is incorrect. Lesions in the optic chiasma cause a see-saw nystagmus.

Pons
Pons is incorrect. Lesions in the pons cause an upbeat nystagmus.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a body mass index of 30 has been taking the oral contraceptive pill. She is admitted with a 10-day history of worsening headaches, which are worse on stooping or coughing, and double vision. On examination she has bilateral sixth nerve palsies and bilateral papilloedema; the examination is otherwise normal. Initial plain computed tomography (CT) of the brain and orbits is normal. Later the same day, she develops sudden-onset right hemiparesis and speech disturbance. Repeat CT performed as an emergency shows a cortical low-density area with a haemorrhagic component in the left posterior temporal lobe. Which of the following investigations would be the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Cranial magnetic resonance venography
The initial symptoms and signs indicate a raised intracranial pressure, followed by sudden deterioration due to a haemorrhagic ischaemic lesion in the left hemisphere. The differential diagnosis after the initial normal CT scan is between idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), which is more common in obese female patients, and CVST, for which she has a risk factor (on the oral contraceptive pill). Her deterioration is due to a venous infarct (typically haemorrhagic, often cortical and not corresponding to arterial territory). CVST must be urgently looked for with either MRI venography or CT venography as she is at risk of continuing deterioration. If confirmed, treatment is hydration with intravenous fluids and anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin.

4-Vessel cerebral angiography
4-Vessel cerebral angiography is incorrect. 4-vessel arterial angiography is a test to investigate arterial disease such as aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation (AVM) or vasculitis. It is not designed to detect cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).

CT angiography
CT angiography is incorrect. CT angiography is a test to investigate arterial disease such as aneurysm, AVM or vasculitis. It is not designed to detect CVST.

Diffusion-weighted MRI
Diffusion weighted MRI is incorrect. Diffusion-weighted MRI is highly sensitive to ischaemic stroke but does not specifically help to detect CVST.

Gradient echo MRI
Gradient echo MRI is incorrect. Gradient echo MRI will show haemorrhage and blood products with high sensitivity but does not detect CVST.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of severe pain in his lower back after lifting a heavy box at work. The pain radiates to his right buttock and thigh. He has had no urinary symptoms. On examination he can straight-leg raise to 90 degrees on the left side, but only to 30 degrees on the right. Sciatic stretch test is positive. He has difficulty plantar flexing his right ankle and has abnormal sensation on the plantar aspect of the foot. His right ankle reflex is absent, but all other reflexes are normal. There is no other sensory disturbance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
L5/S1 disc prolapse
The L5 and S1 nerve roots are commonly subject to compression through lateral prolapse of the L4/L5 or L5/S1 discs. Patients present with low back pain and ‘sciatica’ and the problem occurs commonly after lifting a heavy weight. Signs include limited straight-leg raising, loss of ankle reflex on the affected side, weakness of plantar flexion and sensory loss in the affected dermatome. In this patient’s case, S1 involvement appears predominant given the pattern of sensory loss on the sole of the foot and the weakness of plantar flexion (S1) rather than dorsiflexion (L5). The likely level of compression is therefore L5/S1 disc, which compresses the S1 neve root.

Cauda equina syndrome
Cauda equine syndrome is incorrect. The cardinal features of cauda equina syndrome are asymmetrical leg weakness with sphincter involvement.

Common peroneal nerve palsy
Common peroneal nerve palsy is incorrect. A common peroneal nerve palsy would present with a footdrop. Although this can occasionally be confused with an L5 nerve root lesion, this is not the case here given the weakness of ankle plantar flexion rather than dorsiflexion.

L3/L4 disc prolapse
L3/L4 disc prolapse is incorrect. As described, the likely level of compression is the L5/S1 disc which compresses the S1 nerve root. This makes L3/L4 disc prolapse unlikely.

L4/L5 disc prolapse
L4/L5 disc prolapse is incorrect. As described, the likely level of compression is the L5/S1 disc which compresses the S1 nerve root. This makes L4/L5 disc prolapse unlikely.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a several-month history of increasing limb weakness, muscle cramps and some slurring of speech. He has no visual or urinary symptoms. He has a sister who is well, and so are both parents. His past medical history includes diabetes mellitus, and he is being investigated for infertility. On examination, he is noticed to have gynaecomastia, atrophy of the tongue, muscle fasciculations, including perioral fasciculations, mild predominantly proximal weakness of the limbs and decreased deep-tendon reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Spinal bulbar muscular atrophy
Spinal bulbar muscular atrophy, also known as Kennedy syndrome. The patient presents with proximal weakness and cramps, typical symptoms of the disease. Wasting, fasciculations, weakness and hyporeflexia are seen on examination. The finding of perioral fasciculations is highly suggestive. Androgen insensitivity is part of the syndrome which explains the gynaecomastia and infertility. It is an X-linked recessive condition caused by a trinucleotide repeat (CAG).

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is incorrect. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis presents with progressive weakness, usually starting distally in one limb or in the bulbar region. Patients have a combination of upper motor neurone signs (spasticity, hypereflexia) and lower motor neurone signs (wasting, fasciculations). There is no association with gynaecomastia or infertility and perioral fasciculations are rare.

Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
Limb girdle muscle dystrophy is incorrect. Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy could explain the proximal weakness but not the fasciculations or the gynaecomastia. It is therefore a less likely diagnosis.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis presents with episodes of neurological dysfunction that relapse and remit, although a primary progressive form of the condition also exists. Lower motor neurone findings such as wasting and fasciculations are not seen as it is a CNS disorder. There is no association with either gynaecomastia or infertility.

Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy is incorrect. Myotonic dystrophy may present in adulthood with cramps and distal weakness. Myotonia can be elicited on examination. Although mild distal wasting can occur, fasciculations are not seen. It is associated with cardiac conduction problems, cataracts, insulin resistance and mild learning difficulties. The mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant so a family history in keeping with this would be expected.

stem: A 60-year-old hypertensive man who is a non-smoker presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden onset of headache, vomiting and vertigo. On neurological examination he has marked ataxia on the left-hand side of his body. Two hours later his pupils have become small and symmetrical, his breathing has become irregular and he cannot move one side of his body. What is the next step in his management?
options: Urgent CT scan of the head
explanation:
Urgent CT scan of the head
The most probable diagnosis is an expanding mass such as a haemorrhage in the posterior fossa, causing brainstem compression, so the best next step is an urgent CT scan of the head.

Electroencephalogram
Electroencephalogram (EEG) is incorrect. Apart from the fact that EEG would be practically impossible to arrange in this setting, it is very unlikely to help you make a diagnosis.

Intravenous naloxone
Intravenous naloxone is incorrect. Although this might be considered, the small pupils in this case are more likely to be due to disruption of descending sympathetic tracts in the brainstem rather than the effects of opiates. The history and other neurological signs present make this answer less likely.

Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture (LP) is incorrect. LP would be contraindicated in this setting due to the presence of a probable posterior fossa mass.

Trial of mannitol
Trial of mannitol is incorrect. The use of mannitol might form part of the management of a patient with raised intracranial pressure but would not be recommended empirically. The priority in this case should be cerebral imaging in order to define the cause of the acute deterioration.

stem: A 45-year-old keen walker in previously good health presents with headache, photophobia, bilateral facial weakness and fever some 2 months after a holiday in Germany. The headache was of acute onset. He remembers that he developed a skin rash over his right arm and generalised arthralgia 2 weeks before the onset of these symptoms. Computed tomography (CT) brain is normal. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals 150 cells/mm 3, over 90% lymphocytes, with a protein level of 1.0 g/l and a glucose level just less than two-thirds that of serum glucose. What is the most likely cause of this meningitis?
explanation:
Borrelia burgdorferi
Lyme disease is a spirochaetal, tick-borne illness caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. The disease typically evolves over time with fever, headache, erythema migrans, arthralgia, followed by cranial neuropathies (a common cause of bilateral facial weakness) and lymphocytic meningitis. The mainstay of therapy is treatment with antibiotics (tetracycline or ceftriaxone).

Carcinomatous meningitis
Carcinomatous meningitis is incorrect. The fact that the patient was previously healthy excludes carcinomatous meningitis. This occurs due to seeding or secondary to a malignancy. Skin rash is not a common presentation. CT may show meningeal infiltrations. These infiltration are well noted in patients with cerebral Chatlymphoma. with Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is incorrect. It usually presents with chronic headache and constitutional symptoms. CSF would usually show a much higher protein level and a lower glucose level (about one-third that of serum glucose). A skin rash does not occur.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis presents with fever, weight loss and fatigue, and is usually not acute in onset. Lymphadenopathy, acute granulomatous uveitis, erythema nodosum and hypercalcaemia are common symptoms. The rash in Lyme disease is erythema migrans and the rash of sarcoidosis is erythema nodosum. There are multiple cranial nerve palsies, with the commonest being the seventh nerve, and the eight nerve being the second commonest. Peripheral neuropathies are common. Chest X-ray shows hilar adenopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows changes. CSF shows a lymphocytic predominance with elevated proteins. 699

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. This bacterial meningitis with a polymorphonuclear predominance. Bilateral facial weakness and rash are against the diagnosis.

stem: A 69-year-old woman presents with a sudden onset of weakness in her left arm and leg. She is known to be hypertensive. There has been no headache, loss of consciousness, visual, speech or sensory symptoms. On examination, her blood pressure is 180/90 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal. There is no carotid bruit. Higher mental function tests are normal. There is no apraxia or neglect. Speech, swallowing and sensation are all normal. There is no visual field defect. There is a mild facial weakness sparing the forehead. The left arm and leg are flaccid and weak. Mild changes in temperature and touch sensations are also noticed.Reflexes and tone are normal. There is a left extensor plantar response. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
options: Right internal carotid artery atheroembolic stroke
explanation:
Lacunar stroke
This patient’s symptoms are suggestive of a cerebrovascular event given the acute onset of weakness. A sudden onset of focal symptoms and signs strongly suggests stroke. The presence of left-sided weakness involving the face, arm and leg, in the absence of language disturbance, hemineglect or visual field defect favours a small deep (lacunar) infarct affecting the corticospinal tract at the level of either the internal capsule or the upper pons. Mild sensory changes in temperature and touch sensations also favor a small infarct. The sparing of the forehead, indicating upper motor neurone facial weakness, favours the former diagnosis. The term ‘lacune’ refers to a small deep infarct resulting from occlusion of a penetrating branch. Infarcts occur predominantly in the basal ganglia, internal capsule, thalamus and pons. Hypertension and diabetes are the main risk factors. Common lacunar strokes include a pure motor hemiparesis, pure hemisensory loss, ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria clumsy-hand syndrome.

Cardioembolic stroke
Cardioembolic stroke is incorrect. The emboli arise from a cardiac source, the commonest of these being intracranial and mural thrombi created by atrial fibrillation, dilated cardiomyopathy, with reduced ejection fraction and wall motion abnormalities. Valvular heart disease (rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral regurgitation or stenosis, prosthetic heart valves, endocarditis) is a common cause for cardioembolic stroke. Cardiac emboli produce both large and small branch occlusion of the major cerebral arteries.

Right internal carotid artery atheroembolic stroke
Right internal carotid artery atheroembolic stroke is incorrect. Internal carotid artery disease can produce typical syndromes of middle cerebral artery and anterior cerebral artery infarction. Embolisation to the retinal arteries causes ipsilateral monocular blindness which can be transient (amaurosis fugax) or permanent. Internal carotid artery occlusions can be asymptomatic or can produce holohemispheric infarction.

Right internal carotid artery dissection
Right internal carotid artery dissection is incorrect. This can occur following trauma to the neck or spontaneously. The symptoms can be typical of the syndromes of middle cerebral artery and anterior cerebral artery infarction. Sometimes they can be asymptomatic or produce holohemispheric stroke. 712 Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke A 53-year-old hospital porter is referred to you with aching and fatigue in his legs. His symptoms started 2 months ago with difficulty walking up stairs. On direct questioning, he says it takes him increased effort to get dressed. He also complains of a dry mouth, but there are no speech or swallowing difficulties. On systematic questioning, he has a long history of mild breathlessness on exertion and a chronic cough that he attributes to his heavy smoking. However, over the last 2 weeks he has noticed blood streaks in his sputum. On examination he has a predominantly proximal weakness, more so on the left. Deep tendon reflexes are depressed, but with repeated muscle contraction. There are no sensory changes or extraocular muscle abnormalities.

Right vertebral artery atheroembolic stroke
Right vertebral artery atheroembolic stroke is incorrect. A right vertebral artery stroke will present with features hiccups, Tutor of posterior fossa symptoms such as diplopia, vertigo, hearing loss, circumoral numbness, dysphagia, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms including dysconjugate gaze, Horner syndrome, nystagmus, unilateral pharyngeal weakness, bilateral or crossed motor and sensory defects.

stem: A 32-year-old IV drug abuser is admitted with a one-day history of double vision, droopy eyelids, and a dry throat. Over the next 24 hours, her symptoms worsen and she begins to notice limb weakness and breathing difficulties. Examination reveals poorly reactive pupils, ptosis, restricted eye movements, decreased deeptendon reflexes, and symmetrical upper and lower limb weakness, but sensation is normal. Cerebrospinal fluid examination is normal. Electromyography shows a decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Miller–Fisher variant of the Guillain–Barré syndrome
explanation:
Botulism
Botulism is caused by a toxin produced by the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium botulinum, which blocks the release of acetylcholine from the motor nerve terminal (thus, it is a pre-synaptic disorder). Botulism can be spread by the ingestion of foods contaminated by inadequate sterilisation, or, as in this case, through wound contamination in drug abusers after subcutaneous injection of heroin (the poor venous access of chronic addicts may preclude intravenous heroin administration). Early symptoms are blurred vision, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Pupillary responses to light are impaired, tendon reflexes reduced, and typically there is progressive symmetrical limb weakness. Most patients have evidence of autonomic dysfunction such as dry mouth, constipation, or urinary retention. Electromyography in botulism typically shows a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.

Lambert–Eaton syndrome
Lambert–Eaton syndrome is incorrect. Lambert Easton Myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) could conceivably present with similar signs (reduced reflexes, autonomic signs), but the clinical context is less suggestive of this diagnosis. LEMS is most often a paraneoplastic disorder and in addition, the rapid decline here would be very atypical of LEM.

Miller–Fisher variant of the Guillain–Barré syndrome
Miller–Fisher variant of the Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. Cerebrospinal fluid examination is associated with a high protein content in Guillain–Barré syndrome, including the Miller Fisher variant (that is associated with oculoparesis and sensory ataxia). The normal sensation seen here alse makes this diagnosis most unlikely.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. In myasthenia gravis, there is decrement seen on electromyography with repetitive nerve stimulation. In addition the pupillary abnormalities would not be expected. 253 Clostridium BotulinumPoliomyelitis
Poliomyelitis is incorrect. Poliomyelitis would not present with oculoparesis and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is usually cellular.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is seen in the Neurology Clinic and tells you that her father and her older brother have Huntington’s disease. They both developed symptoms slowly, over a number of years. Her mother is in good health. What is the patient's chance of developing Huntington’s disease?
explanation:
50%
The mode of genetic transmission for Huntington’s disease is autosomal-dominant. Therefore, if one parent is affected each child has a 50% risk of inheriting the condition. There is no effect of sex on inheritance. Huntington’s disease can now be screened for in children of affected patients by measuring the length of the abnormal trinucleotide repeat. However, the screening test should only be offered with the back-up of skilled counselling to ensure the patient has considered the effect of testing on themselves and their family.

0%
0% is incorrect. There would be a 0% risk of transmission of an X-linked disorder from an affected father to his son, as he would pass his Y-chromosome on to all his sons, for example Alport syndrome.

25%
25% is incorrect. There would be a 25% risk of transmission of an autosomal-recessive condition where both parents are carriers, for example cystic fibrosis. They would also have a 50% chance of being a carrier.

75%
75% is incorrect. There would be a 75% risk of transmission of an autosomal-dominant condition where both parents are heterozygotes (Aa), each of their children has a 50% chance of being heterozygous (Aa), a 25% chance of being homozygous for the dominant allele (AA) and a 25% chance of being homozygous for the recessive allele (aa). Huntington’s Disease100%
100% is incorrect. There would be a 100% risk of transmission of an autosomal-recessive condition where both parents were affected.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with sudden right-sided weakness and dysphagia, dysarthria and diplopia. On examination she has a right hemiparesis, slurred speech and abnormal eye movements, with left VIth nerve palsy. She is also noted to have left-sided facial weakness. She has a history of hypertension managed with ramipril 10 mg daily, and diabetes mellitus managed with metformin 1 g bd. Her BP is 165/90 mmHg. A recent HbA1c was 66.12 mmol/mol (8.2%). Where is the most likely site of her lesion?
explanation:
Left pons
The clinical pattern of contralateral limb weakness with bulbar involvement and ipsilateral VIth and VIIth nerve palsies is typical of a pontine stroke. Cerebral MRI is likely to reveal a localised area of ischaemia in the left pons. This woman is at significant vascular risk and should be managed aggressively with statins, tighter control of blood pressure and anti-platelet therapy. Although the value of dual anti-platelet therapy with dipyridamole and aspirin was proved in the ESPS-2 study, in patients with a completed stroke, clopidogrel is now recommended. Tighter control of glucose has a relatively blunt effect on vascular risk; recent studies (ACCORD, VADT and ADVANCE) showed no significant association of tighter glycaemic control with a reduction of macrovascular events.

Left hemisphere
Left hemisphere is incorrect. A hemispheric or internal capsule lesion would cause a contralateral hemiparesis, but not the ipsilateral brainstem signs seen in this case.

Left internal capsule
Left internal capsule is incorrect. A hemispheric or internal capsule lesion would cause a contralateral hemiparesis, but not the ipsilateral brainstem signs seen in this case.

Right cerebellum
Right cerebellum is incorrect. A lesion here would cause ipsilateral ataxia, not the features described in this case. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke Which one of the following statements is most accurate about chronic subdural haematoma?

Right pons
Right pons is incorrect. In pontine stroke, the brainstem signs are ipsilateral to the site of the lesion.

stem: A 32-year-old woman was noted by her GP to have anisocoria (unequal pupils), with a dilated right pupil of 3mm compared to the left. The anisocoria was more pronounced in the light. There was poor constriction to light of the right eye, however accommodation was normal. Ocular movements were normal with normal lid position bilaterally. She was otherwise in good health. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adie’s tonic pupil
Absent or poor constriction to light with normal accommodation/light-near dissociation is indicative of Adie’s tonic pupil. Anisocoria is more noticeable in the light compared to the dark due to damage of the parasympathetic supply to the ciliary ganglion, causing impaired constriction and a dilated pupil. This usually occurs in otherwise healthy young women, and is commonly unilateral. Diagnosis is confirmed with low dose pilocarpine (0.125%) which shows constriction in the affected eye only due to hypersensitivity of the sphincter pupillae.

Argyll Robertson pupil
Argyll Robertson pupil is incorrect. Argyll Robertson pupil is encountered in the tertiary stage of syphilis, and is rarely seen nowadays in the U.K. There is accommodation but no or poor constriction to light, similar toTutor Adie’s tonic pupil, however pupils are typically bilaterally and irregularly smaller than usual. Anisocoria is more noticeable in the dark. There may be iris atrophy. Syphilis serology is required to help establish the diagnosis.

Horner’s syndrome
Horner’s Syndrome is incorrect. Horner’s syndrome is a result of damage to the sympathetic supply to the eye. The affected pupil is therefore constricted, with normal response to light and accommodation. Anisocoria is more pronounced in the dark due to impaired dilatation. The patient will also have mild ptosis of the affected eye +/- anhydrosis. Pharmacological tests with apraclonidine and cocaine are required to confirm the diagnosis and level of injury.

Third nerve palsy
Third nerve palsy is incorrect. Presentation of a third nerve palsy is variable, however typically the pupil is dilated and “down and out” (depressed and abducted) due to paralysis of the ocular muscles supplied by the third nerve, thus affecting ocular movements. The pupil may not always be affected in a pupil-sparing nerve palsy, however there is usually complete ptosis of the eye. The patient may complain of double vision and/or pain. Holmes–Adie SyndromePhysiological anisocoria
Physiological anisocoria is incorrect. Physiological anisocoria is the most common cause of anisocoria. It is usually less than or equal to 2mm in difference, which remains the same in all light conditions. There is normal constriction to light and accommodation with no symptoms.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the clinic with a tremor. He tells you that it is interfering with his job as an electrician, and that his father also suffered from a tremor and problems with head nodding. On examination you notice a low-amplitude tremor, slightly more marked on the left than the right. Tone and reflexes are normal, and he can easily perform the finger-pinching test without loss of amplitude or speed of pinch. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Propranolol
The positive family history and absence of parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia (finger-pinching test is normal) and rigidity (tone is normal) support a diagnosis of essential tremor. Unfortunately, symptoms of essential tremor tend to be slowly progressive. Both propranolol and primidone (not offered as an answer here) are effective therapies for the condition, and can be used as maintenance treatments. However, once patients are reassured that essential tremor is benign, some will prefer not to start pharmacotherapy at all. Others may be prescribed propranolol that they take only if they are attending a job interview, for example.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Benzodiazepines are sedative medications and are also used to manage alcohol withdrawal due to their GABAergic effects. Typically, alcohol improves symptoms in essential tremor, and patients may report this in their history. Therefore, it is logical that benzodiazepines would be effective for essential tremor; however, they are avoided due to the potential for dependency, and also because of a lack of long-term efficacy data.

L-dopa
L-dopa is incorrect. This is a therapy for Parkinson’s disease and will not be effective in essential tremor: L-dopa increases brain dopamine levels, which is helpful in parkinsonian tremor (where part of the mechanism for the tremor is lack of dopamine) but not in essential tremor where brain dopamine levels are normal.

Risperidone
Risperidone is incorrect. This is an atypical antipsychotic commonly used in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. This will not be effective in essential tremor, as it does not affect the neurochemical pathways responsible for essential tremor. Essential TremorRopinirole
Ropinirole is incorrect. This is a dopamine agonist used in Parkinson’s disease, and will not be effective in essential tremor as the neurochemical mechanism of a parkinsonian tremor is different to that of essential tremor (a parkinsonian tremor is caused by dopamine deficiency, which is improved by using dopamine agonists; the exact mechanism of essential tremor is unclear, but dopamine agonists have not been shown to be helpful in the condition).

stem: Which one of the following additional features might you expect to find on examination?
explanation:
Loss of deep tendon reflexes
This woman has Adie’s tonic pupil and the common association with this is areflexia – sometimes referred to as the Holmes-Adie syndrome. It is a benign condition thought to be due to mild autonomic neuropathy.

Pale optic disc
Pale optic disc is incorrect. A pale optic disc would suggest previous optic neuropathy and this does not produce symptoms of bright light intolerance.

Nystagmus
Nystagmus is incorrect. Nystagmus is not associated with Adie’s tonic pupil so this finding would require appropriate investigation.

Ataxia
Ataxia is incorrect. Ataxia is not associated with Adie’s tonic pupil so this finding would require appropriate investigation.

Intention tremor
Intention tremor is incorrect. Intention tremor is not associated with Adie’s tonic pupil so this finding would require appropriate investigation. Holmes–Adie.

stem: A 40-year-old man notices he has had difficulty in walking for a number of months, and slight drooping of his eyelids. On examination he has mild bilateral ptosis, mild weakness of the proximal upper limb muscles with some winging of the scapula and bilateral foot drop with distal wasting and pes cavus. The reflexes are generally difficult to elicit, and the ankle jerks are definitely absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy
Fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHMD) is an autosomal-dominant condition with variable presentation that may go unrecognised until later life. Facial weakness, winging of the scapula, proximal upper limb weakness and foot drops are typical.

Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy
Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy is incorrect. Patients with the X-linked condition Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy die at a young age (mean 25 years).

Miller–Fisher syndrome
Miller–Fisher syndrome is incorrect. The presence of distal wasting and pes cavus indicates a very chronic neuromuscular disorder with axonal loss; this does not occur in the Guillain–Barré syndrome variant of Miller– Fisher syndrome, which is an illness characterised by oculoparesis and sensory ataxia.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. The presence of distal wasting and pes cavus indicates a very chronic neuromuscular disorder with axonal loss; this does not occur in myasthenia gravis.

Paraneoplastic polymyositis
Paraneoplastic polymyositis is incorrect. Paraneoplastic polymyositis is usually an acute or subacute illness with proximal limb weakness and wouldnot cause such chronic signs.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a long history of alcohol abuse and diabetes was admitted with a subacute illness, consisting of headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. On examination, he was also observed to be ataxic, dysarthric, dysphagic and to have gaze-evoked nystagmus. MRI brain demonstrated a high-signal abnormality of the brainstem. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 15 polymorphs/mm 3, glucose concentration of 2 mmol/l (serum 6 mmol/l) and a protein concentration of 0.9 g/l. The patient has failed to after 3 days of intravenous cefuroxime treatment. What is the most likely cause of the meningitis?
explanation:
Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria meningitis should always be considered in the elderly population, diabetics, and alcohol abusers and in patients on immunosuppressive treatment. Both a polymorphonuclear pleocytosis or lymphocytic predominance may be seen, with low CSF glucose and high protein levels are seen. Brainstem involvement is common. It does not respond to cephalosporin treatment. Ampicillin is the treatment of choice.

Haemophilus influenzae
Haemophilus influenzae is incorrect. H. influenzae meningitis does not usually involve the brainstem.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is incorrect. It causes a lymphocytic meningitis, usually with evidence of pulmonary tuberculosis infection and chronic deterioration.

Nocardia asteroides
Nocardia asteroides is incorrect. It causes a lymphocytic meningitis and is usually associated with very widespread infection, not only including the CNS but also the brain, soft tissue, lungs and skin. 698 Bacterial Meningitis

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis does not usually involve the brainstem.

stem: A 42-year-old male is involved in a road traffic collision. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals that he may have hemisection of cord. Which one of following findings is most likely to occur?
options: Contralateral segmental anaesthesia at the level of the lesion
Ipsilateral hyperreflexia below the level of the lesion
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation
explanation:
Ipsilateral hyperreflexia below the level of the lesion
Spinal cord hemisection, also known as the Brown–Séquard syndrome (BSS), is associated with symptoms affecting dorsal columns, spinothalamic tract and corticospinal tract. There is ipsilateral paralysis, loss of vibration and position sense, and hyperreflexia below the level of the lesion. Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, usually beginning about two to three segments below the level of the lesion, is also seen. In the clinical situation, a mix of these signs is usually seen as hemisection is rarely complete.

Contralateral loss of position sense
Contralateral loss of position sense is incorrect. Dorsal column tract fibres also cross in the brainstem and, as such, deficits from lesions in the spinal cord are ipsilateral.

Contralateral paralysis
Contralateral paralysis is incorrect. Corticospinal tracts have already crossed in the medullary pyramids before they enter the spinal cord. Therefore, paralysis in BSS is ipsilateral.

Contralateral segmental anaesthesia at the level of the lesion
Contralateral segmental anaesthesia at the level of the lesion is incorrect. Afferent fibres destined for the spinothalamic tracts (pain and temperature sensation) ascend about two segments once they enter the spinal cord and then cross. Therefore, in BSS, the pain and temperature sensation deficits are ipsilateral at the level of the lesion and contralateral below. In the ipsilateral few segments before this crossing occurs, there is segmental anaesthesia as both spinothalamic and dorsal column tract fibres are affected.

Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation is incorrect. Afferent fibres destined for the spinothalamic tracts (pain and temperature sensation) ascend about two segments once they enter the spinal cord and then cross. Therefore, in BSS, the pain and temperature sensation deficits are ipsilateral at the level of the lesion and contralateral below. In the ipsilateral few segments before this crossing occurs, there is segmental anaesthesia as both spinothalamic and dorsal column tract fibres are affected.

stem: A 69-year-old woman has become progressively weaker over a 3-month period. Her symptoms fluctuate diurnally, being worse when she awakes. Although her greatest difficulty is climbing stairs, she also has difficulty raising her arms. The patient denies the presence of pain, numbness, diplopia, difficulty swallowing and bladder abnormalities, but has noted dryness of her mouth. She has been a heavy smoker for years. On examination there are no abnormalities of the cranial nerve, cerebellar or sensory function. Her weakness is diffuse and mild, with strength increasing with exertion. Reflexes are absent but are obtainable after exertion. Plantar responses are flexor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an antibody-mediated syndrome (anti-voltage-gated calcium antibodies) often associated with small-cell lung carcinoma or with autoimmune diseases. It starts insidiously, often several years before a tumour becomes evident. Patients present with proximal weakness, which is typically worse in the morning and resolves with exertion. There are accompanying autonomic features, especially dry mouth. It is a presynaptic neuromuscular disease with inhibition of acetylcholine release from the presynaptic junction. The patient in the described case scenario has proximal weakness, with diurnal fluctuation which is worse in the mornings and improves with exercise. She has dryness of mouth which is an autonomic syndrome which is a feature of LEMS. Further, LEMS is a paraneoplastic syndrome. The fact that she is a smoker is a risk factor for lung malignancies and often LEMS predates the malignancy.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease presents with muscle weakness and atrophy, altered tendon reflexes (hyperactive if upper motor neurones are affected and hypoactive or absent if lower motor neurones are affected). Babinski sign is positive if upper motor neurones are involved; that is there can be a mixture of upper motor and lower motor signs as in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or there may be only a predominant upper motor neurone type pattern in progressive lateral sclerosis. In patients there is pure or predominant bulbar involvement. In motor neurone disease overt cognitive and sensory changes are absent.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis usually presents as episodic or progressive multifocal symptoms and signs. Onset is usually in healthy young adults. MRI shows abnormal findings. The disease sclerosis, or course may be relapsing or remitting, clinically isolated syndrome, secondary progressive multiple primary progressive multiple sclerosis. There is no evidence of diurnal variation. The clinical scenario is not suggestive of multiple sclerosis. Multiple sclerosis is diagnosed using the McDonald criteria or the MAGNIMS criteria which is a combination of both clinical and imaging findings.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is characterised by fluctuating, fatigable weakness of commonly used muscles. This often includes ocular, bulbar and respiratory muscles. Other muscle groups can be involved in the later stages. Presence of antibodies to acetylcholine receptors is present in most patients. There is diurnal variation in myasthenia gravis where weakness is more prominent in the evenings or after exertion (opposite of LEMS).

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis usually occurs after 30 years, with a myopathy count distribution of weakness (proximal weakness). About one-third of patients have prominent muscle pain and tenderness. Serum creatinine kinase will be markedly elevated. EMG shows spontaneous activity and muscle biopsy shows evidence of endomysial infiltration of the muscle by inflammatory cells and this provides a definitive diagnosis. 711 Lambert-Eaton.

stem: A 40-year-old man has developed progressive weakness and wasting of both upper limbs over the last 5 months. He has noticed that his grip is poor, being worse on the right, and some muscles have become thinner. He has also noticed some ‘flickering’ of the muscles, particularly over the right thenar eminence and the left forearm. There are no sensory symptoms. On examination the asymmetrical weakness and wasting are confirmed, as well as intermittent fasciculation. The upper limb deep tendon reflexes are all present with reinforcement. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. He undergoes nerve conduction studies and electromyography, which show evidence of demyelination and conduction block in his upper limbs, and normal sensory conduction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multifocal motor neuropathy
The answer is Multifocal motor neuropathy (Option D). Given the absence of sensory features, the main differential clinical diagnosis here is between motor neurone disease (MND) and multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN). The latter is an inflammatory neuropathy that causes multifocal demyelination with conduction block, in contrast to MND where axonal degeneration is seen. The neurophysiological findings in this case are typical of MMN and allow us to exclude MND. Prognosis is very different, with MMN being responsive to immunomodulatory therapies such as intravenous immunoglobulins.Positive GM1 anti-ganglioside antibodies may be present in around 50% of cases.

Bilateral brachial neuritis
Bilateral brachial neuritis is incorrect. Brachial neuritis (Parsonage Turner syndrome) is an inflammatory disorder of uncertain aetiology affecting the brachial plexus. It is characteristically unilateral but can be bilateral in up to 30% of cases. The syndrome is characterised by severe and acute shoulder pain and subsequent weakness, usually around the shoulder girdle, with winged scapula commonly seen. The history, examination findings (especially lack of sensory involvement) and neurophysiology findings are not at all typical of brachial neuritis.

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is incorrect. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is a clinically variable disorder, although one would expect a combination of motor and sensory signs, likely affecting all four limbs and often in a non-length-dependent pattern.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. As outlined this can be discounted by the neurophysiological findings being more typical of MMN.

Paraneoplastic brachial plexopathy
Paraneoplastic brachial plexopathy is incorrect. The lack of sensory involvement makes paraneoplastic brachial neuritis, where one might also expect some clinical features to suggest underlying malignancy, unlikely.

stem: Which one of the following statements is most accurate about chronic subdural haematoma?
options: Injury to the middle meningeal artery is the usual cause of the haematoma
Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis should be done immediately on patient arrival
Neck stiffness is an early feature
The trauma to the head is usually minor and often forgotten by the patient
explanation:
The trauma to the head is usually minor and often forgotten by the patient
After minor head trauma, especially in an elderly patient, symptoms may develop weeks and even months later. Headache is the earliest feature and may be present almost from the time of the injury; subsequently, subtle mental changes may occur such as lethargy, loss of initiative, somnolence and even confusion. If untreated, patients may progress to signs and symptoms of tentorial herniation.

Headache is often absent
Headache is often absent is incorrect. Headache is a common feature of chronic subdural haematoma.

Injury to the middle meningeal artery is the usual cause of the haematoma
Injury to the middle meningeal artery is the usual cause of the haematoma is incorrect. Bleeding from the middle meningeal artery is associated with extradural haemorrhage. Subdural haematomas are caused by venous bleeding.

Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis should be done immediately on patient arrival
Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis should be done immediately on patient arrival is incorrect. Those with a space-occupying lesion should generally not undergo lumbar puncture for fear of causing brain herniation (‘coning’).

Neck stiffness is an early feature.

stem: Which one of the following findings best supports a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS)?
options: Multiple grey matter lesions on 1.5T MRI
explanation:
Intrathecal synthesis of IgG
The answer is Intrathecal synthesis of IgG. MS is the most common demyelinating diseases of the central nervous system. It most often affects young adults between the ages of 20 and 50, with a 2:1 female:male ratio. Cerebrospinal fluid is typically examined for the presence of increased intrathecal synthesis of IgG and also for the presence of a discrete set of proteins, called oligoclonal bands, which appear on gel electrophoresis. Note that oligoclonal bands and increased rates of IgG synthesis are found in about 90% of patients with definite MS, but may also be present in other diseases.

CSF protein of > 1.2 g/dl
CSF protein of > 1.2 g/dl is incorrect. A raised CSF protein can be seen in MS but is very non-specific. A protein level this high would be more consistent with either an inflammatory neuropathy (eg Guillain–Barré syndrome) or a meningitic condition.

Low CSF:serum glucose ratio
Low CSF:serum glucose ratio is incorrect. A low CSF glucose level when compared to the serum level is indicative of a bacterial/mycobacterial/fungal/malignant (but not viral) meningitis.

Multiple grey matter lesions on 1.5T MRI
Multiple grey matter lesions on 1.5T MRI is incorrect. MS is classically thought of as a disease of the cerebral white matter, not grey matter. Multiple Sclerosis

Normal visual evoked potentials
Normal visual evoked potentials is incorrect. Abnormality of visual evoked potentials may be used to support a diagnosis of MS.

stem: A 65-year-old man is admitted via the Emergency Department. He has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months after retiring from his job as an accountant due to difficulty in concentrating. He was originally diagnosed with depression but has not responded to SSRIs. He is now very confused and over the past 48 h has not been able to get out of bed. On examination his BP is 135/85 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. Mini-mental state examination reveals a score of 12/30. He has increased tone bilaterally, an ataxic gait and has myoclonic jerks when startled by a nurse slamming a door on the ward. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
The rapid deterioration to very significant dementia, coupled with myoclonic jerks, fits very well with an underlying diagnosis of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Criteria suggest that there is probable CJD if the following features are seen: progressive dementia and at least two out of the following four clinical features: Myoclonus Visual or cerebellar disturbance Pyramidal/extrapyramidal dysfunction Akinetic mutism and Atypical EEG during an illness of any duration and/or A positive 14-3-3 CSF assay with a clinical duration to death less than two years MRI high-signal abnormalities in caudate nucleus and/or putamen on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Furthermore, routine investigations should not suggest an alternative diagnosis. Given that this patient has progressive dementia, myoclonic jerks and cerebellar signs, he meets the criteria above. Investigations would include a lumbar puncture to check for 14-3-3, a biochemical marker in the CSF, MRI and potentially a brain biopsy (though this is usually only performed if there is diagnostic uncertainty). Unfortunately no treatment affecting disease course exists, and management is supportive.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. You would not expect Alzheimer’s disease to cause such a rapid deterioration in cognitive ability; it would be a more gradual process. Myoclonic jerks are not a feature of Alzheimer’s disease.

Endogenous depression
Endogenous depression is incorrect. Although depression is a dementia mimic, it would be highly unusual for it to cause such a severe dementia. You would also expect some response to SSRI therapy if this was depression. Depression would not cause objective neurological signs: this patient has ataxia, bilaterally increased tone and myoclonic jerks, none of which can be explained by a diagnosis of depression.

Multi-infarct dementia
Multi-infarct dementia is incorrect. You would not expect such a rapid cognitive decline in multi-infarct dementia: it is a more gradual (albeit step-wise) process. Myoclonic jerks are not a feature of multi-infarct dementia.

Pick’s disease
Pick’s disease is incorrect. This is also known as frontotemporal dementia. Personality changes and language difficulty are early features of Pick’s disease; neither of these symptoms is described here. Pick’s disease also would not explain the ataxia, bilaterally increased tone and myoclonic jerks: there are no specific neurological signs associated with frontotemporal dementia unless it is part of an overlap syndrome with motor neurone disease or Parkinson’s-plus syndromes.

stem: During a routine insurance medical examination, a GP notices that a 30-year-old female patient has absent ankle jerks and unequal pupils. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Holmes–Adie syndrome
Adie’s pupil can be attributed to a postviral degeneration in the ciliary ganglion The pupil is initially dilated, with a tonic reaction to light and sectorial vermiform movements • The pupil is hypersensitive to 0.125% pilocarpine. A normal pupil will be unaffected by this weak dilution of pilocarpine, whereas an Adie pupil will constrict due to denervation hypersensitivity The near vision is impaired by accommodative spasm, but this recovers in a few months The pupil sphincter later becomes fibrosed and the pupil miosed (‘little old Adies’) Holmes–Adie syndrome is the combination of Adie’s pupil with hyporeflexia and typically occurs in women in this age group.

Horner syndrome
Chat but withthe Horner syndrome is incorrect. Horner syndrome is another cause of anisocoria (unequal pupils), affected pupil is smaller. Horner syndrome is not typically associated with abnormal deep tendon reflexes.

IIIrd nerve palsy
IIIrd Nerve palsy is incorrect. Third nerve palsies do cause anisocoria and an abnormally large pupil, but are mainly characterised by reduced ocular motility and an associated ptosis.

Mescaline ingestion
Mescaline ingestion is incorrect. Recreational drug use (eg mescaline) can cause abnormalities in pupil size, but these are bilateral and unlikely to cause anisocoria. Holmes–Adie SyndromeArgyll Robertson pupils
Argyll Robertson pupil is incorrect. Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral small pupils which constrict to accommodation, ie there is light-near dissociation (the pupils accommodate but do not react).

stem: A 46-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presents to the clinic complaining of pain, pins and needles and loss of sensation in her feet. Her diabetes has been poorly controlled over a number of years, with her HbA1c averaging around 72.68 mmol/mol (8.8%) on a basal bolus insulin regime. You suspect she might have diabetic neuropathy. What would be the expected findings on nerve conduction study?
options: Increased nerve conduction velocity on peripheral nerve testing
Decreased nerve conduction velocity on peripheral nerve testing
More marked loss of motor nerve conduction velocity
explanation:
Decreased sensory nerve amplitude responses
The patient has diabetic polyneuropathy, which is typically a predominantly sensory, length dependent axonal neuropathy. In such neuropathies the main neurophysiological finding is reduced sensory nerve amplitude potentials.

Increased nerve conduction velocity on peripheral nerve testing
Increased nerve conduction velocity on peripheral nerve testing is incorrect. In neuropathy one will not see increases in the speed of nerve action potential transmission.

Increased sensory nerve amplitude responses
Increased sensory nerve amplitude responses is incorrect. One will see a decreased amplitude of response, not an increase.

Decreased nerve conduction velocity on peripheral nerve testing
Decreased nerve conduction velocity on peripheral nerve testing is incorrect. Decreased conduction velocities are the hallmark of demyelinating neuropathies (like CIDP) not axonal neuroapthies such as the sort seen in diabetes.

More marked loss of motor nerve conduction velocity
More marked loss of motor nerve conduction velocity is incorrect. Decreased conduction velocities are the hallmark of demyelinating neuropathies (like CIDP) not axonal neuroapthies such as the sort seen in diabetes. In addition, in diabetes the sensory nerves are typically more affected than the motor nerves.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents to the Neurology Clinic for review. She has suffered from gradually worsening weakness over the past 6–8 weeks. She reports easy fatigability on minimal exercise and tiredness affecting her eyes at the end of the day, with diplopia and drooping of her eyelids. She is otherwise well, apart from flitting small joint pains, which she puts down to arthritis. On examination, her BP is 110/70 mmHg and her pulse is 72 bpm and regular. She has 4/5 proximal power weakness affecting the upper and lower limbs andyou note fatigability in her voice on asking her to count to 50. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis
The gradual onset of proximal muscle weakness with fatigability fits well with a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. It is most commonly caused by antibodies binding to the acetylcholine receptor andis treated with steroids and cholinesterase inhibitors.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is characterised by CNS inflammation, manifesting as either discrete relapses or a slow progression of symptoms, which can include optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, subacute cerebellar symptoms and bowel or bladder symptoms.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is usually associated with a much more gradual onset of a mixed pattern of upper and lower motor neurone symptoms and signs, rather than with proximal weakness with fatigability.

Lambert-Eaton syndrome
While the proximal weakness is consistent, Lambert–Eaton syndrome is far less common than myasthenia gravis and is associated with underlying carcinoma, usually bronchial carcinoma. The lack of a smoking history or chest disease clearly counts against this. Myasthenia Gravis

Guillain-Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is associated with acute ascending motor and/or sensory symptoms, often after a GI infection. The proximal symptoms and fatigability count against this diagnosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man describes intermittent unilateral pain above and behind his left eye, which has woken him from sleep every night for the previous 7 days. The pain is described as severe and stabbing, lasting about 30 minutes and making him restless and agitated. It is associated with tearing from his left eye and nasal stuffiness. When he looked in the mirror during attacks he had noted his left eyelid drooping. He remembers he had experienced similar symptoms for about a month last year, but that they had resolved spontaneously and he had not sought medical attention. Physical examination is normal. He is a lifelong smoker. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Cluster headache
The symptoms are very suggestive of cluster headache, the most common of a group of headache disorders known as the ‘trigeminal autonomic cephalgias’. This commonly presents in middle-aged men, and occurs in clusters lasting weeks to months. Headaches classically occur at night-time, are severe and are associated with autonomic features such as ptosis, lacrimation and nasal running/stuffiness.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. Migraine headaches are characterised by throbbing pain, nausea, photo-, phono- and mechanophobia. The attacks are not usually nocturnal.

Paroxysmal hemicrania
Paroxysmal hemicrania is incorrect. Paroxysmal hemicrania is another type of trigeminal autonomic cephalgia, but is much rarer, tends to occur multiple times throughout the day and is commoner in women. It is exquisitely sensitive to indomethacin.

Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis is incorrect. Temporal arteritis does not occur in individuals < 50 years of age. Cluster Headache

Trigeminal neuralgia
Trigeminal neuralgia is incorrect. Trigeminal neuralgia is sometimes mistaken for cluster headache, but the attacks are much shorter and autonomic activation is rare. The pain has a sharp, lancinating quality. There is no night-time tendency to attacks and the pain is often triggered by touching the face.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents with Guillain–Barré syndrome. Her weakness continues to worsen after admission to hospital. Which one of the following should be used to monitor her respiratory function?
options: Forced expiratory volume 1/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) ratio
explanation:
Vital capacity
Vital capacity is the most sensitive measure of respiratory muscle weakness associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome. Respiratory failure is the major complication associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome, and some form of ventilatory support may be needed for between 10% and 20% of patients. For patients with respiratory muscle weakness, intensive nursing is necessary to prevent secondary respiratory infection.

Arterial blood gases
Arterial blood gases is incorrect. Arterial blood gases often remain normal (due to compensation) until established respiratory muscle weakness has occurred. Vital capacity is more useful, as deteriorating vital capacity can be detected prior to the onset of overt respiratory failure, allowing preventative measures to be taken.

Chest expansion size
Chest expansion size is incorrect. This is of no meaningful use in this setting.

Forced expiratory volume 1/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) ratio
Forced expiratory volume 1/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) ratio is incorrect. This ratio is used to estimate the contribution of ‘obstructive’ and ‘restrictive’ defects to respiratory failure and is unhelpful in this setting. Guillain-Barré Syndrome

Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is incorrect. PEFR often remains normal (due to compensation) until established respiratory muscle weakness has occurred. Vital capacity is more useful, as deteriorating vital capacity can be detected prior to the onset of overt respiratory failure, allowing preventative measures to be taken.

stem: Lesions to which structure are most likely to be associated with a left superior homonymous quadrantanopia?
explanation:
Right temporal lobe
A superior quadrantanopia indicates a lesion in the temporal optic radiations or inferior bank of the calcarine (visual) cortex. The lesion is contralateral to the field defect, thus the left superior homonymous quadrantanopia in this question will be due to a lesion in the right temporal lobe.

Left occipital cortex
Left occipital cortex is incorrect. Left occipital cortex lesions produce right-sided homonymous field defects.

Left parietal lobe
Left parietal lobe is incorrect. A lesion in the right parietal lobe may produce a left-sided inferior quadrantanopia.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm is incorrect. A lesion in the optic chiasm will produce bitemporal hemianopia.

Right optic tract
Right optic tract is incorrect. A lesion in the right optic tract produces a left homonymous hemianopia. Visual Field Defects A 62-year-old alcoholic man presented to the Emergency Department with confusion for the past week. He is known to be a heavy drinker. Clinically, he was able to answer questions, but was confused with respect to a number of his answers. He had a mild, left-sided hemiparesis. Blood investigation.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive dementia, generalised myoclonus and paroxysmal sensory symptoms of four months’ duration. A diagnosis of Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) needs to be excluded. Which of the following investigations would be the best diagnostic test?
explanation:
Lumbar puncture
RT-QuIC peptide assay has a 95.8% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity for sporadic CJD diagnosis.

CT brain
No conclusive evidence for the disease can be obtained from a CT.

EEG
The EEG shows non-specific abnormalities such as background slowing, or it is normal in new-variant CJD. In comparison in sporadic CJD (sCJD) there are periodic sharp wave complexes or other EEG abnormalities in 60– 70% of patients.

MRI brain
MRI brain is the most useful non-invasive test. Although it previously was the gold standard for investigation, with increased signal on T2 weighted scans in the posterior thalamus indicating possible CJD, it has now been superseded by RTC-Qulc protein assay on LP. Notes: New-variant CJD disease was first recognised in 1996. The affected individuals are usually younger. Psychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety and psychosis are prominent early in the disease and may be the presenting symptom in 85% of patients. Painful paresthesiae are common due to thalamic involvement. Other symptoms appear rapidly within months including, cognitive impairment, cerebellar ataxia, abnormal movements (chorea, myoclonus and dystonias). Symptoms progress and the patients usually die within 14 months of symptom onset. The disease affects the lymphoreticular system, thus a tonsillar biopsy may be of diagnostic value, showing the presence of protease-resistant PrP. A definitive diagnosis would need a brain biopsy with characteristic histopathologic changes and the presence of typical protease-resistant PrP protein on western immunoblot assay, although RT-QulC peptide assay now represents a promising way to confirm the diagnosis of sporadic CJD on LP alone.

stem: A 44-year-old man with an unremarkable past medical history developed dizziness, tinnitus and mild left-sided hearing loss. The symptoms presented over several months and were slowly progressive, with tinnitus being continuous over the past 2 months. The initial evaluation by his GP was unremarkable with a normal neurological examination and normal otoscopy. Audiometry revealed a mild degree of sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. What would be your next course of action?
explanation:
MRI brain scan
The symptoms are consistent with a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), and the patient should be investigated with an MRI brain scan. The most common symptoms of vestibular schwannomas are unilateral sensorineural hearing loss (96%), unsteadiness (77%), tinnitus (71%), headache (29%), mastoid pain or otalgia (28%), or less frequently facial numbness, diplopia and vertigo. In most patients the initial symptom is unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, which may have been present for 1–5 years (mean 3.7 years).

Repeat audiometry at 6 months
Repeat audiometry at 6 months is incorrect. Repeat audiometry would not allow a diagnosis to be made – it only measures the symptom.

Prescribe a hearing aid
Prescribe a hearing aid is incorrect. This only treats the symptoms and a potentially serious diagnosis may be missed by a failure to investigate appropriately.

Prescribe a vestibular sedative
Prescribe a vestibular sedative is incorrect. A vestibular sedative only treats the symptoms and the potentially serious diagnosis may be missed by failure to investigate appropriately. Acoustic Neuroma

CT brain scan with contrast
CT brain scan with contrast is incorrect. CT scanning does not have sufficient resolution to exclude this diagnosis.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension attends the general practitioner with his wife. She is concerned about a sudden deterioration in his speech. Whilst he appears to understand what his wife says to him, she is concerned that his responses have become halting and non-fluent, and he appears to be expending great effort when he talks. He can, however, repeat phrases when asked. You suspect that he has transcortical motor aphasia. He is right handed. Which one of the following areas of the brain is most likely to have been affected?
explanation:
Left inferior frontal gyrus
The combination of effortful, non-fluent spontaneous speech with relatively preserved repetition and comprehension is suggestive of transcortical motor aphasia. The lesion is usually in the dominant inferior frontal region although Broca’s area itself is spared. Stroke is the commonest cause.

Left orbito-frontal region
Left orbito-frontal region is incorrect. Lesions in the orbitofrontal regions tend to produce alterations in behaviour, particularly problems with disinhibition.

Left parietal lobe
Left parietal lobe is incorrect. Left parietal lobe lesions may cause problems in reading, writing, calculation and praxis, but shouldn’t cause a non-fluent aphasia.

Right inferior frontal gyrus
Right inferior frontal gyrus is incorrect. In a right handed person the right hemisphere is non-dominant so lesions here will not affect language. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Left posterior temporal lobe
Left posterior temporal lobe is incorrect. A posterior left temporal lesion may affect Wernicke’s area so a fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension is produced.

stem: A 58-year-old farmer from Northern Ireland presents with a progressive neurological illness over 3 weeks. He complains of double vision and has some slurring of speech and unsteadiness on his feet, as well as malaise and tiredness. He also admits to having lost 6.25 kg (1 stone) in weight over a 6-week period. On examination he has a bilateral VIth nerve palsy, facial asymmetry and marked dysarthria. The deep tendon reflexes are sluggish throughout and the plantar responses equivocal. He has lymphadenopathy of the axilla and groins, and a temperature of 38.6°C. Chest X-ray shows some evidence of right upper lobe changes. MRI of the brain shows diffuse meningeal enhancement. Lumbar puncture shows an elevated protein of 1.2 g/l, an elevated white cell count of 87/mm 3 (mostly lymphocytes) and a low CSF/blood glucose ratio (CSF glucose 1.2 mmol/l, blood glucose 6.7 mmol/l). Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to be found on further investigation?
explanation:
Tuberculous meningitis
The patient's symptoms, including progressive neurological deficits, significant weight loss, and fever, are consistent with TB meningitis. The presence of bilateral 6th nerve palsy, facial asymmetry, and marked dysarthria further supports a central nervous system involvement. The CSF findings, particularly the elevated protein, increased white cell count with lymphocytic predominance, and very low CSF/blood glucose ratio, are classical for tuberculous meningitis. Moreover, the chest X-ray showing right upper lobe changes suggests a possible primary or reactivated TB infection, reinforcing the likelihood of TB meningitis.

Brucellosis
Although brucellosis can present with fever, malaise, and weight loss, it typically does not cause the very low CSF glucose seen in this case. Neurological involvement in brucellosis is less common and, when present, usually does not present with such prominent meningeal signs or diffuse meningeal enhancement on MRI. Additionally, brucellosis is more common in regions where the disease is endemic, and Northern Ireland is not a high-risk area for brucellosis.

Lyme disease
Lyme disease can cause neurological symptoms such as cranial nerve palsies, especially facial palsy, but it usually does not lead to a very low CSF glucose. The CSF in Lyme neuroborreliosis typically shows a mild to moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein. Additionally, Lyme disease is more common in areas with high tick populations, and the patient's history does not suggest recent tick exposure or a characteristic erythema migrans rash.

Malignant meningitis
While malignant meningitis can present with cranial nerve palsies and low CSF glucose levels, the presence of fever and a high white cell count in the CSF suggests an infective process rather than a neoplastic one. Malignant meningitis would also likely show abnormal cells on CSF cytology, which has not been mentioned here. Furthermore, the patient’s systemic symptoms, including fever and weight loss, align more with an infectious etiology like TB rather than a malignancy.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis can cause neurological symptoms and meningeal enhancement, but it typically does not cause such a pronounced decrease in CSF glucose. The CSF in neurosarcoidosis usually shows an elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis, but the glucose levels are generally normal or only mildly decreased. Moreover, sarcoidosis usually presents with other systemic signs like uveitis, erythema nodosum, or pulmonary involvement, which are not described in this case.

stem: Which of the following is the most important immediate management?
options: IV Pabrinex ® (vitamin B substances with ascorbic acid)
explanation:
Chlordiazepoxide
This man has symptoms of alcohol withdrawal, with tachycardia, sweating and tremor, on a background of alcohol excess. Patients with alcohol withdrawal should be treated with benzodiazepines, such as chlordiazepoxide, to prevent progression to delirium tremens or alcohol withdrawal seizures.

Hydroxycobalamin
Vitamin B 12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, diarrhoea or constipation, peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. It is important to replace vitamin B 12 in people who are malnourished, such as those with chronic alcohol dependence, but this is not the most important immediate management.

IV 0.9% sodium chloride
Although the patient is tachycardic and slightly hypotensive, the most important issue to address is the alcohol withdrawal, which, if left untreated, could progress to more serious complications.

IV 20% glucose
Although this patient has hypoglycaemia, with a blood glucose level of 3.9 mmol/l, the patient is awake and alert. Therefore, the first-line treatment should include oral glucose before administering IV glucose, if necessary.
