IV Pabrinex ® (vitamin B substances with ascorbic acid).

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an explosive headache, vomiting and photophobia. On initial assessment, there is marked neck stiffness. Cranial nerve examination reveals a dilated right pupil, unreactive to light and accommodation. Eye movements are painful and he is unable to adduct, elevate or depress his right eye on conjugate gaze. There are no other neurological findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cerebral glioma with raised intracranial pressure
explanation:
Ruptured posterior communicating artery aneurysm
The clinical combination of sudden severe headache and meningismus suggests a subarachnoid haemorrhage. The painful non-‘pupil-sparing’ third cranial nerve palsy in this setting implicates an aneurysm arising from the posterior communicating artery or an internal carotid artery aneurysm near the origin of the posterior communicating artery. Therefore, ruptured posterior communicating artery aneurysm is correct.

Cerebral glioma with raised intracranial pressure
Cerebral glioma with raised intracranial pressure is incorrect. It would be unusual for a space-occupying lesion to present in such an abrupt manner, apart from with seizure.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes can be associated with ‘medical’ ‘pupil-sparing’ third nerve palsies. However, the thunderclap headache and involvement of the pupil in this case make this option very unlikely.

Intracerebral haemorrhage
Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) is incorrect. ICH can present with headache and focal neurology. However, the clinical signs in this case indicate that there is a brainstem lesion and ICH seldom occurs in this location.

Ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
Ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm is incorrect. The anterior communicating artery connects the left and right anterior cerebral arteries and is located close to the optic chiasm. Aneurysms can manifest with visual field defects but not oculomotor dysfunction.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her neurological symptoms?
explanation:
Transient ischaemic attack
The sudden onset of negative symptoms is typical of transient ischaemic attack. This lady has a history of recurrent miscarriage and previous deep vein thrombosis. She also has a raised activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) on investigation. This raises the possibility of presence of the ‘lupus anti-coagulant’ or an underlying diagnosis of the anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome. This patient would require detailed investigation for this possibility as well as other prothrombotic states.

Functional disorder
Functional disorder is incorrect. Functional hemiplegia is a potential stroke mimic and might be considered in this case. However, a patient with functional weakness will often display physical signs that are incongruent with any given vascular territory (for example, dense right-sided hemiplegia without aphasia). Furthermore, positive findings, such as Hoovers sign, should be elicited before a diagnosis of functional weakness is made.

Haemorrhagic stroke
Haemorrhagic stroke is incorrect. In this case, by definition, because her symptoms have resolved within the 24h period, this is a transient ischaemic attack as opposed to stroke. Furthermore, it would be unusual for a haemorrhagic stroke to present with such transient symptoms and CT brain is very sensitive for identifying intracerebral bleeding (and is normal in this case).

Ischaemic stroke
Ischaemic stroke is incorrect. In this case, by definition, because her symptoms have resolved within the 24-h period, this is a transient ischaemic attack as opposed to stroke.

Migraine with aura
Migraine with aura is incorrect. Migraine is common but should not be diagnosed in this case. First, there is no headache. Although acephalgic migraine can occur, it is uncommon. Second, the symptoms have acute onset. In a migrainous aura, the symptoms should evolve gradually over at least 5 min. Third, negative symptoms (weakness and loss/disturbance of speech) are much less common in migraine than positive symptoms (tingling, flashing dots/lines in the visual field).

stem: An elderly man presented with progressive lower limb weakness, particularly with hip flexion, preserved knee flex but absent ankle reflex with bilateral extensor plantars. He had a history of prostate carcinoma. Investigations: raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP), normal calcium, normal parathyroid hormone (PTH). What is the investigation most likely to reveal the underlying diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine
explanation:
Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine
This patient is likely to have compression at the level of the conus medullaris, as suggested by the mixture of upper and lower motor neurone signs. Extradural tumours principally involved in causing spinal cord compression include carcinomas of the bronchus, breast, prostate and thyroid, lymphoma and malignant melanoma. Acute management involves use of corticosteroids to reduce oedema, followed by referral for local radiotherapy.

Bone density scan
Bone density scan is incorrect. This investigation would not be performed in this setting.

Computerised tomography of spine
Computerised tomography (CT) of spine is incorrect. CT of the spine can yield high-resolution images of bony structures, but are unable to show detailed soft tissue anatomy, meaning that the CT is less useful than MRI in this setting.

Myelogram
Myelogram is incorrect. Prior to the advent of CT and MRI, myelography would have been performed to identify the site of spinal cord compression. However, it is an invasive procedure with attendant risks and is rarely performed in modern times.

Plain films of the spine
Plain films of the spine is incorrect. Plain films may show degeneration of vertebrae and destruction, but MRI is the best investigation for identifying the size and nature of any destructive lesion.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with an established diagnosis of multiple sclerosis presents with new weakness in the left leg. Intercurrent infection is excluded and there is no suggestion that the presentation marks disease progression. Two days have elapsed since her symptoms began; she has no history of psychological conditions. Which of the following should be the next step in management of her acute attack?
options: Methylprednisolone 0.5 g once daily (OD) orally (PO) for five days
Methylprednisolone 0.25 g OD PO for five days
Methylprednisolone 1 g OD intravenously (IV) for 3–5 days
Vitamin D two tablets od PO for five days
explanation:
Methylprednisolone 0.5 g once daily (OD) orally (PO) for five days
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has produced a guideline for the management of multiple sclerosis (MS) in adults (CG186). This clearly states that treatment for a relapse of MS should be with oral methylprednisolone (0.5 g daily for five days). IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days) should be considered as an alternative for people with MS, but only in those patients: in whom oral steroids have failed or not been tolerated, or who need admitting to hospital for a severe relapse or monitoring of medical or psychological conditions, such as diabetes or depression.

Methylprednisolone 0.25 g OD PO for five days
The NICE guideline explains that oral methylprednisolone should not be used at doses lower than 0.5 g daily for five days when treating an acute relapse of MS, lest it is ineffective.

Plasma exchange for 5–7 days
There is no robust evidence that the use of plasma exchange in the setting of an acute MS relapse is effective.

Methylprednisolone 1 g OD intravenously (IV) for 3–5 days
The question indicates that there is no prior medical or psychological history of relevance. This is designed to draw your attention to the fact that the NICE guideline only advocates the use of IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days) for people with MS: in whom oral steroids have failed or not been tolerated, or who need admitting to hospital for a severe relapse or monitoring of medical or psychological conditions, such as diabetes or depression. There is no evidence that either of these conditions are met in this instance.

Vitamin D two tablets od PO for five days.

stem: An 83-year-old woman is brought to clinic by her son. She lives independently, but her son has noticed that she has become increasingly forgetful over the last 6 months. There are no neurological abnormalities on examination. Which one of the following features would most support a diagnosis of early Alzheimer's disease?
explanation:
Word-finding difficulties
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) most commonly presents with insidious progressive memory loss, to which other types of cognitive impairment are added over the course of several years. Functions commonly affected after the development of memory loss include language disorders (e.g. word-finding problems and poor spelling) and impaired visuospatial skills. Thus in a patient with progressive memory problems the finding of word retrieval difficulties is supportive of the diagnosis of AD.

Disinhibition
Disinhibition is incorrect. Disinhibition is a frontal lobe sign and in the context of a slowly progressive cognitive syndrome usually suggests the diagnosis of frontotemporal dementia.

Drowsiness
Drowsiness is incorrect. The presence of drowsiness goes greatly against the diagnosis of AD, in which conscious level and alertness is preserved. Patients who are encephalopathic (for instance due to hepatic failure) are typically drowsy in a fluctuating manner. This fluctuation in levels of alertness may also be seen in dementia with Lewy bodies.

Mutism
Mutism is incorrect. Mutism is rare in AD, but may be seen in advanced frontotemporal dementia and primary progressive aphasia.

Visual hallucinations
Visual hallucinations is incorrect. The presence of visual hallucinations, in the context of progressive cognitive decline, strongly suggests the diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies. Alzheimer’s.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of progressive difficulty with speech and swallowing. On examination she is dysarthric, with a brisk gag reflex. Tongue movements are slow and effortful. Tone is increased in all four limbs, with a pyramidal distribution of weakness. Sensation is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Motor neurone disease
The combination of a pseudobulbar palsy and a spastic quadriparesis with preserved sphincters and sensation makes motor neurone disease the best-fit diagnosis.

Brainstem glioma
Brainstem glioma is incorrect. Apart from the rarity of infratentorial gliomas in adults, an intrinsic lesion here would more likely cause deficits of multiple cranial nerves with progression over a shorter period of time.

Cervical myelopathy
Cervical myelopathy is incorrect. A lesion here would not cause a pseudobulbar palsy.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. The presentation here is of a pure upper motor neurone syndrome with no sensory involvement. Guillain–Barré syndrome would cause a lower motor neurone syndrome with some sensory involvement and by definition would not progress over a 3-month period.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis, particularly the primary progressive form of the disease, could potentially explain the signs observed here. However, the lack of sensory involvement would be very unusual.

stem: An 82-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic for review. He has a history of Parkinson’s disease. His wife complains that he is agitated during sleep. This started before the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease and has been exacerbated since. He is not particularly tired during the day. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Melatonin
The most likely diagnosis here is rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, which is common in patients with Parkinson’s disease and may indeed be the harbinger of the condition. Treatment strategies include melatonin or clonazepam.

Modafinil
Parkinson’s disease is associated with a number of sleep disorders. This is most likely rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder. Excessive daytime sleepiness may be helped by modafinil. This is not the case here.

Olanzapine
The diagnosis here is most likely rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder. Hallucinations and delusions are common in Parkinson’s disease and affect the patient during the day. Quetiapine or clozapine are reasonable treatments. However, olanzapine is not recommended as it can worsen parkinsonism.

Quetiapine
Quetiapine is a drug primarily used in the treatment of schizophrenia and depression. Where sleep disturbance is present in both conditions, this patient does not show any signs or symptoms of schizophrenia or depression. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s Disease

Sertraline
Sertraline is a selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitor which can exacerbate symptoms of rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder.

stem: A 30-year-old man has been admitted to the hospital for investigation of worsening muscle weakness in his upper and lower limbs over the last 10 years. The patient says he had never been keen to participate in sports at school and that his father had problems with his gait for years. On examination, cognition, bulbar function and cranial nerves are all normal. Examination of the limbs shows distal symmetrical wasting and weakness in his arms and legs. There is areflexia. Tone is normal. There are no visible fasciculations. Vibration, pain and temperature are impaired in both hands and feet. There is kyphoscoliosis and bilateral pes cavus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease
This patient presents with polyneuropathy. The presence of difficulties since school, musculoskeletal deformities such as kyphoscoliosis and pes cavus and a possible family history of gait difficulties suggest a hereditary basis for his neuromuscular symptoms and signs. The presence of areflexia and symmetrical lower motor neurone weakness and sensory loss suggest a polyneuropathy. The commonest inherited polyneuropathy is Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (also known as hereditary motor sensory polyneuropathy).

Acquired chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP)
Acquired chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is incorrect. CIDP is characterised by gradual progressive weakness over at least 2 months, areflexia, and increased CSF protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). Acquired CIDP lacks skeletal deformities such as pes cavus or kyphoscoliosis.

Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is incorrect. Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia which is characterised by chronic, slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, and absent lower limb tendon reflexes. Onset is usually between 2 years and 25 years. Cardiomyopathy is common.

Spinal muscular atrophy
Spinal muscular atrophy is incorrect. Spinal muscular atrophy is a common autosomal recessive motor neurone disease. It presents with subacute weakness with variable age at onset. Characteristic features include weakness, wasting and fasciculations, areflexia and hyporeflexia. Cognitive changes are absent. The are no sensory changes or symptoms. 713

Vitamin B 12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a peripheral neuropathy. It often involves the dorsal columns with loss of joint position sensation. Skeletal deformities and pes cavus are not seen in vitamin B12 deficiency.

stem: A 16-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of weakness and heaviness of her arms and legs, which has been developing over an hour. She has generalised weakness of all muscle groups in her upper and lower limbs, together with hyporeflexia. Blood tests show: Na 143 mmol/l; K 2.8 mmol/l; urea 6.2; creatinine 80; glucose 4.0; urine dipstick negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Periodic paralysis
This woman has hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, which is an autosomal dominant disorder with onset usually in the teens. It occurs usually on awakening from sleep or after rest. Large carbohydrate or sodium-rich meals are usual precipitating factors. It never occurs during exercise.

Cocaine overdose
Cocaine overdose is incorrect. Patients with cocaine overdose present with aggressive behaviour, excessive sweating and acute stroke.

Ecstasy overdose
Ecstasy overdose is incorrect. Ecstasy overdose is incorrect. Patients present with severe nausea, abdominal cramps and loss of consciousness.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction disorder typically causing fatigable diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness. It is not associated with hypokalaemia and reflexes are normal. Periodic ParalysisParamyotonia congenita
Paramyotonia congenita is incorrect. Paramyotonia congenita presents with myotonia (sustained muscle spasms) during exercise. The myotonia is exaggerated by continuing exercise or cold. There is no limb weakness and there is no hypokalaemia during the attack.

stem: A 45-year-old man with epilepsy who is on carbamazepine has a history of mild and stable hepatic impairment. His seizure control is poor and he requires the addition of a second-line agent. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate?
explanation:
Levetiracetam
In mild to moderate liver failure the pharmacokinetics of levetiractam are unchanged. In severe liver failure the dose is usually halved. It is therefore a good choice in this setting. In addition levetiracetam will not interact with his carbamazepine.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect. Lamotrigine dose needs to be significantly reduced in patients with liver disease so this option is less correct than levetiracetam.

Oxcarbazepine
Oxcarbazepine is incorrect. Oxcarbazepine may be safe in mild liver disease, but there is little available data to guide the decision and therefore this answer is less correct than levetiracetam. In addition it is not appropriate to add this drug to carbamazepine as a second-line agent as they are very similar in action.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is incorrect. Phenytoin is only used with caution in liver disease. Epilepsy and Seizures

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. Sodium valproate is avoided in liver disease due to the risk of hepatotoxicity with this drug.

stem: A 23-year-old homeless man is admitted with a history of becoming unwell after sleeping rough for the last week. A few days previously he had complained of feeling rather dizzy and slightly nauseated. The following day he developed double vision and slurred speech. His gait became unsteady and he was found collapsed by police officers. He is brought to the Emergency Department. When asked, he complains of mild pain situated in the back of his neck. He is drowsy and his speech is very slurred, but comprehensible. On examination of his eye movements, the left eye moves fully but the right eye does not abduct. He has right-sided facial numbness. In the limbs, he is mildly weak in the left arm and leg. The reflexes in all four limbs are all very brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. Tests of co-ordination are reasonably well performed on the bed, but when you get him out of bed, his gait is very unsteady and he needs to be supported. His chest is clear and he is apyrexial. The rest of the examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vertebral artery dissection
He has a progressive brainstem syndrome, confirmed on neurological examination, which demonstrated impaired consciousness, dysarthria, sixth and seventh cranial nerve palsies, bilateral upper motor neurone signs and ataxia. This is most likely caused by thrombosis of the vertebral artery after spontaneous dissection (consider the neck pain), which has spread, or embolised, up the basilar artery to occlude the brainstem perforating arteries. Vertebral artery dissection is therefore the best answer.

Drug-induced cerebral arteritis
Drug-induced cerebral arteritis is incorrect. There is no history of drug abuse, but cocaine and heroin can cause cerebral vasculitis with multiple infarcts. However, the history is more likely to represent vertebral dissection and thrombosis than a drug-induced vasculitis, which is rare.

Right subdural haematoma
Right subdural haematoma is incorrect. These focal posterior circulation symptoms and signs cannot reasonably be accounted for by a subdural haematoma.

Tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculous meningitis is incorrect. Tuberculous meningitis can cause a basal meningitis, ‘picking off’ cranial nerves, but he is afebrile with no chest signs, therefore making it less likely, although still worth considering.

Wernicke’s encephalopathy
Wernicke’s encephalopathy is incorrect. Wernicke’s encephalopathy presents with ataxia, eye movement problems and confusion, so would be worth considering here, but it does not fully explain all the signs such as asymmetric weakness and brisk reflexes.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents with slowly progressive facial weakness and loss of taste. He has also noticed that he is more sensitive to loud sounds than usual and has begun to develop tinnitus. He has no other medical illnesses. . On examination there is weakness of the facial muscles on the right (including the forehead), a small patch of altered sensation on the right cheek and decreased taste sensation. Where is the most likely location of this lesion?
explanation:
Cerebellopontine angle
This patient has evidence of VIIth and Vth cranial nerve involvement. At the cerebellopontine angle cranial nerves V, VII and VIII are all in close proximity to each other, so this seems the best option.

Internal auditory canal
Internal auditory canal is incorrect. Lesions in the internal auditory canal can produce VIIth and VIIIth cranial neuroapathies but not trigeminal nerve lesions.

Parotid gland
Parotid gland is incorrect. Lesions in the parotid gland can cause facial nerve palsies but not trigeminal sensory loss.

Petrous temporal bone
Petrous temporal bone is incorrect. Lesions affecting the tip of the petrous temporal bone result in Vth and VIth nerve palsies (sometimes known as Gradenigo syndrome). Gradenigo syndrome itself was previously described in patients with chronic otitis media, it’s much more rarely seen now in the modern antibiotic era.

Stylomastoid foramen.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department one morning after an episode of unconsciousness, a convincing history of which was obtained from his mother. She had witnessed his eyes rolling upwards, a fall to the floor, jerking of all four limbs and his lips going blue. He had been incontinent. He had been assessed in a general paediatric clinic 3 years earlier complaining of sudden brief bilateral ‘jerks’ occurring largely in the morning after waking. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
This is a classic history of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, one of the most common primary generalised epilepsy syndromes. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy typically appears in the second decade and is characterised by myoclonic seizures, associated at times with generalised tonic–clonic seizures (as in this case) or absence seizures. Both myoclonic seizures and generalised tonic–clonic seizures have a special circadian pattern, in that they occur almost exclusively on or soon after awakening, either from all-night sleep or from a nap. The condition is usually treated first-line with levetiracetam.

Hypoxic myoclonus
Hypoxic myoclonus is incorrect. There is no history to suggest hypoxia.

Localisation related epilepsy
Localisation related epilepsy is incorrect. Localisation related epilepsy refers to epilepsy characterised by seizures with focal onset and is not usually associated with this picture of early morning myoclonus. It is the most common sort of epilepsy in adults.

Non-epileptic attack disorder
Non-epileptic attack disorder is incorrect. This history sounds entirely compatible with a primary generalised epilepsy and there are no ‘red flags’ to suggest non-epileptic attack disorder.

Wilson’s disease.

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the Neurology Clinic. He unfortunately suffered a seizure during a routine visit to the dentist. Apparently, he stared vacantly for a period of 10–15 seconds and was unresponsive. Later after the consultation was abandoned he was again unresponsive with a period of tonic posturing, followed by limb jerking, and he lost control of his urine. On examination at the clinic he is neurologically normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Mixed absence and tonic–clonic jerk epilepsy
explanation:
Mixed absence and tonic–clonic jerk epilepsy
Mixed absence and tonic–clonic epilepsy, as the first episode was, is clearly suggestive of absence and the second seizure was a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. His first seizure sounds like a typical absence seizure with a period of vacant staring followed by recovery. Absence seizures are typically associated with loss of consciousness lasting a few seconds, with abrupt recovery and no postictal phase. The second event is typical of tonic–clonic seizure. Generalised tonic–clonic seizures occur with or without premonition. During the tonic phase the eyes are open and roll up, pupils dilate, elbows flex, arms pronate and it may be associated with incontinence, moaning, cyanosis and apnoea. During the clonic phase there are clonic movements with the frequency of movements gradually decreasing and amplitude increasing. This phase may be associated with tongue biting, cyanosis and apnoea. This is usually followed by a postictal phase where the patient may be drowsy, confused or lethargic. Regular respiration resumes and there may be a residual headache and muscle soreness. An EEG would be the investigation of choice here. In this patient, levetiracetam is likely to be the most appropriate choice to reduce the frequency of both absence and tonic–clonic seizures.

Atonic seizures
Atonic seizures is incorrect. Atonic seizures are typically drop attacks which last seconds. The spectrum varies from head drop to complete loss of tone in the entire body.

Generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy
Generalised tonic clonic epilepsy is incorrect. He had an absence seizure followed by a tonic–clonic seizure.

Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure is incorrect. Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure is unlikely as the semiology is different. They tend to have vigorous thrusting of shoulder and hip girdle and trunk as opposed to limb movements. Further, incontinence is rare. Epilepsy and Seizures

Temporal lobe epilepsy
Temporal lobe epilepsy is incorrect. Temporal lobe epilepsy is a type of focal seizure. It could present as focal aware seizure or a focal impaired awareness seizure. It usually begins with an aura (focal aware seizure). There wiping, lip may be involuntary complex motor activity during impaired consciousness like gum chewing, nose smacking. These seizures may evolve into secondary generalised seizures. His semiology did not correspond to the above pattern.

stem: In a patient with diplopia which one of the following findings is most suggestive of myasthenia gravis?
options: Absent pupillary light reflex with preserved accommodation reflex
Loss of pin-prick sensation around the chin area
Thymoma on computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest
explanation:
Thymoma on computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest
Myasthenia gravis is an acquired autoimmune disorder associated with acetylcholine receptor antibodies which block the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (ligand gated ion channels) on the motor end plate. Direct blocking, as well as a reduction in receptor numbers secondary to the inflammatory response induced by antibody binding, leads to dysfunction in neuromuscular transmission. The ocular muscle involvement is usually bilateral and associated with ptosis and diplopia. Pupillary and accommodation reflexes are characteristically normal. Two-thirds of patients with myasthenia gravis have thymic hyperplasia and 10–15% will have thymoma. The role of thymectomy is clear in those with thymoma, but remains controversial in those with thymic hyperplasia only. The creatinine kinase (CK) is typically normal in myasthenia gravis and proptosis is not a feature.

Absent pupillary light reflex with preserved accommodation reflex
Absent pupillary light reflex with preserved accommodation reflex is incorrect. Argyll Robertson pupils can be seen in neurosyphilis, but not myasthenia gravis.

Elevated creatine kinase (CK)
Elevated creatine kinase (CK) is incorrect. CK is often measured by neurologists screening for muscle disease. It is not usually raised in myasthenia gravis.

Loss of pin-prick sensation around the chin area
Loss of pin-prick sensation around the chin area is incorrect. The numb chin syndrome, or mental nerve neuropathy, is an uncommon manifestation of metastatic malignancy.

Proptosis
Proptosis is incorrect. Proptosis is suggestive of thyroid eye disease. In thyroid eye disease there are restricted eye movements not secondary to weakness, but due to swelling and fibrosis of the extraocular muscles.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her stroke?
explanation:
Pontine haemorrhage
Massive pontine haemorrhage carries a poor prognosis, with a mortality of around 80% at 48 h. Smaller haemorrhages may present with focal neurological signs and no disturbance of consciousness. Prognosis is directly related to the level of consciousness at presentation. Intubation and ventilation, followed by urgent CT scan, is the management of choice for this patient. The features that help localise here are the loss of the doll’s eye reflex (which confirms a nuclear rather than supranuclear gaze palsy) and the bilateral pinpoint pupils (which are often a feature of pontine lesions).

Lacunar haemorrhage
Lacunar haemorrhage is incorrect. Lacunar haemorrhages may be associated with a range of motor and sensory signs rather than the specific picture of a pontine lesion seen here.

Lateral medullary syndrome
Lateral medullary syndrome is incorrect. Lateral medullary syndrome is characteristically associated with altered facial sensation ipsilaterally and altered limb sensation contralaterally. There may be ipsilateral ataxia and Horner’s syndrome as well as dysarthria and dysphagia.

Left middle cerebral artery infarct
Left middle cerebral artery infarct is incorrect. Left middle cerebral artery infarction is associated with typical signs of an anterior circulation stroke and usually involves unilateral face and arm weakness as well as language dysfunction or hemineglect, depending on whether the dominant or non-dominant hemisphere is affected.

Thalamic haemorrhage.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with unilateral hearing loss, and an acoustic neuroma is demonstrated on MRI scan. What other finding would you most expect?
explanation:
Loss of corneal reflex
This patient has a clinical presentation consistent with an acoustic neuroma, with unilateral tinnitus and hearing loss. In almost all cases, extension into the internal acoustic meatus causes a widening at one end, giving the internal acoustic meatus the appearance of a trumpet on CT imaging. On MRI, acoustic neuromas can be difficult to see, but in T2-weighted imaging will appear relatively bright in comparison to normal brain tissue. Loss of the corneal reflex due to compression of the trigeminal nerve or its nucleus is seen relatively early in patients with acoustic neuroma. If the acoustic neuroma is at the cerebellopontine angle, it is often the first sign to appear; if there is hearing loss, it is likely that the Vth cranial nerve is also affected. Therefore, loss of the corneal reflex is the most likely additional finding on examination.

Facial weakness
Facial weakness is incorrect. Eventually, facial weakness would be an expected consequence of a growing mass lesion at the cerebellopontine angle, because the facial nerve passes through this space and then through the internal auditory meatus. However, the facial nerve is relatively resistant to pressure or stretching, and is therefore much less likely to be involved than the trigeminal nerve.

Lateral rectus (VIth nerve) palsy
Lateral rectus (VIth nerve) palsy is incorrect. VIth nerve palsy is associated with raised intracranial pressure from any cause, due to its long course and passage over the petrous temporal bone. Raised intracranial pressure is rarely seen in acoustic neuromas ? only with very large tumours. Some even larger tumours may cause direct pressure on the VIth cranial nerve, but this is extremely uncommon. Consequently, a lateral rectus palsy is not the most likely additional finding.

Loss of taste
Loss of taste is incorrect. This finding would be due to involvement of the facial nerve (which supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani). This is a late clinical finding, and therefore less likely than loss of the corneal reflex.

Third nerve palsy
Third nerve palsy is incorrect. Third nerve palsy is not associated with the condition: the oculomotor nerve does not emerge or travel with the vestibulocochlear nerve, which is the origin of the acoustic neuroma (aka vestibular schwannoma). It is therefore unlikely that a mass arising from the vestibular nerve could affect the oculomotor nerve.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with a resting tremor in her left arm. She is dysarthric and ataxic. An ECG reveals first-degree heart block. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Wilson disease
The combination of cerebellar signs and tremor in a young patient makes Wilson disease the most likely diagnosis. Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is a rare inherited autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. Clinical signs: Ophthalmic examination may reveal Kayser–Fleischer rings (a rusty-coloured ring around the iris), and eye movements may be restricted. Central nervous system signs may include ataxia, tremor, parkinsonism and cognitive decline. There may be signs of liver failure. The heart may be involved, manifesting in rhythm abnormalities, especially heart block and atrial fibrillation. Investigations: Serum ceuruloplasmin and copper are usually low in spite of the copper deposits in tissues. However, they may be normal. Urinary copper is high and a 24-hour urine collection is the investigation of choice when screening for Wilson disease. The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic analysis of the ATP7B gene.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. The patient is far too young, even for a familial form of Alzheimer’s disease.

Functional illness
Functional illness is incorrect. Functional disorders can occur in this age group but should only be considered if there are positive signs to support such a diagnosis (eg Hoover’s sign).

Huntington’s chorea
Huntington’s chorea is incorrect. The Westphal variant of Huntington disease (HD) can present in this age group, but parkinsonism, dystonia, long-tract signs, dementia and epilepsy are the predominant features. Interestingly, chorea is usually not prominent in the Westphal variant of HD. Furthermore, cardiac abnormalities, as in this case, are not a feature.

Neuroacanthocytosis
Neuroacanthocytosis is incorrect. Neuroacanthocytosis can present in this age group and some variants can cause cardiomyopathy, but the neurological presentation is usually characterised by dystonia and chorea rather than tremor and ataxia. A cardinal feature of neuroacanthocytosis is orolingual dystonia and even self mutilation (lip biting). Wilson’s.

stem: A 75-year-old man is noted by his family to be increasingly confused and for the last 12 months things have been worsening. His mental state fluctuates considerably and he appears to be hallucinating at times. His daughter commented that his gait has become abnormal over the preceding months, and that his GP had tried a tablet for the nocturnal confusion that apparently made him much worse. On examination he has a Mini-Mental Score of 20/30, has generally increased tone and difficulty in performing rapidly alternating movements. His tendon reflexes are normal, as are the plantar responses; no primitive reflexes are detected. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation of this clinical scenario?
explanation:
Dementia with Lewy bodies
A fluctuating confusional state with well-formed visual hallucinations (as described in this case) is typical of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Patients often have clinical evidence of Parkinsonism at presentation, but this is not necessary for diagnosis. Cognitive deficits are found in the realms of memory, attention, visuospatial function and executive function. This condition is now recognised to be the second most common cause of neurodegenerative dementia in older people (after Alzheimer’s). Typically, standard antipsychotic drugs such as haloperidol worsen DLB, and indeed potentially fatal neuroleptic sensitivity reactions can occur. It is one of a group of conditions caused by abnormal aggregation of the synaptic protein α-synuclein. Symptomatic treatment with cholinesterase inhibitors is recommended.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Alzheimer’s disease typically presents with an insidious onset of progressive memory loss followed by word-finding difficulties, visuospatial impairment and executive problems. Fluctuations and hallucinations are uncommon.

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is incorrect. Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is a form of prion disease and results in a rapidly progressive dementia, often with prominent ataxia and myoclonic jerks. The history in this case suggests a slower neurodegenerative pathology than CJD.

Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia is incorrect. Frontotemporal dementia is typically an early onset dementia, presenting before the age of 65 (and often much younger - in the 40s or 50s). The condition is characterised by altered social behaviour and personality change. Fluctuating confusion is uncommon and visual hallucinations occur only in a minority of patients.

Vascular dementia
Vascular dementia is incorrect. Vascular dementia can present with similar features but the degree of fluctuation is usually less and well-formed visual hallucinations occur less frequently, so DLB is the better answer. In addition, patients with vascular dementia may have upper motor neurone signs such as brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars.

stem: A patient complaining of diplopia has nystagmus of the right eye on rightward gaze. The left eye fails to adduct. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
explanation:
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
These are the features of an internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), with a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the side of the eye that fails to adduct – making the left medial longitudinal fasciculus correct. The medial longitudinal fasciculus is a brainstem structure connecting the 6th and 3rd nerve nuclei on opposite sides of the brainstem in order to co-ordinate abduction of one eye with adduction of the other (horizontal conjugate gaze).

Left frontal eye field
Left frontal eye field is incorrect. Frontal eye fields are in the frontal lobes of the brain (one on each side); they initiate voluntary horizontal eye movements. A lesion in the left frontal eye field results in conjugate deviation of the eyes to the left (toward the lesion).

Right cerebellum
Right cerebellum is incorrect. Cereballar lesions produce ataxia, nystagmus and dysarthria. There is no actual oculoparesis.

Right frontal eye field
Right frontal eye field is incorrect. Frontal eye fields are in the frontal lobes of the brain (one on each side); they initiate voluntary horizontal eye movements. A lesion in the right frontal eye field produces conjugate deviation of the eyes to the right. Eye Movements and StrabismusRight medial longitudinal fasciculus
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus is incorrect. A lesion in the right medial longitudinal fasciculus would produce a right INO with failure of right eye adduction on looking to the left.

stem: A 27-year-old female who delivered a healthy baby 36 hours ago under epidural anaesthesia complains of worsening headaches. Shortly afterwards she has two fits. She has a temperature of 37.8°C and the full blood count reveals a mild neutrophilia. Neurological examination shows a left hemiplegia and bilateral upgoing plantar reflexes. There is no meningism. The optic discs appear mildly swollen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ischaemic stroke due to patent atrial septal defect
explanation:
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
The presence of headaches, seizures and focal neurological deficits strongly suggests the diagnosis of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. The post-partum period is a risk factor because of potential hypovolaemia and increased viscosity in the early post-partum period. Given the expectation that the lumbar puncture is carried out under aseptic technique, infection wouldn’t be expected.

Bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis is incorrect. Bacterial meningitis is a potential complication of the epidural, but the lack of meningism and the focal signs go greatly against this diagnosis.

Eclampsia
Eclampsia is incorrect. Eclampsia could cause seizures, but one might expect hypertension and it is hard to explain the focal neurological signs with this diagnosis.

Ischaemic stroke due to patent atrial septal defect
Ischaemic stroke due to patent atrial septal defect is incorrect. Ischaemic stroke could explain the left hemiparesis but not the bilateral upgoing plantars and papilloedema.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. Subarachnoid haemorrhage would typically present with a thunderclap haeadache and meningism. There are often no focal neurological signs.

stem: Which one of the following pathological abnormalities is characteristically found in patients with Parkinson’s disease?
explanation:
Lewy bodies
The characteristic finding in Parkinson’s disease is the Lewy body. A cytoplasmic inclusion, the eosinophilic Lewy body, typically consists of a dense core surrounded by a less intensely stained region and a faint halo. The main component of these bodies is alpha synuclein. Lewy bodies are also seen in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB).

Mallory bodies
Mallory bodies is incorrect. Mallory bodies are found in the liver and are associated with alcoholic liver disease.

Negri bodies
Negri bodies is incorrect. Negri bodies are seen in rabies infection.

Neurofibrillary tangles
Neurofibrillary tangles is incorrect. Neurofibrillary tangles are a feature of Alzheimer’s diseases. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s Disease

Pick bodies
Pick bodies is incorrect. Pick bodies are neuronal tangles found in Pick’s disease (a tau based type of frontotemporal dementia).

stem: A 35-year-old migraineur presents to the Emergency Department with a 48-hour history of headache and leftsided visual disturbance. On examination you find a left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. There is abnormal optokinetic response when the target is moved towards the right. What is the most likely site of his lesion?
explanation:
Right parietal lobe
A lesion in the right parietal lobe will produce a contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. Such parietal lesions may also cause a loss of the normal optokinetic response when the target is moved toward the side of the lesion.

Left optic tract
Left optic tract is incorrect. A lesion in the left optic tract will produce a right-sided homonymous hemianopia.

Left parietal lobe
Left parietal lobe is incorrect. A left parietal lobe lesion will produce a right-sided inferior homonymous quadrantanopia.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm is incorrect. An optic chiasm lesion will produce a bitemporal hemianopia.

Right occipital lobe
Right occipital lobe is incorrect. A lesion in the right occipital lobe will most likely produce a left-sided homonymous hemianopia.

stem: An 85-year-old woman is referred for neurology review. In the course of an admission to the Geriatric Unit for investigation of anaemia, a full neurological examination has been carried out by the registrar. Several signs have been found and he is unsure which of these are significant. She has small pupils that react sluggishly to light; impaired upward gaze and poor convergence. She has reduced hearing in both ears, left more than the right, with a sensorineural pattern. The knee and the ankle jerks are absent. There is a mildly positive palmomental reflex. Vibration sense is diminished to the ankles. Her posture is stooped and she has an ‘unsteady’ gait. In this patient, which one of these signs, when found, should prompt further investigation?
explanation:
Absent knee jerks
While absent or reduced ankle jerks are not uncommon after the age of 75 years, the absence of knee jerks implies a pathological process (assuming that they were previously present) such as neuropathy or radiculopathy.

Absent ankle jerks
Absent ankle jerks is incorrect. Absent or reduced ankle jerks are not uncommon after the age of 75.

Impaired upgaze
Impaired upgaze is incorrect. The neuro-ophthalmic signs may all occur as part of the normal ageing process. When considering eye signs in the elderly it is common to see impaired upgaze, but loss of downgaze is usually pathological (seen, for instance, in PSP).

Impaired vibration sense
Impaired vibration sense is incorrect. Reduced vibration sense may occur distally. In elderly subjects it is not unusual to find it is impaired in the feet, but usually can be felt again in the ankles.

Positive palmomental reflex
Positive palmomental reflex is incorrect. A weakly positive palmomental reflex (retraction of one side of the mouth and chin caused by contraction of the mentalis muscle, when the thenar eminence of the palm is stroked) is said to be present in as many as half of elderly people, although other primitive reflexes would suggest the presence of frontal lobe disease.

stem: A 67-year-old male who drinks 10 units of alcohol per day presents to the Emergency Department with poor memory and a wide-based, stamping gait. He has had some urinary incontinence recently and has been given a course of trimethoprim. On examination, he is confused with a MMSE of 16/30 and appears to have gazeevoked nystagmus, as well as impaired vertical gaze. His family reports that his gait and memory issues have been worsening over the past few weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Wernicke’s encephalopathy
Wernicke’s encephalopathy is characterised by the classic triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, which fits the presentation of this patient. The patient's chronic alcohol use is a significant risk factor for thiamine deficiency, which is the underlying cause of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. The wide-based, stamping gait is indicative of ataxia and peripheral neuropathy, which are common in this condition. Prompt recognition and treatment with thiamine are essential to prevent progression to Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic and debilitating amnesic disorder.

HIV encephalitis
While HIV encephalitis can present with cognitive impairment and confusion, it typically does not present with the specific eye movement abnormalities such as gaze-evoked nystagmus and impaired vertical gaze seen in this patient. HIV encephalitis often has a more gradual onset and may include other signs such as fever or generalised neurological deficits. The patient's history of heavy alcohol use also makes Wernicke’s encephalopathy more likely than HIV encephalitis. Additionally, urinary incontinence is not a common feature of HIV encephalitis.

Meningovascular syphilis
Meningovascular syphilis can present with a range of neurological symptoms, including cognitive impairment and confusion, but it typically does not involve the specific ophthalmoplegia (gaze-evoked nystagmus and impaired vertical gaze) seen in this patient. The condition usually presents with signs of meningitis or strokelike symptoms due to vascular involvement. The patient's history of alcohol use and the acute onset of symptoms are more consistent with Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Additionally, urinary incontinence is not commonly associated with meningovascular syphilis.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) can present with a triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive impairment, which makes it a feasible diagnosis. However, NPH does not typically present with specific eye movement abnormalities such as gaze-evoked nystagmus and impaired vertical gaze seen in this patient. The patient's history of chronic alcohol use and the presence of these specific neurological findings make Wernicke’s encephalopathy a more likely diagnosis. Furthermore, NPH is usually diagnosed with characteristic findings on brain imaging, such as enlarged ventricles without cortical atrophy.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is a disorder of the spinal cord that results from the formation of a cyst or cavity within the spinal cord. It typically presents with symptoms such as loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution over the shoulders and arms. Syringomyelia does not usually present with encephalopathy, confusion, or the specific eye movement abnormalities seen in this patient. The patient's symptoms and history are more consistent with Wernicke’s encephalopathy than with a spinal cord disorder.

stem: A 27-year-old scriptwriter is referred because of worsening disorientation and confusion over the last five months. Initially, her work colleagues noticed she was neglecting deadlines. She has been found in a supermarket with no idea of where she was or how she got there. Her mood has been variable, with crying episodes occurring without provocation. She has been given leave from her job because of problems with recognising colleagues and managing simple information. Her partner feels her condition is rapidly worsening. He tells you she had a miscarriage two months ago. Tests for HIV and syphilis serology were performed as part of prenatal screening: they were normal. There is no family history of neurological disease. Physical examination shows her to be withdrawn and poorly communicative. Her Abbreviated Mental Test score is 6/10. There are no cranial nerve abnormalities. Tone is increased globally, and there are recurrent, asymmetrical, jerks in all four limbs. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI of the brain
This kind of rapid cognitive decline in a young person with myoclonus and little else abnormal in the neurological examination suggests variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob (vCJD) disease. The differentials for a rapidly progressive dementing syndrome are wide, but would include sporadic CJD, HIV-related disease, CNS vasculitis and limbic encephalitis. In vCJD magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain may show abnormalities involving deep brain areas such as the thalami.

Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is incorrect. Testing for the 14-3-3 or S100b protein markers in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has a diagnostic sensitivity of only 50% in vCJD but is much more sensitive in sporadic CJD.

Serum ACE level
Serum ACE level is incorrect. Serum ACE levels are often elevated in sarcoidosis, which may rarely present with a rapidly progressive dementia, but this test has poor sensitivity and specificity.

Tonsillar biopsy
Tonsillar biopsy is incorrect. It is possible to isolate abnormal prion proteins from tonsillar tissue in cases of vCJD, but non-invasive tests such as MRI and a newly developed blood assay are first line investigations in suspected vCJD.

EEG
EEG is incorrect. In later disease stages of vCJD, an EEG may show nonspecific abnormalities, but doesn’t show the typical sharp wave periodic complexes seen in sporadic CJD.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of drooling when he tries to eat, difficulty closing his eyes and inability to smile. On examination he has weakness of eye closure, which is worse on the left, and weakness of other muscles of facial expression. Facial sensation is normal, as are eye movements, hearing and bulbar function. The remainder of both the neurological and general examination is likewise normal. There is a family history of stroke. His previous health has been good with no recent illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bilateral Bell’s palsy
The clinical signs are those of bilateral lower motor neurone seventh (facial) nerve palsy – lower motor neurone as eye closure is impaired. There are a few causes of this, including sarcoidosis, Lyme disease and bilateral parotid infiltration (eg by a lymphoma). However, in this case, with no preceding illness and no associated signs, the cause is most likely to be Bell’s palsy, which can occasionally present bilaterally. Sometimes bilateral facial nerve palsy can be the first presenting sign of Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Basilar artery territory stroke
Basilar artery territory stroke is incorrect. Basilar artery territory stroke would usually present with a constellation of brainstem signs, not isolated facial weakness.

Lyme disease
Lyme disease is incorrect. Sarcoidosis and Lyme disease are less likely. In the case of Lyme disease one would expect a history of tick bite exposure and the typical rash (erythema chronicum migrans), in addition the absence of signs and symptoms of systemic illness make this less likely.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is a reasonable differential diagnosis but the lack of ptosis, oculoparesis, bulbar weakness and proximal limb involvement make it a less likely answer.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. The lack of signs and symptoms of systemic illness make sarcoidosis less likely. Bell’s.

stem: Which one of the following neurological findings is most helpful in differentiating subacute combined degeneration of the cord secondary to b12 deficiency from multiple sclerosis (MS)?
explanation:
Absent ankle jerk
The syndrome of subacute combined degeneration of the cord is most commonly caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. It is associated with degeneration of the white matter in the dorsal and lateral columns of the spinal cord. As the illness progresses, the patient may develop Babinski’s sign and sensory ataxia. In addition, vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with sensory peripheral neuropathy, with absent distal tendon reflexes and distal sensory loss. Therefore, a mixture of central and peripheral signs is seen clinically. MS should not cause absent ankle jerks. MS is a disease limited to pathology of the central nervous system and does not cause neuropathy. The other options are incorrect as these could occur in either MS or subacute combined degeneration of the cord and, therefore, do not aid differentiation.

Ataxia
Ataxia is incorrect. This could occur in either MS or subacute combined degeneration of the cord and therefore would not aid differentiation.

Bilateral Babinski’s sign
Bilateral Babinski’s sign is incorrect. This could occur in either MS or subacute combined degeneration of the cord and therefore would not aid differentiation.

Optic atrophy
Optic atrophy is incorrect. This could occur in either MS or subacute combined degeneration of the cord and therefore would not aid differentiation. Multiple Sclerosis A 40-year-old man describes intermittent unilateral pain above and behind his left eye, which has woken him from sleep every night for the previous 7 days. The pain is described as severe and stabbing, lasting about 30 minutes and making him restless and agitated. It is associated with tearing from his left eye and nasal stuffiness. When he looked in the mirror during attacks he had noted his left eyelid drooping. He remembers he had experienced similar symptoms for about a month last year, but that they had resolved spontaneously and he had not sought medical attention. Physical examination is normal. He is a lifelong smoker. What is the diagnosis?

Pyramidal pattern weakness
Pyramidal pattern weakness is incorrect. This could occur in either MS or subacute combined degeneration of the cord and therefore would not aid differentiation.

stem: A patient with HIV presents with gradual and progressive memory loss. His magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows brain atrophy and mild white matter hyperintensity without any other significant changes or contrast enhancement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
HIV associated dementia
HIV associated dementia is thought to be primarily due to the direct effect of HIV on the brain, although other factors, such as cerebrovascular disease, may contribute. The typical MRI scan findings are atrophy and hazy white matter signal change. Unlike many of the opportunistic infections that can occur in HIV, it is not usual to see discrete lesions or contrast enhancement.

Cytomegalovirus infection
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is incorrect. CMV infection of the brain occurs only in very immunosuppressed individuals and is usually rapidly progressive.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect. Lymphoma of the CNS is more common in HIV and may present with cognitive decline. Discrete contrast enhancing lesions are normally seen on MRI and atrophy is not an imaging feature of this condition.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is incorrect. PML is caused by JC virus and most frequently occurs in very immunosuppressed individuals with HIV, although it can be seen as a complication of certain biologic immunospuppressive drugs. White matter signal change is seen on MRI, classically in posterior brain regions. It may present with cognitive decline, but there are often accompanying focal neurological signs; it therefore seems less likely to be the correct diagnosis here.

stem: A 75-year-old woman had a left total hip replacement yesterday. Today she has developed weakness and numbness of her left foot. On examination there is weakness of all ankle movements (dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, eversion and inversion) and numbness over the dorsum of her foot and lateral aspect of her leg. The left ankle jerk is absent. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Left sciatic nerve
Sciatic nerve damage is a common complication of total hip replacement.It causes global weakness of the ankle owing to the involvement of both its branches (common peroneal and tibial nerves). The ankle jerk is absent owing to the involvement of the tibial nerve. Sensory loss is variable but most commonly occurs around the dorsum of the foot and lateral aspect of the leg.

Left common peroneal nerve
Left common peroneal nerve is incorrect. A pure common peroneal nerve palsy causes weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and eversion.

Left femoral nerve
Left femoral nerve is incorrect. A pure femoral nerve palsy causes weakness of hip flexion and knee extension.

Left obturator nerve
Left obturator nerve is incorrect. A pure obturator nerve palsy causes weakness of hip adduction.

Left tibial nerve
Left tibial nerve is incorrect. A pure tibial nerve palsy causes weakness of ankle plantar flexion and inversion, as well as loss of the ankle jerk. Overall, the combination of motor deficits here indicates a lesion of the sciatic nerve.

stem: A 21-year-old obese woman presents to her GP complaining of worsening headaches over the past 4 months. The only medication of note is the combined oral contraceptive pill. She also reports blurring of vision and says that her headaches are worse in the morning. On examination of the fundi, the GP is concerned that there may be optic disc swelling bilaterally. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
IIH occurs most commonly in overweight young women. The disease is characterised by optic disc swelling and is associated with headaches that are worse when lying down, coughing or straining. Transient visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus are also features, which typically occur when the patient changes posture. In serious cases, visual loss can occur. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure is elevated when measured during lumbar puncture (which must be performed in the lateral position for an accurate reading). CSF constituents are normal.Thiazide diuretics and acetazolamide reduce intracranial pressure, but should only be seen as short-term measures. Weight loss (aiming for at least 10% reduction in weight) is the mainstay of treatment and referral to a weight management clinic is sometimes appropriate. Visual acuity and fields should be monitored carefully. Occasionally surgical decompression or shunting may be necessary, particularly if there is a threat to vision.

Macroprolactinoma
Macroprolactinoma is incorrect. Lesions of the pituitary only rarely cause headache. Pituitary lesions can cause visual field defects (classically a bitemporal hemianopia) and optic atrophy, but do not usually raise intracranial pressure and, as such, do not usually cause optic disc swelling.

Microprolactinoma
Microprolactinoma is incorrect. Lesions of the pituitary only rarely cause headache. Pituitary lesions can cause visual field defects (classically a bitemporal hemianopia) and optic atrophy, but do not usually raise intracranial pressure and, as such, do not usually cause optic disc swelling.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Normal pressure hydrocephalus is incorrect. Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with a classical triad of incontinence, dementia and gait apraxia. Headaches are not usually a feature and intracerebral pressure is normal.

Saggital sinus thrombosis
Saggital sinus thrombosis is incorrect. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) should always be considered in this setting, and investigations are usually performed to exclude this possibility. Secondary causes of raised intracranial pressure should be excluded before a diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension is made. However, CVST usually presents more acutely with a severe (sometimes thunderclap) headache and neurological deficits. Seizures are also a common occurrence with CVST. Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension A 23-year-old homeless man is admitted with a history of becoming unwell after sleeping rough for the last week. A few days previously he had complained of feeling rather dizzy and slightly nauseated. The following day he developed double vision and slurred speech. His gait became unsteady and he was found collapsed by police officers. He is brought to the Emergency Department. When asked, he complains of mild pain situated in the back of his neck. He is drowsy and his speech is very slurred, but comprehensible. On examination of his eye movements, the left eye moves fully but the right eye does not abduct. He has right-sided facial numbness. In the limbs, he is mildly weak in the left arm and leg. The reflexes in all four limbs are all very brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. Tests of co-ordination are reasonably well performed on the bed, but when you get him out of bed, his gait is very unsteady and he needs to be supported. His chest is clear and he is apyrexial. The rest of the examination is normal.

stem: A 46-year-old man who has been on haemodialysis for 12 years complains of insidious onset of painful nocturnal dysaesthesia involving the thumb and three fingers, relieved by shaking the hand. Physical examination of the hand reveals thenar wasting and numbness over the fingers. Blood tests are normal. Which one of the following statements fits best with this clinical picture?
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome would explain these findings
Deposition of amyloid of the AL (associated with light chains) type would be likely
Deposits of β2-microglobulin-associated amyloid are extremely unlikely to be a contributory cause
These findings are most likely to be associated with generalised peripheral neuropathy
These symptoms suggest compression of the ulnar nerve
explanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome would explain these findings
Clinically, the patient has carpal tunnel syndrome, an entrapment neuropathy in which the median nerve is compressed within the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome itself may be managed with surgical division of the flexor retinaculum, but unfortunately patients often present late, after at least some nerve damage has become established.

Deposition of amyloid of the AL (associated with light chains) type would be likely
Deposition of amyloid of the AL (associated with light chains) type would be likely is incorrect. A type of amyloid protein identified as β2-microglobulin has been demonstrated in bone and carpal tunnel tissue of patients undergoing long-term haemodialysis (usually more than 10 years). It is hoped that modifications of dialysis membranes will result in improved β2-microglobulin clearance with diminished tissue deposition and that switching to newer dialysis membranes may symptoms of β2-microglobulin deposition.

Deposits of β2-microglobulin-associated amyloid are extremely unlikely to be a contributory cause
Deposits of β2-microglobulin-associated amyloid are extremely unlikely to be a contributory cause is incorrect. A type of amyloid protein identified as β2-microglobulin has been demonstrated in bone and carpal tunnel tissue of patients undergoing long-term haemodialysis (usually more than 10 years). It is hoped that modifications of dialysis membranes will result in improved β2-microglobulin clearance with diminished tissue deposition and that switching to newer dialysis membranes may symptoms of β2-microglobulin deposition.

These findings are most likely to be associated with generalised peripheral neuropathy
These findings are most likely to be associated with generalised peripheral neuropathy is incorrect. This is unlikely to be associated with a generalized peripheral neuropathy. Mononeuropathies A 30-year-old woman with a body mass index of 30 has been taking the oral contraceptive pill. She is admitted with a 10-day history of worsening headaches, which are worse on stooping or coughing, and double vision. On examination she has bilateral sixth nerve palsies and bilateral papilloedema; the examination is otherwise normal. Initial plain computed tomography (CT) of the brain and orbits is normal. Later the same day, she develops sudden-onset right hemiparesis and speech disturbance. Repeat CT performed as an emergency shows a cortical low-density area with a haemorrhagic component in the left posterior temporal lobe. Which of the following investigations would be the most appropriate next step?

These symptoms suggest compression of the ulnar nerve
These symptoms suggest compression of the ulnar nerve is incorrect. These symptoms are caused by median nerve compression.

stem: A 59-year-old woman has intermittent spasms affecting her neck. Her head has a tendency to turn involuntarily towards the left when this happens. The episodes can last for up to 15 minutes at a time. She has no other symptoms and neurological examination between episodes is normal. At the time of these spasms the right sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles are hard and contracted. A diagnosis of cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis) is made at the Neurology Clinic. What treatment is likely to be proposed?
options: Local baclofen injection to the affected muscles
Local botulinum toxin injection to the affected muscles
explanation:
Local botulinum toxin injection to the affected muscles
There is good evidence (level A, Class I–II) for the usefulness of botulinum toxin in cervical dystonia, which is the most frequent form of focal dystonia. Botulinum toxin is also effective in treating blepharospasm and other focal and generalised dystonias. It is given as a series of local injections via a specialist clinic service, sometimes with electrophysiological guidance, depending on the anatomical region involved. Local botulinum toxin injection to the affected muscles is the best treatment choice here.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline has no significant utility in treating focal dystonia. It is frequently used in the treatment of neuropathic pain.

Baclofen orally
Baclofen orally is incorrect. Baclofen orally can be used to treat spasticity, but is not particularly effective for focal dystonia.

Gabapentin
Gabapentin is incorrect. Gabapentin has no significant utility in treating focal dystonia. It is frequently used in the treatment of neuropathic pain.

Local baclofen injection to the affected muscles
Local baclofen injection to the affected muscles is incorrect. Baclofen is not injected into muscles, although in severe spasticity it can be administered intrathecally via a special pump.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with tingling and weakness affecting her left arm and leg. She tells you about a fall some 6 weeks earlier, following which she has had a sore neck, especially on flexion or lateral rotation. On examination there is 4/5 power weakness affecting her left arm and left leg, with lower motor neurone signs in the arm, upper motor neurone signs in the leg including bilateral upgoing plantar responses. Loss of vibration and joint position sense is more marked in the hands than the feet. More minor sensory loss is also detectable on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cervical myelopathy
The symptoms described here are consistent with cervical myelopathy related to extrinsic cord compression, most likely as a result of bony injury which occurred during the fall. Urgent MRI and neurosurgical review to further elucidate the nature of any neck injury are indicated. In cervical myelopathy bladder or bowel dysfunction is caused primarily by a bilateral upper motor neuron lesion. Cervical myelopathy is generally due to degenerative changes of the middle and lower cervical spine. Therefore, the impairment of hand function in this patient can be attributed mainly to lower motor neuron function.

Cervical radiculopathy
Cervical radiculopathy is incorrect. Cervical radiculopathy implies injury of one nerve root, which would not fit with these symptoms.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is incorrect. Syringomyelia is associated with sensory loss over a cape-like distribution over the upper body, rather than peripheral sensory loss.

Syringobulbia
Syringobulbia is incorrect. This occurs when a syrinx forms in the brainstem. It is associated with syringomyelia and can affect the cranial nerves.

Brachial plexus injury
Brachial plexus injury is incorrect. Brachial plexus injury would not be associated with lower limb signs.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with increasing weakness. She has no past medical history of note apart from a recent diarrhoeal illness, which she puts down to an undercooked chicken meal. Her husband says that she has been unable to get up out of a chair for the past day. On examination there is obvious bilateral limb weakness more marked in the lower limbs and areflexia. You notice that if she lies flatter in the bed her oxygen saturations fall by around 2% on the pulse oximeter and she is unable to perform spirometry. Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate management of choice in this patient?
options: ITU review for consideration of ventilation
explanation:
ITU review for consideration of ventilation
This woman has a history that is suggestive of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS). This may be precipitated by Campylobacter, her history of recent diarrhoeal illness being a pointer. Certain features point to a poor prognosis, these include: Rapidity of onset Reduced vital capacity or respiratory failure Age >40 Proven associated bacterial infection Reduced amplitude of compound muscle action potential. Her inability to perform spirometry and desaturation on lying flat are pointers to impending respiratory muscle weakness; therefore, the correct answer here is ITU review for consideration of ventilation.

Ciprofloxacin 500 mg po bd
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg po bd is incorrect. Ciprofloxacin has no role in treating GBS and she has no current symptoms of bacterial infection.

High-dose intravenous corticosteroids
High-dose intravenous corticosteroids is incorrect. High-dose intravenous corticosteroids are ineffective for GBS.

Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is incorrect. Lumbar puncture is a useful test in GBS and one expects to see raised CSF protein, but normal CSF white cell count. In this case the need for ITU support must come before the lumbar puncture. Guillain-Barré Syndrome

Plasma exchange
Plasma exchange is incorrect. Plasma exchange is a possible treatment for GBS, although intravenous immunoglobulin is generally used first line. In this case the need for ITU support supercedes the instigation of plasma exchange.

stem: A 59-year-old man is referred to the Stroke Clinic after an episode of confusion. He had just got out of the shower when he started to behave in a manner that worried his wife. When she questioned him about what was the matter, he appeared not to know where he was, what day it was or indeed who the next-door neighbour that his wife called for help was. He did, however, know who he himself was. His wife mentioned that he also complained of having had a headache, so she suggested he should go to bed to sleep off the attack. He went to bed and slept for the rest of the day and night. On waking he felt well but was unable to recall exactly the events of the previous day. He is a non-smoker. On examination there are no abnormalities other than an elevated blood pressure of 170/90 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Transient global amnesia
The features, particularly the retention of knowledge regarding his own identity, are characteristic of transient global amnesia (TGA). No investigations are required, as this is a clinical diagnosis. TGA is a benign condition, the aetiology of which is not clear. Its occurrence does not increase the risk of subsequent vascular events. The risk of recurrence is approximately 10%.

Cerebral venous thrombosis
Cerebral venous thrombosis can manifest in many ways, often with headache, seizures and Chat focalwith neurological deficits. This presentation, however, with spontaneous resolution would be very unlikely.

Right caudate haemorrhage
Caudate infarction or haemorrhage may cause cognitive dysfunction and be mistaken for depression, but symptoms would persist for longer than in this patient.

Right hemisphere transient ischaemic attack (TIA)
Right hemisphere transient ischaemic attack (TIA) would not present with an amnestic syndrome. Rather, it would produce left-sided limb symptoms of either weakness or sensory loss.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a thunderclap headache and does not produce a focal amnestic syndrome.

stem: Over the next few hours the headache and weakness resolve. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give her sumatriptan to take when the headache begins
Give her a card to show to obtain high flow oxygen therapy
explanation:
Stop the oral contraceptive pill
This woman is having migraines with aura, particularly with focal neurological symptoms, are an indication to discontinue the pill immediately because of significantly increased risk of ischaemic stroke. She should be offered alternative contraception.

Give her sumatriptan to take when the headache begins
Give her sumatriptan to take when the headache begins is incorrect. Triptans can be used to treat migraines, but would not be an appropriate option in this case as the patient is on the combined oral contraceptive pill.

Give her a card to show to obtain high flow oxygen therapy
Give her a card to show to obtain high-flow oxygen is incorrect. High-flow oxygen is used in the treatment of cluster headache, whereas this patient is presenting with classical migraine symptoms.

Start amitriptyline
Start amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline is used as prophylaxis against migraine, but would not be an appropriate option in this case as the patient is on the combined oral contraceptive pill.

Start aspirin
Start aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin can be used to treat migraines, but would not be an appropriate option in this case as the patient is on the combined oral contraceptive pill. Useful external weblinks bnf.org ( (related to stop the oral contraceptive).

stem: A 49-year-old man hit his forehead getting into his car. A few hours later he developed diplopia, vomiting and severe headache. On examination he is slightly drowsy, and has dilated right pupil, partial right ptosis, little movement in any direction of gaze in his right eye, with reduced sensation over the right forehead. He had a postural systolic BP drop of 20 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pituitary apoplexy
The patient is exhibiting signs of pituitary apoplexy with right III, IV, VI nerve palsy and V1 affected indicating extension into the right cavernous sinus. The fact that he hit his head on the car in the first place may imply a visual field defect. His blood pressure drop is the result of glucocorticoid insufficiency.

Bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis is incorrect. Bacterial meningitis will present with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and possibly signs of sepsis.

Middle cerebral artery infarction
Middle cerebral artery infarction is incorrect. Middle cerebral artery will result in contralateral hemiparesis, not the cranial nerve signs seen here.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. Subarachnoid haemorrhage may present with a thunderclap headache and, if the responsible aneurysm arises from the posterior communicating artery, one may see a third nerve palsy; however, the other cranial nerve signs seen here cannot be explained with this diagnosis.

Vertebral artery dissection.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has developed difficulty walking over the last two months. Tone and power are normal in the lower limbs. Knee jerks are preserved yet ankle jerks are absent. Plantar responses are extensor. She has had some difficulty emptying her bladder. What is the most likely cause of her problems?
explanation:
Conus medullaris lesion
Absent reflexes imply a lower motor neurone (LMN) lesion, but extensor plantars an upper motor neurone (UMN) lesion. The causes of this combination are therefore those disorders that can cause a mixture of UMN and LMN signs. These include vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration of the cord with peripheral neuropathy), tertiary syphilis (taboparesis), motor neurone disease, Friedreich’s ataxia, a conus medullaris lesion or diabetes mellitus.

Beriberi
Beriberi is incorrect. Beriberi is caused by thiamine deficiency and may present with a peripheral neuropathy, but UMN signs would not be seen.

Cervical spondylosis
Cervical spondylosis is incorrect. Cervical spondylosis is common and often just causes neck pain. Severe spondylosis may cause a compressive myelopathy with UMN in the legs.

Parasagittal meningioma
