Parasagittal meningioma is incorrect. Parasagittal meningioma is a cause of bilateral leg weakness with upper motor neurone signs. Absent ankle jerks are not seen.

stem: A patient presented with acute onset of mild right hemiparesis affecting the body. He also has evidence of sensory loss on the right-hand side of his body but on the left-hand side of his face. There is evidence of Horner syndrome on the left. Which one of the following structures is involved?
explanation:
Brainstem
There is evidence of the lateral medullary syndrome. The commonest cause is thromboembolic disease affecting the vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries. The key feature that localises the lesion clinically to the brainstem is the ‘crossed’ nature of the signs (i.e. left side of face and right side of body). Hemiparesis in the lateral medullary syndrome is mild or absent as the descending motor tracts run medially. Horner syndrome is caused by disruption of the ipsilateral descending sympathetic tract.

Frontal lobe
Frontal lobe is incorrect. A contralateral hemiparesis would be the most likely consequence of a lesion affecting the frontal lobe.

Medial temporal lobe
Medial temporal lobe is incorrect. The feature of lesions in the temporal lobe again depends upon whether the dominant (eg aphasia) or non-dominant (eg prosopagnosia) lobe is affected, although a contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia can occur as a result of a lesion affecting either lobe.

Occipital lobe
Occipital lobe is incorrect. A lesion here would cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Parietal lobe
Parietal lobe is incorrect. Parietal lobe lesions can be difficult to localise and clinical features depend on whether the dominant (eg Gerstmann syndrome – acalculia, agraphia, finger anomia and right–left disorientation) or non-dominant (eg anosagnosia, constructional apraxia) lobe is affected. A hemisensory syndrome may be seen, but the ‘crossed signs’ described here would not occur.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset severe headache and vomiting. She was decorating her ceiling that morning when the headache began, felt mainly at the occiput with neck pain. Some 2 hours later she felt nauseated, vomited and was unable to walk. She takes no regular medication and has no significant past history. Examination is difficult due to severe nausea and vertigo, but does reveal normal limb power on the bed but an inability to mobilise due to ataxia. She has upbeat nystagmus in all directions of gaze. Her speech is slurred and the uvula is deviated to the right. The tongue appears normal. The left pupil is reduced in diameter when compared to the right. There is reduced pinprick sensation in the left side of the face and in the right arm and leg. Where is the most likely site of her lesion?
explanation:
Left lateral medulla
This woman has a left lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), which is usually caused byocclusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) secondary to vertebral artery dissection. Recent trauma or activities involvingunusually prolonged or excessive neck extension are risk factors for vertebral artery dissection. The PICA supplies the posteroinferior cerebellar hemisphere as well as the lateral portion of the medulla, where structures damaged include the: Vestibular nucleus (causing nystagmus and vomiting) Inferior cerebellar peduncle (causing ipsilateral limb ataxia) Spinothalamic tract (causing contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the limbs and torso) Spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve (causing ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face) Nucleus ambiguus (causing in ipsilateral laryngeal, pharyngeal and palatal paralysis by disruption of projections to the vagus nerve. Allows the uvula to be pulled away from the side of the lesion) Descending sympathetic fibres (causing an ipsilateral Horner syndrome)

Left cerebellar hemisphere
Left cerebellar hemisphere is incorrect. An isolated cerebellar lesion would not cause crossed signs (where deficits are noted on one side of the face but the other side of the body) or the cranial nerve deficits seen.

Left lateral pons
Left lateral pons is incorrect. A lesion in the lateral pons could cause all of the features listed, apart from deviation of the uvula. In a lateral pontine syndrome, an ipsilateral‘lower motor neuron’ facial palsy (due to disruption of the facial nerve nucleus) would be expected and therefore left lateral pons is incorrect.

Right lateral medulla
Right lateral medulla is incorrect. In the lateral medullary syndrome the lesion is ipsilateral to the side of the Horner syndrome, facial sensory dysfunction, palatal palsy and limb ataxia. You are asked to see a 72-year-old who comes to the Emergency Department complaining that she is unable to walk. She had a resection for a Dukes C colonic carcinoma some 9 months earlier. Since then she has been well and has returned to looking after her grandchildren each weekday. On examination, she looks anxious. Her BP is 149/88 mmHg, her pulse 90 beats/min and regular. Cardiovascular and respiratory examination is unremarkable. Neurology reveals left-sided lower limb paralysis, with increased tone and an upgoing plantar on the left side. There is contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation with ipsilateral loss of fine touch and vibration sense. Investigations:

Right medial medulla
Right medial medulla is incorrect. Lesions in the medial medulla cause the Dejerine syndrome. In this syndrome, the hypoglossal nucleus is damaged causing ipsilateral deviation of the tongue and there is contralateral limb weakness due to disruption of descending corticospinal fibres. Right medial medulla is therefore incorrect. It is also worth noting that Horner syndrome does not occur in the Dejerine syndrome.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with ascending paralysis of her lower and then upper limbs, which evolved over a 4-day period. She also has paraesthesias of her legs and hands. On examination she has normal cranial nerve examination. She has grade 3/5 weakness of both legs as well as weakness of grip, and is areflexic throughout. After admission to the Neurology Unit she undergoes nerve conduction studies (NCS), which show a reduced conduction velocity, conduction block and small compound motor and sensory potentials. The report states that this ‘would be in keeping with the clinical suspicion of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS)’. What is the likely underlying pattern of peripheral nerve pathology giving rise to these neurophysiological changes?
explanation:
Segmental demyelination
The most frequent form of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) can be more accurately called ‘acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP)’, although axonal forms of the disease do occur. The nerve conduction study (NCS) changes described here are typical of segmental demyelination, confirmed by the presence of conduction block. This occurs because of focal degeneration of the susceptible myelin sheath (due to an inflammatory antibody reaction), leaving the underlying axon intact. Recovery of function may therefore be relatively rapid, as remyelination occurs (weeks and months).

Accumulation of β-amyloid plaques
Accumulation of β-amyloid plaques is incorrect. Accumulation of β-amyloid plaques is the hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease and has nothing to do with Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Axonal degeneration
Axonal degeneration is incorrect. Axonal degeneration occurs in many neuropathies and on neurophysiology you see relatively intact conduction velocities but reduced action potential amplitudes.

Ischaemic demyelination
Ischaemic demyelination is often associated found in the periventricular region and is often associated with vessel disease due to hypertension.

Wallerian degeneration.

stem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has been suffering from increasingly frequent migraines over the past few months, and was particularly concerned today as her usual aura of flashing multi-coloured lights in front of her right eye, followed by a severe right-sided headache, was accompanied by transient arm weakness which resolved after approximately 30 min. Her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination her BP is 155/95 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. The limb weakness has resolved and there are no abnormal neurological findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?
explanation:
Stop the oral contraceptive pill
This patient has had an episode of hemiplegic migraine, which puts her at increased risk of an ischaemic stroke if she continues to use the combined oral contraceptive pill. That being the case, the key intervention is to switch to some other form of contraception such as the progesterone-only pill.

Reassurance
Reassurance is incorrect. This patient is at increased risk of stroke if she continues to use the combined oral contraceptive pill. In addition, her migraines have been increasing in frequency and she mayChat require with migraine prophylaxis if her symptoms do not resolve after switching to a different contraceptive.

Start regular amitriptyline
Start regular amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline is an appropriate first-line medication for migraine prophylaxis, which is usually offered to patients experiencing more than two migraines per month. However, the most important step is to stop the combined oral contraceptive as she is at increased risk of stroke. This may help to resolve her migraines, and prophylaxis may not be necessary.

Start regular atenolol
Start regular atenolol is incorrect. Although atenolol is an acceptable first-line treatment in the prophylaxis of migraines, it would be appropriate to stop the combined oral contraceptive pill first: this may remove the need for prophylaxis by improving or stopping her migraines. Furthermore, she is at increased risk of stroke as she is experiencing migraines on the oral contraceptive pill, and therefore this must be switched as soon as possible.

Start regular topiramate
Start regular topiramate is incorrect. Topiramate is an antiepileptic and a second-line option for migraine prophylaxis; it can be associated with significant drowsiness, lethargy and nausea, and hence is not a first-line option. All predisposing factors should be addressed before starting prophylactic medication. Migraine A 60-year-old engineer who was previously well was found collapsed on the floor. When he was admitted, examination revealed weakness of the right side of his body, with his arm and face more severely affected than his leg, and severe aphasia.

stem: A 21-year-old man comes to the Neurology Clinic. He is making troublesome, uncontrolled movements including swinging out his arm, twitching of his neck, unintentional grunting and inappropriate swearing/commentary whilst interacting with other individuals. Clinical examination, including CNS exam, is entirely normal. During the examination, he continues with bizarre tics and swearing. Blood work-up is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for control of his tics?
explanation:
Risperidone
This patient is most likely to be suffering from Tourette syndrome. Systematic reviews and case series mostly support the use of risperidone in this individual, although the minimum effective dose should be used in an attempt to avoid extra-pyramidal side effects.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Diazepam is likely to be associated with unacceptable sedation and is inappropriate as a long-term solution.

Ropinirole
Ropinirole is incorrect. Smaller studies suggest the possible benefit of ropinirole, buspirone, carbamazepine or metoclopramide, but there is a dearth of RCT data for this condition and further trials are needed.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. This is an antiepileptic medication which can be used for epilepsy, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Carbamazepine is an antiepileptic which has some effect on Tourette syndrome, but would not be considered first-line treatment.

stem: A 72-year-old man attends the clinic accompanied by his wife. She reports that he has become gradually confused over the past few months. He has also suffered from episodes of urinary incontinence. There is a history of atrial fibrillation for which he takes digoxin and aspirin, and hypertension for which he takes ramipril. On examination his BP is 142/82 mmHg, with pulse 72/min. There is no papilloedema on fundoscopy. He has a rather flat affect and a shuffling and broad-based gait when you ask him to walk across the consulting room. CT head reveals evidence of cerebral atrophy and ventricular enlargement. What would be the most appropriate next step in management to address the likley cause of this patient's deterioration?
explanation:
Lumbar puncture
The triad of dementia, gait disturbance and urinary incontinence raises the possibility of normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and the CT findings of enlarged ventricles supports this. The gait disturbance in normalpressure hydrocephalus is not a true ataxia, but a gait apraxia caused by distortion of the sacral motor fibres travelling within the corona radiata: it tends to be slow and shuffling, similar to a parkinsonian gait (except that you would not expect the gait to be broad-based if it were simply parkinsonian). It is this damage to the sacral nerve supply which also leads to the urinary incontinence seen in normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Damage to the limbic system, which is located next to the ventricles, causes the dementia. The condition is a cause of reversible dementia, and therefore should be treated. The first-line management would be a therapeutic lumbar puncture, though the definitive management is to surgically insert a CSF shunt, either as a ventriculo-peritoneal shunt or ventriculo-atrial shunt, if the patient is fit for surgery.

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin is incorrect. There is no indication here that the patient has dyslipidaemia. If this was vascular dementia, it would be important to modify any vascular risk factors. Although this patient does have vascular risk factors (hypertension), the clinical picture is not consistent with a vascular cause of dementia. The triad of features seen here (dementia, gait disturbance and incontinence) can be those of vascular dementia, but you would expect progression to be stepwise (with clinical worsening when a vascular event occurs), not gradual (as in this case).

Memantine
Memantine is incorrect. Memantine is an NMDA antagonist used in moderate-severe Alzheimer’s disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. You would not expect to find ventricular enlargement on CT in Alzheimer’s disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, and the clinical triad of incontinence, dementia and gait disturbance is more suggestive of normal-pressure hydrocephalus. The gait disturbance seen here is broad-based, and therefore is not quite parkinsonian (which is the gait pattern seen in dementia with Lewy bodies). As normal-pressure hydrocephalus is reversible using lumbar puncture and then CSF shunting, there is no indication for memantine.

Ropinirole
Ropinirole is incorrect. Ropinirole is used in Parkinson’s disease. You would not expect to see ventricular with AIslow Tutor and enlargement on CT if this were Parkinson’s disease, and the gait disturbance described hereChat – though shuffling – is broad-based, which does not fit with Parkinson’s. Urinary incontinence is also not a feature of Parkinson’s. The clinical features of this case are more consistent with normal-pressure hydrocephalus; there is no indication for ropinirole (a dopamine agonist) in this condition.

stem: A 17-year-old girl who is part-way through her A-level exams is admitted to the Emergency Department. She collapsed during a geography exam, suffering a fit, but she was not incontinent of urine. On examination, her BP is 115/72 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. She appears unconscious, with resistance to eye opening. When you try and wake her she remains unresponsive with eyes closed and presents rhythmic trunk and pelvic movements, with bicycling of her legs. The episode of abnormal movements waxes and wanes over 5 min. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure
The pointers towards psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (NES) are: functional rather than organic loss of consciousness (resistance to eye opening); atypical duration, 5 min being much longer than the usual seizure duration of 1–2 min; and the waxing/waning pattern of movements. The nature of movements as described is also evocative of NES, but remember that frontal seizures can involve complex behaviour and rhythmic movements (but never lasting as long as 5 min and not with a waxing/waning pattern). The fact that these episodes occur when the patient is stimulated, coupled with the fact they have begun during a period of exam stress, fits with psychogenic episodes, but some patients with epilepsy also experience seizures triggered by stress, or have a past history of traumatic psychological events, so beware of purely circumstantial ‘evidence’ when making a diagnosis of possible NES. The gold standard diagnosis is through recording a habitual event on video-EEG with interpretation by an expert team. Effective communication of an unambiguous diagnosis is the most important first step in the therapeutic process. A multi-disciplinary approach to management is ideal, with neurology, psychology and psychiatry input, though in practice few centres are equipped with specialist teams. Be aware of the high prevalence of associated psychiatric morbidity (anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder) and the possibility of childhood psychological (or psycho-sexual) trauma. Other somatic complaints with a functional basis are not uncommon. Reference: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures—Definition, etiology, treatment and prognostic issues: A critical review. Bodde et al. Seizure 2009. Vol. 18(8): 543–53

Non-convulsive status epilepticus
Non-convulsive status epilepticus is incorrect. Status epilepticus is a prolonged seizure due to failure of seizure termination mechanisms, or frequent seizures without full recovery of consciousness in-between episodes. For non-convulsive status epilepticus, the duration must be at least 10 min. Symptoms can be negative with aphasia, mutism, amnesia and catatonia, as well as positive symptoms of rhythmic twitching, eye deviation or dystonia. The clinical description does not match this as she has regular movement of her legs and is physically resisting eye opening.

Temporal lobe seizure
Temporal lobe seizure is incorrect. In a focal aware seizure (previously termed simple partial seizure) of the temporal lobe there can be feelings of déjà vu, jamais vu, amnesia or change in emotion. There can also be hallucinations which are often auditory in nature. There can also be a focal impaired awareness (complex partial) seizure originating in the temporal lobe with motionless starting, automatic movements, changes in speech and aphasia, as well as change in mental state. Either type of seizure can lead to secondary general seizure. In the absence of the above features being described, this is unlikely.

Frontal lobe seizure
Frontal lobe seizure is incorrect. Frontal lobe seizures have a wide array of different symptoms and signs due to the various neurological functions controlled by the frontal lobe. The evidence is often motor, with changes in motor function which can result in repetitive jerking. An alternative is a change in tone. There is often an associated aura. This patient does not have distinct seizure episodes, making this very unlikely.

stem: A 32-year-old woman develops sudden-onset weakness and numbness of her left arm and leg and pain in the right neck while taking part in an exercise class. She is on the oral contraceptive pill. There are no other risk factors for stroke identified. On examination she has a mild upper motor neurone weakness of her left face, arm and leg, left-sided hemisensory loss, a left homonymous hemianopia and left-sided inattention. Brain CT and diffusion-weighted MRI both show a recent single infarction in the territory of the right middle cerebral artery. Which of the following mechanisms should be suspected to be the most likely cause pending further investigation?
explanation:
Dissection of right carotid artery
Cervical vascular dissection that occurs spontaneously or is provoked by minimal trauma (a clue in this case being the fact that she is taking an exercise class) is likely to be commoner than previously recognised, and is the most common cause of stroke in patients under 40 with no vascular risk factors, as here. The clinical presentation described here is that of a right total anterior cerebral syndrome (TACS), indicating that the internal carotid and its middle cerebral branch are the likely vessels involved. Thus dissection of the right carotid artery is correct. In carotid artery dissection ipsilateral Horner’s sign may also be present.

Cardioembolic from atrial septal defect
Cardioembolic from atrial septal defect is incorrect. When an ischaemic event occurs in the context of exercise, the possibility of a Valsalva manoeuvre precipitating embolism from a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect should also be considered. However, when the event is provoked by exercise an arterial dissection should be considered most likely until proven otherwise, as this presents the highest risk of further stroke.

Dissection of basilar artery
Dissection of basilar artery is incorrect. Dissection of the basilar artery would present with posterior circulation stroke symptoms.

Inherited thromboembolic disorder
Inherited thromboembolic disorder is incorrect. Inherited thromboembolic disorder is more likely to present with recurrent venous thrombosis than arterial stroke; a family history of such clots may also be present. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke You review a 32-year-old woman who is 2-days postpartum and has suffered two generalised tonic–clonic seizures in the space of 1 hour on the maternity ward. Apparently she has been complaining of an increasingly severe headache over the previous 24 hours, which was unrelieved by paracetamol and codeine. She received an epidural during delivery. On examination she is very drowsy and has a BP of 134/87 mmHg. She is unable to comply with your questions with respect to neurological examination, but you do determine that she has bilateral papilloedema. Her temperature is 37.4°C. Investigations reveal:

Thromboembolic secondary to carotid atherosclerosis
Thromboembolic secondary to carotid atherosclerosis is incorrect. Thromboembolism secondary to carotid atherosclerosis is unlikely in a 32-year-old woman.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of severe left earache with a burning sensation in the ear, vertigo and loss of taste. There is left-sided weakness of both the upper and the lower facial muscles. Facial sensation is normal. You note a vesicular rash over the left ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Ramsay Hunt syndrome is caused by infection of the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, together with invasion of the VIIIth nerve ganglia, by the herpes zoster virus. This produces ear pain, hearing loss, vertigo and facial nerve paralysis. A vesicular rash is usually present in the outer ear, and sometimes also the soft palate or anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Lymphocytes in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and a mildly elevated CSF protein are recognized.

Bell’s palsy
Bell’s palsy is incorrect. Bell’s palsy is probably the most common cause of a lower motor neurone VIIth nerve lesion. However, the burning pain and vertigo make herpes zoster infection more likely.

Lateral medullary syndrome
Lateral medullary syndrome is incorrect. Lateral medullary syndrome is a brainstem stroke causing ipsilateral Horner syndrome, facial numbness and contralateral limb numbness. Lower cranial nerve nuclei may be involved and this can produce hoarseness and dysphagia.

Otitis media
Otitis media is incorrect. Otitis media is often chronic and is rarely complicated by multiple cranial neuropathies.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for his neurological findings?
explanation:
No intervention required
This patient has a small, chronic subdural, which has occurred as a result of his recent fall. At this stage (2-3 weeks after the injury), with a small subdural and no focal neurology, there is no indication for intervention. He should of course be advised to reduce his drinking, and be offered access to support through his GP and a group such as Alcoholics Anonymous.

Anticoagulation for AF
Anticoagulation for atrial fibrulation (AF) is incorrect. This patient has a subdural haematoma: giving him anticoagulant medication at this stage could cause further bleeding with potentially catastrophic results.

Bed rest
Bed rest is incorrect. Bed rest does not affect the resolution of a subdural haematoma, and this patient’s falls are secondary to his alcohol intake. To modify his risk of further head injury, he should reduce his alcohol intake: bed rest is not a long-term solution.

Evacuation of subdural
Evacuation of the subdural haematoma is incorrect. This patient has only a small subdural haematoma, which is chronic. He has no red flags such as focal neurology or decreased consciousness level. Evacuation would only be indicated if these red flags were present.

Vitamin K
Vitamin K is incorrect. Vitamin K is used to correct coagulopathy when INR >2.0. Here the INR is 1.4 and therefore vitamin K is not indicated. Subdural HaematomaA 45-year-old alcoholic man who has previously presented with confusion and walking difficulties was given a diagnosis of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. This was treated with thiamine replacement, and over time he made a good recovery. He reattends the Emergency Department with his partner. He has apparently started drinking again and stopped taking his vitamin supplements.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with episodic pain in the right side of his face, which has been going on for 2 months. In addition, he complains of a buzzing sound in his right ear and right-sided hearing loss. Two weeks earlier he also complained of numbness in his face, but the GP was unable to find any abnormal signs. When you see him, he is in pain. He does appear to have hearing loss and a reduced corneal reflex on the right, but nothing else. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vestibular Schwannoma
The combination of unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and trigeminal neuropathy (as evidenced by reduced corneal reflex) is classical of a vestibular Schwannoma.

Ménière’s disease
Ménière’s disease is incorrect. Ménière’s disease causes recurrent episodes of hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo; it is not painful.

Multiple sclerosis with brainstem plaque
Multiple sclerosis with brainstem plaque is incorrect. A brainstem plaque due to MS is possible, but the time course and hearing loss would be highly atypical.

Trigeminal neuralgia
Trigeminal neuralgia is incorrect. Trigeminal neuralgia causes sharp lancinating facial pain, but not these focal neurological deficits.

Viral labyrinthitis
Viral labyrinthitis is incorrect. Viral labyrinthitis cannot account for the trigeminal nerve signs, and is usually an acute condition. Acoustic Neuroma A 32-year-old woman, who works as a croupier and is normally fit and well, had woken 3 weeks before with weakness in her left hand. She had noted numbness at the base of the thumb on the dorsum of the hand. She is on the oral contraceptive pill. She drinks alcohol in binges, one of which had occurred the night before her symptoms started, and smokes 15 cigarettes per day. She has a normal general examination, normal cranial nerves and normal muscle tone, but mild weakness of the left brachioradialis and moderate weakness of wrist and finger extension. She has full power in her other arm muscles including elbow extension. Reflexes are normal.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a resting tremor of his right arm. You also note that he has a shuffling gait and freezes when he crosses the door frame when he enters the consulting room. His symptoms are interfering with his passion for walking. A diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson's disease is made. Which of the following medications would be first-line treatment?
explanation:
Co-careldopa
Co-careldopa or co-beneldopa (levodopa in combination with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor) are the usual first-line treatments for Parkinson’s disease. In the recent past, concern about late motor complications (eg dyskinesia) limited the use of levodopa in early disease and dopamine agonists were often preferred. However, this has become less of an issue more recently, particularly with the advent of invasive therapies such as deep brain stimulation or apomorphine, which can be used to ameliorate late motor complications (largely as a result of allowing for a reduced levodopa dose to be used).

Amantadine
Amantadine is incorrect. Amantadine does have modest anti-parkinsonian effects but is usually used as an addon therapy in later disease to help with the management of dyskinesia.

Benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl)
Benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl) is incorrect. Benzhexol is an anticholinergic medication which is sometimes used in tremor dominant disease. However, side effects (particularly memory disturbance and gastrointestinal symptoms such as dry mouth, cramps and constipation) often limit its use.

Ropinirole
Ropinirole is incorrect. Ropinirole and pramipexole are synthetic dopamine agonists. Ropinirole and pramipexole are reasonable first-line treatments for Parkinson’s disease. However, they are usually not as efficacious as levodopa and impulse control disorder is increasingly noted as a significant adverse effect. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s Disease Which one of the following is a cause of second-order-neurone Horner syndrome?

Selegiline
Selegiline is incorrect. Selegeline and rasagaline are monoamine oxidase inhibitors which can be used to augment treatment with levodopa, particularly in later disease, to reduce motor fluctuations.

stem: Once the diagnosis of epilepsy is confirmed, which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment option with respect to prophylaxis against further fits?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
Given this woman has had three tonic-clonic seizures in the past month, and that such generalised seizures may put her baby at risk, it would seem appropriate to intervene with antiepileptic therapy. The treatment of choice here would be lamotrigine. The underlying origin of the seizures should also be determined and investigation with cerebral MRI would be indicated.

No treatment
No treatment is incorrect. Given that three seizures have already occurred, the risk of further seizures is relatively high and the consequent potential for harm from such events must be considered.

Gabapentin
Gabapentin is incorrect. Regardless of any effect on the foetus, gabapentin has poor efficacy as an antiepileptic and would not be used as a first line agent.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate should not be commenced in any patient < 55 years of age unless two consultants agree there is no alternative. This is due to the evidence from various international pregnancy registers, including the UK, that the rate of major congenital malformations is particularly elevated for sodium valproate. In men, it may result in reduced fertility. Epilepsy and Pregnancy

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is incorrect. Phenytoin is not recommended for use during pregnancy. Furthermore, phenytoin is not an agent that would usually be considered as a first choice for the treatment of epilepsy, although it continues to have a role in the treatment of status epilepticus.

stem: A 42-year-old man has been in the Intensive Therapy Unit for 6 weeks following a road traffic collision in which he had crashed his car after drinking heavily. You are called to see him as it has been noticed that he appears to have developed painless limb weakness over the past 7–10 days. On examination of the lower limbs there is symmetrical, predominantly distal, weakness with absent ankle and knee reflexes. In the upper limbs there is some wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles bilaterally, worse on the right. The upper limb reflexes are retained. He has possible peripheral sensory loss to pinprick and light touch in a ‘glove and stocking’ distribution. Cranial nerves are normal. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Critical illness polyneuropathy
Prolonged stays (as a patient) on the Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU), irrespective of the underlying pathology, are associated with a risk of developing critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy. The neuropathy is axonal and can be predominantly sensory, predominantly motor, or mixed. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography may be indicated to confirm the diagnosis and exclude any other conditions (eg Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS)).

Alcoholic polyneuropathy
Alcoholic polyneuropathy is incorrect. Despite being oft quoted as a cause of neuropathy, there is a great deal of controversy as to whether alcohol can cause a neuropathy due to direct toxic effects on the peripheral nerve or if its effects are solely mediated through secondary nutritional deficiencies.

Critical illness myopathy
Critical illness myopathy is incorrect. Muscle wasting might raise suspicion of a critical illness myopathy but this is incorrect as it would not explain the obvious clinical features of neuropathy (reflex loss, sensory disturbance). Axonal loss is a key feature of critical illness polyneuropathy and therefore, although it might be possible for the wasting seen in the hands to be a manifestation of a myopathic process, it is more likely to be secondary to axonal loss due to neuropathy in this case.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is incorrect. It would be unusual for patients with GBS to have retained reflexes in the upper limb. Furthermore, facial weakness is common in GBS. Obviously it goes without saying that it would also be very unlucky for this gentleman to not only crash his car but then also develop a completely different and unrelated illness while he was in hospital. If doubt remains, the CSF should show cytoalbumologic dissociation in GBS, whereas it is usually normal in critical illness polyneuropathy. NCS/EMG would (usually) show a non-length-dependent demyelinating neuropathy (ie reduced velocities and conduction block) in GBS, although can be normal early in the disease course.

Nutritional polyneuropathy (beriberi)
Nutritional polyneuropathy (beriberi) is incorrect. Although nutritional polyneuropathy is a reasonable choice given the history of alcohol use and the fact that dry beriberi can mimic GBS, it is a less likely explanation for this presentation. Beriberi is usually associated with marked hyperalgesia/allodynia and burning dysesthesia, which is not mentioned here. Furthermore, nystagmus is common, as are other clinical features of alcohol misuse or malnutrition.

stem: A wheelchair-bound 19-year-old woman presents to clinic with difficulty reading. She has a known ArnoldChiari malformation that has progressively decreased her mobility. She says that the words appear to jump as she tries to follow text. On examination, she has a normal range of eye movements and normal ophthalmoscopy. However, the examiner notes nystagmus. Given the presenting symptom, which one of the following types of nystagmus might you expect to find in this patient?
explanation:
Downbeat
This is associated with lesions at the cervico-medullary junction. The difficulty in reading stems from upward deflections of the eyes when trying to follow stationary text on looking down. You can ask the patient whether they still have difficulty if they try reading the menu at coffee shops, which is usually positioned above their heads, when downbeat nystagmus should normally lessen or even disappear.

Brun’s
Brun’s is incorrect. This occurs in lesions of the cerebello-pontine angle, with peripheral vestibular nystagmus contralateral to the lesion and ipsilateral slow, large-amplitude, gaze-evoked nystagmus due to brainstem compression. Look in the question for other features of a large cerebello-pontine angle mass, such as V, VII and VIII cranial nerve palsies on the ipsilateral side to the low-amplitude nystagmus.

Convergence retraction
Convergence retraction is incorrect. This describes convergence retraction movements due to co-contraction of the extra-ocular muscles on attempted upgaze, and is due to a lesion in the dorsal midbrain.

Pendular
Pendular is incorrect. This describes nystagmus with no fast phase and is not cause-specific. It can be seen in multiple sclerosis.

Upbeat
Upbeat is incorrect. This is caused by lesions in the brainstem or occasionally by lesions in the cerebellar vermis. It is much rarer than downbeat nystagmus.

stem: Which of the following is likely to be most useful in confirming the diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI brain
The combination of sudden-onset severe headache (an indicator of an acute rise in ICP) and bitemporal hemianopia (an indicator of central optic chiasmal compression) suggest the phenomenon of “pituitary apoplexy” secondary to acute haemorrhage within the pituitary gland. This often occurs with pituitary adenomas which is suggested by the following: elevated prolactin – this is not because of prolactin secretion by the adenoma (as there are no premorbid symptoms such as galactorrhea or gynaecomastia) but rather an indication that the normal hypothalamic inhibitory pathways which influence anterior pituitary prolactin secretion have been damaged by the haemorrhage (loss of inhibition à increased secretion) mild hyponatraemia – either due to low ACTH secondary to direct corticotroph damage (which results in low cortisol and subsequently hyponatraemia) or inappropriate secretion of ADH (preferential retention of water dilutes serum Na concentrations) low TSH – due to direct damage of thyrotrophs by the haemorrhage. With all the above in mind, the investigation which is most likely to yield a diagnosis is an MRI brain as it will visualise the pituitary haemorrhage.

Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is incorrect. Although this patient has a sudden-onset headache, the presence of bitemporal hemianopia localises the problem to the optic chiasm, making pituitary pathology much more likely than a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Lumbar puncture is an important investigation in subarachnoid haemorrhage, following a CT scan. In this case, investigations are aimed at demonstrating or ruling out pituitary pathology; a lumbar puncture will not be discriminatory.

MRA
MRA is incorrect. MRA is useful for examining the vascular architecture, such as for identifying aneurysms. It is unnecessary in this case; the MRI will demonstrate whether there is a pituitary mass, and whether there is any bleeding or ischaemia within the pituitary itself.

Pituitary function testing
Pituitary function testing is incorrect. Although pituitary function testing (thyroid function tests, LH and FSH, prolactin, cortisol, IGF-1) is likely to be abnormal, it will not confirm whether the underlying cause is a tumour or apoplexy.

Visual evoked potentials.

stem: He is given an iv cephalosporin. Which of the following is the most appropriate procedure to deliver the diagnosis?
explanation:
CSF PCR
The sub-acute presentation, coupled with a very high cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis is consistent with tuberculous meningitis. Viral meningitis presents similarly, but CSF would be clear and CSF glucose would be greater than 60% of serum glucose. Fungal meningitis is rare and affects the immunocompromised, which is not described in this patient’s history. However, he is from West Africa, so TB meningitis is more likely than a typical bacterial meningitis, especially given the insidious nature of symptom onset. CSF PCR delivers rapid and accurate diagnosis, enabling anti-tuberculous therapy to commence promptly. Treatment of CNS TB consists of an intensive phase (4 drugs administered for 2 months) followed by a continuation phase (2 drugs administered for an additional 7 to 10 months), for a total treatment duration of 9 to 12 months. For adults, the intensive phase consists of four drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) administered for two months. And the continuation phase consists of 2 drugs (isoniazid and rifampin) for 7-10 months.

Blood culture
Blood culture is incorrect. A history of headaches, drowsiness, agitation, neck stiffness and a turbid CSF sample points to a diagnosis of bacterial, fungal or tuberculous meningitis. The subacute presentation, coupled with a very high cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis, is consistent with tuberculous meningitis. Blood culture may be abnormal if there is a bacteraemia, but will not give a definitive histological diagnosis of TB meningitis.

Chest x-ray
Chest X-ray is incorrect. Chest X-ray may be abnormal if he had pulmonary TB, but will not give a definitive histological diagnosis of TB meningitis.

CSF culture
CSF culture is incorrect. CSF microscopy and culture for acid-fast bacilli and subsequent ZN staining is often difficult, time-consuming and lacks sensitivity. On average a positive microscopy sample for tuberculosis is only identified in 25% of patients, although this increases to around 60% after culture.

MRI whole spine
MRI whole spine is incorrect. MRI spine may detect areas of spinal meningitis, or another cause of his back pain, but will not give a definitive histological diagnosis of TB meningitis.

stem: You are referred a 57-year-old woman with a marked change in personality over the last 5 years. She has become increasingly sexually flirtatious with inappropriate behaviour in social situations. Impairment of abstract thinking, memory and planning has become increasingly obvious. However, the ability to perform arithmetic tasks is relatively preserved. Speech output is diminished. There is no motor impairment. Physical examination is unremarkable except for the presence of grasp reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is associated with early personality change, although the exact nature of this change varies. Patients may present with disinhibition, or alternatively with apathy, loss of initiative and drive with impairment of frontal executive tasks. Speech gradually deteriorates and many patients develop aphasia. Neuroimaging might reveal isolated frontotemporal lobar atrophy. It usually presents in patients between the ages of 40 and 65. This patient has progressive behavioural change and dysexecutive symptoms so frontotemporaldementia is a likely diagnosis

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Alzheimer’s disease typically presents with poor memory and associated deficits in language, praxis and visuospatial functioning. Behaviour and insght are usually preserved until the advanced stages of the disease. It therefore seems unlikely in this case.

Frontal lobe meningioma
Frontal lobe meningioma is incorrect. Frontal lobe meningioma may present with a progressive frontal lobe disorder so is a reasonable differential diagnosis. The length of the presentation and lack of additional neurological signs probably favour FTD.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis can cause frontal signs and occasionally presents in a progressive manner in older individuals, but is likely to have prominent motor and sensory signs on examination. Frontotemporal DementiaYou are asked to review a 25-year-old man who complains of pain in his upper limbs exacerbated by coughing. You suspect he may have syringomyelia. Which one of the following is a typical early finding associated with a cervical syrinx?

Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is incorrect. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus presents with gait disturbance, cognitive deterioration and bladder symptoms. The absence of a gait disorder on neurological examination effectively excludes this diagnosis.

stem: A 20-year-old man with known epilepsy presents to the Emergency Department in status epilepticus. He has not responded to two doses of 10 mg rectal diazepam and has been having a seizure for over 10 minutes. Blood glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
explanation:
Phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenously
The patient has been seizing for over 10 minutes and there has been a failure of benzodiazepines. The patient can thus be said to be in ‘established status epilepticus’. At this stage, general consensus would be to load with intravenous phenytoin or valproate.

Diazepam 10 mg intravenously
Diazepam 10 mg intravenously is incorrect. Further use of benzodiazepines is unlikely to be of benefit and may cause respiratory depression. Second-line therapies should be commenced.

IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg
IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg is incorrect. Further use of benzodiazepines is unlikely to be of benefit and may cause respiratory depression. Second-line therapies should be commenced.

Propofol infusion
Propofol infusion is incorrect. The use of anaesthetic agents is usually restricted to the ‘refractory’ phase of status epilepticus and as such would only be administered if there is a failure of the second-line treatments.

Thiopental bolus
Thiopental bolus is incorrect. The use of anaesthetic agents is usually restricted to the ‘refractory’ phase of status epilepticus and as such would only be administered if there is a failure of the second-line treatments. Epilepsy and Seizures A 30-year-old woman with no relevant past medical history has presented with acute, binocular horizontal diplopia and severe headache. On examination there is a partial ptosis on the left and a dilated and unreactive left pupil. The left eye is abducted when looking straight ahead. Eye movement testing reveals moderate underaction of adduction, elevation and depression of the left eye. The right eye moves normally. There is intorsion of the left eye in downgaze. The rest of the neurological examination, including fundal examination, is normal. Blood pressure and blood glucose testing were normal in the Emergency Department.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is sent to see you with an unsteady gait. She reports that this has been coming on over about 9 months. She specifically has trouble on stairs, coming down as well as going up, but is not too bad on the flat. There are no symptoms in her arms or head/face. On examination, she has a broad-based gait, with impaired heel–toe walking. Tone power and reflexes are normal. There are no upper limb abnormalities. The only abnormality on testing the cranial nerves is that there is evidence of downbeat nystagmus. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Chiari malformation
The history of difficulty coming down stairs and the presence of downbeat nystagmus is highly suggestive of a structural lesion at the foramen magnum. Chiari malformation seems most likely in the absence of other signs.

Adult-onset cerebellar ataxia
Adult-onset cerebellar ataxia is incorrect. Adult-onset cerebellar ataxias are a heterogeneous group of rare genetically determined conditions (eg the numerous variations of spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA), numbered 1– 27 at present, with identified genetic mutations), presenting with a variety of cerebellar, pyramidal, peripheral nerve and extraocular signs. In general presentation of such inherited progressive cerebellar ataxias occurs earlier in adult life, and the relatively late presentation, as well as the absence of other signs, makes such a diagnosis less likely in this case. Structural lesions need to be ruled out before making suchChat a diagnosis. with Brainstem lacunar stroke
Brainstem lacunar stroke is incorrect. The slow onset of symptoms is not consistent with a stroke, making this a less likely option.

Foramen magnum meningioma
Foramen magnum meningioma is incorrect. A meningioma at the foramen magnum could certainly cause this picture, but it might also be associated with corticospinal signs in her legs.

Paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia.

stem: A 24-year-old male, injecting heroin addict presented with rapidly progressive, mild, generalised limb weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia and a dry mouth. Some 12 hours after admission he suddenly deteriorated resulting in a respiratory arrest, following which he required ventilation. On examination in the Intensive Therapy Unit he was alert and orientated. He had bilateral ptosis, dilated unreactive pupils, diplopia on both horizontal and vertical gaze, with restriction of eye movements in all directions and profound bilateral facial weakness. He now has marked weakness in all four limbs with depressed reflexes. Both plantar responses are flexor. Sensory testing is normal. He had recently been prescribed antibiotics by his GP for an infected injection site in his groin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Botulism
Wound botulism should be considered in any injecting drug user who presents with descending motor weakness and autonomic signs. This typically presents as a descending paralysis, starting with cranial nerves, and also has involvement of the autonomic system. Early diagnosis and treatment are vital. The main differential diagnosis is a variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), which could produce a similar clinical picture of cranial nerve palsies and autonomic dysfunction, but this syndrome was pure motor, which would be unusual. The dilated pupils are unusual in GBS but can be seen in Miller–Fisher variants, although in those cases significant motor weakness is rare.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. As outlined the pure motor syndrome picture makes this less likely a diagnosis when compared to botulism.

Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is incorrect. LEMS rarely presents with such profoundly abnormal eye movements and pupil dilation would be unusual. He has no obvious risk factor for LEMS (small-cell lung cancer, for example), whereas he has an obvious risk factor for botulism.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is another possibility, but would not explain the dry mouth, fixed pupils or areflexia.

Posterior circulation stroke
Posterior circulation stroke is incorrect. The signs do not suggest an upper motor neurone lesion, so posterior circulation stroke is unlikely.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of severe progressive incapacitating headaches. She spends most of her time lying flat, as in this position she is headache-free. She has no other complaints. She is using up to eight co-codamol tablets a day. She has suffered from migraine since the age of 13 years. Examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic daily headache secondary to analgesic overuse
explanation:
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension
The most important aspect in this patient is the postural nature of the headache, pointing strongly to this diagnosis. Low cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure headache is a distinct and familiar syndrome that is seen most frequently following lumbar puncture, but may also occur either following an episode of possible minor trauma to meninges (eg sports injury to neck or back) or without apparent cause. The lower limit of the normal range for CSF pressure is generally considered to be 10 cm H 2O. The mechanism of SIH is thought to be insidious CSF leak that leads to low CSF pressure, expressed clinically as orthostatic headache in association with one or more of numerous symptoms including nausea, vomiting, horizontal diplopia, unsteadiness or vertigo, altered hearing, neck pain/stiffness, interscapular pain and occasionally visual-field abnormalities. The headache may be gradual, subacute or thunderclap in onset. Diagnosis may be confirmed by measuring CSF opening pressure at lumbar puncture: by very definition, the opening CSF pressure is low, and often a ‘dry’ tap is encountered. However, the pressure may be normal, especially with intermittent leaks and may vary tap to tap. CSF fluid analysis is normal. MRI studies typically reveal diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement, frequently in association with ‘sagging’ of the brain, tonsilar descent and posterior fossa crowding. Although conservative measures are often undertaken first (bed rest, analgesia, increased fluid intake) epidural blood patch is the treatment of choice.

Chronic daily headache secondary to analgesic overuse
This possibly should be considered as it often complicates chronic headaches. However, the positional nature of the headache in this case indicates the correct answer.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is a high-pressure headache that tends to be worse when lying flat and is worse in the morning, often associated with papilloedema. This syndrome is often observed in association with obesity or various medications including vitamin-A derivatives, tetracyclines and steroids. In such cases, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis should be excluded.

Migraine
Migraine is usually associated with episodic pain, which may be unilateral or bilateral, throbbing or sharp, and is commonly accompanied by nausea, photophobia, phonophobia and vomiting.

Tension headache
Tension headache presents with a band-like sensation around the head that is usually bilateral and not aggravated by physical activity. 252 Headache -.

stem: A 70-year-old man is sent to the Memory Clinic for assessment by his GP. He has become increasingly forgetful and confused, having lost his bearings in the local supermarket twice in the past few months, and his wife is finding he puts items in inappropriate places around the house. On examination his BP is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. His chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender, and he has a BMI of 26. There is no focal neurological deficit, although his MMSE is reduced at 23/30. CT head reveals changes consistent with cerebral atrophy. Which of the following is most likely to accumulate in his brain?
explanation:
Amyloid
A variety of amyloid plaques are observed in Alzheimer’s disease, the most likely diagnosis here. Diffuse amyloid plaques have a loose accumulation of β/A4 amyloid without surrounding abnormal neurites, and are considered to be precursors of neuritic plaques. The mature neuritic plaque consists of a dense core of β/A4 amyloid surrounded by a halo and ring of abnormal neurites. A hypermature plaque has a dense core of β/A4 amyloid surrounded by reactive astrocytes but without abnormal neurons.

Acute-phase proteins
Acute-phase proteins is incorrect. Acute-phase proteins such as CRP are elevated in patients with Alzheimer’s disease, but they are not the primary cause of protein plaques in patients with the condition.

Immunoglobulins
Immunoglobulins is incorrect. Immunoglobulins do not normally accumulate in the brain parenchyma in patients with Alzheimer’s disease, but are seen in some inflammatory brain conditions.

β2-Microglobulin
β2-Microglobulin is incorrect. It accumulates and can aggregate into amyloid fibres in patients who are on longterm haemodialysis. It can also be elevated in patients with multiple myeloma and lymphoma. Alzheimer’s Disease

Transthyretin
Transthyretin is incorrect. Transthyretin is a transport protein for thyroid hormone and retinol binding protein, and accumulates in patients with familial amyloidosis, leading to peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 45-year-old man was involved in a motorcycle accident and suffered a thoracic spine fracture, paralysis and a sensory level below T4. He presents to the neurology clinic some 3 years later with sensory loss in a shawl-like distribution over his shoulders, and weakness affecting both hands that has been gradually progressing. On examination, he has a spastic paraparesis below T4. Altered sensation is noted to C8. There is decreased tone in both upper limbs, and movement appears limited by pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Post-traumatic syringomyelia
The slowly progressive sensory and motor symptoms seen here are consistent with development of a posttraumatic syrinx. Post-traumatic syringomyelia often presents with pain, which spreads upwards from the initial injury site. MRI of the spinal cord is the diagnostic modality of choice. Serial examinations are needed to document progression and to help correlate MRI appearance with symptoms. Surgery is required to prevent expansion of the syrinx, and timing of this is dependent on symptoms and MRI progression.

Anterior spinal artery thrombosis
Anterior spinal artery thrombosis is incorrect. This is the most common spinal cord infarction and is characterised by loss of motor function below the level of injury, loss of pain and temperature sensations, and preservation of proprioception, fine touch and vibration.

Autonomic dysreflexia
Autonomic dysreflexia is incorrect. Autonomic dysreflexia occurs due to unopposed sympathetic outflow below the level of a spinal cord lesion.

Myofascial pain syndrome
Myofascial pain syndrome is incorrect. Myofascial pain is a syndrome of chronic pain, where multiple focal tender points exist that are thought to correspond to areas of fascial restriction.

Post-traumatic spinal stenosis
Post-traumatic spinal stenosis is incorrect. This would result in neurological changes below the level of stenosis.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. She has noticed that his walking has deteriorated over the past few months. He has also become incontinent of urine and she feels he may be confused. A history of shingles 1 month ago is noted. They admit to his drinking two glasses of wine per day. On examination he has a broad-based shuffling gait and poor short-term memory. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical history?
explanation:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) presents with the classic triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia. This appears to be what is described in the clinical case here and this patient should be investigated with a MRI brain scan to look for dilated ventricles. If present, a lumbar puncture could be performed, with large-volume CSF removal, to look for clinical evidence of improvement.

Alcoholic dementia
Alcoholic dementia is incorrect. Alcohol-related dementia is unlikely given the modest alcohol intake.

Herpes zoster encephalitis
Herpes zoster encephalitis is incorrect. Despite the recent shingles, herpes zoster encephalitis seems unlikely, as this would be an acute illness with headache, fever, confusion and possibly seizures.

Intracerebral neoplasm
Intracerebral neoplasm is incorrect. Intracerebral neoplasm would need to be considered here given the relatively short duration of the history. However, the presence of the classic triad for NPH and lack of focal signs, headache or seizures make a brain tumour less likely.

Multi-infarct dementia
Multi-infarct dementia is incorrect. Multi-infarct dementia typically presents with stepwise deterioration, not described here, and may be associated with focal upper motor neurone signs on examination.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 4-year history of a progressive difficulty in speaking. Her friends have noticed that she struggles to remember their names and struggles to find the correct word for certain objects, often resorting to calling them ‘thingy’. Physical examination is normal. A neuropsychological profile identifies deficits only when performing tasks that involve naming or assigning meaning to objects. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Semantic dementia
The history is suggestive of semantic dementia, a form of frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Frontotemporal dementia tends to affect individuals at a younger age than Alzheimer’s disease. The peak age of onset is 55–65 years. FTD comprises three principal forms: Behavioral variant: the most common form (~60%), usually presenting with change in social skills, emotions, personal conduct and self-awareness. Many are misdiagnosed with a psychological illness. Pathology primarily affects the frontal lobes. Semantic dementia: accounts for approximately 20% of cases of FTD. Presents with a very specific deficit in semantic memory (the ability to associate meaning to objects presented via visual or auditory modalities). As in this case, difficulties recognising faces (prosopagnosia) and naming objects are common. Patients will often use ‘higher order substitutions’ when attempting to name objects. For example, when struggling (often with great frustration) to find the word for ‘apple’ a patient will resort to calling it simply ‘fruit’. Pathology primarily affects the temporal lobes. Progressive non-fluent aphasia: accounts for the remaining 20% of cases of FTD. In this disorder, semantic memory is maintained but the patient is unable to verbalise normally. Speech becomes slow and laboured, with speaking on the telephone being particularly difficult. Pathology primarily affects the left perisylvian region.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. It would be reasonable to opt for this answer, given that Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is by far the most common form of dementia worldwide, but there are a number of features here that make this answer less likely. First, the patient is quite young for AD. Although familial forms of AD can present in presenile years, these are exceedingly rare. Second, there is a very focal deficit in this case and, importantly, no deficits in other domains of memory are apparent. Although problems with semantic memory and indeed the fluency of speech can occur in AD, it would be unusual for the deficits to be restricted to only these areas. Furthermore, people with AD have prominent problems with episodic memory (eg remembering what happened yesterday). The absence of this deficit in FTD means that patients often go misdiagnosed for many years.

Corticobasal degeneration
Corticobasal degeneration is incorrect. Corticobasal degeneration is a rare neurodegenerative disorder in which language problems (usually a non-fluent aphasia) occur in combination with prominent physical abnormalities (parkinsonism and apraxia). The normal physical examination in this case and the fact that the language problem is one of a deficit in semantics rather than the fluency of speech, make this answer incorrect.

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is incorrect. CJD is a prion disease which can present with a rapidly progressive dementia. The lack of any physical abnormalities after 4 years virtually excludes this possibility.

Depressive pseudo-dementia
Depressive pseudo-dementia is incorrect. Low mood can cause apparent problems with memory, primarily through a lack of attentiveness and motivation. The deficits presented in this case, along with the progressive deterioration over 4 years make this possibility unlikely. Frontotemporal DementiaYou are referred a 57-year-old woman with a marked change in personality over the last 5 years. She has become increasingly sexually flirtatious with inappropriate behaviour in social situations. Impairment of abstract thinking, memory and planning has become increasingly obvious. However, the ability to perform arithmetic tasks is relatively preserved. Speech output is diminished. There is no motor impairment. Physical examination is unremarkable except for the presence of grasp reflexes.

stem: A 23-year-old man attends the neurology clinic for review. He was previously injured in a motorcycle accident where he suffered a T9 fracture and extensive damage to the spinal cord. Although he had significant muscle weakness below the level of the lesion, pain and temperature sensation had been preserved. He now reports pain and temperature loss over part of his body. He admits to drinking 5 units of alcohol per day. On examination you can demonstrate loss of pain and temperature sensation over the upper back, shoulders and upper arms. Fine touch appears to be preserved. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Syringomyelia
Post-traumatic syringomyelia is a well-recognised long-term complication of extensive spinal cord injury. Classically it causes sensory disturbance with a loss of pain and temperature sensation, but preservation of light touch (as seen here). The syrinx is a fluid-filled cyst existing in the central spinal cord, and compresses the anterior horn (lower motor neurones) and spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature sensation); this causes weakness (not evident here, as there was pre-existing weakness from the accident) and sensory disturbance. Usually the dorsal columns (light touch and proprioception) are spared, but as the syrinx expands it may involve these tracts. It is not clear exactly why the syrinx develops, but possible causes include: liquefaction of intraparenchymal haematoma; ischaemia due to tethering; arterial or venous obstruction; release of intracellular lysosomal enzymes; and mechanical damage from cord compression. MRI is indicated to confirm the diagnosis, followed by a neurosurgical opinion to inform management.

Delayed scar fibrosis
Delayed scar fibrosis is incorrect. Delayed scar fibrosis leads to a tethering of the cord to the dura, and usually causes further weakness in the muscles at the level of the original injury (ie at the level of T9 in this patient). Occasionally it can also cause pain at the level of the injury (again, at T9). This patient does not describe any change in strength, or any pain. The clinical picture here is of a central cord syndrome, not of tethering related to scar fibrosis.

Functional disorder
Functional disorder is incorrect. Although functional neurological disorders are not uncommon, and can co-exist with organic disease, it should be a diagnosis of exclusion. This patient clearly has symptoms and signs consistent with a central cord syndrome, of which the most likely cause is syringomyelia, and therefore this is not a functional disorder.

Peripheral neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy is incorrect. Peripheral neuropathy does cause sensory disturbance, beginning distally and progressing proximally. However, where pain and temperature fibres are affected, usually there is neuropathic pain; this patient does not describe any pain. If this was peripheral neuropathy, you would expect associated loss of light touch and vibration sense, which is preserved in this patient. Instead, syringomyelia causes a dissociated sensory loss: light touch and vibration sense are either unaffected or affected across a different distribution to pain and temperature sensory loss.

Spinal osteoarthritis
Spinal osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis would not cause a dissociated sensory loss (affecting pain and temperature without affecting light touch and vibration sense). Osteophytes and degenerative disease can Chatloss withdescribed cause a radiculopathy, leading to pain in the upper limb, but you would not expect the sensory here.

stem: Which of the following would best fit with the clinical picture?
explanation:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
The triad of gait disturbance, memory loss and urinary incontinence fits best with a diagnosis of normalpressure hydrocephalus. Neuroimaging with either CT or MRI, coupled with large-volume lumbar puncture and assessment of neurological status post-lumbar puncture, are the assessments of choice.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Urinary incontinence and gait unsteadiness would be expected late in Alzheimer’s disease rather than being seen early as here.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. Gait unsteadiness and urinary incontinence are not features of depression.

Multi-infarct dementia
Multi-infarct dementia is incorrect. Multi-infarct dementia might be considered here given the vascular risk factor of hypertension, but would typically be associated with a step-wise rather than gradual progression, frequently in the context of an established history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack.

Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is incorrect. Wernicke-Korsakoff is not expected as his alcohol intake is not excessively high, his alanine transaminase is normal and there is no evidence of confabulation, a prominent feature of memory loss associated with thiamine deficiency.

stem: A 45-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic presents with a 72-hour history of horizontal diplopia. The images separate wider on rightward gaze. Covering his right eye on right gaze results in the disappearance of the outer image. Dysfunction of which cranial nerve is most likely to be causing these problems?
explanation:
Right abducens
The effects of paresis on diplopia can be easily predicted by three rules. The direction in which the distance between the images is at a maximum is the direction of action of the paretic muscles. Paresis of the horizontally acting muscles tends to produce mainly horizontal diplopia. Finally, the image projected further from the centre belongs to the paretic eye. In this case the patient has a right abducens nerve palsy as there is horizontal diplopia on looking to the right and the outer image disappears when the right eye is covered.

Left abducens
Left abducens is incorrect. A left abducens palsy produces diplopia, with horizontal separation of images on looking to the left.

Left trochlear
Left trochlear is incorrect. Trochlear nerve palsies produce diplopia on looking downward due to failure of the superior oblique muscle.

Right oculomotor
Right oculomotor is incorrect. A right oculomotor palsy would produce ptosis, deviation of the eye in a ‘down and out’ position and possibly a dilated pupil (depending on whether autonomic fibres were compromised).

Right trochlear
Right trochlear is incorrect. Trochlear nerve palsies produce diplopia on looking downward due to failure of the superior oblique muscle. Eye Movements and StrabismusA 22-year-old university student exhibits involuntary head twitching and flicking of his hands. He also says that he suffers from embarrassing grunting which can affect him at almost any time. When he is in lectures at the university he manages to control it, but often when he comes home and relaxes the movements and noises get the better of him. His girlfriend who attends the consultation with him tells you that he seems very easily distracted and often is really very annoying, repeating things which she says to him and mimicking her. On further questioning it transpires that this has actually been a problem since childhood. On examination his BP is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 74 beats/min and regular. His heart sounds are normal, respiratory, abdominal and neurological examinations are entirely normal. Investigations.

stem: A 62-year-old woman complains of unsteadiness when walking. On examination she has pyramidal weakness of her left lower limb, and reduced pain and temperature sensation of her right leg and right side of her trunk up to the level of the umbilicus. Joint position sense is impaired at her left great toe but is normal elsewhere. She has a definite left extensor plantar response, and the right plantar response is equivocal. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Left mid-thoracic cord
The clinical signs are those of the Brown–Séquard syndrome, or hemicord syndrome. This is characterised by ipsilateral pyramidal signs, ipsilateral dorsal column sensory loss and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss, because of the anatomical arrangement of these tracts in the cord. The sensory level is around T10 and therefore the lesion is likely to be above this; however, there are no symptoms or signs in her upper limbs and therefore a cervical cord lesion is unlikely. As a result the lesion localises to the thoracic cord. In Brown–Séquard syndrome the lesion is on the same side as the pyramidal tract signs so left mid-thoracic cord must be correct.

Left cervical cord
Left cervical cord is incorrect. In a lesion of the left cervical cord one would expect a Brown–Séquard pattern of symptoms and signs to affect both upper and lower limbs.

Left lumbosacral plexus
Left lumbosacral plexus is incorrect. A lesion of the left lumbosacral plexus would result in lower motor neurone signs in the left leg, potentially with sensory loss/alteration crossing multiple dermatomes in that limb. There would be no upper motor neurone signs.

Midline mid-thoracic cord
Midline mid-thoracic cord is incorrect. Midline thoracic cord lesions would produce bilateral signs in the trunk and lower limbs, depending on the precise size of the lesion.

Right mid-thoracic cord
Right mid-thoracic cord is incorrect. Right mid-thoracic cord lesions would produce the opposite pattern of symptoms and signs described here.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends your clinic and gives a description of recurrent early morning and nocturnal attacks of severe throbbing unilateral orbital pain over the last 2 months. There is tearing and conjunctival injection corresponding to the headaches. Each attack lasts about 1 hour, but leaves a dull ache around the eye lasting for a few hours. These have not occurred previously. She feels that her lifestyle is severely compromised and is becoming depressed. There are no abnormalities on examination. Blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cluster headaches
The patient’s symptoms are characteristic of cluster headache. Severe, brief headaches occurring with diurnal variation are typical. The presence of autonomic symptoms is common and such problems should be specifically enquired about.

Analgesic overuse headaches
Analgesic overuse headaches is incorrect. There is no history given of analgesic overuse and, in addition, this usually produces a chronic daily headache syndrome.

Migraine without aura
Migraine without aura is incorrect. Migraine is possible, but the length of attack (too short), the frequency and the occurrence first thing in the morning and at night are all suggestive of cluster headache.

Paroxysmal hemicrania
Paroxysmal hemicranias is incorrect. Paroxysmal hemicranias cause pain of much shorter duration.

Parotid tumour.

stem: Which one of the following is a cause of second-order-neurone Horner syndrome?
explanation:
Pancoast’s tumour
Horner syndrome is also known as oculo-sympathetic paresis and is characterised by miosis, ptosis and anhydrosis. Lesions along the sympathetic chain along the head and neck region can cause these clinical appearances. The causes of Horner syndrome can vary with age, and can be elicited by thinking about lesions that could affect its path. The first-order (central) neurone descends from the hypothalamus to the cervical spine. The second-order (preganglionic) neurone exits the spinal cord and heads towards the head and neck. It travels along its path with the cervical sympathetic chain, the brachial plexus, lung apices (Pancoasttumour) to synapse at the superior cervical ganglion. This is located near the angle of the mandible and is in close proximity to the common carotid artery. The third-order (postganglionic) neurone begins at the superior cervical ganglion and travels along the wall of the internal carotid artery into the cavernous sinus. Lesions along its path affecting the internal carotid artery or within the cranium can affect its function.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis is incorrect. Cavernous sinus lesions are classed as third order (post-ganglionic) cause of Horner syndrome

Craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma is incorrect. The first-order (central) neurone descends from the hypothalamus to the cervical spine (ciliospinal centre of Budge), and can be affected by craniopharyngioma.

Internal carotid artery aneurysm
Internal carotid artery aneurysm is incorrect. Lesions of the third-order neurone affect the internal carotid artery.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is incorrect. The first-order (central) neurone descends from the hypothalamus to the cervical spine (ciliospinal centre of Budge), and can be affected by syringomelia.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy for him?
explanation:
Propranolol
This patient has essential tremor for which propranolol or topiramate are the usual first-line therapies. Primidone can also be used, but often causes drowsiness. Essential tremor is characterised Chat by upper limb with postural and action tremor without rest tremor. Parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia or rigidity are absent. The neck and voice (due to involvement of the larynx) can also become tremulous. There is a positive family history in over 50% of cases and the tremor classically improves after the consumption of alcohol.

Co-careldopa
Co-careldopa is incorrect. Co-careldopa is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease.

Pramipexole
Pramipexole is incorrect. Pramipexole is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease.

Ropinirole
Ropinirole is incorrect. Ropinirole is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease. Essential TremorSelegiline
Selegiline is incorrect. Selegiline is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is sent to the Emergency Department urgently. She is 36 weeks’ pregnant. She describes headache and simultaneous onset of right-sided numbness and dysphasia. She initially developed tingling in the right side of her face that spread over a matter of several minutes to the right hand. Some 10 minutes later she noticed she was having word-finding difficulty and that her right arm felt clumsy. The whole attack resolved completely within 20–30 minutes. By the time she arrived in the Emergency Department her neurological examination was normal. There is a previous history of headaches and vomiting as a teenager, which varied according to her menstrual cycle. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spontaneous dissection of the right internal carotid artery
Transient ischaemic attack secondary to left hemisphere small-vessel disease
explanation:
Migraine with aura
The spread of symptoms over 10–15 minutes is indicative of migraine aura. Word-finding difficulty is a common migraine aura symptom. The previous history of migrainous headache is supportive.

Cerebral venous thrombosis
Cerebral venous thrombosis is incorrect. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is more common in late pregnancy and the puerperium, but spontaneously resolving symptoms would be unusual and there may be other signs on examination such as papilloedema.

Partial epileptic seizure
Partial epileptic seizure is incorrect. The spread of symptoms is too slow for a partial seizure and the total duration of the attack is too long for this diagnosis to be considered likely.

Spontaneous dissection of the right internal carotid artery
Spontaneous dissection of the right internal carotid artery is incorrect.
