Spontaneous dissection of the right internal carotid artery may be asymptomatic or may result in ipsilateral face and neck pain, possibly with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. If a thrombus forms and then embolises, an ischaemic anterior circulation stroke or TIA may occur. The history here of spreading sensory deficits is not suggestive of an ischaemic stroke.

Transient ischaemic attack secondary to left hemisphere small-vessel disease
Transient ischaemic attack (TIA) secondary to left hemisphere small-vessel disease is incorrect. TIA secondary to left hemisphere small vessel disease would be expected to produce a sudden onset of sensory and motor symptoms. Dysphasia does not usually occur in subcortical small-vessel disease.

stem: A 54-year-old man is diagnosed with Huntington’s disease, and comes to the Neurology Clinic with his family to discuss implications of the diagnosis. He has two children who are aged 19 and 15. He asks about the risks for his children with respect to Huntington’s disease. Which of the following is correct?
options: Symptoms are likely to occur at a younger age
Symptoms are likely to occur at an older age
Symptoms are likely to be less severe
There is only a 25% chance of inheriting the disease
There is a 100% chance of inheriting the disease
explanation:
Symptoms are likely to occur at a younger age
Huntington’s disease is caused by mutations in the Huntingtin gene (HTT). HTT is present in humans. People with Huntington’s disease have a trinucleotide repeat that is longer than normal, which makes the gene defective and creates the Huntingtin protein that is the result of symptoms. The mutation is dominant with nearly full penetration. Because of this, it is an autosomal dominant disease. As the number of repeat trinucleotides builds over generations, there is earlier onset of disease with increased penetrance. This is termed genetic anticipation.

Symptoms are likely to occur at an older age
Symptoms are likely to occur at an older age is incorrect. If a child is affected with the gene there is likely to be genetic anticipation and therefore earlier, rather than later, onset of disease.

Symptoms are likely to be less severe
Symptoms are likely to be less severe is incorrect. The symptoms and severity of Huntington’s may vary over generations according to the number of trinucleotide repeats, although the disease is invariably progressive.

There is only a 25% chance of inheriting the disease
There is only a 25% chance of inheriting the disease is incorrect. The chance of inheritance is 50% as this is an autosomal dominant condition. If it had been an autosomal recessive condition and the partner was a carrier, then the risk of inheritance would be 25%.

There is a 100% chance of inheriting the disease
There is a 100% chance of inheriting the disease is incorrect. This chance of inheritance would occur when a mother has a mitochondrial disease, or if a condition with the affected gene on the Y chromosome has a son. Huntington’s DiseaseA 26-year-old female intravenous drug user attends the Emergency Department with increasing muscle rigidity and difficulty closing her mouth. On examination, she has globally increased tone with neck stiffness and trismus. She finds it very difficult to sit up owing to abdominal muscle spasm. Her BP is measured at 155/90 mmHg, with a pulse of 88 beats/min. You notice necrotising areas around multiple recent puncture sites.

stem: A 42-year-old former motorcyclist comes to the Neurology Clinic for review some 2 months after hemitransection of his cord at the level of T10 after an accident. What would you expect one of the neurological findings to be?
options: Contralateral loss of pinprick and temperature sensation below T10
Contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception below T10
explanation:
Contralateral loss of pinprick and temperature sensation below T10
This occurs because the lateral spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature sensations, crosses to the opposite side of the spinal cord shortly after entering. Thus, damage to one side of the spinal cord affects these sensory pathways on the opposite side. In Brown-Séquard syndrome, the lesion interrupts the lateral spinothalamic tract on the same side, but since these fibres have already crossed, the sensory loss manifests contralaterally. This is a hallmark feature of Brown-Séquard syndrome, where the patient experiences contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion.

Contralateral gross muscle wasting
Muscle wasting typically results from lower motor neuron damage or disuse and is more pronounced on the same side as the injury in lower motor neuron lesions. In the context of a spinal cord hemitransection, we would expect muscle wasting to be ipsilateral due to corticospinal tract involvement. The corticospinal tract  (responsible for motor control) does not cross over until it reaches the medulla, leading to ipsilateral effects, not contralateral.

Contralateral increased tone
Increased muscle tone, or spasticity, is usually associated with upper motor neuron lesions, which in this case would be on the same side as the spinal cord lesion. The corticospinal tract, which is involved in controlling voluntary movements, descends ipsilaterally in the spinal cord and crosses at the medulla. Therefore, damage to this tract results in increased tone on the same side as the lesion.

Contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception below T10
The dorsal columns, which carry vibration and proprioception sensations, remain uncrossed in the spinal cord and only decussate (cross) at the medulla. Therefore, damage to these pathways within the spinal cord causes ipsilateral deficits below the level of the lesion. Patients with a T10 hemitransection would experience loss of vibration and proprioception on the same side as the lesion, not the opposite side.

Contralateral weakness
The corticospinal tract, responsible for motor control, crosses at the medulla, meaning the effects of a spinal cord lesion occur on the same side as the lesion. Therefore, damage to the corticospinal tract within the spinal cord results in ipsilateral weakness, not contralateral. In the case of a T10 hemitransection, the patient would exhibit weakness on the same side as the lesion, consistent with the pattern of upper motor neuron lesions.

stem: She is concerned about tremor as a possible drug side-effect. Which one of the following medications is most appropriate for her?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine would probably be the best medication to start in this setting. Apart from potential drowsiness, lamotrigine is relatively free of CNS side-effects, the most common reported adverse event Chat being rash. It also with doesn’t interfere with the metabolism of the oral contraceptive pill and is relatively safe versus other options in early pregnancy.

Clonazepam
Clonazepam is associated with sedation and would not be used in this setting routinely; clonazepam is not a first-line treatment for focal epilepsy.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is associated ataxia and nystagmus, even in some patients at doses within the therapeutic range. It also leads to gum hypertrophy. It can not be used in this setting as it is an old AED and is no longer considered a first line option.

Primidone
Primidone is primarily associated with sedation and would not be used in this setting routinely; primidone is not a first-line treatment for focal epilepsy. Primidone can be used to treat essential tremor. Epilepsy and Pregnancy

Topiramate
Whilst topiramate is a useful antiepileptic agent it is not first line. Additionally it is contraindicated in pregnancy or those planning pregnancy due to teratogenicity.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after moving a number of heavy boxes at home. On examination there is pain on straight-leg raising and movement of the lower limbs is limited by pain. There is mild weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and weakness of big toe extension. Ankle jerk reflexes are normal. Sensation is altered over the lateral border of the shin. This suggests an L5 nerve root lesion. Which one of the following represents the management of choice in this case?
explanation:
Gentle mobilisation and physiotherapy
This patient has symptoms typical of lumbar radiculopathy due to disc disease. Gentle mobilisation and physiotherapy represents the management of choice in this case, as most patients will make a spontaneous improvement within 4–6 weeks.

Immobilisation and complete bed rest
Immobilisation and complete bed rest is incorrect. A prolonged period of immobilisation may prolong recovery time and duration of pain.

Local corticosteroid injection
Local corticosteroid injection is incorrect. Local corticosteroid injection may be tried in patients with ongoing symptoms who do not wish to have surgery, or who are otherwise unfit for surgery.

Referral for microdiscectomy
Referral for microdiscectomy is incorrect. Microdiscectomy is a potential treatment options for patients with radiologically proven nerve root compression and severe symptoms or symptoms that do not resolve with conservative measures.

Referral for open discectomy
Referral for open discectomy is incorrect. Open discectomy is a potential treatment option for patients with radiologically proven nerve root compression and severe symptoms or symptoms that do not resolve with conservative measures.

stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic atrial fibrillation is on warfarin. He has had two unprovoked tonic–clonic seizures that were witnessed by his wife. CT brain shows only some diffuse ischaemic changes in the white matter. The GP wants to start him on an antiepileptic drug. Which one of the following antiepileptic drugs does not have important drug interactions with warfarin?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine has no effect on liver enzymes and does not interact with warfarin. Drug interactions and side effect profiles should always be considered before introducing antiepileptic drugs (AEDs). Choice of AED should be made in collaboration with the patient, particularly taking into account the patient’s other medical problems and other medications (particularly oral contraceptives) taken.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Carbamazepine is a liver enzyme inducer.

Phenobarbital
Phenobarbital is incorrect. Phenobarbital is a liver enzyme inducer.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is incorrect. Phenytoin is a liver enzyme inducer.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with increasing headaches around his left forehead over the past few months, and has now developed left third nerve palsy. He has a past medical history of osteoarthritis of the right knee and he smokes five cigarettes per day. On examination the left eye looks down and out. Movements of the right eye are normal. Blood pressure is 172/95 mmHg, with pulse 74 bpm; he is obese. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
A posterior communicating artery aneurysm is characteristically associated with a third nerve palsy. Not only can these aneurysms present with a typical subarachnoid haemorrhage, but also they can present with an isolated oculomotor nerve palsy (OMNP) or a non-traumatic subdural haematoma (SDH). They are treated either surgically or endovascularly.

Anterior communicating artery aneurysm
Anterior communicating artery aneurysm is incorrect. Anterior communicating artery aneurysms are associated with a bitemporal hemianopia.

Internal carotid artery aneurysm
Internal carotid artery aneurysm is incorrect. Internal carotid artery aneurysms are associated with increased risk of embolic phenomena and, as such, symptoms of an anterior territory stroke may be seen.

Middle cerebral artery aneurysm
Middle cerebral artery syndrome is incorrect. Contralateral hemiparesis and hemi-sensory loss in the face and upper and lower extremities is the most common presentation of middle cerebral artery syndrome.

Vertebral artery aneurysm
Vertebral artery aneurysm is incorrect. Vertebral artery aneurysms are rare; dissections are seen, however, and are associated with symptoms of a posterior territory stroke. Oculomotor Nerve (cranial nerve III).

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with a brief episode of dysphasia associated with mild right arm weakness. The symptoms resolved spontaneously after 4 hours. She has no previous history of note, and no identifiable stroke risk factors. After being seen at the TIA clinic, she undergoes MRI with carotid angiography. This shows a tiny infarct in the left middle-cerebral artery territory. In addition, there is an abnormal appearance of the middle portion of the internal carotid arteries, described as being like a ‘string of beads’, with areas of concentric stenosis. Which cause of her vascular disease is most likely?
options: Underlying previously undiagnosed autoimmune collagen disease
explanation:
Fibromuscular dysplasia
Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory condition that principally affects the carotid and renal arteries. It occurs in woman much more than in men, most often between 15 and 50 years of age, but it can present even later in individuals in whom it has been clinically silent for many years. The aetiology is unknown; there are associations with certain other disorders, including Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan syndrome, phaeochromocytoma and Takayasu’s disease. The classic ‘string of beads’ appearance (seen in this case) is caused by medial hyperplasia. Treatment involves both optimal management of other vascular risk factors and angioplasty where appropriate.

Atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis is incorrect. Atherosclerosis is unlikely in a younger person without conventional vascular risk factors.

Spontaneous internal carotid artery dissection
Spontaneous internal carotid artery dissection is incorrect. Carotid artery dissection is a relatively common cause of stroke in younger patients but typically occurs unilaterally, whereas the imaging changes in this case affect both carotids. A ‘string of beads’ appearance is not usually seen.

Underlying previously undiagnosed autoimmune collagen disease
Underlying previously undiagnosed autoimmune collagen disease is incorrect. There are no clinical cues that this patient may have an undiagnosed autoimmune collagen disease so this answer is unlikely. Transient Ischaemic Attack

Vasculitis
Vasculitis is incorrect. There are no clinical indicators of vasculitis (fever, constitutional symptoms, headache, raised inflammatory markers), so this answer is less likely.

stem: A 40-year-old banker came to the Emergency Department complaining of intense headache of 2 hours’ duration. The pain is localised around the right eye and is associated with tearing and redness of the eye. The patient reported he has had similar episodes over the last year. He also admits that these episodes occurred every day for a few weeks with one to three attacks a day, which last for 1 to 2 hours, frequently at night. After 6 weeks, the attacks stopped. He lost his job 6 months ago and has noticed an increase in the intensity of the pain since. Examination reveals drooping of the eyelid and small pupil on the right side. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Cluster headache
The features presented here are typical of cluster headache. Cluster headache afflicts less than 1 in 1000 in the general population. The majority of sufferers are men. The syndrome is characterised by frequent attacks of intense pain localised in and around the eye on one side, characteristically accompanied by conjunctival injection and lacrimation in this eye, along with nasal stuffiness on the same side and sometimes Horner syndrome. All signs and symptoms are strictly unilateral and occur during attacks lasting between 15 min and 3 h, often at night. The attacks occur with a frequency from one to eight daily during a period lasting from some weeks to months (the ‘cluster’). After a remission of varying duration, the same pattern recurs. In contrast to migraine, during an attack the cluster patient prefers to pace about. Sumatriptan injection or oxygen inhalation aborts pain attacks in most patients. The most frequently used prophylactic agents used are verapamil and lithium.

Cerebral tumour
Cerebral tumour is incorrect. Perhaps of most concern, many patients with brain tumours do not have headache. However, a brain tumour may cause raised intracranial pressure and focal neurological deficits. The headache will have ‘red flag’ features in keeping with this (headache with vomiting occurring in the morning or induced by Valsalva manoeuvre etc).

Iritis associated headache
Iritis associated headache is incorrect. Ophthalmic pathology (including iritis and glaucoma) should always be remembered as rare causes of headache, but the description in this case is so typical of cluster headache that this option can be discounted.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. Although migraine can cause many symptoms, the autonomic features described here are not typical. A migrainous headache usually lasts between 3 hours and 3 days. There is usually a prodrome of lethargy or irritability and a slow build-up of throbbing head pain, which is usually unilateral. Accompanying nausea, photophobia and phonophobia are common. Cluster Headache

Tension-type headache
Tension-type headache is incorrect. Tension headaches are probably a variant of migraine and, with detailed questioning, accompanying migrainous symptoms can usually be elicited from the patient.

stem: A 19-year-old student presents with pain in his shoulders and upper arms, particularly on the left. The pain began overnight a few weeks before his presentation to the doctor. He works part time as a supermarket stacker and has noticed difficulty placing items on high shelves. He has no gait disturbance. On examination there is slight wasting around the shoulder, with weakness of shoulder abduction, as well as elbow flexion on the left. There is no bony pain on palpation of the neck. The biceps and supinator reflexes are absent, but the triceps reflex is present. There is subjective reduction of sensation over the lateral aspect of the arms extending down to the thumbs and index fingers bilaterally. Examination of the legs is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bilateral idiopathic brachial plexopathy
Idioapthic brachial plexopathy is usually unilateral, but it can be bilateral. It often involves the C5 and C6 segments of the brachial plexus. It can begin suddenly or present over a number of days, with a severe stabbing pain that may last from hours to weeks. There is usually associated weakness and profound wasting of the muscles involved. Recovery may take months to years and may be incomplete.

Bilateral cervical ribs
Bilateral cervical ribs is incorrect. Bilateral cervical ribs usually cause damage to C8 and T1 nerve roots, not C5 and 6 as seen in this case.

Cervical syrinx
Cervical syrinx is incorrect. A cervical syrinx causes a loss of pain and temperature sensation in theupper limbs. In chronic cases, weakness and wasting can develop. Upper motor neurone signs may be seen in the lower limbs.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis would not cause sensory or reflex signs. Brachial Plexus Regional AnatomyProlapsed C5/6 intervertebral disc
Prolapsed C5/6 intervertebral disc is incorrect. A prolapsed C5/6 intervertebral disc is a possible differential diagnosis, but the pain might reasonably be more severe in the neck initially.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of loss of consciousness with associated limb jerking. This occurred at 0600 hours after she had been at an all-night party. Her father is said to have epilepsy and she has a cousin who has ‘blank spells’ of some kind. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis
explanation:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
The family history of epilepsy and the provocation of a generalised seizure by sleep deprivation (with or without alcohol) in a young patient are strongly suggestive of a primary generalised epilepsy syndrome. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is the most common primary generalised epilepsy, but is underdiagnosed partly owing to the lack of awareness of the condition by doctors. Absence seizures may start in childhood but can be subtle and remain undiagnosed. Myoclonic jerks, especially of the upper limbs, which predominantly occur in the mornings shortly after waking are often reported on direct questioning. (These may be so subtle as to be interpreted as ‘clumsiness’ when eating breakfast). There may be a positive family history, although the condition is not monogenic.

Alcohol-induced seizure
Alcohol-induced seizure is incorrect. Alcohol-induced seizure would be a possibility here but the positive family history raises the suggestion of a primary generalised epilepsy syndrome.

Drug-induced seizure
Drug-induced seizure is incorrect. Drug-induced seizure would be a possibility here but the positive family history raises the suggestion of a primary generalised epilepsy syndrome.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis
Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis is incorrect. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis would typically present with focal onset seizures. Patients often have complex partial seizures with an aura (smell/taste/pilioerection/rising abdominal sensation) followed by a spell of altered awareness with or without automatisms (eg lip smacking/gulping/hand movements).

Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure is incorrect. There is nothing in the case described to support a diagnosis of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures.

stem: A 39-year-old keen camper presents with a 2-week history of headaches, a ‘droopy face’, joint pains and a lowgrade temperature. He had returned from a camping holiday 1 month earlier. The only abnormality on neurological examination is left facial weakness. A lumbar puncture was carried out and the results of the CSF analysis are as follows: 250 cells/μl, over 90% lymphocytes, protein 2.1 g/l, glucose 4.0 mmol/l (serum glucose 8.0 mmol/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Borrelia burgdorferi meningitis
All the options listed (ie Borrelia burgdorferi meningitis, Bell’s palsy, sarcoidosis, Guillain–Barré syndrome and tuberculous meningitis) could cause facial weakness. However, the headache, fever, arthralgia and possible exposure to tick bites favour Borrelia burgdorferi meningitis, also known as Lyme disease. Lyme disease is a tick-borne disorder that results from systemic infection with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Neurological manifestation may occur weeks or months after the characteristic skin lesion (erythema migrans), and includes lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuritis and radiculoneuritis. The CSF usually shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, with elevated protein and normal glucose. The treatment of choice for the meningitis of Lyme disease is intravenous penicillin or ceftriaxone.

Bell’s palsy
Bell’s palsy is incorrect. Bell’s palsy is a common cause of facial weakness but could not explain the rest of the clinical picture or the abnormal CSF.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. There are no additional features to suggest Guillain–Barré syndrome and the high number of WBC in the CSF essentially excludes this diagnosis.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is a reasonable differential diagnosis here. The fever would be unusual in sarcoidosis and suggests an infective cause should be considered first.

Tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculous meningitis is incorrect. Tuberculous meningitis is once again a reasonable differential diagnosis. Usually CSF glucose is very low in tuberculous meningitis.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with a gradually worsening difficulty in walking up stairs, light-headedness on standing and a dry mouth. He tends to feel better at the end of the day. He has a mild ptosis, normal tone in his limbs but proximal weakness in his lower limbs and global hyporeflexia. There is some evidence of increased muscle strength with reinforcement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lambert–Eaton syndrome
This man has Lambert–Eaton syndrome, which is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against the voltage gated calcium channels. This syndrome occurs in males more often than females (5:1). Patients complain of autonomic symptoms (especially dry mouth).It is commonly associated with small-cell lung carcinoma.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is incorrect. MG is an autoimmune disorder caused by the production of antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Patients often present with episodic diplopia and ptosis. There may be facial weakness, slurring of speech, dyspnoea and limb weakness, which is usually proximal. The symptoms are worse on exertion and typically by the end of the day.ReflexesChat are usually normal with or increased in MG and autonomic features are not seen.

Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) is incorrect. OPMD is a progressive, inherited, autosomal dominant disorder and family history is common. The onset is in the fifth or sixth decade with ptosis and dysphagia, but there is no fluctuation of symptoms.

Poliomyelitis
Poliomyelitis is incorrect. Poliomyelitis is characterised by rapid onset flaccid weakness and wasting of the limb muscles with areflexia, and is usually asymmetric. The history of fluctuation and symmetrical weakness is against this diagnosis. Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic SyndromeA 58-year-old farmer from Northern Ireland presents with a progressive neurological illness over 3 weeks. He complains of double vision and has some slurring of speech and unsteadiness on his feet, as well as malaise and tiredness. He also admits to having lost 6.25 kg (1 stone) in weight over a 6-week period. On examination he has a bilateral VIth nerve palsy, facial asymmetry and marked dysarthria. The deep tendon reflexes are sluggish throughout and the plantar responses equivocal. He has lymphadenopathy of the axilla and groins, and a temperature of 38.6°C. Chest X-ray shows some evidence of right upper lobe changes. MRI of the brain shows diffuse meningeal enhancement. Lumbar puncture shows an elevated protein of 1.2 g/l, an elevated white cell count of 87/mm 3 (mostly lymphocytes) and a low CSF/blood glucose ratio (CSF glucose 1.2 mmol/l, blood glucose 6.7 mmol/l). Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to be found on further investigation?

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy that may be associated with an underlying malignancy. It has an insidious onset of proximal and lower limb weakness and can be associated with muscle pain. Ocular symptoms are rare and if present should alert you to consider a different diagnosis.

stem: A 71-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a suspected stroke. He has previously suffered from posterior territory TIAs and is already taking clopidogrel. The most junior doctor in the team sees the patient first and tells you she suspects a left posterior inferior cerebellar artery stroke. Which of the following findings would you expect on examination?
options: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body
explanation:
Ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome
Ipsilateral Horner syndrome is seen in lateral medullary syndrome, which is caused by a stroke affecting the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Features of the lateral medullary syndrome are listed below: Dysfunction Effects Vestibular nuclei Vomiting, vertigo, nystagmus Inferior cerebellar peduncle Ipsilateral cerebellar signs including ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia Central tegmental tract Palatal myoclonus Lateral spinothalamic tract Contralateral deficits in pain and temperature sensation from body Spinal trigeminal nucleus & tract Ipsilateral loss of pain, and temperature sensation from face Nucleus ambiguus (which affects vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves) Ipsilateral laryngeal, pharyngeal and palatal hemiparalysis: dysphagia, hoarseness, diminished gag reflex Descending sympathetic fibres Ipsilateral Horner syndrome

Contralateral cerebellar signs
Contralateral cerebellar signs is incorrect. Although you would expect to see cerebellar signs in lateral medullary syndrome, these would be ipsilateral, not contralateral.

Contralateral Horner syndrome
Contralateral Horner syndrome is incorrect. Horner syndrome is a feature of lateral medullary syndrome due to damage to the descending sympathetic tracts. However, this damage is ipsilateral, not contralateral.

Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face is incorrect. You would expect to see loss of pain and temperature sensation over the ipsilateral face, not the contralateral face. Sensory information from the face travels from the trigeminal ganglion to synapse in the spinal trigeminal nucleus, which is in the ipsilateral medulla. The second-order neurons decussate before terminating in the thalamus. Consequently, injury at the level of the lateral medulla will affect ipsilateral fibres.

Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body is incorrect. You would expect to see loss of pain and temperature sensation from the contralateral side of the body, not the ipsilateral side. This is because sensation from the body travels separately to sensation from the face, in the spinothalamic tract. Fibres in the spinothalamic tract decussate in the spinal cord before travelling to the thalamus, and hence fibres affected by pathology in the medulla are contralateral, not ipsilateral.

stem: A 32-year-old man has a 4-day history of progressive weakness which began in his lower limbs. He has been healthy except for an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago. His temperature is 37.8°C, blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, pulse 94 bpm and respiratory rate 42 breaths/min. He has symmetrical weakness of both sides of the face and of the proximal and distal muscles of the extremities. Sensation is intact. No tendon reflexes can be elicited and the plantar responses are flexor. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Guillain–Barré syndrome
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) or Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute neuropathy characterised by progressive weakness of one or more limbs, areflexia and characteristic findings on neurophysiology. The face is commonly involved. GBS occurs more commonly in females and is preceded by an infection in about one-third of patients. The peak of disability is usually seen within the first 3 weeks. Steroids are not found to be effective but intravenous immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis are.

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is incorrect. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis can be considered as a very severe and acute form of multiple sclerosis (MS) which is more common in children and usually follows a viral infection or vaccination. As with MS, pathology is restricted to the central nervous system Chatand withas AI such Tutor the signs on examination are ‘upper motor neuron’, rather than the ‘lower motor neuron’ signs seen in this case.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Although myasthenia gravis should be considered in the differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with an acute flaccid paralysis, the areflexia and lack of eye movement disorder seen in this case make this possibility less likely.

Poliomyelitis
Poliomyelitis is incorrect. Polio is very rare in the western world and tends to present with asymmetrical weakness.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Pure polymyositis (without any features of co-existing connective tissue disorder) is actually very rare. Furthermore, it would be unusual to have areflexia and such prominent distal weakness in polymyositis. Guillain-Barré.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department with a sudden blurring of vision affecting her left eye and pain at the back of the eye. She also describes that there has been a loss of colour vision affecting the eye. Her past medical history includes an episode of poor co-ordination affecting her right hand, some 2 months ago and she has Type 1 diabetes which is managed with a basal bolus insulin regimen. There is a relative afferent pupillary defect affecting the left eye, and some right sided loss of coordination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis
The episode of poor co-ordination followed a few months later by unilateral optic neuritis raises the possibility of a demyelinating disease. An MRI and LP are next steps confirming the diagnosis.

CMV retinitis
CMV retinitis is incorrect. There is no suggestion of immunosuppression, and CMV retinitis is associated with hard exudates and retinal haemorrhages.

DIDMOAD syndrome
DIDMOAD syndrome is incorrect. Although this patient has diabetes mellitus, gradually progressive visual loss, rather than a sudden unilateral episode would be expected in optic atrophy.

Ischaemic optic neuritis
Ischaemic optic neuritis is incorrect. There is no suggestion of thrombophilia, arteritis or vascular disease to point towards an ischaemic cause for her symptoms.

Space occupying lesion.

stem: A 45-year-old man complains of numbness of his left thigh. He feels his balance may be poorer than usual but is not sure of this. He has put on 6.25 kg (1 stone) in weight over the past 6 months. He has mild, chronic, low back pain. There is a family history of a neurological condition, in that his father’s brother is said to have multiple sclerosis. On examination he is overweight. He has some reduction of pinprick sensation over the anterolateral part of his thigh on the left, with no motor signs. Tendon reflexes are normal. There are no cerebellar signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Inflammatory disease of the lumbosacral plexus
Lumbar canal stenosis with nerve root entrapment
explanation:
Meralgia paraesthetica
Meralgia paraesthetica is a syndrome that includes numbness, paraesthesias and pain in the anterolateral thigh, which may result from either an entrapment neuropathy or a neuroma of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN). The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve branches off of the lumbar plexus and conveys fibers from the L2 and L3 nerve roots. The nerve courses through the pelvis, running adjacent to the lateral edge of the psoas muscle. It enters the leg underneath or through the inguinal ligament, medial to the anterior superior iliac spine; it is in this location that entrapment can occur. The nerve is purely sensory, relaying sensory information from the anterolateral and lateral thigh. Obesity or weight gain is a risk factor for this as it predisposes to nerve compression. The diagnosis is mainly clinical (including the absence of other signs). Electrophysiological studies can help to exclude other, more generalised neuroradiculopathy, but will only rarely confirm the lesion.

Familial multiple sclerosis
Familial multiple sclerosis is incorrect. The family history of MS, as well as the history of a possible balance problem in this case, are ‘red herrings’. The symptoms and signs indicate a mononeuropathy. MS does not affect the peripheral nervous system.

Inflammatory disease of the lumbosacral plexus
Inflammatory disease of the lumbosacral plexus is incorrect. The brachial and lumbosacral plexus may be involved in an inflammatory process. However, this is rare and would present with pain and weakness in the distribution of multiple peripheral nerves.

Lumbar canal stenosis with nerve root entrapment
Lumbar canal stenosis with nerve root entrapment is incorrect. Although the area of sensory abnormality could potentially be mistaken with the L2 dermatome, lumbar canal stenosis with L2 nerve root entrapment is very rare and would usually be associated with radicular (shooting) pain.

Sporadic multiple sclerosis.

stem: A 35-year-old man has developed an involuntary jerky movement with poor motor coordination and degenerated mental skills. He first presented to the GP some 6 months earlier where he was diagnosed with mild depression. On further questioning it transpires that his father killed himself although the patient doesn’t know the reason why. Examination in the clinic reveals evidence of chorea and some short term memory loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Huntington’s chorea
Huntington’s initially presents with a mood disorder, and this is followed by abnormalities in short term memory with progressively worsening abnormal choreform movements. It is caused by the presence of an autosomaldominant lethal gene (i.e. the huntington gene) on the short arm of chromosome 4 and results in progressive neurodegeneration. Genetic anticipation is exhibited with patients presenting at a younger age with progression through the generations.

Lewy body disease
Lewy body disease is incorrect. Lewy body dementia follows a similar pathological process to Parkinson’s disease, with patients exhibiting features of Parkinsonism coupled with memory loss and visual hallucinations.

General paralysis of the insane (GPI)
General paralysis of the insane (GPI) is incorrect. This is chronic meningoencephalitis associated with neurosyphillis.

HIV dementia
HIV dementia is incorrect. HIV associated dementia complex presents late in the disease, the absence of evidence of chronic infection and opportunistic illnesses counts against HIV as an underlying diagnosis.

Normal-pressure hydrocephalus.

stem: An 80-year-old woman with hypercholesterolaemia, ischaemic heart disease and hypertension complains of tingling and numbness in both feet that has been worsening over 6 months. Examination shows her to have altered pinprick sensation over both feet and absent ankle reflexes. Urea and electrolytes are normal, blood glucose is normal and there is no history of alcohol ingestion. She is, however, taking a number of medications for the secondary prevention of vascular problems. Which of the medications listed below is most likely to have caused her symptoms?
explanation:
Simvastatin
The symptoms and examination findings are most consistent with an axonal, length-dependent peripheral neuropathy. Statins have been associated with peripheral neuropathy and therefore simvastatin seems the best answer here. There is currently no firm evidence that this association infers causality, but from the options given in this question simvastatin is the best choice. Epidemiology studies suggest a 14-fold increase in peripheral neuropathy versus matched controls.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide is not associated with peripheral neuropathy.

Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is incorrect. Clopidogrel is not associated with peripheral neuropathy.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Ramipril is not associated with peripheral neuropathy.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone is incorrect. Spironolactone is not associated with peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 48-year-old man, with a history of chronic injectiondrug use, presents with sequential footdrop and then wrist drop associated with pain and occurring over a 3-week period. Nerve conduction studies show evidence of a multifocal axonal neuropathy. He is also noted to have nailfold infarcts in his hands and feet, purpura and hepatomegaly. Which one of the following diagnoses is the most likely?
explanation:
Hepatitis C related cryoglobulinaemia
A subacute painful multifocal neuropathy (‘mononeuritis multiplex’) occurring in association with features of systemic inflammation (in this case, seen as nail fold infarcts) raises the possibility of vasculitis (specifically involving the vasa nervorum to give rise to neurological manifestations). Vasculitic neuropathies can occur secondary to: Cryoglobulinaemia Polyarteritis nodosa Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss syndrome) Rheumatoid arthritis Systemic lupus erythematosus Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Hepatitis C infection may be associated with cryoglobulinaemia (proteins that become insoluble at reduced temperatures), which causes a vasculitic syndrome including neuropathy.

Cytomegalovirus polyradiculopathy
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polyradiculopathy is incorrect. CMV infection is a rare cause of a polyradiculopathy. Neurological manifestations of this infection more commonly involve retinitis and encephalitis occurring in the immunosuppressed patient (eg HIV infection). Sensory features usually predominate in those with radiculopathy and the nerve conduction studies characteristically show normal sensory potentials in nerves innervating areas affected by sensory loss (indicating a lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion). These factors make this choice less likely than Hepatitis C related cryoglobulinaemia.

Hepatitis B related Guillain–Barré syndrome
Hepatitis B related Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. This is not a presentation typical of the Guillain–Barré syndrome (for many reasons, not least the nerve conduction studies which should show evidence of peripheral nerve demyelination – reduced velocities and conduction block).

Hepatitis C related Guillain–Barré syndrome
Hepatitis C related Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. This is not a presentation typical of the Guillain–Barré syndrome (for many reasons, not least the nerve conduction studies which should show evidence of peripheral nerve demyelination – reduced velocities and conduction block).

Systemic toxoplasmosis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with an intermittent attack disorder. She describes that she has a ‘funny feeling’ in her head at the onset of an attack but is unable to give any more history. The description from her partner is that she looks pale and distressed, and then collapses to the floor. She occasionally has some shaking or twitching movements of her arms and legs, but more often lies still for the duration of the attack. During them she is unresponsive. The attacks last from 15 to 30 minutes. Afterwards she may appear ‘dazed’ and does not know what has happened, but always recognises her family. Occasionally she seems upset and cries after the attack. The attacks occur on average once a fortnight and they are all similar. Clinical examination, including lying and standing blood pressure, routine blood tests and 12-lead ECG, is normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next investigation to try and reach a definitive diagnosis?
explanation:
Video-EEG recording
Certain clinical features in the history are suggestive of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) as the most likely diagnosis. These include the prolonged nature of the attacks (15–30 min) with the patient lying still; this pattern is typical of neither epilepsy nor cardiogenic attacks. The presence of crying after the attacks, while not specific, is also suggestive. It is extremely important to try to make a definitive diagnosis. Misdiagnosis as epilepsy or another condition may lead to inappropriate drug treatment (risk of toxicity or teratogenicity from antiepileptic drugs, AEDs), among other potential problems, as well as failure to offer appropriate psychological therapy. For this reason a ‘trial of AEDs’ is not recommended and referral to a specialist, preferably an epileptologist, is recommended by recent guidelines. Although diagnosis can be made on clinical grounds in some cases, video-EEG recording of habitual events is often required and remains the gold standard diagnosis, so this option is correct. It is a specialist investigation and is generally performed in video telemetry units under the supervision of an epileptologist.

24-hour ambulatory ECG
24-hour ambulatory ECG is incorrect. 24-hour ambulatory ECG is a potential investigation in the management of patients with syncopal collapses that do not sound simply vasovagal in nature. That is not the case here however based on the clinical information provided.

48-hour ambulatory EEG with ECG
48-hour ambulatory EEG with ECG is incorrect. 48-hour ambulatory EEG with ECG is occasionally a useful test in the diagnosis of epilepsy, but due to a low diagnostic yield overall it is now being used less and less.

Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is incorrect. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is a potential investigation in the management of patients with syncopal collapses that do not sound simply vasovagal in nature. That is not the case here however based on the clinical information provided.

Cardiac memo prolonged ECG recording
Cardiac memo prolonged ECG recording is incorrect. Cardiac memo prolonged ECG is a potential investigation in the management of patients with syncopal collapses that do not sound simply vasovagal in nature. That is not the case here however based on the clinical information provided. Non-epileptic.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is referred with a single fall. She has been well all her life and has rarely had to see her doctor. She smokes ten cigarettes per week. Examination is unremarkable other than a right-sided ptosis and some slight thinning and weakness of the muscles of her right hand, which she thinks might be long-standing. What is the most likely cause of her ptosis?
explanation:
Horner syndrome
The causes of unilateral ptosis include disinsertion of the aponeurosis of the levator palpebrae superioris, Horner syndrome and a third nerve palsy. In addition, local inflammation of the conjunctiva may cause ptosis. In this case weakness of the patient’s hand muscles suggests a T1 root lesion, and therefore a Horner syndrome is the most likely. Miosis can be subtle and easy to miss.

Levator disinsertion
Levator disinsertion is incorrect. Disinsertion of the aponeurosis of the levator palpebrae superioris is common and is characterised by the loss of the crease normally seen on the upper eyelid. It cannot explain the wasted hand.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is far more likely to result in bilateral ptosis, but it may be asymmetrical. There is often a degee of extra-ocular muscle weakness and facial weakness as well. Myasthenia cannot account for the wasted hand, but may cause proximal limb weakness.

Ocular pharyngeal muscular dystrophy
Ocular pharyngeal muscular dystrophy is incorrect. Ocular pharyngeal muscular dystrophy is very rare and would cause bilateral ptosis. Horner Syndrome A woman presented to the Emergency Department with collapse and vomiting preceded by occipital headache of acute onset. After 8 h, she was conscious, alert with photophobia and mild neck stiffness. Computed tomography (CT) brain scan was carried out and was normal. Which one of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

Third nerve palsy
Third nerve palsy is incorrect. A third nerve palsy would cause weakness of extraocular muscles (sparing lateral rectus – CN VI and superior oblique – CN IV), leaving the eye deviated in a ‘down and out’ position. In addition there may be a dilated pupil.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents following a fall. She reports pain and weakness in her hands for several months, stiff legs and swallowing difficulties and has bilateral wasting of the small muscles of her hands. Reflexes in the upper limbs are absent. Tongue fasciculations are present and both legs show increased tone, pyramidal weakness and hyperreflexia with extensor plantars. Pain and temperature sensation are impaired in the upper limbs, but with preserved fine touch and proprioception. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Syringobulbia
This patient presents with lower motor neurone (LMN) signs in her arms and upper motor neurone (UMN) signs in her legs. There is also a dissociated sensory loss of spinothalamic sensations, with sparing of posterior column function, in the upper limbs. This pattern is seen when a syrinx (an expansion of the cord’s central canal) expands, causing compromise of decussating spinothalamic fibres and then, as the syrinx gets larger, involvement of cervical anterior horn cells and the descending corticospinal tracts. The fasciculating tongue suggests that the lower brainstem (XIIn nuclei) is also involved; this is termed syringobulbia, rather than the more common syringomyelia that only affects the cord.

Cervical spondylosis
Cervical spondylosis is incorrect. Cervical spondylosis could cause similar limb signs but cannot account for the tongue fasciculations and swallowing problems that this patient has.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease (MND) is incorrect. This patient has clear sensory signs that are not seen in MND.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. In multiple sclerosis you would not see lower motor neurone signs, so this diagnosis can be excluded.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is incorrect. As described this affects only the cord, in contrast to syringobulbia where the lower brainstem is also involved.

stem: Where is the most likely site of the lesion which has led to her visual disturbance?
explanation:
Optic chiasm
Bitemporal hemianopia raises the possibility of compression at the level of the optic chiasm. This is usually caused by a pituitary tumour. The feelings of tiredness seen here also raise the possibility of reduced production of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and other anterior pituitary hormones. She requires a full battery screen of pituitary hormones including TSH, gonadotrophins, growth hormone and prolactin and an MRI brain scan. Patients with a pituitary macroadenoma need rapid referral for surgery to reduce the chances of permanent visual loss.

Frontal lobe
Frontal lobe is incorrect. A lesion in the frontal lobe could cause monocular visual failure due to direct compression of the optic nerve. A sufficiently large lesion can also cause contralateral optic disc swelling due to raised intracerebral pressure, as seen in Foster–Kennedy syndrome.

Occipital lobe
Occipital lobe is incorrect. A lesion in the occipital lobe causes a contralateral homonomous hemianopia.

Optic nerve
Optic nerve is incorrect. A lesion here would cause monocular visual failure.

Temporal lobe
Temporal lobe is incorrect. A lesion here may cause a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.

stem: A 72-year-old woman was referred to the Neurology Clinic with a history of fluctuating cognitive decline and hallucinations. Her GP had noticed rigidity with bradykinesia but initial response to levodopa therapy has been poor. Most recently she has had a number of falls and has become incontinent of urine. On examination she is hypotensive with a postural drop of 35 mmHg. She is confused, with a Mini-Mental State Score of 11/30. There is bradykinesia, tremor and rigidity. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) presents with fluctuating cognitive decline, hallucinations and parkinsonism. Autonomic dysregulation is also seen. It can be hard to treat the parkinsonism, as levodopa therapy may worsen confusion. Cholinesterase inhibitors can be useful in reducing the hallucinations and confusion.

Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is incorrect. FTD causes a progressive change in personality, behaviour and cognition. Although hallucinations are recognised to occur, they are unusual. Parkinsonism may occur as a latestage finding.

Multiple system atrophy
Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is incorrect. MSA produces a combination of parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure. Significant cognitive impairment and hallucinations are uncommon.

Parkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease is incorrect. Parkinson’s disease could explain the physical signs, although a good response to levodopa would be expected. In addition, the cognitive impairment of Parkinson’s disease is typically seen later, not as an early-presenting feature.

Progressive supranuclear palsy
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is incorrect. PSP causes early gait failure with falls; patients have a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy on examination. A fronto-subcortical dementia is common, but hallucinations are rare.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted with dysarthria, tremor and parkinsonian symptoms. On examination you notice yellow–brown rings on examination of the eyes, seen at the limbus of the corneae. Given the most likely diagnosis, which part of the brain is predominantly affected by her underlying condition?
explanation:
Basal ganglia
This woman has Wilson’s disease, the appearance of her corneae being highly suggestive of Kayser–Fleischer rings, confirming the diagnosis. The basal ganglia are most affected. Wilson’s disease is a degenerative disease where there is progressive hepatolenticular degeneration. It is an autosomal recessive disease involving chromosome 13, resulting in a defective copper transporting ATPase involved in the vesicular transport of copper. Copper binds to ceruloplasmin and is secreted into the circulation. In Wilson’s disease, this is impaired and there is abnormal accumulation of copper with affinity for the brain and liver. Imaging may show normal or generalised atrophy. CT may show bilateral putaminal hypodensity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows T2 hyperintensities in the thalamus, putamen, dentate nucleus and occasionally in the brainstem.

Brainstem
Brainstem is incorrect. The brainstem is rarely affected. When involved it shows a central core of decreased signal intensity – rarely the face of the panda sign in the mid-brain on the MRI.

Cerebellum
Atrophy of the cerebellum is incorrect. Cerebellar involvement is rare and usually occurs in the late stages of the disease. Changes in T2 signal on MRI are seen in the cerebellum, and cortical atrophy may be seen in latestage disease.

Cerebral cortex
Cerebral cortex is incorrect. Cortical atrophy may occur in the late stages of the disease. Wilson’s Disease

Frontal lobes
Frontal lobes is incorrect. There are no specific changes in the frontal lobes in Wilson’s disease.

stem: A 69-year-old man with known cerebrovascular risk factors presents with a brainstem stroke. As well as ataxia, dysarthria and bilateral pyramidal tract signs, he is noted to have impaired upward and downwards gaze, with preservation of horizontal eye movements, as well as of the doll’s eye reflexes. There is convergent nystagmus. Pupils are dilated and sluggishly reactive. Infarction of which part of the brainstem is most likely to have produced his eye signs?
explanation:
Dorsal midbrain
Vertical eye movements are under bilateral control of the cortex and the upper brainstem. Dorsal midbrain lesions are associated with a failure of vertical gaze. This may be called Parinaud syndrome, and is usually associated with convergent nystagmus, as well mydriasis and impaired pupillary reflexes. Upgaze is more often affected than downgaze. Hence dorsal midbrain is correct.

Dorsal pons
Dorsal pons is incorrect. Pontine lesions do not affect vertical eye movements.

Lateral medulla
Lateral medulla is incorrect. Medullary lesions do not affect vertical eye movements.

Ventral midbrain
Ventral midbrain is incorrect. Vertical eye movements are not controlled in the ventral midbrain although the 3rd nerve nuclei are here, so 3rd nerve palsies may occur with lesions in this location.

Ventral pons
Ventral pons is incorrect. Pontine lesions do not affect vertical eye movements.

stem: A 40-year-old man has been complaining for the last 2 months of progressively unsteady gait. He also reported an attack of blurring of vision 2 years ago which lasted for 3 weeks. He is known to drink 50 units of alcohol weekly. On this most recent visit to the GP he complained of more unsteadiness. Examination revealed bilateral reduced/absent reflexes in the lower limbs, increased tone and spastic weakness. There is loss of pin-prick, light touch and joint position sensation in both feet. He has impaired vibration sensation to the anterior superior iliac spines bilaterally. Examination of eye movements and visual fields appeared normal. Which one of the following is the initial investigation most likely to provide a diagnosis?
explanation:
Serum vitamin B12
This patient has features consistent with subacute combined degeneration of the cord, associated with vitamin B 12 deficiency, resulting from his consumption of large quantities of alcohol. This syndrome is a myeloneuropathy and consists of spinal cord signs (increased tone, high level of vibration sensation loss) and peripheral neuropathic signs (reduced reflexes). The previous episode of visual disturbance sounds like optic neuritis but the current signs are not in keeping with a central nervous system demyelinating relapse (all the signs would be upper motor neurone (UMN))

CT brain
CT brain is incorrect. The patient has no current signs that sound like they could be due to acute brain pathology so a CT brain is uneccessary.

MRI brain
MRI brain is incorrect. The patient has no current signs that sound like they could be due to acute brain pathology so MRI brain is uneccessary. Given the signs an MRI scan of the spine would be a reasonable precaution and may show high signal in the posterior columns, consistent with subacute combined degeneration.

Nerve conduction studies
Nerve conduction studies is incorrect. Given some of the lower motor neurone (LMN) signs it is not unreasonable to consider nerve conduction studies, and indeed these may well show a neuropathic picture. However the aetiology will not be clear from this so B12 levels are a better answer.

Thyroid function testing
Thyroid function testing is incorrect. Thyroid dysfunction could not produce this myeloneuropathic picture.

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted with a 6-week history of proximal muscle weakness. He has been having difficulty climbing stairs and getting up from a sitting position in a chair. He is a lifelong smoker and his alcohol intake is 30 units per week. He does not admit to any recent change in his weight and his BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Which of the following results points most strongly towards an underlying medical condition known to result in proximal myopathy?
options: Abnormal liver function tests and macrocytosis
A suppressed 0900-h serum cortisol level after an overnight dexamethasone suppression test
Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and normal free thyroxine levels
explanation:
Abnormal liver function tests and macrocytosis
Alcohol excess is commonly associated with deranged liver function and macrocytosis. It also causes proximal myopathy.

A suppressed 0900-h serum cortisol level after an overnight dexamethasone suppression test
A suppressed 0900-h serum cortisol level after an overnight dexamethasone suppression test is incorrect. This is a diagnostic screening test for Cushing’s syndrome. Suppression of cortisol is a normal response. In those with Cushing’s syndrome, cortisol level fails to suppress to <50 nmol/L.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. In vitamin D deficiency, proximal myopathy is associated with hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, raised alkaline phosphatase and low 25-OH vitamin D (<30 nmol/l).

Low serum vitamin B12 level
Low serum B 12 level is incorrect. Vitamin B 12 deficiency causes macrocytosis but it does not cause proximal myopathy or abnormal liver function. 610

Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and normal free thyroxine levels
Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and normal free thyroxine levels is incorrect. This biochemical picture is consistent with subclinical (compensated) hypothyroidism. Proximal myopathy is a feature of thyrotoxicosis, not subclinical hypothyroidism. Mainly upper limb girdle muscles are affected. In thyrotoxicosis, TSH is suppressed and free thyroxine (T4) and tri-iodothyronine (T3) levels are elevated.

stem: A 48-year-old man is admitted to hospital after being brought in by an ambulance unconscious. On taking a collateral history from his wife, you learn that after having breakfast he developed left sided weakness, difficulty in understanding others, appeared to have a headache and collapsed a short time later. He also has a background of insulin dependent type 2 diabetes, poorly controlled hypertension, a significant 20-pack year smoking history and an average alcohol consumption of 50 units per week. On examination, he remains unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Score of 3 and a left sided hemi-paresis. There is also a dysconjugate gaze with the right eye being deviated laterally and the right pupil being larger than the left with no response to light. What is the most likely cause of his coma?
options: Midbrain haemorrhage involving the cerebral peduncle
Midbrain infarction of the dorsomedial midbrain
explanation:
Temporal lobe haemorrage with oedema
This patient has focal neurological signs suggestive of a right sided temporal lobe stroke (fluent, receptive dysphasia and headache), as well as evidence of a right third nerve palsy and left sided hemiparesis. He has significant risk factors for both ischemic and haemorrhagic stroke, but given the presence of the ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis, the most likely diagnosis in this case is a haemorrhagic temporal lobe stroke with associated oedema, causing uncal herniation with brainstem compression.

Midbrain haemorrhage involving the cerebral peduncle
A stroke in this location results in an ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis. This is also eponymously known as Weber syndrome. It would not however, be associated with headache and a fluent, receptive dysphasia as is observed in this question.

Midbrain infarction of the dorsomedial midbrain
A stroke in this location results in an ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral upper and lower limb ataxia. This is also eponymously known as Claude syndrome. It would not however, be associated with hemiparesis, headache and a fluent, receptive dysphasia as is observed in this question.

Lateral pontine haemorrhage
A stroke in this location would produce an ipsilateral limb ataxia, facial paralysis, hearing loss, vertigo and nystagmus, as well as contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation and contralateral hemiparesis. This is known as lateral pontine syndrome or eponymously as Marie-Foix syndrome. It would not produce any of the symptoms or signs seen in this question.

Inferior pontine infarction.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents with a weak grip and tingling of her right hand. On examination, you find weakness of the right abductor pollicis brevis and mild weakness of thumb flexion. Finger abduction and adduction appear to be within normal limits. There is sensory loss to pinprick affecting the thumb, index and middle finger. Sensation in the thenar eminence is spared. The left-hand sensorimotor examination is normal. The deep tendon reflexes are symmetrical. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
options: Compression of the right median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Compression of the right median nerve in the forearm
Compression of the right ulnar nerve at the elbow
explanation:
Compression of the right median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Pregnancy is a risk factor for carpal tunnel syndrome, as are other conditions that promote fluid retention or thickening of the subcutaneous tissues (eg hypothyroidism), factors that alter the configuration of the wrist structures (eg osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis) and conditions that predispose to neuropathy (eg diabetes, hereditary tendency to pressure palsy). The median nerve supplies the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis . However, weakness may be absent or incomplete, whereas sensory symptoms and signs are common. Phalen’s sign involves placing pressure over the carpal tunnel with the wrist flexed – it is considered positive if this reproduces the patient’s symptoms. Tinel’s test involves tapping over the wrist in an effort to reproduce symptoms.

Compression of the right median nerve in the forearm
Compression of the right median nerve in the forearm is incorrect. Sensation over the thenar eminence is supplied by the palmar branch of the median nerve which does not pass through the carpal tunnel. Therefore, if there is altered sensation here a more proximal lesion of the median nerve should be considered, but this is not the case here.

Compression of the right ulnar nerve at the elbow
Compression of the right ulnar nerve at the elbow is incorrect. No motor or sensory deficits in regions supplied by the ulnar nerve are described here.

Right brachial plexopathy
Right brachial plexopathy is incorrect. Brachial plexus lesions give rise to deficits affecting a mixture of peripheral nerves rather than the pure median nerve syndrome described here.

Right C8 nerve root irritation
Right C8 nerve root irritation is incorrect. C8 contributes to median and ulnar nerves via the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. Therefore, a mixture of signs affecting both of these distributions would be expected.

stem: A 49-year-old woman was placed on warfarin therapy because of pulmonary embolism. While she has been on therapy, she has developed pain, numbness and paraesthesias from her left anterior thigh extending to her medial leg, plus weakness of knee extension and hip flexion. The left knee jerk is absent. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Left femoral nerve
All of the abnormalities are indicative of a left femoral neuropathy.The patient has weakness of knee extension (quadriceps) and hip flexion (iliopsoas).She has decreased sensation in her anterior thigh and medial distal leg, which is the cutaneous distribution of the femoral nerve. A patient on anticoagulation therapy can suffer a retroperitoneal haematoma, which can damage the femoral nerve.

Left common peroneal nerve
Left common peroneal nerve is incorrect. Common peroneal neuropathy causes foot drop, sensory loss in the lateral aspect of the foot and anterolateral aspect of the shin.

Left obturator nerve
Left obturator nerve is incorrect. Injury to the obturator nerve causes numbness in the medial aspect of the thigh and weakness of hip adduction.

Left sciatic nerve
Left sciatic nerve is incorrect. Injury to the left sciatic nerve causes numbness of the foot and lower part of the leg, weakness of knee flexion, ankle plantar flexion, dorsiflexion, inversion and absent ankle reflex.

Left superior gluteal nerve
Left superior gluteal nerve is incorrect. Damage to the left superior gluteal nerve causes weak hip abduction and a Trendelenburg gait.

stem: A 28-year-old woman was diagnosed 3 months ago with schizophrenia. Her psychiatrist started her on haloperidol. She has now presented to the Emergency Department with confusion and drowsiness. On examination she is pyrexial (39.5°C), disoriented and her blood pressure is 200/100 mmHg. She has severe bilateral rigidity. What treatment is most likely to be effective?
explanation:
Dantrolene
The most likely diagnosis is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is a known complication of neuroleptic treatment. It presents with an altered mental state, pyrexia, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction. Management consists of muscle relaxants, such as dantrolene and intravenous fluids. Dopamine agonists need to be considered but may exacerbate the psychiatric condition.

Aciclovir
Aciclovir is incorrect. Aciclovir is the treatment of choice for herpes simplex encephalitis, which is a reasonable differential diagnosis here, given the fever and altered mental state. However, the rigidity, hypertension and history of exposure to neuroleptics make neuroleptic malignant syndrome a more probable diagnosis.

Cefuroxime
Cefuroxime is incorrect. Cefuroxime is an antibiotic of cephalosporin class (β-lactam).It has no role in this condition unless there are markers of infection.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is incorrect. Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker and is avasodilator. The primary indication of this drug in neurology is to prevent vasospasm of the cerebral blood vessels after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Propranolol
Propranolol is incorrect. Propranolol is a non-cardioselective β-blocker and is commonly used in migraine prophylaxis.

stem: A 68-year-old man was referred as an emergency by his GP because of left-sided foot drop. The foot drop had come on 3 weeks earlier. He had noted slight tingling on the dorsum of his foot. He had tripped a few times, and on one occasion turned his ankle, which had become slightly swollen. The foot drop had substantially improved over the last 10 days. His knee had been bandaged for support after a fall had led to recurrent knee pain on walking a few days before the foot drop began. He has mild weakness of his left ankle dorsiflexors and evertors, and moderate weakness of the extensor hallucis and extensor digitorum; other movements, including ankle inversion and hip abduction, are normal. Reflexes are normal. There is sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot from the base of the hallux to the ankle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common peroneal palsy
This man has a left-sided common peroneal nerve palsy that is likely to have occurred after external compression of the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head from his tight knee bandage.

Ischaemic stroke
Ischaemic stroke is incorrect. Ischaemic stroke is an important consideration, but there are no upper motor neurone signs.

L5 radiculopathy
L5 radiculopathy is incorrect. Preserved ankle inversion and hip abduction indicate this is probably not an L5 radiculopathy. In addition the sensory loss would likely extend onto the shin.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease (MND) is incorrect. The presence of sensory disturbance rules out motor neurone disease and to make a diagnosis on motor neurone disease one would expect a mixture of upper and lower motor neurone signs. In addition the problem seems to be improving spontaneously, which is unlikely to happen in MND, as it is a progressive neurodegenerative process.

Sciatic nerve palsy.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of lower back pain. More recently he has developed weakness of and paraesthesias in his legs. On the day of admission, he was unable to stand, and developed difficulty in initiating micturition. He is a long-standing, insulin-dependent diabetic and his diabetic control is poor. His most recent HbA 1c is 70 mmol/mol (8.6%). On examination he has a temperature of 38°C. He has increased tone and pyramidal distribution weakness in his lower limbs. Lower limb reflexes are brisk with extensor plantars. Sensory examination is variable. Straightleg raising produces pain. CRP is elevated at 210 mg/l. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Spinal epidural abscess
This man clearly has an upper motor neurone lesion, most likely in the spinal cord. The fever, back pain and very high CRP are suggestive of a spinal epidural abscess.

Anterior spinal artery thrombosis
Anterior spinal artery thrombosis is incorrect. Anterior spinal artery thrombosis typically causes sudden-onset severe flaccid paraparesis. The high CRP and fever cannot be explainedby this diagnosis.

Prolapsed L3/4 intervertebral disc
Prolapsed L3/4 intervertebral disc is incorrect. A prolapsed disc at L3/4 would produce a lower motor neurone syndrome due to spinal nerve root compression (the spinal cord ends at L1 vertebral level).

Spinal arteriovenous malformation
Spinal arteriovenous malformation is incorrect. Spinal arteriovenous malformation can present suddenlydue to thrombosis or bleeding, but once again cannot account for the high CRP and fever.

Tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculous meningitis is incorrect. Tuberculous meningitis is more likely to present with a several-week historyof headache and meningism.

stem: A 25-year-old obese woman presents with severe headaches over the last 3 months, which are worse in the morning. A CT of her head is normal. A lumbar puncture is performed and shows an opening pressure of 30 cm of CSF. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral optic disc swelling. What is the most likely abnormality seen on examination of the visual fields?
explanation:
Enlarged blind spot
This lady has a raised pressure headache syndrome. In the absence of an underlying cause (including venous sinus thrombosis and tetracycline antibiotic usage), the diagnosis will be idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) (sometimes called benign intracranial hypertension or pseudotumour cerebri). In this syndrome, swelling of the optic nerve head causes enlargement of the blind spot.

Altitudinal field defect
Altitudinal field defect is incorrect. Altitudinal field defects (classically loss of the inferior hemifield) are usually the result of an ischaemic optic neuropathy and are not a feature of raised intracranial pressure.

Bitemporal hemianopia
Bitemporal hemianopia is incorrect. A bitemporal field defect is caused by a lesion at the optic chiasm (usually a pituitary adenoma). This is not a feature of IIH.

Central visual field defect
Central visual field defect is incorrect. A central field defect can rarely occur in IIH, although typically even in the most severe cases the central field is retained. However, central field defects are more commonly caused by optic nerve ischaemic or inflammatory disorders. Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension A 28-year-old-female is admitted with recurrent epileptic fits. She is known to have epilepsy and has been taking phenytoin for five years, but her fits are not controlled. During her stay, the resident doctor was able to make the patient respond to verbal commands during the fit and he thought that the fits he witnessed were probably psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (pseudoseizures). In this patient the presence of which one of the following features would be most helpful in establishing the diagnosis of genuine epileptic fits?

Left homonymous hemianopia
Left homonymous hemianopia is incorrect. Homonymous field defects are caused by lesions of the optic radiation. These are not a feature of IIH.

stem: A previously well 58-year-old woman is referred by her General Practitioner to the hospital. She complains of recurring attacks of the room spinning around her in a horizontal plane, which is happening on multiple occasions every day. Each attack lasts about ten seconds and seems to occur whenever she turns in bed, lies down or sits up from the supine position. There are no other associated symptoms. She is taking no medication. Standard neurological examination is normal. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Epley manoeuvre
This patient has benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, a common, self-limiting condition characterised by brief bouts of vertigo triggered by head movement. The diagnosis can be confirmed clinically by examining for rotatory nystagmus brought on by the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre. The Epley manoeuvre can then be carried out to treat the condition.

Aspirin
Aspirin is used in the management of an acute stroke. In patients with vertigo, careful consideration is needed to rule out a posterior circulation stroke. Posterior circulation ischaemia would not present with repetitive, stereotyped, short-lived attacks of vertigo triggered by movement.

Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre
The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre is used in the assessment and diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). A positive test is indicated by rotatory nystagmus and the onset of symptoms. It is not a treatment option. The Epley manoeuvre can be performed immediately after diagnosis to manage BPPV.

Prochlorperazine
Prochlorperazine can provide symptomatic relief from vertigo, including BPPV and labyrinthitis. Labyrinthitis usually presents with an acute or subacute onset of hearing change, vertigo and vomiting. It is not usually purely episodic or purely triggered by movements, although moving around does make the symptoms of labyrinthitis more severe. Prochlorperazine, however, is not necessarily a curative measure for BPPV and the Epley manoeuvre should be tried initially.

Sumatriptan
Sumatriptan is used in the treatment of migraine. Migraine may produce symptoms of vertigo, although this usually happens in the context of a throbbing headache. In addition, vertigo seen in migraine lasts longer than a few seconds and is not specifically related to head movement, although many migraineurs are generally motion-sensitive.

stem: A 24-year-old man with a family history of myotonic dystrophy visits you for advice about starting a family. He has the typical features of frontal male pattern balding and is beginning to develop features of muscle weakness. He has read on the internet about a phenomenon called ‘anticipation’ which is associated with the condition. What does anticipation mean in this setting?
options: Symptoms develop which prevents fathering children
Symptoms begin at an earlier stage in successive generations
Symptoms are less severe in successive generations
Warning signs appear which can pre-date the main symptoms associated with the condition
Patients can anticipate the severity of their condition by looking at their parents
explanation:
Symptoms begin at an earlier stage in successive generations
Genetic anticipation occurs in conditions caused by trinuceotide repeats (such as Myotnic dystrophy type 1). The unstable nature of the repeat means that successive generations have a longer repeat length and this generally produces an earlier age of onset and sometimes a more severe phenotype.

Symptoms develop which prevents fathering children
Symptoms develop which prevents fathering children is incorrect. Anticipation does not imply a problem with fertility.

Symptoms are less severe in successive generations
Symptoms are less severe in successive generations is incorrect. Symptoms tend to be more severe in successive generations.

Warning signs appear which can pre-date the main symptoms associated with the condition
Warning signs appear which can pre-date the main symptoms associated with the condition is incorrect. In many genetic disorders there are early signs that can be detected prior to obvious symptom onset – this is sometimes referred to as the prodromal stage.

Patients can anticipate the severity of their condition by looking at their parents
Patients can anticipate the severity of their condition by looking at their parents is incorrect. Anticipation refers to an earlier age of symptom onset in each successive generation.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents with clinical features consistent with an embolic stroke. Which one of the following conditions is most associated with an increased risk of embolic stroke?
explanation:
AF (rheumatic heart disease)
AF in the context of rheumatic heart disease increases the relative risk of stroke by a factor of 17. In this setting, AF associated with mitral valve lesions (caused by rheumatic heart disease) leads to left atrial clot and forming thrombo-embolic condition.
