Mitral annular calcification
While mitral annular calcification doubles the relative risk of stroke, this is not as significant as the risk increase seen with AF in the context of rheumatic heart disease (× 17).

Atrial fibrillation (AF) (non-rheumatic heart disease)
Although AF in the context of non-rheumatic heart disease does increase the relative risk of stroke by a factor of 6, this is not as significant as the risk increase seen with AF in the context of rheumatic heart disease by a factor of 17.

Coarctation of the aorta
Coarctation of the aorta is associated with upper body hypertension and berry aneurysms, which predispose to intracranial haemorrhage as opposed to embolic stroke.

Patent foramen ovale.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to an out of hours service with headache, drowsiness, fever and neck stiffness. The fundi appear normal. There is a purpuric rash on his body. Previous medical history and family history are unremarkable. The GP phones you for advice as to what he should do while awaiting urgent ambulance transfer to hospital. What advice should be given?
options: Do nothing pending blood cultures and CSF analysis
explanation:
Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin
The scenario is suggestive of meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitides. Initial ‘blind’ treatment of suspected bacterial meningitis (especially meningococcal disease, as is likely given the rash) involves urgent transfer to hospital and parenteral benzylpenicillin before transfer (IV being preferable to intramuscular, if possible). Cefotaxime may be an alternative in penicillin allergy, and chloramphenicol may be used if there is a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin or cephalosporins. In hospital the current guideline is to give IV cefotaxime pending confirmation of the organism and antibiotic sensitivities; thereafter the regimen of choice for confirmed meningococcal meningitis is intravenous benzylpenicillin, 2.4 g every 4 h for 5–7 days or IV cefotaxime.

Do nothing pending blood cultures and CSF analysis
Do nothing pending blood cultures and CSF analysis is incorrect. Where there is a non-blanching rash, current guidelines advocate pre-hospital immediate antibiotic administration.

Give bolus IV cefotaxime
Give bolus IV cefotaxime is incorrect. Although this may be effective, current guidelines advocate benzylpenicillin as first-line therapy pre-hospital.

Give single high-dose oral benzylpenicillin
Give single high-dose oral benzylpenicillin is incorrect. Benzylpenicillin is ineffective when administered orally.

Give single high-dose oral cephalosporin
Give single high-dose oral cephalosporin is incorrect. Oral antibiotics would be inappropriate owing to slower onset and lower bioavailability. Bacterial Meningitis A 38-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with longstanding thoracic back pain and progressive problems with walking. He is now unable to stand. He has no past medical history. On examination he has a spastic paraparesis, upgoing plantars, bilateral hyperreflexia and a sensory level to all modalities at T10. Investigations.

stem: You suspect this patient has epilepsy. Where is the likely site of the seizure onset?
explanation:
Temporal lobe
Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common type of partial seizure. The patient’s subjective abdominal symptoms, and then staring, followed by lip smacking and a period of disorientation, are in keeping with a description of temporal lobe seizures. Inter-ictal EEGs are abnormal in one third of individuals with TLE. MRI is the imaging modality of choice, looking for an underlying cause such as hippocampal or temporal sclerosis, temporal lobe dysplasia or tumour, and PET may add further information.

Brainstem
Brainstem is incorrect. Myoclonus is associated with the brainstem.

Frontal lobe
Frontal lobe is incorrect. Frontal lobe seizures are usually characterised by prominent motor signs, and sometimes more complex automatisms including laughing, crying or vocalisations if prefrontal regions are involved. Speech arrest and dystonic posturing may also be seen.

Occipital lobe
Occipital lobe is incorrect. Occipital lobe seizures are characterised by visual hallucinations.

Parietal lobe
Parietal lobe is incorrect. Parietal lobe seizures are rarer, and may manifest somatosensory phenomena; patients may, for instance, describe abnormal sensation travelling up a limb during the course of a seizure.

stem: After a traumatic injury to her left upper limb, a 36-year-old woman presents with acute weakness and numbness of her left arm. On examination she has a wrist drop with marked weakness of the extensor digitorum longus, brachioradialis and subtle triceps muscles. There is sensory loss over the posterior forearm and a small area of numbness over the dorsum of her hand. The triceps reflex is diminished but other reflexes are intact. Where is the likely anatomical location of the nerve injury?
options: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Medial cord of the brachial plexus
Proximal median nerve in the axilla
Radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus
Ulnar nerve in the ulnar groove
explanation:
Radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus
The radial nerve is composed of fibres from C6 to C8 cervical spinal roots, but mainly from C7; it is the continuation of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. It is particularly susceptible to compression or traumatic damage as it winds around the humerus (including ‘Saturday night palsy’, a pressure palsy sustained while sleeping in an awkward position under the influence of alcohol), and may also be compressed in the axilla (eg from using a crutch). It supplies the muscles controlling elbow, wrist and finger extension as well as sensation over the posterior forearm and a small patch at the dorsal base of the thumb. The long and medial heads of triceps are supplied proximal to the spiral groove, but a branch to the lateral head emerges within the spiral groove, so some degree of triceps weakness could be expected in lesions at this site.

Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Lesions affecting the lateral cord of the brachial plexus is incorrect. Lateral cord of the brachial plexus will result predominantly in weakness of biceps and partially of median nerve innervated muscles, with sparing of radial nerve innervated muscles.

Medial cord of the brachial plexus
Medial cord of the brachial plexus is incorrect. Lesions affecting the medial cord of the brachial plexus will result in weakness of ulnar (and some median) nerve innervated muscles.

Proximal median nerve in the axilla
Proximal median nerve in the axilla is incorrect. A lesion of the proximal median nerve in the axilla will produce weakness in the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis) as well as flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis.

Ulnar nerve in the ulnar groove.

stem: A 65-year-old presents with sudden-onset visual disturbance. He denies any other symptoms. He is known to be a heavy smoker and hypertensive. On examination he has a right homonymous hemianopia, with sparing of the central field. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Left occipital lobe
The vascular risk factors and hyper-acute cadence of onset suggest that a stroke affecting the occipital lobe, the territory of the posterior cerebral artery, is the most likely cause of the presentation. Classically, strokes here will spare the occipital pole, the area topographically representing the macula. This is thought to be a consequence of dual supply of this area from anterior and posterior circulations. Hanzi Strokes affecting the occipitallobe will cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular (central field) sparing, as seen in this case.

Left optic nerve
Left optic nerve is incorrect. A complete optic nerve lesion would cause a unilateral blindness, whereas incomplete lesions would cause a scotoma.

Left optic tract
Left optic tract is incorrect. A lesion of the optic tract (ie the part of the visual pathway between the superior colliculus and the optic chiasm) would cause a homonymous hemianopia without sparing of the macula.

Left temporal lobe
Left temporal lobe is incorrect. A temporal lobe lesion causes a superior homonymous quadrantanopia. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Optic chiasma
Optic chiasma is incorrect. An optic chiasm lesion classically causes a bitemporal hemianopia.

stem: A 27-year-old motorcyclist comes to the neurology clinic some 6 months after suffering a significant motor vehicle accident. He is complaining of sensory symptoms affecting both upper limbs. You suspect a diagnosis of syringomyelia. Which of the following is the most likely finding?
options: Preserved pain and temperature sensation in the upper limbs
Spastic weakness with bilateral up going plantars in both lower limbs
explanation:
Spastic weakness with bilateral up going plantars in both lower limbs
This is a well-established finding in patients with syringomyelia.

Dysphonia and tongue atrophy
Dysphonia and tongue atrophy is incorrect. These are features of syringobulbia, which is more likely to be associated with congenital craniocervical malformation rather than trauma.

Hyperreflexia in the arms
Hyperreflexia in the arms is incorrect. There is loss of arm reflexes associated with syringmyelia rather than hyperreflexia.

Nystagmus
Nystagmus is incorrect. Nystagmus is more likely to be associated with syringobulbia and disease in the upper portion of the cord.

Preserved pain and temperature sensation in the upper limbs
Preserved pain and temperature sensation in the upper limbs is incorrect. There is ‘dissociate sensory loss’, where there is impaired perception of pain and temperature with preserved light touch and proprioception perception in the neck, arms and upper trunk.

stem: A 50-year-old man complains of a sharp pain over his left shoulder and upper trunk, exacerbated by coughing. He has noticed that when he places his left hand in the bath he is unable to feel the temperature accurately. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: T1 root lesion secondary to Pancoast’s tumour
explanation:
Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia represents the formation of a fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord. It may result from spinal cord trauma, tumours of the spinal cord, or congenital defects. Sensory manifestations arise primarily from interruption of decussating spinothalamic fibres, affecting pain and temperature sensation, while light touch, vibration and joint position sense are preserved (a ‘dissociated sensory loss’). Typically with a cervical syrinx, pain and temperature sensation are lost in a cape-like distribution. Syrinx extension into the anterior horns of the spinal cord damages motor neurones and causes diffuse muscle atrophy that begins in the hands and progresses proximally.

Atlanto-axial subluxation
Atlanto-axial subluxation is incorrect. Atlanto-axial subluxation occurs in rheumatoid arthritis and causes a high cervical myelopathy; this typically produces symptoms and signs in all four limbs, so does not match the history given here.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an acute demyelinating neuropathy that, although sometimes asymmetric, typically affects all four limbs. Patients usually have prominent weakness.

T1 root lesion secondary to Pancoast’s tumour
T1 root lesion secondary to Pancoast’s tumour is incorrect. A T1 root lesion may produce pain in the medial arm and weakness with wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles, thus it does not seem to fit the history given here.

Vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B 12 deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin B 12 deficiency produces subacute combined degeneration of the cord. This gives rise to symmetric weakness and sensory ataxia, predominantly affecting the lower limbs.

stem: A 28-year-old woman reports to her GP that her vision has become blurred in her right eye over the course of a few days. She has been rubbing the eye a lot, and now she also mentions that there is a dull ache in the eye. She has previously been fit and well. Her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill, which she has been taking for 8 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Demyelinating optic neuritis
Either compression or demyelination could cause this subacute onset of symptoms, but the aching favours demyelination.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is incorrect. Glaucoma characteristically causes halos around bright lights, which is not reported here.

Ischaemic optic neuritis
Ischaemic optic neuritis is incorrect. Ischaemic optic neuritis would likely cause her symptoms to come on more rapidly than reported.

Occipital lobe infarction
Occipital lobe infarction is incorrect. Occipital lobe infarction would produce a painless homonymous hemianopia. Optic Neuritis

Optic nerve compression
Optic nerve compression is incorrect. As outlined the aching described in the scenario makes demyelination more likely.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to her GP with mood swings and depression. She is prescribed Prozac, but returns a few months later with pains and numbness in both legs. Her antidepressant is changed but her mood worsens and she starts to have problems with her memory and motivation. She is referred to your clinic where, in addition to mild cognitive impairment, you notice slight increased tone in her limbs and occasional myoclonic jerks. Her MRI scan reveals thalamic hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, but her EEG is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
New-variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
New-variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) classically presents with psychiatric symptoms in young adults, followed by non-specific painful sensory symptoms, most often in the lower limbs.Cognitive impairment, pyramidal signs, myoclonus and primitive reflexes may then develop.Mean disease duration is approximately 14 months. MRI commonly shows a high signal on T2-weighted images in the pulvinar (posterior aspect of thalamus). EEG is often normal, compared with sporadic CJD in which biphasic or triphasicperiodic complexes are observed.

Corticobasal degeneration
Corticobasal degeneration is incorrect. Corticobasal degeneration presents as an asymmetric syndrome with rigidity, apraxia, myoclonus and alien limb phenomena. It usually presents after the age of 55.

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is incorrect. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is a primary epilepsy syndrome comprising earlymorning myoclonus and generalised tonic–clonic seizures, sometimes with absence seizures. The history here sounds quite different.

Progressive severe depression
Progressive severe depression is incorrect. The abnormal neurological signs on examination mean this cannot simply be severe depression.

Wilson’s disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic with sudden slurring of his speech, facial pain and vertigo. A diagnosis of lateral medullary syndrome is made. Abnormalities in which of the following vessels is most frequently associated with lateral medullary syndrome?
explanation:
Vertebral artery
In lateral medullary syndrome, the most commonly affected artery is the vertebral artery, followed by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, superior middle and inferior medullary arteries.

Anterior cerebral artery
The internal carotid arteries branch to form two major cerebral arteries: the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Together, they form the anterior circulation that supplies the forebrain; lesions in the anterior circulation present as: dysarthria/aphasia unilateral, contralateral motor weakness (leg/shoulder more than arm/hand/face) minimal sensory changes (two-point discrimination) in the same distribution as above left limb apraxia urinary incontinence.

External carotid artery
The external carotid artery is a major artery of the head and neck. It arises from the common carotid artery when it splits into the external and internal carotid artery. The external carotid artery supplies blood to the face and neck; it is not responsible for lateral medullary syndrome.

Middle cerebral artery
The middle cerebral artery is another internal carotid artery. As mentioned, it is one of the two arteries that form the anterior circulation that supplies the forebrain.

Internal carotid artery
The internal carotid artery is a terminal branch of the common carotid artery; it arises around the level of the fourth cervical vertebra when the common carotid bifurcates into this artery and its more superficial counterpart, the external carotid artery. It can be conceptually divided into three main segments: cervical, petrosal, and intracranial. It is not responsible for lateral medullary syndrome.

stem: A 32-year-old nurse presents to the Emergency Department for review. She has a history of increasing shortness of breath particularly when she lays flat in bed and weakness affecting her legs over the past few days. She remembers a diarrhoeal illness a few days earlier that she attributes to off milk. On examination oxygen saturations are 90% on air and she has absent lower limb reflexes bilaterally. You arrange a lumbar puncture which shows raised protein in the CSF but no organisms. Which one of the following is the most appropriate acute treatment for her underlying condition?
explanation:
Intravenous Immunoglobulin
This woman has Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), most probably related to previous Campylobacter infection. The only treatments of proven value are plasma exchange therapy and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). In the UK IVIG is generally used as first line therapy. The decreased oxygen saturations and shortness of breath are related to respiratory muscle weakness, and patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome should be managed with regular spirometry and reviewed on a High Dependency Unit

Pyridostigmine
Pyridostigmine is incorrect. Pyridostigmine is a symptomatic treatment for myasthenia gravis but has no effect in GBS. The areflexia, lack of oculobulbar symptoms and raised CSF protein make myasthenia unlikely clinically.

Physiotherapy
Physiotherapy is incorrect. Whilst mild forms of GBS can spontaneously (with physio for rehab) any patient who is non-ambulant or who has respiratory compromise needs active treatment.

IV corticosteroids
IV corticosteroids is incorrect. IV corticosteroids are not effective in GBS. Guillain-Barré Syndrome

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent is incorrect. Some patients with GBS have quite severe back pain, which may be helped by NSAIDs but they have no disease modifying effect.

stem: A 39-year-old man notices that he sustained a burn to his right hand while cooking, without being aware of it. On further questioning he admits that his grip on both sides has become gradually weaker over several months. On examination he has wasting and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, with occasional fasciculation seen in the abductor pollicis brevis. There is sensory loss to pinprick and temperature in both arms and trunk in a hemicape distribution. Other sensory modalities are normal. He has a right Horner syndrome. His lower limbs have normal power but slightly increased tone, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses. The remainder of the examination is normal. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for his symptoms and signs?
options: Neurofibromas in the cervical cord and brachial plexus
explanation:
Syringomyelia
The combination of gradual spinothalamic sensory loss in the described distribution, Horner syndrome, lower motor neuron signs in the upper limb and upper motor neuronsigns in the lower limbs is highly suggestive of syringomyelia, an abnormal cavitation within the central spinal cord. This usually occurs in the cervical region but may extend upwards into the brainstem (syringobulbia) or downwards to the thoracic or even lumbar cord There may be associated craniovertebral abnormalities such as a scoliosis or vertebral fusion, and about 90% of patients have a type-1 Chiari malformation (descent of the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum). Treatment is neurosurgical.

Meningioma of the cervical cord
Meningioma of the cervical cord is incorrect. As described the pattern of sensory loss in this patient make this a less likely diagnosis.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease could be given consideration (given the mixture of upper motor neurone (UMN) and lower motor neurone (LMN) features) but the sensory abnormalities in this case effectively rule motor neurone disease out.

Neurofibromas in the cervical cord and brachial plexus
Neurofibromas in the cervical cord and brachial plexus is incorrect. As described the pattern of sensory loss in this patient make this a less likely diagnosis.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis (in all of its forms) produces a pure upper motor neuron (UMN) clinical picture. Therefore, as well as the sensory findings being highly atypical for MS, the lower motor neuron (LMN) features seen in the upper limb make primary progressive multiple sclerosis very unlikely.

stem: A 18-year-old man presented with recurrent convulsions. The convulsions usually occur at night and are confirmed by an eyewitness. Clinical examination revealed three café-au-lait spots (15 mm in diameter) on the lower limbs, and four on his back. Which one of the following would be most helpful in confirming the suspected underlying diagnosis?
options: Genetic testing with protein truncation assay
explanation:
Slit-lamp examination of the eye
The implication is that this young man may have type-1 neurofibromatosis (NF). The seven clinical criteria used to diagnose NF1 (of which at least two should be present) are as follows: Six or more café-au-lait spots or hyperpigmented macules greater than or equal to 5 mm in diameter in pre-pubertal individuals and 15 mm in post-pubertal individuals Two or more neurofibromas (of any type) or one plexiform neurofibroma Axillary or inguinal freckles Two or more iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), often identified only through slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist Optic nerve glioma Sphenoid dysplasia or typical long-bone abnormalities, such as pseudarthrosis Therefore, the presence of Lisch nodules on slit-lamp examination of the eye allows one to make a positive clinical diagnosis of NF1 without further investigation.

Computed tomography (CT) brain
Computed tomography (CT) brain is incorrect. CT scan of the brain may be helpful in some cases (although MRI scan would be preferred), but is unlikely to allow a positive diagnosis to be made as per the criteria above.

Cutaneous biopsy of buttock lesion
Cutaneous biopsy of buttock lesion is incorrect. Skin lesions of those with NF1 are often biopsied to confirm their aetiology. However, café-au-lait spots are recognised based on their clinical features alone.

EEG
EEG is incorrect. EEG will not assist in defining the underlying diagnosis.

Genetic testing with protein truncation assay
Genetic testing with protein truncation assay is incorrect. Genetic testing in NF1 is complex, as a multitude of genetic abnormalities of the NF1 gene (Chrom 17) can result in the condition. Furthermore, current diagnostic criteria do not include genetic confirmation and allow for diagnosis to be made on the basis of clinical features alone.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment at this stage?
explanation:
Supportive care
The patient’s symptoms and clinical course are likely secondary to polio. Paralytic polio, as in this case, is seen in < 1% of all polio cases. There may be an initial prodrome of a flu-like illness or gastroenteritis which subsides. Paralytic polio often presents with severe muscle spasms of the back and lower limbs and flaccid muscle tone is usually seen unilaterally. The patient should also be placed in an isolation unit, as the major route of transmission for polio is faecal–oral. The patient should be closely monitored for respiratory failure, because even though lower limb paralysis is most common, a bulbar form does exist. Where paralysis does occur, some residual weakness is seen in up to 90% of cases.

Acyclovir
Acyclovir would be indicated for herpes encephalitis or varicella zoster central nervous system infection. In this case, both of these are less likely than polio given the prodromal flu like illness and asymmetrical lower motor pattern of weakness..

Intravenous ceftriaxone
Intravenous ceftriaxone is the treatment for bacterial meningitis. While muscle aches, neck pain and meningism suggest meningitis, the additional features of back pain, severe muscle spasms and decreased tone are not typically seen in meningitis and should point towards polio.

Intubation and ventilation
There is no current indication in the clinical scenario that the patient is in respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support. Respiratory failure occurs only if there is bulbar involvement in the later flaccid weakness stage of polio. Approximately 95% of patients with poliomyelitis are asymptomatic or have only mild systemic symptoms. The other 5% may display different severities of central nervous system involvement. The preparalytic stage involves a viral prodrome, headache, fever, irritability and meningism. This stage may then develop into paralytic polio, involving severe muscle pain and spasm, followed by flaccid weakness.

Methylprednisolone
Methylprednisolone has not been found to be beneficial in paralytic polio.

stem: A 70-year-old man is referred for increasing unsteadiness of gait. He has not fallen, but has taken to using a walking stick. In addition, he is finding his fingers to be increasingly stiff. His wife adds that she thinks he is also forgetful, something he denies. Over the last ten years, he has had some problems with urinary urgency and hesitancy, but his urinary symptoms have worsened over the past 3 months and he has had urinary incontinence on a number of occasions. He does not smoke, but has been a heavy drinker in the past. On examination of his gait, he takes short shuffling steps and found turning difficult, using a wide base. His writing is a little small and he does have slowness of fine finger movement bilaterally, but the muscle tone is normal. The Mini-Mental Test examination is 16/30, which he puts down to rushing to get to the hospital on time and still feeling flustered. What is most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
The triad of dementia, urinary symptoms and gait disturbance is classically associated with normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH).This man has had urinary symptoms for 10 years, so these may be due to simple prostatic hypertrophy, but the significant change in bladder symptoms more recently suggests something else may be going on.Disturbance of fine motor control of the fingers is equally prevalent in NPH, but less well recognised. NPH, therefore, seems the best choice.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Alzheimer’s disease very rarely presents with a gait disorder and mobility issues are only really seen in the late stages of the condition.

Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is incorrect. FTD presents with altered behaviour and social conduct. Patients may have a dysexecutive syndrome on cognitive testing. Patients with FTD may develop Parkinsonism as the disease progresses, but gait failure is rarelya presenting feature.

Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease
Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease is incorrect. This patient does not have the clinical signs of idiopathic Parkinson’s disease. There is no evidence of asymmetric, upper limb predominant tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity. In addition, it is unusual to have significant cognitive impairment at presentation.

Multi-infarct dementia
Multi-infarct dementia is incorrect. Multi-infarct dementia is a good differential diagnosis in this case, although one might reasonably expect a ‘step-wise’ deterioration and neurological examination often reveals upper motor neurone signs.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents with progressive cognitive impairment and personality change. He gives a history of a stroke 2 years before, which has left him with mild left hemiparesis, and prior to that he had had several ‘mini-strokes’. He has a long history of migrainous headaches. His brother has a similar history, in that he, too, had several strokes between the ages of 40 and 55. Their mother died at 60 of ‘dementia’ and his father’s medical history is unknown. He has four children in their late 20s. His daughter suffers from migraine and had what seemed to be a transient ischaemic episode during her first pregnancy. Another son also has frequent headaches, sometimes with associated transient weakness of one side of his body. On examination, the patient has signs of left hemiparesis, generally brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars. He has an apraxic gait. His MiniMental State Examination score is 24/30 with slow responses. What possible unifying diagnosis should be considered when investigating his cognitive problem?
options: Autosomal-dominant form of cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Cerebral autosomal-dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
Mitochondrial encephalopathy with leukoencephalopathy and stroke-like features
explanation:
Cerebral autosomal-dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
Cerebral autosomal-dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) is the most common genetic form of vascular dementia. It has a very variable phenotype but is characterised by a high prevalence of migraine with aura (often atypical aura), strokes at a young age and early vascular (subcortical) dementia. Variability in presentation may partly reflect environmental factors, eg smoking is associated with an earlier age of onset. The affected locus is on chromosome 19q12 – the ‘NOTCH 3’ gene – and several different possible mutations have been identified (missense mutations or deletions). MRI scanning shows subcortical white matter change, often involving the temporal poles. Given the symptoms and suggestion of an autosomaldominant inheritance pattern, CADASIL is the best answer here.

Autosomal-dominant form of cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Autosomal-dominant form of cerebral amyloid angiopathy is incorrect. Hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy can cause autosomal-dominant strokes and vascular dementia (sometimes with epilepsy), but the strong history of migraine could not be explained.

Familial hemiplegic migraine
Familial hemiplegic migraine is incorrect. Familial hemiplegic migraine cannot really explain the progressive cognitive problem, and although the auras can be severe and prolonged, a permanent hemiparesis would be unusual.

Hyperhomocysteinaemia
Hyperhomocysteinaemia is incorrect. Hyperhomocysteinaemia is a risk factor for thrombotic events and cardiovascular disease. It can be due to genetic polymorphisms in 5-MTHF reductase, but it is not a cause of autosomal-dominant hereditary cerebrovascular disease with dementia, as described in this case. Dementia

Mitochondrial encephalopathy with leukoencephalopathy and stroke-like features
Mitochondrial encephalopathy with leukoencephalopathy and stroke-like features (MELAS) is an important differential diagnosis in young onset stroke. It is a mitochondrial disease, so maternal patterns of inheritance are typically seen. Other ‘mitochondrial’ features such as diabetes, deafness and seizures are often also present in the patient or the family history.

stem: A 75-year-old woman with a long history of hypertension and diabetes presents with a sudden onset of involuntary movements of her right arm and leg. On examination she has right hemiballistic involuntary movements. Which structure has most likely been damaged?
explanation:
Subthalamic nucleus
This is a diabetic and hypertensive patient presenting with hemiballism. Hemiballism is a complication of subthalamic nucleus damage. Other causes include tumours and abscess. Dopamine antagonists are the treatment of choice. The commonest cause is stroke.

Ventral pallidum
Ventral pallidum Caudate nucleus is incorrect. Damage to the caudate nucleus causes chorea. The ventral pallidum is a component of the basal ganglia which forms part of the limbic loop and is involved in the reward system.

Dentate nucleus
Dentate nucleus is incorrect. Damage to the dentate nucleus is associated with ataxia.

Hippocampus
Hippocampus is incorrect. Damage to the hippocampus is associated with memory impairment.

Red nucleus
Red nucleus is incorrect. Damage to the red nucleus is associated with tremor. 715 CNS Tumours A 52-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is found unconscious on a park bench near to the hospital. According to his fellow rough sleepers he has been increasingly sleepy and confused over the past few days. He has been drinking up to 3 bottles of strong cider per day. On examination he is very drowsy and has bruising above his left eye and towards the left hand side of his head. There is bruising over both arms and across the right hand side of his chest consistent with rib injury. His BP is 155/85 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular, temperature is 38.2 oC. He has signs of left sided consolidation. You eventually manage to partially wake him, and he appears to have a focal weakness of his left arm. Investigations;.

stem: A 55-year-old right-handed woman with breast cancer presents with symptoms suggestive of brain metastasis. Which neuropsychological finding is most likely to suggest a right parietal lesion?
explanation:
Visual inattention
Parietal lobe damage manifests as a defect of attention in the contralateral visual field, astereognosis, constructional apraxia (non-dominant), dressing apraxia (non-dominant) and ideomotor apraxia (dominant). Right hemisphere (ie non-dominant) parietal lesions are particularly prone to producing visual neglect. Thus visual inattention is the best answer here.

Acalculia
Acalculia is incorrect. Gerstmann syndrome consists of acalculia, agraphia, impaired right/left discrimination and finger agnosia, and is caused by a lesion in the dominant (ie usually left hemisphere) angular gyrus (part of the inferior parietal lobe). Therefore acalculia is incorrect.

Finger agnosia
Finger agnosia is incorrect. Gerstmann syndrome consists of acalculia, agraphia, impaired right/left discrimination and finger agnosia, and is caused by a lesion in the dominant (ie usually left hemisphere) angular gyrus (part of the inferior parietal lobe). Therefore finger agnosia is incorrect.

Receptive aphasia
Receptive aphasia is incorrect. Receptive aphasia classically involves damage to Wernicke’s area in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus.

Reduced digit span
Reduced digit span is incorrect. Reduced digit span is a sign of impaired working memory and usually occurs in left-sided temporoparietal lesions, although sometimes frontal damage can produce a poor digit span as well.

stem: Autonomic neuropathy is least likely to occur in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis
Autonomic neuropathy commonly associates with other forms of neuropathy. It can be asymptomatic or cause incapacitating disability, especially as a result of severe postural hypotension. Three types of dysfunction are prominent: Gastrointestinal: gastroparesis, episodic nocturnal diarrhoea and colonic dilatation Cardiovascular: postural hypotension, elevated heart rate, loss of respiratory sinus arrhythmia Genitourinary: large residual volume, retrograde ejaculation and impotence. Causes of autonomic neuropathy:- CNS (central nervous system) Multiple system atrophy Parkinson’s disease Wernicke’s encephalopathy (as a result of chronic alcoholism) Syringomyelia/syringobulbia Peripheral nervous system Familial dysautonomia (Riley–Day syndrome) Familial amyloidosis Guillain–Barré syndrome Diabetes mellitus Tabes dorsalis Alcoholic nutritional neuropathy Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). This presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder which is associated with anti-voltage gated calcium channel antibodies in those with small-cell lung cancer is associated with autonomic dysfunction, but myasthenia gravis (a post synaptic disorder) is not. Therefore, myasthenia gravisoption is correct.

Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is incorrect. Autonomic neuropathy is likely to occur in Amyloidosis.

Chronic alcoholism
Chronic alcoholism is incorrect. Autonomic neuropathy is likely to occur in chronic alcoholism.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. Autonomic neuropathy is likely to occur in Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Multiple system atrophy
Multiple system atrophy is incorrect. Autonomic neurophathy is likely to occur in multiple system atrophy.

stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis is found to have horizontal nystagmus on abduction. There is also impaired adduction on the left side. Where is the lesion responsible likely to be?
explanation:
Medial longitudinal bundle
The phenomenon above is called internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and is caused by a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which is responsible for coordinating lateral gaze movements. It causes ipsilateral reduced/absent eye adduction.

Cerebellar peduncle
Cerebellar peduncle is incorrect. Lesions in the cerebellar peduncle usually affect saccadic and smooth pursuit eye movements.

Hypothalamus
Hypothalamus is incorrect. The hypothalamus and the pituitary gland are in close proximity to the optic chiasm, and therefore lesions in these structures can also give rise to visual field defect.

Oculomotor nucleus
Oculomotor nucleus is incorrect. Lesions in the oculomotor nucleus will cause third cranial nerve palsy (full or partial), where individuals can present with symptoms of blurry vision, diplopia and a droopy eyelid, and an eye that appears to be in a down and out position.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm is incorrect. Lesions affecting the optic chiasm will give rise to visual defect, particularly bitemporal hemianopia.

stem: A 32-year-old woman, who works as a croupier and is normally fit and well, had woken 3 weeks before with weakness in her left hand. She had noted numbness at the base of the thumb on the dorsum of the hand. She is on the oral contraceptive pill. She drinks alcohol in binges, one of which had occurred the night before her symptoms started, and smokes 15 cigarettes per day. She has a normal general examination, normal cranial nerves and normal muscle tone, but mild weakness of the left brachioradialis and moderate weakness of wrist and finger extension. She has full power in her other arm muscles including elbow extension. Reflexes are normal. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
explanation:
Radial nerve at the spiral groove
The history is consistent with ‘Saturday night palsy’. A lesion of the radial nerve at the spiral groove is the most likely answer. This causes weakness in radial-innervated muscles distal to the site of the lesion.

C7 nerve root lesion
A C7 nerve root lesion is incorrect. C7 nerve root lesion is unlikely because the triceps was not involved and the brachioradialis (C5, 6) was involved.

Posterior interosseous nerve
Posterior interosseous nerve is incorrect. A posterior interosseous nerve lesion is unlikely because there was involvement of muscles outside the posterior interosseous nerve territory (brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus).

Right cerebral cortex
Right cerebral cortex is incorrect. A lesion in the right cerebral cortex would be unlikely to produce such a focal pattern of weakness and sensory loss. In addition there may be brisk reflexes in the affected limb.

Ulnar nerve
Ulnar nerve is incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies the small muscles of the hand, and a different sensory territory (medial border of hand and little finger). Mononeuropathies A patient presents with eye pain and diplopia of 2 days’ duration. On examination there is no proptosis, but a left-sided VIth nerve palsy, a partial left IIIrd nerve palsy, and left Vth nerve sensory changes over the maxilla are present.

stem: A 22-year-old man develops a depressive illness that fails to respond to drug treatment. He complains of pins and needles over the left-hand side of his body. Within 5 months his gait has become unsteady and he has difficulty in performing fine-motor tasks. On examination he has a depressed affect with mild short-term memory impairment and difficulty in copying a clock-face diagram. There are bilateral cerebellar signs and the reflexes are all pathologically brisk with equivocal plantar responses. He has occasional writhing movements of his left upper limb. A clinical diagnosis of variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is suspected. A cranial MRI is performed. Which one of the following MRI findings would be most supportive of this diagnosis?
options: Diffuse white-matter disease on T2-weighted imaging
Increased signal in the caudate nucleus
Increased signal in the pineal body
Increased signal in the pulvinar of the thalamus
explanation:
Increased signal in the pulvinar of the thalamus
The clinical picture given is typical of variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (vCJD), the human form of bovine spongiform encephalopathy. This is a rare condition with a median age of onset of 28 years. Typical symptoms include persistent painful sensory symptoms and neuropsychiatricdisturbance followed by a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia, myoclonus and sometimes dystonia. A definitive diagnosis requires postmortem tissue confirmation, but some investigations allow categorisation into ‘possible’ or ‘probable’ cases. MRI scanning is usually the first step. The ‘pulvinar sign’ on cranial MRI has been found in > 90% of pathologically confirmed cases of vCJD (but not sporadic or other forms) so it is the correct answer here.

Diffuse white-matter disease on T2-weighted imaging
Diffuse white-matter disease on T2-weighted imaging is incorrect. Diffuse white-matter disease on T2weighted imaging is typical of vascular dementia.

Increased signal in the caudate nucleus
Increased signal in the caudate nucleus is incorrect. Increased signal in the caudate nucleus is one of the radiological markers of sporadic CJD, together with cortical ribbon hyperintensity. These changes are often seen on T2-weighted imaging but are best appreciated using DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging) sequences.

Increased signal in the pineal body
Increased signal in the pineal body is incorrect. Increased signal in the pineal body is not associated with any form of prion disease and would most likely represent a simple pineal cyst.

Normal scan.

stem: A 42-year-old woman complains of nocturnal tingling and pain in her right hand. The pain is reproduced on tapping over the median nerve at the wrist. Given the probable explanation for her symptoms, what is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Idiopathic
This patient most probably has carpal tunnel syndrome, which is a common condition causing median nerve compression at the wrist. There is nocturnal tingling and pain in the hand (and forearm at times), followed by weakness of the thenar muscles. Tinel’s sign occurs when the symptoms are reproduced by tapping over the median nerve.

Acromegaly
Acromegaly is incorrect. Whilst it may cause carpal tunnel syndrome, the majority of cases are idiopathic.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. Whilst it may cause carpal tunnel syndrome, the majority of cases are idiopathic.

Pregnancy
Pregnancy is incorrect. Whilst it may cause carpal tunnel syndrome, the majority of cases are idiopathic. Mononeuropathies You are called to see a 23-year-old woman who, after delivery (of a term infant), developed unrelated severe diarrhoea and vomiting over 24 hours. She has become confused, had a generalised tonic–clonic seizure and developed a left hemiparesis. Her BP is 115/60 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. Over the past 24 hours she has received 4.5 l of IV fluid replacement according to the chart, and has passed 2.2 l of urine.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Whilst it may cause carpal tunnel syndrome, the majority of cases are idiopathic.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with dense left-sided hemiparesis of more than 8 hours duration. A CT scan shows an acute infarct involving the right middle cerebral artery. A carotid ultrasound scan shows 80% stenosis of the left carotid artery and 45% stenosis of the right carotid artery. He suffered a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) in the same arterial territory last year and is taking aspirin 75 mg. What is the most appropriate treatment for long-term stroke prevention?
explanation:
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is the correct option, as NICE guidance currently recommends it as the first-line treatment for secondary prevention after an ischaemic stroke. This recommendation is based on clinical trials demonstrating clopidogrel’s efficacy in reducing recurrent stroke risk and better tolerability compared to other antiplatelet therapies. Clopidogrel’s action inhibits platelet aggregation, contributing to a decrease in subsequent thrombotic events. Its once-daily dosing also improves patient adherence and convenience.

Aspirin 300 mg
This dosage is prescribed for the initial two weeks following an ischaemic stroke or TIA to prevent immediate recurrence. For long-term prevention, a lower maintenance dose or alternative medications are recommended. Continuing aspirin at 300 mg indefinitely may increase the risk of bleeding complications. Thus, it is not suitable for chronic secondary prevention of stroke.

Aspirin and dipyridamole in combination
Aspirin and dipyridamole in combination is incorrect because while it was previously recommended, current NICE guidance supersedes this with clopidogrel for secondary prevention of stroke. The combination could Tutor offer benefits in preventing recurrent strokes, yet clinical evidence now supports the efficacy and safety profile of clopidogrel. Using this combination adds complexity in managing potential side effects and adherence compared to single-agent therapy. Consequently, it is not preferred for this patient.

Carotid endarterectomy
Although it can be beneficial in certain cases of significant carotid stenosis, the patient’s right carotid artery— associated with the symptomatic area—is only 45% stenosed. NICE guidelines generally recommend endarterectomy for stenosis greater than 50% in symptomatic patients unless they have a disabling stroke. The patient's dense hemiparesis likely limits the potential benefits, making surgery less advantageous.

stem: A 45-year-old migraineur presents having had an episode of sudden onset posterior headache associated with nausea and vomiting. He is afebrile with no neck stiffness or photophobia, and the neurological examination is normal. CT of his head performed 12 hours after the onset of symptoms is normal. What is the best course of action?
explanation:
Lumbar puncture
Although the patient has a history of migraine, sudden onset posterior headache is not typical of migraine and is an emergency situation; subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) has to be excluded. Small aneurysmal bleeds might not present with neck stiffness or photophobia. Plain CT brain with in the first 24 hours of the event is diagnostic in 95% of the cases; however, a negative scan means there is still a 5% chance of missing the bleed. Lumbar puncture for spectrophotometry, done after 12 hours following the event, is very sensitive and increases the yield for the diagnosis of SAH. Lumbar puncture would also help exclude CNS infections.

Discharge with analgesia
Discharge with analgesia is incorrect. Discharge with analgesia in this situation is not ideal as every sudden onset headache with a good history needs to be investigated.

Monitor for 24 hours
Monitor for 24 hours is incorrect. Monitoring for 24 hours is not the right option because if there is SAH or CNS infection the patient may deteriorate rapidly and this can be life threatening. Prompt diagnosis is essential.

MRI (brain)
MRI (brain) is incorrect. MRI (brain) confers no extra benefit over CT in this situation andit might be difficult to obtain in an emergency situation.

Urgent neurology outpatient appointment
Urgent neurology appointment is incorrect. Urgent neurology outpatient appointment is again not ideal as this is an emergency situation.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with epilepsy not responding to pharmacological treatment has undergone pre-surgical assessment for a unilateral temporal lobectomy. She wants to continue her hobby as an artist if possible. Which of the following visual field defects may be seen post-operatively?
explanation:
Superior homonymous quadrantonopia
The visual field defect and their corresponding lesion may be remembered with the acronym “PITS” namely Parietal lobe, Inferior homonymous quadrantonopia, Temporal lobe, Superior homonymous quadrantonopia. Notably, a temporal lobe lesion may progress to a homonymous hemianopia.

Bi-nasal hemianopia
Bi-nasal hemianopia is incorrect. This is a rarely encountered visual field defect. Anatomically, this is due to compression or damage of the uncrossed fibres of the optic nerve.

Bi-temporal hemianopia
Bi-temporal hemianopia is incorrect. This is due to a lesion of the optic chiasm, causes including a pituitary tumour or a craniopharyngioma.

Central scotoma
Central scotoma is incorrect. Central scotomas may occur due to defects of the macula, such as age-related macular degeneration. Visual Field Defects

Inferior homonymous quadrantonopia
Inferior homonymous quadrantonopia is incorrect. This would correspond to a parietal lobe lesion, not a temporal lobe lesion (see Answer for Option E).

stem: A 33-year-old man presents with a 10-year history of arm tremor. However, it has become worse recently, such that he now finds it embarrassing at work and is worried about losing his job. His father had a similar problem, although this was mild and always put down to benign tremulous Parkinson’s disease. On examination he has a fine postural tremor, but normal tone. Fine finger movements are normal, as is his gait. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Essential tremor
The fine postural tremor is typical of essential tremor. It is often familial. The absence of other neurological signs helps to support this diagnosis.

Familial cerebellar degeneration
Familial cerebellar degeneration is incorrect. A familial cerebellar degeneration seems unlikely in the absence of cerebellar signs.

Familial Parkinson’s disease
Familial Parkinson’s disease is incorrect. The lack of extrapyramidal signs and a rest tremor makes familial Parkinson’s disease unlikely.

Severe anxiety
Severe anxiety is incorrect. Severe anxiety is often associated with a tremor, but the family history and lack of clear anxiety symptoms make this less likely than essential tremor.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. There are no extrapyramidal or cerebellar signs to suggest Wilson’s disease, and no mention is made of the presence of KF rings.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with two episodes of right, painless, transient, monocular visual loss lasting up to a minute: each episode was like a curtain descending from the upper visual field to affect the whole vision of her right eye. Neurological examination is normal. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), glucose and lipids are all within the normal ranges. Resting electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus rhythm and a 72-hour tape reveals no arrhythmias. Computed tomography (CT) brain is normal. Doppler of the carotid arteries shows a 40% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery. She is otherwise well apart from hypertension managed with two oral agents. What is the treatment of choice for secondary prevention of further thrombus formation?
explanation:
Clopidogrel
This patient has amaurosis fugax of the right eye, characterised by painless transient monocular visual loss. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent used for secondary prevention of thrombus formation and is often the drug of choice for long-term secondary prevention of ischaemic events. However, the initial treatment when a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is suspected remains high-dose aspirin 300 mg daily for a period of 2 weeks.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Amaurosis fugax is a manifestation of an emboli phenomenon where a transient clot passes through the retinal artery causing the transient loss of vision. Prednisolone has no place in the management of a vascular event. Further, a normal ESR and other investigations exclude the possibility of giant cell arteritis or other vasculitis causes.

Right carotid artery angioplasty
The right carotid artery supplies the retinal artery to the right eye. Angioplasty is not the intervention of choice in carotid artery stenosis. It is still in the experimental stages and has not been accepted as a standard procedure in clinical practice guidelines. Further, this lady has only a 40% stenosis, which does not warrant interventions

Right carotid artery endarterectomy
The right carotid artery is the artery that supplies the right retinal artery. However, a 40% stenosis is not an indication for carotid endarterectomy. Carotid endarterectomy is indicated only if there is a moderate or worse (> 50%) stenosis of the symptomatic carotid artery.

Aspirin and dipyridamole.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation:
Heptavalent antitoxin
This man has symptoms and signs consistent with food-borne botulism, and administration of antitoxin as soon as possible after the diagnosis is made is an important component of management. As the antitoxin is produced from equine serum, hypersensitivity to the infusion may occur. Clinical improvement may take weeks to months, Tutor but recovery is eventually seen in around 95% of patients. Supportive care, including monitoring for,AI and treatment of, respiratory failure is crucial.

Benzylpenicillin
Benzylpenicillin is incorrect.Chloramphenicol
Chloramphenicol is incorrect. Chloramphenicol has good penetration of the blood brain barrier and can be used to treat CNS infections including Neisseria meningitides. However, it does not have a role in the treatment of botulism.

Intravenous immunoglobulin
Intravenous immunoglobulin is incorrect. Intravenous immunoglobulin is used to treat several neurological conditions, including Guillain–Barré syndrome and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, but would not be the treatment of choice here. Clostridium BotulinumIntravenous methylprednisolone
Intravenous methylprednisolone is incorrect. Intravenous methylprednisolone is used in the acute treatment of central nervous system inflammatory disorders and can shorten the duration of multiple sclerosis relapses. However, it would not be the treatment of choice here.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the neurology clinic for review. He is very concerned that his 78-year-old father has recently been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, and requests information on assessment of his The son’s) possible risk factors for developing the disease. He has mild hypertension, controlled with ramipril 5 mg daily; he also takes ibuprofen after exercise because of a previous knee injury. He works as an accountant, which he tells you can be very stressful. Examination reveals a BP of 138/82 mmHg, with pulse 74/min and regular. His BMI is 28. Which of the following would be considered the most important risk factor for developing Alzheimer’s in this case?
explanation:
Family history of Alzheimer’s
Although hypertension and obesity are also risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease, this patient’s hypertension is well controlled and his BMI is only mildly elevated. Consequently, family history represents the most important risk factor for this patient. Other risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease include: Vascular risk factors, such as insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, uncontrolled hypertension, obesity APOE4 genotype Traumatic brain injury Down’s syndrome

NSAID use
NSAID use is incorrect. In fact, NSAID use may be a protective factor against developing Alzheimer’s disease.

BMI 28
BMI 28 is incorrect. A BMI of 28 means that this patient is overweight, but he is not obese. Obesity is an independent risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease, but being overweight is not. Therefore, in this case, his family history is a more significant risk factor.

Controlled hypertension
Controlled hypertension is incorrect. Hypertension is a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease, but as this patient’s hypertension is well controlled, his family history is a more important risk factor.

Stressful job as an accountant
Stressful job as an accountant is incorrect. Having a complex job that intellectually engages you may in fact be a protective factor against developing Alzheimer’s disease. Alzheimer’s.

stem: A 19-year-old man has had a tendency to complex tics since childhood. He repeatedly squats down on the ground and also has another repetitive action of rubbing his nose. He is prone to loud vocalisations, sometimes swear-words. The symptoms significantly interfere with his attempts to get work. A diagnosis of Gilles de la Tourette syndrome has been made. How might this be best treated?
explanation:
Risperidone
Gilles de la Tourette syndrome is a rare tic syndrome consisting of multiple tics involving both motor actions and vocalisations. Onset is in childhood. Utterance of obscenities (coprolalia) is a dramatic manifestation; echolalia and palilalia may also occur. The underlying cause is unknown, with no particular imaging or standard histopathological abnormalities having been identified.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline is not used in the treatment of Tourette syndrome.

Cognitive-behavioural therapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy is incorrect. Cognitive behavioural therapy can be used in Tourette syndrome and is perhaps more effective for milder tics.

Chlorpromazine
Chlorpromazine is incorrect. Chlorpromazine was one of the first antipsychotics to be developed and has a significant adverse effect profile; it is not used to treat Tourette syndrome.

stem: A 79-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit after suffering a subarachnoid haemorrhage. His GCS is 3 and the team is evaluating him for the possibility of brain death. The oculovestibular response is not intact. Which of the following represents the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Brainstem
The vestibulo-ocular reflex is tested by the caloric test. No eye movements are seen during or following the slow injection of at least 50 ml of ice-cold water over 60 s into each external auditory meatus in turn. Clear access to the tympanic membrane must be established by direct inspection, and the head should be at 30° to the horizontal plane, unless this positioning is contraindicated by the presence of an unstable spinal injury. Testing of the reflex forms part of the confirmation of a diagnosis of brainstem death. Diagnosing brainstem death requires a certain code of practice, written by the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges.

Optic nerves
Optic nerves is incorrect. The visual pathways are not responsible for the doll’s eye reflex. A lesion at one or both of the optic nerves would cause total blindness in the ipsilateral eye.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm is incorrect. The visual pathways are not responsible for the doll’s eye reflex. A lesion at the optic chiasm would cause a bitemporal hemianopia.

Occipital lobes
Occipital lobes is incorrect. The visual pathways are not responsible for the doll’s eye reflex. A lesion at the one of occipital lobes would cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Cortical blindness can be caused by bilateral lesions at the occipital lobes. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

Cerebellum
Cerebellum is incorrect. The cerebellum plays a role in motor learning to correct the damaged vestibule-ocular reflex to allow for accurate movement of the eyes.

stem: A 35-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia. During the next 24 hours he developed a dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, breathlessness and progressive weakness of his upper and lower limbs, initially affecting the proximal muscles. On examination, he has fixed dilated pupils, generalised ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria and pharyngeal weakness. His cough is weak. He has a global weakness of his upper and lower limbs. Tone is reduced, reflexes depressed and plantar responses flexor. Sensation is normal. General medical examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Botulism
The clinical picture is highly suggestive of botulism, a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disordercaused by a toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum that prevents the release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal. Botulism presents with cranial neuropathies, autonomic dysfunction (particularly mydriatic pupils and dry mouth) and limb weakness which is classically descending. Reflexes are absent or depressed. Sensation is normal. Respiratory failure is a frequent complication. As with Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), repetitive nerve stimulation shows an incremental response Diagnosis is made by demonstrating the presence of toxin in serum, stool or vomit and is supported by neurophysiology. Treatment is largely supportive. The early administration of antitoxin may be of value in some cases. Prognosis is good if appropriate supportive treatment is initiated early (ie in an ITU setting).

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is incorrect. In GBS the weakness is classically ascending, rather than the descending pattern seen here. The mydriasis and lack of any sensory findings would also be unusual for GBS.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. The cadence of onset is far too rapid for motor neurone disease.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder which does bear some similarities to botulism (and LEMS). However, the autonomic involvement seen here is not in keeping with MG and is seen only in the presynaptic disorders (LEMS and botulism).

Poliomyelitis
Poliomyelitis is incorrect. Although the encephalitic form of polio can cause autonomic dysfunction, the lack of fever and other encephalitic features (eg stupor) make poliomyelitis unlikely.

stem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the neurology clinic for review. He has been diagnosed with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), predominantly leading to jerking affecting his upper limbs. He continues to have 3 or more episodes per week, mainly in the hour after waking. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication for him?
explanation:
Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is correct. Whilst it is slightly less effective than valproate, valproate is not recommended for use in patients < 55 years old. Levetiracetam is usually well tolerated with the exception of mood disturbance in a low number of patients.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. It is contraindicated in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and can exacerbate myoclonus.

Topiramate
Topiramate is a third line option in the treatment of JME. It may result in mood disorder and weight loss and is slightly less effective than levetiracetam or lamotrigine.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect. It should not be offered as a first line as it can exacerbate myoclonus. It is usually preferred as a second-line agent.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with a 1-day history of left-sided neck pain and right-sided sensorimotor disturbance. Shortly after the neck pain had begun, he had noted that his left eyelid was ‘drooping’, and that he had developed weakness and altered sensation in his right arm and leg. He had recently visited a chiropractor for neck pain after a road traffic collision. Examination reveals a left Horner syndrome and weakness and sensory disturbance on the right-hand side with an extensor right plantar. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Carotid artery dissection
The constellation of symptoms and signs is best explained by a left carotid artery dissection causing left hemispheric ischaemia, and subsequent right-sided signs. Carotid and vertebral artery dissection are reported after chiropractic manipulation and episodes of neck trauma, but are often spontaneous. The association of pain in the neck with an ischaemic stroke syndrome should always raise dissection as a possibility. Carotid dissection commonly causes Horner syndrome because of the intimate association of sympathetic nerve fibres and the carotid artery.

Lateral medullary infarction
Lateral medullary infarction is incorrect. There are no posterior circulation symptoms or signs to support a diagnosis of lateral medullary infarction, although this does cause Horner syndrome.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. A subarachnoid haemorrhage might present with sudden-onset symptoms, but rarely with focal signs like these and not with Horner syndrome.

Venous sinus thrombosis
Venous sinus thrombosis is incorrect. Venous sinus thrombosis might cause right hemiplegia, but does not explain the Horner syndrome and is not usually of sudden onset.

Vertebral artery dissection.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with Alzheimer’s disease currently on lorazepam and haloperidol presents with increasing immobility associated with falls. On examination in the clinic she is confused, her BP is 155/72 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. There is no postural drop. She has bradykinesia with evidence of cog-wheel rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Dopamine blocking or depleting drugs are an important cause of parkinsonism. In this case the haloperidol is likely to be responsible for the patient’s clinical picture, which suggests drug-induced parkinsonism. Antipsychotics should be avoided in dementia wherever possible, as such patients may be particularly susceptible to extra-pyramidal side effects and such drugs also seem to increase the risk of stroke in this population.

Brain tumour
Brain tumour is incorrect. A brain tumour is more likely to present with seizures, headache or focal neurological signs. The findings of bradykinesia and rigidity on examination make this diagnosis less likely than extrapyramidal drug side effects to be the cause for her presentation.

Concomitant Parkinson’s disease
Concomitant Parkinson’s disease is incorrect. Concomitant Parkinson’s disease is always possible, but the fact that haloperidol is among her regular medications means that a drug-induced parkinsonism is much more likely.

Deteriorating Alzheimer’s disease
Deteriorating Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Although deteriorating Alzheimer’s disease can be associated with mild parkinsonism, the fact that haloperidol is among her regular medications means that a drug-induced parkinsonism is much more likely.

Subdural haematoma
Subdural haematoma is incorrect. A subdural haematoma is an important cause of physical deterioration in frail, elderly patients, especially those who are prone to falls. However, the findings of extra-pyramidal signs on examination make this diagnosis less likely to be the cause for her presentation. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s.

stem: Which one of the following features is most typical of cavernous sinus thrombosis?
options: Ipsilateral lower motor facial nerve palsy
Loss of pin-prick sensation around the chin area
explanation:
Double vision on looking upwards
Cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually due to a suppurative process in the orbit, nasal sinuses, or upper half of the face, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus infection. The condition is severe with high fever, headache, malaise, nausea, vomiting and convulsions. Chemosis, oedema and cyanosis of the upper face occur due to obstruction of the ophthalmic vein. Ophthalmoplegia is secondary to damage to the third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves. Eye pain and hyperaesthesia of the forehead (not the chin) is due to damage to the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1, the ophthalmic branch).

Difficulty in swallowing
Difficulty in swallowing is incorrect. Bulbar failure is not a feature of the cavernous sinus syndrome.

Ipsilateral lower motor facial nerve palsy
Ipsilateral lower motor facial nerve palsy is incorrect. The facial nerve does not pass through the cavernous sinus.

Loss of pin-prick sensation around the chin area
Loss of pin-prick sensation around the chin area is incorrect. Ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve pass through the cavernous sinus, but the mandibular branch does not. Cavernous Sinus SyndromePapilloedema is an early feature
Papilloedema is an early feature is incorrect. Retinal haemorrhage and papilloedema are late events and the absence of these signs should not be relied upon to rule out the condition.

stem: A 20-year-old female presents with right unilateral ocular pain, which is worse on eye movement, and blurred vision in the same eye. Her visual acuity is RVA 6/24, LVA 6/6. Colour vision is impaired on the right and there is a right, relative, afferent pupillary defect. Visual field examination shows a right central scotoma. The patient has read about multiple sclerosis and wishes to know what her risk is of developing this condition. MRI brain is performed and shows an area of high signal within the white matter. What are the approximate chances of the patient developing multiple sclerosis in the next 15 years?
explanation:
50%
The five cardinal features of optic neuritis are reduced visual acuity, impaired colour vision, pain on eye movement, relative afferent pupillary defect and scotoma. Visual function generally improves spontaneously over weeks, and 95% of patients return to visual acuity of at least 36/60 within 12 months. Optic neuritis may occur as an isolated self-limiting presentation or may represent the first episode of demyelination in some patients, who will go on to develop multiple sclerosis (MS). Studies have shown that the presence or absence of demyelinating lesions on MRI can help prognosticate by stratifying the risk of MS in patients with acute isolated optic neuritis. In the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (2006), the 15-year risk of MS in the group of patients with at least one MRI T2 lesion was 50%, whereas the 15-year risk with a normal baseline MRI was 25%. Therefore, 50% is correct and 25% is incorrect. The other choices are inaccurate estimates based on this evidence.

2%
2% is incorrect. As described this does not match the findings of the Optic Neuritis Treatment trial for patients with at least one MRI T2 lesion.

25%
25% is incorrect. As described this does not match the findings of the Optic Neuritis Treatment trial for patients with at least one MRI T2 lesion.

80%
80% is incorrect. As described this does not match the findings of the Optic Neuritis Treatment trial for patients with at least one MRI T2 lesion.

100%
100% is incorrect. As described this does not match the findings of the Optic Neuritis Treatment trial for patients with at least one MRI T2 lesion.

stem: A 86-year-old man presents with difficulty in walking and foot drop. There is weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion of the right foot, with sensory loss over the dorsum of that foot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common peroneal nerve lesion
The common peroneal nerve arises from the division of the sciatic nerve in the popliteal fossa. It contains nerves fibres originating from the L4–S1 nerve roots. It divides into a superficial (supplying muscle that everts the foot and sensation to the dorsum of the foot) and a deep (supplying foot and great toe extensors, as well as a small patch of sensation around the dorsum of the great toe) branch.Inversion of the foot is preserved. It passes close to the head of the fibula and can be damaged by pressure in this area (eg from habitual leg crossing).

Deep peroneal nerve lesion
Deep peroneal nerve lesion is incorrect. Lesions of the deep peroneal nerve are associated with a much more localised area of sensory disturbance and the preservation of ankle eversion power.

L5 root lesion
L5 root lesion is incorrect. Lesions of the L5 root can cause a similar distributionof sensory impairment, but this should extend proximally onto the lateral border of the calf. L5 lesions are also associated with more proximal leg weakness due to disruption of other nerves originating at L5 (eg superior gluteal nerve, which supplies hip abductors such as tensor fasciae latae).

Sciatic nerve lesion
Sciatic nerve lesion is incorrect. A sciatic nerve lesion is likely to affect portions of both the common peroneal and tibial nerve. Mononeuropathies

Tibial nerve lesion
Tibial nerve lesion is incorrect. A tibial nerve lesion does not cause a footdrop and would present with sensory disturbance on the lateral border of the foot (sural nerve) and weakness of ankle plantarflexion and inversion.

stem: A 25-year-old woman who works as a chef comes to the clinic because she has increasingly been dropping objects and getting burns on her hands. At age 18, she had a fall whilst horse-riding, resulting in a fracture and minor spinal injury of T5 & T6. She recovered with minimal residual deficit. She pays privately for an MRI scan, and this shows evidence of syringomyelia extending from C4-T1. Which of the following findings would you most expect?
options: Exaggerated tendon reflexes in the upper limbs
Loss of pain sensation over the shoulders
Loss of light touch in the hands
Loss of power predominantly in the upper arms
Loss of temperature sensation in the feet
explanation:
Loss of pain sensation over the shoulders
Characteristically, the first sensory loss to be seen is loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders, in a cape-like distribution.

Exaggerated tendon reflexes in the upper limbs
Exaggerated tendon reflexes in the upper limbs is incorrect. Syringomyelia is associated with loss of tendon reflexes.

Loss of light touch in the hands
Loss of light touch in the hands is incorrect. The dorsal column is usually spared in syringomyelia, leaving light touch intact.

Loss of power predominantly in the upper arms
Loss of power predominantly in the upper arms is incorrect. Muscle wasting of the upper arms occurs much later in the disease time course. It affects the hands initially, which is why our patient kept dropping things.

Loss of temperature sensation in the feet
Loss of temperature sensation in the feet is incorrect. As the syrinx enlarges, light touch, vibration and proprioception are lost in the feet.

stem: A 21-year-old student presents to the Emergency Department with a headache which has got steadily worse over the past four months and is now present as severe throbbing pain ﬁrst thing in the morning and last thing at night. She also complains of blurring/greying out of her vision when she bends down to pick something up off the ﬂoor. She is obese, with a body mass index of 33 kg/m2, and has a progesterone contraceptive implant. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 152/90 mmHg and a pulse of 78 bpm and regular. There is bilateral papilloedema, but neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 115 - 155 g/l WCC 8.1 x 109/l 4 - 11 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 182 x 109/l 150 - 400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Computed tomography (CT) head + CT venogram: Normal ventricular size, no mass lesion identiﬁed, no thrombosis identiﬁed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
C Lumbar puncture In this situation, lumbar puncture is both diagnostic (because of its ability to measure the opening pressure) and therapeutic, in that removal of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) will result in a rapid improvement in headache symptoms. As such, it is the most appropriate next step in this case of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). While CSF will be replaced within hours of the procedure, it is thought, in some patients, the temporary drop in CSF pressure ‘resets’ the system and reduces the headache burden over the long term. Except in the case of a threat to vision, and while awaiting emergency neurosurgical intervention, there is no role for serial lumbar punctures after diagnosis. A Acetazolamide Diuretic therapy, including acetazolamide, can be used in the management of IIH, although it is important to conﬁrm the diagnosis ﬁrst. The primary treatment is weight control. However, acetazolamide may be used alongside weight control as a bridging treatment or in resistant cases. B Bendroﬂumethiazide Like acetazolamide, bendroﬂumethiazide can be used as a treatment for IIH. In this case, however, it is important to make the diagnosis ﬁrst, and in an obese patient, thiazides can negatively impact on glucose tolerance, increasing the risk for diabetes mellitus over the longer term. D Opiate analgesia In this situation, with IIH, it will only mask, and not treat, the underlying symptoms. For this reason, it should be avoided here. E Prednisolone

Prednisolone can be considered for short-term treatment of IIH, although its efﬁcacy is often not maintained in the long term. It is primarily used when there are acute severe visual symptoms.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a tremor. This mainly affects her hands but she has also noticed that her head has a tendency to nod, especially when she is under stress or embarrassed. The hand tremor is worse when she is carrying things such as a cup and saucer. She has noticed that the symptoms are improved when she drinks alcohol. Her mother had a similar tremor. Examination reveals a 4–6 Hz tremor, most marked when her arms are outstretched, and titubation. She has difficulty in neatly copying a spiral diagram. Other neurological examination is normal. Thyroid function is normal. Based on the likely clinical diagnosis, which one of the following treatments would be the most appropriate first-line therapy?
explanation:
Propranolol
This patient has the typical features of essential tremor and first line treatment is with propranolol. Primidone is a suitable alternative for those who cannot take propranolol or for whom it is ineffective.

A dopamine agonist
A dopamine agonist is incorrect. A dopamine agonist would be a suitable first line choice in Parkinson’s disease.

An L-dopa preparation
An L-dopa preparation is incorrect. An L-dopa preparation would be a suitable first line choice in Parkinson’s disease.

Clonazepam
Clonazepam is incorrect. Clonazepam can be used in myoclonic disorders and certain sleep disorders (eg REM sleep behaviour disorder).

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the neuropathy seen here?
explanation:
Alcohol abuse
This patient’s investigations are consistent with alcohol abuse: there is a macrocytic anaemia; hypocalcaemia which may be linked to alcohol-related hypomagnesaemia and poor dietary intake of calcium and vitamin D; and abnormal liver function.
