In addition, there are supportive features in the history: he has had ankle and Colles’ fractures suggesting falls, and it is possible that his separation from his wife was related to alcohol abuse. Alcohol is a common cause of peripheral neuropathy, and would explain the clinical picture here.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. This is a very common cause of glove-and-stocking peripheral neuropathy, as seen here. However, although the glucose is elevated, it is only mild at 6.8 mmol/l. It is unlikely that the patient has diabetes mellitus, and even more unlikely that he would have developed microvascular complications related to diabetes.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Peripheral neuropathy as seen here is not a feature of haemochromatosis. Neurological sequelae of haemochromatosis are not common, but the most frequent is dyskinesia, which is not described here.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. Although hypothyroidism can cause peripheral neuropathy, there is no indication that this patient has any symptoms or signs of thyroid disease. In addition, you might expect hyponatraemia in significant hypothyroidism, but here the sodium is normal.

Pernicious anaemia
Pernicious anaemia is incorrect. Pernicious anaemia is caused by antibodies directed against intrinsic factor, which in turn affects the absorption of B12. B12 deficiency is a cause of peripheral neuropathy; however, typically the hands are affected very late. It is also much more unusual for pain and temperature fibres to be affected; if this was B12 deficiency, you might expect the light touch and vibration sense to be affected out of proportion to pain and temperature. Here both are equally affected.

stem: A 70-year-old retired gardener was admitted to an Orthopaedic Ward 2 weeks ago following a fall in which he sustained a fractured femoral neck. His family report that he was last completely well 4 months ago. At that time, a change in his personality was noted with frequent unprovoked emotional outbursts directed at those close to him, inappropriate tearfulness and laughter. Over the next few weeks, he was reported to be increasingly forgetful. In the following weeks, his family have noticed that he has been increasingly clumsy, often spilling drinks and having difﬁculty dressing. His walking became increasingly unsteady with frequent falls precipitating his current admission. The surgical team are concerned about continued cognitive deterioration, despite treatment for a recent suspected urinary tract infection, and have referred him for medical advice. Over the last week, jerking movements have also been noted in his arms. On examination he is agitated, bed-bound and catheterised with spontaneous and stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. Mini-Mental State Examination reveals a score of 8 out of 30, with global deﬁcits. A bilateral grasp reﬂex together with pout and snout reﬂexes are present. Tone is increased in all of the limbs, with symmetrically brisk reﬂexes and bilateral extensor plantars. Although he has difﬁculty following commands, there is demonstrable ataxia and apraxia of the upper limbs. Haematological investigation results: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 128 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.4 × 10 /l 9 4–11 × 10 /l9 Platelets 281 × 10 /l 9 150–400 × 10 /l9 Sodium (Na ) + 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) + 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatine 101 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Haematocrit 0.565 Urea 8.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 11.0µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 22 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 50g/l 35–55 g/l Alkaline phosphatase 14 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Corrected Ca 2+ 2.35 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) 2.15µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l fT4 13.5pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l Vitamin B12 245 ng/l 160–900 pmol/l Folate 13.9 μg/l 2.0–11.0 µg/l Random glucose 5.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 8 mm/h 0–10 mm in the 1 hourst C-reactive protein (CRP) 4 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Serum protein electrophoresis Normal Rheumatoid factor Positive Anti-nuclear antibody Negative ANTA Negative Random cholesterol 8mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l Treponema pallidumhaemagglutination test Negative Anti-neuronal antibodies Negative Chest X-Ray Unremarkable Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 92.1 fl 76–98 fl Cerebrospinal fluid examination: Cells 3mm <5/mm (WCC) Protein 0.47 g/l < 0.45 g/l Glucose 4.3 mmol/l 2.5–3.9 mmol/l Cytology No abnormal cells detected Which one of the following investigations is most speciﬁc in securing the diagnosis in this case?
options: CSF analysis for 14.3.3 protein and RTQuIC
Serial blood ﬁlm for examination of acanthocytes
Polymerase chain reaction of CSF for herpes simplex virus detection
Axial T2 weighted, diffusion weighted, and Fluid Attenuation Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI series
explanation:
A CSF analysis for 14.3.3 protein and RTQuIC The clinical scenario is suggestive of sporadic CJD. MRI, EEG and CSF tests all have their place to play in investigating this condition. The recently developed RTQuIC (Real-Time Quaking Induced Conversion) test appears to be the most sensitive and speciﬁc test to date, providing higher levels of accuracy than the well- established 14.3.3 protein test. B Serial blood ﬁlm for examination of acanthocytes Neuroacanthocytosis describes a range of diseases characterised by hyperkinetic movement disorder and cognitive impairment. The features in this case favour CJD. C Electroencephalography (EEG) EEG examination in sporadic CJD may demonstrate generalised bi- or triphasic periodic sharp wave complexes with a frequency of around 1–2 per second. In an appropriate clinical context, the appearance of this EEG pattern is strongly supportive of a diagnosis of sporadic CJD. In 60 to 80% of cases of sporadic CJD, the characteristic periodic picture will eventually develop.

D Polymerase chain reaction of CSF for herpes simplex virus detection The long history seen in this case makes viral encephalitis very unlikely. E Axial T2 weighted, diffusion weighted, and Fluid Attenuation Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI series Magnetic resonance imaging is generally undertaken to exclude other illnesses. However, in addition, in a proportion of cases, abnormalities of signal may be seen in the anterior basal ganglia and sometimes in the cortex. These changes may be helpful in supporting a diagnosis of sporadic CJD.

stem: A 72-year-old man is referred to the general medical clinic with a history of about 15 attacks of pins and needles in his left arm and leg over a period of 6 weeks. His GP is concerned that this patient will soon have a completed stroke despite already being on aspirin. Typical attacks lasted for about 5 minutes and there were no additional symptoms. On closer enquiry he said that the sensation started in his left foot and then, over a period of about 1 minute, spread ‘like water running up my leg’ to involve his whole leg and arm. Each attack was identical. His past medical history includes hypertension and ischaemic heart disease, for which he already takes aspirin. There are no abnormalities on neurological examination, but his blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transient ischaemic attacks affecting the right hemisphere
explanation:
Focal aware seizures
The positive sensory features (tingling rather than numbness), the stereotyped and repetitive nature of attacks and the ‘march’ of symptoms suggest epilepsy rather than transient ischaemic attacks; therefore, the correct answer here is focal aware seizures (previously named partial seizures).

Cerebral venous thrombosis
Cerebral venous thrombosis is incorrect. Cerebral venous thrombosis would be unlikely to present such with recurrent and stereotyped events.

Migraine equivalent
Migraine equivalent is incorrect. Although symptoms of migrainous aura without headache (migraine equivalent) do spread, it is usually over 10–30 minutes, and the frequency of attacks would be very unusual.

Recurrent deep white-matter microhaemorrhages
Recurrent deep white-matter microhaemorrhages is incorrect. The history of hypertension and aspirin does raise the possibility of microhaemorrhages, but the stereotyped nature of the attacks is against this diagnosis. Epilepsy and Seizures

Transient ischaemic attacks affecting the right hemisphere
Transient ischaemic attacks affecting the right hemisphere is incorrect. Isolated positive symptoms (particularly sensory ones) are very rarely vascular in origin and a typical sensory transient ischaemic attack would be characterised by loss of sensation. Therefore this is not the best option.

stem: A 67-year-old teacher suddenly lost her memory after walking her dog. Her husband noted that she still knew the names of close friends, but she was disorientated in time and place, and seemed perplexed. She could follow complex commands, but was unable to recall something she had been told 5 minutes before. The episode resolved after 10 hours, although she did not remember the event. She has a history of migraine, but the episode of memory loss was not associated with headache. CT brain imaging, Doppler ultrasound of the extracranial cervical vessels and electroencephalography are normal. What is your clinical diagnosis?
options: Complex partial seizure and post-ictal phase
explanation:
Transient global amnesia
The history is most consistent with an attack of transient global amnesia. Typically, the onset is abrupt, and anterograde memory is profoundly impaired. Patients are disorientated in time, and often in place, but never in person. Retrograde memory is variably disturbed, lasting for hours to years. Patients often do not recognise acquaintances, but they can usually recall their own name and recognise close relatives. Patients recognise their memory deficits and repeatedly ask questions to try and orientate themselves, and also ask ‘Why can’t I remember?’. Both immediate memory, as demonstrated by the patient’s ability to immediately repeat several digits or words, and procedural memory, as demonstrated by the patient’s ability to do complex tasks (eg driving), are preserved. No other major neurological symptoms occur. Resolution is gradual, with subjective recovery occurring in two-thirds of patients within 2–12 hours and, in almost all, within 24 hours. Recognised precipitating events include strenuous exercise, intense emotion, sexual intercourse, pain, temperature extremes, cervical manipulation, coughing spells and medical procedures (eg cerebral and cardiac angiography).

Complex partial seizure and post-ictal phase
Complex partial seizure and post-ictal phase is incorrect. A complex partial seizure may go unnoticed except for the post-ictal phase, during which patients may appear confused. However, the duration of this attack is far too long for simple post-ictal confusion.

Global hypoxia after arrhythmia
Global hypoxia after arrhythmia is incorrect. Global hypoxia after arrhythmia is an unsatisfactory answer as no significant loss of consciousness has been described and the idea of ‘global hypoxia’ producing just a focal amnesia is not biologically plausible.

Migraine aura without headache
Migraine aura without headache is incorrect. Migraine aura without headache is more likely to take the form of a spreading visual field or sensory deficit and would not be expected to last as long as this attack.

TIA.

stem: A 56-year-old man is referred to you with a 2-year history of ascending lower limb numbness and, more recently, foot drop. In the last 6 months he has also developed numbness in his fingers. He has a distal reduction to pinprick, relatively preserved muscle power, except for ankle dorsiflexion and hyporeflexia in his legs. The GP has already organised nerve conduction studies and the report is sent along with the patient. Which one of the following is suggestive of an axonal neuropathy?
explanation:
Reduced compound muscle action-potential amplitude
Reduced compound muscle action-potential amplitude is the only finding from this list suggestive of an axonal neuropathy. One must remember that, broadly, reduction in velocities or blocks are associated with myelin disorders whereas loss of action potential size/amplitude is associated with axonal disorders.

Abnormally slow F-response
Abnormally slow F-wave response is incorrect. Slow F-wave response is associated with demyelinating neuropathies.

Conduction block
Conduction block is incorrect. Conduction block is associated with demyelinating neuropathies.

Delayed P100 latency
Delayed P100 latency is incorrect. Delayed P100 latency is a feature of performing visual Chat evoked potentials with in those with optic nerve disease.

Reduced conduction velocity
Reduced conduction velocity is incorrect. Reduced conduction velocity is associated with demyelinating neuropathies.

stem: A 69-year-old woman was taken to hospital with a sudden-onset, mild, right hemiparesis and an inability to speak. CT scan showed evidence of a recent left hemisphere infarction. She was found to be in atrial fibrillation and was anticoagulated. While in hospital she had a right-sided focal seizure and was treated with phenytoin. She made a good recovery over the next 6 weeks and was discharged home with instructions to use a walking frame because of unsteadiness on her feet. Phenytoin 300 mg at night was continued, as was warfarin. When she was seen in the follow-up clinic 3 months later, atrial fibrillation was still present and anticoagulation was continued, but the phenytoin was tailed off to zero. Now, 2 months later, she has been re-admitted having developed a mild right hemiparesis and drowsiness over the previous 10 days. On further questioning her husband remembers that she tripped over the rug in the lounge about 10 days earlier. Her INR is 5.1. What is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
explanation:
Left subdural haematoma
The initial story suggests that she suffered a cardioembolic stroke secondary to atrial fibrillation, and that her symptoms were the result of cortical infarction from a left middle cerebral artery branch occlusion. However, her second admission with gradual onset of symptoms over days is more likely to result from a subdural haematoma secondary to excessive anticoagulation than a recurrent stroke. Her INR has risen due to the cessation of phenytoin, which is an enzyme inducer. Thus without the phenytoin she metabolises relatively less warfarin and her INR goes up.

Concurrent lobar pneumonia
Concurrent lobar pneumonia is incorrect. Intercurrent infection such as pneumonia could cause deterioration in general, but not specifically of the right hemiparesis.

Further cardioembolic stroke
Further cardioembolic stroke is incorrect. The gradual onset of symptoms makes recurrent stroke less likely than subdural haematoma secondary to excessive anticoagulation.

Left hemisphere intracerebral haemorrhage
Left hemisphere intracerebral haemorrhage is incorrect. Left hemisphere intracerebral haemorrhage would present with an acute hemiparesis, potentially with other left hemisphere signs such as aphasia.

Recurrent seizures
Recurrent seizures is incorrect. Recurrent seizures are generally uncommon after ischaemic stroke, but could cause deterioration if she was in partial status epilepticus – however, there is really no history to suggest uncontrolled seizure activity.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate for her with respect to prophylaxis against further migraine?
explanation:
Propranolol
First-line options for migraine prophylaxis include tricyclic antidepressants, ß-blockers and antiepileptics such as topiramate. Amitriptyline may be particularly useful if there are associated symptoms of depression or insomnia or if the ß-blocker is not tolerated. In this case intolerance may arise due to hypotension secondary to the propranolol however propranolol is a non-cardioselective ß-blocker and its blood pressure effects may, therefore, be mild and tolerable.

Diclofenac
Diclofenac is incorrect. These medications would not be used for migraine prophylaxis, but might have a role in treatment of acute migraine attacks.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. Sodium valproate does have anti migraine properties but is avoided in women of childbearing potential because of the high risk of teratogenicity.

Pizotifen
Pizotifen is incorrect. Pizotifen may be used for migraine prophylaxis, but is now generally avoided due to the adverse effect profile (sedation, dry mouth, increased appetite and weight gain) and general lack of efficacy.

Sumatriptan
Sumatriptan is incorrect. These medications would not be used for migraine prophylaxis, but might have a role in treatment of acute migraine attacks. Migraine A 28-year-old woman reports to her GP that her vision has become blurred in her right eye over the course of a few days. She has been rubbing the eye a lot, and now she also mentions that there is a dull ache in the eye. She has previously been fit and well. Her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill, which she has been taking for 8 years.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with sudden onset double vision and right arm weakness. Examination reveals a left-sided ptosis with the left eye deviated downwards and outwards during attempts to look straight ahead. Which of the following would best describe this presentation?
explanation:
Weber syndrome
Weber syndrome is a midbrain stroke syndrome usually occurring as a result of occlusion of the paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery. Clinical features include: Ipsilateral CNIII palsy. This helps localise the lesion to the midbrain. Contralateral hemiparesis and hemiparkinsonism due to involvement of the corticospinal tract and substantia nigra, respectively. The ‘crossed’ nature of these features (ie contralateral to the CNIII palsy) indicates that the lesion is within the brainstem and above the medullary decussation.

Binswanger’s disease
Binswanger’s disease is incorrect. Binswanger’s disease is a cerebral white matter disorder occurring in those with a multitude of vascular risk factors.The MRI appearance can occasionally be confused with demyelination (‘MS’) but, in the case of Binswanger’s disease, the lesions are a reflection of diffuse small occlusive vessel disease. Patients will often have experienced multiple previous transcient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or lacunar strokes and the disorder can culminate in dementia, pseudobulbar palsy and gait apraxia. The presentation here is not in keeping with this.

Millard-Gubler syndrome
Millard–Gubler syndrome is incorrect. Millard–Gubler syndrome is a pontine brainstem syndrome. An ipsilateral CN VI palsy helps to localisethe lesion. This case describes a CNIII palsy and therefore this choice is incorrect.

Moya moya disease
Moyo moya is incorrect. Moya moya is an occlusive vasculopathy. Occlusion of the terminal segments of the intracranial internal carotid arteries and extensive collateral vascularisation gives a typical ‘hazy’ appearance on cerebral angiogram (the so-called ‘puff of smoke’). This condition often presents with headaches, recurrent ‘TIAs’ (secondary to small parenchymal haemorrhages) and seizures.

Wallenberg syndrome
Wallenberg syndrome is incorrect. Wallenberg syndrome is also known as the lateral medullary syndrome. An ipsilateral pharyngeal/palatal palsy helps localise the lesion to the medulla and the combination of an ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face and contralateral loss of pain and temperature in the body help localise to the lateral brainstem. These features are not described in this case.

stem: A patient with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy – Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) – who was admitted with only mild sensory symptoms, is deteriorating in hospital. He has become progressively weaker over the last 12 hours, and is finding it harder to breathe. Which of the following interventions would NOT be considered?
explanation:
Intravenous methylprednisolone
Steroids (oral or IV) have never been shown to outcomes in GBS.

Intravenous immunoglobulin
Acute treatments for GBS have been subjected to randomised trials, and these have been systematically assessed in a series of Cochrane reviews. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is equal in efficacy to plasmapheresis and could be considered here.

Transfer to MHDU/ITU
Deterioration in acute GBS and the need for IVIG should prompt transfer from a general ward to a high level of care. In this environment, monitoring can be improved, allowing early intervention if respiratory compromise develops.

Monitoring of FVC
A downward trend in FVC or drop < 1 L would raise concerns regarding potential respiratory failure, prompting transfer to a higher dependency area and close monitoring of ABGs and oxygen saturations.

Plasmapheresis
As described, plasma exchange is equal in efficacy to IVIG and could also be considered as a treatment option here. (Choice of IVIG or PE varies from patient-to-patient and physician preference). Guillain-Barré.

stem: A 23-year-old woman complains of double vision. On horizontal eye movement examination, she has nystagmus of the left eye and impaired adduction of the right eye when she tries to look to the left. Her other eye movements are normal. What is the likely anatomical location of the pathology?
explanation:
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus
The clinical picture of weakness of adduction in one eye and contralateral gaze-evoked nystagmus is typical of internuclearophthalmoplegia (INO). This is a disorder of horizontal conjugate eye movements resulting from a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, the bundle of connecting fibres between the IIIrd and VIth cranial nerve nuclei (ie in the brainstem, between the mid-brain and the pons). The ‘side’of the INO or site of the lesion is ipsilateral to that of the adduction failure. In this case the right medial longitudinal fasciculus is therefore correct. A lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus would produce failure of left eye adduction and nystagmus in the right, abducting eye on rightward gaze. Remember INO may be bilateral, in which case there is bilateral failure of adduction and horizontal nystagmus in each abducting eye upon horizontal gaze. Adduction of the eyes still occurs during accommodation.

Left cerebellar peduncle
Left cerebellar peduncle is incorrect. Lesions of the left cerebellar peduncle produce ipsilateral limb ataxia.

Left lateral medulla
Left lateral medulla is incorrect. Lesions of the left lateral medulla produce a well-characterised syndrome sometimes referred to as Wallenberg syndrome. This consists of ipsilateral Horner syndrome, facial numbness and hoarse voice with contralateral limb numbness. Patients may also have nystagmus and ipsilateral limb ataxia.

Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus is incorrect. As described a lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus would produce failure of left eye adduction and nystagmus in the right, abducting eye on rightward gaze. NystagmusRight IIIrd cranial nerve nucleus
Right IIIrd cranial nerve nucleus is incorrect. A lesion in the right IIIrd nerve nucleus would produce a right IIIrd nerve palsy with ptosis, mydriasis and oculoparesis, resulting in the eye being held in the ‘down and out’ position due to unopposed action of lateral rectus and superior oblique. In nuclear lesions there may also be contralateral partial ptosis (due to bilateral innervation of levator) and restriction of upgaze in the contralateral eye (due to superior rectus innervation originating in the nucleus contralateral to that eye).

stem: A right-handed 70-year-old male patient presents with sudden weakness in the right arm and right leg with right hemisensory loss and aphasia. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg and he smokes 20 cigarettes per day. What is the most likely artery involved?
explanation:
Middle cerebral artery
This man is right handed; as such it seems most likely he has suffered a left middle cerebral artery stroke which has led to his aphasia. The middle cerebral artery supplies the internal capsule, and as such a range of different motor and sensory deficits may occur. CT or MRI are the investigations of choice to confirm the diagnosis. After initial recovery, he should be managed with an appropriate anti-platelet agent such as clopidogrel, to BP target and started on a statin.

Anterior cerebral artery
Anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. Anterior cerebral artery stroke presents with leg weakness and to a lesser degree arm weakness, owing to the vascular territory involving the medial frontal lobes.

Posterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery is incorrect. In the case of posterior cerebral artery stroke, one would expect some ‘posterior circulation’ features such as brainstem signs, visual disturbance or ataxia.

Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery is incorrect. A stroke in this territory would present with cerebellar signs or as part of the lateral medullary syndrome.

Vertebral artery
Vertebral artery is incorrect. Vertebral artery stroke also presents with posterior circulation features, which are not seen in this case.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive weakness of his upper and lower limbs, fevers and generalised lethargy. He had abruptly developed pain in his right calf and foot drop 4 weeks ago. One week later he noticed numbness of his right thumb, index and middle finger. Numbness of his left little finger subsequently became apparent. Just 2 days ago he developed a painful left foot drop and numbness over the dorsum of his left foot. He also developed a skin rash over both feet. He has lost 6.4 kg (1 stone) over the last 4 weeks. Routine haematological investigations reveal a normochromic, normocytic anaemia and ESR of 110 mm. What will be the most useful diagnostic test?
explanation:
Nerve biopsy
This patient presented with features of multiple nerve involvement over a period of 4 weeks with constitutional symptoms and a very high ESR. This is very suggestive of mononeuritis multiplex. The skin rash, high ESR and the skin rash make vasculitis the most likely diagnosis. Causes of mononeuritis multiplex include vasculitis, diabetes, sarcoidosis, paraneoplastic syndrome and amyloidosis. A nerve biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment includes prednisolone and cyclophosphamide. Disorders associated with vasculitic neuropathy include polyarteritis nodosa, Churg–Strauss syndrome and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).

Bone marrow aspiration
Bone marrow aspiration is incorrect. It is not an investigation in the diagnostic workup of vasculitis.

MRI spine
MRI spine is incorrect. It is not an investigation in the diagnostic workup of vasculitis.

Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is incorrect. It is not an investigation in the diagnostic workup of vasculitis.

Tumour markers
Tumor markers is incorrect. Mononeuritis multiplex can occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome. However, in this patient the features were consistent with a vasculitis. Thus, tumour markers will not be an appropriate investigation.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with concerns over starting a family. She has been diagnosed with epilepsy with focal onset to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures. She is currently taking phenytoin 300 mg daily and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. Her last seizure was 11 months ago, after which she was started on levetiracetam. She has since had good seizure control. She currently has the copper coil for contraception. She is anxious about the risk of fetal malformations. What would be the most appropriate advice to suggest regarding her long-term management?
options: Start folic acid 5 mg/day and aim to wean from phenytoin
Start folic acid 5 mg/day, stop both antiepileptics and change the patient to lamotrigine
Start folic acid 5 mg/day and trial of withdrawal of all antiepileptics
explanation:
Start folic acid 5 mg/day and aim to wean from phenytoin
Starting high-dose folic acid with the aim of monotherapy with levetiracetam at the lowest dose that provides seizure control is appropriate for this patient. Folic acid supplementation should ideally begin three months before conception and medication changes should be completed before conception. Women of child-bearing age with epilepsy should be told in advance of the potential teratogenic effects of antiepileptic drugs and the desirability of preconception counselling. Making decisions about antiepileptic drugs in this situation depends on many factors, including the type of seizures a patient has, seizure frequency, number of antiepileptics, type of antiepileptics, other risk factors and the individual’s wishes regarding accepting the risk of further seizures versus the risk of fetal malformations. High-dose folic acid 5 mg daily is advised in view of its effect in diminishing the risk of neural tube defects and is recommended from the preconception period throughout at least the first trimester. If antiepileptic drug treatment is necessary, then monotherapy, at the lowest possible dose that controls seizures, is desirable. Levetiracetam has a lower risk of teratogenicity than phenytoin and would be more appropriate here. There is scope for further titration of levetiracetam to 1.5 g twice daily while phenytoin is weaned off.

Start folic acid 400 μg/day
Women at low risk of neural tube defects are advised to take folic acid 400 μg/day as part of their antenatal supplements.

Start folic acid 5 mg/day
Although the patient should be started on high-dose folic acid (5 mg/day), clinicians should also aim for monotherapy with the lowest dose possible of antiepileptic.

Start folic acid 5 mg/day, stop both antiepileptics and change the patient to lamotrigine
Although lamotrigine is considered to have one of the safer side-effect profiles in pregnancy, so does levetiracetam. Ideally the patient should be transitioned to monotherapy with the lowest effective dose of antiepileptic that has a safer side-effect profile in pregnancy.

Start folic acid 5 mg/day and trial of withdrawal of all antiepileptics
High-dose folic acid is important to reduce the risk of congenital malformation and the increased risk of autism seen with antiepileptics. It is equally important to both mother and fetus that seizure control is maintained. Withdrawal of both medications may trigger seizure activity, with the relative risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy and hypoxia to the fetus.

stem: A 28-year-old man comes to your clinic as his father has recently been diagnosed with Huntington’s disease and he would like to know what his risk is of developing the illness. What is the genetic mode of inheritance of Huntington’s disease?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Huntington’s disease (HD) is a trinucleotide repeat expansion mutation (cytosine–adenine–guanine [CAG]) that is autosomal dominantly inherited. Normally this sequence contains 7–30 repeats, but when the number rises above 37, HD occurs. The gene has near 100% penetrance, so everyone who inherits the gene will almost certainly develop the disease. The longer the repeat sequence, the more severe and younger onset the disease occurs. HD also displays a phenomenon known as ‘anticipation’ where each time the mutation is passed down the repeat becomes longer, and so the disease more severe in the next generation. There is a 50% chance that this man will have inherited the abnormal gene and develop the condition.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. The condition is known to be dominantly inherited.

No genetic inheritance identified
No genetic inheritance identified is incorrect. There is a clear autosomal dominant course described.

Polygenic inheritance
Polygenic inheritance is incorrect. Polygenic inheritance is when a characteristic or disease is affected by multiple genes (eg diabetes or skin colour). HD is clearly related to a single mutation in the CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin protein gene on chromosome 4. Huntington’s DiseaseA patient with HIV presents with gradual and progressive memory loss. His magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows brain atrophy and mild white matter hyperintensity without any other significant changes or contrast enhancement.

X-linked-dominant
X-linked-dominant is incorrect. X-linked dominant is a mode of genetic inheritance when the abnormal dominant gene is carried on the X chromosome. The HD gene is known to be on chromosome 4.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents with wasting of both the thenar and hypothenar eminences on one hand, with weakness of thumb abduction, thumb flexion, and finger abduction and adduction. Sensory loss to pinprick is present over the ulnar border of the hand and forearm. The remainder of the neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
explanation:
Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
The thenar eminence (abductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis) is supplied by the median nerve with the exception of the adductor pollicis, which is ulnar. The muscles of the hypothenar eminence are abductor, flexor and opponens digiti minimi and palmaris brevis, and are supplied by the ulnar nerve.The median nerve also supplies the first two lumbricals. The inferior trunk of the brachial plexus (commonly injured by traction on the arm in an abducted position) can be damaged, producing combined C8/T1 lesions that give rise to the symptoms described, which mimic a combined median and ulnar nerve lesion in the hand.

Anterior interosseous nerve
Anterior interosseous nerve is incorrect. This patient’s symptoms cannot be caused by lesions to the anterior interosseous nerve alone.

Median nerve at the wrist
Median nerve at the wrist is incorrect. This patient’s symptoms cannot be caused by lesions to the median nerve alone.

T1 nerve root
T1 nerve root is incorrect. A T1 root lesion would primarily affect the intrinsic muscles of the hand (especially abductor pollicis brevis) and other signs would usually be present, for example Horner syndrome. In addition, the sensory loss would not affect the hand itself (T1 dermatome is on the medial arm). Mononeuropathies

Ulnar nerve at the elbow
Ulnar nerve at the elbow is incorrect. This patient’s symptoms cannot be caused by lesions to the ulnar nerve alone.

stem: A 42-year-old man was riding on a motorcycle, and following a road traffic accident he was thrown off the bike and injured his back and neck. He was given immediate first aid and basic investigations including CT scan of the cervical spine and head which were normal. He was in pain, especially in the left upper limb initially. He was discharged from the Accident and Emergency Department. He continued to have pain and noticed weakness of the hand. He presented 1 week later with global muscle wasting of the left hand. Which is the nerve or nerve root most likely to be involved?
explanation:
T1 nerve root
Global wasting of the hand is a result of wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the hand and indicates damage to both the median and the ulnar nerves, with damage to the T1 nerve root. The T1 root supplies the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

C7 nerve root
C7 nerve root is incorrect. The C7 nerve root has a shared supply along with the C6 root and innervates the muscles involved in the movements of the elbow and wrist.

Median nerve
Median nerve is incorrect. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles – the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis; the ulnar nerve serves the remainder. Injury to the median nerve will not cause global wasting of the hand.

Radial nerve
Radial nerve is incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the extensors of the arm and forearm. It does not supply the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Thus injury to this nerve can be excluded in this case.

Ulnar nerve
Ulnar nerve is incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies some of the intrinsic muscles of the hand – medial aspect of the hand. However, it will not affect all the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Further the type of injury is less likely to result in an ulnar nerve palsy, which will cause weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Only a proximal injury of the ulnar nerve will cause weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with a headache over his left eye spreading across his forehead. During the headache he develops difficulty speaking. Three minutes later he has developed clumsiness in his right hand, and 2 minutes after that he describes his right leg as ‘feeling heavy’. His speech and limb symptoms have disappeared after 20 minutes, but his headache persists for 6 hours. He suffered from migraine as a teenager but has not had an attack in over 15 years. He smokes 25 cigarettes a day. On examination he has a mild left ptosis and a small reactive left pupil, but nothing else is found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Migraine
Spreading (over minutes) sensory and motor symptoms are classical of migraine aura. Word-finding difficulties are also a common migraine aura symptom. Some patients with migraine may develop autonomic symptoms such as a Horner syndrome, as seen here. Migraine seems the most likely diagnosis in this case.

Basilar artery aneurysm
Basilar artery aneurysm is incorrect. Basilar artery aneurysm may result in a brainstem stroke, but this would not produce spreading hemispheric neurological symptoms followed by a 6-hour headache.

Internal carotid artery dissection
Internal carotid artery dissection is incorrect. Internal carotid artery dissection may result in a Horner syndrome and could give rise to an anterior circulation stroke – but one would expect sudden onset of neurological deficit, not the spreading pattern seen here.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. There is nothing in this history to suggest subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Vertebral artery dissection
Vertebral artery dissection is incorrect. Vertebral artery dissection could result in a brainstem/posterior circulation stroke, but this would not produce spreading hemispheric neurological symptoms followed by a 6hour headache.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with pressure-type headache and transient visual change on standing. Which one of the following features is most supportive of the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
options: Enlarged blind spots and constriction of the visual field
Past history of deep venous thrombosis
explanation:
Enlarged blind spots and constriction of the visual field
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) presents with headaches and visual change. Loss of visual acuity when changing posture is called transient visual obscuration and is typical of IIH. The usual finding on visual field testing is an enlargement of the blind spots and circumferential restriction in visual fields. Papilloedema can usually be seen on fundoscopy.

Lateralised motor weakness
Lateralised motor weakness is incorrect. Lateralised motor weakness is not seen in IIH and its presence in a patient like the one described here would once again raise suspicion of a cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

Past history of deep venous thrombosis
Past history of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is incorrect. Past history of DVT would raise suspicion of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which can mimic IIH symptoms by causing raised intracranial pressure. CT venography is used to diagnose this and is usually performed in cases of possible IIH to exclude this potentially serious condition.

Raised ESR
Raised ESR is incorrect. Raised ESR is not seen in IIH.

Reduced visual acuity.

stem: A teacher presents with a 2-week history of increasing malaise, tingling in her hands and feet and difficulty in walking. There is symmetrical distal weakness that is worse in her legs, absent lower limb reflexes, reduced sensation to pinprick and impaired proprioception to the knee bilaterally. Lumbar puncture shows an acellular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with a raised protein level. Which one of the following factors confers the worst prognosis for this illness?
options: Level of protein greater than 1.5 g/l in CSF
explanation:
Preceding diarrhoeal illness
The clinical history given above is of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) Poor prognostic factors in GBS include: age> 40 years rapid symptom progression requirement for ventilatory support previous history of diarrhoeal illness (specifically Campylobacter spp.) a high anti-GM 1 antibody titre

Age less than 40 years
Age less than 40 years is incorrect. As outlined age > 40 years is a poor prognostic factor.

Female sex
Female sex is incorrect. Female sex is not a poor prognostic factor in GBS. In general males are affected 1.5 times more often than women.

Gradual onset
Gradual onset is incorrect. Gradual onset is not typical of GBS as most cases reach nadir by 2 weeks of symptom onset. Very rapid onset over hours is associated with the axonal motor form of the illness and confers a poor prognosis. Guillain-Barré Syndrome

Level of protein greater than 1.5 g/l in CSF
Level of protein greater than 1.5 g/l in CSF is incorrect. The CSF protein level is typically raised in GBS but no particular level has been shown to predict outcome or overall prognosis.

stem: What is the time limit after the onset of symptoms up to which IV thrombolysis should be administered?
explanation:
4.5 h
The clinical scenario describes a 58-year-old man who collapsed at work and neurological examination reveals a left-sided hemiplegia consistent with a diagnosis of acute stroke. The blood investigations done are within normal limits and the CT head shows no intracerebral haemorrhage; hence most likely this patient has suffered an ischaemic rather than a haemorrhagic episode. According to the NICE Guidelines and NICE Pathways for Acute Stroke – “Alteplase is recommended for treating acute ischaemic stroke in adults if treatment is started as early as possible within 4.5 hours of onset of stroke symptoms, and intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded by appropriate imaging techniques”. Where there is confirmed anterior circulation occlusion then thrombectomy should also be offered.

1h
1h 1 h is incorrect. Only offering thrombolysis within 1 hour of a stroke risks missing significant benefit which could be afforded to patients with an acute event.

3h
3h 3 h is incorrect. Although the greatest benefit for thrombolysis is seen in the first 3 hours, there is still a positive benefit risk for thrombolysis out to 4.5 hours.

6h
6h 6 h is incorrect. Thrombolysis out to 6 hours brings with it significant risk of haemorrhagic transformation.

12 h
12 h is incorrect. By 12 hours significant neuronal death has already ensued and any benefit of thrombolysis is minimal.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of occipital headache. Computed tomography (CT) imaging confirms a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). Which of the following agents is most frequently used to reduce the chances of cerebral artery vasospasm, risk for cerebral infarct, and worsening neurologic outcomes?
explanation:
Nimodipine
Nimodipine should be routinely used in the context of SAH. This is based on the largest randomised clinical trial of 554 patients for using nimodipine prophylaxis after acute SAH; systematic reviews also support its use. The key papers are: Pickard JD et al. Effect of oral nimodipine on cerebral infarction and outcome after subarachnoid haemorrhage: British aneurysm nimodipine trial. BMJ 1989; 298(6674): 636-42, and Allen GS et al. Cerebral arterial spasm - a controlled trial of nimodipine in patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage. N Engl J Med 1983; 308(11): 619-24.

Nicardipine
In a large randomised trial, nicardipine decreased the incidence of delayed ischaemic neurological deficits, reduced the need for hypervolaemic hypertensive therapy and reduced angiographic vasospasm, yet it did not the overall outcome after three months.

Diltiazem
Phase I and II safety studies of diltiazem in SAH demonstrated safety, but no effect on vasospasm.

Labetalol
While there is no head-to-head trial comparing labetalol to nimodipine in the setting of SAH, there are studies comparing labetalol with nicardipine. These have found labetalol to be associated with increased in-hospital infections, but no difference in mortality or modified Rankin Score > 2 when compared to nicardipine. Given that nicardipine is inferior to nimodipine, empirical reasoning does not support the preferential use of labetalol over nimodipine in SAH.

Indapamide
Indapamide can have a profound volume depleting effect. Its use in the context of SAH must be judicious; it is without an evidence base.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with a 12-month history of intermittent confusion and visual hallucinations. On examination he has bilateral rigidity and bradykinesia with normal power, reflexes and sensation. Plantar responses are flexor. General medical examination is normal. CT brain scan is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diffuse Lewy body disease
Diffuse Lewy body disease (or dementia with Lewy bodies) accounts for around 10% of cases of dementia. It is less common than Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia. Typical features include intermittent confusion, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, recurrent falls, somnolence (which may occur suddenly during the daytime) and syncope. Dopamine treatment may the parkinsonian symptoms but may exacerbate the confusion and visual hallucinations. Neuroleptics should be avoided as these can worsen symptoms. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine can be helpful for symptomatic treatment.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Hallucinations are unusual in early Alzheimer’s disease and the parkinsonism would also be atypical.

Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease
Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease (IPD) is incorrect. IPD would usually present with the classic motor features (tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia) although non-motor features (anxiety, depression, constipation etc) are common and under-recognised. Although those with IPD can become demented, this is labelled ‘Parkinsons disease dementia’ if it occurs after 2 years following the diagnosis of IPD.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Normal pressure hydrocephalus is incorrect. Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically presents with the triad of gait apraxia (sometimes called a ‘magnetic gait’), dementia (predominantly of the dysexecutive type, causing deficits in planning and organisation of complex tasks) and urinary incontinence.

Prion disease
Prion disease is incorrect. Although prion disease (such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease) should be considered in those with a rapidly progressive dementia with parkinsonism, the prodrome here (12 months) is too long.

stem: After undergoing a right temporal lobectomy for intractable epilepsy, a 30-year-old man is found to have a visual field defect postoperatively. Which one of the following is most likely to be found?
explanation:
Left superior quadrantanopia
The visual tracts retain a topographical representation of the retina as they divide to pass through the temporal and parietal lobes.Temporal lobe lesions are associated with superior quadrantanopic field defects and parietal lesions with inferior quadrantanopic defects.The correct answer is therefore left superior quadrantanopia. Such a defect is frequent after temporal lobe epilepsy surgery, but is usually asymptomatic.

Left homonymous hemianopia
Left homonymous hemianopia is incorrect. A left homonymous hemianopia suggests a lesion involving both the right temporal and parietal lobes or potentially a right occipital lobe lesion.

Left inferior quadrantanopia
Left inferior quadrantanopia is incorrect. A left inferior quadrantanopia is caused by a right parietal lobe lesion.

Right inferior quadrantanopia
Right inferior quadrantanopia is incorrect. A right inferior quadrantanopia is caused by a left parietal lobe lesion. Visual Field Defects

Right superior quadrantanopia
Right superior quadrantanopia is incorrect. A right superior quadrantanopia is caused by a left temporal lobe lesion.

stem: A 45-year-old woman had a right mastectomy 2 years ago for breast cancer. She has now presented with a 2month history of progressive ataxia and dysarthria. On examination, there is gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria, upper limb ataxia and gait ataxia. Power, tone, reflexes and sensation are normal. Plantar response is flexor bilaterally. CT and MRI brain are normal and CSF shows no bacterial growth. What is the most likely cause of her ataxia?
explanation:
Paraneoplastic cerebellum syndrome
In a patient with malignancy (especially lung or breast) and a subacute onset of a cerebellar syndrome a normal MRI, a paraneoplastic syndrome is the most likely diagnosis. The onset of paraneoplastic cerebellar syndrome is usually subacute. It is associated with features such as ataxia, dysarthria, vertigo, oscillopsia, nystagmus and dysmetria. Malignancies of the lungs, breast, ovaries and lymphomas are associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar syndrome. Brain imaging and CSF analysis are normal or show non-specific changes. Serum and CSF may contain anti-Purkinje cell antibodies. Occasionally patients respond to steroids, immunoglobulins or plasmapheresis.

Cerebellum metastasis
Cerebellum metastasis is incorrect. The CT and MRI are normal making a cerebellar metastasis unlikely.

Malignant meningitis
Malignant meningitis is incorrect. Malignant meningitis usually presents with headache, decreased mental abilities and confusion.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Cerebellar signs are a common presentation of multiple sclerosis. However, multiple sclerosis is an episodic or progressive disease and the symptoms and signs are multifocal. Onset is most often in healthy young adults. There are abnormal finding in the MRI in >95% of the patients. 720

Wernicke’s encephalopathy
Wernicke’s encephalopathy is incorrect. Wernike’s encephalopathy presents with acute global confusional state, abnormal eye movements and ataxic gait.

stem: A woman presented to the Emergency Department with collapse and vomiting preceded by occipital headache of acute onset. After 8 h, she was conscious, alert with photophobia and mild neck stiffness. Computed tomography (CT) brain scan was carried out and was normal. Which one of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid examination after 12 h has elapsed
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain with contrast
Repeat CT scan of the brain in 24 h
explanation:
Cerebrospinal fluid examination after 12 h has elapsed
This history is suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). In a patient who complains of sudden-onset severe occipital headache it is important to rule out SAH before other potential causes are considered. CT scan is the initial investigation of choice and subarachnoid or intraventricular blood is usually seen. Where the CT scan is negative or equivocal, lumbar puncture (LP) is the next investigation of choice. Xanthochromia appears several hours after SAH; red blood cells may also be seen. Sequential bottles of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) should be sent for analysis to rule out a false-positive from a traumatic tap.

Cerebral angiography
Cerebral angiography is incorrect. Cerebral angiography is useful in detecting aneurysms, but only after the presence of subarachnoid haemorrhage has been confirmed.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain with contrast
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain with contrast is incorrect. CT scan of the brain with contrast is not routinely used in this setting.

Magnetic resonance imaging brain
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain is incorrect. MRI brain is not routinely used in this setting.

Repeat CT scan of the brain in 24 h
Repeat CT scan of the brain in 24 h is incorrect. In fact, subarachnoid blood becomes more difficult to detect on CT as time elapses.

stem: A 56-year-old man develops arm weakness after an injury to his elbow. He has weakness of the long flexors of the right thumb and index finger, and is unable to pronate his forearm on that side. There is no sensory loss. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged?
explanation:
Anterior interosseous nerve
The median nerve gives off its motor branch, the anterior interosseous nerve, below the elbow as it descends between the two heads of the pronator teres muscle. A lesion of either nerve may occur in this region, sometimes after trauma or owing to compression from, for example, a fibrous band.With anterior interosseous nerve involvement, there is no sensory loss and weakness is confined to the pronator quadratus, flexor pollicis longus and the flexor digitorum profundus to the second and third digits.

Median nerve
Median nerve is incorrect. Weakness is more widespread and sensory changes occur in an appropriate distribution when the median nerve itself is affected.

Posterior interosseous nerve
Posterior interosseous nerve is incorrect. Posterior interosseous nerve lesions produce weakness of finger extension and milder weakness of wrist extension with radial deviation due to preserved extensor carpi radialis (radial nerve).

Radial nerve
Radial nerve is incorrect. Radial nerve lesions give rise to weakness of wrist extension and there may be a patch of altered sensation on the dorsum of the hand, around the base of the thumb. Mononeuropathies A 40-year-old woman with a history of Graves’ disease presents with a 6-month history of progressive tingling and weakness of her legs. On examination of the lower limbs, there is bilateral pyramidal weakness, depressed deep tendon reflexes and flexor plantar responses. There is reduced joint position sense and vibration sensation in her lower limbs but no other sensory abnormalities.

Ulnar nerve
Ulnar nerve is incorrect. Ulnar nerve lesions produce weakness of finger abduction and adduction with weakness of hypothenar muscles. Sensory loss occurs along the ulnar border of the hand.

stem: A 36-year-old woman reports diplopia, particularly at the end of the day. She first noted the symptoms 48 hours earlier. A diagnosis of myasthenia gravis is made. Which of the following treatment options is the most appropriate in treating the acute attack?
options: Prednisolone 5 mg once daily (OD) orally (PO) for three days
Pyridostigmine 30 mg four times daily (QDS) PO for 2–4 days
Prednisolone 30 mg OD PO for five days
Pyridostigmine 60 mg QDS PO for five days
explanation:
Pyridostigmine 30 mg four times daily (QDS) PO for 2–4 days
According to guidelines issued by the Association of British Neurologists’ in 2015, the treatment of ocular myasthenia should begin with pyridostigmine; 'titrate up to find the lowest effective dose'. 'Initially 30 mg four times daily for 2–4 days' should be used.

Prednisolone 5 mg once daily (OD) orally (PO) for three days
In 2015, the Association of British Neurologists issued management guidelines for myasthenia gravis. Steroids are suggested as the third step in the treatment of ocular myasthenia, after pyridostigmine and thymectomy. When steroids are used, they should be dosed as follows: 'Start 5 mg on alternate days for three doses and increase by 5 mg every three doses until symptoms . The maximum dose is 50 mg on alternate days or 0.75 mg/kg/alternate day for ocular myasthenia gravis'.

Thymectomy
Thymectomy 'If the serum anti-acetylcholine receptor (ACh-R) antibody is positive and the patient is aged under 45 years: consider thymectomy at presentation'. This is the second (not first) line of treatment in ocular myasthenia, according to guidelines issued by the Association of British Neurologists in 2015.

Prednisolone 30 mg OD PO for five days
The dosing of steroids in ocular myasthenia should be on an alternate day basis as per the guidelines issued by the Association of British Neurologists in 2015.

Pyridostigmine 60 mg QDS PO for five days
This option represents the second step in the dose titration of pyridostigmine according to guidelines issued by the Association of British Neurologists in 2015; initially 30 mg four times daily for 2–4 days then 60 mg four times daily for five days then increase to 90 mg four times daily over one week if required. The duration of action varies, and some patients require five divided daily doses. If pyridostigmine does not control symptoms satisfactorily within a few weeks, start prednisolone.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of involuntary neck movements. There is no history of trauma. He is on no drugs. There is no relevant family history. On examination he has an episodic right torticollis. The rest of his neurological examination is normal. MRI of his cervical spine is normal. The neurologist in the Movement Disorders Clinic has diagnosed cervical dystonia. Which of the following treatments will be most beneficial?
explanation:
Botulinum toxin
This gentleman with involuntary neck movements and episodic right torticollis with a normal cervical spine has a diagnosis of cervical dystonia. Botulinum toxin injection is the first-line treatment for cervical dystonia (torticollis). Secondary causes need to be excluded such as drugs (neuroleptics) and cervical spine abnormalities. If a primary cervical dystonia is diagnosed botulinum toxin is the drug of choice. Botulinum toxin injections are useful in spasticity and hemifacial spasms.

Baclofen
Baclofen is incorrect. Baclofen is a muscle relaxant and is not very useful in the treatment of cervical dystonias.

Haloperidol
Haloperidol is incorrect. Antidopaminergic drugs such as haloperidol are not very useful in the treatment of cervical dystonias, and used long term can worsen movement disorder.

L-Dopa
L-Dopa is incorrect. Dopa-responsive dystonia is a rare syndrome and is generally associated with a positive family history. The dopa-responsive dystonias present most commonly with progressive gait disturbances and increased muscle tone. Rarely focal presentations can occur.

Propranolol
Propranolol is incorrect. Propranolol is a non-selective β blocker and has no role in the management of cervical dystonias.

stem: A 67-year-old man has a history of chronic neck pain. However, on this occasion he presents acutely to his doctor with pain over his left shoulder blade and axillary region, which radiates down his arm involving the arm and ending in the fingers, especially the index and middle finger. He also has tingling in these fingertips. He has some tenderness in the triceps region, and a reduced range of neck movements (which is painful). There is mild weakness of the forearm extensors and wrist extension. There is slight loss of pinprick sensation over the index and middle finger. The biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are equal and symmetrical, and the triceps reflex is diminished on the left compared with the right. Otherwise examination is unremarkable. His doctor thinks that a cervical disc prolapse is the most likely cause. Which cervical level would be most likely, given his symptoms and signs?
explanation:
C.6,7
Disc prolapse at the C.6,7 level causes compression of the C.7 nerve root. His symptoms and signs are typical of this level, with weakness predominantly involving radial nerve-supplied muscles (triceps, extensor carpus radialis). The diminished triceps reflex (C.6,7) but preserved biceps and brachioradialis (both C.5,6) is also characteristic. The diagnosis can usually be confirmed with a combination of MRI and neurophysiology. The latter may be particularly helpful in patients with chronic spondylitic disease, in helping to determine which of the levels of compression is most acute.

C.4,5
C.4,5 is incorrect. C.5 root compression would cause altered sensation in the upper arm and shoulder with weakness in biceps and shoulder abduction. The biceps jerk would be diminished.

C.5,6
C.5,6 is incorrect. C.6 root compression would also cause weakness of biceps and shoulder abduction. However, the sensory loss would be in the forearm and hand.

C.7,8
C.7,8 is incorrect. C.8 root compression would cause weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and sensory loss in the hand and forearm.

C.8, T.1
C.8, T.1 is incorrect. T.1 root lesions also cause weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, but the sensory loss is more proximal in the forearm and does not affect the hand.

stem: A 40-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of initial headache, altered level of consciousness, aphasia, fever and a complex tonic–clonic seizure. He has been intubated and ventilated to protect his airway. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, are normal. An unenhanced computed tomography scan shows hypodense areas in both temporal lobes. A lumbar puncture is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Intravenous aciclovir
The clinical history is most consistent with a diagnosis of herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE). Inflammatory markers are often normal in HSE, and computed tomography head imaging findings are suggestive of HSE (temporal lobe imaging changes suggest this diagnosis). Prompt treatment with intravenous aciclovir is required. In HSE, the time left untreated correlates with mortality and morbidity, so postponing treatment while polymerase chain reaction results return is inappropriate.

Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics is an appropriate treatment for meningitis. The clinical history and investigation findings are not in keeping with this diagnosis. Meningitis may present with a stiff neck and raised inflammatory markers, with indicators of sepsis and potentially a rash. In meningitis, computed Chattomography with brain is usually normal and the cerebral-spinal fluid has neutrophil leukocytosis and a low glucose ratio.

Diazepam
Diazepam may be used to treat the seizures the patient is experiencing, however, it is not the most appropriate treatment in this case. The most appropriate treatment for the current presentation is aciclovir.

Intravenous levetiracetam and intravenous antibiotics
Intravenous levetiracetam and antibiotics are not a suitable management plan. A loading dose of levetiracetam is appropriate in status epilepticus. The history suggests herpes simplex encephalitis, so it is important to include aciclovir.

Intravenous steroids
Intravenous steroids may help with cerebral oedema. The evidence, however, for reduced mortality and morbidity is much greater for aciclovir.

stem: You are asked to review a 25-year-old man who complains of pain in his upper limbs exacerbated by coughing. You suspect he may have syringomyelia. Which one of the following is a typical early finding associated with a cervical syrinx?
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensation
Muscle wasting in the small muscles of the lower limbs
explanation:
Loss of pain and temperature sensation
Classical syringomyelia is most commonly associated with the Arnold–Chiari malformation and presents at 20– 30 years of age. Upper limb pain exacerbated by coughing or laughing is typical. Spinothalamic sensory loss (pain and temperature) leads to painless upper limb burns and trophic changes. Difficulty in walking and paraparesis develop later. The condition is gradually progressive. Surgical decompression may slow progression.

Flaccid paraparesis
Flaccid paraparesis is incorrect. Spastic paraparesis with hyperreflexia in the lower limbs is seen due to disruption of descending upper motor neurons. Lower motor neurone signs can be seen in the upper limb (at the level of the syrinx) as the syrinx disrupts the anterior horn cells at this level.

Loss of light touch
Loss of light touch is incorrect. The central nature of the syrinx picks off decussating sensory fibres. These consist of the spinothalamic tracts and therefore loss of pain and temperature sensation occurs, usually in a ‘cape’ distribution affecting the torso and upper limbs. Light touch fibres are spared.

Loss of lower limb reflexes
Loss of lower limb reflexes is incorrect. Spastic paraparesis with hyperreflexia in the lower limbs is seen due to disruption of descending upper motor neurons. Lower motor neurone signs can be seen in the upper limb (at the level of the syrinx) as the syrinx disrupts the anterior horn cells at this level.

Muscle wasting in the small muscles of the lower limbs
Muscle wasting in the small muscles of the lower limbs is incorrect. Spastic paraparesis with hyperreflexia in the lower limbs is seen due to disruption of descending upper motor neurons. Lower motor neurone signs can be seen in the upper limb (at the level of the syrinx) as the syrinx disrupts the anterior horn cells at this level.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of hypertension is brought to the Emergency Department with sudden onset severe occipital headache and left sided weakness. On examination, her GCS is 13. Her BP is 190/100 mmHg. She has a left-sided hemiplegia. An urgent scan confirms a large right-sided subarachnoid haemorrhage. Over the course of the next 30 minutes, she becomes increasingly drowsy and begins to vomit. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the vomiting and decreased consciousness?
options: Decreased CSF absorption at arachnoid granulation
explanation:
Mass effect
In the presence of a significant bleed, local pressure/cerebral oedema leads to decreased consciousness and vomiting due to raised intracranial pressure. Meningism primarily leads to occipital pain on neck flexion or straight leg raise.

Neuronal death
Neuronal death is incorrect. At this stage, the neuronal death would not be enough to attribute these symptoms. Mass effect, however, is the reason for the vomiting and decreased consciousness.

Decreased CSF absorption at arachnoid granulation
Decreased CSF absorption at arachnoid granulation is incorrect. Hydrocephalus after SAH is thought to be caused by obstruction of CSF flow by blood products or adhesions, or by a reduction of CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations. The former occurs as an acute complication; the latter tends to occur two weeks or later, and is more likely to be associated with shunt dependence.

Elevated blood pressure
Elevated blood pressure is incorrect. Elevated systolic blood pressure contributes to the subarachnoid haemorrhage (especially aneurysmal SAH) and is managed with IV antihypertensives, such as IV beta blockers. It is associated with poor outcomes. Mass effect, however, is the reason for the vomiting and decreased consciousness.

Meningism
Meningism is incorrect. This would be characterised by nuchal rigidity and/or Kernig’s sign and/or Brudzinski’s sign.

stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the clinic with a GP diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease. He has read about ropinirole on the internet and wants to try this as initial therapy instead of l-dopa. What is the mode of action of ropinirole?
explanation:
Dopamine-receptor agonist
Ropinirole is a dopamine agonist, and acts at the D2/D3 receptor. Parkinson’s disease is a loss of dopaminergic transmission in the substantial nigra of the basal ganglia, so treatment focuses on giving dopamine (in the form of levodopa, the amino acid precursor to dopamine) or dopamine receptor agonists, such as ropinirole. Levodopa is given in conjunction with drugs which reduce its peripheral breakdown, such as dopa-decarboxylase inhibitors (benserazide, carbidopa) and COMT-inhibitors (entacapone). Combination drugs such as cobeneldopa (levodopa and benserazide, trade name Madopar) and co-careldopa (levodopa and carbidopa, trade name Sinemet) are the most commonly used initial treatments for Parkinson’s disease. Other dopamine agonists used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease include bromocriptine, cabergoline, pergolide, pramipexole, rotigotine (available as patch) and apomorphine (available as a subcutaneous infusion). They can be used at all stages of the disease, either as monotherapy or in conjunction with levodopa.

COMT inhibitor
COMT inhibitor is incorrect. Entacapone is an example of a COMT inhibitor, and it works by reducing peripheral breakdown of levodopa.

Dopa Decarboxylase Inhibitor
Dopa decarboxylase inhibitor is incorrect. Benserazide and carbidopa are examples of dopa decarboxylase inhibitors, and they work by reducing peripheral breakdown of levodopa. They are used to avoid nausea associated with levodopa therapy.

Dopamine transport inhibitor
Dopamine transport inhibitor is incorrect. This would also reduce dopamine transmission, so would not work as treatment for Parkinson’s. Dopamine transport inhibitors are currently under investigation for the treatment of cocaine and amphetamine addiction.

Dopamine antagonist
Dopamine antagonist is incorrect. Parkinson’s disease is a loss of dopaminergic transmission in the substantial nigra of the basal ganglia, so treatment focuses on giving dopamine (in the form of levodopa, the amino acid precursor to dopamine) or dopamine receptor agonists. Dopamine antagonists would reduce dopamine transmission. They are used in the treatment of psychotic disorders. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the clinic because of intermittent blurring of vision in her right eye. She has no past medical history of note, and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. Her blood pressure is normal. Her right pupil is more dilated than the left (>3mm), but has a relatively normal accommodation reflex. It constricts poorly when she moves from dark to light. The left is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Holmes-Adie pupil
Anisocoria (difference in pupil size) may be physiological (usually <2mm difference), pathological or pharmacological. Pathological causes may be classified as damage to the sympathetic pathway and damage to the parasympathetic pathway causing impaired dilation and constriction respectively. Sluggish accommodation/light-near dissociation with absent or poor constriction to light is indicative of Adie’s tonic pupil (Holmes-Adie pupil). Anisocoria in cases of Holmes-Adie pupil is more noticeable in the light compared to the dark due to damage of the parasympathetic supply to the ciliary ganglion, causing impaired constriction and a dilated pupil. This usually occurs in otherwise healthy young women, and is commonly unilateral. Diagnosis is confirmed with low dose pilocarpine (0.125%) which shows constriction in the affected eye only due to hypersensitivity of the sphincter pupillae.

Argyll Robertson pupil
Argyll Robertson pupil is incorrect. Argyll Robertson pupil is encountered in the tertiary stage of syphilis, and is rarely seen nowadays in the U.K. There is accommodation but no or poor constriction to light, similar to Adie’s tonic pupil, however pupils are typically bilaterally and irregularly smaller than usual. Anisocoria in this case would be more noticeable in the dark. There may be iris atrophy. Syphilis serology is required to help establish the diagnosis.

Horner’s syndrome
Horner’s syndrome is incorrect. Horner’s syndrome is a result of damage to the sympathetic supply to the eye. The affected pupil is therefore constricted, with normal response to light and accommodation. Anisocoria is more pronounced in the dark in Horne's syndrome due to impaired dilatation. The patient will also have mild ptosis of the affected eye +/- anhydrosis. Pharmacological tests with apraclonidine and cocaine are required to confirm the diagnosis and level of injury.

Sixth nerve palsy
Sixth nerve palsy is incorrect. The patient commonly complains of double vision with a sixth nerve palsy. This usually manifests as a loss of abduction of the affected eye due to paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle. Pupils are not commonly affected unless there is an associated third nerve palsy. Holmes–Adie SyndromeThird nerve palsy
Third nerve palsy is incorrect. Presentation of a third nerve palsy is variable, however typically the pupil is dilated and “down and out” (depressed and abducted) due to paralysis of the ocular muscles supplied by the third nerve, thus affecting ocular movements. The pupil may not always be affected in a pupil-sparing nerve palsy, however there is usually complete ptosis of the eye. The patient may complain of double vision and/or pain.

stem: A 26-year-old female intravenous drug user attends the Emergency Department with increasing muscle rigidity and difficulty closing her mouth. On examination, she has globally increased tone with neck stiffness and trismus. She finds it very difficult to sit up owing to abdominal muscle spasm. Her BP is measured at 155/90 mmHg, with a pulse of 88 beats/min. You notice necrotising areas around multiple recent puncture sites. What is the most appropriate antibiotic to use in this case?
explanation:
Metronidazole
This woman has signs of tetanus caused by Clostridium tetani. The likely vector of infection is through one of the most recent injection sites, because of a contaminated needle. Management involves administration of intravenous tetanus immunoglobulin, followed by debridement of the wound. Antibiotic therapy involves the use of either penicillin or metronidazole, and is important particularly when there are generalised symptoms as seen here.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. This antibiotic option would be less effective in the treatment of tetanus. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that is primarily used second line for the treatment of gastrointestinal and urinary tract infections.

Gentamicin
Gentamicin is incorrect. This antibiotic option would be less effective in the treatment of tetanus. Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic which is particularly effective against Gram-negative bacteria such as pseudomonas.

Vancomycin
Vancomycin is incorrect. This antibiotic option would be less effective in the treatment of tetanus. Vancomycin is usually reserved for the treatment of methicillin-resistant Staph. Aureus and Clostridium difficile infections.

Erythromycin
Erythromycin is incorrect. This antibiotic option would be less effective in the treatment of tetanus. Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic primarily used to treat respiratory tract infections.

stem: A 64-year-old smoker presents to the Emergency Department with a 12-hour history of weakness in his legs and inability to pass urine. Physical examination reveals that he is hypertensive with flaccid paresis of the lower limbs. Pain and temperature sensation are impaired to T7 but joint position sense is unaffected in the lower limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anterior spinal artery occlusion
Branches of the anterior spinal artery supply the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, with the posterior spinal arteries supplying the posterior third. Most of the spinal vascular supply comes from two or three major arterial branches, so segments of the cord in the watershed area between the branches (around T2–T4) are vulnerable to ischaemia. Sudden pain in the back and the distribution of the affected segment is associated with bilateral flaccid weakness and dissociated sensory loss with impaired pinprick and temperature sensation below the level of the infarct. In anterior spinal artery occlusion proprioception and vibration sense are typically spared because they are conducted in the posterior columns. This syndrome is described in the case presented here.

Acute transverse myelitis
Acute transverse myelitis is incorrect. Acute transverse myelitis presents over hours to days and gives rise to a range of different myelopathic symptoms and signs depending on the location of the inflammatory lesion. The dissociation of pain and temperature sensation from proprioception would be unusual in transverse myelitis so make it a less likely answer.

Cauda equina syndrome
Cauda equina syndrome is incorrect. Cauda equina syndrome could cause weakness of both legs (although it is usually asymmetric) and affects bladder control. However, the sensory level at T7 localises the lesion to the spinal cord and not the more distal cauda equina.

Cervical spondylosis with acute decompensation
Cervical spondylosis with acute decompensation is incorrect. Cervical spondylosis would produce symptoms in all four limbs and would not spare dorsal column sensations.

Spinal tumour
Spinal tumour is incorrect. A spinal tumour would usually present with a more slowly progressive syndrome over weeks to months.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with an episode of memory loss. Three days earlier he had become confused. His wife led him into the house – he apparently sat down at her request and had a cup of tea. He then wandered around the house, confused, but remained conscious and able to have some conversation with his wife, although continuing to ask similar questions repeatedly. After 3 h, he abruptly returned to normal and had no recollection of the events. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Transient global amnesia
The exact cause of transient global amnesia is unclear. It occurs most commonly among patients above 50 years of age. Despite the apparent severity of symptoms during the attack, there is always complete recovery.

Alcohol-related amnesia
Alcohol-related amnesia is incorrect. It is difficult to see how this diagnosis could cause a discrete episode of anterograde amnesia, as described in this case. Rather, it would cause longer-term symptoms.

Chronic subdural haematoma
Chronic subdural haematoma is incorrect. It is difficult to see how this diagnosis could cause a discrete episode of anterograde amnesia as described in this case. Rather, it would cause longer term symptoms.

Complex partial status epilepticus
Complex partial status epilepticus is incorrect. Complex partial status epilepticus is possible but less likely. Transient epileptic amnesia (TEA) can mimic transient global amnesia, although it would usually be shorter in duration and associated with other features of focal seizure activity (eg distal limb automatism). The paralysis associated with myasthenia gravis is thought to result from the influence of autoimmune antibodies that bind to the ligand-gated ion channel known as:

Hysterical fugue state
Hysterical fugue state is incorrect. Hysterical fugue state is also possible, although in a 60-year-old man it would be improbable. In addition, this disorder is usually characterised by wandering and an apparent change in belief or a confusion about one’s identity.

stem: A 69-year-old man has diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and hypertension. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for the last 43 years. His son contacts his General Practitioner as he mentioned that during a telephone conversation, his father ‘wasn’t making sense’. At the Emergency Department, the patient is orientated and alert, with normal power, tone and reflexes throughout. Assessment of his speech reveals some difficulty with word identification and repetition and a lack of fluency. He has difficulty naming examples within a category, eg, types of animals. He can follow instructions, however. An MRI scan of the brain shows a small localised infarct. Where is the lesion most likely to be located?
explanation:
Inferior frontal lobe (Broca’s area)
