This patient has an expressive dysphasia. Space-occupying lesions, strokes and surgery may produce very focal cortical lesions. However, language production involves many different areas of the brain acting in concert and it is unusual to get a ‘pure’ speech disturbance of the kind described in this patient. Comprehension, fluency and repetition are the three main variables that allow for localisation of aphasia. Broca’s area (inferior frontal lobe), is the centre for the motor part of speech and sentence formation. Lesions in this area produce impaired fluency, intact comprehension and impaired repetition.

Angular gyrus
The angular gyrus is part of the inferior parietal lobule. Lesions here in the dominant hemisphere cause Gerstmann syndrome, also known as angular gyrus syndrome, which include agraphia (inability to communicate in writing), acalculia (inability to complete simple math problems), finger agnosia (impairment in discriminating their own fingers) and left-right disorientation.

Arcuate fasciculus
The conduction pathway (arcuate fasciculus) connects Wernicke area and Broca areas. Lesions in the arcuate fasciculus impair the transmission of information between these two regions. This injury leads to impaired repetition, but normal fluency and normal comprehension. Thus this is a conduction aphasia, a rare form of aphasia.

Left cerebral hemisphere
The infarctions of the left cerebral hemisphere, typically involving the occlusion of the internal carotid or middle cerebral artery typically result in global aphasia in which the patient has deficits in all aspects of language including spontaneous speech, naming, repetition, auditory comprehension, reading and writing. Global aphasia may result from strokes, tumours, dementia, or other causes. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Posterior, superior temporal lobe (Wernicke’s area)
Wernicke’s area (posterior, superior temporal lobe), is the centre for comprehension and planning of words. The lesions in this area present with patients unable to understand written and/or spoken words, while their speech remains fluent but meaningless (a receptive dysphasia).

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a no-no head tremor and tremor of the outstretched hands. There are no other neurological abnormalities. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Propranolol
This patient is most likely to have essential tremor. Essential tremor is a very common movement disorder, and presents with a postural tremor that may have its onset anywhere between the second and sixth decades of life. The specific pathophysiology of essential tremor remains unknown. There is often a positive family history. Although it is typically a postural tremor, essential tremor may occur at rest in severe and very advanced cases. It most commonly affects the hands but can also affect the head, voice, tongue and legs. In some, the tremor is alleviated by small amounts of alcohol, an effect not found in Parkinson’s disease. The most widely used drugs for essential tremor are the β-adrenergic blocker propranolol and the anticonvulsant topiramate. Selegiline, l-dopa and amantadine are all therapies used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease (PD) and would not be recommended in this setting. Although occasionally there is some diagnostic confusion, the tremor of PD can usually be differentiated from essential tremor due to the fact that it occurs at rest. In PD there are usually other motor (rigidity, bradykinesia) and non-motor (depression, urinary disturbance, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder) features which act as clues to the diagnosis.

Amantadine
Amantadine is incorrect. Amantadine is a therapy used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease and would not be recommended in this setting.

Botulinum toxin
Botulinum toxin is incorrect. Botulinum toxin therapy can be used as part of the management for refractory or disabling essential tremor, but would not be recommended at this stage. It is also a treatment for dystonic tremor.

L-Dopa
L-Dopa is incorrect. L-dopa is a therapy used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease and would not be recommended in this setting. Essential TremorSelegiline
Selegiline is incorrect. Selegiline is a therapy used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease and would not be recommended in this setting.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department complaining of progressive weakness of both legs that has been getting progressively worse over the last 2 weeks. The weakness appears to be symmetrical and he is now struggling to walk. He is also complaining of pain in his lower back and buttocks. He has noticed that the left side of his face has become weak and this is evident in his speech, as the left mouth does not move properly and his speech sounds slurred. On further questioning, he reports that he has recently recovered from a ﬂu-like illness. He admits to intermittent use of intravenous (IV) heroin. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this clinical picture?
explanation: B Human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) This patient is at risk of contracting HIV, given his use of IV heroin. HIV seroconversion illness is associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) and HIV can also cause a radiculitis, mimicking GBS. Classic GBS is an acute, ascending, progressive neuropathy characterised by ﬂaccid limb weakness, paraesthesia and hyporeﬂexia. In severe cases, muscle weakness may involve the respiratory muscles leading to progressive respiratory failure, which is the major cause of mortality. Autonomic involvement can also occur leading to cardiac arrhythmia. GBS is thought of as a post-infectious disorder. The body mounts a misdirected immune response against the nervous system due to molecular mimicry. Two-thirds of patients have a history of gastrointestinal (GI) or respiratory infection from 1–4 weeks before the onset of weakness. Common infections preceding GBS include Campylobacter jejuni (25%), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), inﬂuenza A virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, HIV and Haemophilus inﬂuenzae. Other infections can mimic GBS, including diphtheria and Lyme’s disease. D Shigella This patient has GBS. Species within the Shigella genus can cause dysentery, and are also associated with haemolytic uraemic syndrome. However, Shigella is not associated with an acute paralytic neuropathy. A Streptococcus pneumoniae Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause pneumonia, sinusitis and meningitis but is not known to cause an acute paralytic neuropathy. C Mycobacterium tuberculosis TB has a myriad of neurological manifestations (e.g. intracranial abscess, arachnoiditis, meningitis) and this patient might be considered at high risk of contracting TB. If the syndrome was conﬁned to the legs, one might consider Pott’s disease of the spine, or arachnoiditis, as a cause. However, TB is not a common cause of an acute paralytic neuropathy. E Yersinia Species within the Yersinia genus are associated with diarrhoeal illnesses (yersiniosis), Crohn’s disease and reactive arthritis. Yersinia is not commonly associated with any neurological manifestations.

stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of chronic back pain presents for review. He is aware of a dragging feeling affecting his left foot when he tries to walk. This has developed since a minor injury to his left knee. On examination he has weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot. The right is unaffected and plantar flexion and inversion are normal on the left. MRI of the spinal cord shows degenerative disc changes at multiple levels but no evidence of cord or nerve root impingement. Nerve conduction studies and EMG are awaited. What sensory loss would you expect to find in association with this motor defect?
options: Sensory loss affecting the big toe only
Sensory loss over the entire foot to the level of the ankle
Sensory loss over the plantar aspect of the foot
Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg
explanation:
Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg
The most likely diagnosis is a mononeuropathy affecting the left common peroneal nerve. This would lead to sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg on the left. This picture of nerve injury may be seen after trauma (eg blow to the back of the knee) or other causes of mononeuritis such as diabetes mellitus.

No associated sensory loss
No associated sensory loss is incorrect. The common peroneal nerve is not a pure motor nerve so there will be sensory loss.

Sensory loss affecting the big toe only
Sensory loss affecting the big toe only is incorrect. Lesions of the deep peroneal nerve can cause sensory loss in the first web space of the foot (in addition to a foot drop), but not sensory loss affecting just the big toe.

Sensory loss over the entire foot to the level of the ankle
Sensory loss over the entire foot to the level of the ankle is incorrect. This distribution of sensory loss is not compatible with a focal mononeuropathy causing foot drop.

Sensory loss over the plantar aspect of the foot
Sensory loss over the plantar aspect of the foot is incorrect. The sensation to the plantar aspect of the foot is from the tibial nerve and its branches. A lesion of this nerve does not produce a foot drop, rather weakness of plantarflexion.

stem: A 78-year-old female is referred by her GP with intermittent confusion over the last 2 weeks. She has a history of hypertension for which she takes bendrofluazide. Four weeks ago she suffered a fall that was complicated by a Colles’ fracture and minor head injury. She was treated in the Emergency Department at the time, and a skull X-ray was normal. On this occasion, examination is normal, including mental state assessment. The night following admission she is noted to be slightly confused. Routine bloods, resting ECG and chest radiograph are all normal. Which one of the following diagnoses must be excluded?
explanation:
Subdural haematoma
In the context of fluctuating confusion and a recent minor head injury subdural haematoma must be excluded. A CT scan of her head should be performed.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. The acute and fluctuating nature of the history suggests Alzheimer’s disease is not the cause.

Intercurrent urinary tract infection
Intercurrent urinary tract infection is incorrect. Intercurrent infection is a more common reason for this type of presentation, but it is more important to exclude a subdural haematoma.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. The absence of a thunderclap headache and meningism make subarachnoid haemorrhage unlikely. Subdural HaematomaA 67-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension attends the general practitioner with his wife. She is concerned about a sudden deterioration in his speech. Whilst he appears to understand what his wife says to him, she is concerned that his responses have become halting and non-fluent, and he appears to be expending great effort when he talks. He can, however, repeat phrases when asked. You suspect that he has transcortical motor aphasia. He is right handed. Which one of the following areas of the brain is most likely to have been affected?

Transient ischaemic attack
Transient ischaemic attack is incorrect. Non-specific confusion with no focal signs is unlikely to be caused by transient ischaemic attack.

stem: A 66-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a history of dizziness and vomiting. He had been symptomatic for the past 2 days and noticed that he had a tendency to sway towards his right side while walking. He had been hypertensive for the past several years and was taking atenolol 100 mg/day. On examination, the blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg, with a pulse of 78 bpm. He was alert and orientated to place and time. Fundi were unremarkable. Conjugate lateral gaze to the right side was impaired, and a right- sided gaze-evoked nystagmus was evident. The right orbicularis oculi and oris were mildly weak. Right upper and lower limbs were hypotonic and ataxic. Plantar were ﬂexors on both sides. Pinprick sensation was impaired over the left-sided trunk and limbs. What is the most likely vascular territory involved?
explanation:
C Right anterior inferior cerebellar artery The correct answer is Right anterior inferior cerebellar artery (Option C). The occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery causes a lateral inferior pontine infarction. The principal ﬁndings are vertigo, vomiting, horizontal and vertical nystagmus and ipsilateral tinnitus. A lower motor neurone facial weakness, paresis of the conjugate lateral gaze, cerebellar ataxia, Horner syndrome and, rarely, deafness all occur ipsilaterally. On the contralateral side, impaired pain and temperature over the half of the body is observed due to spinothalamic tract involvement. E Right middle cerebral artery Right middle cerebral artery (Option E) is incorrect. Features of

middle cerebral artery infarction include: Contralateral hemiplegia and hemianesthesia Dysphagia Dysarthria and dysphasia Hemianopia Hemineglect. A Right posterior cerebral artery Right posterior cerebral artery (Option A) is incorrect. Depending upon the location and severity of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) occlusion, signs and symptoms may vary. Blockages of the proximal portion of the vessel produce only minor deﬁcits due to collateral blood ﬂow from the opposite hemisphere via the posterior communicating artery. In contrast, distal occlusions result in more serious complications. Visual deﬁcits, such as agnosia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnosia), prosopagnosia or cortical blindness, may be a product of ischaemic damage to the occipital lobe. Occlusion of the branches of the PCA that supply the thalamus can result in central post-stroke pain, and lesions to the subthalamic branches can lead to a wide range of deﬁcits. B Right superior cerebellar artery Right superior cerebellar artery (Option B) is incorrect. Headache, nausea and vomiting, vertigo, gait imbalance and diplopia are the most common complaints at onset of the occlusion. Other common ﬁndings include dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, dysarthria, ataxia and vertigo. D Right anterior cerebral artery Right anterior cerebral artery (Option D) is incorrect. Depending upon the area and severity of the occlusion, signs and symptoms may vary. Blockages to the proximal segment of the vessel produce only minor deﬁcits due to collateral blood ﬂow from the opposite hemisphere via the anterior communicating artery. Occlusions distal to this segment will result in more severe presentations. Contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss of the lower extremity is the most common symptom associated with anterior cerebral artery occlusion.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with a history of Graves’ disease presents with a 6-month history of progressive tingling and weakness of her legs. On examination of the lower limbs, there is bilateral pyramidal weakness, depressed deep tendon reflexes and flexor plantar responses. There is reduced joint position sense and vibration sensation in her lower limbs but no other sensory abnormalities. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Vitamin B12 deficiency
There is selective involvement of the dorsal columns and pyramidal tracts, plus evidence of peripheral nerve involvement; this is classical for subacute combined degeneration of the cord due to B 12 deficiency. On presentation, 50% of patients have absent ankle reflexes with hyper-reflexia at the knees. Plantars are initially flexor, and later extensor. The history of autoimmune disease suggests that intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies should be measured in order to determine the cause of the vitamin B 12 deficiency.

Anterior spinal artery thrombosis
Anterior spinal artery thrombosis causes acute paraparesis with impaired spinothalamic sensations but preserved dorsal column sensations, so does not fit with this clinical presentation.

HTLV-1 infection
HTLV-1 infection causes a chronic, progressive myelopathy, often with prominent bladder disturbance. The history does not suggest this and, in addition, the depressed reflexes are not compatible with this diagnosis.

Hypothyroid associated peripheral neuropathy
Hypothyroid associated peripheral neuropathy is incorrect. The peripheral neuropathy associated with hypothyroidism is typically a painful sensory neuropathy, so the pyramidal weakness and preservation of pinprick sensation (inferred from the details in the question) do not make this diagnosis likely.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with a 48-hour history of pain behind her right ear followed by drooping of the right side of her face. She also describes having an ‘odd taste’ in her mouth and soreness on swallowing. She had previously been fit and well. On examination there is right-sided facial weakness affecting both the upper and lower parts of her face and impaired taste sensation over the right anterior part of her tongue. You notice a vesicular rash on the pinna. There is no sensory loss over her face. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a syndrome in which there is a presumed herpes zoster virus infection of the geniculate ganglion, resulting in facial nerve palsy in association with a vesicular eruption involving the ear, palate, pharynx or neck.

Bell’s palsy
Bell’s palsy is incorrect. Bell’s palsy is the most common cause of lower motor neurone facial paralysis.It is not associated with a vesicular rash. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, anterior two-thirds of the tongue, stapedius muscle in the inner ear, lacrimal gland and salivary glands.

Glomus jugulare tumour
Glomus jugulare tumour is incorrect. A glomus jugulare tumour is slow growing and presents with unilateral hearing loss and cranial nerve palsies affecting CN IX–XI.

Left hemisphere lacunar stroke
Left hemisphere lacunar stroke is incorrect. A left hemisphere lacunar stroke could produce an upper motor neurone type facial weakness, which would partially spare the upper part of the face.

Parotid tumour
Parotid tumour is incorrect. A parotid tumour may cause a facial palsy, but could not account for the vesicles.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his deteriorating conscious level?
explanation:
Subdural haematoma
Chronic deterioration in a patient with alcoholism raises the possibility of a subdural haematoma. Given a history of alcoholism and likelihood of a coagulopathy, even a trivial injury can result in haematoma formation. CT scanning is the investigation of choice, followed by evaluation of the scans by a neurosurgeon to decide with respect to necessary intervention. It is quite possible that there may also be a pneumonia related to hypoventilation because of pain from a rib injury, but this is unlikely to be responsible for the deteriorating conscious level.

Bacterial pneumonia
Bacterial pneumonia is incorrect. Given the evidence of a head injury and focal neurology, a primary neurological event is much more likely to be the cause of his symptoms.

Cerebral abscess
Cerebral abscess is incorrect. This is the main differential, and would be considered in the absence of the significant alcohol history and evidence of a head injury.

Cerebral infarct
Cerebral infarct is incorrect. The position of the injury/bruising to the head fits with a traumatic bleed rather than an infarct. Subdural HaematomaExtradural haematoma
Extradural haematoma is incorrect. Extradural haematomas are associated with rapid bleeding and consequent development of focal neurology.

stem: An 18-year-old female presents with a 3-day history of progressive weakness and numbness of her legs, urinary retention and back pain some 2 weeks following an upper respiratory infection. On examination there is spastic paraparesis, pinprick sensory level up to T5, impaired vibration sense to her knees and extensor plantars. Examination of her cranial nerves and upper limbs is normal. MRI of the spine is normal. CSF analysis reveals 50 cells/mm 3, over 90% lymphocytes with normal protein and glucose levels and negative oligoclonal bands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Post-infectious transverse myelitis
This patient has post-infectious transverse myelitis. The patient has complete cord syndrome with involvement of anterior spinothalamic tracts causing a sensory level, lateral corticospinal tracts causing upper motor neurone (UMN) signs and dorsal column causing vibration loss. The predominant lymphocytes in CSF, with normal protein, normal glucose and negative oligoclonal bands favour a post-viral infective inflammatory process rather than a primary autoimmune inflammation.

Anterior spinal artery occlusion
Anterior spinal artery occlusion is incorrect. Anterior spinal artery occlusion more commonly presents with acute onset of flaccid weakness and areflexia (spinal shock); there would be no posterior column involvement. CSF would be normal.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is incorrect. GBS causes a flaccid paraparesis, areflexia and Chat therewith willAInot be a Tutor sensory level.CSF typically has normal white cell count and elevated protein level.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is incorrect. MS can present in a similar pattern clinically, however, back pain is rare. CSF white cell count of up to50 can be seen MS, but the absence of CSF oligiclonal bands is against this diagnosis.

Thoracic disc prolapse
Thoracic disc prolapse is incorrect. Disc prolapses at this level are uncommon; the usual sites of disc prolapse are cervical and lumbar spinal levels. The clinical presentation can be similar, however, CSF would be normal and the MRI scan would demonstrate the disc prolapse.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with a 6-day history of progressive ascending numbness and weakness of her lower and, subsequently, upper limbs. The day after admission to the General Medical Unit she is noted to have developed bilateral facial weakness. She is areflexic. The Neurology Registrar on call has advised performing a lumbar puncture pending transfer to the Neurology Unit that day. Which one of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings would be most likely?
options: Elevated lymphocyte count with a low CSF:serum glucose ratio
Elevated polymorph count and high protein
Normal cell count, high protein and normal glucose ratio
Normal cell count, high protein and positive oligoclonal bands
Normal cell count, normal protein and positive anti-ganglioside antibodies
explanation:
Normal cell count, high protein and normal glucose ratio
This clinical picture suggests worsening Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS). Typically, the CSF is under normal pressure, is acellular,with a normal glucose ratio and a high protein level that probably reflects the widespread inflammation of the spinal nerve roots. Therefore, normal cell count, high protein and normal glucose ratio is the best option. The protein may be normal in the first few days of the illness but reaches a peak in 4–6 weeks.

Elevated lymphocyte count with a low CSF:serum glucose ratio
Elevated lymphocyte count with low CSF:serum glucose ratio is incorrect. Elevated lymphocyte count with a low CSF:serum glucose ratio is suggestive of a malignant process, or certain infections such as tuberculosis.

Elevated polymorph count and high protein
Elevated polymorph count and high protein is incorrect. Elevated polymorph count and high protein is the CSF pattern seen in bacterial infections.

Normal cell count, high protein and positive oligoclonal bands
Normal cell count, high protein and positive oligoclonal bands is incorrect. Normal cell count, high protein and positive oligoclonal bands may be seen in multiple sclerosis, although protein levels are often normal and a level of greater than 1 g/l would be unusual. Although oligoclonal bands are seen in GBS, this is not universal, meaning it isn’t the correct answer here. Guillain-Barré Syndrome

Normal cell count, normal protein and positive anti-ganglioside antibodies
Normal cell count, normal protein and positive anti-ganglioside antibodies is incorrect. Normal cell count, normal protein and positive anti-ganglioside antibodies is an unlikely correct response as antiganglioside antibodies are not usually checked in CSF but can be checked in blood and are positive in a range of acute and chronic inflammatory neuropathies. Their use in routine clinical practice is not currently well established.

stem: Which drug is most likely to have caused this problem?
explanation:
Isoniazid
The nerve conduction study values above are consistent with an axonal sensory neuropathy where sensory action potential amplitudes are reduced. In demyelinating neuropathies the conduction velocities are typically prolonged with relative preservation of action potential amplitudes. Isoniazid is the commonest antituberculous drug to cause peripheral neuropathy, which is usually axonal. Prescribing pyridoxine with the isoniazid can reduce the risk. Isoniazid is also associated with hepatotoxicity.

Ethambutol
Ethambutol is incorrect. Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis but not a peripheral neuropathy. For this reason visual acuity and colour vision testing should be performedon patients taking this drug.

Paracetamol
Paracetamol is incorrect. Paracetamol is not associated with peripheral neuropathy.

Pyrazinamide
Pyrazinamide is incorrect. Pyrazinamide does not cause peripheral neuropathy. The main side effects are GI disturbance and hepatotoxicity.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is incorrect. Rifampicin does not cause peripheral neuropathy but is an enzyme inducer so can decrease the effectiveness of other drugs.

stem: Interferon beta is a licensed treatment in the United Kingdom for which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS)
Interferon beta is licensed for use in patients with RRMS who are able to walk unaided. RRMS is defined as having at least two attacks of neurological dysfunction (‘relapses’) over the previous 2 years. Clinical trials have shown that interferon is associated with a modest reduction in relapse frequency (around 30%),but convincing evidence regarding the effect on long-term prognosis and disease progression (eg time taken to evolve into secondary progressive MS) remains elusive. Interferon beta is given as either subcutaneous injection three times per week or intramuscular injection once weekly. Adverse effects include local inflammatory reactions at injection sites, flu-like symptoms and depression. Some patients develop anti-drug antibodies against interferon that limit its efficacy. In this case, a switch to an alternative drug (eg glatiramer acetate) is usually advocated. Interferon beta is also licensed (although used much less commonly) for use in patients with a single demyelinating event if it is severe and the patient is thought to be at high risk of developing MS. Interferon beta-1b is also licensed for use in patients with secondary progressive MS but its efficacy in this condition has not been confirmed. It is not licensed for the treatment of primary progressive MS. It is also important to understand that just because a medication has been licensed, does not mean that it is available for prescription on the NHS. This requires further authorisation through processes such as the NICE Technology Appraisal scheme. To add further complication, NICE actually rejected interferon beta and glatiramer acetate (copaxone) for use in MS. However, their use was ultimately allowed through the AI advent Tutor of the ‘NHS risk-sharing scheme’.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. GBS is a demyelinating neuropathy and (for the purposes of this exam especially) does not affect the central nervous system. Interferon (and steroids) have no role in the treatment of GBS.

Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B is incorrect. Interferon alpha has a role in treatment of Hepatitis B but not interferon beta.

Hepatitis C
Hepatitis C is incorrect. Interferon alpha has a role in the treatment of Hepatitis C but not interferon beta.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis is incorrect. As described interferon beta is not licensed for the use of primary progressive MS.

stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia presents with sudden-onset rightsided weakness, hemianopia and aphasia. This occurred an hour previously while he was eating his breakfast. He is taking aspirin, simvastatin, ramipril and digoxin. What action would you recommend?
options: Admission to a stroke unit, with CT in the next 24 hours
CT within the next 4 hours, and transfer to an acute stroke unit
Immediate CT with a view to heparinisation
Immediate CT with a view to IV thrombolysis
Immediate oral aspirin, then CT as soon as possible
explanation:
Immediate CT with a view to IV thrombolysis
Intravenous thrombolysis (0.9 mg/kg IV rtPA (recombinant tissue plasminogen activator) over 1 hour) is now licensed in the UK for acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours. Both evidence from randomised trials and a Cochrane meta-analysis support this treatment. This is therefore the correct answer.

Admission to a stroke unit, with CT in the next 24 hours
Admission to a stroke unit, with CT in the next 24 hours is incorrect. This course of action does not allow for timely administration of IV thrombolysis.

CT within the next 4 hours, and transfer to an acute stroke unit
CT within the next 4 hours, and transfer to an acute stroke unit is incorrect. This course of action does not allow for timely administration of IV thrombolysis.

Immediate CT with a view to heparinisation
Immediate CT with a view to heparinisation is incorrect. Heparin has never been shown in randomised trials to benefit ischaemic stroke. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke

Immediate oral aspirin, then CT as soon as possible
Immediate oral aspirin, then CT as soon as possible is incorrect. Aspirin should be administered only after CT, and should be avoided for 24 hours if the patient is thrombolysed.

stem: A 70-year-old female with a 2-month history of proximal upper limb pain and right-sided headaches develops sudden-onset right-sided visual blurring. On examination there is an altitudinal field defect in the right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Giant cell arteritis
The history of proximal limb aching, headache and visual loss is highly suspicious of giant cell arteritis (GCA). Altitudinal field defects are typically seen in ischaemic optic neuropathy, including that caused by GCA.

Carotid artery dissection
Carotid artery dissection is incorrect. Carotid artery dissection could cause ipsilateral neck pain and headache and can lead to an anterior circulation stroke.

Cluster headache
Cluster headache is incorrect. Cluster headache is characterised by short-lived spells of severe unilateral pain, often occurring at night. Autonomic features such as ptosis, redness of the eye and nasal stuffiness are usually seen. It usually presents in men aged 30–40.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is incorrect. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is usually seen in young, overweight women and causes headache with papilloedema. Giant Cell Arteritis An elderly man presented with progressive lower limb weakness, particularly with hip flexion, preserved knee flex but absent ankle reflex with bilateral extensor plantars. He had a history of prostate carcinoma. Investigations: raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP), normal calcium, normal parathyroid hormone (PTH). What is the investigation most likely to reveal the underlying diagnosis?

Ophthalmoplegic migraine
Ophthalmoplegic migraine is incorrect. Ophthalmoplegic migraine is a rare headache syndrome associated with temporary oculoparesis.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is referred for an evaluation of dysphagia. On examination she has bilateral ptosis, facial weakness and atrophy of the temporalis. She says she has difficulties relaxing her grip, especially in cold weather, and that her father had similar problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myotonic dystrophy type 1
The patient has difficulties relaxing her grip, indicating clinical myotonia. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an autosomal-dominant condition that presents with ptosis, facial weakness dysphagia, sleep apnoea, distal weakness, atrophy of the temporalis, frontal balding, cardiac conduction problems, cataracts and impaired mental function. Thus myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the best explanation for the symptoms described here.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease (MND) is incorrect. Although it can present with dysphagia, the prominent features are usually limb weakness, wasting and fasciculations of the affected muscles, and there would be interposed upper motor neurone signs such as increased tone, hyper reflexia and/or extensor plantars.Myotoniais not observed in this condition. Ptosis is uncommon in MND.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. It can present with dysphagia, but wasting of the facial muscles and myotonia are not features of multiple sclerosis.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. It presents with fluctuating and fatigable weakness symptoms. Facial muscle wasting and myotonia are not characteristic of this condition.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. It can present with dysphagia; however, the prominent feature is proximal limb weakness. Facial muscle wasting and myotonic features are not present.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has a history of idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, first diagnosed 2 years ago. Although she was initially symptomatically well controlled on a low dose of a levodopa preparation, she is now complaining of increasing rigidity and tremor. She currently takes a preparation of levodopa combined with the peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor carbidopa (Sinemet 100/25), one tablet three times per day (at 0800, 1500 and 2000 h). She feels that the effect of the medication wears off after a couple of hours, and now has frequent, fairly prolonged ‘off’ periods. Her only other medical history is irritable bowel syndrome. What would be the most appropriate initial change to her medication regime?
options: Add a fourth dose of Sinemet and adjust to regimen so that doses are taken at 0800, 1200, 1600
Apomorphine injections as required for “off” periods
explanation:
Add a fourth dose of Sinemet and adjust to regimen so that doses are taken at 0800, 1200, 1600
Add a fourth dose of Sinemet and adjust to regimen so that doses are taken at 0800, 1200, 1600 and 2000 h The patient is relatively early in to the disease. The post-dose (i.e. predictable) ‘wearing off’ phenomenon described is suggestive of under-treatment with levodopa. Initial options would be to increase each individual dose of sinemet but leave as a three times per day regimen, or switch to a four times per day regimen. The latter is preferred as this gives a more even distribution of levodopa over the day. However, patient preference (e.g. trouble remembering to take tablets in the middle of the day) may prevent this.

Addition of amantadine
Addition of amantadine is incorrect. The use of amantadine is usually restricted to treating dyskinesia occurring later in disease.

Addition of entacapone (a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor)
Addition of entacapone (a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor) is incorrect. Entacapone is used to ease motor fluctuations that occur in later disease and is used as an adjunct to levodopa. At this stage, simply more levodopa is required. Furthermore, entacapone frequently causes constipation and may worsen the patients’ irritable bowel syndrome.

Addition of ropinirole (a dopamine agonist)
Addition of ropinirole (a dopamine agonist) is incorrect. This answer is potentially correct. However, in recent times, the use of dopamine agonists has fallen out of favour, particularly because of fears about the common (and under-recognised) complication of impulse control disorder. Overall, the patient in this case is receiving a relatively modest dose of levodopa and increasing this is the most straightforward solution to the problem presented.

Apomorphine injections as required for “off” periods
Apomorphine injections as required for “off” periods is incorrect. Apomorphine injections can be used as a ‘rescue’ type therapy for ‘off’ periods, particularly in late disease where such occurrences can become unpredictable. It would be better at this stage to simply increase the amount of levodopa taken and even it out over the course of the day. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset double vision. On examination she has a normal range in up- and downgaze in both eyes. On left gaze the left eye fails to abduct, while the right eye appears normal. On right gaze the right eye appears to abduct normally but the left fails to pass the midline. Her visual acuity and pupil reactions are normal. You also notice that she has a left facial weakness. What is the likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Brainstem
The clinical scenario is difficult as there are several problems: Inability to abduct the left eye. This movement is mediated by the lateral rectus muscle under the control of the VI cranial nerve, the Abducens. Therefore, there is a left-sided VI cranial nerve lesion. Left-sided facial weakness indicating a left-sided VII cranial nerve lesion. Lastly, the left eye fails to cross the midline (medial rectus, III cranial nerve) when the right lateral rectus abducts (VI cranial nerve). We know there isn’t a III cranial nerve palsy – all other eye movements are intact. This is an internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). The lack of abnormality in pupillary reactions and vision localise the lesion to the area of the VI cranial nerve nucleus, horizontal gaze centre, medial longitudinal fasciculus and the facial colliculus. The brainstem is the only unifying affected area.

Cerebello-pontine angle
Cerebello-pontine angle is incorrect. Cranial nerves V, VII and VIII palsies are the classic syndrome here.

Cavernous sinus
Cavernous sinus is incorrect. Cranial nerves III, IV, V and VI travel in the cavernous sinus. Consider this diagnosis in pregnancy and acne when cavernous sinus thrombosis risk is higher.

Frontal cortex
Frontal cortex is incorrect. The frontal eye fields control saccades. Frontal cortex lesions that stimulate frontal eye fields, such as an epileptogenic focus, create abnormal conjugate gaze away from the lesion, while destructive processes such as a tumour create abnormal gaze towards the side of the lesion.

Orbital apex
Orbital apex is incorrect. Cranial nerves II, III, IV, and VI all travel through the orbit into the eye. Tumours of the orbit classically create oculomotor dysfunction with loss of vision due to optic neuropathy.

stem: A 17-year-old girl was admitted to the Emergency Department after suffering a generalised tonic–clonic seizure at 0700 hours. She had been to a nightclub the night before and only went to bed at 0300 hours. She denies taking any illegal substances but admits to drinking around 10 units of alcohol throughout the evening. A detailed history reveals that her upper limbs twitch daily in the early morning, but only for a few seconds, sometimes causing her to spill her morning cup of tea. Neurological examination is normal. CT scan of the brain has been requested. Tox screen is positive for alcohol only. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Diagnosis cannot be made with the above information
explanation:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is a common type of idiopathic generalised epilepsy. It is characterised by generalised tonic–clonic seizures, usually provoked by sleep deprivation and/or excessive alcohol intake. Early morning myoclonic jerks mainly involving the upper limbs are common but under-reported by patients. Absence seizures can also occur. Brain imaging is normal and inter-ictal EEG shows generalised poly-spike and wave discharges.

Diagnosis cannot be made with the above information
Diagnosis cannot be made with the above information is incorrect. It must be remembered that, in the main, brain scans and EEGs are not used to diagnose epilepsy, only to refine a diagnosis that has been made clinically.

Focal epilepsy
Focal epilepsy is incorrect. Focal epilepsy, including seizures arising from the temporal lobe, involve focal seizures (or ‘partial seizures’) which may become generalised (secondary generalisation). The history (especially Tutor from witnesses) is therefore very important. In focal seizures with secondary generalisation, it is usually possible to identify preceding focal seizure signs and symptoms such as a progressive shaking of a single limb (Jacksonian march) or the patient complaining of a rising abdominal sensation or déjà vu prior to the onset of generalised convulsion. Myoclonic jerks (as in this case) are not focal seizures, but in fact involve pan-cerebral epileptic discharges, albeit for a brief period.

Frontal lobe epilepsy
Frontal lobe epilepsy is incorrect. Frontal lobe epilepsy can be difficult to diagnose as seizures often have an unusual appearance (for example, cycling type movements of the legs) and occur nocturnally. EEG can be normal, even ictally, due to poor coverage of the deep sulci of the frontal lobe by surface EEG electrodes.

Temporal lobe epilepsy
Temporal lobe epilepsy is incorrect. Focal epilepsy, including seizures arising from the temporal lobe, involve focal seizures (or ‘partial seizures’) which may become generalised (secondary generalisation). The history (especially from witnesses) is therefore very important. In focal seizures with secondary generalisation, it is usually possible to identify preceding focal seizure signs and symptoms such as a progressive shaking of a single limb (Jacksonian march) or the patient complaining of a rising abdominal sensation or déjà vu prior to the onset of generalised convulsion. Myoclonic jerks (as in this case) are not focal seizures, but in fact involve pancerebral epileptic discharges, albeit for a brief period.

stem: A 20-year-old man went to see his GP because of recent onset of difﬁculty in breathing on mild exertion. He gave a 6-year history of weakness of his limbs, such that he was never able to pursue athletic activities in his school. His father and mother are cousins. Neither of his parents has any medical problem and he has two normal younger siblings. There was no history of muscle cramps and no discoloration of his urine. On examination, he had weakness of the shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles. Truncal muscles were also weak. On deep inspiration, the anterior abdominals had a tendency to retract. Tendon reﬂexes were reduced in all four limbs. There were no sensory signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Acid maltase deﬁciency Acid maltase deﬁciency (glycogen storage myopathy type 2) has three clinical forms. The adult form that is depicted in this scenario

is a slowly progressive weakness of the shoulder, pelvic girdle and truncal muscles. At times the diaphragmatic weakness is the prime difﬁculty, which brings the patient to the Accident and Emergency Department, and so the differential diagnosis would include motor neurone disease, myasthenia gravis and nemaline rod myopathy. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by muscle biopsy. The sarcoplasm of affected cells is vacuolated and the vacuoles contain Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive diastase digestible material. The glycogen particles lie in aggregates. Electron microscopy shows some of these to occupy lysosomal vesicles (i.e. this is a lysosomal disease), and others to lie free. Positive ischaemic forearm tests may occur in patients with other forms of glycogen storage disorder (namely, Cori disease, McArdle disease and Tarui disease). However, a normal test result would be expected in acid maltase deﬁciency. Acid maltase deﬁciency presenting in adulthood carries a better prognosis than the infantile form, and patients are known to survive until the 6th or 7th decade. A Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Classical amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is associated with bulbar palsy, and the long duration of symptoms, including difﬁculty performing sports at school, counts against ALS as the diagnosis. B Polymyositis Polymyositis is associated with muscle weakness, although a shorter disease course accompanied by muscle pain and other signs of connective tissue disease would be expected. C Familial hypokalaemic periodic paralysis Familial hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is associated with marked muscle weakness during the recovery period after intense exercise. D Tarui disease Tarui disease is usually associated with more marked muscle weakness than that seen here, and with myoglobinuria, which can lead to urine discoloration.

stem: A 53-year-old hospital porter is referred to you with aching and fatigue in his legs. His symptoms started 2 months ago with difficulty walking up stairs. On direct questioning, he says it takes him increased effort to get dressed. He also complains of a dry mouth, but there are no speech or swallowing difficulties. On systematic questioning, he has a long history of mild breathlessness on exertion and a chronic cough that he attributes to his heavy smoking. However, over the last 2 weeks he has noticed blood streaks in his sputum. On examination he has a predominantly proximal weakness, more so on the left. Deep tendon reflexes are depressed, but with repeated muscle contraction. There are no sensory changes or extraocular muscle abnormalities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
LEMS is a neuromuscular junction disorder with a well-recognised association with malignancy (50–60% of cases), most commonly small-cell lung carcinoma. It is characterised by proximal muscle weakness, particularly in the legs, which improves for a short while after exercise (post-exercise facilitation). Extraocular and bulbar muscles are usually spared. In addition, tendon reflexes are usually depressed or absent and are characteristically enhanced with repeated muscle contraction. Autonomic disturbances (eg dry mouth and impotence, as in the above case) are common.

Metabolic myopathy
Metabolic myopathy is incorrect. Metabolic myopathy usually causes proximal limb weakness but one cannot accountfor the reflex changes and autonomic symptoms with this diagnosis.

Paraneoplastic neuropathy
Paraneoplastic neuropathy is incorrect. Paraneoplastic neuropathy is usually motor and sensory so one would expect sensory signs. In addition the phenomenon of post-tetanic contraction reflex improvement would not be seen.

Tuberculous myeloradiculopathy
Tuberculous myeloradiculopathy is incorrect. Tuberculous myeloradiculopathy should cause motor and sensory signs and symptoms. It may be painful and is often associated with fever.

Vasculitic neuropathy
Vasculitic neuropathy is incorrect. Vasculitic neuropathy would produce multifocal motor and sensory neuropathic signs (mononeuritis multiplex) and is usually painful. Lambert-Eaton.

stem: A 23-year-old secretary in a law ﬁrm presents with a one-day history of sudden-onset left-sided facial weakness. She ﬁrst noticed this when she was putting her make-up on in the morning. She has noticed hyperacusis in her left ear and altered taste. She is very anxious because two years ago she had problems with her vision and was told that multiple sclerosis was a possibility. At this time, she declined further investigation when it was offered. Past medical history of note includes type 1 diabetes mellitus. Regular medications include insulin and the combined oral contraceptive pill. She denies any tick bites, head injury or recent painful blistering on her outer ear. On examination, she has entire paralysis of the 7th cranial nerve, including weakness of the forehead and some difﬁculty closing her left eye. There is no objective hearing loss, and no sensory signs. Examination of the auditory meatus and canal is unremarkable. The remainder of the neurological examination is normal. There are no visible rashes. You offer her an eye patch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Bell’s palsy Bell’s palsy is an idiopathic palsy or paralysis of the 7th cranial nerve. It typically has a sudden onset of action and affects regions innervated by the facial nerve. The present scenario includes altered taste and hyperacusis. The lower motor neurone presentation here, with all facial muscles involved, is the key differentiating factor when comparing Bell’s palsy to a stroke, which spares the forehead. Treatment includes oral prednisolone and an eye patch to protect the eye, given the inability to close it. D Ramsay Hunt syndrome Ramsay Hunt syndrome, also known as herpes zoster oticus,

presents with painful blisters on the outer ear. There was no evidence of this in the scenario and therefore it is not the best answer. A Stroke This is false because in a stroke you have an upper motor neurone presentation whereby there is sparing of the forehead muscles. This lady clearly has a lower motor neurone lesion in view of the fact that she has entire paralysis of the facial nerve including the forehead. B Lyme’s disease This is a favourite of the MRCP but in this case is not correct. Although this can cause facial palsy, one would expect a history of tick bites and a rash to be present. Without any further evidence to support Lyme’s disease, it simply cannot be the best answer. C Multiple sclerosis Multiple sclerosis was a possible diagnosis when this lady had optic neuritis previously. This option is not the best answer because MS typically presents as an upper motor neurone lesion. This basic knowledge can allow you to rule out MS when considering which option is the most correct.

stem: A 30-year-old rugby player is admitted to the Emergency Department with an enlarging swelling of the neck. She had been involved in a particularly bad rugby tackle three days ago. Since then, she has noticed swelling occurring over the left side of her neck and some weakness affecting the left shoulder, although she has attributed this to a muscle strain. What worries her most is a speciﬁc problem with swallowing, which has come on within the last 48 h. She is a ﬁt woman with no known history and is not taking any regular medication. On examination, she has a large, hard swelling over the left lateral aspect of the neck. Inspection of her eyes is demonstrated below: Examination of the cranial nerves reveals reduced palatal elevation on the left and weakness of shoulder elevation on the left. Sensation and ocular movements are intact. Examination of the limbs does not reveal any abnormalities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Extracranial carotid artery dissection This patient presents with a history in keeping with the diagnosis of extracranial carotid artery dissection. This is associated with blunt

trauma, arteriopathies (of which ﬁbromuscular dysplasia is the commonest) and other collagen vascular disorders. The neck swelling is an expanding haematoma and she has subsequently developed left-sided compressive cranial nerve palsies (IX, X and XI) and a left-sided Horner syndrome, miosis and ptosis are evident on the photograph, as a result of compression of the sympathetic chain. E Intracranial vertebral artery dissection This presents with posterior circulation ischaemia and subarachnoid haemorrhage in some cases A Intracranial carotid artery dissection This condition presents with headache followed by major anterior circulation stroke. Some intracranial dissections present as subarachnoid haemorrhage. B Extracranial vertebral artery dissection This condition presents with neck pain and ischaemia of the posterior circulation. D Lateral medullary syndrome Infarcts of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery cause the lateral medullary syndrome. This is characterised by ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral reduced pain and temperature sensation of the face and other ipsilateral cranial nerve involvement, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation of the limbs.

stem: A 67-year-old right-handed woman is referred to the Stroke Unit. She is a lifelong heavy smoker but has no past medical history. She describes rapid onset facial paralysis that has persisted for a day. She further describes an awareness of sounds seeming louder on the left. On examination, there is ﬂattening of the nasolabial fold on the left, and she is unable to raise her eyebrow or close her eye on that side. Blood pressure is 155/70 mmHg. There is no rash or adenopathy. The remainder of neurological examination, including auroscopy, assessment of parotids and mucous membranes, is normal. Choose the most appropriate management plan.
options: Admission to an acute stroke unit
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
explanation:
B Oral steroids and eye taping Complete facial paralysis with no sparing of the frontalis muscle suggests a lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy. The most

common cause is Bell’s palsy. There are no other features in this case to suggest an alternative cause. Optimal management of a suspected case of Bell’s palsy has been traditionally controversial. Most results from systematic reviews of steroids and antivirals have been conﬂicting. However, an adequately powered randomised controlled trial conducted in Scotland, of early (<72 h after symptom onset) treatment by oral prednisolone, oral aciclovir or both was published in 2007 (Sullivan et al., NEJM 2007; 357:15981607). This study found a signiﬁcant effect of steroids but not aciclovir in 3- and 9-month assessment of facial power recovery. No adverse effects occurred. D Eye taping and ophthalmology referral Protecting the exposed cornea is certainly important, but steroids will also confer a better recovery. A Admission to an acute stroke unit This patient has evidence of a lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy, so stroke care is not indicated. C Oral aciclovir and eye taping Antiviral drugs do not have a beneﬁt in Bell’s palsy compared to steroids. E Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain There are no additional cranial nerve or upper motor neurone signs here to suggest that MRI is indicated

stem: A 53-year-old man is referred by his general practitioner with a tremor affecting his left wrist and hand. This has been observed for the past 8 months and is present intermittently, but seems to worsen with stress or anxiety. He also reports feeling generally fatigued and low in mood. He has noticed a subtle decrease in dexterity and lack of coordination with activities such as playing golf. On examination, he is noted to have a simple oscillating tremor of the left hand, which is present at rest. The same tremor is noticed with the arms outstretched. Assessment of tone reveals cogwheeling in the distal left upper limb. Examination of his gait demonstrates small steps, with reduced arm swing of the left upper limb and mild postural instability on tests of retropulsion. Which of the following therapeutic strategies is most appropriate in this case?
explanation:
B Co-careldopa 100 mg three times daily The clinical scenario is suggestive of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Onset is typically asymmetrical, with the most common initial ﬁnding being resting tremor in an upper extremity. Over time, patients notice symptoms related to progressive bradykinesia, rigidity and gait difﬁculty. Other initial symptoms of PD may be non-speciﬁc and include fatigue and depression. The three cardinal signs of PD are resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia. Of these features, two of three including bradykinesia are required to make the clinical diagnosis. The goal of medical management in PD is to provide control of signs and symptoms for as long as possible while minimising adverse effects. Medications usually provide good symptomatic control for 4–6 years. After this, disability progresses despite best medical management, and many patients develop longterm motor complications including ﬂuctuations and dyskinesia. Levodopa, coupled with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (PDI), remains the mainstay of symptomatic treatment for PD. It provides the greatest anti-parkinsonian beneﬁt with the fewest adverse effects. A Amantadine 100 mg twice daily Amantadine is a weak antagonist of the NMDA-type glutamate receptor, increases dopamine release and blocks dopamine reuptake. This makes it a weak therapy for Parkinson's disease. It can be used to treat L- DOPA-related motor ﬂuctuations (i.e. shortening of L-DOPA duration of clinical effect, probably related to progressive neuronal loss) and L-DOPA-related dyskinesias (choreiform movements associated with long-term L-DOPA use, probably related to chronic pulsatile stimulation of dopamine receptors). C Entacapone 200 mg three times daily Entacapone is a selective and reversible inhibitor of the enzyme catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). When taken together with levodopa (L-DOPA) and carbidopa, entacapone prevents catecholO-methyltransferase from breaking down and metabolising levodopa, resulting in an overall increase of levodopa levels remaining in the brain and body. This can be used to help manage motor ﬂuctuations. D Propranolol 80 mg twice daily Propranolol is usually ineffective in treating the tremor of Parkinson’s disease. E Ropinirole 0.25 mg daily Whilst a dopamine agonist would be a reasonable ﬁrst-line therapy, most clinicians now favour L-Dopa as it is more effective in

relieving symptoms. In addition, there are increasing concerns with dopamine agonists regarding side effects, such as impulse control disorder.

stem: A 62-year-old man presented with a progressive worsening of memory over a 3-month period since arriving back from a summer holiday in Australia. His wife said that he had initially put this down to the fact he had been having difﬁculties sleeping while on holiday and his concentration had suffered. However, he now had difﬁculty remembering what day it was or where he was. His past history included recent depression and also stable angina, hypertension and asthma. On examination he had severe cognitive impairment but cranial nerve and limb examination appeared, normal apart from occasional jerky movements of the hands and a somewhat ataxic gait. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed signal changes in the putamen and head of the caudate. Which further investigation would help support the diagnosis?
explanation:
A Electroencephalography The most likely diagnosis is sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (sCJD). He has rapidly progressive cognitive impairment with prodromal insomnia and depression. Myoclonus is often a prominent feature and other features include seizures, cerebellar signs, extrapyramidal signs and cortical blindness. Electroencephalography (EEG) may reveal characteristic bi- or triphasic periodic complexes superimposed on a slow background rhythm. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) examination may reveal a positive 14-3-3 protein (which is a marker of rapid neuronal destruction), and the newly developed RTQuIC test can also be performed – this helps support the diagnosis and is the other investigation which should be considered. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain may show signal changes in the putamen, head of the caudate and cortex, in comparison to the ﬁndings in variant CJD in which increased signal in the pulvinar may be seen. D Serum syphilis serology Neurosyphilis may produce neurological symptoms such as abnormal gait, blindness, confusion, sudden personality changes and dementia. In this case the MRI already strongly suggests sCJD. B Genetic testing

Genetic testing would be normal in sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. Inherited prion diseases do occur due to mutations in the PRNP gene, but are rarer disorders than sporadic CJD. C Serum antinuclear antibodies Serum antinuclear antibodies would be normal in Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. Anti-nuclear antibodies are elevated in autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus. E Serum vitamin B12 Vitamin B12 deﬁciency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord and a peripheral neuropathy. It can also cause optic atrophy and cognitive impairment.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycaemia, muscle weakness and fatigue. He has a history of delayed puberty and short stature. He reports difﬁculty maintaining energy levels between meals and has frequent dizziness and confusion when fasting. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly and a BMI of 18 kg/m2. Laboratory investigations show hypoglycaemia (3.0 mmol/l), elevated lactate levels and hyperlipidaemia. Genetic testing conﬁrms glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke disease). What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?
options: Frequent small meals with cornstarch supplementation
explanation:
B Frequent small meals with cornstarch supplementation In adults with glycogen storage disease type I, managing fasting hypoglycaemia remains critical. Frequent small meals supplemented with uncooked cornstarch provide a slow and steady release of glucose, preventing hypoglycaemia and reducing metabolic complications. D Glucagon injections during hypoglycaemia Glucagon is ineffective in glycogen storage disease type I because the enzymatic block prevents glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis from producing glucose. A High-protein diet to support gluconeogenesis While protein intake can beneﬁt patients with some glycogen storage diseases, those with type I disease cannot utilise

gluconeogenesis effectively due to glucose-6-phosphatase deﬁciency. C Initiation of a ketogenic diet A ketogenic diet is contraindicated in glycogen storage diseases due to the risk of worsening lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia, as patients cannot metabolise ketones efﬁciently. E Liver transplantation Liver transplantation is reserved for severe, refractory cases or complications such as hepatocellular carcinoma. It is not the ﬁrstline management in stable adults.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with no past medical history is admitted as an emergency. Initial presentation was with headache, fever and meningism. Her husband also described her as becoming increasingly drowsy for around 48 h prior to admission, They have recently returned from a weekend away in France. Her temperature on admission was noted to be 38.2 °C, with a BP of 110/70 mmHg and a pulse of 90 bpm. She was given intravenous (IV) benzylpenicillin, and cerebrospinal ﬂuid was obtained by the emergency team. The on-call microbiologist calls to report Gram- positive rods on the initial Gram stain. What would be the most appropriate medication for this patient?
explanation:
C IV ampicillin and gentamicin The Gram-positive rods reported on the Gram stain probably represent Listeria monocytogenes. Listeria is the second most common form of meningitis in the elderly and immunosuppressed (including the mild relative immunosuppression occurring in pregnant women). Clinical infection often spreads to involve brain parenchyma, in particular the brainstem. Thus a meningoencephalitic picture with headache, meningism and cranial nerve palsies is common. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid Gram stain yields an organism in less than 50% of cases of Listeria meningitis. The cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) examination further differs from the more common bacterial meningitis with a lower white cell count and protein. Some cases may resemble a viral CSF proﬁle. Treatment consists of ampicillin and gentamicin; however, even with treatment mortality remains high (>60 % in some series). Listeria are similarly susceptible in vitro to ampicillin and penicillin, and acquired resistance to the most commonly used

drugs is rare. However, ampicillin and penicillin G demonstrate delayed in vitro bactericidal activity at concentrations attainable in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF). As a result, for listerial CNS infections, we add gentamicin, which is bactericidal, to ampicillin or penicillin to achieve synergistic effects. B IV cefotaxime and rifampicin In cases where there is a relevant travel history or where drugresistant Pneumococcus is suspected, rifampicin is added to cefotaxime. However, here the Gram stain result suggests that Pneumococcus is not the pathogen involved. A IV cefotaxime and dexamethasone The role of steroids is proven in paediatric practice and there is some evidence for its use in adults with pneumococcal meningitis. At present steroids are not recommended for proven Listeria meningitis in adults. D IV cefotaxime and aciclovir In cases where initial clinical details and results fail to discriminate between a bacterial and viral cause, it is common practice to cover for both in this way, but here the Gram stain has conﬁrmed a bacterial pathogen so aciclovir is not needed. E IV chloramphenicol This drug is used in cases of suspected meningitis when there is a history of true allergy to penicillin or cephalosporins.

stem: A 73-year-old woman who is known to have Alzheimer’s disease is admitted to the ward, having suffered a fall at home. She is known to be unsteady on her feet and has carers four times a day who provide all her personal care and meals. For some time, carers have recommended she be moved to a residential home. You mention to her that this is an option and she refuses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Make the patient go to a residential home
explanation:
A Assess the patient’s capacity In this situation, assessing capacity is the key next step. If the patient has capacity, then it is possible they can return home with maximal support from social services. If they do not have capacity and are, in effect, therefore unable to comprehend the potential dangers of going home, a residential home may be appropriate. D Let the local court decide Asking the local court to decide is also unnecessary at this stage. If there is disagreement over the patient’s capacity, then it may be required, but this is always a last resort. B Ask the family to decide Asking the family to decide is not appropriate as, in all likelihood, they will be unable to give an objective opinion, and until the

patient’s capacity is assessed, no decision should be made. C Discharge the patient home This is the worst option, as without assessing the patient’s capacity, we could potentially be exposing the patient to signiﬁcant risk by putting her back into an unsafe environment. E Make the patient go to a residential home It is important for us ﬁrst to make an assessment of the patient’s capacity. If they are deemed to not have capacity, then a residential home may be appropriate, but this should be a multidisciplinary decision made in conjunction with the family and any previous wishes the patient has expressed.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a history of occasional slurring of speech associated with reduced facial expressions. She also complains of intermittent regurgitation of food through her nose, a situation that she has found to be terribly embarrassing. Her symptoms tend to be worst at the end of the day. There is no past medical history of note and she takes no regular medication. On examination, her observations are within normal limits. Her cardiorespiratory examination is normal and there is no deﬁcit in motor or sensory function. She describes blurred vision during visual ﬁeld testing. Given the likely underlying diagnosis, what is the ﬁrst-line investigation to request?
explanation:
A Anti-Ach receptor antibodies The diagnosis of this patient is myasthenia gravis (MG), which is an autoimmune disorder characterised by the formation of antibodies against acetylcholine (ACh) receptors. Testing of these antibodies is now recommended as ﬁrst-line. In MG, patients typically present with painless weakness that becomes worse on repetitive movement or activity. Patients may complain of general weakness, ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia and difﬁculty chewing, especially tough foods such as meat. The condition is slightly more prevalent in women. The range of presentations is wide and depends on the severity of the disease. Thyroid disorders may be seen in as many as 10% of patients with MG. The diagnosis is based on the characteristic history and general examination and two positive tests, preferably serological (serum anti-ACh antibodies) and electrodiagnostic (eg repetitive nerve

stimulation). Treatment modalities include cholinesterase inhibitors, immunosuppressive drugs, plasmapheresis and immunotherapy. In patients with MG, the application of an ice pack for several minutes to the patient’s eyelids can result in improvement of ptosis, with a sensitivity and speciﬁcity of a diagnosis of MG of over 90%. This transient improvement occurs as the cooling results in the slower breakdown of ACh at the neuromuscular junction. E Tensilon® test The Tensilon® test involves injecting an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (edrophonium) which temporarily reduces muscle weakness. It was previously used as an investigation of choice. However, due to the risk of cardiac arrhythmias, it is less frequently used. B Creatine kinase levels Creatine kinase would be tested in patients with suspected polymyositis. It tends to be normal in patients with MG. C Lumbar puncture A lumbar puncture is used in the diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome and multiple sclerosis. However, the fatiguability of symptoms seen in this patient’s presentation is more characteristic of MG. D Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) head An MRI head is used in the diagnosis of many neurological diseases, including multiple sclerosis, an important differential diagnosis in this patient. However, it plays no role in the diagnosis of MG.

stem: A 52-year-old builder presents to his general practitioner having developed weakness of his right hand. He complains of reduced grip, which he has noticed signiﬁcantly while at work. His symptoms have come on over a period of months following an accident when he fell from some scaffolding. More recently he has noticed some slight weakness and pain of his right shoulder, particularly when trying to lift building materials above his head. He has a history of asthma and is a smoker of 40 cigarettes per day. He complains that his breathing has been steadily worsened over the last few weeks particularly when lying in bed. On examination, he is of slim build. Chest examination is normal and there is a full range of movement at the neck. There is evidence of dorsal interossei wasting over the right hand. In addition, there is evidence of wasting affecting the thenar eminence. Tone is reduced at the right wrist and elbow, and triceps jerk is absent. The bicep and supinator jerks are present with re-enforcement. On examination of power, there is signiﬁcantly reduced right wrist extension, ﬁnger ﬂexion and extension and opposition of the thumb. There is some slight weakness affecting right shoulder abduction, but rhomboid testing is normal. There is some reduced sensation affecting the right middle, ring and little ﬁnger and the medial aspect of the forearm. The rest of the neurological examination is normal Chest X-ray shows hyperinﬂated lung ﬁelds and slightly raised right diaphragm. Electromyogram/nerve conduction studies show: Fibrillation potentials and positive waves affecting small muscles of right hand and wrist extensors Sensory nerve action potentials absent No abnormalities in the left arm. In view of the above history and ﬁndings, what is the likely location of the lesion in this patient?
explanation: C Brachial plexopathy This patient presents with a history consistent with traumatic brachial plexopathy following a fall. He has a distribution of weakness, which does not ﬁt with an individual mononeuropathy, and the root levels involved are C5–T1. A Ulnar nerve palsy The distribution of weakness and sensory loss are wider than simply ulnar innervated structures (small muscles of hand and sensation to medial border of hand). B C8 and T1 root lesion Involvement of muscles such as the shoulder abductors means this must be more widespread than just C8 and T1 roots. Absent sensory nerve action potentials on NCS point to a lesion distal to the dorsal root ganglion. Therefore, multiple root lesions are unlikely in this patient and the lesion must lie within the brachial plexus. D Anterior horn cell disease Whilst this diagnosis could cause progressive weakness and wasting, there would be no sensory signs or sensory problems on neurophysiology. E High cervical myelopathy This would cause a spastic weakness of the upper and lower limbs.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a long history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus presents as an emergency appointment to the clinic with severe burning pain affecting her right thigh and proximal limb weakness. She has some peripheral sensory loss and has had previous laser therapy in both eyes. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 132/72 mmHg, and pulse is 75 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 22. Her right thigh is painful on light touch, and there is evidence of proximal muscle weakness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Diabetic amyotrophy The correct answer is Diabetic amyotrophy (Option B). This scenario is typical of diabetic amyotrophy (although the

condition is rarer in type 1 vs type 2 diabetes). Weakness and wasting are limited to proximal muscle groups, and sensory loss is minimal. The condition is thought to be at least partially immunedriven, although it is also associated with periods of inadequate glucose control and may be precipitated by a period of rapid improvement in glucose levels. D Lumbar spine disc prolapse Lumbar spine disc prolapse (Option D) is incorrect. In lumbar disc prolapse, motor and sensory loss can be related to impingement of a particular nerve root, which is not the case here. A Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option A) is incorrect. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a type of motor neurone disease. It is characterized by worsening weakness and progressive difﬁculty in speaking, swallowing and eventually breathing. The cause is genetic in 5–10% of cases, and unknown in the remaining 90–95%. Sensory nerves and the autonomic nervous system are generally unaffected. C Lumbar spondylosis Lumbar spondylosis (Option C) is incorrect. Lumbar spondylosis is associated with back pain and usually with bilateral lower limb symptoms. E Spinal stenosis Spinal stenosis (Option E) is incorrect. Spinal stenosis is associated with back pain and bilateral lower limb pain.

stem: A 52-year-old woman attended her GP and reported that she had noticed difﬁculty holding her head up for the last few months. She had been previously well and her only existing medical condition was hypothyroidism, for which she took 50 micrograms of levothyroxine. On examination, she had weakness of neck ﬂexion and extension and and her facial appearance is shown below. There was also mild weakness of shoulder abduction, but the remainder of the neurological examination was normal. Which one of the following is the most useful investigation in making a diagnosis?
explanation:
B Nerve conduction studies and electromyography

The most likely diagnosis in this case is myasthenia gravis, as evidenced by the right eye ptosis and neck and limb weakness. This is an autoimmune condition and patients may be positive for acetylcholine receptor antibodies or antibodies to muscle-speciﬁc kinase (MuSK). These antibodies are positive in at least 85% of cases. The diagnosis can be conﬁrmed by completing nerve conduction studies, which show a decrement with repetitive nerve stimulation testing. A Tensilon test where Tensilon, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is administered intravenously, has been used in the diagnosis of the condition but this is less common now as it can result in life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Patients diagnosed with myasthenia gravis should have imaging of their mediastinum as there is an association between the condition and thymoma. Treatment is with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and immunosuppression. In severe presentations or acute deteriorations, intravenous immunoglobulins or plasma exchange may be considered. D Lumbar puncture This investigation would not help in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. It may be useful in the diagnosis of a range of conditions including multiple sclerosis, where oligoclonal bands may be seen, and Guillain–Barré syndrome, where the CSF protein can be raised. The history in this case is not suggestive of either of these conditions. A MRI cervical spine This investigation would not help in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. It would be useful in the diagnosis of cervical spinal pathology such as degenerative disease, bony lesion, nerve root compression or spinal cord compression. The history and examination ﬁndings in this case are not suggestive of any of these conditions, with fatiguable weakness and no sensory symptoms. C Nerve biopsy This investigation would not help in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. This investigation can be useful in the diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy. The examination ﬁnding of fatiguable weakness in this case is not suggestive of peripheral neuropathy. E Serum creatine kinase This investigation would not help in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Creatinine kinase is raised in inﬂammatory myopathies, including polymyositis and dermatomyositis. The history in this case is not suggestive of either of these conditions, which would present with proximal weakness and muscle pain. A heliotrope rash may also be seen in dermatomyositis.

stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to the Accident and Emergency Department by his neighbour, who found him lying on the ﬂoor of his sitting room, unable to move. He is known to have non-insulindependent diabetes mellitus and ischaemic heart disease and takes multiple medications. On examination, he is conscious and alert. His blood pressure is 190/100 mmHg, with a pulse of 85 bpm, irregular. He understands but cannot communicate except by blinking and vertical eye movements. He cannot swallow and has weakness of eye closure on both sides. There is a ﬂaccid quadriplegia. Both plantar responses are extensor. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potasium (K+) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c 77.05 mmol/mol (9.2%) < 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Basilar artery occlusion The above scenario depicts a clinical state in which the patient is awake but is unable to respond in any way except by vertical gaze and blinking. This is consistent with ‘locked-in syndrome’ and is due to basilar artery occlusion. The lesion is in the ventral pons, and it essentially interrupts the corticobulbar and corticospinal pathways and spares the somatosensory pathways and the ascending neuronal functions responsible for arousal and wakefulness, as well as certain mid-brain elements that allow certain eye movements.
