Typical treatment for suspected staphylococcal intracerebral abscess includes gentamicin and ﬂucloxacillin. Data on the brain penetration of linezolid are variable. E Aspergillus fumigatus Fungal infection is usually diagnosed after failure to respond to antibacterials, and is more often a cause of pulmonary infection. A Streptococcus viridans

S. viridans is associated with dental infection and is a recognised cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis. It isn’t usually seen after skin/scalp laceration. C Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an environmental pathogen and is often found in wounds that are heavily contaminated, for example with soil. D Clostridium perfringens Clostridium perfringens is responsible for gas gangrene and results in subcutaneous emphysema. It is therefore inconsistent with the picture seen here.

stem: A 73-year-old woman presented to the Hyperacute Stroke Unit ﬁve hours ago with new-onset dizziness, vomiting, drowsiness and a headache. She was last seen well 12 hours before that. She has a past medical history of hypertension, type II diabetes and depression. She takes regular amlodipine and metformin. Clerking records indicate she was opening her eyes to sound and obeying commands. Her BP was 155/72 mmHg and her heart rate was 78 bpm and regular. She is documented to have had past pointing on the right side. Investigations at presentation: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 115 g/dl 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.9 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 162 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 98 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l CT of the brain Well-defined area of volume loss in the left frontal lobe,with a low-density appearance consistent with encephalomalacia. No haemorrhage MRI was requested, and aspirin 300 mg was commenced. On reassessment, she is now opening her eyes to pain, localising to pain and able to state her name and seems to be answering yes and no inconsistently. Her BP is 195/90, and her heart rate is 111 bpm. What is the most likely cause of this patient's deterioration?
explanation: B Hydrocephalus This patient most likely initially presented with an acute cerebellar infarct, evidenced by past pointing, drowsiness and nausea. Her initial GCS score was 14, and on reassessment, this has dropped to 11. Such a change in GCS score should prompt urgent reimaging, with hydrocephalus as the main differential. Posterior fossa infarcts are susceptible to rapid increases in oedema, which can result in closure of the aqueduct or fourth ventricle, thereby causing obstructive hydrocephalus. The Neurosurgical and Intensive Care Teams should review the patient as appropriate. D Seizure Seizures following a stroke can occur acutely or in the chronic phase. Post-ictal drowsiness could result in a low GCS score, although no seizure activity is described. Given this patient is on a Hyperacute Stroke Unit, she is likely to be closely observed. A Malignant middle cerebral artery syndrome Malignant middle cerebral artery (MCA) syndrome describes acute-onset swelling which occurs following an MCA infarct. Here, with pointers to a cerebellar infarct (dizziness, past pointing), the most likely diagnosis is hydrocephalus due to swelling in the posterior fossa post-infarction. The initial CT report is consistent with an old infarct in the left frontal lobe. C Further cerebral infarction Repeat cerebral infarction is possible but usually occurs in cases where there is a possible proximal source such as AF, signiﬁcant carotid stenosis or, more rarely, atrial myxoma. It would usually cause new neurological signs and symptoms, rather than worsening GCS score, as is the case here. E Hypertensive emergency Malignant hypertension can result in acute neurological signs and symptoms, including encephalopathy and papilloedema. However, here, it is likely that hypertension stems from pain from posterior fossa swelling and hydrocephalus secondary to a cerebellar infarct.

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents with severe dizziness, vertigo and nausea. She has suffered a number of attacks over the past two months. The attacks come on at their worst when she lies down in bed, with her head turned to the right-hand side, and last for around 20 s to a minute. There is no tinnitus. Examination reveals no focal localising neurological signs. You move her rapidly from a sitting position to a supine one with her head tilted at 45 degrees. After waiting for 30 s, you return her to the sitting position having noted obvious nystagmus. Given the likeliest origin of her symptoms, which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment in this case?
explanation: D Epley manoeuvre This patient gives the classical history of benign positional vertigo (BPPV) and the absence of focal neurological signs gives credence to this as the most likely diagnosis. The onset of BPPV is typically sudden, with frequent attacks occurring for days to weeks, occasionally for months or years afterwards. The symptoms often resolve spontaneously until the next episode and occur in a spectrum of severity. In patients with extreme cases, the slightest head movement may be associated with nausea and vomiting. The Epley manoeuvre looks to reposition any free-ﬂoating particles within the semi-circular canals and resolve positional vertigo. A Prochlorperazine In most cases of medical treatments are not indicated. The treatment of choice is the Epley manoeuvre. In acute severe exacerbations which are not responsive to the Eply manoeuvre or similar, anti-histamine and anti- cholinergic drugs may be considered. B Diazepam Long-term medical therapy, such as diazepam, is not the treatment of choice as the Epley manoeuvre carries a high chance of relieving symptoms. This manoeuvre is well documented and attempts to move the free-ﬂoating particles which exist in the semi-circular canals, with a series of planned movements of the head. C Hall-pike manoeuvre The Hall-pike manoeuvre, which is described in the question, is the standard clinical test for BPPV. It is used for diagnosis, not treatment and is therefore an incorrect option. The ﬁnding of classic rotatory nystagmus with latency and limited duration is considered pathognomonic. A negative test result does not exclude the diagnosis. E Betahistine Long-term medical therapy, such as betahistine, is not the treatment of choice. This patient’s signs and symptoms are suggestive of benign positional vertigo (BPPV). The treatment of choice is the Epley manoeuvre.

stem: A 19-year-old university student presented with progressive unsteadiness of walking over the previous year. She had been otherwise well, apart from recent difﬁculty hearing her lecturer in classes. She took no prescription medication but had occasionally taken cocaine during her ﬁrst year of college. She drank up to 30 units of alcohol per week and smoked 10 cigarettes a day. Her parents were both well, but she remembers her father’s sister having problems with walking before she died. Examination revealed normal tone and power throughout all four limbs. Reﬂexes were normal in the upper limbs but decreased at the knees and absent at the ankles. Coordination was normal in all four limbs but her gait was ataxic. Sensation in the upper limbs was normal, but there was decreased vibration sense and proprioception to the ankles bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Friedreich’s ataxia Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder that normally starts before the end of the teens. It has an annual incidence of around 1 in 50,000. Neurological features are of a progressive ataxia, cerebellar dysarthria, lower limb areﬂexia, decreased vibration and proprioception, pyramidal weakness and extensor plantar reﬂexes. Pes cavus and scoliosis are both seen. Cardiomyopathy occurs in over 70% of cases. Less common features are optic atrophy, diabetes mellitus and deafness. E Vitamin B12 deﬁciency Peripheral loss of vibration and position sense are the earliest features of B12 deﬁciency. Loss of reﬂexes and mild to moderate weakness are much later features of low vitamin B12. A Ataxia telangiectasia Ataxia telangiectasia presents in childhood with symptoms of cerebellar dysfunction and ataxia in childhood, rather than for the ﬁrst time in the late second decade. C Multiple sclerosis Multiple sclerosis usually presents with a patchwork of neurological signs rather than the prominent ataxic gait seen here as an initial feature. D Dentatorubropallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) DRPLA presents with symptoms similar to those of Huntington’s disease, and is most prominent amongst the Japanese population.

stem: A 56-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of progressive leg weakness, with particular problems walking up the stairs. This was associated with intermittent pains in his thighs anteriorly. In the previous year he had also noticed problems unscrewing lids from jars, which he felt was due to his grip being generally weaker. He had been well otherwise with no recent weight loss or other symptoms. Examination revealed wasting of the forearms and the quadriceps, with distal weakness in the upper limb and proximal weakness in the lower limb. Reﬂexes were present with ﬂexor plantar responses. Sensation and coordination were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Inclusion body myositis (IBM) Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is the most common acquired myopathy in those aged over 50 years, being more common in men than women. There is often fairly selective muscle involvement, with wasting and weakness of the quadriceps and the long ﬁnger ﬂexors being the most common. Muscles can also be affected asymmetrically. The pattern of muscle involvement is thus different to polymyositis (PM) or dermatomyositis (DM), and the rate of progression is generally slower than with these diseases. Creatine kinase (CK) is raised (around 1000 IU/l) but generally not as high as in PM or DM. Electromyography (EMG) and sometimes muscle biopsy will help in the diagnosis. IBM is much less responsive to immunosuppressive treatment than PM or DM. B Motor neurone disease The selective muscle involvement seen here is much more consistent with inclusion body myositis than motor neurone disease. A Myotonic dystrophy Symptoms of myotonic dystrophy generally present during the third decade with muscle weakness and myotonia (failure of muscles to relax for a prolonged period after use). Other features include infertility/subfertility and frontal balding in men. C Addison’s disease Although adrenal insufﬁciency is associated with proximal muscle weakness, other features that would suggest a diagnosis of adrenal insufﬁciency are absent here. E Polymyositis The selective muscle weakness seen here is inconsistent with polymyositis, with wasting of the quadriceps being the only proximal symptom seen here.

stem: A 45-year-old painter is admitted from his place of work after collapsing in the afternoon. He is a smoker of 20 cigarettes per day but is otherwise well. On rousing at the building site, he was noted to have slurred speech, dizziness and some transient symptoms affecting the right side of the body. This had recovered by the time he reached the Emergency Department. Angiography revealed a proximal stenosis of the left subclavian and carotid arteries. EEG showed no evidence of spike activity. Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
C Subclavian steal syndrome Subclavian steal syndrome is associated with retrograde ﬂow in the vertebral artery due to a proximal subclavian artery stenosis. Neurological symptoms are precipitated by vigorous use of the arm on the side of the stenosed subclavian artery, e.g. painting a wall. Rather than being related to embolic phenomena, they are in fact related to reduced blood ﬂow, demonstrated by a difference in blood pressure between the affected and unaffected arms. The diagnosis is often confused with transient ischaemic attacks or epilepsy. Duplex ultrasound and magnetic resonance angiography are the investigations of choice. The syndrome is associated with diseases that cause the lumen of the artery to be diminished: Takayasu’s arteritis (a type of vasculitis), thoracic outlet compression or post-surgical repair of aortic abnormalities. Medical management is similar to that of peripheral arterial disease: smoking cessation, lipid and blood pressure control and anti-platelet agents. Endarterectomy and stenting are common surgical methods involved in relieving symptoms associated with this condition. D Complex partial seizure Complex partial seizures cause loss of awareness without loss of consciousness, along with the other, well- known features such as a prodrome of ﬂuttering sensation in the abdomen, and automatisms like lip-smacking. This patient has had loss of consciousness, and no history of prior lip-smacking or prodrome. Therefore, this is not a complex-partial seizure. A Transient Ischaemic attack

Transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) might be a plausible answer given he has focal symptoms such as hemi- sensory disturbance and slurred speech. However, loss of consciousness is uncharacteristic of a TIA. Moreover, we are told that there is a proximal stenosis in the left subclavian and carotid arteries, whereas a TIA would usually be caused by stenosis in the mid- to distal carotids, with the subclavians being unaffected. B Migraine attack Migraines can come on at work, at times of stress, but there is usually an aura with wave-like lines moving across the affected visual ﬁeld, followed by a unilateral or global thumping headache that gets better with rest. Loss of consciousness is not a feature of migraine. Therefore, this is not the correct answer. E Generalised epilepsy There are no features to suggest this man has had a seizure, such as a prodrome, a history of witnessed limb rigidity or jerking, or postictal confusion or fatigue. Even if there were features of seizure activity in the history, generalised epilepsy (a tendency to have seizures) cannot be diagnosed from a history of a single seizure without supportive evidence from an EEG.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with stereotyped episodes of facial pain. He describes ‘electric shocks’ to the lower half of his right face. Attacks last a second only, but he can experience multiple attacks in an hour, often with a residual ache. He identiﬁes a number of triggers to attacks including laughing and shaving. There is no past medical history. On examination, you note normal pupils and full range of ocular movement. There is reduced corneal reﬂex and reduced sensation in the mandibular and maxillary division of the trigeminal. The remainder of examination is unremarkable. What is the most important management step?
explanation: E MRI of the brain The history given is characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia, with paroxysms of pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. However, two features in the history should alert the clinician that this is unlikely to be ‘classic’ trigeminal neuralgia. Trigeminal neuralgia should not be associated with any physical signs: note the cranial nerve signs in this patient. Furthermore, trigeminal neuralgia is a disease of middle-to-late age, most often affecting women. Thus in this young male patient, imaging to exclude a structural lesion – for instance an area of demyelination related to multiple sclerosis – should be performed before therapy is instituted. Usual treatment for trigeminal neuralgia would be a titrated dose of carbamazepine. A number of surgical procedures are available for intractable pain but are associated with signiﬁcant potential side effects. D Peripheral nerve block with phenol Nerve blockade may be considered in patients who fail to respond to medical therapy alone. A Carbamazepine Carbamazepine is an initial ﬁrst-line option for trigeminal neuralgia, but a structural cause for the patient’s symptoms should be excluded ﬁrst. B Amitriptyline There is little evidence to support use of tricyclic antidepressants in the management of trigeminal neuralgia, although they are often added as a second-line therapy. C Reassurance The pain associated with trigeminal neuralgia is signiﬁcant, and may itself drive depression because of its severity. As such, reassurance alone isn’t an appropriate option.

stem: A 32-year-old painter presented with a two-day history of suddenonset occipital headache associated with nausea and vomiting. The next day his right hand became weak for a few hours. Later that day he had an episode of sensory disturbance in his right upper limb, consisting of tingling in his hand that spread up the arm to his shoulder over the 60 s and lasted 120 s in total. On the day of admission, he had a similar episode of sensory disturbance lasting 30 s in total. Fundoscopy appearances are similar bilaterally and one retina is shown below: On examination, he had bilateral papilloedema, no neck stiffness and an otherwise normal neurological examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) has an annual incidence of 0.22 per 100 000 and is associated with headache (>90% of cases), seizures (focal, with or without secondary generalisation – almost 50%), focal weakness (40%) and papilloedema (40%), all seen in this patient. (The fundoscopy image is typical of the picture seen in papilloedema). Risk factors for CVST include genetic or acquired prothrombotic disorders, pregnancy, the oral contraceptive pill, vasculitis, malignancy, dehydration and infection. However, there are multiple other associated factors. A Migraine Migraine is not usually associated with an occipital headache; presentation with a frontal headache, preceded by an aura and accompanied by nausea and vomiting, would be expected. Papilloedema is not seen. B Viral meningitis Papilloedema would be unusual in the context of viral meningitis, and there are no features to suggest acute viral infection. D Multiple transient ischaemic attacks Multiple TIAs usually occur in the same territory, are not associated with headaches and we are given no evidence of vascular risk factors here.

E Carotid dissection Carotid dissection is associated with amaurosis fugax, partial Horner syndrome and other features such pulsatile tinnitus and change in taste, depending on the extent of any underlying dissecting aneurysm.

stem: You are called to the vascular ward during the evening to assess a 68-year-old diabetic, who had undergone balloon angioplasty to his right leg that morning. Post-procedure recovery was uneventful although he had required sedation for anxiety. He awoke with rightsided weakness and language difﬁculty. From past medical history you note poorly controlled diabetes and hyperlipidaemia. On examination, his blood pressure is 158/95 mmHg and he is in sinus rhythm with a Glasgow coma scale of 14/15. A bedside glucose test is 9.5 mmol/l. He has a dense right hemiparesis, homonymous hemianopia and expressive dysphasia. Initial computerised tomography (CT) scan has been performed and is unremarkable. He has been given 300 mg of aspirin. Ward staff tell you that it was 16.20 when he awoke; it is now 18.35. What is the optimal management of this patient?
options: Admit to the acute stroke unit
Thrombolysis with intravenous tissue plasminogen activator
explanation:
A Admit to the acute stroke unit The clinical picture is consistent with a dominant middle cerebral artery infarct. Evidence-based strategies for infarct in the acute stage include aspirin, admission to a dedicated stroke unit and, if eligible, thrombolysis. Thrombolysis has been proven to reduce disability in nonhaemorrhagic infarcts when given within 3 h of symptom onset, and guidelines support thrombolysis for some patients out to a 4.5 h limit. Important contraindications include recent trauma; hypertension (systolic pressure over 180 mmHg); and active bleeding. His recent angioplasty would not exclude him from therapy. However, as he awoke with symptoms there is no certainty over the time of stroke onset and as such, thrombolysis cannot be advised. It has been shown that patients who suffer a stroke on a non-medical ward and are subsequently managed in that ward have poor outcomes. C Intravenous labetalol This is an effective treatment for acute blood pressure control, but there is no clear indication for that in this patient. NICE guidance on acute stroke care suggests lowering blood pressure only if there is

hypertensive emergency (or if BP is >185/110 and thrombolysis is being considered). B Thrombolysis with intravenous tissue plasminogen activator The precise time of onset of his stroke is not known. D Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin infusion NICE guidelines suggest maintaining blood glucose between 4-11 mmol/l. E Thrombolysis with intravenous streptokinase There is no role for use of streptokinase in acute stroke. Where thrombolysis is indicated, it is with TPA rather than with streptokinase.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department by her GP for a bilateral 6th nerve palsy. She reports severe, dull headaches, worse in the mornings, over the past 3 months. There has also been a deterioration in her vision, with intermittent diplopia, particularly when she strains or bends forward. The only medication of note includes the combined oral contraceptive pill. Examination reveals a BP of 155/90 mmHg, and pulse is 75 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 34. There is bilateral papilloedema and bilateral 6th nerve palsy. Routine blood testing is unremarkable. MRI scanning reveals ﬂattening of the sclera and distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space. Magnetic resonance venography is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
D Lumbar puncture New-onset morning headaches should always be investigated with cerebral imaging to rule out a space- occupying lesion or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. The history and demographic of this patient is consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Most patients present with postural headaches, transient visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus. Clinical examination will reveal papilloedema, potentially enlarged blind spot with impaired visual acuity and sometimes cranial nerve VI palsies. A diagnosis is made by demonstrating raised intracranial pressure on lumbar puncture (>25 cm CSF) – often the patient will have instantaneous relief of their symptoms. The major morbidity associated with IIH is visual loss (hence the change in name from benign intracranial

hypertension), and therefore patients should have an ophthalmology review for regular retinal photography and visual ﬁeld assessment. The most effective and enduring treatment is weight loss. Pharmacological therapy aims to reduce CSF production, such as with acetazolamide or topiramate. For patients with progressive visual loss, surgical intervention can be considered – optic nerve sheath fenestration and/or CSF shunts. A Acetazolamide Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production. This is a recognised pharmacological treatment for IIH, but ﬁrst the diagnosis needs to be conﬁrmed with a lumbar puncture. B Furosemide Furosemide is a loop diuretic and is a recognised pharmacological treatment for IIH, but ﬁrst the diagnosis needs to be conﬁrmed with a lumbar puncture. C Indomethacin Indomethacin is a NSAID which is used in the treatment of indomethacin-responsive primary headache disorders, such as hemicrania continua and paroxysmal hemicrania. These are sidelocked headaches often associated with unilateral autonomic symptoms. E Prednisolone Corticosteroids have previously been used in the treatment of IIH. However, they are no longer recommended as they can cause weight gain which is disadvantageous, withdrawal can cause rebound IIH associated with marked visual loss and there are signiﬁcant deleterious side effects from prolonged steroid use. In any case, the diagnosis should be conﬁrmed with a lumbar puncture in the ﬁrst instance.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is brought into the hospital with a 2-day history of left-sided headaches and blurred vision. She does not usually suffer from headaches and ﬁnds the persistent pain worrying. Her past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension. However, previous clinic letters suggest non- compliance with medication. On examination, she has a heart rate of 65 bpm with a BP of 188/105 mmHg. The remainder of her cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Her neurological examination showed the following ﬁndings (as shown below): What is the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation?
explanation:
A Carotid artery dissection This patient has features of Horner syndrome including ptosis and miosis of the left eye. Horner syndrome is caused by disruption of the sympathetic chain that produces ptosis (secondary to loss of sympathetic innervation to the smooth muscle of the superior tarsal muscle), miosis (through un-antagonised parasympathetic stimulation to the iris) and anhidrosis. There are numerous causes of Horner syndrome including carotid artery dissection. The history of a headache and past medical history of hypertension and medication non-compliance makes this diagnosis even more likely. The current BP of 188/105 mmHg also supports non-compliance with medication. B Facial nerve schwannoma This would give rise to the clinical picture of facial nerve palsy with paralysis of the muscles innervated by the facial nerve. Facial nerve palsy would not give rise to the clinical presentation seen here and does not cause pupillary changes. C Microvascular oculomotor nerve palsy The most common cause of oculomotor nerve palsy is diabetes mellitus and its microvascular complications. Symptoms of oculomotor nerve palsy include complete ptosis and an eye that is turned outwards and downwards. An important reminder is that microvascular oculomotor nerve palsy may not necessarily cause pupil dilatation. This is because the parasympathetic ﬁbres carried from the Edinger Westphal nucleus are spared. However, traumatic causes of oculomotor nerve palsy are more likely to cause pupil changes.

D Uncal herniation The uncus is located within the medial portion of the temporal lobe. In cases of raised intracranial pressure, the uncus can herniate through its intracranial compartment and cause extrinsic compression of the oculomotor nerve, giving rise to an oculomotor nerve palsy with pupillary involvement (eg ptosis, pupil dilatation and a ‘down and out’ facing eye). E Varicella zoster virus reactivation This can give rise to shingles or Ramsay–Hunt syndrome (or herpes zoster oticus), a syndrome that causesN ipsilateral facial nerve palsy and a vesicular rash within the ear canal that causes ear pain and occasionally tinnitus and vertigo.

stem: You assess a 78-year-old man in the medical receiving unit. His history is of sudden onset weakness and diplopia. On examination, pupils are equal and reactive. The right pupil is difﬁcult to visualise due to a low-hanging eyelid and displacement of the eye in a temporal–inferior direction. There is ﬂaccid weakness of the left arm and leg with an upgoing left plantar. The consultant neurologist phones to discuss the patient. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation:
A Ventrolateral midbrain This patient’s symptoms are consistent with that of Weber syndrome, which is a result of infarction of the midbrain – speciﬁcally the ventrolateral aspect. This is usually secondary to occlusion of the paramedian branches of the basilar artery or the posterior cerebral artery. The condition presents with an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy (causing ptosis, eye deviation down and out, afferent pupillary defect and resultant diplopia) and a contralateral weakness. Occasionally, the patient may also present with contralateral parkinsonian rigidity. D Right hemi-cord Hemi-cord lesions give rise to Brown–Séquard syndrome, which consists of ipsilateral paresis and dorsal column sensory loss (vibration and proprioception) and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss (pain and temperature) a few levels below the lesion. B Left lateral medulla

A lesion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery would cause Wallenberg’s syndrome. This consists of nystagmus, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, ipsilateral temperature and pain facial sensory loss, contralateral limb sensory loss (pain and temperature), ipsilateral limb ataxia and ipsilateral palatal and vocal cord paralysis. C Left parietal lobe Cortical pathology in the dominant parietal lobe (including the angular and supramarginal gyri) can cause Gerstmann’s syndrome: ﬁnger agnosia; left–right disorientation; dysgraphia and acalculia. E Corpus callosum The corpus callosum connects the left and right cerebral hemispheres and aids interhemispheric communication. Pathology of the splenium of the corpus callosum can give rise to alexia without agraphia. Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome is caused by callosal degeneration from chronic alcohol abuse and causes dementia, spasticity, dysarthria and an inability to walk.

stem: You are asked to review a 72-year-old man in the Neurology Clinic. He has a past medical history of hypertension for which he takes lisinopril and amlodipine. There is a convergent squint and a leftsided facial weakness. Where is the most likely site of his lesion?
explanation:
A Pons The 6th-nerve nucleus is encircled by seventh-nerve ﬁbres in the pons, so pontine lesions of the seventh cranial nerve are often associated with a convergent squint (due to lateral rectus palsy). Causes include pontine tumours (such as a glioma), demyelination due to multiple sclerosis and vascular lesions. D Cerebellum Cerebellar dysfunction would result in ataxia rather than the 6th and 7th cranial nerve lesions seen here. B Medulla Medial medullary lesions lead to hypoglossal nerve injury, corticospinal tract dysfunction and damage to the medial lemniscus. Lateral medullary syndrome is well described.

C Parietal lobe Parietal lobe lesions do not result in 6th and 7th cranial nerve lesions, although they may result in inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. E Upper spinal cord Upper spinal cord lesions can affect cranial nerve XI, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with weakness in both legs, which has signiﬁcantly worsened over the past week. She also has a history of intermittent paraesthesiae in both legs over this period. She is normally a keen runner, regularly running half-marathons, and initially noted the symptoms became worse after her runs. She does not recall any recent diarrhoeal or viral illnesses. On ﬂexion of the neck, she experiences an electric shock sensation down her back. She is apyrexial, and there is no evidence of photophobia or neck stiffness.
options: Computed tomography (CT) thorax, abdomen and pelvis
explanation: D MRI brain with gadolinium The MRI scan shows a short segment lesion in the cervical spine. Paraesthesiae, alongside the cervical MRI ﬁndings, hint at transverse myelitis. However, a cause needs to be identiﬁed. This stem and the MRI ﬁndings conﬁrm a ‘clinically isolated syndrome’. An MRI brain may show lesions which, if they were non-enhancing, would satisfy criteria for Multiple sclerosis (MS) as dissemination in time and space. The younger age of the patient, lack of features of optic neuritis and radiological features hint toward MS being more likely than Neuromyelitis optica (NMO). Clearly, viral infections would need considering, but these are not listed as an answer to potentially investigate. A Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) Gram stain While this patient presents with a relatively acute deterioration in neurological symptoms, for which a neurological infection would be an important differential, the long history of previous neurological impairment and lack of meningitis symptoms make a bacterial infection less likely. Therefore, CSF Gram staining would not be the most useful investigation. B Nerve conduction studies The purpose of this question is to identify the underlying cause of the transverse myelitis suggested in the stem. While nerve conduction studies may conﬁrm transverse myelitis, displaying features such as active denervation, they will not investigate the underlying cause. MS is important to be ruled out as an underlying cause. According to the McDonald criteria, we have evidence of a ‘clinically isolated syndrome’ at present. An MRI brain may show lesions which, if they were non-enhancing, would satisfy criteria as dissemination in time and space, providing a diagnosis of MS. C Computed tomography (CT) thorax, abdomen and pelvis A neurological malignancy would need to be followed up with screening for metastases. However, in this case, there is no history pointing to malignancy, instead favouring transverse myelitis. E Neuromyelitis optica (NMO) immunoglobulin The history and MRI ﬁndings point to a diagnosis of transverse myelitis, a focal inﬂammatory disorder of the spinal cord. This has a number of causes, including NMO. While NMO is a possibility here, MS is more common, and therefore a more likely cause in this scenario. Additionally, the radiological features are less supportive of NMO, which manifests as a longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion expanding three or more spinal segments.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after suffering from ﬂorid visual hallucinations and disturbed sleep over the past few days since his medications for symptoms of Parkinson’s disease were increased. According to his wife he had memory problems and some limited hallucinations even before the Parkinson’s was diagnosed. Current medications include both ropinirole and levodopa for Parkinson’s disease and amlodipine for management of blood pressure. Other history of note includes episodes of incontinence. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 145/72 mmHg, with no signiﬁcant postural drop. His pulse is 80 bpm and regular. Respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. He has cogwheeling and a tremor, worse on the right than on the left, and a festinant gait. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.7×109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 303×109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Computed tomography (CT) head: Generalised atrophy consistent with his age. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Lewy body dementia The symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, coupled with the development of ﬂorid hallucinations on uptitration of dopaminergic medication, are typical of Lewy body dementia. Treatment is difﬁcult as patients often require relatively high doses of anti-parkinsonian medication to enable movement, although this can drive signiﬁcantly worsening confusion and hallucinations. Typical antipsychotics should be avoided, and data on atypical antipsychotics are conﬂicting with respect to tolerability, although risperidone and olanzapine are both used as options when intervention is required. A Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is seen primarily in overweight women and is classically associated with headaches and visual disturbances. Patients often have papilloedema on fundoscopy. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed on assessing a patient’s opening pressure while performing a lumbar puncture. C Multi-infarct dementia Multi-infarct dementia is not associated with parkinsonian symptoms. It is caused by a number of small infarctions that cause a stepwise deterioration in brain function. Treatments involve

modifying ongoing vascular risk factors and use of memantine. D Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) NPH is an abnormal build-up of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) in the cerebral ventricles or cavities. Patients usually present with an apraxic gait, cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence. The gait deﬁcit is usually responsive to CSF drainage. E Progressive supranuclear palsy Progressive supranuclear palsy is characterised by less marked symptoms of parkinsonism than those reported here, features of dementia, loss of upward gaze and autonomic neuropathy. It is one of the ‘Parkinson plus’ syndromes.

stem: A 29-year-old woman from Malawi is admitted with a 2-week history of weight loss, fever, difﬁculty walking and abnormal speech. In the Accident and Emergency Department she is witnessed to have a focal seizure involving her right arm and right leg. On examination, she has mild right-sided weakness, ataxia and dysphasia. A CT brain scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres. An HIV antibody test is positive. An MRI brain scan conﬁrms bilateral cerebral and cerebellar ring-enhancing lesions. CSF ﬁndings are unremarkable. The images above shows the ﬁndings from a CT brain scan (A) with contrast and a T2-weighted MRI brain scan (B). Which drugs would be included in empirical therapy for this condition?
explanation:
C Sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine and folinic acid

The likely diagnosis in the setting of HIV infection is cerebral toxoplasmosis. This presents in the setting of advanced immunosuppression, but is still seen as a ﬁrst presentation of HIV infection. The most common presenting symptoms are fever, focal neurological symptoms and seizures. Patients are nearly always seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii, so negative serology should suggest an alternative diagnosis. Imaging studies characteristically show multiple ring-enhancing lesions. The main differential diagnoses are primary cerebral lymphoma, tuberculosis, cryptococcal disease and progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy (PML). Often, empirical therapy for toxoplasmosis is started on the basis of ﬁndings from imaging studies, and therapy should result in radiological improvement within 2–3 weeks. The initial treatment of choice is sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid. If there is no improvement, then brain biopsy is indicated. Steroids are often used if there is signiﬁcant oedema or mass effect, but there is no evidence for their use otherwise. B Ceftriaxone and amphotericin B This would cover bacterial infection and also fungal infections such as Cryptococcus. The multiple ring- enhancing lesions favour toxoplasmosis. A Dexamethasone and ceftriaxone This is the treatment for suspected pneumococcal meningitis, but the ring-enhancing lesions seen here suggest toxoplasmosis. D Foscarnet and ganciclovir This is the treatment for CMV encephalitis. The presentation with seizures and the ring-enhancing lesions on MRI make CMV less likely. E Aciclovir This is the treatment for herpes simplex encephalitis. Whilst this can present with seizures, the 2-week prodrome and imaging ﬁndings make this an unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden-onset left-sided hemiparesis left facial weakness and leftsided limb twitching. In the ED she was noted to be drowsy. Prior to the event, she had been out shopping with her sister when she had started to develop one of her migraine attacks and vomiting. Her past medical history included troublesome migraine with aura, for which she was taking pizotifen and sumatriptan, and impaired glucose tolerance diagnosed several years ago. She had recently visited her general practitioner (GP), complaining of progressive weakness in her legs. On examination, she had short stature and was initially drowsy, but easily rousable. Her temperature was 37.3 ºC, blood pressure 135/75 mmHg, pulse 88/min and body mass index 21.2. There was evidence of a left UMN (upper motor neuron) facial weakness. Fundoscopy was normal. On examination of the limbs, there was evidence of proximal muscle weakness of the legs and arms, and associated left-sided pyramidal tract signs: all left-sided reﬂexes were pathologically brisk and the left plantar response was extensor. There was no myoclonus. She was investigated with blood tests and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)/MRV (MR venogram) brain scan. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 125 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 245 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Glucose 11.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.4 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 128 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lactate 3.0 mmol/l 0.5–2.2 mmol/l MRI brain scan showed several areas of cortical high signal intensity abnormality on T2-weighted imaging, particularly in the occipital lobes. No intracranial haemorrhage or space-occupying lesion was detected. MRV was normal. In light of the current ﬁndings, what is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
options: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes)
CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leucoencephalopathy
explanation:
C MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes) This patient presents with a typical history for MELAS. Clues to the diagnosis include history of migraine, glucose intolerance, short stature, proximal myopathy and the current stroke-like event with seizure activity. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows multiple cortical lesions, which do not respect vascular territories. The diagnosis can be conﬁrmed with mitochondrial DNA genetic analysis. B Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) It is an important differential diagnosis in a young patient presenting with stroke and seizures. However, one would expect to ﬁnd a ﬁlling defect on MRI and MRV (MR venogram) imaging in this patient. A Hemiplegic migraine Whilst this could account for the acute event, this diagnosis cannot explain all the other important points in the history and examination.

D Right anterior circulation infarct This could produce a left hemiparesis but cannot account for the other features described in the case. In addition, the MRI changes do not suggest this diagnosis. E CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leucoencephalopathy CADASIL, which causes strokes in young migraineurs, is not associated with myopathy and does not cause a high lactate. Mutations in the NOTCH 3 gene can be found and support the diagnosis.

stem: A 32-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of progressive weakness. Initially, he developed a foot drop on the right and some weakness of hand grip on the left, but over the next few days this progressed to weakness of all four limbs. He had just come back from a three-week holiday to Spain where he had spent the ﬁrst few days in bed with a cough and feeling generally unwell. On examination, there was weakness, decreased tone and areﬂexia in all four limbs. Plantar responses were downgoing. Cranial nerves, coordination and sensation were normal. Which one of the following is the most useful investigation in making a diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
D Lumbar puncture The likely diagnosis in this case is Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), as evidenced by the acute onset of rapidly progressive lower motor neurone pattern of weakness and the history of prodromal illness. Lumbar puncture is important in the diagnosis of this condition as it can be used to exclude other potential causes of similar presentations, such as infection or malignancy. A raised protein count and normal white cell count in the CSF are characteristic ﬁndings in GBS. In almost 70% of cases there is a prodromal infection, with the most common types being Campylobacter jejuni, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus. In a number of cases, anti-ganglioside antibodies are found (particularly GM1, and in the Miller–Fisher variant GQ1b). Treatment is usually with intravenous immunoglobulins and supportive interventions, including monitoring of respiratory function, prophylactic anticoagulation and monitoring for cardiac arrhythmias. Early and regular measurement of forced vital capacity (FVC) is extremely important, and any suggestion of low or decreasing vital capacity requires immediate intensive care team involvement. A Atypical pneumonia serology This would not help to arrive at a diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome in this case. Although infection with atypical pathogens can precipitate the development of GBS, a positive result would not conﬁrm the diagnosis.

B Serum immunoglobulins Although serum immunoglobulins may be raised in Guillain–Barré syndrome, this is not a response that is speciﬁc to this condition. Raised serum immunoglobulins may be seen in response to a range of different infections, and therefore this does not help conﬁrm the diagnosis in this case. C CT of the whole spine This investigation would not help make a diagnosis of Guillain– Barré syndrome. CT of the spine is useful to identify bony abnormalities such as fractures or bony lesions. The ﬁndings in this case could not be attributed to a spinal or central cause of weakness as the examination ﬁndings are in keeping with a lower motor neurone distribution. E Serum creatinine kinase This investigation would not help make a diagnosis of Guillain– Barré syndrome. This investigation would be useful in the diagnosis of inﬂammatory myopathies such as polymyositis or dermatomyositis, which do present with weakness but with reﬂexes preserved.

stem: A 26-year-old man recently arrived in the UK from New York, attends the Accident and Emergency Department. He has a past history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. He describes a few days of fever, headache and myalgia. Admission was prompted by worsening headache and back pain. While waiting in the medical receiving unit he becomes progressively drowsier. Examination revealed ﬂaccid paralysis and depressed tendon reﬂexes. He was reviewed by the intensive care team and arrangements were made for ventilation. A computerised tomography (CT) brain is performed, that is normal. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid examination reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Protein 0.9 g/l () < 0.45 g/l Glucose 4 mmol/l 2.5–3.9 mmol/l WCC 230/mm3 (mostly lymphocytes) < 5/mm3 Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 150 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets (PLT) 600 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l WCC 12.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 7.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 6.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l What is the most likely infective process?
explanation: B West Nile disease West Nile virus (WNV) is a single-stranded RNA ﬂavivirus transmitted via the culex mosquito. This previously ‘tropical’ disease has become topical in recent years following a large-scale outbreak in the New York area. The virus has spread rapidly, with reports of infection across the continent. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), over 15,000 people in the US have tested positive for WNV infection since 1999. To date there have been over 500 deaths; recent hurricanes and subsequent damage to water infrastructure may increase these numbers. The number of subclinical or mild infections not presenting to hospital is likely to be much higher still. Incidence of neurological involvement is usually quoted at around 1%, although some suggest that the incidence of meningoencephalitis in the USA is higher than in other parts of the world. Risk factors for neurological involvement include increasing age, and any form of immunosuppression. The usual picture is of sudden-onset fever and myalgia with nausea and vomiting and a non-speciﬁc rash. Transient meningitis is occasionally seen. Frank meningoencephalitis is seen in two-thirds of cases with neurological involvement; 15% progress to coma. A ﬂaccid paralysis similar to acute Guillain–Barré is increasingly recognised. Diagnosis is initially clinical with subsequent serological conﬁrmation. Treatment is supportive; results from trials of antivirals have yielded disappointing results. C Human immunodeﬁciency virus HIV is unlikely given the short history of illness and no signiﬁcant prodrome. A Lyme disease Lyme disease is associated with a tick bite, and we’re given no evidence to support exposure to a tick such as an eschar or erythema chronicum migrans. As well as encephalitis, mononeuritis and heart block are possible features. D Tuberculosis TB meningitis is lymphocytic, and the absence of chest symptoms or other features such as chronic night sweats counts against TB infection. E Lassa fever Lassa is acute viral haemorrhagic fever, and is endemic amongst the rodent population of West Africa. Ribavirin, if given early enough, may be an effective intervention.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of headache and neck pain. She says it started on waking 12 hours ago and the pain has become unbearable now. She gives no history of trauma. There is no signiﬁcant past medical or family history. On examination, her blood pressure is 138/84 mmHg and her heart rate is 84 bpm and regular. Neurological examination reveals rightsided pronator drift but no other focal neurology in the limbs.
explanation:
D Initiate dual antiplatelet therapy This patient has presented with acute symptom onset of severe headache and neck pain. In addition, there is left-sided ptosis and miosis (note the unequal pupils on the patient), raising suspicion of Horner syndrome. This combination of signs and symptoms makes the diagnosis of spontaneous carotid artery dissection likely. In such patients in whom the bleeding risk is minimal (small/no infarct), prompt initiation of anticoagulation to decrease the risk of stroke is recommended. Note that Horner syndrome in carotid artery dissection is partial and not complete, ie only ptosis and miosis are present, but not anhidrosis. In these patients, Horner syndrome is indicative of pressure over the cervical sympathetic ﬁbres, rather than ischaemia. The right-sided pronator drift may be a consequence of a secondary infarction. This patient should be investigated with an MRI brain scan. Treatment of patients where an ischaemic stroke is suspected can include thrombolysis and thrombectomy if the patient presents within the appropriate time windows (4.5 hours and 6 hours respectively). In patients who present later, as in this case, with extracranial dissection and a suspected stroke, antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation is indicated for a time period of usually 6 months, dependent on follow up imaging. Antiplatelets are usually initiated as a dual antiplatelet regimen (loading doses of 300mg of aspirin and clopidogrel followed by 75mg of each, daily) for 21 days, followed by long term clopidogrel monotherapy (75mg). C Endovascular stenting There is no role for endovascular stenting in patients with carotid

artery dissection and may result in propagation of any clot which forms around the area of dissection. It may be performed in patients with carotid artery stenosis. A Analgesic therapy with indomethacin Whilst appropriate analgesia is indicated, non-steroidal analgesics, except aspirin, lead to an increased risk of stroke and should therefore be avoided in carotid artery dissection. Here paracetamol and potentially opiate based analgesia, such as codeine, would be preferable. B Carotid endarterectomy Carotid endarterectomy has no role in carotid artery dissection and may result in propagation of any clot which forms around the area of dissection. It may be performed in patients with carotid artery stenosis. E Reperfusion with alteplase Patients with acute ischaemic symptoms may be candidates for reperfusion therapy. It is not indicated in this patient due to the presentation some 12 hours after symptom onset. When used outside of the licenced window (4.5 hours) the beneﬁt is outweighed by the risk of haemorrhage.

stem: A 48-year-old man has been seen in Emergency Department (ED) by the orthopaedic team with a suspected disc prolapse. He presented to his GP with stiffness and weakness in both legs, which developed over the last week. He has started to develop difﬁculty passing urine over the last 12 hours. He has long-standing back pain. There is no other medical history. When seen in ED he is able to walk, although he has a stiff-legged gait. Tone is increased in both legs. Power is 4±5 with pathologically brisk reﬂexes and sustained beats of clonus at both ankles. The plantars are up-going bilaterally. There is decreased soft touch sensation until a level around the umbilicus. There are no neurological abnormalities in the arms. The cranial nerve examination is also normal. The orthopaedic registrar reviewed the patient earlier in the day and requested urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine. This was reviewed by the radiologist and was reported as showing no structural lesions. The scan shows from the T9 vertebrae down to the sacral area. The orthopaedic registrar feels that this is not a surgical problem and wonders whether it might be multiple sclerosis. He asks you, the medical registrar, what you would like to do with the patient. You examine the patient and agree with the physical signs. What are you going to suggest?
options: Admission to a medical bed overnight pending neurology review
MRI of the entire thoracic spine
Urgent MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine
Catheterise and discharge with urgent neurological outpatient appointment
explanation:
D Urgent MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine This man’s syndrome, with spastic paraparesis and urinary symptoms, is a medical/surgical emergency. Although the examination suggests a level at around T10, it must be remembered that these levels can be misleading. In particular, the lesion can be several levels higher than the sensory signs suggest and any delay in identifying and treating a structural problem could result in permanent neurological deﬁcit, impotence and incontinence. C Urgent nerve conduction studies The examination ﬁndings clearly indicate an upper motor neuron lesion, so neurophysiology will not be helpful. A Admission to a medical bed overnight pending neurology review This case is an emergency and the patient requires MRI of the spine to exclude a treatable compressive lesion. B MRI of the entire thoracic spine

This is a reasonable suggestion and would likely identify the problem. However, with acute myelopathic conditions in the cervical area, the signs in the arms can occasionally be very subtle (perhaps just inverted supinator reﬂexes), so in this situation it is best to be cautious and image cervical and thoracic segments. E Catheterise and discharge with urgent neurological outpatient appointment This would be medically negligent as the case described is an emergency and the patient requires MRI of the spine to exclude a treatable compressive lesion

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department for review. He complains of global weakness and feels unable to walk. He says the weakness came on suddenly around two hours after he had returned home from a run. He reports a similar episode some two weeks earlier following a run which resolved spontaneously. He has no past medical history of note. Apparently, after his ﬁrst run, he reports an urticarial rash on his legs which lasted for a few hours. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg; pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. He has a marked 3/5 proximal myopathy affecting his hip ﬂexors. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.0 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis

Intermittent weakness a few hours after exercise is classical of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis. At the time of symptoms, blood tests indicating hypokalaemia are very helpful in conﬁrming the underlying disease process. Potassium supplementation is the ﬁrstline treatment for patients suffering frequent attacks. Alternative options would be acetazolamide or potassium-sparing diuretics, such as spironolactone. A Acid maltase deﬁciency Acid maltase deﬁciency is associated with proximal muscle weakness from childhood. Therefore, this diagnosis is unlikely in this case. C Insulinoma While hyperinsulinaemia may play a role in the pathogenesis of hypokalaemia periodic paralysis, an insulinoma is very unlikely to be the diagnosis given that the weakness occurred straight after exercise. Typically, a patient cannot point toward a speciﬁc situation in which weakness occurs in an insulinoma due to the sporadic secretion of insulin. D Myasthenia gravis There is no other feature of proximal muscle weakness seen in this scenario to suggest myasthenia gravis. Given the intermittent nature of the weakness after exercise, coupled with the fact that it resolves, further makes this diagnosis seem unlikely. E Thyrotoxicosis Although thyrotoxicosis should be screened for, there are no symptoms suggestive of thyrotoxicosis in this patient’s presentation. There are forms of periodic paralysis related to thyrotoxicosis and these should always be screened for in patients who present with periodic paralysis.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with increasing weakness. She consulted her general practitioner (GP) 4 days earlier, unable to get out of a chair. Her husband has brought her to the Emergency Department as she is choking when she eats and seems only able to mumble sounds. On examination, there appears to be global weakness with absent reﬂexes bilaterally. On further questioning, there is a history of recent food poisoning around three weeks ago. Electrophysiological studies show evidence of conduction block at multiple sites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) GBS is an acute inﬂammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy, which may follow Campylobacter infection. Nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction velocity and conduction block due to impaired transmission along demyelinated nerves. E Botulism Botulism and other neuromuscular junction disorders, such as myasthenia gravis, are key differentials when considering a patient with an acute ﬂaccid paralysis. There is a history of ‘food poisoning’ in this case, but the onset of food-borne botulism is usually within 48 h of exposure. Furthermore, the ﬁnding of conduction block on neurophysiology is typical of peripheral nerve demyelination, rather than dysfunction of the neuromuscular junction. A Motor neurone disease (MND) The evolution of symptoms is too rapid for motor neurone disease, which usually evolves over a period of many months. B Multiple sclerosis (MS) As MS is a disease of the central nervous system, one would expect to see upper motor neurone signs. These are not present in this case. D Poliomyelitis Polio is very rare in the developed world. Furthermore, it would be very unusual for polio to evolve so rapidly and involve the nervous system so diffusely.

stem: A 20-year-old patient is referred to the tertiary Neurology Clinic because of a possible diagnosis of juvenile Parkinson’s disease. His symptoms began predominantly with dystonia affecting the lower limbs, but he now has more classical signs of Parkinson’s disease including tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity. You map out his family tree and understand that one of his two sisters developed Parkinson’s at the age of 16, but that his parents do not have signs of Parkinson’s. Which of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance?
explanation:
Autosomal recessive
This option is correct because in autosomal recessive inheritance, both parents can be carriers of a single copy of the mutated gene without showing any symptoms. Each child has a 25% chance of inheriting two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) and, therefore, expressing the disease. The described scenario where two out of three siblings have the condition fits within the statistical framework of autosomal recessive inheritance. The lack of symptoms in the parents aligns with this mode of inheritance, as carriers do not show the disease.

Autosomal dominant
This option is incorrect because if the condition were autosomal dominant, we would expect one of the parents to be affected since only one copy of the mutated gene is necessary for the condition to manifest. In an autosomal dominant pattern, there would typically be a 50% chance of passing the condition to offspring if one parent is affected. The absence of symptoms in both parents argues strongly against an autosomal dominant inheritance. Therefore, the lack of disease in the parents does not support this mode of inheritance.

Autosomal dominant with genetic anticipation
Autosomal dominant with genetic anticipation is incorrect. Although one might hypothesise that this could be because of autosomal dominant inheritance with genetic anticipation (i.e. the parents do in fact have very mild disease, compared to the patient’s obvious disease), this is less likely than the pattern observed being reflective of an autosomal recessive disease.

Autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance
This option is incorrect because, in autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance, some individuals who carry the dominant gene may not express the disease at all, even though they can pass the gene to their offspring. However, in such cases, we would still typically expect to see the condition manifesting in at least one of the parents or more extended family members with varying degrees of severity. The complete absence of symptoms in both parents makes this explanation less likely. The given family history, where both parents are asymptomatic and two out of three siblings are affected, is more consistent with an autosomal recessive pattern.

X-linked
This option is incorrect for several reasons. In X-linked recessive inheritance, males are more often affected because they have only one X chromosome, which they inherit from their mother. Females would require two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) to manifest the disease, which is less common. Since the patient’s sister is affected while neither parent shows symptoms, this pattern does not support an X-linked mode of inheritance. X-linked conditions also tend to show a distinct pattern where male offspring of carrier mothers are primarily affected, which is not observed in this scenario. Parkinsonism and Parkinson’s.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of confusion and dizziness. On the way to the hospital, she fell onto the footpath twice and has now signiﬁcantly bruised her left knee. Her past medical history includes Crohn’s disease for which she had a terminal ileal resection six weeks ago and epilepsy, for which she takes phenytoin. She denies smoking or alcohol use. On examination, she is confused with a GCS score of 14 (E4V4M6). Her temperature is 36.5 °C, her heart rate is 90 bpm and regular and her BP is 110/65mmHg. Auscultation of the chest sounds clear and her abdomen is soft. She has horizontal-gaze-evoked nystagmus. Her BMI is 17 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 110 g/l 115–155 g/l Mean cell volume (MCV) 71 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ WCC 10.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 3.0 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 46 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected calcium 1.9 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l Phosphate 0.4 mmol/l 0.8–1.5 mmol/l Magnesium 0.60 mmol/l 0.85–1.10 mmol/l Albumin 18 g/l 34–54 g/l CRP 3.5 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Wernicke’s encephalopathy This patient has features of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, including horizontal-gaze-evoked nystagmus, ataxia (suggested by recurrent falls) and confusion. Classically, Wernicke’s encephalopathy is characterised as being secondary to excessive alcohol intake. However, there are multiple causes including malnutrition (eg secondary to recent gastrointestinal surgery or poor oral intake). The globally low electrolyte levels, anaemia, low MCV and hypoalbuminaemia in association with a BMI of 17 kg/m2 are all suggestive of malnutrition that is likely to be the precipitant of this patient’s presentation. B Miller–Fisher syndrome Miller–Fisher syndrome is a rare neurological disease with similar features to Guillain–Barré syndrome. The onset of symptoms typically follows a viral illness, and features include ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areﬂexia. However, confusion and cognitive impairment are rarely seen and suggest an alternative diagnosis. A Acute encephalitis Acute encephalitis is a reasonable differential diagnosis given the confusion and neurological features. However, the normal inﬂammatory markers and lack of fever make encephalitis a less likely diagnosis. C Normal-pressure hydrocephalus Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by ataxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment. It is more common in the older population and is associated with diabetes mellitus and vascular disease. It does not explain the nystagmus. D Phenytoin overdose Phenytoin toxicity is an important differential diagnosis to consider and the features of toxicity are very similar to other causes of encephalopathy. It presents with ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, cognitive dysfunction and nystagmus. In severe cases, phenytoin toxicity can cause life-threatening arrhythmias and seizures and

coma. However, the blood results indicate either an inadequate intake or inadequate absorption of nutrition. This, combined with the lack of cardiovascular signs or symptoms, make an alternative diagnosis like Wernicke’s encephalopathy more likely.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-week history of increasing headaches, which have become dramatically worse over the past 10 days. She describes a constant pain behind her eyes that is unrelieved by paracetamol. Initially, the headaches would only appear in the morning, but now they are constant throughout the day. She has also noticed that her vision becomes occasionally blurred when she gets up in the mornings. She has been feeling much more tired during the day for the past month, but attributes this to poor sleeping due to her headache. Her boyfriend feels that she is depressed. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history of note, and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. She smokes 20 cigarettes per day, and drinks 12 units of alcohol per week. On examination, she is tearful. Her body mass index (BMI) is 31 kg/m2. Her temperature is 36.8 °C. There is no obvious neck rigidity. Her pulse is 70 bpm, regular, and jugular venous pressure and heart sounds are normal. Her blood pressure is 126/76 mmHg. Respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Her fundoscopic appearance of the right eye is shown below, the left eye was similar. The remainder of the neurological examination was unremarkable. CT head is reported as normal. Which investigation would be most useful in guiding treatment?
explanation:
E Lumbar puncture This patient likely has idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The term ‘idiopathic’ is now preferred to ‘benign’, as the clinical course may have signiﬁcant morbidity. There is raised intracranial pressure in the absence of a mass lesion or hydrocephalus. Incidence is 1/100 000, with a female preponderance (F:M 3.8:1). Up to 90% of patients are overweight. Other risk factors include smoking and oral contraceptive pill use. Symptoms include headaches which are worse in the mornings, and with coughing or straining. This is attributable to the raised intracranial pressure. Other symptoms include blurred vision, scotomata and horizontal diplopia. The commonest sign is papilloedema. Lumbar puncture is required to demonstrate an elevated opening pressure and to exclude chronic meningitic illnesses that could mimic this presentation. Magnetic resonance venography is important in excluding venous sinus thrombosis as a secondary cause of raised pressure. Treatment includes weight loss if the patient is obese; intracranial pressure may be controlled by serial lumbar puncture. Drugs that may be successful include acetazolamide and thiazide diuretics. Visual loss is the single most threatening complication of idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and treatment is with urgent largevolume lumbar puncture, followed by shunting if required. Optic nerve fenestration is an alternative, although there are no comparative studies between the two interventions. D Overnight pulse oximetry Nocturnal hypoxia and hypercapnia can cause headache, but the features seen here are suggestive of raised ICP and so lumbar

puncture is required. A Electroencephalogram (EEG) EEG is useful in the investigation of epilepsy (especially primary generalised epilepsy) and encephalopathy, but there would be no indication for it here. B Visual evoked potentials This test can be used to assess causes of visual failure, particularly if one is trying to demonstrate optic neuropathy. C Thyroid function tests Whilst this patient does have some non-speciﬁc general symptoms that could be compatible with hypothyroidism, the headache and papilloedema suggest that raised intracranial pressure is the issue that needs to be addressed.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the GP surgery complaining of a general feeling of weakness. He says that he has also noticed that towards the evenings his eyelids begin to droop. On clinical examination, you are able to demonstrate fatiguability. There is no muscle tenderness and no rashes on examination of his skin. His blood pressure is 128/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular and his BMI is 28. Which of one the following may be associated with his neurological condition?
explanation: C Hypothyroidism The hallmark of myasthenia gravis is fatiguable weakness. The disease tends to affect two age groups, with one peak in the second and third decade, which usually affects women, and a second peak in the sixth and seventh decade, usually affecting men. The following muscle groups are commonly affected, in decreasing order of likelihood: extra-ocular, bulbar, face, neck, limb girdle, distal limbs and trunk. Treatment modalities include the use of the cholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine for symptom control, immunosuppression with prednisolone and azathioprine for longerterm maintenance. Disorders associated with myasthenia include: thyrotoxicosis, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes mellitus, dermatomyositis, pernicious anaemia and thymic tumour. E Orofacial dyskinesia Orofacial or tardive dyskinesias are involuntary repetitive movements of the mouth and face. In most cases, these occur following long-term treatment with antipsychotic drugs. This is not associated with myasthenia gravis. A Diabetes insipidus Diabetes insipidus is a condition characterised by large amounts of dilute urine and increased thirst due to ADH deﬁciency or lack of response to ADH. This is not associated with myasthenia gravis. B Friedrich’s ataxia Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal recessive inherited disease that causes progressive damage to the nervous system. It manifests in initial symptoms of poor coordination, such as gait disturbance; it can also lead to scoliosis, heart disease and diabetes, but does not affect cognitive function. This is not associated with myasthenia gravis. D Myotonia congenita Myotonia congenita is a congenital neuromuscular channelopathy that affects skeletal muscles. It is a genetic disorder. The hallmark of the disease is the failure of initiated contraction to terminate, often referred to as delayed relaxation of the muscles (myotonia) and rigidity. This is not associated with myasthenia gravis.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful long term intervention?
explanation:
Diet and exercise
The diagnosis here is idiopathic intracranial hypertension with a severe headache and papilloedema indicating raised intracranial pressure. Given her, BMI is 35 and fasting glucose is 6.0, the most appropriate intervention is weight loss. In the event that she is unable to lose weight with diet and exercise alone, both liraglutide and referral for surgery are potential options.

Acetazolamide
Acetazolamide is incorrect. Acetazolamide is the most effective diuretic option, although it is poorly tolerated due to symptoms of GORD in a large number of cases, and doesn’t impact on BMI.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide is less effective than acetazolamide in controlling intracranial pressure, and has a negative impact on glucose tolerance.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. This has a modest impact on blood glucose and weight and is inferior to a structured diet and exercise program.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Prednisolone can be considered as an acute intervention but is ineffective over the longer term.

stem: A 59-year-old man has shown a change in his mood and personality over a 9-month period. He has subsequently developed difficulty with memory and concentration, and then progressive ‘fidgety’ movements of his limbs and facial musculature. By the time of medical assessment he has frank choreiform movements and a Mini-Mental State Examination of 21/30. Other examination is normal. He was adopted and therefore no information on his family history is available. He has three adult children (aged 27, 30 and 33 years) of whom the two youngest are asymptomatic. However, the oldest son has recently been investigated by the Neurology Department for slightly erratic behaviour and fidgety restless movements of both legs. Based on the likely clinical diagnosis, which one of the following genetic patterns of this condition is most likely?
explanation:
Autosomal-dominant inheritance with anticipation
The clinical scenario is that of Huntington’s disease. This is often characterised by slowly progressive subcortical dementia with early personality changes (irritability, disinhibition) followed by the onset of a progressive choreiform movement disorder. However the disease is heterogeneous, with some patients presenting with a circumscribed movement disorder of chorea or, in some early onset forms, Parkinsonism. Age of onset is very variable, with both juvenile forms (< 25 years) and late-onset forms existing, but most patients present at around 35–45 years of age. It has an autosomal-dominant mode of inheritance and is one of the trinucleotide-repeat disorders (CAG repeat, on the ‘huntingtin’ gene, chromosome 4p16.3). Increasing repeat length in offspring gives rise to the phenomenon of anticipation (clinical onset at an earlier age in subsequent generations). Thus autosomal-dominant inheritance with anticipation is correct.

Autosomal-dominant with variable penetrance
Autosomal-dominant with variable penetrance is incorrect. Autosomal-dominant with variable penetrance could potentially explain the inheritance pattern described in this case, but in light of the clinical information suggestive of Huntington’s disease, autosomal-dominant inheritance with anticipation is a better choice.

Autosomal-recessive inheritance
Autosomal-recessive inheritance is incorrect. With autosomal-recessive inheritance one would not expect transmission from affected parent to affected offspring.

Mitochondrial disorder
Mitochondrial disorder is incorrect. With mitochondrial disease one usually sees maternal transmission (with mitochondrial DNA being inherited via the ovum only), but some mitochondrial disease can be transmitted in an autosomal-dominant or recessive manner due to somatic mutations in nuclear genes that encode proteins involved in mitochondrial pathways (eg POLG1).

X-linked inheritance.

stem: A 74-year-old diabetic male presents to the clinic. He has had type 1 diabetes controlled with insulin for the past 60 years. He gives a history of transient left-sided facial weakness, which recovered spontaneously after two weeks. He previously presented three months earlier with a left common peroneal nerve palsy leading to motor and sensory loss. Again this recovered spontaneously after three to four weeks. On examination his BP is 110/70 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. There is peripheral sensory loss affecting both feet. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mononeuritis multiplex
Two discrete incidents of neuropathy, accompanied by gradual recovery and affecting both sensory and motor function in the case of the common peroneal nerve palsy, fit best with a diagnosis of mononeuritis. Ensuring tight glucose control may reduce the risk of future episodes occurring.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. The presence of sensory symptoms rules out motor neurone disease, as this affects motor neurones only.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis is more usually associated with focal neurological signs and focal areas of demyelination, and predominantly upper motor neurone signs on examination. Although it can affect any age, it is most commonly diagnosed in those between 15 and 60 years old.

Churg Strauss syndrome
Churg-Strauss syndrome is incorrect. Churg-Strauss would be highly unusual without symptoms of asthma.

Multiple TIAs
Multiple transcient ischemic attacks (TIAs) is incorrect. The normal blood pressure, duration of symptoms and isolated nerve involvement goes against a diagnosis of TIAs. TIAs are cerebrovascular events that last less than 24 h. Mononeuropathies A 19-year-old college student is noted by her flatmate to seem confused. She has been complaining of a diffuse headache and general malaise for the past 24 hours. On examination she has a temperature of 38 °C. She is restless and mildly dysphasic. The remainder of the general and neurological examination is normal. CT brain scan shows hypodensity in both temporal lobes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination shows a white cell count of 16/mm 3 (lymphocytes), a slightly raised protein concentration of 0.75 g/l and a normal CSF/blood glucose ratio.

stem: A 36-year-old painter and decorator presents with sudden-onset back pain. He was sitting on the ﬂoor painting a fence when he realised after some time that he was unable to get up. On examination, he has bilateral leg weakness with lower limb hyporeﬂexia. He has pinprick sensory loss to the level of the umbilicus. Vibration sense is clearly present at the knee. He is in urinary retention. Past medical history of note includes hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily. Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Anterior spinal cord syndrome This artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. Symptoms occur because there is complete motor paralysis below the level of the lesion due to interruption of the corticospinal tract. There is loss of pain sensation below the level of the lesion due to interruption of the spinothalamic tract.
