There is, however, relatively good preservation of vibration sense due to intact dorsal column function.

D Guillain–Barré syndrome This usually presents with ascending weakness beginning in the lower limbs, with sensory loss and neuropathic pain. Onset is usually approximately 3 weeks after a viral illness. B Cervical cord compression Cervical cord compression is essentially ruled out because of the sensory level at the umbilicus. C Transverse myelitis This occurs against a background of inﬂammatory disease (i.e. multiple sclerosis) or due to infection. The very sudden onset in this case favours an acute vascular cause. E Miller Fisher syndrome This condition typically leads to a triad of weakness of the eye muscles, abnormalities of coordination and absent reﬂexes. It is a variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of diplopia, difficulty with swallowing and unsteadiness. He had an upper respiratory tract infection three weeks ago. He is otherwise fit and well. On examination, there is bilateral partial ptosis, complete ophthalmoplegia, areflexia and gait ataxia. Sensory examination reveals reduced vibration sensation to the knees bilaterally and absent right ankle reflex, including with a reinforcement manoeuvre. Given the most likely clinical diagnosis, which of the following investigations should be completed before deciding on the treatment modality?
explanation:
Immunoglobulin A levels
It is important to check IgA levels before starting immunoglobulin therapy for the likely diagnosis of Miller– Fisher syndrome: a Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) variant. It presents with a triad of ophthalmoplegia, areflexia and ataxia. It may follow gastroenteritis or an upper respiratory tract infection. The Brighton criteria can be used to determine the diagnostic certainty for GBS and its variants. The treatment of choice for severe cases is either intravenous (IV) immunoglobulins or plasma exchange; there is no current significant difference between the two. However, anaphylaxis with immunoglobulins is significantly increased in those with immunoglobulin A deficiency. Immunoglobulin A levels should be checked before starting treatment. Miller–Fisher syndrome does not always require IV immunoglobulins. The patient in this case, however, has bulbar involvement, as indicated by his difficulty with swallowing.

Cerebrospinal fluid glucose concentration
A cerebrospinal fluid cell count of < 50/μl and a cerebrospinal fluid protein concentration greater than the reference range are both indicative of Guillain-Barré syndrome/Miller Fisher syndrome.

Immunoglobulin G levels
It is important to check immunoglobulin A, not immunoglobulin G, levels before starting immunoglobulin therapy for Miller–Fisher syndrome.

Magnetic resonance imaging head
It is important to consider alternative causes of the presenting symptoms. The patient’s clinical picture and examination findings indicate a severe form of Miller–Fisher syndrome requiring intervention and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is unlikely to provide any additional information.

Nerve conduction studies
Nerve conduction studies are part of the Brighton criteria for diagnosing Guillain–Barré syndrome or Miller– Fisher syndrome and can provide key diagnostic information in confirming the diagnosis. As a likely diagnosis of Miller–Fisher syndrome has been made, this is unlikely to change treatment modality at this stage.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressively worsening double vision over several weeks. He has also suffered a boring pain behind his eye, and loss of sensation to light touch over the left side of his face. On examination, he appears to have almost complete ophthalmoplegia of his left eye, with a left ptosis and dilated, poorly reactive, left pupil. There is reduced pinprick over the left forehead. His right eye movements are normal, as is the remainder of the neurological examination. His ESR is 80 mm/1st hour and he has a normochromic normocytic anaemia. Given the cranial nerves involved, where is the likely lesion?
explanation:
Left cavernous sinus
Tolosa–Hunt syndrome (THS) is caused by a granulomatous inflammatory process that involves the anterior cavernous sinus/superior orbital fissure region. This is associated with lesions of cranial nerves III, IV, VI and the first (ophthalmic) division of V, and seems to be the likely diagnosis here. However, any lesion in the left cavernous sinus needs to be considered in a case like this. A cavernous sinus syndrome can also occur because of aneurysms or thrombosis of the cavernous sinus, or following invasive tumour spread from the sella turcica or from within the sinus.

Frontal sinus
Frontal sinus with Frontal sinus is incorrect. A lesion in the frontal sinus will not produce these multiple cranialChat neuropathies.

Left lateral pons
Left lateral pons is incorrect. A left lateral pontine lesion might result in loss of facial pain and temperature sensation ipsilateral to the lesion but also loss of sensation (pain and temperature) in the contralateral limbs. In addition, there may be ipsilateral facial weakness, ipsilateral deafness and ipsilateral ataxia. Oculoparesis is not seen.

Left medial pons
Left medial pons is incorrect. A left medial pontine lesion may cause an ipsilateral facial weakness and contralateral limb weakness. There is weakness of abduction in the ipsilateral eye, but other extra-ocular movements are spared. Cavernous Sinus SyndromeA 58-year-old man with a history of multiple sclerosis presents with horizontal diplopia. Clinically, the diplopia is most apparent while looking to the left. The outer image disappears when the right eye is occluded. On examination he has weakness of adduction of the right eye and nystagmus on attempted lateral gaze to either side, worse on looking to the left.

Left retro-orbital space
Left retro-orbital space is incorrect. A lesion in the left retro-orbital space may produce oculoparesis but cannot explain the sensory loss.

stem: A 56-year-old woman has a history of headaches occurring on average 4–8 times per month, sometimes in clusters. They are left-sided and associated with nausea and photophobia. Sometimes she has associated tingling and clumsiness of her right hand for a few hours. They are increasingly disabling, to the extent that she has had to phone in sick to work on the last six occasions. She tends to take paracetamol and metoclopramide in combination, and in fact takes this up to ten times a week when she is going through a ‘bad spell’. She previously tried sumatriptan but found that this made her feel dizzy. She has a past history of asthma and is on hormone replacement therapy. Which treatment would be most appropriate to recommend at this stage?
options: Acute treatment with a different triptan, eg naratriptan
Acute treatment with codeine and domperidone
explanation:
Prophylactic treatment with topiramate
Topiramate is an anticonvulsant that has been shown to be effective in reducing the frequency and severity of migraines. Given the patient's frequent and disabling headaches, a prophylactic approach is warranted to her quality of life. Topiramate does not have the respiratory side effects that make β-blockers unsuitable for this asthmatic patient. Additionally, it has a favourable side effect profile compared to other prophylactic options like methysergide.

Acute treatment with a different triptan, eg naratriptan
While triptans are effective for acute migraine attacks, the patient experiences headaches 4-8 times per month. Using triptans frequently can lead to medication-overuse headaches, which can exacerbate her condition. Additionally, the patient previously had dizziness with sumatriptan, indicating a potential intolerance to triptans.

Acute treatment with codeine and domperidone
Codeine is an opioid, and frequent use can lead to dependence and medication-overuse headaches. This patient already experiences frequent migraines, and adding codeine could worsen her headache pattern. Domperidone is an antiemetic that may help with nausea but does not address the primary issue of headache frequency and intensity.

Prophylactic treatment with a propranolol
Prophylactic treatment with a propranolol β-blockers like propranolol can trigger bronchospasm and worsen asthma symptoms. While propranolol is effective for migraine prevention, it is contraindicated in asthmatic patients. Therefore, an alternative prophylactic treatment must be considered.

Prophylactic treatment with methysergide
Methysergide is rarely used due to its significant side effects, including endocardial and retroperitoneal fibrosis. These serious adverse effects limit its use to very specific and refractory cases. Safer and more effective options, such as topiramate, are preferred for routine migraine prophylaxis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman weighing 90 kg and 162 cm tall presents with visual loss and headaches. On examination she has a sixth nerve palsy and swelling of the optic disc. MRI of the brain is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
The diagnosis is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) (previously known as benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) or pseudotumor cerebri). This is more common in women, particularly in those who are obese and between the ages of 15 and 40. It is important to exclude secondary causes, including drug-induced IIH (nitrofurantoin, oral contraceptives, tetracyclines, nalidixic acid, corticosteroids and etretinate) and other causes of raised intracranial pressure, including cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. The sixth cranial nerve palsy is a ‘false localising sign’ as the abducens nerve is vulnerable to downwards pressure of the brainstem.

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. Hypoparathyroidism can have some neurological manifestation as a consequence of hypocalcaemia (including papilloedema) but would not cause the presentation described here.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Normal pressure hydrocephalus is incorrect. Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically presents with the triad of dementia, gait apraxia and incontinence.

Paraneoplastic syndrome
Paraneoplastic syndrome is incorrect. Paraneoplastic syndromes (particularly those associated with antiCRMP5 antibodies) can be associated with optic neuropathy (and consequent swollen appearance of the optic disc). However, this is very rare and, given the other factors described in this case, this possibility is therefore less likely. Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension A 33-year-old-female teacher presents with a subacute onset of weakness, numbness and paraesthesia in the right leg. She says this previously happened to a lesser extent on the left-hand side and resolved after a few months. She has light headedness and an electric-shock-like feeling from the neck down the spine whenever she bends her head forward. She denies any history of fits but her brother who is 16 years old suffers with epilepsy. On examination there is evidence of profound weakness and reduced pinprick sensation in the right leg. Horizontal nystagmus on looking to the right is evident. Apart from MRI scanning, which of the following is a potentially helpful test?

Venous sinus thrombosis
Venous sinus thrombosis is incorrect. This should be considered and can be a cause of raised intracranial pressure. However, the factors described in this case (obesity, normal brain scan) make this possibility less likely.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward. He complains of sudden-onset headache with vomiting. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15/15. Computed cerebral angiography free blood identified in both ventricles, with an 8 mm cerebral artery aneurysm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Endovascular coil
This patient has experienced a brain aneurysm as suggested by his sudden severe headache and nausea/vomiting. The most appropriate management in this case is use of an endovascular coil. Coiling is typically preferred, having shown better outcomes in the long run. In some cases, however, patient anatomy (tortuous vessels or plaque in the carotid arteries) may preclude this procedure and the patient may need to be transferred to another centre.

Catheter-directed nicardipine
Catheter-directed nicardipine can be useful in situations where there is demonstrable vascular spasm; however, this is not the case here.

Neurosurgical clipping
Neurosurgical clipping of an aneurysm is less preferable than use of an endovascular coil. The international subarachnoid aneurysm trial and barrow ruptured aneurysm trial demonstrated that endovascular coiling generally yields superior outcomes, compared to neurosurgery.

Prophylactic phenytoin
Although seizure prophylaxis in subarachnoid haemorrhage should be considered, phenytoin is associated with poorer outcomes. Levetiracetam is generally the preferred agent for seizure prophylaxis, based on its safety profile.

Tranexamic acid
The ULTRA randomised controlled trial (RCT) of early tranexamic acid failed to show benefit in terms of clinical outcomes (with a trend that actually seemed to favour placebo). This is a large, modern multicentre RCT which should guide our practice.

stem: A 65-year-old man complained of a limp in his right leg that had developed over the last few months, associated with pain in his back and down the front of his leg. On examination, of his lower limbs he had normal tone, weakness of knee extension, foot inversion and foot dorsiﬂexion on the right but full power in other groups; a decreased knee reﬂex on the right, but all other reﬂexes were present and plantars were ﬂexor. Sensation to pin-prick and light touch was decreased over the medial part of the right calf. Which nerve root on the right side is affected?
explanation:
C L4 The L4 dermatome is over the anteromedial part of the shin. L4 is also part of the knee reﬂex and is involved in hip adduction, knee extension, ankle dorsiﬂexion and foot inversion. The back pain and radicular pain down the leg are clues to the diagnosis of a radiculopathy. It is important to consider red ﬂags for spinal cord or cauda equina compression. Careful examination of the reﬂexes and sensation is usually most helpful in localising the lesion. Weakness is not usually prominent. The cause of the lesion is best evaluated with an MRI scan of the lumbosacral spine. E S1 The S1 dermatome is mainly over the sole of the foot. S1 is part of the ankle reﬂex and is involved in hip extension, ankle plantar ﬂexion and foot eversion. A L2 The L2 dermatome includes the anterior aspect of the thigh. The L2 nerve root contributes to hip ﬂexion and adduction power. B L3 The L3 dermatome includes the medial aspect of the thigh and knee (this can be easily remembered as ‘three’ rhymes with ‘knee’). The L3 nerve root contributes to knee extension and hip adduction power. D L5

The L5 dermatome is over the anterolateral shin and dorsum of the foot. L5 is involved in hip extension, knee ﬂexion, ankle dorsiﬂexion and big toe extension.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with weakness in his hands and legs. In particular, he reports difﬁculties playing football with his sons. On examination, bilateral ptosis with a smooth forehead is noted. Fundoscopy proves difﬁcult because of bilateral cataracts. Facial expression is reduced, with wasting of the temporalis muscles, masseters and sternomastoids. Slow release of hand grip is present bilaterally, with distal weakness and wasting in the upper limb muscles. There is bilateral foot drop. Deep tendon jerks are depressed. Which one of the following best explains the underlying aetiology of this condition?
options: Trinucleotide repeat disorder affecting the DMPK gene
Antibodies directed against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Disorder due to mutation in gene-encoding dystrophin
explanation:
B Trinucleotide repeat disorder affecting the DMPK gene This man has features consistent with myotonic dystrophy type 1, which is caused by excessive repeats of the nucleotides C-T-G in an untranslated region of the dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. The other clinical features of myotonic dystrophy are frontal balding, a lean face due to wasted temporalis and masseter muscles; cardiac dysrhythmias such as heart block (look for a pacemaker); smooth muscle abnormalities resulting in abdominal pain; dysphagia and pseudo-obstruction; respiratory muscle weakness; insulin resistance or diabetes; hypogonadism; and susceptibility to cancer. As a trinucleotide repeat disorder (like Huntington’s disease), myotonic dystrophy type 1 becomes symptomatic progressively earlier in each successive generation due to expansion of the trinucleotide repeat - a phenomenon called anticipation. This can lead to neonates presenting with hypotonia and respiratory muscle weakness – congenital myotonic dystrophy. EMG changes are found in almost any muscle (waxing and waning of potentials, termed the ‘dive bomber effect’). D Antibodies directed against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor This option alludes to myasthenia gravis (MG), which can present with fatiguable ptosis. We are not told that his ptosis is fatiguable. His muscle weakness is distal, whereas MG features fatiguable

proximal weakness (shoulders and hips). Muscle wasting, myotonia and cataracts are not usually seen in MG. A Inherited phosphofructokinase deﬁciency While phosphofructokinase deﬁciency (PFKD) can present in adulthood with progressive weakness, it usually presents in childhood with muscle cramps and fatigue. Patients do not usually have cataracts C Underlying mitochondrial DNA mutation Whilst ptosis can be a feature of mitochondrial disease, it is usually accompanied by diplopia, ophthalmoplegia and proximal muscle weakness. This man’s weakness is more distal. He has evidence of wasted facial musculature, and myotonia, which are not usually seen in mitochondrial disease. E Disorder due to mutation in gene-encoding dystrophin Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene. They start in childhood or adolescence, affect mostly males (they are inherited in an X-linked fashion) and cause muscle pseudo-hypertrophy (especially in the calves) rather than wasting. Cataracts and myotonia are not features of these muscular dystrophies. Some female carriers may have clinically detectable weakness and high serum creatine kinase concentrations, but are only fully affected clinically if a copy of the X-chromosome is deleted (i.e. if they also have Turner syndrome), or inactivated.

stem: A 25-year-old man visits his general practitioner (GP) complaining of a resting tremor in one hand that has become progressively more noticeable over the last few months. He has also found getting dressed in the mornings to be particularly difﬁcult due to a lack of co-ordination. On further questioning, he reports that he 'feels tired all the time' and admits to feeling depressed and lonely. He has not worked since leaving college and lives with his parents. On examination, the patient has a relatively expressionless face with a paucity of blinking. His eyes have a symmetrical appearance and an image of his left eye is shown below. A ﬁne resting tremor of the left hand is noted. Examination of the patient's wrists shows rigidity of movement on ﬂexion and extension. Mental examination shows some slowing of higher functions and a mildly blunted affect. Observing the patient walking shows the left arm not to swing fully and the left foot mildly scraping the ﬂoor. Given this clinical presentation, which one of the following conditions should be considered within the differential diagnosis?
explanation:
D Wilson’s disease Wilson's disease is a neurodegenerative disease of copper metabolism. It typically presents in childhood or adolescence and rarely presents after the 3rd decade. Clinical manifestations are predominantly hepatic, neurologic and psychiatric. Patients who present with fulminant liver failure have a mortality rate as high as 70%. Liver disease is the most common initial manifestation in children. Older individuals often present with neuropsychiatric symptoms. Neurological symptoms and signs include parkinsonism, but may present in many other forms including dystonias, particularly of the face (rictus), eye movement disorders and psychiatric changes including emotional lability, personality changes and depression. This condition should therefore be excluded in any young person presenting with a movement disorder; this includes liver biochemistry, serum ceruloplasmin, 24 h urinary copper excretion and slit-lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings, which can be seen here. Kayser-Fleischer rings are dark rings which encircle the iris, as they can be difﬁcult to see with fundoscopy, slit-lamp examination is warranted even if fundoscopy appears normal. B Epidemic pleurodynia Epidemic pleurodynia (Bornholm disease) is a febrile illness caused by Coxsackie B viral infection. Symptoms include paroxysmal chest pain, fever, headache and myalgia. It does not ﬁt this patient’s presenting symptoms. A Erythema induratum Erythema induratum (Bazin’s disease) is an inﬂammatory disorder of subcutaneous fat tissue. It can be associated with TB, autoimmune

conditions, inﬂammatory bowel disease and haematological conditions. It does not ﬁt this patient’s presenting symptoms. C Menetrier’s disease Protein-losing hypertrophic gastropathy (Menetrier’s disease) is an acquired gastrointestinal condition most frequently affecting middle-aged males. Symptoms include epigastric pain, fatigue, anorexia and weight loss. It does not ﬁt this patient’s presenting symptoms. E Whipple’s disease Infection with Tropheryma whipplei can give rise to neurological symptoms in 10–40% of patients, but isolated neurological disease is rare. Cognitive impairment is the most common neurological manifestation. Oculomasticatory myorhythmia and oculo-facial-skeletal myorhythmia are considered pathognomonic. Wilson’s disease should always be ruled out ﬁrst in a young patient with the combination of a psychiatric condition and movement disorder.

stem: A 48-year-old accountant presents to the Outpatient Clinic with weakness of the left lower extremity that has been gradually developing over the past 4 months. On further questioning, he also describes occasional brief and unprovoked episodes of rhythmic jerking along the length of the left limb and less marked weakness affecting the right leg. He also reports headache, which is worst in the morning. Neurological examination reveals weakness of both lower limbs that is more pronounced on the left side, and bilateral extensor (upgoing) plantar responses. Sensory examination reveals mild reduction of vibration sense of the left leg, but is otherwise normal. Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate to complete ﬁrst?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic and lumbar spine
Computed tomography (CT) of the dorsal and lumbar spine
explanation:
C MRI of the head The patient’s bilateral lower limb weakness could be due to either a spinal cord lesion in the dorsal (thoracic) region or a midline/parasagittal brain lesion. The presence of headache, sensory symptoms on the same side as the weaker limb and the patient’s account of partial seizure activity in the same area all point to the brain as the location of the lesion. A para-sagittal meningioma will often manifest in this manner. For this reason, an MRI of the head is the most appropriate ﬁrst investigation in this case. A Visual evoked potentials (VEPs) This is an investigation used to test for evidence of demyelination of the optic nerve in patients with suspected multiple sclerosis. It is not usually the ﬁrst test to be completed and would usually be done after MRI imaging of the brain and spine had been completed. B Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic and lumbar spine The pattern of symptoms and signs in this case is more suggestive of

a brain lesion. However, given that there is bilateral leg weakness and up-going plantar responses, which can be present in spinal lesions, MRI imaging of the spine would certainly be a consideration after brain imaging and especially if the MRI brain did not show an abnormality. D Computed tomography (CT) of the dorsal and lumbar spine The pattern of symptoms and signs in this case is more suggestive of a brain lesion. If imaging of the spine was required, MRI would be the more useful modality in this case and so would be preferable to CT. E Electroencephalography (EEG) This is an investigation used to determine seizure activity. This investigation may be useful in this case, as the patient does describe some partial seizure activity, but the pattern of signs and symptoms is suggestive of a brain lesions and so brain imaging should be completed in the ﬁrst instance.

stem: A 64-year-old woman was admitted with a history of urinary incontinence of 3 months duration. Her daughter noticed that she had become clumsy and forgetful even before she had developed incontinence. Her handwriting had deteriorated, with her hand shaking too much to produce anything legible at all. On examination, her BP was 152/82 mmHg, pulse 85 bpm and regular. She was quiet and subdued, failed the 7 subtraction test but could identify her daughter and remember her date of birth. With respect to objects, whilst she could name them correctly she was unable to recall them. Tremor was clearly evident when you asked her to stretch out both her hands. Tendon reﬂexes were brisk, with down-going plantars. When you asked her to walk her gait was slow and wide-based with only small steps. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 45 U/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 18 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l CSF Normal constituents, opening pressure 22 cm H 0 6–20 cmH O Once the suspected diagnosis is conﬁrmed, what is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: D CSF drainage The triad of cognitive impairment, gait disturbance and incontinence raises the possibility of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Drainage of 20–30 ml of CSF may lead to clinical improvement. The degree of cognitive improvement determines whether future therapeutic lumbar puncture is planned or whether the patient is a candidate for shunting. Computed tomography (CT) or MRI of the head shows hydrocephalus with no obstruction to CSF ﬂow. On T2-weighted images, periventricular oedema may be seen. A Memantine Memantine NMDA receptor antagonist which is used in the treatment of dementia. The raised opening CSF pressure, however, means that normal-pressure hydrocephalus should ﬁrst be excluded as a diagnosis. B Donepezil This is a cholinesterase inhibitor used for the treatment of Alzheimer’s dementia. The CSF opening pressure, however, suggests that hydrocephalus should be excluded ﬁrst before considering pharmacotherapy for memory loss. C Piracetam Piracetam is prescribed in the UK for myoclonus, and as such it has no role here in the treatment of normal- pressure hydrocephalus. E Deep brain stimulation Deep brain stimulation is a treatment for Parkinson’s disease resistant to pharmacological intervention.

stem: You are called to the Geriatric Psychiatry Ward to assess a new inpatient. A 66-year-old man was admitted yesterday for elective investigation of cognitive dysfunction. His wife describes a background of worsening memory problems and poor mobility. The pattern is one of ‘good days’ with minimal symptoms, followed by periods of sudden deterioration. In the weeks prior to admission, he has suffered frequent falls. He has no psychiatric history, although he has recently complained of ﬂeeting visual hallucinations. He had no regular medication prior to admission. On the night of his admission, he became acutely distressed, complaining of ‘seeing monsters’ in his peripheral vision. His agitation was such that he required emergency sedation. On examination, he is drowsy and unable to give a coherent history. Tone is increased in all four limbs, although power seems normal. He has symmetrical upper limb rigidity and bradykinesia. His wife claims the involuntary movements are new. What is the most appropriate management for the underlying neurological condition that has precipitated his admission to hospital?
explanation:
B Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors This patient’s underlying diagnosis is very suggestive of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). This is a neurodegenerative disease caused by deposition of Lewy bodies (abnormal protein aggregates) in the cerebral cortex and brain stem. The consortium on DLB international workshop diagnostic criteria suggests the diagnosis is likely if, in the context of dementia, there are also present two of the three following core features: ﬂuctuating attention and concentration, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations and spontaneous parkinsonian motor signs. Further suggestive features include rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder, and a severe sensitivity to the extra-pyramidal side effects of neuroleptics. There is some evidence in the form of a small number of randomised controlled trials and open label studies to suggest that acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors, such as rivastigmine, may reduce hallucinations, ﬂuctuations and parkinsonian symptoms and improve attention. C Aspirin and statins This combination would be appropriate for a patient suffering from vascular dementia, a dementing illness caused by series of repeated cerebral infarctions, usually in the context of risk factors such as hypertension. The disease manifests in a step-wise manner, and so periods of stability between deterioration can appear as the ﬂuctuant stage of DLB. Neurological symptoms may also occur in vascular dementia, making these conditions difﬁcult to differentiate. However, the patient’s tetrad symptoms of dementia, ﬂuctuant course, parkinsonism and visual hallucination point more towards a diagnosis of DLB. A Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are a class of antidepressant drugs that are typically used to treat depression and anxiety. This patient’s presentation is not in keeping with either of these diagnoses, and therefore this would not be the most appropriate agent to use in his management. D Copper-chelating agents Wilson’s disease, which is treated with copper-chelating agents, is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that results in copper accumulation in body tissues, particularly the liver, brain, eyes and

kidneys, and can present with neuro-psychiatric symptoms, including parkinsonism symptoms. However, it will usually also present with symptoms of liver disease and the classical KayserFleischer rings on eye exam. The disease is most commonly diagnosed between the ages of 5 and 35 years. E Dopamine agonists Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors can be seen as a ﬁrst-line treatment in DLB as they can have an improvement on neuropsychiatric and motor symptoms. Dopamine agonists such as ropinirole and rotigotine are used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease. For the severe parkinsonian symptoms of DLB, dopamine agonists have been used but they have been associated with worsening psychotic and behavioural symptoms. For this reason, small doses of levodopa are generally the preferred treatment for motor symptoms, as this agent has a lower side effect proﬁle.

stem: A 36-year-old self-employed designer presents to the Emergency Department, complaining of problems with his vision. These began suddenly while he was working late at night at home. He has a highpressure and stressful job (‘If I don’t ﬁnish on time, I can’t pay the mortgage’) and, as a result, he tends to work long hours. He reports reaching up for a ﬁle on an upper shelf when he felt dizzy and unwell. He sat down and noticed that he could not see the left side of his computer screen clearly. He denies headache or pain in his neck. He is a smoker and drinks around 35–40 units of alcohol per week. Past medical history includes sinusitis, for which he has bought a nasal steroid inhaler, he takes no other regular medications. On examination, he appears well although he is anxious. His pulse is 90/min and regular with a blood pressure of 128/84 mmHg. Cranial nerve examination reveals left homonymous hemianopia. There are no eye movement abnormalities and the remainder of the neurological examination is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 354 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is most likely to assist with the diagnosis?
options: Detailed enquiry about illicit drug use
explanation: E Detailed enquiry about illicit drug use Stimulant drug use (especially cocaine) is prevalent among young professionals and is a not uncommon association with young-onset ischaemic events, both cerebral and coronary. Cocaine is thought to cause acute vasospasm and so may lead to vascular events taking place with no visible arterial wall abnormalities. A detailed drug history is very important, particularly in younger age-group patients presenting with ischaemic events. Most patients will not volunteer it unless asked and may not recognise its importance. B ESR Vasculitic conditions can cause young strokes but in someone without any signiﬁcant systemic symptoms (rashes, hair loss, joint pains, fevers) the ESR is not likely to lead to a diagnosis. In older patients (>50 years) the possibility of giant cell arteritis would have to be borne in mind and ESR is a useful test. A Fundoscopy The ﬁnding of homonymous hemianopia means the lesion is behind the optic chiasm, so fundoscopy is unlikely to reveal anything speciﬁc in this case (although all patients with neurological symptoms should have a thorough examination that includes this). C Urinary catecholamines analysis This test can be done to investigate phaeochromocytoma, which is a rare cause of secondary hypertension. This man’s blood pressure seems normal so there is no indication for this test at the current time. D Fasting blood sugar analysis Whilst diabetes is a risk factor for young strokes, it would be an extremely unusual presenting feature (i.e. no known history of poorly controlled diabetes).

stem: A 58-year-old man is brought to the Neurology outpatient clinic by his daughter. She is extremely concerned and he has been displaying some very odd behaviour and has had some weakness in his lower limbs. She reports that about a year ago she and her family noticed that their father’s business was beginning to lose money as he had become unable to manage his ﬁnances. They had also had complaints from staff who felt their father’s behaviour to clients was often rude and disinhibited, laughing or crying at inappropriate times. He had developed a ‘sweet tooth’ and would hoard such items, eating little else. The daughter reported that over the last few weeks she had noticed her father’s speech sounded different and he had difﬁculty getting out of his chair. He had previously been ﬁt and well, with no past medical history and took no medications. On examination, the patient’s speech has a nasal quality and he has an impaired swallow with tongue fasciculations. The remainder of the cranial nerve examination is normal and there is no papilloedema. He has proximal limb weakness of 4/5 bilaterally and fasciculations of his left quadriceps. His reﬂexes are brisk. His sensory exam is normal. His mini-mental state examination (MMSE) scores 28/30, with some subtle word- ﬁnding difﬁculties. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C FTD-MND The frontotemporal dementias (FTD) are a group of clinically and neuropathologically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorders characterized by prominent changes in social behaviour and personality or aphasia accompanied by degeneration of the frontal and/or temporal lobes. Some patients with FTD also develop concomitant motor neurone disease, like this man is demonstrating. Likewise some patients with classical MND develop FTD. In FTD, memory is often less severely affected than in Alzheimer’s and performance on MMSE is often surprisingly high; a detailed behavioural and cognitive history taken from an informant (patients typically lack insight) is required to make the diagnosis. Neuroimaging with MRI or CT may show focal atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes, but these are not diagnostic tests. MND can be conﬁrmed using EMG in the usual manner. There is often a hereditary trait to FTD, with 10-25% showing autosomal dominant inheritance. Hexanucleotide expansions in the C9ORF72 gene are especially associated with FTD-MND. D Motor neurone disease (MND) Whilst the patient has clinical features to support this diagnosis, the cognitive and behavioural aspects must be accounted for, so FTDMND is a more accurate diagnosis. A Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) Whilst this patient does have features of FTD, one needs to account for the motor signs so FTD-MND is a more accurate diagnosis. B Alzheimer’s disease This will usually present with memory symptoms, but prominent behavioural and emotional changes are rare. In addition, there is no link with MND. E Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) PSP is characterised by a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, parkinsonism, decreased balance and early falls. Behavioural changes are seen, but features of MND would not be present in PSP.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of personality changes, disinhibition and altered dietary habits with a preference for sweet foods. He lost his job as an accountant because of inappropriate social behaviour. There is no memory deficit. The neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia is a neurodegenerative disease and is characterised by prominent changes in personality and behaviour. The patient presents with personality and behavioural changes, altered eating and sexual habits, speech disturbances and disinhibition. Short-term memory is intact until the end stage of the disease. The age of onset is 45–65 years. Primary progressive aphasia is present. This could be progressive expressive non-fluent aphasia or progressive receptive aphasia with loss of semantic knowledge for environmental objects. Frontal and temporal dysfunction (personality, language and memory impairment) with preservation of parietal lobe function (visual–spatial skills) is seen. Brain imaging usually shows atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes. It is associated with motor neurone disease. Some cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Alzheimer’s disease has an insidious onset and a gradual progression of memory loss. There is impairment of one or more other cognitive domains, including aphasia, apraxia, agnosia or executive functioning. Thus the history is not suggestive of Alzheimer’s disease. This gentleman of 60 years has a fairly rapid onset of symptoms (6 months) with an alteration of executive functions which is not characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease, especially with the fact that the patient has no memory deficit.

Diffuse Lewy body disease
Diffuse Lewy body disease is incorrect. Diffuse Lewy body dementia presents with cognitive impairment and is often preceded or associated with extrapyramidal symptoms. Patients also have fluctuating levels of attention and alertness. Recurrent visual hallucinations, auditory hallucinations and delusions are usually present, along with sleep disturbances. This patient has disturbances in executive functions and social disinhibition, which is not a feature that characterises diffuse Lewy body disease, and a normal neurological examination.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Multiple sclerosis is an episodic or progressive disease and the symptoms are and signs are multifocal. Onset is most often in healthy young adults. There are abnormal findings in the MRI in >95% of the patients.

Vascular dementia
Vascular dementia is incorrect. Vascular dementia presents with a subcortical pattern of cognitive changes. Clinical stroke with radiological evidence of cerebral infarcts is evident. There is a temporal relationship between the dementia and strokes. There may be associated motor dysfunction including gait disorders. Urinary dyscontrol, usually incontinence or frequency, can occur.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with urinary retention and weakness in his legs. Past history of note includes hypertension, type-2 diabetes, and colonic carcinoma for which he underwent an anterior resection some 5 years earlier. On examination his BP is 142/72 mmHg, pulse is 80 beats per min and regular. There is left-sided loss vibration and joint position sense at the level of T10, right-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation a few segments below the level of T10, and there is 1/5 power weakness affecting his left leg. He is in urinary retention. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Brown-Séquard syndrome
The combination of leg weakness and urinary retention should alert the clinician to a diagnosis of spinal cord involvement, especially with a history of malignancy. The clinical picture described fits best with BrownSéquard syndrome, the suspicion being that it may be owing to metastatic disease from his colonic carcinoma. While spinal metastases are seen less frequently in association with colon cancer, they are recognised as a late phenomenon. MRI is the imaging modality of choice. Brown-Séquard syndrome, also known as hemisection of the cord, arises due to damage to all structures on one side of the spinal cord, in this case the left side. This causes ipsilateral weakness (the descending corticospinal pathway having already decussated at the medulla), ipsilateral loss of vibration sense, proprioception and joint position sense (ascending dorsal column not yet decussated), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature (ascending spinothalamic tract has decussated). Prognosis is poor with colonic carcinoma metastases as they are less likely to be responsive to high-dose corticosteroids versus other tumours such as lymphomas.

Spinal stenosis
Spinal stenosis, or narrowing of the spinal canal, due to disc herniations, osteophyte formation, spondylosis, facet or ligament hypertrophy (but in this case, probably due to bony metastasis), will affect the peripheral structures of the spinal cord first, but will not tend to cause different features involving both the left and right side of the body simultaneously as described here.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia arises from fluid-filled cysts in the central canal of the spinal cord, and causes dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain and temperature, preserved light touch, vibration and joint position sense), but, again, symptoms tend to be bilateral.

Anterior spinal infarction
Anterior spinal infarction is expected to lead to bilateral symptoms below the level of the cord, rather than the picture consistent with hemisection seen here.

Anterior spinal artery haemorrhage
Anterior spinal artery haemorrhage is associated with rapid onset bilateral symptoms below the level of the for Tutor haemorrhage, rather than the hemi-section picture seen here, and there are no significant risk factors arterial haemorrhage.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is noted to have poor self-care with symptoms of early morning wakening and decreased appetite. She has poor concentration, is easily agitated and lacks motivation. There is a history of recent death in the family. She also recently lost her job as a volunteer. She has difficulty in answering shortterm recall questions and has an MMSE of 21. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Depressive pseudodementia
Early morning wakening and decreased appetite are symptoms of depression, and there have clearly been life events that may have precipitated the illness in this patient. Short-term memory loss may occur in conjunction with depression as well as being seen in dementia. The memory loss improves with treatment of the depression. Other physical signs of depression include weight loss, constipation, loss of libido, impotence in men, fatigue and generalised body aches and pains.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Although a neurodegenerative conditions might be considered in this scenario, a diagnosis of dementia requires that there is insidious onset of interference with the ability to perform one’s usual activities as a result of progressive deterioration in at least two cognitive domains (eg memory, executive, visuospatial, language). Delirium and major psychiatric disorders must also be excluded. The information provided in this case is not sufficient to meet the criteria for dementia and therefore it is not appropriate to begin to attempt differentiating between dementia sub-types.

Delirium
Delirium is incorrect. Delirium is characterised by acute onset concurrent disturbances of consciousness and attention, perception, thinking, memory, psychomotor behaviour, emotion and the sleep-wake schedule, and can result from innumerable medical causes. The features in this case are not those of delirium.

Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia is incorrect. Although a neurodegenerative conditions might be considered in this scenario, a diagnosis of dementia requires that there is insidious onset of interference with the ability to perform one’s usual activities as a result of progressive deterioration in at least two cognitive domains (eg memory, executive, visuospatial, language). Delirium and major psychiatric disorders must also be excluded. The information provided in this case is not sufficient to meet the criteria for dementia and therefore it is not appropriate to begin to attempt differentiating between dementia sub-types. Depression

Personality disorder
Personality disorder is incorrect. According to the ICD-10, personality disorder represents a persistent behaviour pattern of clinical significance which appears to be the expression of the individual's characteristic lifestyle and mode of relating to himself/herself and others. The features in this case are not those of personality disorder.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with transient weakness in his left arm and collapse. He recovers within 24 hours and has a carotid ultrasound scan. This reveals a 45% stenosis affecting the right internal carotid artery and a 60% stenosis affecting the left internal carotid artery. Other risk factors include smoking 30 cigarettes per day (which he refuses to stop) and hypertension. Blood pressure in the clinic is 145/80 mmHg. He is in sinus rhythm and his cholesterol level is 5.1 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management to reduce risk of a further stroke affecting the same territory?
explanation:
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is recommended by NICE guidelines for secondary stroke prevention because it has been shown to be more effective than aspirin in reducing the risk of recurrent cerebral infarctions. Clopidogrel works by inhibiting platelet aggregation, which helps to prevent the formation of new clots that could lead to another stroke. In patients with a history of transient ischaemic attack (TIA) or stroke, clopidogrel has been demonstrated to provide superior protection against future events compared to aspirin alone. Therefore, clopidogrel is the preferred antiplatelet agent for this patient to minimise the risk of further strokes.

Aspirin therapy
Aspirin, while effective in reducing the risk of stroke, is not as effective as clopidogrel for secondary stroke prevention. Aspirin works by inhibiting cyclooxygenase, which decreases platelet aggregation, but clopidogrel's mechanism of action provides a more substantial reduction in the risk of recurrent strokes. Given the patient's significant risk factors, including smoking and hypertension, it is crucial to use the most effective agent available. Therefore, while aspirin would still reduce stroke risk, it is not the optimal choice in this scenario.

Right carotid endarterectomy
The stenosis in the right carotid artery is 45%, which is below the threshold typically considered for surgical intervention. Carotid endarterectomy is usually reserved for patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70% or greater. Performing surgery on a 45% stenosis would not be justified as the risks of the procedure could outweigh the potential benefits. Furthermore, the patient's symptoms suggest that the left carotid artery may be more relevant to his clinical presentation.

Left carotid endarterectomy
Although the left internal carotid artery has a higher degree of stenosis at 60%, this is still below the 70% threshold generally considered for endarterectomy in symptomatic patients. Additionally, the patient's symptoms (transient weakness in the left arm) imply that the right side is more likely to be the affected territory, making surgery on the left side less pertinent. Carotid endarterectomy is a significant surgical procedure and should be reserved for cases where the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. Therefore, in this patient, medical management with antiplatelet therapy is more appropriate.

Statin therapy
Statins are important for managing overall cardiovascular risk, including reducing cholesterol levels, which can help prevent future cardiovascular events. However, in the context of secondary stroke prevention, the primary goal is to prevent new clot formation, which is more effectively achieved with antiplatelet therapy such as clopidogrel. While lowering cholesterol can contribute to long-term vascular health, it does not provide the immediate protection against recurrent strokes that antiplatelet agents do. Therefore, while statins should be part of the overall management plan, they are not the most critical intervention for preventing a further stroke in this case.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of severe occipital headache, vomiting and neck stiffness. He says it was the worst headache he has ever had. Neurological examination is normal. CT brain is normal. A lumbar puncture is going to be performed. How many hours after the onset of headache should the lumbar puncture be performed?
explanation:
12 hours
The sudden onset of a severe headache raises the possibility of a subarachnoid haemorrhage. A CT brain is mandatory in these situations. It is sensitive up to 95% in the first 24 hours. However, a normal CT brain cannot exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage altogether. A lumbar puncture needs to be performed to look for xanthochromia (using spectrophotometry). You need to wait 12 hours after the onset of the headache, as this is the time it takes for the breakdown of haemoglobin to bilirubin.

1 hour
1 hour is incorrect. This would be too soon to do the lumbar puncture.

2 hours
2 hours is incorrect. This would be too soon to do the lumbar puncture.

6 hours
6 hours is incorrect. This would be too soon to do the lumbar puncture.

8 hours
8 hours is incorrect. This would be too soon to do the lumbar puncture.

stem: A previously well, 70-year-old woman develops episodes of severe, lancinating facial pain affecting the left side of her face; these have increased in frequency over the past few months. They typically affect the upper part of her face, are very sudden and last a few seconds or so. They can occur in clusters over several hours. Her General Practitioner (GP) has already prescribed carbamazepine, which has helped to some degree. There are no specific activities or movements that can bring on the pain, although it is perhaps a little worse in the cold. On examination she has reduced pinprick sensation over the left side of her face (all III divisions of the Vth nerve) and a reduced corneal reflex on that side. The remainder of the examination appears to be within normal limits. Which possible diagnosis would you consider as the most likely at this stage?
options: Herpes zoster of the trigeminal nerve
Local tumour compressing the trigeminal nerve
explanation:
Local tumour compressing the trigeminal nerve
Although this patient is in the typical age group for trigeminal neuralgia, and the description of the pain is suggestive of this, there are nevertheless atypical features that exclude this diagnosis. As well as the absence of ‘trigger factors’ (induction of pain by specific movements, which can include speaking, chewing, brushing the teeth and touching a particular point on the face), the most important atypical feature is the presence of fixed sensory loss. This indicates that a structural cause for her trigeminal neuropathy must be looked for, and in this age group a tumour is most likely.

Hemifacial spasm
Hemifacial spasm is incorrect. Hemifacial spasm is an idiopathic movement disorder with involuntary contraction of facial muscles; it is not usually painful and is not associated with sensory loss.

Herpes zoster of the trigeminal nerve
Herpes zoster infection would be associated with a vesicular rash.

Idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia
Idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia is incorrect. As described while idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia is typical in this patient age group, and the described pain is suggestive of the diagnosis, there are other atypical features that exclude the diagnosis, the most important one being the presence of fixed sensory loss which is more suggestive of a structural cause for the trigeminal neuropathy.

Paroxysmal hemicrania
Paroxysmal hemicrania is incorrect. Paroxysmal hemicrania is a primary headache syndrome and the fixed sensory loss excludes this diagnosis.

stem: You consider both CNS toxoplasmosis and cryptococcosis as possible diagnoses. Which of the following is the most useful differentiator?
explanation:
Ring-enhancing lesions on CT brain
Ring-enhancing lesions on CT scan are a typical finding in cerebral toxoplasmosis, but in CNS cryptococcosis CT findings may be non-specific or even normal, or show meningeal enhancement, granuloma formation, cerebral oedema or hydrocephalus. Cryptococcal pseudocysts may also be seen, appearingChat as non-enhancing with hypodense lesions. The best way to definitely diagnose either condition is with CSF culture for Cryptococcus neoformans, or CSF PCR for Toxoplasma gondii DNA. There may also be a role for meningeal or brain biopsy in either case.

CSF appearance
CSF appearance is incorrect. CSF appearance may be abnormal for both diagnoses, so is not a useful differentiator. In toxoplasmosis, CSF findings may include elevated protein and variable glucose and WBC counts. In cryptococcosis, CSF may be normal in 25% of patients, and only minimally abnormal in 50%. It can appear clear or turbid, with elevated protein levels in up to two-thirds of cases. The glucose level is usually normal. Close to 100% of CSF culture results are positive for Cryptococcus neoformans.

CSF glucose
CSF glucose is incorrect. CSF glucose may be abnormal, most likely low, for both diagnoses, so it is not a useful differentiator.

CSF lymphocytosis
CSF lymphocytosis is incorrect. CSF cell count may be abnormal for both diagnoses, so is not a useful differentiator. In toxoplasmosis, CSF findings may include elevated protein and variable glucose and WBC counts. In cryptococcosis, CSF may be normal in 25% of patients, and only minimally abnormal in 50%, with elevated protein levels in up to two-thirds of cases.

Toxoplasma antibodies
Toxoplasma antibodies is incorrect. Antibodies may be unreliable in immunodeficient individuals, as they could fail to produce significant titres of specific antibodies. The other theory is that toxoplasma antibodies could be prevalent in a high proportion of individuals owing to historical exposure, and IgM may persist for a number of years, leading to a high false-positive rate. Toxoplasmosis A 52-year-old man with a long history of alcohol abuse and diabetes was admitted with a subacute illness, consisting of headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. On examination, he was also observed to be ataxic, dysarthric, dysphagic and to have gaze-evoked nystagmus. MRI brain demonstrated a high-signal abnormality of the brainstem. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 15 polymorphs/mm 3, glucose concentration of 2 mmol/l (serum 6 mmol/l) and a protein concentration of 0.9 g/l. The patient has failed to after 3 days of intravenous cefuroxime treatment.

stem: You are called to see a 23-year-old woman who, after delivery (of a term infant), developed unrelated severe diarrhoea and vomiting over 24 hours. She has become confused, had a generalised tonic–clonic seizure and developed a left hemiparesis. Her BP is 115/60 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. Over the past 24 hours she has received 4.5 l of IV fluid replacement according to the chart, and has passed 2.2 l of urine. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Sagittal sinus thrombosis
This condition often arises under circumstances leading to dehydration, such as severe diarrhoea and vomiting, which the patient experienced. The seizure and subsequent focal neurological deficits, such as hemiparesis, fit the profile of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, where a blood clot forms in the dural venous sinuses. Predisposing factors include postpartum changes and fluid imbalances, making this diagnosis highly probable given the context and clinical presentation.

Amniotic fluid embolism
Amniotic fluid embolism is not the correct answer. It is a rare but severe obstetric emergency in which amniotic fluid enters the maternal bloodstream, causing a sudden reaction. This typically occurs during labour or immediately postpartum, not 24 hours later, as in this case. Furthermore, the main symptoms of amniotic fluid embolism include respiratory distress, cardiovascular collapse, and disseminated intravascular coagulation, which are not observed here.

Eclampsia
Although eclampsia can occur postpartum and involve seizures, it generally presents with high blood pressure and proteinuria, neither of which are noted here. The patient's blood pressure is normal, and the focal neurological deficit observed is more suggestive of a vascular event rather than eclampsia. Additionally, the history of severe diarrhoea and vomiting leading to dehydration does not correlate well with typical eclampsia triggers.

Severe hyponatraemia
While hyponatraemia can cause symptoms like confusion, seizures and occasionally focal neurological deficits, the patient has been receiving significant intravenous fluid replacement. This management would likely prevent severe hyponatraemia, reducing the probability of this diagnosis. The link between dehydration and the neurological symptoms suggests a different underlying cause than a sodium imbalance.

Vertebral artery dissection
This condition typically results from trauma or severe neck movements and is characterised primarily by posterior circulation symptoms, which can include dizziness, difficulty swallowing and ataxia. Seizures would be uncommon in vertebral artery dissection. Moreover, the detailed history of severe diarrhoea, vomiting and dehydration leading to the patient's symptoms does not align with the usual presentation of vertebral artery dissection, making it an unlikely explanation.

stem: An 82-year-old man who is known to have prostatic carcinoma presents to the Emergency Department complaining of lower back pain. He also complains of his legs feeling heavier than usual, with reduced sensation. On examination, he is found to have percussion tenderness of his spine, loss of sensation to the level of the umbilicus, a distended bladder and reduced anal tone. He has markedly reduced power of the lower legs, with hyperreﬂexia and upgoing plantar responses. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to request?
options: Immediate computed tomography (CT) of the whole spine
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) whole spine within 24 hours
MRI whole spine within one week
explanation:
C Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) whole spine within 24 hours The diagnosis in this patient is acute spinal cord compression, as evidenced by the upper motor neurone pattern weakness and sensory symptoms described, along with bladder and bowel dysfunction. Signs of cord compression include percussion tenderness over the spine, which is especially prominent with metastatic carcinoma, paraparesis, a sensory level and corticospinal reﬂex changes, with increased tone, hyperreﬂexia and clonus below the level of the lesion. This is a medical emergency – diagnosis should not be delayed and urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 hours is indicated. In patients with a history of carcinoma, bony metastases are the most common cause of cord compression, and as

prostate carcinoma commonly metastasises to bone, this is the most likely cause in this case. Timely administration of dexamethasone is important and discussion with Oncology regarding consideration of radiotherapy would be vital in the management of this patient. D MRI whole spine within one week An MRI of the whole spine is needed for the diagnosis of spinal cord compression. This should be done within 24 hours, especially if neurological signs are present on examination. An MRI of the whole spine within one week is reserved for patients with suspected spinal metastases without neurological signs. A Immediate computed tomography (CT) of the whole spine This investigation cannot be used to conﬁrm spinal cord compression. A CT could offer detailed imaging of bony injury or disruption; however, it is not useful in characterising the spinal cord and so is not the most useful modality to conﬁrm spinal cord compression. B Nerve conduction studies Nerve conduction studies are useful in determining between axonal and demyelinating neuropathies. However, this patient has signs and symptoms of spinal cord compression, which nerve conduction studies would not be able to diagnose. E Myelography This investigation is less useful than MRI in the diagnosis of spinal cord compression. While it can image the spinal canal effectively, it is less useful in characterising the neural tissue.

stem: A 56-year-old woman attends the Chest Clinic following chemotherapy for a localised small cell lung carcinoma. She complains of gradual-onset limb weakness and muscle tenderness, associated with intermittent diplopia. On examination, she has a right-sided ptosis, proximal myopathy and reduced tendon reﬂexes. Which neuroimmunological test would most help in diagnosis?
explanation:
E Anti-VGCC (voltage-gated calcium channel) The clinical picture is Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). This is an autoimmune paraneoplastic phenomenon most often associated with small cell lung cancer (SCLC). LEMS can present up to 2 years before a primary is discovered, and in a minority of cases no primary is ever found. Clinical features of LEMS are weakness and pain especially in limb girdle muscle groups. Ocularbulbar features are usually less severe than in myasthenia gravis. The underlying pathophysiology involves production of autoantibodies against voltage- gated calcium channels (VGCC) at the neuromuscular junction. A Anti-Yo Anti-Yo antibodies are associated with cerebellar degeneration and are especially seen in lung and gynaecological malignancy.

B Anti-AChR (acetylcholine receptor) These are associated with thymoma and occur in myasthenia gravis. C Anti-Hu Anti-Hu antibodies are associated with small cell lung cancer and lead to encephalomyositis or sensory neuropathy associated with small cell lung cancer. D Anti-Purkinje cell These are associated with small cell lung cancer and lead to cerebellar degeneration.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden-onset headache that peaked in intensity within seconds of onset. The pain was the worst she had ever experienced. The headache has been present for eight hours but is lessening. There is associated nausea, vomiting and photophobia. She has no past history of note and has not experienced severe headache before. General and neurological examination is unremarkable. A number of investigations have already been performed by the casualty ofﬁcer. He admits that the lumbar puncture was a difﬁcult procedure and he obtained a ‘bloody tap’. Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain is normal. Spinal ﬂuid: 500 RBC/cm3; < 5 WBC/cm3; no organisms on Gram stain; no xanthochromia. Which of the following is the next most important management step?
explanation:
D Magnetic resonance angiogram The history is classical for subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). Any patient with a ﬁrst-onset, explosive headache needs admission and investigation for SAH. The lack of meningism or other clinical signs should not put you off the diagnosis. The initial investigation of choice is computerised tomography (CT) of the brain. The sooner the CT is performed, the greater the sensitivity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is less effective at detecting fresh blood. If performed within 24 h, a modern CT scanner will diagnose SAH with 90–95% sensitivity. If the CT is normal the next investigation is cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)

examination, preferably 12 h after headache onset. Xanthochromia, the breakdown product of red blood cells, will not be detected until around 12 h post-bleed. If available, a better biochemical test would be spectrophotometry of spun cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF should have been spun down and formal spectrophotometry requested at the time of analysis, though this casualty ofﬁcer did not request this. In addition, the LP has been performed too soon after the headache onset). If imaging already provides a diagnosis, there is no need to subject the patient to an unnecessary lumbar puncture. It is recognised that headache can accompany expansion of an aneurysm prior to bleed and so if the history is good, even with negative CT and xanthochromia, the patient should undergo non-invasive imaging of cerebral vessels. As such, MRA is the correct answer from those given as possible options. This patient should receive adequate analgesia, balancing pain relief against interfering with Glasgow coma scale measurement. E IV dexamethasone There is no evidence to suggest that corticosteroids are helpful in managing thunderclap headache or subarachnoid haemorrhage. A Repeat lumbar puncture In this case there is no value in repeating spinal tap to look for xanthochromia, as blood from the previous procedure will make interpretation impossible. B Reassurance and simple analgesia The history is very suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage, and investigations performed to date have not adequately excluded this. Further investigation is warranted. C Subcutaneous sumatriptan The history is of a thunderclap headache and there is no previous suggestion of any habitual migraines presenting with this sort of severe headache. As such, this presentation requires full investigation.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents with slowly worsening walking over the last few years. He has become increasingly slower in his walking and has particular difﬁculty turning around. In the last 2 years he has developed shaking of his right hand and he has difﬁculty doing his buttons up on his shirt. On neurological examination, he is hypomimic with a hypophonic voice, and he has a resting tremor prominent on the right side. He has increased tone with cogwheeling that is greater in the right arm than the left. He also has difﬁculty with ﬁne ﬁnger movements on the right side. He has a stooped gait with decreased arm swing. The rest of his neurological examination is normal. Which of these drugs would be the most effective initial treatment for this patient?
explanation: A Levodopa The most likely diagnosis in this gentleman’s case is idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, exhibiting the classical triad of rigidity, bradykinesia and tremor. Levodopa is the most effective treatment in terms of controlling the motor symptoms. Levodopa is, however, associated with an earlier development of motor ﬂuctuations compared to dopamine agonists. The disadvantage of dopamine agonists is that they are less effective in controlling motor symptoms and are more likely to cause side effects such as impulse control disorder and daytime sleepiness. Thus patient involvement in treatment decision-making is crucial in Parkinson’s disease management. D Benzhexol This is an old anticholinergic drug that is now rarely used. It has some modest beneﬁt in treating the tremor of Parkinson’s disease. B Entacapone This is a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor and can be added to levodopa to try and reduce motor ﬂuctuations. It is not a ﬁrst-line treatment. C Selegiline This is a monoamine oxidase B (MOAB) inhibitor with only modest ability to relieve motor symptoms. For some patients early in the disease course, with mild symptoms, it can be a useful ﬁrst drug. It can also be added later to try and relieve motor ﬂuctuations, with levodopa. E Propranolol Beta-blockers are rarely effective in managing the tremor of Parkinson’s disease, although they can be useful in treating essential tremor.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the GP complaining of difﬁculty walking up the stairs at home. He tells you that his father died in his early 50s after a severe pneumonia, but he had to sleep propped up in bed and seemed short of breath for many months before his death. You understand that his parents were ﬁrst cousins. The patient tells you that he has always found exercise difﬁcult, and struggled particularly with sport at school. He now has a sedentary job in an ofﬁce. On examination, he has proximal weakness in his legs, with lower motor neurone signs. There is mild upper limb weakness, but this is much less marked than in the lower limbs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 3 The hereditary spinal muscular atrophies comprise a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterised by progressive lower motor neurone weakness. Type 3 SMA is known as the chronic juvenile form, the symptoms of which ﬁrst appear after the age of 18 months. It may be associated with a normal life expectancy, and patients may have near normal motor function apart from difﬁculties climbing the stairs due to proximal lower limb weakness. Bulbar palsy occurs late in the disease and may have been responsible for the recurrent pneumonia and progressive respiratory failure suffered by his father. Pathological study reveals the progressive loss of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and cranial nerve nuclei. A Myotonic dystrophy Myotonic dystrophy is an inherited condition associated with progressive muscle wasting and weakness, with delayed relaxation of grip due to myotonia. Frontal hair loss, cataract formation and male infertility are further features (the male infertility making it unlikely to be the diagnosis here). B Myasthenia gravis Myasthenia gravis presents with gradually worsening proximal muscle weakness and is autoimmune in origin. It is not inherited. C Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Features seen in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, such as earlier bulbar palsy, muscle weakness affecting both upper and lower limbs, and fasciculations, are absent here. D Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 1 This leads to death a few weeks after birth due to rapid motor neuron death.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is referred to a neurologist. She complains of several years’ history of feeling tired in the mornings. Her new partner who accompanied her says that he has been awoken on multiple occasions during the night. He describes her sitting up abruptly, vocalising incomprehensibly, lifting her arms in the air and promptly returning to sleep within 1 minute. He ascribes these events to dreaming but has noticed an increase in their frequency and is genuinely concerned. The patient cannot recollect any of these events; however, they appear to be stereotyped, associated with vocalisation but with no apparent post-event confusion. Other than having a past history of appendectomy and irritable bowel disease, she is well in herself. She has, however, lost her job and been under signiﬁcant amounts of emotional stress recently. Neurological examination is grossly normal; an electrocardiogram shows heart rate 71/min and in sinus rhythm, with blood pressure is 122/71 mmHg; full blood count and biochemistry are normal. EEG shows sharp wave activity in bifrontal regions. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: B Frontal lobe seizures This patient appears to be presenting with a history compatible with nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy. The clues here include short stereotyped events, abrupt onset and termination of motor symptoms associated with bizarre vocalisation, nocturnal nature of the events and relatively little post-ictal confusion. Videosomnography best differentiates frontal lobe seizures from other conditions, showing epileptiform activity in frontal lobe epilepsy. D Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep disorder This is an important differential, which can range from semipurposeful automatisms to full enactment of dreams often with violent activity and with detailed recall of a nightmare the next day. A Non-epileptic attack disorder These episodes are less stereotyped, and are much more likely to be seen during the day rather than at night. C Temporal lobe seizures Temporal lobe seizures usually last for a few minutes and are associated with automatisms, and are followed by a period of postictal confusion. E Paroxysmal kinesogenic choreoathetosis PKC is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterised by a range of abnormal movements including ballism, chorea and dystonia.

stem: An 18-year-old female patient was brought to the Emergency Department by her mother for the evaluation of episodic unawareness that had troubled her for the past couple of years. During the spells, she would stare and would seem stupeﬁed. She could also have some ﬂuttering of her eyelids. The episode would end in few minutes; and she would be normal again. However, for the past 12 months she had also been experiencing a few sudden shock-like contractions of her limbs, in the early morning. These features were intriguing for the family. A day before the present consultation, she lost consciousness for the ﬁrst time and had jerky movements of the limbs that continued for a couple of minutes. There was no family history of note. Choose the most likely diagnosis
explanation:
C Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is the most common form of idiopathic generalised epilepsy in young adults. The patient seeks

medical attention because of generalized seizures, often after awakening or because of myoclonic jerks in the morning involving the entire body. Sometimes absence seizures are prominent, as in this patient. Electroencephalogram (EEG) characteristically shows 4–6 Hz irregular poly-spike and slow wave activity. Intelligence remains unimpaired and the disorder tends not to be progressive. Sodium valproate, lamotrigine and levetiracetam are all useful drugs and medication should be continued indeﬁnitely. MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate, unless two consultants agree that there is no suitable alternative treatment. E Non-epileptic attack disorder The features described in this case are consistent with absence seizures, myoclonus and a probable generalised tonic-clonic seizure, making JME highly likely. NEAD is a psychologically mediated disorder with attacks that can look somewhat like generalised epileptic seizures. Several features suggest that an attack may be non- epileptic – back arching, pelvic thrusting, sideto-side head movement, waxing and waning shaking and prolonged spells of pseudo-sleep are all seen in NEAD. A Variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease This is a very rare disease that historically occurred due to ingestion of beef infected with bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or iatrogenically from products such as human-derived growth hormone. There have been no new cases in recent years. The illness is characterised by rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus and ataxia. B Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis This is a progressive and usually fatal condition related to measles infection in childhood. It is characterised by encephalopathy, myoclonus, a movement disorder and eventually coma. Characteristic periodic complexes are seen on EEG. D Rasmussen encephalitis This is a rare inﬂammatory brain disease of unknown aetiology. It typically affects one hemisphere and results in seizures (often epilepsy partialis continua) and progressive hemiparesis.

stem: A 74-year-old man attends with a 6-month history of heaviness and discomfort in his upper legs, which is only present after walking for 5 minutes. He has always been a keen walker, being a member of the local Ramblers’ Association, but he is now unable to participate as he would like. He is, however, still able to cycle to his parttime job as a librarian. He has been previously fit and well, although was recently started on antihypertensive medication. He is an ex-smoker, having given up 5 years ago when his wife died. On examination his blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg. His pulse was 56 and regular. His peripheral pulses are all palpable, but the capillary return in his toes is slow. Neurological examination of his arms and legs is normal, apart from diminished ankle jerks, and reduced vibration sense distally in the lower limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lumbar canal stenosis
Lumbar canal stenosis (LCS) is the most likely diagnosis given this patient’s symptoms and history. Neurogenic claudication, characterised by heaviness and discomfort in the legs after walking, is a hallmark feature of LCS. This patient’s ability to cycle without symptoms is highly characteristic of LCS, as the flexed position of the spine while cycling increases the diameter of the spinal canal, alleviating nerve compression. Examination findings of diminished ankle jerks and reduced vibration sense may be seen in older adults with coexisting mild peripheral neuropathy, but they do not exclude LCS. The absence of motor weakness and the presence of palpable peripheral pulses further support LCS over vascular or muscular causes. Overall, the clinical picture aligns with degenerative changes in the lumbar spine leading to canal narrowing.

Abdominal aortic stenosis
Abdominal aortic stenosis typically presents with vascular claudication, which can be confused with neurogenic claudication. However, vascular claudication often results in pain rather than heaviness and discomfort and is not relieved by changes in spinal posture, such as flexion during cycling. Examination in vascular claudication would usually reveal diminished or absent peripheral pulses in the lower limbs, which is not the case here. Additionally, vascular claudication would not explain the neurological findings of reduced vibration sense and diminished ankle reflexes.
