B Tropical spastic paraparesis This syndrome, rare in the UK, is caused by HTLV1, which is negative in this case. A Taboparesis Tertiary syphilis could produce all of these symptoms and signs, but the investigations have ruled this illness out (negative VDRL and TPHA). One would expect cellular CSF in tertiary syphilis. C Multiple sclerosis Whilst this may present in a progressive manner, especially in older men, the reﬂexes would be brisk and prominent neuropsychiatric change is rare at the outset. E Disseminated encephalomyelitis This is a reasonable consideration in terms of explaining the symptoms and signs. However, the macrocytic anaemia and posterior column MRI signal change make subacute combined degeneration more likely.

stem: As the CT2 on call, you are asked to review a previously well 45year-old farmer on the ward. He was admitted with severe lower respiratory tract infection post inﬂuenza, and after multiple cutaneous abscesses were noted he was commenced on ﬂucloxacillin and gentamicin. According to the notes, his neurological examination on admission was entirely normal. You are asked to see him by the nurses some 48 hours later as he is complaining of upper limb and neck weakness, and the nurses note that he has difﬁculty when asked to open his eyes, shown below: There is a lack of facial expression and his saturations are dipping to below 90% as he is hypoventilating. He reports that his arms were not affected yesterday On examination, it appears that the upper limb weakness is worse proximally. There is no lower limb weakness. Deep tendon reﬂexes are diminished, and sensation is preserved. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 124 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Staphylococcus aureus is cultured from cutaneous abscesses. What is the diagnosis most suggested by this clinical picture?
explanation:
C Botulism The clinical photograph here shows bilateral ptosis and the clinical features are in keeping with 'descending paralysis'. This can be seen with botulism. Here, the skin abscesses may be the source of infection. B Guillain–Barré syndrome

GBS typically presents as an acute motor sensory neuropathy. This patient has reduced reﬂexes but other features like descending paralysis and eye involvement with cutaneous abscess points toward botulism. A Myasthenia gravis The acute onset and development of weakness in a clear descending pattern following abscess and antibiotic treatment would make MG less likely. However, it is important to realise that aminoglycosides such as gentamicin should not be given to patients with MG in view of their detrimental effect on neuromuscular transmission. This is a key piece of knowledge that the MRCP examiners like to test. In MG it ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness and limb weakness would be expected, but not in a descending pattern, like here. D Clostridium difﬁcile There is no history of diarrhoea, and it would not satisfactorily explain the neurological signs that are described here. Diagnosis of C. difﬁcile is by stool microscopy. E Organophosphate poisoning Whilst organophosphate poisoning is a possibility given his occupation as a farmer, it seems unlikely given that the symptoms of weakness started after the abscesses.

stem: You assess a 28-year-old woman in the Outpatient Clinic. She was diagnosed with myasthenia gravis 3 years ago and initially improved with oral anticholinesterase medication and immunosuppression. In the last 6 weeks, she has worried about a return of her symptoms despite compliance with medication. She describes generalised lethargy as worse at the end of the day and occasional diplopia. On systemic enquiry, she admits weight gain and ankle oedema. On general examination, you note palmar erythema, and resting tachycardia. What is the ﬁrst-line investigation?
explanation:
D Human chorionic gonadotrophin assay This patient describes some symptoms suggestive of myasthenia relapse. The majority of her other symptoms and signs are consistent with pregnancy, a common cause of myasthenia relapse. Pregnancy has a variable effect on the course of myasthenia. Women with

myasthenia that is stable prior to pregnancy are likely to remain stable throughout pregnancy, although a small proportion may have post-partum worsening. In poorly controlled myasthenia before pregnancy, ﬂares are most likely to occur in the ﬁrst trimester and the postpartum period. E Rheumatoid factor assay Rheumatoid antibodies are found in 10-40% of the population and there is an increased incidence of rheumatoid arthritis in myasthenia patients. However, this investigation would not help explain her symptoms and is not the best option provided. A Thyroid function testing and autoantibodies Autoimmune thyroid disease is common (3-8%) in those with myasthenia gravis, and should form part of the initial diagnostic work up. In this case, however, although resting tachycardia and palmar erythema are associated with hyperthyroidism, weight gain and ankle oedema would be associated with hypothyroidism. B Echocardiogram It may be used to investigate oedema and tachycardia but would not be a ﬁrst-line investigation in this context. C Computerised tomography (CT) chest This may be used to investigate for thymoma in myasthenia patients, but the presence of a thymoma would not explain her deterioration. Furthermore, the pregnancy status of a woman of child-bearing age should be established prior to exposing her to such high doses of radiation.

DR. JAM Alzheimer’s Disease Dementia is a progressive impairment of cognition that has an impact on daily functioning.  Overview Key Facts  Dementia is a progressive impairment of cognition that has an impact on daily functioning.  The most common form of dementia is Alzheimer's disease, which accounts for over 50% of all dementia cases.  Alzheimer's disease is associated with progressive degeneration of the cerebral cortex with associated widespread cortical atrophy.  Affected neurones become surrounded by amyloid plaque deposits, with reduced acetylcholine production.  This causes irreversible global, progressive impairment of brain function and eventually reduced intellectual ability (without impairment of consciousness).  There is no one clear cause, but numerous risk factors are implicated, with advancing age being the most common.  Other risk factors include smoking, hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and genetics.  Loss of short-term memory is often the first sign of the condition (often many years after neurodegeneration has begun).  Other changes may include changes in behaviour, personality, speech, perception, thought processes and mood.  It is important to exclude reversible causes of dementia before the diagnosis is formally made.  Management is dependent on the stage of the condition and may involve social and family/carer support, as well as drug treatment.  The condition is progressive; drug treatments aim to temporarily ease symptoms and slow progression. Epidemiology  Alzheimer’s disease makes up over 50% of all cases of dementia.  Of people living in the United Kingdom with dementia, it is estimated that 520 000 people have Alzheimer’s disease (Alzheimer's society).  Although prevalence increases with age, the prevalence of Alzheimer’s and in specific age groups has decreased over the last 20 years  this may be due to a reduction in vascular risk factors and better health education.  However, as life expectancy is increasing, overall, the number of people living with dementia is expected to continue rising.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  Risk factors for dementia include:  increasing age – main risk factor  genetics – positive family history, apolipoprotein E gene  cardiovascular disease risk factors – diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension  smoking  reduced activity levels  comorbidities such as stroke, Parkinson's disease and depression.  Other factors which may also have an effect on the development of the condition include:  heavy alcohol intake  low educational attainment  low cognitive stimulation  low social engagement/support. Pathophysiology  Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in the hippocampus and cerebral cortex.  Widespread atrophy of the cortex.  Loss of acetylcholine and synapses at the neurone level.  Epsilon 4 of the apolipoprotein E gene is a major risk factor.  Early-onset disease implicated by APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 genes.  Clinical Presentation  The hallmarks of presentation of Alzheimer's dementia may include the following, with a progressive course:  short-term memory loss  dysphasia  dyspraxia  behavioural changes, eg wandering, aggression, agitation, disinhibition  psychotic/psychiatric symptoms, such as depression, delusions and hallucinations  apathy  altered eating patterns  incontinence (late stages of disease).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include other forms of dementia: Signs/symptoms Clinical features Vascular dementia Gait disturbance Personality change Stepwise progression

DR. JAM Labile mood Urinary symptoms Insight preserved Cardiovascular disease risk factors Dementia with Lewy bodies/Parkinson’s disease dementia Fluctuating dementia Delirium Parkinsonism Visual hallucinations Sleep disorders Frontotemporal degeneration Stereotyped behaviours Personality change Loss of insight Expressive dysphasia Preserved memory Primitive reflexes Progresses slowly Family history More common in women, with early-onset before

Huntington’s disease Schizophrenialike psychosis Choreiform movement Depression Irritability Dementia Presents in earlier life during 20–40 years Family history Normal-pressure hydrocephalus Apathy Inattention Urinary incontinence Gait apraxia Presents in 50–70year-olds Reversible dementia Prion disease Myoclonic jerks Seizures Cerebellar ataxia Starts at < 50 years Rapid onset Rapid progression  Other differentials to consider:  depression/pseudodementia  mild cognitive impairment  delirium  other psychiatric disorders – schizophrenia, psychosis and mania  transient global amnesia  epilepsy  drugs – anticholinergics.  Diagnosis/Investigation  If dementia is suspected, diagnostic testing may involve:  history/examination – distinguishing between causes; history ideally from the patient and someone who knows the patient well

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  cognitive testing – mini-mental state examination and Addenbrooke’s cognitive examination  Baseline bloods – full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, vitamin B12/folate, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), syphilis and HIV  radiography – chest X-ray  brain imaging – CT/MRI  electroencephalogram (EEG)  NICE guidance recommends the use of the National Institute of Neurological and Communicative Disorders and Stroke and the Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders Association (NINCDS/ADRDA) diagnostic criteria for the assessment of Alzheimer's disease.  If the diagnosis remains uncertain and Alzheimer's disease is suspected, either:  FDG-PET (fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography CT), or perfusion SPECT (single-photon emission CT) if FDG-PET is unavailable, or  examine cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for either total tau or total tau and phosphorylated-tau 181 and either amyloid-beta 1–42 or amyloid-beta 1–42 and amyloid-beta 1–40.  Management Alzheimer’s disease management should involve the assessment and management of the patient's functional and social needs, as well as considering the supportive needs of the carer of the patient. Management should be based on a case-by-case basis. Non-pharmacological management  Patients should be given written information regarding:  the course of the condition and prognosis  medical treatment options available  support groups and associations  sources of legal and financial advice  driving advice (DVLA must be informed of all drivers diagnosed with Alzheimer's).  People with mild-to-moderate dementia should be given the opportunity to participate in structured group cognitive stimulation programmes to help maintain cognitive skills and day-to-day functioning.  Memory enhancement strategies should be discussed, such as using reminder notes, lists and reorganisation of possessions.  Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may be helpful for patients with symptoms of depression or anxiety, involving their carers.  Other non-pharmacological approaches for those with anxiety, depression or behaviour issues may include exercise, aromatherapy and multi-sensory stimulation.

DR. JAM  Palliative and end-of-care life should be discussed and planned as appropriate.  Social support should be initiated and progressed as the condition advances.  Pharmacological management  Medical management options for Alzheimer's disease include:  cholinesterase inhibitors, eg donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine:  indicated for mild-to-moderate disease  improve cognitive and behavioural symptoms  increase acetylcholine availability.  memantine:  indicated for moderate-to-severe disease  N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor antagonist.  Other pharmacological treatments for associated symptoms may be required, such as antidepressants for depression (avoid anticholinergics and tricyclic antidepressants).  Prognosis  The condition is a progressive disease with a 5–8 years average life expectancy from diagnosis.  There is currently no cure for the condition.  The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that people with dementia can expect to be:  in a mild or early-stage (forgetful, some language difficulties) for the first year or two  in a moderate stage (very forgetful, increasing speech difficulty, needs help with self-care) from the second to fourth or fifth year  in a severe or late-stage (near-total dependence and inactivity) from the fourth to fifth year onwards. Amyloidosis Amyloidosis is a clinical disorder caused by abnormal amyloid fibrils deposited in the tissues, altering their function.  Overview Key Facts  Amyloidosis is a clinical disorder caused by abnormal amyloid fibrils deposited in the tissues, altering their function.  It is a rare but fatal disease, responsible for 1 in 1500 deaths in the United Kindom (UK).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The main classifications are AA amyloidosis, AL amyloidosis (the most common) and ATTR amyloidosis – classified by the type of amyloid fibril deposition.  AL amyloidosis is of unknown cause and also called ‘primary amyloidosis’. It has associations with myeloma.  Clinical presentation depends on the site of deposition but can range from nephrotic syndrome to heart failure.  Diagnosis is by histological examination with Congo red stain classically showing green birefringence under polarised light. Immunoglobulins and serum or urine immunofixation show the presence of monoclonal protein.  Treatment of AL amyloidosis is usually chemotherapy – standard regimes include melphalan followed by stem cell transplant if eligible.  AA amyloidosis is associated with inflammatory arthropathies and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The mainstay of treatment is controlling the underlying condition.  Prognosis is variable but the presence of amyloid cardiac disease is a poor prognostic indicator. Epidemiology  Amyloidosis is a rare disease but the specific incidence is dependent on the type of amyloidosis.  It is a fatal disease, responsible for 1 in 1500 deaths in the UK.  AL amyloidosis is the most common, with an incidence of nine cases per million per year.  Age of diagnosis is around 65 years and less than 10% of patients are under 50.  Men have a higher prevalence and incidence than women. Aetiology  Dependent on the type of amyloidosis  AL amyloidosis – unknown cause but has associations with myeloma. No genetic, occupation or environmental risk factors have been identified for AL amyloidosis.  AA amyloidosis – 60% are secondary to inflammatory polyarthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ankylosing spondylitis and other types of arthritis.  Other causes include other inflammatory conditions such as IBD, chronic infections, etc.  The risk of developing AA amyloidosis without a background of an inflammatory disorder is very unlikely. Pathophysiology  There are around 23 different proteins that can form amyloid fibrils.  Amyloid diseases are classified chemically by the fibril protein – AA amyloidosis, AL amyloidosis, transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), described below.  Classification AA amyloidosis:

DR. JAM  Mainly an acute phase reactant.  Only a small number develop amyloidosis with elevated serum amyloid A levels – usually the kidney, liver and spleen are the main sites for deposition.  Systemic AA amyloidosis is a complication of chronic inflammation caused by rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn’s disease, malignancies, etc.  Treatment of these reduces the incidence of AA amyloidosis.  It will often present with nephrotic syndrome or renal dysfunction.  If not adequately treated, then AA amyloidosis end-stage renal failure (ESRF) can develop and dialysis is required.  Prognosis is overall poor even with treatment. AL amyloidosis:  Previously called ‘primary amyloidosis’.  Extracellular fibril-forming monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains accumulate in organs such as the heart, kidney, nervous system, lungs, colon.  Majority of patients have monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or asymptomatic myeloma.  Clinical presentation is variable – dyspnoea, weakness, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, impaired renal function, cardiomyopathy and heart failure.  Diagnosis is by histological examination and Congo-redpositive stain of the amyloid deposits, with classic green birefringence under polarised light.  Treatment is usually chemotherapy – standard regimes include melphalan followed by stem cell transplant.  Amyloid cardiac disease should be treated supportively. Amiodarone and pacemakers may be required for arrhythmias. A heart transplant can be considered.  Prognosis is variable but the presence of amyloid cardiac disease is a poor prognostic indicator. Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR)  An autosomal dominant disease that is associated with a large number of mutations.  Each variant involves a different organ – eg peripheral neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, renal impairment and proteinuria.  The requirement of dialysis is a poor prognostic indicator. Other types of amyloidosis:  These include heavy chain amyloidosis, beta-microglobulin amyloidosis (associated with CKD), hereditary renal amyloidosis, central nervous system amyloidosis (eg in Alzheimer's disease or prion proteins in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Other classifications of amyloidosis:  Localised.  Systemic.  Familial periodic fever syndromes – familial Mediterranean fever, Muckle–Wells syndrome, hyper IgD.  Inherited forms of amyloidosis – TTR amyloidosis, fibrinogen amyloidosis, gelsolin amyloidosis, apolipoprotein amyloidosis.  Senile systemic amyloidosis.  Dialysis amyloidosis.  Clinical Presentation  Variable clinical presentations dependent on which system is involved.  Symptoms:  fatigue  weight loss  easy bruising  breathlessness  oedema  peripheral neuropathy  autonomic symptoms.  Signs:  proteinuria  signs of heart failure – raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, murmurs  hepatomegaly, jaundice and ascites  glove and stocking neuropathy  autonomic disturbance – postural hypotension  GI bleeding  skin lesions – orbital purpura, enlarged goitre.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  chronic kidney disease (CKD)  other causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy  MGUS-associated nephropathy  membranous glomerulopathy  multiple myeloma  sarcoidosis  diabetes  lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Amyloidosis is suspected on the basis of symptoms and diagnosed with biopsy.

DR. JAM  Serum immunofixation – positive in 60% – shows the presence of monoclonal protein.  Urine immunofixation – positive in 80% with AL.  Immunoglobulin free light chain assay – very sensitive for diagnosing AL – with raised kappa lambda ratio.  Bone marrow aspirate should be done on all patients and will show clonal plasma cells.  Beta-2 microglobulin can help predict prognosis.  Biopsy of the affected organ will stain red with Congo red.  Any organ-specific investigations may be helpful such as an echocardiogram or cardiac MRI.  Management  Treatment of amyloidosis is dependent on the type.  Generally, the goal of treatment is to reduce the plasma cell clone which is responsible for the production of the immunoglobulin light chain. By reducing production, this means deposition is also reduced, in an attempt to halt progressive organ failure. Treatment of AL  Any patient who has biopsy-proven amyloidosis within any organs should be considered for chemotherapy or stem cell transplant.  Those who are candidates for stem cell transplant can be offered chemotherapy. Monitoring of immunoglobulin free light chains is used to assess response to treatment. Treatment of AA  The aim of the treatment of AA is to control the underlying inflammatory process.  Colchicine has been shown to be useful in reducing the development of AA in patients with familial Mediterranean fever.  Prognosis  Again, this is dependent on the type of amyloidosis.  The prognosis of AL amyloidosis is dependent on the response to therapy for suppression of light chain synthesis.  7-year survival rate sits around 80% in those who completely respond; this reduces to 57% for a partial response.  In patients who fail to respond, the survival at 7 years is around 30%.  The main predictor of mortality is the severity of cardiac involvement, which is now used as part of severity staging.  Prognosis of AA amyloidosis is hugely variable on the extent of the underlying disease.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Bacterial Meningitis Meningitis is an acute infection caused by inflammation of the meninges – that is the outer membranous lining covering of the brain and the spinal cord.  Overview Key Facts  Meningitis is an acute infection caused by inflammation of the meninges – that is the outer membranous lining covering of the brain and the spinal cord.  Meningitis can be caused by either bacterial, viral or fungal infections or non-infective causes like tumours, autoimmune disorders, trauma, and certain drugs.  Bacterial meningitis affects all ages – most commonly seen in children. It is a life-threatening condition.  Route of transmission is close contact (droplets or secretions from the upper respiratory tract).  The cardinal symptoms of meningitis include headache, fever, photophobia, vomiting and neck stiffness.  Diagnosis is made with blood tests, computed tomography (CT) scan and lumbar puncture.  Intravenous (IV) Ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice for bacterial meningitis. Epidemiology  Developed countries – 2 to 5 cases per 100 000 annually.  Meningococcal infection (mostly caused by Men B subtype) is more common compared to pneumococcal infection.  Neisseria Meningitidis is the causative organism of recurring epidemics of meningitis every 8–12 years.  Most cases are sporadic, outbreaks occur especially in adolescents.  Influenza A, asplenia and complement deficiencies predispose to infection. Aetiology  In the United Kingdom (UK), the most common causative organisms of acute bacterial meningitis in children > 3 months and adults include:  Neisseria meningitidis (Meningococcal infection)  Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcal infection)  Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).  Most common causative organisms in neonates < 1 month of age:  Streptococcus agalactiae  Escherichia coli

DR. JAM  S. pneumoniae  Listeria monocytogenes (also a concern in the elderly). Pathophysiology Bacteria initially colonise in the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells ⇢ transported across the cells to intravascular space by creating separations in the apical tight junctions of columnar epithelial cells ⇢ bloodborne bacteria reach intraventricular choroid plexus ⇢ directly infect choroid plexus epithelial cells and gain access to the CSF ⇢ bacteria adhere to cerebral capillary endothelial cells and migrate through the cells to reach the CSF ⇢ rapid multiplication of bacteria within CSF due to absence of effective host immune defence system ⇢ elevated consequence of elevated levels of CSF cytokines and chemokines ⇢ clinical signs and symptoms.  Clinical Presentation  Triad of fever, headache, nuchal rigidity (pathognomonic sign of meningeal irritation).  Level of consciousness decreased – ranging from lethargy to coma.  Diffuse erythematous non-blanching maculopapular rash.  Photophobia.  Capillary refill time > 2 seconds.  Kernig's and Brudzinski's sign positive – signs of meningeal irritation.  Kernig's sign -pain and resistance on passive knee extension with hips fully flexed.  Brudzinski's sign - hips flex on bending the head forward.  Focal seizures due to focal arterial ischaemia or infarction or focal oedema.  Cushing's reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration, cerebral herniation).  Non-specific signs like fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, decreased appetite, chills.  Differential Diagnosis  Fungal meningitis  Viral encephalitis  Central nervous system malignancy  Brain or spinal epidural abscess  Para meningeal infection  Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever  Non-infective causes like SLE, Beçhet’s syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full Blood Count

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Polymerase chain reaction  CT or magnetic resonance imaging  Lumbar puncture – CSF abnormalities in bacterial meningitis:  opening pressure > 180 mmH2O  white blood cells 10 microL to 10,000 microL : neutrophils predominate  CSF glucose – < 0.4  glucose < 2.2 mmol/l  protein > 0.45 g/l.  Glass test for rashes.  Management Non-pharmacological  Adequate rest  Adequate hydration and nutrition. Pharmacological Suspected Meningococcal infection with a nonblanching rash:  hospital admission  single dose of Benzylpenicillin at the earliest in the outpatient set up:  dose:  child < 1 year – 300 mg  child 1 – 9 years – 600 mg  adults and child 10 years and above 1200 mg. Suspected Meningococcal infection without non- blanching rash:  hospital admission  empirical antibiotics – either Benzylpenicillin, Cefotaxime, Chloramphenicol  vancomycin is added if the patient has a history of travel outside the UK. Chemoprophylaxis for post-exposure or close contacts:  given to all individuals who were in close contact with the patient for seven days prior to the onset of the illness  medical professionals involved in the care of the patient  ciprofloxacin is preferred antibiotic over rifampicin. Ciprofloxacin is preferred as a STAT dose  dexamethasone is added to reduce the risk of complications.  Prognosis  The mortality rate ranges between 3%–7%

DR. JAM  Risk of death increases with various factors including low level of consciousness, children, decreased CSF glucose.  Complications of meningitis include the following:  hearing loss  memory Impairment  seizures  gait disturbances  motor deficits  hydrocephalus  visual disturbances. Behçet Syndrome Behçet syndrome is a vasculitis that manifests with a variety of mucocutaneous, vascular, gastrointestinal, ophthalmological and central nervous system symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Behçet syndrome is a vasculitis that manifests with a variety of mucocutaneous, vascular, gastrointestinal, ophthalmological and central nervous system (CNS) symptoms.  There are no specific investigative tests but pathergy testing, as well as autoimmune screening, can help to rule out other diagnoses.  The mainstay of treatment for severe disease is corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapies, eg azathioprine.  Symptoms usually improve with time and treatment over a course of 1–2 years. Epidemiology  It is often seen in patients from Turkish, Israeli and EastAsian backgrounds.  It is most common in young adults aged between 20 and 30 years.  Symptoms tend to be more severe in men. Aetiology  Aetiology is unclear, with studies showing possible genetic predisposition, with increased inflammation and immunological activity.  Distinction between whether it is an auto-inflammatory or auto-immune disorder is not well established.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology is unclear, with theories suggesting the presence of neutrophil hyper-reactivity.  Clinical Presentation  Diagnosis based on clinical criteria of:  recurrent oral ulcers  plus two other clinical manifestations of:  recurrent genital ulcers around the scrotum or labia  skin manifestations such as erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions or papulopustular and/or nodular lesions  eye involvement, eg uveitis, hypopyon  positive pathergy test which involves the formation of a pustule/papule 48 hours after the skin is pricked with a sterile needle  gastrointestinal involvement, eg crampy abdominal pain, diarrhoea  blood vessel involvement (rare), eg deep vein thrombosis, thrombophlebitis  CNS involvement, eg seizures, cranial nerve palsies, dizziness, memory impairment.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  aphthous stomatitis  Crohn’s disease/ulcerative colitis  herpes simplex  necrotising vasculitis  seronegative spondyloarthropathies  acne vulgaris  erythema nodosum  superficial thrombophlebitis  rheumatoid arthritis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There are no specific diagnostic tests for Behçet syndrome, but tests are performed to rule out alternative diagnoses.  Pathergy testing:  subcutaneous skin prick forms an induration in the skin within 48 hours that may be present with a papule/pustule  positive in Behçet syndrome.  Rheumatoid factor:  to rule out rheumatoid arthritis if associated joint symptoms  negative in Behçet syndrome.

DR. JAM  Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs):  to rule out autoimmune diseases  negative in Behçet syndrome.  Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs):  to rule out necrotising vasculitis  negative in Behçet syndrome.  HLA-B51:  strongly associated genetic factor in Behçet syndrome  positive in Behçet syndrome.  Lumbar puncture:  to rule out tuberculosis (TB), herpes simplex or listeriosis if neurological involvement  may find lymphocytosis or polymorphonuclear cells.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain:  may find white matter changes if CNS involvement suspected.  Colonoscopy/endoscopy:  to rule out inflammatory bowel disease if GI symptoms  may find inflammation and aphthous-type ulcers in Behçet syndrome.  Computed tomography (CT) chest/pulmonary angiography:  indicated if haemoptysis to rule out pulmonary aneurysm.  Management  Mucocutaneous ulcers:  first line – topical corticosteroids, eg triamcinolone – used for mild symptoms  second line – colchicine, oral corticosteroids, eg prednisolone, or immunosuppressive therapy, eg azathioprine – used for 1–2 years for active lesions resistant to topical treatment  third line – TNF-α inhibitors, eg infliximab – used for 1–2 years for disease resistant to corticosteroids or oral immunosuppressant drugs.  Eye involvement:  mild/moderate – prednisolone + azathioprine  severe – prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg infliximab or adalimumab).  GI involvement:  prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg infliximab).  CNS involvement:  prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg infliximab).  Major vascular involvement:  prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg ciclosporin).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Remission often occurs with treatment over 1–2 years.  If symptoms are controlled during this time doses can be tapered down.  Involvement of ocular, major vascular and GI systems carries a poorer prognosis.  Behçet eye disease can lead to blindness.  Other  Monitoring:  patients are likely to require monitoring every 2–3 months when using immunosuppressants  includes blood tests such as full blood count, liver function tests, urea and electrolytes and annual ophthalmological examinations. Bell’s Palsy Bell’s palsy is a unilateral facial palsy with acute onset evolving within 72 hours.  Overview Key Facts  Bell’s palsy is a unilateral facial palsy with acute onset evolving within 72 hours.  Diagnosis of exclusion is often made clinically.  Treated with high-dose prednisolone in most cases with the addition of antiviral agents and/or surgical decompression in severe cases.  Return of facial tone and movement should be present within 4–6 months.  More common in younger age groups (15–45 years old). Epidemiology  Most common in those aged between 15 and 45 years of age, with an incidence of 23–32 cases per 100 000 per year.  Equal distribution between men and women.  Affects the left or right side of the face in an equal distribution. Aetiology  Linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) that may be caused by immune suppression. The underlying aetiology is not yet certain.

DR. JAM  Risk factors include pregnancy, diabetes, intranasal flu vaccine, family history, Hispanic ethnicity and cold climates. Pathophysiology  HSV-1 causes infection of Schwann cells and destruction to ganglion cells.  Facial nerve conduction blockade occurs proximal to the geniculate ganglion meaning all branches are affected equally.  Subsequently results in demyelination and inflammation of neurones of the facial nerve:  somatomotor axons – affects muscles of facial expression  axons supplying stapedius muscle – hyperacusis  gustatory fibres – hypogeusia/dysgeusia  sensory fibres – otalgia and posterior auricular pain  parasympathetic axons – dysfunction of salivary glands and lacrimal glands.  Clinical Presentation  Single episode (recurrent episodes may suggest an alternative diagnosis to Bell’s palsy).  Unilateral facial involvement.  Involvement of all facial nerve branches – unequal distribution of weakness essentially rules out Bell’s palsy.  Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes).  Otalgia.  Facial synkinesis.  Absence of constitutional symptoms. Characteristic features of Bell’s palsy – unilateral face weakness/loss of movement:  There are multiple classification systems that can be used to determine the severity of facial dysfunction, however, these are rarely used in practice in the context of Bell’s palsy, and are very subjective.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  Ramsay Hunt syndrome  Lyme disease  facial nerve tumour (benign/malignant)  blunt force trauma  chronic otitis media  cholesteatoma  idiopathic orofacial granulomatosis  uveoparotid fever  cerebrovascular accident.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The majority of cases are a diagnosis of exclusion made by clinical diagnosis.  First investigations to order:  electroneuronography – indicated if complete facial paralysis showing more than 90% decrease in muscle action potential on the affected side compared with the unaffected side of the face  needle electromyography – absence of voluntary motor unit potentials  Borrelia burgdorferi – exclusion of Lyme disease.  Investigations to consider:  pure tone audiometry – normal  tympanometry and stapedius reflex – impaired reflex of the ipsilateral efferent limb  magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) – normal, used to exclude alternative diagnoses  computed tomography (CT) – normal, used to exclude alternative diagnoses.  Management  First-line:  corticosteroids – prednisolone  eye protection – to prevent keratoconjunctivitis sicca.  In severe cases of complete paralysis:  antiviral therapy – aciclovir, valaciclovir  surgical decompression.  Prognosis  Ninety-four per cent of patients with incomplete paralysis will recover fully compared with only 61% of patients with complete facial paralysis.

DR. JAM  Other factors that affect prognosis include older age, diabetes, pregnancy and disturbance of taste on first presentation.  Other  Complications:  keratoconjuncivitis sicca (dry eye)  ulcerative keratitis  ectropion  gustatory hyperlacrimation  contracture and synkinesis. Benign Neck Lumps And Swellings Benign neck lumps and swelling can be either congenital or acquired, and can arise from a number of anatomical structures in the neck.  Overview Key Facts  Benign neck lumps and swelling can be either congenital or acquired, and can arise from a number of anatomical structures in the neck.  The most common benign soft tissue tumours found in the neck are lipomas, which usually present as asymptomatic, soft, poorly-defined masses deep to the skin.  Other benign neck lumps include:  cystic hygroma  thyroglossal cyst  branchial cyst  ranula  laryngocele  sialadenitis/sialithiasis (covered separately)  pharyngeal pouch (covered separately).  Occasionally what a patient might identify as a lump is actually part of their normal anatomy, eg structures such as:  transverse process of C1 vertebra  hyoid bone  thyroid or cricoid cartilage.  If the diagnosis is uncertain, referral should not be delayed by undertaking investigations in primary care, particularly in high-risk individuals. Epidemiology Cystic hygroma

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Cystic hygromas occur in approximately one per cent of children with no particular gender or ethnic preponderance. Thyroglossal cyst  Occurs in around 7% of the population and most commonly presents in childhood. Branchial cyst  The most common cause of congenital neck masses, the majority present in childhood.  Occasionally they may present later in life, usually by early adulthood. Ranula  Ranulas usually present in childhood or early adulthood. Laryngocele  The condition is rare, and believed to be more frequent in wind instrument players and glassblowers. Aetiology  Congenital:  thyroglossal cyst  branchial cyst  cystic hygroma.  Most common acquired benign neck masses are:  ranula  laryngocele  pharyngeal pouch. Pathophysiology Thyroglossal cyst  Persistent connection between the caecum of the tongue and the pyramidal lobe of the thyroid gland causing a mass in the midline. Branchial cyst  Congenital epithelial cysts occurring lateral from the midline, thought to be due to failure of obliteration of the second branchial cleft in embryonic development. Cystic hygroma  A cystic lymphatic lesion that occurs in the posterior triangle of the neck.  Most present at birth or before the age of two years. Ranula  A type of mucocele in the floor of the mouth originating from the sublingual glands.  The two principal causes are:  a blocked duct causing a swelling  a ruptured cyst that leads to extravasation of mucin. Laryngocele

DR. JAM  An air pocket that arises from the deepest point of the laryngeal ventricle.  Clinical Presentation Thyroglossal cyst  Midline cystic lump that is near the hyoid bone and moves upwards when the individual swallows or protrudes their tongue. Branchial cyst  painless, slow-growing, smooth, fluctuant swellings in the lateral neck. Cystic hygroma  Can be seen on antenatal ultrasound scans in pregnancy, commonly found in neck and axillae, soft painless swellings, sometimes translucent. Ranula  Clear/bluish cysts usually contained within the floor of the mouth (mylohyoid) but can push through. Laryngocele  An air-filled cyst can bulge internally into the larynx, externally into the neck or be combined (where the connection is through the thyrohyoid membrane).  They usually present with an intermittent neck swelling, which becomes palpable when the the valsalva manoeuvre is performed.  Differential Diagnosis  Thyroid lump/swelling – may be nodular or diffuse  Inflammatory lymphadenopathy  Malignant lesions  Normal anatomical structures.  Diagnosis/Investigation General investigations:  bloods (FBC, U+Es, CRP)  plain neck radiograph  ultrasound scan imaging.  Management  NICE guidance of management of a neck lump of unknown cause:  admit the person immediately if there are symptoms such as stridor, or signs of superior vena cava obstruction  consider admission if the person has dysphagia, signs of aspiration, or symptoms or signs of sepsis.  Consider an urgent referral using suspected cancer pathway if:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  there is an unexplained neck lump in a person aged 45 years or older  there is a persistent and unexplained neck lump in a person younger than 45 years of age.  Consider arranging an ultrasound scan if there is an unexplained lump that is increasing in size:  For adults 25 years of age and older refer for an urgent ultrasound appointment (within two weeks).  Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral if ultrasound scan findings are uncertain or suggestive of soft tissue sarcoma.  For children and young people up to and including 24 years of age, refer for a very urgent ultrasound appointment (within 48 hours).  Consider a very urgent referral if ultrasound findings are uncertain or suggestive of soft tissue sarcoma.  Specific management options Thyroglossal cyst  Referral to ENT to consider a Sistrunk's procedure. Branchial cyst  Referral to ENT, antibiotics to treat infections or abscess, definitive treatment is with excision. Cystic hygroma  Sclerotherapy or surgical removal. Ranula  Treatment is by surgical excision, which must include excision of the sublingual gland. Laryngocele  Treatment is by surgical excision (endoscopic or external approach depending on size and location).  Prognosis  Will be dependent on the extent of swelling, whether it has affected surrounding structures and the underlying pathology. Thyroglossal cyst  Excellent prognosis after Sistrunk's procedure, approximately 10% recur. Branchial cyst  Persistent problems with infection or drainage is usually resolved with surgical excision. Cystic hygroma  Dependent on the size and time of detection. Ranula  some ranulas may spontaneously resolve without treatment; usually excision is required.

DR. JAM  Following excision symptoms usually resolve completely. Laryngocele  Enlargement can cause hoarseness and in severe cases can cause airway obstruction.  Laryngoceles can also become infected (laryngopyocele).  Laryngoceles may also be associated with laryngeal malignancy. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is a short-lived attack of vertigo, often lasting less than 30 seconds. Prognosis  Overview Key Facts  Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a short-lived attack of vertigo, often lasting less than 30 seconds.  The majority of cases are due to displaced otolith particles, which usually work with the hair cells to allow motion sensing within the semi-circular canals.  It is diagnosed with the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre.  It can be treated with the Epley Manoeuvre.  Surgery is reserved for the most extreme and refractory cases. Epidemiology  One of the commonest causes of vertigo.  Incidence peak in those between 50–70 years.  Lifetime prevalence of 2.4% in European countries.  1-year prevalence of 1.6%. Aetiology  Majority of cases are primary BPPV.  Others may be associated with other inner ear conditions, including vestibular neuronitis and labyrinthitis. Pathophysiology  BPPV results from the displacement of otoliths (crystals within the ear), which normally allow the sensing of motion.  These otoliths travel from the otolith membrane and enter the semi-circular canals.  Eventually, the accumulation of these displaced otoliths (canaliths) becomes great enough to move the cupula (the structure containing the motion sensing hair cells).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  This allows the cupula to detect linear motion – eg gravity – which it would not normally detect.  This triggers the vestibulo-ocular reflex causing nystagmus and vertigo. The position of the otoliths (Otoconia) in the posterior canal: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BPPV_otoconiaweb.jpg This file is licensed under the Creative Commons AttributionShare Alike 4.0 International license.  Clinical Presentation  Short-lived episodes of vertigo typically lasting 20–30 seconds.  These episodes are usually triggered by a change in head position, but there may be a lag period of 5–20 seconds between the movement and the vertigo.  There should be no hearing deterioration, unless there is another underlying condition.  There is no associated tinnitus.  Nausea is common, but vomiting is not a typical feature.  The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre is used to diagnose the condition:  the patient is lying on a couch such that their head overhangs the head of the couch  the examiner stands to one side of the patient  the patient sits up and turns their head to face the examiner  the examiner holds the patient’s head in that position and quickly lays the patient flat  the eyes must remain open  repeat this test on the other side.  The reproduction of symptoms or nystagmus is considered a positive test.  It is important to check for any neck problems or any back problems as not to injure the patient.  Differential Diagnosis  Labyrinthitis/vestibular neuronitis.  Meniere's disease.  Transient ischaemic attack (TIA) and stroke.  Multiple sclerosis.  Acoustic neuroma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Clinical diagnosis using history and exam as above.

DR. JAM  Management Non-pharmacological  The mainstay of management of this condition is a movement known as the Epley Manoeuvre.  This is performed initially in the same way as the Dix– Hallpike test, but slower and in a controlled manner:  positioned as above  turn patient’s head to the affected (bad) side, hold this position here for 30 seconds  lie the patient flaw slowly, keep the head turned towards the affected side, with the neck in extension over the edge of the bed  the head remains turned like this for 30 seconds  turn the head towards the good side by 90°  keeping the head still, ask the patient to lie on the hip and shoulder of the unaffected (good) side  turn the head a further 90° towards the good side, maintain 30 seconds  keep the head close to the shoulder on the good side, bring the patient to a sitting position, maintain this for 30 seconds  turn the head to the centre and flex the neck to place on the chin, maintain this for 30 seconds.  After the manoeuvre, the patient should not drive home, they should not lie flat for two nights, and for a further five nights they should not lie on the bad side.  If it is not possible for the patient to attend an appointment, they can perform Brandt–Daroff exercises at home, but these are not as effective as an Epley Manoeuvre performed by a health professional.  Pharmacological  Pharmacological management of this condition is not effective. Surgical  Surgery is the last resort of management.  It involves denervation of the semi-circular canals.  This has a risk of deafness but is very effective.  Prognosis  The normal course of BPPV is spontaneous remission, but there is a high chance of recurrence.  This recuurance rate is approximately 50% in five years.  BPPV itself is not a dangerous condition, but it does increase the risk of falls, especially in the older age group.

DR. JAM Clostridium Botulinum Clostridium botulinum is a Gram-positive, anaerobic bacillus.  Overview Key Facts  Clostridium botulinum is a Gram-positive, anaerobic bacillus.  It produces a neurotoxin responsible for botulism – a neuroparalysis characterised by cranial nerve palsies, oculobulbar weakness and symmetrical flaccid paralysis.  Diagnosed by detection of the toxin in bodily fluids.  Treatment consists of supportive care and administration of antitoxin. Patients should have their vital capacity, oxygen saturation and inspiratory force monitored in an intensive care setting.  Long-term complications include fatigue, weakness and dyspnoea on exertion.  Respiratory dysfunction is a potential complication and may occur due to upper airway obstruction or diaphragmatic muscle weakness.  The mortality rate is 3–5% overall and < 1% in infant botulism. Epidemiology  Spores are ubiquitous in the soil worldwide and are found in agricultural products and the intestinal tract of animals, including fish.  Extremely rare in the United Kingdom (UK), more common in the United States of America (USA).  Men and women affected equally.  Wound botulism is the most common form in the UK, whereas infant botulism is the most common in the USA.  Food-borne botulism is most commonly seen in outbreaks.  Intravenous (IV) drug users are at particular risk of wound botulism. Aetiology  Clostridium botulinum exists as a spore until environmental conditions are optimal to allow germination.  There are three naturally occurring forms of botulism:  food-borne botulism – ingestion of preformed toxin in contaminated foods, most commonly home-canned fruits and vegetables and smoked or preserved meats and fish.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  wound botulism – spores germinate within contaminated wounds.  infant botulism – ingestion of spores (commonly from honey or soil) which germinate in the intestinal tract and release neurotoxin.  Inhalation botulism is another form, but does not occur naturally and is caused by the release of the toxin in aerosol, such as bioterrorism.  There are seven distinct neurotoxins produced by the organism and human disease is caused by toxins A, B and E. Pathophysiology  Botulism occurs from entry of the toxin into the systemic circulation via the mucosa or a break in the skin.  Once in the circulation, the toxin is transported to the presynaptic nerve terminal of peripheral and cranial nerves.  The toxin is a metalloproteinase that cleaves SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction.  This prevents the fusion of transmitter-containing vesicles with the presynaptic membrane and therefore inhibits the release of acetylcholine.  This results in paralysis or autonomic dysfunction.  Clinical Presentation  All three types of botulism present with neuroparalysis, including:  blurred vision, diplopia and ptosis secondary to cranial nerve lll, lV and Vl palsies  dysarthria and dysphagia secondary to oculobulbar weakness or cranial nerve lX, X and Xll palsies  oculobulbar weakness can also contribute to blurred vision and diplopia  symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes  in infants, there may be hypotonia, feeding difficulties and weakened cry  urinary retention, constipation, postural hypotension and dry mouth secondary to autonomic dysfunction.  Food-borne and infantile botulism are associated with GI symptoms, such as cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.  Fever is characteristically absent.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  Guillain–Barré syndrome  myasthenia gravis  Lambert–Eaton syndrome  toxicity, eg magnesium, shellfish.

DR. JAM  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bioassay for botulinum toxin in samples from serum, vomit, gastric secretions, stool or foods.  Culture of samples may be performed in food-borne or infantile botulism.  Electromyography (EMG) testing may be considered and is useful for investigating other differentials such as Lambert– Eaton syndrome. In botulism, sensory nerve studies are normal, but muscle action potentials are significantly reduced.  Management  Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment and patients should have their vital capacity, oxygen saturation and inspiratory force monitored in an intensive care setting.  Mechanical ventilation is appropriate in any patient with upper airway compromise.  Rapid administration of the antitoxin is essential, of which there are several types:  intravenous (IV) human botulism immunoglobulin is preferred in infants  horse-derived heptavalent botulism antitoxin is preferred in adults.  Gastric lavage may be attempted in adults with food-borne botulism if exposure was recent.  Surgical debridement is performed in wound botulism.  Prognosis  Respiratory dysfunction is a potential complication and may occur due to upper airway obstruction or diaphragmatic muscle weakness.  Mortality rate is 3–5% overall and < 1% in infant botulism.  Full recovery takes weeks to months.  Long-term complications include fatigue, weakness and dyspnoea on exertion. Cluster Headache Headache is a common non-specific symptom and may be divided into primary headache (no clear underlying cause) and secondary headache (occurs due to underlying pathology).  Overview Key Facts  Headache is a common non-specific symptom and may be divided into primary headache (no clear underlying cause) and secondary headache (occurs due to underlying pathology).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Causes of primary headache include:  migraine  cluster headache  tension-type headache.  Causes of secondary headache include:  infection  neoplasm  medication overuse  trauma  vascular disorders.  Cluster headache describes a rare type of primary headache in which attacks occur in series lasting for weeks or months (socalled cluster periods).  These series of attacks may be separated by remission periods, usually lasting months or years.  The pain associated with cluster headache can be so severe that patients may consider or even commit suicide.  Men are more often affected than women and the onset of attacks is typically between ages 25 and 50 years.  About 10–15% of patients have chronic cluster headache, without such remission periods.  Attacks consist of:  severe, strictly unilateral pain, which is orbital, supraorbital or temporal, or in any combination of these sites  lasting 15–180 minutes  occurring from once every other day to eight times a day.  The pain is often associated with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms:  ipsilateral conjunctival injection  lacrimation  nasal congestion  rhinorrhoea  forehead and facial sweating  miosis  ptosis and/or eyelid oedema  restlessness or agitation.  Diagnosis is clinical, based on fulfilling International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICD, third edition) diagnostic criteria.  Further testing may be required to exclude secondary causes or to diagnose them if there is clinical suspicion.  Cluster headaches can be subdivided into episodic (up to 90% of cases) and chronic (around 10% of cases).  Episodic cluster headache:  attacks occur in periods lasting from seven days to one year and are separated by pain-free periods lasting at least one month  cluster periods usually last between two weeks and three months.

DR. JAM  Chronic cluster headache:  attacks occur for more than one year without remission, or with remission periods lasting less than 1-month  chronic cluster headache may arise de novo or evolve from episodic cluster headache.  The aetiology is unclear and treatment can be difficult.  Management of the acute attack includes inhaled oxygen (via face mask) and subcutaneous sumatriptan.  A reducing course of steroids may be helpful, and intranasal lidocaine and occipital nerve blocks or stimulation have been used with some effect.  Verapamil is the first-line agent for prophylaxis; topiramate, sodium valproate and lithium can be used in cases resistant to treatment.  Patients may continue to have episodes throughout their lives, although periods of remission in between clusters of episodes tend to lengthen as the patient ages. Epidemiology  Cluster headache is a rare condition, with an estimated 1-year prevalence of around 50 per 100 000 adults, with a lifetime prevalence of around 125 per 100 000 (NICE).  The typical age of onset of cluster headache is 25–50 years, although most patients report onset before 30 years.  Men are affected about four times more than women, overall. Aetiology  The cause is not clearly understood, but may be a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Pathophysiology  Aetiology is unclear, but the basic pathophysiology seems to be related to hypothalamic grey matter dysfunction, leading to dilatation of cranial vessels.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation of primary headache includes various characters of headache, ie dull, throbbing or stabbing.  Associated features may include:  nausea and vomiting  dizziness  photophobia  lacrimation  pericranial tenderness  aura (focal and transient neurological symptoms associated with migraine).  Differential Diagnosis  Headaches may be due to a wide range of causes including:  paroxysmal hemicrania  migraine

At least one of the following symptoms or signs, ipsilateral to the headache: conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhoea eyelid oedema forehead and facial sweating forehead and facial flushing sensation of fullness in the ear miosis and/or ptosis

A sense of restlessness or agitation D – Attacks have a frequency between one every other day and eight per day for more than half of the time when the disorder is active.  National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend referral to secondary care with urgency depending on the clinical situation if there are any red flags or serious causes of headache suspected, such as:  new, sudden or severe or unexpected headache  progressive or persistent headache  fever  neck pain and/or stiffness  photophobia  papilloedema  new-onset neurological deficit  atypical aura or new-onset aura in a patient on combined oral contraceptive  visual disturbance or vomiting (unless a diagnosis of migraine is clear)  contacts with similar symptoms  recent head trauma (within the last three months)  headache worse on standing or lying down  current or recent pregnancy  history of malignancy  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)/immunosuppression.  If the diagnosis is unclear and serious causes have been ruled out:  ask the patient to keep a headache diary  arrange a review of the results  possibly arrange neurology consultation.  Management  High-flow oxygen and sumatriptan have been shown to be effective in the acute treatment of cluster headache.  Sufferers may be given a card to present at the Emergency Department to gain rapid access to oxygen or may have a home supply.  Sumatriptan is available as a subcutaneous injection (6 mg) or nasal spray (20 mg).  A reducing course of steroids may be helpful, and intranasal lidocaine and occipital nerve blocks or stimulation have been used with some effect.  Verapamil is the treatment of choice for the prevention of cluster headaches. The starting dose is usually 240 mg daily in three divided doses, titrating gradually to effect.

CNS Tumours Cerebral tumours can be classed as either primary (arises in the brain) or secondary (due to cerebral metastasis from distant sites).  Overview Key Facts  Cerebral tumours can be classed as either primary (arises in the brain) or secondary (due to cerebral metastasis from distant sites).  Cerebral metastasis (secondary brain tumour) is the most common cause of brain tumours overall.  Primary tumours can be classed as:  Glial cell origin (‘glioma’ – account for 50% of primary brain tumours):  astrocytoma  oligodendroglioma  ependymoma.  Non-glial cell origin:  mesenchymal tumours (meningioma)  pituitary lesions  nerve sheath tumours (schwannoma, neurofibroma)  haematopoietic tumours (primary cerebral lymphoma)  germ-cell tumours (germinoma, teratoma)  neuronal tumours  others, including craniopharyngioma.  There may be a history of progressive onset of neurological deficit.  History, physical examination, chest radiographs, tumour markers and CT scanning usually help establish diagnosis.  A more specific diagnosis is usually confirmed after biopsy.  Treatment depends on the cause and type of tumour as well as stage of disease.

DR. JAM Epidemiology Cerebral metastasis  30–50% of brain tumours are metastases from other primaries  15% of patients with malignancy present with brain metastasis as the presenting symptom  50% of brain metastases are solitary on CT (30% on MRI). Primary brain tumours  Glioma (50% of primary brain tumours): three-quarters are high grade  Meningioma (15% of primary brain tumours)  Pituitary lesions (5% of primary brain tumours). Aetiology Cerebral metastasis  Most commonly due to primary tumours from:  lung  breast  bowel  melanoma  renal cell. Meningioma  Arises from arachnoid cap cells. Pituitary tumours  5% of pituitary tumours are locally invasive.  Distant spread (CSF or blood-borne) is rare. Pathophysiology Pituitary tumours  Functional tumours secrete excessive amounts of pituitary hormones.  The symptoms are due to the secreted hormones.  Non-functional tumours do not secrete pituitary hormones.  The symptoms associated with these are due to the mass effect (compression), such as bitemporal hemianopia due to pressure on the nearby optic chiasma. Glioblastoma multiforme  Histology:  regional heterogeneity within a single lesion  highly anaplastic glial cells  vascular proliferation and thrombosis (diagnostic)  necrosis (diagnostic)  The macroscopic appearance is of:  greyish ill-defined mass  areas of necrosis and haemorrhage.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Anaplastic Astrocytoma  Histology shows:  diffusely infiltrating astrocytes  nuclear atypia  no microvascular proliferation or necrosis (seen only with GBM).  The macroscopic appearance is of:  white ill-defined mass, sometimes expanding into a gyrus. Meningioma  Histology shows:  many types (meningothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, and many more)  calcification, not uncommon (psammoma bodies)  whorls and lobules of cells are present in some types  sheets of spindle-shaped cells in others  histological type does not correlate with prognosis.  Macroscopic appearance is of:  rubbery, round, lobulated mass  firmly attached to dura.  Clinical Presentation  There is progressive onset of neurological deficit (compared with more acute in cerebral vascular accidents), usually the deficit is motor.  Signs of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) due to mass effect from the tumour or oedema around the tumour.  Seizure (consider cerebral tumours especially in a new seizure disorder in an adult).  Sudden onset of symptoms:  if presentation is due to a bleeding into a tumour. Pituitary tumours  Functional tumours  acromegaly (excess of growth hormone)  Cushing’s disease (excess of ACTH)  galactorrhoea (milky nipple discharge) and infertility in women (excess of prolactin)  hyperthyroidism (excess of thyroid stimulating hormone), rare condition.  Non-functional tumours  visual field defects or deteriorating visual acuity due to pressure on optic chiasma  headache  cranial nerve palsy/proptosis (if invading cavernous sinus)

Primary brain tumours  CT, pre-contrast and post-contrast scans are usually required:  lesion enhancement with contrast is possible only if there is a defect in the blood–brain barrier in the lesion  some lesions are relatively homogeneous and show quite uniform enhancement with contrast (eg meningioma)  some lesions are heterogeneous with areas of increased attenuation (whiter) and areas of decreased attenuation (darker), and show non-uniform enhancement (e.g. GBM)  CT scan (even with contrast) may miss small lesions that may be demonstrable on MRI. Primary brain tumours  Radiotherapy:  this is mainly used for malignant neoplasms  it is the standard adjuvant therapy for treatment of most high-grade gliomas  radiotherapy has more impact on survival than the type of surgery.  Stereotactic radiosurgery:  this is high-dose radiation therapy from multiple trajectories converging on the target tumour tissue  maximises treatment to the target, minimises effect on normal tissue  the target is identified with a modified stereotactic frame  the target needs to be small (< 3 cm). Stereotactic radiosurgery can be done as a one-shot day case or a fractionated course.  accepted indications are:  AVM – useful for lesions not amenable to clipping or coiling, or as part of a combined procedure  vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)  metastasis. Pituitary tumours  Radiotherapy is primarily used for residual or recurrent tumour after surgery. Meningioma  Sometimes a watch-and-wait policy is indicated, especially if symptoms can be controlled by other means (eg low-grade gliomas causing seizures that can be controlled with anticonvulsants).  It is uncertain how to predict if and when a low-grade tumour will convert into a higher-grade lesion.

Primary brain tumour  Chemotherapy:  this is routine for high-grade gliomas (AAs and GBM) in all, but the most unfit/elderly may not be suitable  can be administered either intravenously (temozolomide) or via wafers left in the operative bed at the end of debulking surgery (carmustine, Gliadel).  Corticosteroids:  these reduce oedema and the associated mass effect  give dexamethasone 4 mg orally four times daily, usually with gastric protection.  Anticonvulsants: give as necessary to control symptoms. Pituitary tumours  Prolactinomas: most will shrink with dopamine agonists. Surgical Cerebral metastasis  Metastasectomy - This can be performed through a small incision and ‘mini-craniotomy’. It requires accurate localisation of the lesion in theatre to allow accurate siting of the incision and craniotomy.  This is facilitated by:  ‘Neuro-navigation’ devices which allow surgical instruments to be tracked relative to the lesion’s position in real time during surgery  stereotactic frame.  This is indicated if:  patient is fit  symptomatic lesion is in an accessible location  there is a good prognosis of the primary (extracerebral) lesion. Primary brain tumour  Debulking surgery for malignant primary brain tumours.  Curative resection is not possible for GBM and AA.  Debulking (cytoreductive) surgery increases median survival (but not drastically) in younger, fitter patients.

Coeliac Disease Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten (dietary protein found in barley, wheat and rye) activates an abnormal mucosal response causing characteristic damage and chronic inflammation to the lining of the small intestine.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten (dietary protein found in barley, wheat and rye) activates an abnormal mucosal response causing characteristic damage and chronic inflammation to the lining of the small intestine.  Coeliac disease is also known as:  gluten-sensitive enteropathy  coeliac sprue  non-tropical sprue.  Refractory coeliac disease is the recurrence of malabsorptive clinical signs and symptoms associated with villous atrophy in coeliac patients who have, for more than 12 months, adhered to a gluten-free diet.  Coeliac disease commonly affects the proximal part of small intestine.  Treatment is largely adhering to a gluten-free diet.  Prognosis is generally good, with recovery from symptoms in up to 90% of patients with gluten avoidance. Epidemiology  There is a rise in patients being diagnosed with coeliac disease worldwide; the prevalence globally is estimated to be 1%.  Incidence of coeliac disease in the United Kingdom is 1 in 100 people.  Coeliac disease is twice as common in women than men.  It is prevalent in any age, but peaks in childhood and 50–60 years old. Aetiology  Gluten peptides are found in barley, wheat and rye.  There is an increased immunological response to ingested gluten; the reason for this is unknown, but there are predisposing factors:  genetic predisposition:  association to HLA antigens  presence of HLA-DQ2 in 95%, the rest are DQ8.  immunological factors:  patients with autoimmune conditions, eg type I diabetes mellitus and autoimmune thyroid disease have an increased risk of developing coeliac disease.  The prevalence of coeliac disease also correlates with a high wheat consumption.  First-degree relatives of patients with coeliac disease have a 10–15% risk of coeliac disease themselves. Pathophysiology  Symptoms are due to a genetically predisposed individual developing an immunological response to gluten peptide

DR. JAM antigens which are derived from prolamins in wheat (gliadin), rye (secalin), barley (hordein), and related grains.  In coeliac disease, these gluten peptides are resistant to human proteases, enabling them to persist in the small intestinal lumen.  these peptides trigger immune activation in the intestinal submucosa – mediated by T helper cells.  Tissue transglutaminase is released in response of gluten consumption and modifies gluten peptides into a form that stimulates the immune system more effectively.  Epithelium of small intestine is damaged, causing:  loss of brush border  villous atrophy  crypt hyperplasia.  Resorption of nutrients in the small intestine is impaired, leading to malabsorptive symptoms.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for coeliac disease include:  diarrhoea: either chronic or intermittent  bloating  abdominal pain/discomfort: recurrent abdominal pain, distention or cramping  failure to thrive (children)  weight loss  fatigue  iron-deficiency causing a microcytic anaemia  vitamin B12/folate deficiency causing a macrocytic anaemia  osteopenia/osteoporosis.  Associated conditions include:  dermatitis herpetiformis (intensively itchy and widespread rash)  Down syndrome  selective immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency  autoimmune conditions, eg:  type I diabetes mellitus  thyroid disease  liver disease.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for coeliac disease include:  Crohn’s disease  ulcerative colitis  malignancy, eg gastrointestinal and haematological cancers  peptic ulcer disease  giardiasis

Delirium Delirium describes an acute state of confusion.  Overview Key Facts  Delirium describes an acute state of confusion.  Patients who are age 65 or over are most likely to be affected.  It occurs in 20–30% of medical inpatients and 10–50% of patients who have had surgery.  It is characterised by the presence of a combination of features which may include:  disorientation  fluctuating consciousness  inattention  altered sleep–wake patterns

DR. JAM  agitated behaviour  apathy (a lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern)  hallucinations, misperceptions and delusions.  Delirium in itself is not an aetiological diagnosis; therefore, further investigation and treatment for the cause of the delirium is required.  There are many causes of delirium which can most easily be separated into two categories:  systemic syndromes (extracranial) causes  central nervous system (CNS)-specific (intracranial) causes  investigations to identify cause of delirium  infection screening  arterial blood gas (ABG)/venous blood gas (VBG)  blood tests  blood sugar and ketone analysis  drug/toxin screen  computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) head  abdominal ultrasound  electrocardiogram (ECG).  Management can be divided into general measures:  to optimise the environment and reduce disorientation  to identify and treat the cause of the confusional state  symptomatic treatment such as a short course of sedatives.  Delirium generally has a fluctuating course and recovery can be rapid or take weeks to months.  There is increased morbidity and mortality, as patients are likely to require increased hospital stay times and, as a consequence, be at a higher risk hospital acquired complications. Epidemiology  Recorded in 20–30% of medical inpatients and 10–50% of patients post-operatively.  Risk factors:  age 65 or older  cognitive impairment (past or present) and/or dementia  current hip fracture  severe illness (clinical condition which is deteriorating or at risk of deteriorating). Aetiology  There are many potential causes of delirium which can best be split into:  systemic syndromes (extracranial)  CNS-specific (intracranial) causes.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Systemic Causes  Metabolic and endocrine:  hypo-/hypernatraemia  hypo-/hyperglycaemia  hepatic failure  renal failure  hypercalcaemia  hyperammonaemia  hypoxaemia  hypercapnia  acidosis  vitamin deficiency (eg thiamine, vitamin B12).  Endocrine:  hypo/hyperthyroidism  Addisonian crisis  diabetic ketoacidosis.  Infection:  any sufficiently severe infection (eg pneumonia, urinary tract infection).  Toxic and drug-induced:  alcohol (excess and withdrawal)  benzodiazepines  lithium  carbon monoxide.  CNS-specific Causes  Infection:  meningitis (viral, bacterial, fungal)  encephalitis (viral, bacterial,fungal)  cerebral or (para-meningeal) abscess.  Malignant:  cerebral metastases  malignant meningitis  primary brain tumour (eg high-grade glioma).  Inflammatory:  vasculitis  systemic lupus erythematosus  neurosarcoidosis  multiple sclerosis  acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)  Behçet’s disease.  Antibody-associated encephalitis:  paraneoplastic  non-paraneoplastic

JAM  Hashimoto’s encephalitis (now called steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAAT)).  Vascular:  stroke (especially thalamic or multiple infarcts)  cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Pathophysiology  Delirium is characterised by an acute onset of confusion and a fluctuating course.  It usually develops over 1–2 days.  Delirium can be hypoactive or hyperactive, but some people show signs of both (mixed).  People with hyperactive delirium have heightened arousal and can be restless, agitated and aggressive.  People with hypoactive delirium become withdrawn, quiet and sleepy.  Hypoactive and mixed delirium can be more difficult to recognise.  Clinical Presentation  Patients need to be assessed for signs of delirium if they have a recent change (within hours or days) or fluctuation in their behaviour. This may be self-reported or reported by a relative or carer.  These behavioural changes may affect:  cognitive function – worsened concentration*, slow responses*, confusion  perception – usually in the form of visual or auditory hallucinations  physical function – reduced mobility*, reduced movement*, restlessness, agitation, changes in appetite*, sleep disturbance  social behaviour – lack of co-operation, withdrawal*, alterations in communication, mood and/or attitude. (* indicates hypoactive delirium)  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  dementia (treat for delirium first if there is difficulty distinguishing between the diagnoses of delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia)  delirium tremens (similar features but specifically related to alcohol withdrawal)  mental illness, eg depression, bipolar, psychosis and/or anxiety  acute alcohol/drug intoxication  traumatic head injury  Charles–Bonnet syndrome (rare).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  In the acute setting, delirium can be rapidly screened for using the 4AT test.  This generates a score which suggests the likelihood of delirium based on four key features:  alertness  abbreviated mental test 4 (AMT 4) – ask the patient their name, date of birth, location and present year  attention – ask the patient to recite the months of the year backwards starting from December, for example  acute change/fluctuating course.  If delirium is suspected, a healthcare professional who is trained and competent in diagnosing delirium should carry out a clinical assessment based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-V) criteria or the shortConfusion Assessment Method (CAM) to confirm the diagnosis.  Patients experiencing delirium may exhibit changes on an electroencephalogram (EEG), irrespective of the cause.  Once delirium has been diagnosed, it is important to investigate and treat the cause:  infection screening – includes urine dipstick and microscopy, culture and sensitivity (MC+S), blood cultures, chest X-ray, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis  ABG/VBG – quick way of assessing for hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, electrolyte imbalances, hypo/hyperglycaemia and/or hyperlactataemia  blood tests – urea and electrolytes, full blood count, liver function tests, bone profile, clotting, C-reactive protein, and/or antibody assays if required  blood sugar and ketone analysis  drug/toxin screen  computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) head – to assess for intracranial lesions  lumbar puncture – CSF analysis for blood, protein, glucose, micro-organisms and/or antibodies  electrocardiogram (ECG) – to check for arrhythmia or an acute coronary event.  Management  Prevention of Delirium  There are a number of poor outcomes associated with developing delirium, so prevention is key. A number of steps may be taken to help reduce the risk of patients developing delirium:  try to keep the environment (room, ward and staff) as consistent as possible  assess the patient's risk factors < 24 hours after admission  address cognitive impairment/disorientation (provide appropriate lighting and signage, a clock and a calendar,

JAM verbally re-orientate the patient and facilitate regular visits from family and friends)  address dehydration and/or constipation  assess for hypoxia (optimise O2 saturations)  address infection (look for and/or treat infection and avoid unnecessary procedures, eg catheterisation)  encourage mobility (ensure necessary walking aids are available)  ensure regular aids are available (eg glasses, hearing aids, dentures etc.)  assess and manage pain appropriately  assess and manage poor nutrition  promote good sleep patterns (eg avoid procedures during sleeping hours, reduce noise and schedule medications for the daytime).  General Management  It is important to identify and manage potential causes of delirium as soon as possible.  Try to implement advice as above (eg ensuring you re-orient the patient, keep them in a suitable care environment, arrange regular family and friend visits etc.).  Specific Management  This depends on the identified cause of the delirium, but may consist of non-pharmacological and pharmacological methods with input from the appropriate specialties.  Symptomatic Management  If patients are acutely distressed (can occur in hypoactive as well as hyperactive delirium) or are considered a risk to themselves or others, then try:  verbal and non-verbal de-escalation techniques  a short-term (usually < one week) course of haloperidol at the lowest possible dose, gradually titrating the dose against the severity of their symptoms (if de-escalation techniques fail)  use caution in using anti-psychotic medication in patients with conditions such as Parkinson’s disease or Lewy-body dementia.  Prognosis  There is a significant burden associated with delirium.  Compared with patients who do not develop delirium, people who develop delirium may:  need to stay longer in hospital or in critical care  have an increased incidence of dementia  be more likely to develop delirium again in the future  have more hospital-acquired complications, such as falls and pressure sores
