Dementia With Lewy Bodies Reactive arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis that occurs as a reaction to an infection in another part of the body, typically involving joint pain, swelling and stiffness.  Overview Key Facts  Dementia is a progressive impairment of cognition that has an impact on daily functioning.  Loss of short-term memory is often the first sign of the condition.  Other changes may include changes in behaviour, personality, speech, perception, thought processes and mood.  Prevalence increases with age.  The most common cause of dementia is Alzheimer's disease, which makes up over 50% of cases.  Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia and, similar to Alzheimer's disease, predominantly affects people aged over 65 years.  Pathologically, the hallmark is the accumulation of Lewy bodies, which are intracellular aggregates made up of αsynuclein.  These accumulate in the brainstem and cortex.  From a pathological point of view, these Lewy bodies are the same as the aggregates seen in Parkinson’s disease and also in multiple system atrophy (MSA).  In DLB there are multiple neurotransmitter deﬁciencies but notably affected are the cholinergic and dopaminergic systems.  The clinical presentation of DLB may be similar to Alzheimer's disease with problems in memory, language and visuospatial functioning.  However, there are some characteristic features that set it apart:

DR. JAM  patients with DLB tend to have a ﬂuctuating level of arousal that produces variations in levels of cognitive impairment  at times patients may seem acutely confused and at other times quite lucid  in addition, patients with DLB frequently hallucinate and typically see well-formed, non-threatening, visual hallucinations.  Many patients have symptoms of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder and this can be present for years before the other features of DLB manifest.  On examination, the patient may be parkinsonian, although at presentation this can be subtle.  As the disease progresses, the parkinsonism becomes more obvious.  Cholinesterase inhibitors are used to treat the cognitive symptoms and dopaminergic medication can be used to treat the parkinsonism.  However, a balance must be struck as too much dopaminergic medication tends to worsen confusion and hallucinations.  People who develop cognitive symptoms and motor features of Parkinson's disease within one year are classed as having dementia with Lewy bodies.  Patients with Parkinson’s disease may develop very similar cognitive impairments to patients with DLB, and this is termed ‘Parkinson’s disease dementia’ (PDD). Epidemiology  Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia.  It predominantly affects people aged over 65 years. Aetiology  Risk factors for dementia include:  increasing age – main risk factor  genetics – positive family history, apolipoprotein E gene  cardiovascular disease risk factors – diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension  smoking  reduced activity levels  comorbidities such as stroke, Parkinson's disease and depression.  Other factors which may also have an effect on the development of the condition include:  heavy alcohol intake  low educational attainment  low cognitive stimulation  low social engagement/support. Pathophysiology  Pathologically, the hallmark is the accumulation of Lewy bodies, which are intracellular aggregates made up of αsynuclein.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  These accumulate in the brainstem and cortex.  From a pathological point of view, these Lewy bodies are the same as the aggregates seen in Parkinson’s disease and also in multiple system atrophy (MSA).  In DLB there are multiple neurotransmitter deﬁciencies but notably affected are the cholinergic and dopaminergic systems.  Clinical Presentation  The clinical presentation of DLB may be similar to Alzheimer's disease with problems in memory, language and visuospatial functioning.  However, there are some characteristic features that set it apart:  patients with DLB tend to have a ﬂuctuating level of arousal that produces variations in levels of cognitive impairment  at times patients may seem acutely confused and at other times quite lucid  in addition, patients with DLB frequently hallucinate and typically see well-formed, non-threatening, visual hallucinations.  Many patients have symptoms of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder and this can be present for years before the other features of DLB manifest.  On examination, the patient may be parkinsonian, although at presentation this can be subtle:  parkinsonism is a collective term for the clinical syndrome that includes bradykinesia along with at least one additional symptom of:  tremor  rigidity  gait disturbances.  As the disease progresses, parkinsonism becomes more obvious.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis includes other forms of dementia as well as:  depression  pseudodementia  mild cognitive impairment  delirium  transient global amnesia  epilepsy  cerebrovasclar events  neoplasm  drugs – anticholinergics  other psychiatric disorders:  schizophrenia  psychosis

DR. JAM  mania.  Other forms of dementia: Signs/symptoms Clinical features Alzheimer's disease Short-term memory loss Dysphasia Dyspraxia Behavioural changes, eg wandering Psychotic symptoms Apathy Progressive disease Vascular dementia Gait disturbance Personality change Labile mood Urinary symptoms Insight preserved Stepwise progression Cardiovascular disease risk factors Frontotemporal degeneration Stereotyped behaviours Personality change Loss of insight Expressive dysphasia Preserved memory Primitive reflexes Progresses slowly Family history More common in women with earlyonset before 70 Huntington's disease Schizophrenia-like psychosis Choreiform movement Depression Irritability Dementia Presents in earlier life during 20–40 years Family history Normal-pressure hydrocephalus Apathy Inattention Urinary incontinence Gait apraxia Presents in 50–70year-olds Reversible dementia Prion disease Myoclonic jerks Seizures Cerebellar ataxia Starts at < 50 years Rapid onset Rapid progression  Diagnosis/Investigation  History/examination will help distinguish between causes and form the basis of diagnosis (patients should be referred to a specialist to confirm the diagnosis using the international consensus criteria).  Criteria for diagnosis of probable DLB:  presence of dementia  two out of three core features:  fluctuating attention and concentration  recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations  spontaneous parkinsonism.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  the diagnosis of probable DLB can also be made if there is dementia along with one core feature and at least one suggestive feature including:  rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder  severe neuroleptic sensitivity  low dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia demonstrated by single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) or positron emission tomography (PET) imaging.  Possible DLB can be diagnosed where there is dementia plus one core or suggestive feature. Investigations  Cognitive testing – mini-mental state examination/Addenbrooke’s cognitive examination.  Baseline bloods – full blood count (FBC), electrolytes (U&Es), liver function, thyroid function, vitamin B12/folate, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), antinuclear antibody (ANA), syphilis and HIV.  Radiography – chest X-ray.  Brain imaging – computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).  Electroencephalogram (EEG).  Other special tests – lumbar puncture, cerebral flow studies, neuropsychological testing and genetic testing.  Routine investigations should be carried out to exclude other conditions, such as depression, hypothyroidism and delirium.  Management  Management should involve assessment and management of the patients functional and social needs as well as considering the supportive needs of the carer of the patient.  Management should be based on a case-by-case basis. Non-pharmacological management  Patients should be given written information regarding:  the course of the condition and prognosis  medical treatment options available  support groups and associations  sources of legal and financial advice  driving advice (DVLA must be informed of all drivers diagnosed with dementia).  People with mild-to-moderate dementia should be given the opportunity to participate in structured group cognitive stimulation programmes to help maintain cognitive skills and day-to-day functioning.  Memory enhancement strategies should be discussed, such as using reminder notes, lists and reorganisation of possessions.  Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may be helpful for patients with symptoms of depression or anxiety, involving their carers.

DR. JAM  Other non-pharmacological approaches for those with anxiety, depression or behaviour issues may include exercise, aromatherapy and multi-sensory stimulation.  Palliative and end-of-care life should be discussed and planned for, as appropriate.  Social support should be initiated and progressed as the condition advances.  Arrange admission for people with suspected dementia if:  they are severely disturbed and admission is needed to ensure the health and safety of the person or the safety of others  assessment in primary care is not appropriate, such as complex physical and psychiatric problems.  Treat any identified modifiable risk factors for cognitive impairment:  (such as excess alcohol intake, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity and smoking) where possible.  Pharmacological management  Cholinesterase inhibitors are used to treat cognitive symptoms.  For example, donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine:  indicated for mild-to-moderate disease  improve cognitive and behavioural symptoms  increase acetylcholine availability.  Dopaminergic medication can be used to treat parkinsonism.  Note, a balance must be struck as too much dopaminergic medication tends to worsen confusion and hallucinations.  Avoid neuroleptic drugs for psychiatric and behavioural problems – commonly induce severe sensitivity reactions in patients with LBD.  Prognosis  The condition is a progressive disease with a 5–8 years average life expectancy from diagnosis.  There is currently no cure, treatments primarily aim to manage symptoms.  Patients often experience a steady decline of cognitive function in a pattern that is similar to that in Alzheimer's dementia. Diabetic Neuropathy Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common complications of diabetes and is correlated with poor diabetic control and duration.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common complications of diabetes and is correlated with poor diabetic control and duration.  The most common form of diabetic neuropathy is distal symmetric polyneuropathy, referred to as sock and glove distribution.  Autonomic neuropathy secondary to diabetes can lead to cardiac autonomic neuropathy, gastrointestinal dysmotility, diabetic cystopathy and impotence.  Treatment consists of slowing progression by improving glucose control. Epidemiology  Approximately half of the patients with diabetes develop neuropathy and there is a correlation between patients with a chronically high blood glucose level and a long duration of diabetes. Pathophysiology  Risk factors for diabetic neuropathy include duration of diabetes, glycated haemoglobin levels, insulin resistance and hypertension. Other factors associated with the development of diabetic neuropathy include triglyceride levels, low highdensity lipoprotein levels and abdominal (central) obesity.  The underlying pathology of diabetic neuropathy is still not fully understood; however, there are a number of areas that have been identified as contributing to the peripheral sensory axon loss.  Diabetic neuropathy affects the longest sensory neurones first, leading to the peripheral sensory loss, due to a retraction of the terminal sensory axons. Schwann cells are targeted by hyperglycaemia, and features of demyelination can be seen in some cases, although diabetic neuropathy is not considered a demyelinating condition.  Hyperglycaemic state is believed to lead to oxidative stress of neurones with increased advanced glycation end products, activation of PKC isoforms, altered mitochondrial function and overactivity of the hexosamine pathway. Glucose metabolism may also lead to increased production of oxygen free radicals. Nerve ischaemia may also occur secondary to the microvascular changes seen with diabetes.  Clinical Presentation Diabetic neuropathy exists in different clinical syndromes, the most common of which are:  Distal symmetric polyneuropathy  most common neuropathy  presents with progressive distal sensory loss in a ‘glove and stocking’ distribution  sensory loss tends to account for the majority of cases. Painful neuropathy (burning/stabbing) is slightly less common

DR. JAM  results in axonal loss in nerve conduction studies  motor involvement can occur in severe cases.  Autonomic neuropathy  causes postural hypotension, gastroparesis, gustatory sweating, generalised sweating, altered bowel habit  the earliest clinical sign may be a resting tachycardia.  Diabetic amyotrophy (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy)  non-systemic microvasculitis causes a lumbosacral plexopathy which can affect nerve roots  presents with asymmetric pain then weakness in the proximal leg along with weight loss.  Differential Diagnosis  There is a wide range of causes of peripheral neuropathy, these should be considered in appropriate patients, including:  B12 deficiency  uraemia  hypothyroidism  human immunodeficiency virus/lyme disease  chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy  iatrogenic (chemotherapies, isoniazid, pyridoxine)  paraproteinaemic (i.e myeloma or MGUS)  paraneoplastic.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Distal symmetric polyneuropathy can be diagnosed clinically, providing differential diagnoses have been ruled. In atypical cases investigations can include:  nerve conduction studies in a large fibre polyneuropathy predominantly show sensory axonal loss with reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials in a lengthdependent manner, with the legs being most affected. In severe cases, motor axonal loss can occur with reduced compound motor action potential amplitudes  skin biopsy assessment can be used to look for a small fibre (ie painful) neuropathy.  Autonomic dysfunction can be investigated with:  a lying and standing blood pressure (fall of over ≥ 20 mmHg systolic or ≥ 10 mmHg diastolic being indicative of postural hypotension)  tilt tabling testing  gastrointestinal involvement can be demonstrated by showing delayed gastric emptying on scintigraphy.  Diabetic amyotrophy can be investigated with nerve conduction studies.  Management Diabetic neuropathy is irreversible, the mainstay of treatment is to optimise diabetic control (to slow/prevent progression) and to control symptoms.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Non-pharmacological:  Encourage good foot care (to prevent dry skin) and the wearing of appropriate foot ware to prevent abrasions and cuts which the patient may be unaware of. Patients should be encouraged to inspect their feet daily. Referral to podiatry is important.  Patients with diabetic autonomic neuropathy with postural hypotension should be encouraged to stand up slow, trial elevated the head of the bed, use full leg or body stockings.  Pharmacological:  First-line agents for painful diabetic neuropathy include:  gabapentinoid medications (pregabalin and gabapentin)  antidepressants (amitriptyline and duloxetine)  if the first medication trialled fails to control pain then switch to an alternative first-line agent.  referral to chronic pain should be made if the pain is not controlled despite trials of numerous first-line agents  tramadol should be reserved for acute rescue therapy of neuropathic pain  carbamazepine is the first line agent in trigeminal neuralgia, not for other causes of neuropathic pain.  First-line treatment for diabetic autonomic neuropathy includes:  postural hypotension: fludrocortisone, midodrine and less frequently octreotide  gastrointestinal symptoms should be managed supportively with antidiarrhoeal agents, antiemetics or prokinetics, as appropriate. Treatment of diabetic amyotrophy is also supportive. Encephalitis Encephalitis is defined as an inflammation of the brain, most commonly caused by viral infection, but can also be due to other pathogens or a primary autoimmune process.  Overview Key Facts  Encephalitis is defined as an inflammation of the brain, most commonly caused by viral infection, but can also be due to other pathogens or a primary autoimmune process.  The condition is relatively uncommon but cases can be severe and even fatal, especially in extremes of age.  The most common organism causing encephalitis in the United Kingdom (UK) is Herpes simplex virus type I, which can be severe in the elderly and particularly in neonates.

DR. JAM  Altered behaviour along with features of an acute febrile illness is commonly found.  These symptoms can deteriorate into altered consciousness, seizures and coma.  Diagnosis is often based on clinical and is confirmed with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis along with laboratory testing and neuroimaging.  Acyclovir is commenced for presumed viral encephalitis in the first instance - before plymerase chain reaction (PCR) diagnosis of herpes infection is confirmed. Benzylpenicillin is also often given to cover the possibility of meningitis. Epidemiology  The prevalence of Encephalitis in the UK ranges between 5-8 / 100 000 per year.  Most cases are seen in the extremes of age, ie in children and the elderly population. Aetiology Viral  Herpes Simplex – most common.  Varicella Zoster.  Enterovirus.  Adenovirus.  Parechovirus.  HIV. Bacterial  Mycobacterium Tuberculosis.  Listeria.  Streptococcus Pneumonia.  Neisseria Meningitidis.  Syphilis. Other infective causes  Cryptococcus Neoformans.  Toxoplasma.  Rickettsial.  Fungal. Antibody associated encephalitis  Paraneoplastic.  Non paraneoplastic.  Hashimotos encephalitis.  Steroid responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Patients may initially have flu like symptoms.  The classical presentation is a triad of fever, headache and altered behaviour/mental status.  Other signs and symptoms incude:  meningeal signs - neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting  aphasia  ataxia  tremors  cranial nerve deficits  focal or generalised seizures  coma.  Neonatal herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) usually presents within 4-11 days after birth. Clinically the symptoms and signs include:  lethargy  poor feeding  irritability  bulging fontanelle  shock  jaundice  purpuric/vesicular rash.  Differential Diagnosis  Meningitis.  Lyme Disease.  Whipple’s Disease.  Stroke transient ischaemic attack (TIA).  Cerebral Malaria.  Behçet’s disease.  Syphilis.  Haematological malignancies.  Diagnosis/Investigation Full blood count and blood fill, blood cultures, urea and electrolytes (U&E), LFT, glucose, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and c-reactive protein (CRP).  Computed tomography (CT) to rule out other causes of symptoms and check for raise intracranial pressure which warrants delay of lumbar puncture.  Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis including CSF virology PCR.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan provides detailed imaging for evidence of demyelination.  Electroencephalogram (EEG) is often abnormal.

This should not be delayed by waiting for confirmation of diagnosis.  Broad spectrum antibiotic cover is also added where bacterial infection is suspected.  Other therapy is mainly supportive and may include fluids, antiemetics, sedation and analgesia as required.  Prognosis  Encephalitis is a serious condition with around 70% mortality rate if untreated.  Extremes of age (neonates and the elderly) and immunocompromised are associated with a worse prognosis.  Patients who recover may be left with neuropsychiatric and physical impairment which can range in severity from mild to total dependency for all activities of daily living. Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis  Overview Key Facts  Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EPGA, also called ‘Churg-Strauss syndrome’) is a small to medium-size vessel vasculitis associated with asthma and eosinophilia.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  EPGA is very rare with a prevalence of 10-15 per million people.  Over 90% of patients with EPGA also have a diagnosis of asthma and 30-50% of patients are positive for p-ANCA.  The pathogenesis is still not completely understood.  Asthma usually precedes the development of vasculitis by several years.  Classic symptoms include asthma and sinus or nose symptoms (nasal polyps, allergic rhinitis, paranasal sinusitis).  Vasculitis may also affect the heart, kidney, GI tract skin and neurological system.  Constitutional symptoms may include fever, weight loss and myalgia (as with other forms of vasculitis).  Marked eosinophilia on blood tests may be useful in differentiating EGPA from other vasculitides.  Pulmonary CT may show peripheral opacification, bronchial wall thickening/ bronchiectasis (eosinophilic infiltration) and pleural effusions.  Lung biopsy may show necrotising granulomas with a central eosinophilic core and necrotising vasculitis.  Renal biopsy may show focal or crescentic glomerulonephritis.  Eosinophilia is seen on 33% of patients on bronchoalveolar lavage.  The mainstay of treatment is with corticosteroids but other treatment options involve cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, methotrexate and rituximab.  The 5 year survival rate is 62% with treatment and only 25% without treatment, however the mortality rate is higher in children.  The most common cause of death is from cardiac complications. Epidemiology  Very rare, with a prevalence of 10-15 per million people.  Affects men and women in equal proportions.  May present in childhood, although very rare. Aetiology  EGPA is a small to medium-size vessel vasculitis characterised by eosinophilia.  > 90% of patients have a diagnosis of asthma.  The exact cause is unknown.  30-40% of patients are positive for p-ANCA. Pathophysiology  The pathogenesis of EGPA is still not completely understood.  Most likely the result of a complex process where environmental and genetic factors lead to an inflammatory response involving eosinophils and B and T lymphocytes.

DR. JAM  Clinical Presentation The disease may follow three defined phases (or may present atypically, which makes diagnosis difficult): Phase Description Prodromal phase Most patients suffer from asthma and may also have allergies and sinus symptoms in their teens and early adulthood Eosinophilic phase Blood tests show eosinophilia Vasculitic phase Small and medium-sized vessels affected by vasculitis. This is often preceded by constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fever and lethargy The constellation of symptoms in individual cases vary depending on which organ systems are involved:  Respiratory  asthma (>90% of patients), usually precedes symptoms of vasculitis by several years  allergic rhinitis  paranasal sinusitis  nasal polyps  cough  haemoptysis.  Cardiac  pericarditis or myocarditis  myocardial infarction (secondary to coronary vasculitis)  heart failure.  Renal  hypertension  glomerulonephritis  chronic kidney disease.  Gastrointestinal  bowel ischaemia and perforation  PR bleeding  appendicitis  pancreatitis  Skin  purpura  livedo reticularis  urticaria  necrotic bullae  digital ischaemia.  Neurological  peripheral neuropathy/ mononeuritis multiplex  stroke.  Other

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  fever  myalgia  weight loss.  Differential Diagnosis Differentials include, but are not limited to:  Other vasculitides:  granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)  polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)  microscopic polyangiitis  goodpasture syndrome  Other causes of eosinophilia:  parasitic infections  allergy  asthma  malignancy  chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Laboratory investigations  30-40% of patients will be p-ANCA positive  Eosinophilia (usually > 10% on blood film).  Chest X-ray: may show patchy peripheral consolidation and pleural effusions  Pulmonary CT  Peripheral opacification (consolidation or ground-glass opacities)  Eosinophilic infiltration may cause bronchial wall thickening, bronchiectasis and appearance of centrilobular nodules  Pleural effusions.  Spirometry: 97% of patients have asthma, so will likely present with an obstructive picture on spirometry  Biopsy  Biopsy from an affected organ is the most useful for determining the diagnosis. If this is not possible or if no localised findings are determined, muscle or nerve biopsy may be performed  Lung biopsy may show necrotising granulomas with a central eosinophilic core and necrotising vasculitis  If there is renal involvement, renal biopsy may show focal or crescentic glomerulonephritis.  Bronchoscopic lavage: eosinophilia seen in 33% of cases.  Management  The mainstay of treatment is with corticosteroids.

DR. JAM  Cyclophosphamide may be used if there is life-threatening major organ involvement.  Rituximab may be useful in steroid resistant cases.  Azathioprine or methotrexate may be used if steroid-weaning causes a flare of symptoms.  Prognosis  5 year survival rate:  with treatment = 62%  without treatment = 25%.  Most common cause of death is from cardiac complications (such as cardiac failure or myocardial infarction).  EGPA in children has a higher mortality rate, usually from cardiac complications. Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small and medium vessel vasculitis previously known as Churg–Strauss syndrome, which is characterised by eosinophil-rich, necrotising granulomatous in?ammation.  Overview Key Facts  Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a small and medium vessel vasculitis previously known as Churg–Strauss syndrome, which is characterised by eosinophil-rich, necrotising granulomatous inﬂammation.  EPGA is very rare with a prevalence of 10–15 per million people.  The condition may involve the respiratory tract, the renal system, the skin and peripheral nerves.  It typically presents with a history of asthma, sometimes with atopy and recurrent nasal polyps, often over a number of years prior to diagnosis.  More than 7/10 patients also have mononeuritis multiplex.  Renal involvement is less frequently seen and the condition is associated with less severe renal disease compared with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  The most common renal complication in EGPA is necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, but eosinophilic interstitial nephritis, mesangial glomerulonephritis and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis are also seen.  Renal involvement leads to haematuria and proteinuria, hypertension and raised creatinine levels.  The antibody associated with the condition is pANCA, which is seen in approximately 50% of cases (higher with glomerulonephritis presentations).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  A raised eosinophil count (eosinophilia) is seen in over 90% of patients with advanced disease.  Skin biopsy reveals small-vessel arteriopathy with granuloma formation and is the diagnostic investigation of choice.  Treatment consists of corticosteroids, with or without additional therapy with agents such as methotrexate or cyclophosphamide.  Without treatment, the 5-year survival rate for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is around 25%; with appropriate therapy, this rises to over 60%. Epidemiology  The condition is very rare, with a prevalence of 10–15 per million people.  Affects men and women in equal proportions.  Rarely, the condition may present in childhood. Aetiology  EGPA is a small to medium-sized vessel vasculitis characterised by eosinophilia.  More than 90% of patients have a diagnosis of asthma.  The exact cause is unknown. Pathophysiology  The cardinal feature of EGPA is the necrotising granuloma composed of an eosinophilic core surrounded by macrophages and epithelioid giant cells.  The pathogenesis of EGPA is still not completely understood.  It is most likely the result of a complex process where environmental and genetic factors lead to an inflammatory response involving eosinophils and B and T lymphocytes.  Clinical Presentation  The main presentations are patients with:  asthma (diagnosed or symptoms suggestive of asthma, including wheeze, nocturnal cough)  sensory neuropathy  lung abnormalities  sinus problems such as abnormal growths (polyps).  The disease may follow three defined phases (or may present atypically, which makes diagnosis difficult): Phase Description Prodromal phase Most patients suffer from asthma and may also have allergies and sinus symptoms in their teens and early adulthood Eosinophilic phase Blood tests show eosinophilia Vasculitic phase Small and medium-sized vessels affected by vasculitis. This is often preceded by constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fever and lethargy

JAM The constellation of symptoms in individual cases vary depending on which organ systems are involved:  Respiratory  asthma (> 90% of patients), usually precedes symptoms of vasculitis by several years  allergic rhinitis  paranasal sinusitis  nasal polyps  cough  haemoptysis.  Cardiac  pericarditis or myocarditis  myocardial infarction (secondary to coronary vasculitis)  heart failure.  Renal  hypertension  glomerulonephritis  chronic kidney disease.  Gastrointestinal  bowel ischaemia and perforation  PR bleeding  appendicitis  pancreatitis.  Skin  purpura  livedo reticularis  urticaria  necrotic bullae  digital ischaemia.  Neurological  peripheral neuropathy/mononeuritis multiplex  stroke.  Other  fever  myalgia  weight loss.  Differential Diagnosis Differentials include, but are not limited to:  Other vasculitides:  granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)  polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)  microscopic polyangiitis  Goodpasture syndrome.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Other causes of eosinophilia:  parasitic infections  allergy  asthma  malignancy  chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The condition is diagnosed on finding four out of the following:  asthma  blood eosinophilia > 10%  vasculitic neuropathy  pulmonary infiltrates  sinus disease  extravascular eosinophils on biopsy findings.  It is diagnosed clinically, although a biopsy should be sought for pathological confirmation.  Over 50% of patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis have a positive pANCA (perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) result. Other investigations:  Chest X-ray: may show patchy peripheral consolidation and pleural effusions  Pulmonary computed tomography:  peripheral opacification (consolidation or ground-glass opacities)  eosinophilic infiltration may cause bronchial wall thickening, bronchiectasis and the appearance of centrilobular nodules  pleural effusions.  Spirometry: 97% of patients have asthma, so will likely present with an obstructive picture on spirometry  Biopsy:  biopsy from an affected organ is the most useful for determining the diagnosis. If this is not possible or if no localised findings are determined, muscle or nerve biopsy may be performed  lung biopsy may show necrotising granulomas with a central eosinophilic core and necrotising vasculitis  if there is renal involvement, renal biopsy may show focal or crescentic glomerulonephritis.  Management  Treatment is with corticosteroids, with or without additional therapy with methotrexate, azathioprine or cyclophosphamide.  Glucocorticoids alone usually are adequate for the treatment of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  Cytotoxic drugs are necessary for less than 20% of patients.

DR. JAM  Major life-threatening organ involvement may require treatment with pulse doses of intravenous (IV) corticosteroids as well as other cytotoxic agents.  Other treatments include intravenous immune globulin, interferon-alpha and plasma exchange.  Prognosis  Complications of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis depend on the specific organ system involvement.  The principal causes of morbidity and mortality are myocarditis and myocardial infarction secondary to coronary arteritis.  With treatment, the 1-year survival rate is 90% and the 5-year survival rate is 62%.  Overall, without treatment, the 5-year survival rate is about 25%. Epilepsy And Pregnancy Epilepsy and Pregnancy is a complex medical condition where women with epilepsy face unique challenges and considerations in managing their seizures and medications during pregnancy to ensure the health and safety of both the mother and the baby.  Overview Key Facts  Epilepsy is a neurological disorder in which a person experiences recurring seizures.  The International League Against Epilepsy describes epilepsy as a disease of the brain defined by any of the following conditions:  at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart  one unprovoked seizure and the probability of further seizures similar to the general recurrence risk after two unprovoked seizures, occurring over the next 10 years  diagnosis of epilepsy syndrome.  Most women with epilepsy who become pregnant will have a healthy pregnancy but an increased risk of complications exists.  The risk of death during pregnancy is increased 10-fold in pregnant women with epilepsy compared with those without the condition.  The risk of major congenital malformations is increased, as well as perinatal complications including fetal growth restrictions and stillbirth.  Patients with epilepsy who plan to become pregnant should be referred to a specialist pre-conception to consider substitution

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI and/or alteration of their background medication where necessary.  Although irregular isolated short-lived fits are tolerated in pregnancy, prolonged fits can lead to hypoxia, lactic acidosis, premature rupture of membranes and sometimes fetal death.  Vomiting, altered protein binding of anti-convulsants, altered sleep, altered metabolism and excretion of anti-convulsants all contribute to an increased risk of fit episodes during pregnancy.  Most anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) increase the risk of teratogenicity.  However, most are not contraindicated in pregnancy.  The exception is sodium valproate, which must be stopped in patients who are pregnant or considering conceiving.  High-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) should be advised preconception and for the first three months of pregnancy.  This is particularly important for patients on hepatic-enzymeinducing anti-epileptics such as phenytoin.  A detailed fetal anomaly scan should be performed between 18 and 20 weeks.  If the patient is receiving phenytoin, then vitamin K should be administered to the mother from 36 weeks’ gestation in order to counteract possible neonatal coagulopathy.  Management  Most anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) increase the risk of teratogenicity.  However, most are not contraindicated in pregnancy.  The exception is sodium valproate, which must be stopped in patients who are pregnant or considering conceiving.  High-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) should be advised preconception and for the first three months of pregnancy.  This is particularly important for patients on hepatic-enzymeinducing anti-epileptics such as phenytoin.  A detailed fetal anomaly scan should be performed between 18 and 20 weeks.  If the patient is receiving phenytoin, then vitamin K should be administered to the mother from 36 weeks’ gestation in order to counteract possible neonatal coagulopathy. Epilepsy And Seizures A seizure is the transient occurrence of signs or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  A seizure is the transient occurrence of signs or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain.  Seizures can manifest as a disturbance of consciousness, behaviour, cognition, emotion, motor function or sensation.  There are numerous underlying causes of seizures.  An isolated seizure can be caused by toxic, metabolic, structural and infectious factors and should not be confused with epilepsy:  febrile seizures in children are usually self-limiting after the age of five years  only 25% of all patients who have a seizure will be diagnosed with epilepsy.  Focal seizures originate in networks limited to one hemisphere and may be localised or more widely distributed. Focal seizures are divided into those with retained awareness or impaired awareness.  Generalised seizures originate in bilaterally distributed networks and can include cortical and subcortical structures (but not necessarily the whole cortex). Generalised seizures are divided into motor and non-motor (absence) seizures.  Seizures that continue for more than a brief period of time in patients without known epilepsy (usually < 1 min) are classed as a medical emergency.  Treatment depends upon the type of seizure and severity, as well as the underlying cause.  Epilepsy  Epilepsy is a neurological disorder in which a person experiences recurring seizures.  The International League Against Epilepsy describes epilepsy as a disease of the brain defined by any of the following conditions:  at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart  one unprovoked seizure and the probability of further seizures similar to the general recurrence risk after two unprovoked seizures, occurring over the next ten years  diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.  Risk factors for epilepsy include:  premature birth  complicated febrile seizures  head trauma or infections  genetic causes  brain malformations.  Investigations include imaging to rule out organic causes.  Electroencephalogram (EEG) is done to define the type of epilepsy, not for diagnosis of epilepsy.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Treatment depends upon the type of seizure and severity, as well as the underlying cause.  Complications of epilepsy include:  sudden, unexplained death  physical injury  poor school attainment and/or work absence  depression and anxiety.  It is important to consider driving regulations in patients who hold a driving licence. Epidemiology  Epilepsy is one of the most common serious brain conditions. It affects over 70 million people globally. In the United Kingdom (UK), the prevalence of active epilepsy is estimated to be 5–10 cases per 1000.  Studies suggest that the lifetime risk of having a single seizure is 8–10%, and there is a 3% risk of developing epilepsy.  Peaks of onset of epilepsy occur in early childhood and late adulthood.  Affects both genders equally, though few studies show it is more prevalent in the male population. Aetiology  Seizures are a result of disturbances in the normal balance of excitation and inhibition of impulses within the central nervous system (CNS)  these disturbances can be caused due to various precipitating factors like high fever in children, head traumas, infections etc.  genetic mutations also play an important role, especially in the case of febrile seizures. Risk factors causing a predisposition to epilepsy include:  premature birth  head injury  complicated febrile seizes  genetic conditions associated with seizures  family history of epilepsy  structural abnormalities visible on structural neuroimaging ie stroke, trauma or malformation of cortical development  infections ie tuberculosis, cerebral malaria, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and congenital infection such as Zika virus  metabolic including uraemia (porphyria, amino-acidopathies or pyridoxine deficiency)  immune system related (anti-NMDA (N-methyl Daspartate) receptor encephalitis and anti-LGI1 (leucinerich glioma inactivated-1) encephalitis)  dementia and neurodegenerative disorders.

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Focal seizure activity begins in the discrete region of cortex and then proceeds to fire a large number of local excitatory neurons.  The influx of extracellular calcium and depolarisation of the neural membrane opens sodium channels and a subsequent influx of sodium. This generates a repetitive action potential, causing hyperpolarisation of gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors/potassium channels. This is seen as a spike of discharge on the EEG.  Many intrinsic (second messenger system, cytoplasmic buffering etc) and extrinsic (amount of neurotransmitter at synapse etc) factors contribute to neuronal excitability.  Eliptogenesis is the transformation of normal neuronal network into one that is chronically hyper-excitable. It occurs due to structural changes in the neuronal network following infections, head traumas etc.  Clinical Presentation Tonic–clonic seizures:  No warning signs may be noted.  Loss of consciousness is present.  There is often a brief tonic phase followed by clonic movements after falling to the ground.  Tongue biting and Incontinence may be seen.  Post-ictal confusion is often present. Focal aware seizures (previously termed simple partial seizures):  Consciousness is intact.  Symptoms begin in a very restricted region (like fingers) and over seconds to minutes include larger portion of the extremity – known as the ‘Jacksonian march phenomenon’.  They can develop into a generalised tonic-clonic seizure, now more commonly known as focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.  EEG shows a local discharge starting over the corresponding cortical area. Focal impaired awareness seizure (previously termed complex partial seizures):  Medial temporal (mostly hippocampal) focus is a feature.  Impaired consciousness or loss of consciousness occurs.  An aura usually precedes the seizure, often described as a sense of déjà vu or noting a sudden strong smell, etc.  Automatism is often present – eg chewing, picking movements, lip-smacking etc.  Post-ictal confusion is a feature.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Absence seizure:  Is usually noted in children.  Sudden, brief lapses of consciousness without loss of postural control occur.  It is accompanied by subtle motor signs like blinking or chewing.  The hallmark on EEG is abrupt, generalised, symmetric spike and slow-wave discharge superimposed on a normal EEG background.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  syncope  transient ischemic attacks  psychological disorders including panic attacks  migraine  movement disorders including tics  metabolic disorders including delirium tremens or hypoglycaemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is made after taking an in-depth history and an extensive investigation approach.  Blood tests to rule out electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycaemia renal or hepatic disorders ie full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&Es).  Brain Imaging is done for all patients to determine any underlying structural abnormality.  MRI scan has priority over a CT scan for detection of cerebral lesions associated with epilepsy.  A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed.  EEG is done to establish the type of epilepsy not to diagnose.  Genetic testing may be indicated based on clinical suspicion.  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoid precipitating factors (fasting, excessive tiredness, exposure to loud noise, flashing lights).  Advise the patient or their carers to maintain an epilepsy diary or record further episodes if possible.  Advise the patient to wear an epilepsy bracelet or similar.  Educate family members, carers and other close contacts regarding the management of episodes of seizures.  Avoid cycling and swimming until seizures are controlled.

DR. JAM  Advise the patient to stop driving if they hold a driving licence and to inform the DVLA (Driving and Vehicle Licencing Authority) – guides regarding driving varies depends on the control of the condition, length of seizure-free period and the class of vehicle licence held:  the DVLA needs to be informed after the first episode of seizure  a 6-month cessation of driving for a Group 1 (motor cars and motorcycles) licence is required in case of firsttime seizure attack with normal EEG image  if either or both reports are abnormal, a 12-month cessation of driving is required  driving is allowed only if the patient has been free from any epileptic attack (including auras) for one year, or if they had an epileptic attack while sleeping three years ago and attacks subsequently occurred only when asleep  to obtain a vocational driving license (group 1 license) or group 2 (lorries and buses) license, patients should have been free of epileptic attacks, of all antiepileptic medication and free from a continuing liability to epileptic seizures for ten years.  Pharmacological General principles:  Depending on the underlying cause, a first episode of seizure generally does not require medications. Exceptions include:  first-time seizure onset in an elderly patient – should be investigated to rule out an underlying structural cause.  All patients suspected of having a first epileptic seizure should be referred to a specialist to confirm diagnosis, but may well not need to be admitted initially to hospital.  Anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) are introduced if the patient has more than one episode of seizure and the diagnosis of epilepsy is made by a specialist.  AEDs are initially introduced at a low dose and titrated up until seizures are controlled or the maximum safe dose is reached.  Combination therapy is introduced if monotherapy fails.  All patients with epilepsy who continue to have poor control with medication within two years or despite medication with two drugs should be referred to a tertiary service for further assessment.  The International League Against Epilepsy defines epilepsy as having resolved when people have remained seizure-free for the past 10 years, with no antiepileptic drug treatment for at least the past five years.  In some people who remain seizure-free for more than two years, medication can be slowly withdrawn, although AED withdrawal is associated with an increased risk of seizure recurrence.  first-line AED for generalised tonic-clonic seizures:  sodium valproate (avoided in women of reproductive age due to teratogenicity)  carabamazepine

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  lamotrigine.  first-line AED for focal seizure:  carbamazepine  lamotrigine.  first-line AED for absence seizure:  ethosuximide.  levetiracetam may be substituted for many of the first line agents recommended above.  all AED have potential teratogenics effects including cleft lip, neural tube defects (especially Sodium Valproate), congenital heart defects and urogenital defects.  Emergency management of generalised tonic clonic seizures:  in case of GCTS, more than five minutes in the community either Buccal Midazolam or Rectal diazepam can be administered  if IV line established, then IV Lorazepam is given. Status epilepticus - adult Stage Adult 1. Premonitory (pre-hospital)  10–20 mg diazepam PR repeated once every 15 minutes or 10 mg midazolam PO 2. Early status (0–10 minutes)  secure airway  administer oxygen and gain IV access  lorazepam IV 0.1 mg/kg (usually a 4 mg bolus, repeated once after 10– 20 minutes; rate not critical)  give usual AED medication if already on treatment  for sustained control or if seizures continue, treat as below. 3. Established status (0–160 minutes)  phenytoin infusion at a dose of 15– 18 mg/kg at a rate of 50 mg/min or  posphenytoin infusion at a dose of 15-20 mg phenytoin equivalents (PE)/kg at a rate of 50–100 mg PE/min or  phenobarbital bolus of 10–15 mg/kg at a rate of 100 mg/min. 4. Surgical  Surgical intervention may be considered in patients who continue to be symptomatic despite maximal drug treatment. The goal of epilepsy surgery is to minimise frequency and severity of seizure, and to stop them entirely if possible.  Surgical Procedures include:  temporal lobectomy  amygdalohippocampectomy  lesionectomy  localised neocortical resections  hemispherectomy.  Prognosis  The prognosis of epilepsy varies markedly depending on the:  type epilepsy syndrome  frequency of seizures (the number of seizures in the six months after first presentation is an important predictive factor for both early and long-term remission of seizures)  response to AEDs.  Up to 80% of people with childhood absence epilepsy will be in remission by adulthood; 90% of people with generalised tonic-clonic seizures only will achieve seizure control.  In children and adults with epilepsy, approximately 70% will be in remission (seizure-free for five years on or off drug treatment) but 30% will have ongoing seizures.  The risk of recurrent seizures is highest in the first 12 months and falls to less than 10% after two years.  Most seizures are controlled with appropriate treatment.
