DR. JAM Essential Tremor Essential tremor is typically a postural, symmetrical tremor, most commonly affecting the upper limbs but can also affect the legs, head, jaw and tongue.  Overview Key Facts  Essential tremor is typically a postural, symmetrical tremor, most commonly affecting the upper limbs but can also affect the legs, head, jaw and tongue.  It is the most common cause of debilitating tremor.  Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern in up to 50% of cases, although it can occur with no family history (usually after the age of 40).  The exact pathophysiology is still unknown.  The tremor may be transient at first and become persistent over time.  Tremor usually improves with alcohol and when focusing on specific tasks and worsens with stress, sleep deprivation and caffeine.  Can sometimes be misdiagnosed as Parkinson’s disease, or vice versa.  The diagnosis usually made from history and examination. Other causes of tremor should be excluded, such as alcohol or medications.  Blood tests may help to exclude other causes of tremor such as vitamin deficiencies, hyperthyroidism or Wilson’s disease.  Imaging is not usually required unless concerned about other causes of tremor.  Beta-blockers such as propranolol or primidone (a barbiturate) are the mainstay of pharmacological treatment.  Essential tremor is often poorly responsive to medication.  Deep brain stimulation or radiofrequency thalamotomy can be used for persistent or debilitating cases.  Essential tremor is generally a progressive condition and there is currently no cure. Epidemiology  Essential tremor is the most common cause of debilitating tremor.  Men and women equally affected.  If inherited (autosomal dominant pattern), can present in childhood. If occurs sporadically, usually presents after the age of 40.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  Inherited in an autosomal dominant manner in up to 50% of cases and can be seen in childhood.  May present sporadically (usually after 40 years of age). Pathophysiology  The exact pathophysiology of essential tremor is still largely unknown.  Post-mortem studies have shown that the majority of patients with essential tremor have changes in the cerebellum, including a reduced number of Purkinje cells.  Clinical Presentation  Typically presents as a symmetrical postural tremor, most commonly affecting the upper limbs but can also affect the legs, head, jaw and tongue.  It may be transient at first but often becomes persistent over time.  The tremor does not occur during sleep and may improve or resolve while the person is concentrating on particular tasks.  Does not reduce the speed of movement or cause a decrease in muscle tone.  Many report that the tremor improves following alcohol.  Stress, sleep deprivation or caffeine may worsen the tremor. Classification of tremors: Rest tremor Postural tremor Action/intentio n tremor Characteristi c Occurs at rest while the limb is fully supported Tremor occurs when the limb is raised against gravity Occurs during a voluntary active movement, for example, fingernose test Examples Parkinson’s disease Druginduced parkinsonis m Physiologica l tremor Anxiety Alcohol Wilson’s disease Cerebellar disease  It is important to note that patients may have more than one type of tremor and may present atypically. Therefore, diagnosis can be very challenging.  Differential Diagnosis  Other causes of tremor include:  Parkinson’s disease:  often mistaken for essential tremor as patients are often in the same age demographic and they can present very similarly in the early stages

DR. JAM  classically a unilateral, resting tremor, improved with movement  may have other symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, such as bradykinesia, hypokinesia, gait disturbance, rigidity, depression and cognitive impairment.  drug-induced parkinsonism – typically secondgeneration antipsychotics such as risperidone, olanzapine and clozapine  caffeine  anxiety  hyperthyroidism  hypoglycaemia  drug-induced tremor  multiple sclerosis  Wilson’s disease  cerebellar disease  organophosphate or heavy metal poisoning  basal ganglia lesions  vitamin B1 deficiency.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is made clinically from history and examination.  Medications should be reviewed to rule out drug-induced tremor.  A thorough alcohol history should be taken.  Blood tests may be useful to rule out other causes of tremor such as vitamin deficiencies, thyroid disease or Wilson’s disease.  Imaging not required unless concerned about other causes of tremor.  Management  Treatment is usually initiated in primary care and referral to a neurologist is only necessary if symptoms are debilitating.  Initial pharmacological treatment:  beta-blockers such as propranolol or  primidone (a barbiturate usually used for treating epilepsy).  Essential tremor is often poorly responsive to pharmacological treatment.  For patients with debilitating symptoms or persistent, troubling symptoms despite pharmacological management, surgery may be offered, such as:  deep brain stimulation  radiofrequency thalamotomy.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Essential tremor is generally a progressive condition with no cure. Facial Nerve Ramsay Hunt Syndrome Ramsay Hunt syndrome (also called herpes zoster oticus) occurs due to varicella-zoster virus reactivation affecting the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, resulting in facial nerve paralysis.  Overview Key Facts  Ramsay Hunt syndrome (also called herpes zoster oticus) occurs due to varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation affecting the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, resulting in facial nerve paralysis.  It often occurs in older adults, presenting with unilateral facial palsy, vesicles in/around the area and deafness.  Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, although virological studies can confirm the presence of VZV.  Treatment involves prompt oral steroids (prednisolone) and antivirals (aciclovir), with consideration of eye protection (lubrication and taping eye shut at night).  Complications include corneal ulceration/abrasions, secondary infection of vesicle site, chronic hearing loss (< 5%)/tinnitus/vestibular dysfunction.  Shingles vaccination in the over 70s is a good preventative measure. Epidemiology  The facial nerve is the most common cranial nerve to be affected by a mononeuropathy, with Ramsay Hunt syndrome being a less common cause than Bell’s palsy.  Older people (> 60 years) are affected by shingles more than the young.  Around one-third of all people have shingles in their lifetime, with around 1% of these having Ramsay Hunt syndrome.  Ramsay Hunt, specifically, is more common in women than men. Aetiology  Ramsay Hunt syndrome is due to VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion (the sensory root) of the 7th cranial nerve (aka, VII, the facial nerve).

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Primary VZV infection causes chickenpox; following this, the virus becomes latent in sensory ganglia. Reactivation of VZV globally is also called herpes zoster virus or shingles.  VZV reactivation risk is increased by age and immunocompromise.  The geniculate ganglion is located in the facial canal of the temporal bone.  The geniculate ganglion has nervous involvement from many areas, eg taste fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, motor supply of VII and signals to the lacrimal and salivary glands. This accounts for a lot of the clinical features.  Ramsay Hunt syndrome is classed as a lower motor neurone (LMN) cause of unilateral facial palsy with ipsilateral weakness on the same side where VZV has been reactivated.  The muscles of facial expression can be examined to assess facial nerve function. The upper muscles (eg temporalis) are bilaterally innervated, so if it has been affected at an upper motor neurone level, only the lower half of the face is affected on the contralateral side of the pathology. This is an important examination difference between UMN and LMN pathologies.  Clinical Presentation  Mostly presents in older adults.  Unilateral facial palsy – weak eye closure and weak frontalis muscle movements (eg weak ‘frowning’).  Vesicles, often painful, on the external auditory meatus and/or the soft palate (however, some studies show these only appear in around 1 in 10 cases).  Unilateral dribbling (contralateral side to the palsy).  Deafness – sensorineural hearing loss.  Unsteadiness/vertigo.  Taste loss specifically in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.  Nausea and vomiting.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  Bell’s palsy  other causes of hearing loss, eg Ménière's disease  other causes of ‘unsteadiness’  otitis externa/media  cholesteatoma  Lyme disease  parotid malignancy  upper motor neurone (UMN) lesion, eg stroke, malignancy  post-herpetic neuralgia.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is normally made through clinical examination and history alone.  It is important to first eliminate UMN causes of facial palsy.  Examination – full neurological and cranial nerve examination, ear examination (neurological differences can be mainly seen in testing the muscles of facial expression).  Potential investigation might include PCR testing of swabs from vesicles to determine VZV presence or audiology to further evaluate the associated hearing loss.  Further confirmation of the presence of VZV might be with antibody serology.  Other investigations are used to rule out differentials or to establish an immunological vulnerability of the patient (eg brain imaging for lesions, blood testing for human immunodeficiency virus).  Management  Often requires specialty-specific referral, eg dermatology, ENT, neurology, infectious diseases. Non-pharmacological  Eye protection – eye taping at night, lubricating eye drops.  Pharmacological  Important to start quickly in shingles (< 72 hours from onset), assumed to be similar in Ramsay Hunt:  oral antivirals + steroids (eg in adults – aciclovir 800 mg, 5 times per day, for 7 days + prednisolone 60 mg OD, for 7 days, then reduction).  Analgesia.  Prognosis  Lower rates of recovery than in Bell’s palsy, where more than 2 out of 3 patients fully recover.  Complication risk – corneal ulceration/abrasions, secondary infection of vesicle site, chronic hearing loss (< 5%)/ tinnitus/ vestibular dysfunction.  Prevention:  shingles vaccination (in the United Kingdom > 70 years, regardless of previous VZV infection). Friedreich’s Ataxia Friedreich’s ataxia is a multisystem disorder affecting mainly the central nervous system and heart.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Friedreich’s ataxia is a multisystem disorder affecting mainly the central nervous system and heart.  It is inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion.  Most patients (98%) have a GAA repeat expansion of the frataxin gene.  The most common causes of death are congestive heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias.  Unsteadiness of gait is the usual presenting symptom.  The average life expectancy is 40–50 years. Epidemiology  Prevalence is approximately 1.8 per 100 000 in the United Kingdom.  Symptoms begin between the ages of five and 20 years. Aetiology  Friedreich’s ataxia is inherited as an autosomal-recessive disorder.  It is caused by a defect in the FXN gene, which carries the code for the frataxin protein. Pathophysiology  The majority of patients with Friedreich’s ataxia are homozygous for a GAA repeat expansion in the noncoding region of the gene coding for the mitochondrial protein frataxin.  Mutations cause oxidative injury associated with excessive iron deposits in the mitochondria.  Friedreich’s ataxia involves the spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns in the spinal cord, the pyramidal tracts and the cerebellum and medulla.  Clinical Presentation  Central nervous system:  progressive ataxia:  an early sign of the disease.  absence of deep tendon reflexes (mainly the Achilles’ reflex)  spasticity  peripheral sensory neuropathy  dysarthria:  an early sign of the disease.  difficulty in swallowing  muscle weakness  intelligence is preserved.  Musculoskeletal:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  progressive kyphoscoliosis:  in up to two-thirds of patients.  pes cavus  hammer toes  kyphoscoliosis.  Heart:  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy  myocardial fibrosis  congestive heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias:  the primary cause of death for most patients.  Pancreas:  diabetes mellitus:  present in 10–30% of people with Friedreich’s ataxia.  impaired glucose tolerance.  Eyes:  optic atrophy:  occurs in 25–50% of patients.  Hearing:  hearing loss:  usually in the later stages of the disease.  Differential Diagnosis  Spinocerebellar ataxia.  Dentato-rubro-pallido-luysian atrophy.  Episodic ataxia.  Spastic ataxia.  Abetalipoproteinemia.  Refsum syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis of Friedreich’s ataxia requires a careful clinical examination.  Nerve-conduction studies:  will show motor velocities > 40 milliseconds in the arms and absent sensory action potentials.  Genetic analysis.  Electrocardiogram (ECG):  there may be ventricular hypertrophy and T-wave inversion.  Exclude vitamin E deficiency.  Further investigations:  blood tests:  full blood count  urea and electrolytes  glucose.

DR. JAM  electrocardiogram (ECG):  ventricular hypertrophy  septal hypertrophy  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy  magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain and spinal cord:  shows characteristic atrophic changes, particularly of the cervical spinal cord.  brainstem auditory-evoked responses and visual-evoked potentials:  may be abnormal.  Management Non-pharmacological  Treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia is symptomatic and supportive.  A multidisciplinary treatment strategy is the most appropriate approach given that the condition affects multiple organ systems.  Physiotherapy.  Speech-and-language therapy.  Occupational therapy.  Liaison with educational and social services.  Passive exercises and warming for peripheral cyanosis and cold feet.  Dysphagia may require dietary modification.  Pharmacological  Most trials so far have focused on antioxidant therapy:  coenzyme Q10 and vitamin E have been reported to slow progression in some patients.  Friedreich’s ataxia is a disease with multisystem involvement. Annual reviews should include assessment of:  neurology  cardiac function  musculoskeletal problems  comprehensive systems review  blood tests.  Diabetes (if present) will usually require insulin.  Counselling or antidepressants for depression (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors).  Treatment of cardiac failure and/or arrhythmias, using standard treatments. Surgical  Orthopaedic surgery is necessary if there are symptoms from:  scoliosis  pes cavus

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  equinovarus deformity of the feet.  Gastrostomy:  in the later stages of the disease.  Prognosis  The average life expectancy is 40–50 years, but disease severity and progression vary; some patients live into their seventies.  Loss of the ability to walk typically occurs about 15 years after diagnosis.  The most commonly reported causes of death are cardiac failure and arrhythmias. Frontotemporal Dementia Frontotemporal dementia is a group of neurodegenerative disorders that primarily affect the frontal and temporal lobes of the brain, leading to changes in behaviour, personality and language skills, rather than memory loss, which is more common in other types of dementia such as Alzheimer's disease.  Overview Key Facts  Dementia is a progressive impairment of cognition that has an impact on daily functioning.  Loss of short-term memory is often the first sign of the condition.  Other changes may include changes in behaviour, personality, speech, perception, thought processes and mood.  Prevalence increases with age.  The most common cause is Alzheimer’s disease which makes up over 50% of cases.  Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a less common form of degenerative dementia.  It is also known as Pick's disease and frontal lobe dementia.  It is more commonly first diagnosed in people aged under 65 years and in some cases in patients as young as 45.  It is a heterogeneous condition and there are multiple types of pathological change associated with it.  Approximately half of FTD cases are caused by tau pathology (commonly Pick’s bodies), most of the rest are associated with transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) inclusions.  Pathologically, FTD is linked to many other neurodegenerative conditions.  The pathological changes of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD), both tauopathies, may be seen postmortem.

DR. JAM  Progressive atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes is seen on neuroimaging.  Cases of FTD are more likely to be hereditary than the other neurodegenerative dementias.  Up to 40% of patients with FTD have a family history of dementia or a related neurodegenerative condition.  The ﬁrst two genes identiﬁed were both on chromosome 17 – microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) and progranulin (GRN).  More recently, a hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72 was discovered and is now the most common genetic cause of FTD.  Mutations in C9orf72 can also cause familial motor neurone disease (MND) and some patients develop a combination of FTD and MND.  FTD presents with alterations in behaviour, personality and social conduct and can be broadly broken down into:  behavioural variant FTD  primary progressive aphasia  semantic FTD.  Patients may appear disinhibited or apathetic or have difficulties with language production associated with their behavioural syndrome.  Although patients are typically free of focal neurological deﬁcits, on bedside examination some patients do exhibit frontal release signs such as the grasp reﬂex.  In time patients may develop parkinsonism and some patients develop signs of MND.  There are currently no licensed treatments for FTD:  management is based on optimising social care and educating caregivers to cope with the patient’s behaviours.  The condition typically has a slower course of progression than other forms of dementia, however, this can be variable. Epidemiology  The condition is a rarer form of dementia but may be significantly underdiagnosed.  The condition is slightly more common in women.  FTD is often first diagnosed between the ages of 45 and 65. Aetiology  Cases of FTD are more likely to be hereditary than the other neurodegenerative dementias.  Up to 40% of patients with FTD have a family history of dementia or a related neurodegenerative condition.  The ﬁrst two genes identiﬁed were both on chromosome 17 – microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) and progranulin (GRN).  More recently, a hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72 was discovered and is now the most common genetic cause of FTD.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Mutations in C9orf72 can also cause familial motor neurone disease (MND) and some patients develop a combination of FTD and MND. Pathophysiology  Approximately half of FTD cases are caused by tau pathology (commonly Pick’s bodies).  Most of the rest are associated with transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) inclusions.  A small number of patients have fused-in-sarcoma (FUS) pathology.  Pathologically FTD is linked to many other neurodegenerative conditions.  The pathological changes of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD), both tauopathies, may be seen postmortem.  Progressive atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes is seen on neuroimaging.  Clinical Presentation  Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) presents with alterations in behaviour, personality and social conduct.  The onset of FTD tends to be insidious and progression gradual.  In time patients may develop parkinsonism.  Some patients develop signs of motor neurone disease (MND).  There are three main clinical syndromes of FTD, defined by the predominant symptom at presentation. 1. Behavioural variant FTD (two-thirds of cases)  May present with:  loss of inhibition  inappropriate social behaviour  loss of motivation (not associated with depression)  loss of empathy  loss of sympathy  change in preferences  repetitive or compulsive behaviours, rituals  loss of control over eating or drinking  difficulties with planning, organisation or decision making  memory and visuospatial skills usually preserved in early stages  cognitive deficit less apparent than behavioural changes  lack of insight  loss of awareness of personal hygiene and incontinence as the disease progresses.  On examination:

DR. JAM  there are usually no neurological signs, unless part of an overlap syndrome  neurological examination may show primitive reflexes (forced grasping, rooting, sucking) in later stages  echolalia (repetition of sounds made by others), perseveration (continued repetition of a particular response) or mutism  there may be inappropriate or disinhibited behaviour during consultation. 2. Semantic dementia  May present with:  loss of vocabulary  fluency of speech maintained  may ask the meaning of familiar words  difficulty finding the right word and having to talk around it or describe it  loss of recognition of familiar faces or objects  memory and visuospatial skills comparatively well preserved.  Neurological examination is usually normal. 3. Progressive non-fluent aphasia  Common early symptoms include:  slow, hesitant, difficult speech  grammatical errors in speech  impaired understanding of complex sentences, although recognition of individual words preserved  loss of literacy skills.  On examination:  impairment of orofacial movements such as swallowing, coughing or yawning on command  stuttering, impairment of the ability to write or read, or impaired repetition ability.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include other forms of dementia as well as:  depression  pseudodementia  mild cognitive impairment  delirium  transient global amnesia  epilepsy  cerebrovasclar events  neoplasm  drugs – anticholinergics  other psychiatric disorders:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  schizophrenia  psychosis  mania.  Other forms of dementia: Signs/symptoms Clinical features Alzheimer’s disease Short-term memory loss Dysphasia Dyspraxia Behavioural changes, eg wandering Psychotic symptoms Apathy Progressive disease Vascular dementia Gait disturbance Personality change Labile mood Urinary symptoms Insight preserved Stepwise progression Cardiovascular disease risk factors Dementia with Lewy bodies/Parkinson’s disease dementia Fluctuating dementia Delirium Parkinsonism Visual hallucinations Sleep disorders Progressive disease Frontotemporal degeneration Stereotyped behaviours Personality change Loss of insight Expressive dysphasia Preserved memory Primitive reflexes Progresses slowly Family history More common in women with early-onset before

Huntington’s disease Schizophrenialike psychosis Choreiform movement Depression Irritability Dementia Presents in earlier life during ages 20–40 years Family history Normal-pressure hydrocephalus Apathy Inattention Urinary incontinence Gait apraxia Presents in 50– 70-year-olds Reversible dementia Prion disease Myoclonic jerks Seizures Starts at < 50 years

DR. JAM Cerebellar ataxia Rapid onset Rapid progression  Diagnosis/Investigation  History and examination will help distinguish between causes and form the basis of diagnosis (patients should be referred to a specialist to confirm the diagnosis).  Cognitive testing – mini-mental state examination and Addenbrooke’s cognitive examination.  Baseline bloods – full blood count (FBC), electrolytes (U&Es), liver function, thyroid function, vitamin B12/folate, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), antinuclear antibody (ANA), syphilis and HIV.  Radiography – chest X-ray.  Brain imaging – computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).  Electroencephalogram (EEG).  Other special tests – lumbar puncture, cerebral flow studies, neuropsychological testing and genetic testing.  PET (positron emission tomography) and SPECT (singlephoton emission computerised tomography) may identify reduced frontal/temporal lobe activity before changes can be seen on other modalities such as CT or MRI.  Management  There are currently no licensed treatments for FTD:  management is based on optimising social care and educating caregivers to cope with the patient’s behaviours  psychotropic drugs may be used with caution for depression and psychotic symptoms.  Management should also involve assessment and management of the patients functional and social needs as well as considering the supportive needs of the carer of the patient.  Management should be on a case-by-case basis. Non-pharmacological management  Patients should be given written information regarding:  the course of the condition and prognosis  medical treatment options available  support groups and associations  sources of legal and financial advice  driving advice (DVLA must be informed of all drivers diagnosed with dementia).  People with mild-to-moderate dementia should be given the opportunity to participate in structured group cognitive stimulation programmes to help maintain cognitive skills and day-to-day functioning.  Memory enhancement strategies should be discussed, such as using reminder notes, lists and reorganisation of possessions.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may be helpful for patients with symptoms of depression or anxiety, involving their carers.  Other non-pharmacological approaches for those with anxiety, depression or behaviour issues may include exercise, aromatherapy and multi-sensory stimulation.  Palliative and end-of-life care should be discussed and planned for as appropriate.  Social support should be initiated and progressed as the condition advances.  Arrange admission for people with suspected dementia if:  they are severely disturbed and admission is needed to ensure the health and safety of the person or the safety of others  assessment in primary care is not appropriate, such as complex physical and psychiatric problems.  Treat any identified, modifiable risk factors for cognitive impairment:  such as excess alcohol intake, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity and smoking, where possible.  Prognosis  There is currently no cure for FTD.  The progression of the disease cannot be slowed down; however, the condition progresses more slowly when compared with other forms of dementia.  The prognosis is variable between individuals but there is a gradual decline in social, cognitive and neurological abilities, eventually leading to complete dependence.  The average survival is 8–10 years.  Prognosis is worse when there is overlap with other syndromes, such as with MND. Fungal Infections Fungal infections are very common and usually associated with low morbidity and mortality.  Overview Key Facts  Fungal infections are very common and usually associated with low morbidity and mortality:  onychomycosis – fungal nail infections with thickening and discolouration  candidiasis – oral, oesophageal and vaginal manifestations  ringworm – tinea infection affecting groins, scalp and other skin sites

DR. JAM  histoplasmosis – caused by the fungus histoplasma.  Fungi are important commensals on the skin and within the gastrointestinal tract; immunocompetent hosts are rarely susceptible to severe infection.  Invasive fungal infection is an important problem in immunocompromised patients:  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) co-infection  following chemotherapy or bone marrow transplantation.  Aspergillosis is an important disorder in patients with asthma.  Suspect diabetes mellitus in patients with recurrent presentations with fungal illness.  Organisms causing endemic fungal infections include cryptococcus and histoplasma. Epidemiology  Annual global incidence of fungal infection is estimated at > 1 billion cases.  However, deaths from fungal infection are rare – estimated at < 1.5 million per year with the key risk factor for invasive fungal infection being immunosuppression.  Key risk factor for histoplasmosis is caving (transmitted from bat droppings). Aetiology  Important fungal pathogens include candida albicans, tinea spp, aspergillus spp, cryptococcus neoformans, histoplasma spp and pneumocystis jirovecii. Dermatophytes  Trichophyton rubrum  T. interdigitale  Epidermophyton floccosum (tinea pedis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea unguium) Yeasts  Candida spp. (intertrigo, oral, genital or systemic)  Pityrosporum orbiculare; pityriasis versicolor Pathophysiology  Unlike bacterial infection, the pathophysiology of fungal infections is still poorly understood. Several mechanisms are likely to contribute to virulence in humans.  Fungi have dual morphology – yeast form and filament-like hyphae form.  Either or both may be involved in pathogenesis of certain infections.  Invasive forms of aspergillosis show evidence of disseminated hyphae within tissues.  Clinical Presentation  The presentation of candidiasis depends on the site affected:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  oral candidiasis – white plaques within the oral cavity overlaying raw red mucosa  oesophageal candidiasis – odynophagia  vaginal candidiasis – ‘cottage-cheese’ white discharge.  Tinea infection presents with annular, erythematous skin lesions:  tinea capitis – non-scarring alopecia and overlying scaly changes.  Aspergillosis has a wide range of clinical manifestations, reflecting variation in the host immune status and responses. There are four major sub-types of aspergillosis:  aspergilloma – usually asymptomatic, sometimes mild haemoptysis  invasive aspergillosis – fever, cough with copious sputum production, and pleuritic chest pain  allergic pulmonary aspergillosis – productive cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath  chronic pulmonary aspergillosis – chronic productive cough and shortness of breath.  Cryptococcus infection is usually seen in immunocompromised host:  presents with a subacute history (1–2 weeks) of headache, fevers and confusion  rarer forms of cryptococcosis include wound infection and pulmonary involvement (dry cough, fever, and fatigue).  Typical features of histoplasmosis include:  dry cough and shortness of breath  fever  headache  malaise, fatigue, and arthralgia.  Differential Diagnosis  Oral candidiasis – oral hairy leukoplakia, lichen planus, and malignancy.  Ringworm – psoriasis, alopecia areata, pityriasis versicolor, and vitiligo.  Aspergilloma (haemoptysis) – malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism (PE), and pulmonary-renal syndrome.  Aspergillosis (wheeze and chronic cough) – Churg-Strauss disease and tuberculosis.  Cryptococcal meningitis (headache and fever) – bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, and viral encephalitis.  Histoplasmosis – community-acquired pneumonia, pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), and malignancy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Most simple fungal infections do not require further investigation unless there is significant diagnostic doubt and can usually proceed with trial of treatment:

DR. JAM  tinea infections – consider skin scrapings with potassium hydroxide microscopy  oral candidiasis – consider taking sample beneath white plaque for microscopy.  In patients with recurrent infections, measure fasting glucose to in case of diabetes.  In patients with invasive fungal disease, always perform HIV testing.  Aspergillosis:  imaging:  chest X-ray may demonstrate cavitation, nonspecific consolidation  high resolution computed tomography (CT) is the most sensitive test – pulmonary infiltrates with characteristic ‘halo sign’  serology – aspergillus RAST, IgE, beta-glucan, and galactomannan  BAL (invasive aspergillosis) – fungal hyphae and fungal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of aspirates.  Histoplasmosis:  chest X-ray – may show diffuse reticulonodular changes but no change in 40–50%.  sputum culture  blood tests for histoplasma antigen.  Cryptococcal meningitis:  lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) staining with India ink.  Management Non-pharmacological  Patients with invasive fungal disease are often severely unwell and required good quality supportive care in an High Dependency Unit (HDU) and/or Intensive Care Unit (ITU) setting.  Pharmacological  Oral candidiasis is usually managed with miconazole oral gel or nystatin mouthwash; oral fluconazole may be required for severe or persistent infection.  Oesophageal candidiasis requires a more prolonged course of ‘azole’ drug.  Vaginal candidiasis can be managed using an antifungal pessary or ointment (eg clotrimazole) or short courses of oral fluconazole.  Tinea infection is usually managed with topical antifungals (eg terbinafine) extensive involvement may require oral antifungal treatment.  Invasive aspergillosis is treated aggressively with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B.  Drug treatment for aspergilloma is usually reserved for patients with recurrent haemoptysis, systemic symptoms or with evidence of local fungal invasion:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  intracavitatory instillation of amphotericin paste  oral voriconazole.  Acute and chronic severe forms of pulmonary histoplasmosis are managed with intravenous azole drugs (eg voriconazole).  The treatment of choice for cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B. Surgical  Patients with aspergilloma who present with massive haemoptysis may require bronchial artery embolisation.  Large aspergillomas can also be excised surgically.  Prognosis  Severe fungal infection is rare in immunocompetent individuals.  However untreated infection such as candida can persist for months or years.  Fungal infection of the skin may often relapse following treatment.  Conditions may become chronic in susceptible people.  Despite good supportive care, the prognosis for patients with severe invasive fungal disease is poor.  Other Tinea corporis – note annular erythematous lesion with overlying scaling: Oral candidiasis – loosely adherent white plaques over patient’s tongue:

DR. JAM Guillain-Barré Syndrome Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute, immune polyneuropathy presenting with rapidly evolving weakness and variable sensory loss which is ascending in nature.  Overview Key Facts  Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune polyneuropathy presenting with rapidly evolving weakness and variable sensory loss which is ascending in nature.  Most patients report preceding upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) or urinary tract infection (UTI).  The most commonly identified organism causing GBS is Campylobacter jejuni.  The cardinal feature is post-infection ascending paralysis.  Clinical symptoms include:  flaccid muscle tone  hyporeflexia/areflexia  autonomic disturbances  neuromuscular ventilatory failure  symptoms include shortness of breath on exertion, early morning headache and low forced vital capacity (FVC).  Investigations include:  cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: normal white cell count (WCC) and glucose with raised protein  nerve conduction study: delayed conduction velocities indicating demyelination of peripheral nerves

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  electrocardiogram (ECG): rhythm disturbances  electrolyte study  pulmonary function tests ie spirometry FVC to monitor ventilation.  Treatment includes:  IVIG and plasma exchange  supportive therapy:  feeding care  ventilatory support (the patient may require intubation and ventilation)  pressure care  analgesia.  Prognosis is generally good:  most people make a full recovery, although this may take months  there is a 5% mortality rate, mostly due to the inhibition of ventilation  around 20% of patients go on to experience long-term complications:  weakness  paraesthesia  fatigue. Headache - Primary And Secondary Headache is a common non-specific symptom and may be divided into primary headache (no clear underlying cause) and secondary headache (occurs due to underlying pathology).  Overview Key Facts  Headache is a common non-specific symptom and may be divided into primary headache (no clear underlying cause) and secondary headache (occurs due to underlying pathology).  Causes of primary headache include:  migraine  cluster headache  tension-type headache.  Causes of secondary headache include:  infection  neoplasm  medication overuse  trauma

DR. JAM  vascular disorders.  Assessment includes a detailed history and thorough examination, including vital signs, neurological exam, fundoscopy and examination of extracranial structures.  Diagnosis is often clinical in the case of primary headache; further testing may be required to exclude secondary causes or to diagnose them if there is clinical suspicion.  Investigations that may be indicated include laboratory testing including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), as well as neuroimaging.  Headache diaries may also assist in diagnosis and management.  Management varies depending on the type of headache in the case of primary headache or the underlying cause in the case of secondary headache. Aetiology  Most primary headaches are of unknown aetiology.  lifestyle factors such as stress, alcohol, excess caffeine intake and smoking may exacerbate episodes.  Conditions associated with secondary headache include:  hypertension  disorders of facial and cranial nerves  malignancy  infection  intracranial haemorrhage  giant cell arteritis  central venous thrombosis  carbon monoxide exposure  substance withdrawal  chronic hypoxia.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation of primary headache includes various characters of headache ie dull, throbbing or stabbing.  Associated features may include:  nausea and vomiting  dizziness  photophobia  lacrimation  pericranial tenderness  aura (focal and transient neurological symptoms associated with migraine).  Clinical presentation of secondary headache depends upon the underlying condition but will be any type of headache, which may be associated with:  vomiting  photophobia  loss of consciousness  changes in pupil size

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  fever  changes in heart rate or breathing pattern.  memory disturbances.  Differential Diagnosis Headaches may be due to a wide range of causes including:  migraine  tension-like headache  cluster headache  trigeminal cephalgia and/or neuralgia  optic neuritis  medication overuse headache  substance exposure or withdrawal  intracranial disorders and/or neoplasms  infection  vasculitis  head and/or neck injury  infection – meningitis, encephalitis, herpes zoster or systemic infections  somatisation disorder  sinus infection  glaucoma  otitis media  dental problems.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is usually clinical with primary headaches and is aided by detailed history and thorough physical examination.  The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICD third edition) diagnostic criteria based on history and examination findings are used to classify common types of primary headache including:  migraine without aura  migraine with aura  tension-type headache  cluster headache  medication overuse headache.  National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend referral to secondary care with urgency depending on the clinical situation if there are any red flags or serious causes of headache suspected, such as:  new, sudden or severe or unexpected headache  progressive or persistent headache  fever  neck pain and/or stiffness  photophobia

DR. JAM  papilloedema  new onset neurological deficit  atypical aura or new onset aura in a patient on combined oral contraceptive  visual disturbance or vomiting (unless a diagnosis of migraine is clear)  contacts with similar symptoms  recent head trauma (within the last three months)  headache worse on standing or lying down  current or recent pregnancy  history of malignancy  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)/immunosuppression.  If the diagnosis is unclear and serious causes have been ruled out:  ask the patient to keep a headache diary  arrange a review of the results  possibly arrange neurology consultation.  Management  Management varies depending on the type or cause of headache.  Primary headache may be managed with analgesia and lifestyle modification, but specific therapies may be indicated ie triptans in migraine.  Secondary headache treatment will require management as per the underlying diagnosis ie steroid treatment in temporal arteritis. Holmes–Adie Syndrome Holmes–Adie syndrome is a neurological condition that causes pupil abnormalities (Holmes–Adie pupil) and absent deep tendon reflexes (usually Achilles reflex).  Overview Key Facts  Holmes–Adie syndrome is a neurological condition that causes pupil abnormalities (Holmes–Adie pupil) and absent deep tendon reflexes (usually Achilles reflex).  A Holmes–Adie pupil has an absent or slow response to light (direct and consensual) but normal accommodation reflex.  It most commonly affects young women and presents unilaterally in 80% of cases.  Holmes–Adie syndrome is a clinical diagnosis. There are no specific laboratory or imaging investigations.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Most patients do not require treatment. Reading glasses or pilocarpine eye drops may be considered.  Life expectancy is not reduced. Deep tendon reflexes will not recover. Epidemiology  Holmes–Adie syndrome has a prevalence of 2 cases per 1000 population.  Women are more affected than men (2.6 : 1).  It presents unilaterally in 80% of cases.  It may be associated with other diseases of the nervous system. Aetiology  It is mostly idiopathic and may be associated with infections that damage the ciliary ganglion (eg syphilis).  Other causes include tumours, trauma, autoimmune disease or complications post-operation. Pathophysiology  Damage to the neurones in ciliary and dorsal root ganglia due to a viral infection.  Damage to the ciliary ganglion results in interrupted parasympathetic supply to the ciliary body and iris.  Damage to the dorsal root ganglion results in loss of deep tendon reflexes.  Clinical Presentation  Patients with Holmes–Adie syndrome present with unilateral dilated pupil, which constricts very slowly in response to light (tonic pupil) and loss of deep tendon reflexes.  Ross syndrome is a variant of Holmes–Adie syndrome. Patients with Ross syndrome have a triad of Holmes–Aide pupil, loss of deep tendon reflexes and hypohidrosis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  pharmacological dilation cause of mydriasis  oculomotor nerve palsy  optic nerve diseases  Argyll Robertson pupils.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Holmes–Adie syndrome is a clinical diagnosis.  There are no specific laboratory or imaging investigations.  Management  Most patients do not require treatment.

DR. JAM Non-pharmacological  Reading glasses.  Pharmacological  Pilocarpine eyedrops:  three times daily  constricts the dilated pupil.  Prognosis  Life expectancy is not reduced.  However, the symptoms may progress. If the patient presents with loss of deep tendon reflexes, it is permanent and will not recover. Horner Syndrome Horner syndrome describes the triad of ptosis (eyelid drooping), miosis (pupil constriction) and anhidrosis (reduced/lack of sweating on the affected side).  Overview Key Facts  Horner syndrome describes the triad of ptosis (eyelid drooping), miosis (pupil constriction) and anhidrosis (reduced/lack of sweating on the affected side).  This is caused by interruption of the sympathetic pupillomotor fibres, due to a lesion anywhere along the three-neurone sympathetic pathway.  The condition can be congenital or acquired.  In cases of acquired Horner syndrome, it may be due to serious pathology in the head, neck or chest.  Causes can be divided according to the presence and location of anhidrosis:  central/first order (anhidrosis of face, arm and trunk) – syringomyelia, multiple sclerosis, encephalitis, brain tumours, lateral medullary syndrome  preganglionic/second-order (anhidrosis of face) – cervical rib, thyroid carcinoma/thyroidectomy, bronchogenic carcinoma (Pancoast tumour), trauma, thoracic aortic aneurysm  postganglionic/third-order (no anhidrosis) – cluster headache, carotid artery dissection/aneurysm, cavernous sinus thrombosis, middle ear infection.  The site of the lesion is on the ipsilateral side of the symptoms.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Signs and symptoms include:  miosis – due to inactivation of dilator pupillae  partial ptosis – due to paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle  anhidrosis – due to decreased sympathetic stimulation  apparent enophthalmos  heterochromia iridum (only present in congenital Horner syndrome) due to lack of sympathetic stimulation in childhood interfering with melanin pigmentation of melanocytes.  Diagnosis involves confirming that signs and symptoms are due to Horner syndrome via examination and pharmacological testing, and then investigating to identify the underlying cause.  Treatment and prognosis are dependent on the underlying diagnosis. Aetiology  Causes can be divided according to the presence and location of anhidrosis:  central/first order (anhidrosis of face, arm and trunk):  syringomyelia  multiple sclerosis  encephalitis  brain tumours  lateral medullary syndrome.  preganglionic/second order (anhidrosis of face):  cervical rib  thyroid carcinoma/thyroidectomy  bronchogenic carcinoma (Pancoast tumour)  trauma  thoracic aortic aneurysm.  postganglionic/third order (no anhidrosis):  cluster headache  carotid artery dissection/aneurysm  cavernous sinus thrombosis  middle ear infection. Pathophysiology  Pupil size depends on both pupillodilator (sympathetic) and pupilloconstrictor (parasympathetic) ﬁbres.  Pupils of unequal sizes are not related to optic nerve disease.  Newline pupilloconstrictor ﬁbres travel from the Edinger– Westphal nucleus in the midbrain to the orbit on the third nerve.  The sympathetic (pupillodilator) ﬁbres follow a complex path:  first-order – from the posterior hypothalamus, through the brainstem to the C8–T2 level of the spinal cord – the ciliospinal centre of Budge

DR. JAM  second-order – preganglionic neurones from the cord pass to the paravertebral sympathetic chain and terminate in the superior cervical ganglion  third-order – postganglionic ﬁbres traverse with the internal carotid artery to enter the skull, pass to the cavernous sinus and thence to the orbit, where ﬁbres innervate the dilator pupillae.  Interruption of the sympathetic pupillomotor fibres, due to a lesion anywhere along the three-neurone sympathetic pathway, causes Horner syndrome.  Associated miosis is due to loss of sympathetic stimulation to the eye via Müller’s muscle dysfunction.  Clinical Presentation  Horner syndrome is characterised by signs and symptoms which may include:  miosis – due to inactivation of dilator pupillae  partial ptosis – due to paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle  anhidrosis – due to decreased sympathetic stimulation  apparent enophthalmos  heterochromia iridum different eye colours (only present in congenital Horners syndrome) – due to lack of sympathetic stimulation in childhood interfering with melanin pigmentation of melanocytes.  Patients may be asymptomatic, complain of loss of sweating on the affected side, lid drooping or headache.  The site of the lesion is on the ipsilateral side of the symptoms.  Patients may also present with signs and symptoms related to the underlying cause of the Horner syndrome. Horner syndrome: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Miosis.jpg Waster CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5)

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  involutional changes  prolapsed orbital fat  congenital myogenic ptosis  thyroid eye disease  stye  uveitis  orbital cellulitis  eyelid tumours  chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia  stroke  eyelid foreign body  myasthenia gravis  giant cell arteritis  multiple sclerosis  3rd nerve palsy  Marcus Gunn jaw.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is a clinical one, with history and examination, which can be confirmed with pharmacological testing.  Examine the skin for dryness.  Examine the pupils:  there should be a constricted pupil on the affected side:  this may be more apparent in a darkened room.  constrict the pupil using a torch light and observe dilation when the light is removed, compare both pupils:  the affected pupil will lag behind the other in dilation due to loss of sympathetic tone  note that the test may need to be repeated several times to detect it.  Horner syndrome can be confirmed via pharmacological testing:  cocaine drop test:  cocaine eye drops block the re-uptake of noradrenaline (NA), leading to dilation of the pupil  in Horner syndrome, the lack of NA causes a failure to dilate the pupil.  apraclonidine hydrochloride is a beta-adrenergic receptor agonist:  instillation of 1% apraclonidine into both eyes produces mydriasis in the affected eye only to become larger than the healthy side  the size of the pupil on the unaffected side remains unchanged.  hydroxyamphetamine test:

DR. JAM  this differentiates between a first-, second- or third-order neurone.  the drug leads to dilation of the pupil as a result of NA release from the intact, presynaptic, myoneural junction.  therefore, if there is a first- or second-order cause of Horner syndrome, pupil dilation occurs, but not with a third-order cause.  Once the condition has been confirmed, investigations should be guided by the suspected underlying pathology.  Management  As Horner syndrome is a group of physical signs, the condition itself cannot be managed per se.  The management, therefore, depends upon identifying the underlying diagnosis, which can then be managed as appropriate.  Prognosis  Prognosis is wholly dependent on the underlying cause. Huntington’s Disease Huntington’s disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder; it is the most common hereditary chorea.  Overview Key Facts  Huntington’s disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder; it is the most common hereditary chorea.  Typical onset in patients with the condition is in the third to fourth decades.  It is caused by mutations in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4, encoding a CAG-repeat expansion within the gene.  HD shows genetic characteristics of complete penetrance and anticipation:  earlier age of onset occurs in later generations due to expansion of the CAG repeat.  Genetic testing in at-risk individuals with a family history is available, with appropriate genetic counselling.  Pathological ﬁndings are of neurodegeneration in the cortex and striatum, especially the caudate nucleus.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Chorea, with random ’dancing’ movements flitting from one body part to another, is the characteristic movement disorder of this condition, although parkinsonism is also seen.  Frontal-subcortical cognitive impairment is typically present in HD and a number of behavioural disturbances occur.  In younger-onset patients a hypokinetic rigid picture with parkinsonism is commonly seen – when Huntington's occurs before the age of 20 this is classed as juvenile Huntington's disease.  If there is a known family history of HD, then the diagnosis may be straightforward.  However, in many cases, older affected relatives may have been misdiagnosed or undiagnosed.  It is, therefore, necessary to ask about a history of any neurodegenerative-type illness or psychiatric condition in previous generations.  Diagnosis may include history and examination findings, imaging and genetic testing.  No disease-modifying treatment has been proven in HD, although several agents are in development.  HD is usually managed within a specialist multidisciplinary clinic.  Symptomatic treatment includes management of mood and behavioural changes with SSRIs, and management of chorea with anti-dopaminergic agents such as tetrabenazine.  Overall this is a progressive disease with limited survival and a poor prognosis; death usually occurs between 10 and 30 years from diagnosis. Epidemiology  Huntington’s is the most common hereditary chorea.  The prevalence is estimated to be between 1 in 10 000 and 1 in 20 000.  Typically it presents between the third and fifth decades. Aetiology  HD is caused by mutations in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4, encoding a CAG-repeat expansion within the gene.  HD shows genetic characteristics of complete penetrance and anticipation, whereby earlier age of onset occurs in later generations due to expansion of the CAG repeat. Pathophysiology  Pathological ﬁndings are of neurodegeneration in cortex and striatum, especially the caudate nucleus, in which selective loss of dopamine D2 receptor-bearing medium spiny neurones occurs.  Early caudate atrophy is often seen on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain.

DR. JAM  Clinical Presentation  There is often a prodromal phase of mild psychotic and behavioural symptoms before the development of chorea, due to frontal-subcortical cognitive impairment.  Chorea, with random ’dancing’ movements ﬂitting from one body part to another, is the characteristic movement disorder of this condition, although parkinsonism is also seen as the disease progresses:  initially, chorea may be mild and will then progress to become severe and uncontrollable, often affecting the entire body  with disease progression, movements will change from chloroform to dystonia and parkinsonism.  Slow saccadic eye movements are also characteristic.  In younger-onset patients (juvenile Huntington's disease) a hypokinetic rigid picture with parkinsonism is commonly seen.  Other presentations may include:  schizophrenia-like psychosis  depression  irritability  dementia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  dementia (other causes)  Parkinson's disease/parkinsonism  tardive dyskinesia  epilepsy  psychosis/bipolar disease  neuroacanthocytosis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  anti-phospholipid syndrome  thyroid disease  Wilson's disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Detailed history and examination should raise suspicion of the diagnosis and help exclude other differentials.  If there is a known family history of HD, then the diagnosis may be more straightforward.  However, in many cases, older affected relatives may have been misdiagnosed or not diagnosed at all.  It is, therefore, necessary to ask about a history of any neurodegenerative-type illness or psychiatric condition in previous generations.  MRI and CT scans in moderate-to-severe disease show a loss of striatal volume and increased size of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles.  These changes will not be visible in early disease.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Genetic testing (by blood test at a regional genetic testing clinic) can reveal if the abnormal gene for the condition is present, but not when symptomatic disease will start to occur.  If genetic testing is considered, then extensive genetic counselling in a specialised unit is required.  Testing for alternative causes of movement disorders should be carried out, including for:  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome  thyroid disease  Wilson's disease  dementia.  Management  There is currently no approved disease-modifying therapy.  Long-term management is, therefore, a multidisciplinary team approach looking at symptom management.  A neurologist should be involved to help identify any symptoms that can be managed and medically treated.  A neuropsychiatrist can help with mood and cognitive disturbance.  Involving neuropsychologists is also useful to help ascertain which parts of the patient's condition are causing problems with cognition and help the patient and family come to terms with such a diagnosis.  With involuntary movements, there is often an increased basal metabolic rate, and dieticians can be helpful to ensure they are having sufficient calorie intake.  As the disease progresses, occupational and physical therapists are important to:  help build and improve strength and function  ensure any adaptions are made to the home, workplace and modes of transportation to improve independence.  Areas of current research include deep brain stimulation, neural and stem cell transplantation and pridopidine (a dopaminergic stabiliser).  Prognosis  Overall this is a progressive disease with limited survival.  Symptoms progress steadily until movement disorders and dementia are profound and completely debilitating.  Death usually occurs due to intercurrent infection such as pneumonia, or trauma due to falls.  There is also a high rate of suicide among individuals with the condition.

DR. JAM Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, previously known as benign intracranial hypertension or pseudotumour cerebri, is a condition that is characterised by raised intracranial pressure (RICP) without an associated causative lesion or hydrocephalous.  Overview Key Facts  Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), previously known as benign intracranial hypertension or pseudotumour cerebri, is a condition that is characterised by raised intracranial pressure (RICP) without an associated causative lesion or hydrocephalous.  IIH often presents with headache and profound papilloedema.  The condition is most commonly seen in overweight–obese women.  Symptoms include headache, vision disturbances, tinnitus corresponding to heartbeat and ‘greying out’ of vision.  IIH can cause visual loss, which can be permanent if it is not diagnosed and managed swiftly.  Diagnosis is with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to exclude other causes of RICP.  Treatment is based on symptom relief, which may include prednisolone in the acute phase and diuretics and weight reduction in the longer term. Surgical management such as CSF diversion may be also be of use in some patients.  Any other underlying causes, such as medications, should also be identified and managed. Epidemiology  IIH is relatively rare, with an incidence of around 3 : 100 000 in women and 1 : 100 000 in men.  The condition is most frequently seen in overweight–obese women of childbearing age.  Female : male ratio is thought to be between 3–8 : 1. Aetiology  Sudden weight gain or fluid retention eg pregnancy.  Certain medications such as:  lithium  cimetidine  tetracycline  tamoxifen  vitamin A  nitrofurantoin.  Endocrine conditions:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  thyroid disorders  Cushing’s disease.  Iron deficiency anaemia.  Chronic renal conditions.  Lyme disease. Pathophysiology  The exact cause of IIH is unknown.  Three theories exist to explain the mechanism of IIH: 1. Normal CSF production and absorption, but under higher than normal pressure ⇢ dural venous sinus linings have increased resistance ⇢ features of cerebral oedema and symptoms. 2. Blood flow increases to the brain ⇢ increase pressure ⇢ clinical symptoms (some theories suggest increase in-brain tissue mass causes increased pressure). 3. Narrow transverse sinus ⇢ decreased venous drainage ⇢ congestion and RICP ⇢ clinical symptoms.  Clinical Presentation Clinical presentations include:  headache – typically worse in the morning and may be associated with nausea and vomiting  pulsatile tinnitus  vision disturbances  transient visual obscuration – due to papilloedema  dizziness  gait disturbances  sixth nerve palsy – horizontal diplopia.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  brain tumours  cerebral infections  cerebral abscess  optic neuritis  renal artery or vein occlusion  glaucoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnostic criteria for IIH:  papilloedema

DR. JAM  normal neurological examination except cranial nerve abnormalities  normal neuroimaging – CT/ MRI  normal CSF composition – lumbar puncture (LP)  increased opening pressure of CSF (> 25 cm H2O)  The diagnosis is definite if all these criteria are fulfilled.  The diagnosis is probable if the first four criteria are met but if CSF pressure is lower than specified.  Management Non-pharmacological  The primary long-term management goal is weight reduction.  Lifestyle modifications including diet and exercise is encouraged.  Pharmacological  Acetazolamide or topiramate diuretics may be beneficial in patients.  Steroids can be used to treat acute severe headache and papilloedema.  Series of LPs helps in controlling the intracranial pressure. Surgical Surgical interventions may include:  bariatric surgery to promote weight loss  ventriculoperitoneal shunt for CSF diversion in recurrent disease  optic nerve sheath fenestration may be carried out if there is a significant threat to vision.  Prognosis  The general response to treatment is good.  Relapses and remissions are common.  Around one-third of patients experience recurrence.  Up to half of patients may experience long term visual disturbances, and around 10% may have significant visual loss and associated disability.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by presynaptic autoantibodies to P/Q type calcium channels.  Overview Key Facts  Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is caused by presynaptic autoantibodies to P/Q type calcium channels.  The condition is very rare.  LEMS is most commonly associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung.  Autonomic symptoms are commonly seen in LEMS.  Investigations include creatine kinase (CK), electromyogram (EMG) and muscle biopsy.  Treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine and/or pyridostigmine. Epidemiology  LEMS is very rare. Aetiology  LEMS is most commonly associated most with small cell carcinoma of the lung.  Other neoplastic associations include:  ovarian cancer  breast cancer  lymphoproliferative disorders.  Non neoplastic causes of LEMS include:  diabetes mellitus type I  thyroid disorders. Pathophysiology  Lambert Eaton Myasthenic syndrome is caused by presynaptic autoantibodies to P / Q type calcium channels, resulting in impaired neurotransmitter release.  This ultimately leads to debilitating muscle weakness.  Clinical Presentation  Unlike in myasthenia gravis, eye and bulbar muscle involvement are rare.  Features of LEMS include:  proximal weakness of lower limbs  dry mouth  hypo- or areflexia

DR. JAM  rapid progression in cases of underlying malignancy  difficulty in micturition  impotence  dysphagia  dizziness, especially on standing up.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  myasthenia gravis  motor neurone disease  myopathies  polymyositis  cranial nerve palsy  Graves' disease  botulism.  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnostic investigations include:  computed tomography (CT) scan/positron emission tomography (PET) scan of chest to exclude malignancy  nerve conduction studies  full blood count (FBC).  Management Management of LEMS:  Treat the underlying cause.  Symptomatic treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine (a potassium channel blocker) – 10 mg–20 mg four times per day.  Pyridostigmine may or may not be used.  Corticosteroid therapy may be used.  Plasma exchange and IVIG (rarely).  Prognosis  LEMS has a poorer prognosis, given its relationship to underlying malignancy. Migraine Migraines are the most common cause of primary headaches, affecting approximately 1 : 7 people globally.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Migraines are the most common cause of primary headaches, affecting approximately 1 : 7 people globally.  Symptoms include a unilateral throbbing headache, with associated features such as nausea and vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia and aura (transient focal neurological symptoms).  Migraines can be grouped into:  episodic (< 15 days a month), further divided into migraine with aura and migraine without aura and may also be classed as menstruation-related  chronic (at least 15 days a month).  Diagnosis is predominantly clinical; the focus of investigation is to exclude other serious causes of headache.  Treatment may focus on preventative therapy as well as relieving an acute episode.  Simple analgesia alongside triptans and anti-emetics are treatment options for acute events. Preventative treatments include avoidance of triggers; lifestyle modifications such as medical therapy with beta-blockers or tricyclic antidepressants may be used as prophylaxis. Epidemiology  Migraine affects in 1 : 7 people globally and prevalence is higher in women than men (2 : 1).  Migraine can occur at any age, including childhood.  The condition most commonly affects people between the ages of 25–55 and generally improves with increasing age.  Around 8% of patients with migraine are thought to suffer from the chronic form of migraine. Aetiology Migraine episodes are often triggered by certain factors. These triggers vary between individuals but common triggers include:  stress  menstruation  fasting or missed meals  caffeine  irregular sleep pattern. The risk of developing chronic migraine is increased with the following:  sleep disorders  excessive use of anti-migraine medications  emotional stress and major life events  obesity  increased episodic migraine attacks

DR. JAM  anxiety and/or depression  head injury. Pathophysiology  The exact pathophysiological mechanisms that lead to migraine are not fully understood, although multiple regions of the brain and neurophysiological networks are known to be involved.  There is likely to be a genetic aspect of involvement, as migraines tend to be more frequent in families of sufferers.  Migraine associated with menstruation may be linked to a fall in oestrogen levels.  Clinical Presentation  Often a unilateral pulsatile headache of moderate to severe intensity that restricts activity and lasts anywhere from 4–72 hours.  Associated symptoms that may include one or more of:  photophobia  nausea and vomiting  aura – symptoms may include:  visual symptoms such as zigzags, scotoma or flashing lights in the field of vision  increased sensitivity to smell (hyperosmia)  dizziness  ‘pins and needles’ or altered sensation in limbs  atypical aura symptoms include visual symptoms in one eye, double vision, motor weakness, poor balance and decreased consciousness (these patients may require urgent specialist advice or admission).  Prodromal symptoms (such as fatigue, poor concentration, neck stiffness, and yawning) may occur hours or 1–2 days before the onset of other symptoms of migraine.  Postdromal symptoms (such as fatigue and elated or depressed mood) may occur after resolution of the headache and last up to 48 hours.  Patients may also experience aura symptoms without typical headache.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  tension-type headache  cluster headache  medication overuse headache  head and/or neck trauma  malignancy  central venous thrombosis  trigeminal neuralgia  optic neuritis

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  infection eg meningitis  hypoxia  hypertension  idiopathic intracranial hypertension  cerebrovascular accident (CVA/stroke) or transient ischaemic attack (TIA).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is predominantly clinical and involves taking a detailed history and thorough physical examination.  History should include timing, duration, associated symptoms and possible trigger factors as well as medication history and family history.  Examination should include:  vital signs  extracranial structures:  carotid arteries  temporal arteries  sinuses  temporomandibular joints.  the neck  neurological exam:  cranial nerves  peripheral fundoscopy  gait.  All findings should be normal.  Abnormal findings and red flag symptoms warrant further investigation (urgent referral or admission may be required based on clinical judgment).  Neuroimaging including computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may also be required to rule out other conditions if there is diagnostic uncertainty.  Management Non-pharmacological  Provide patient information regarding migraine and also give information about help groups such as the migraine trust.  Patients should be encouraged to keep a headache diary which may help to identify triggers and measure treatment response.  Advise avoidance of potential triggers, improving sleep hygiene, limiting caffeine, eating regular meals and avoiding stress.  Manage co-morbidities such as obesity, depression and sleep disorders.  Advise limiting acute medication to twice weekly to avoid medication overuse headache.  Stop combined oral contraception in women with migraine with aura.

DR. JAM  Pharmacological Acute treatment (as per NICE):  Simple analgesia, including:  ibuprofen 400 mg (may be increased to 600 mg) or  aspirin 900 mg or  paracetamol 1000 mg.  Triptans may also be used, which should be started at the onset of the headache (not aura):  sumatriptan 50–100 mg orally (PO) is the first choice as recommended by NICE  subcutaneous (SC) and intranasal preparations may be used if vomiting restricts oral use.  Consider an anti-emetic (metoclopramide 10 mg/prochlorperazine 10 mg) in addition to other acute medication, even in patients without nausea and vomiting symptoms. Prophylaxis  Preventative treatment should be considered in:  patients who have significant impact on quality of life (ie prolonged or frequent episodes)  patients in which acute treatments are ineffective or contraindicated  uncommon types of migraine.  NICE recommends:  propranolol 80-160 mg daily in divided doses or  topiramate 50-100 mg daily in divided doses (teratogenic and must not be used in women of child baring potential unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place).  amitriptyline 25-75 mg nocte.  Migraines which are refractory to 2 or more prophylactic agents trialled at maximum tolerated dose for 3 months are suitable for a trial of botulinum toxin or calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor (CGRP) agents.  Prognosis  Migraine tends to improve and even resolve with advancing age.  Female patients may notice an improvement of symptoms following menopause.  In a longitudinal study of migraine in pregnancy  around 60% of women experience remission or improvement  around 35% experience no change  around 5% of women report a worsening of headache.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Mitochondrial Disorders Mitochondrial disorders are a group of genetic conditions that affect the function of mitochondria, leading to a variety of symptoms affecting energy production in cells.  Overview Key Facts  Prevalence of mitochondrial disorders is 1 in 5000, worldwide.  The main abnormality in these genetic disorders is in the mitochondrial respiratory chain function.  The entire mitochondrial DNA comes from the mother of the offspring in the formation of the zygote.  One of the common misconceptions is that mitochondrial disorders are inherited by the mother, but a majority of mitochondrial disorders are due to mitochondrial DNA mutation and only a few mitochondrial disorders occur as a result of the mutation of nuclear DNA.  The brain is the most affected organ due to a mitochondrial disorder. The brain requires the greatest amount of ATP.  Symptoms include headache, stroke, seizures and mental retardation. For diagnosis, there would be involvement of many symptoms and signs and over many organ systems.  Skeletal muscle biopsy and next-generation sequencing (NGS) are key to diagnosis.  Management includes physical exercise along with vitamin, coenzyme Q and amino acid replacement.  Prognosis depends on the type of disease and its severity.  Mitochondrion structure: Epidemiology  Prevalence of mitochondrial disorders is 1 in 5000 worldwide.  In United Kingdom (UK), the prevalence is 1 in 4300 individuals.

DR. JAM  Mitochondrial disorders result from mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations, which are greater in number compared with mutations in nuclear DNA. Aetiology  Genetic mutation in mtDNA.  Mutations in nuclear DNA. Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology is different for different mitochondrial disorders.  Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy:  degeneration of the optic nerve due to a defect in complex 1 called NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase.  Kearns–Sayre syndrome:  degeneration of retinal pigments characterised by ophthalmoplegia, painful eyes and cardiac conduction defects  the defect is in muscle fibres which are ragged red fibres, marked by an irregular contour and structurally abnormal mitochondria.  Mitochondrial encephalopathy lactic acidosis stroke syndrome:  also known as MELAS syndrome  pathogenesis involves energy deficiency, angiopathy and nitric oxide deficiency.  Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (MERF):  the main defect is in the mitochondria of muscular fibres which causes involuntary contractions  the mutation occurs in mitochondrial DNA  more than 80% of patients with MERF harbour an A to G mutation at nucleotide 8344 in mitochondrial MT-TK gene-encoding tRNA (Lys).  Maternally inherited deafness and diabetes (MIDD):  genetic mutation at position 3243 in the tRNA of mitochondrial DNA  defect in insulin secretion which progresses to insulin dependence and cochlear hearing loss.  Pearson syndrome:  mitochondrial DNA deletions  deletions are typically more abundant in blood than any other tissue in the body.  Leigh syndrome:  bilateral symmetric necrotising lesions with spongy changes and microcysts in basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord  includes abnormalities of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and respiratory chain due to nuclear or mitochondrial DNA mutations  genetically heterogeneous pathogenic mutations are identified in over 85 genes.  Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE):

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  gastrointestinal dysmotility and pseudo-obstruction caused by a visceral mitochondrial myopathy  most cases are caused by mutations of the TYMP gene that encodes thymidine phosphorylase leading to secondary depletion or multiple deletions of mitochondrial DNA.  Clinical Presentation  Tissues with maximum oxygen demand such as the brain, skeletal muscle and heart are most susceptible to mitochondrial diseases.  Syndromic presentation, ie multi-organ system involvement of which the nervous system is most commonly affected.  Developmental delay, shortened stature, cochlear deafness, retinopathy, optic atrophy, diabetes mellitus and other endocrine dysfunction, cardiac involvement, renal tubulopathy. Clinical features for some important mitochondrial disorders  Mitochondrial encephalopathy lactic acidosis and stroke (MELAS) syndrome:  neurological – focal or generalised seizures, migraine, hearing loss  stroke-like symptom is the cardinal feature of this disease  musculoskeletal – muscle weakness, paralysis.  Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (MERF):  onset is in early childhood  myoclonus is usually the first symptom  ataxia, myopathy  generalised epilepsy.  Maternally inherited deafness and diabetes (MIDD):  diabetes and sensory-neural hearing loss (cochlear) at age 30–40 years  myopathy  cardiac disorders  renal diseases  gestational diabetes.  Pearson syndrome:  can be fatal in infancy  sideroblastic anaemia  pancreatic dysfunction.  Leigh syndrome – subacute necrotising encephalomyopathy:  neurological manifestations – developmental delay, ataxia, dystonia, peripheral neuropathy, seizures  external ophthalmoplegia  lactic acidosis, vomiting  myopathy.

JAM  Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE):  early satiety, nausea, vomiting  flatulence, diarrhoea, abdominal pain  dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux.  Differential Diagnosis  Mitochondrial disorder should be taken into account in the differential diagnosis of any progressive multisystem disorder:  white matter abnormalities including peripheral neuropathy  diabetes  Alzheimer's disease  Duchenne muscular dystrophy  Lou Gehrig's disease  cancer  Alpers' disease  Friedreich's ataxia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Skeletal muscle biopsy and skin tissue biopsy.  Next-generation sequencing (NGS) panel testing for the causative genes can lead to early and accurate diagnosis in most cases.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or spectroscopy MRS for neurological symptoms.  Retinoscopy or electroretinogram for visual symptoms.  Electrocardiogram and echocardiography for cardiovascular disorders.  Audiogram for hearing loss or auditory symptoms.  Thyroid function tests.  Management Non-pharmacological  Physical exercises, including both endurance exercises and resistance and strength training:  the aim of exercise treatment is to enhance muscle size and strength  endurance activities include outdoor and indoor walking, jogging and running, swimming, dancing, cycling and others  resistance and strength training includes exercises such as sit-ups, arm curls, knee extensions, leg extensions, light weight lifting and many others.  Training of conservation of energy strategy:  patients are trained not to exert too much in a short time period.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Other treatments include speech therapy, physical exercises, respiratory and breathing therapy and occupational and rehabilitation therapy.  Pharmacological  There is no cure for mitochondrial disorders, only symptomatic treatment is targeted.  Treatment response is different for different patients.  The mainstay of pharmacological treatment is vitamins and supplements:  coenzyme Q 10 (ubiquinone)  B complex vitamins  alpha-lipoic acid  carnitor (L-carnitine)  creatine  dichloroacetate  arginine.  Mitochondrial diabetes is treated the same way as ordinary diabetes, such as with insulin and oral hypoglycaemics.  Continuous peritoneal dialysis is used for patients with mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE). Surgical  Corrective surgery for visual disturbance and ptosis.  Cochlear implant and digital hearing aid for hearing loss.  Prognosis  Prognosis depends on the involvement of the organ system.  Multiple organ system involvement makes the prognosis worse and death may occur during infancy.  People with a mild form of the disease may live a normal life.  Other  There is ongoing research for the effective therapeutic treatment of mitochondrial disorders.  Currently used for the mitochondrial disorder, co-enzyme Q10 has no licensed indications as a medicine in the UK.
