Motor Neurone Disease Motor neurone disease is a progressive degenerative, asymmetrical motor neuropathy syndrome involving the upper and lower motor neurones.  Overview Key Facts  Motor neurone disease (MND) is a progressive degenerative, asymmetrical motor neuropathy syndrome involving the upper and lower motor neurones.  The condition is progressive and invariably leads to paralysis and death.  The main types of MND are Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) – the most common form, Progressive bulbar palsy (PBP), Progressive muscular atrophy (PMA) and Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS).  Clinical symptoms include muscle weakness and wasting, fasciculation, brisk reflexes and spasticity.  Diagnosis is usually clinical, investigations to confirm diagnosis include computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain, nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG).  Presence of upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) signs in bulbar, arm and leg regions is consistent with the diagnosis of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS PROGRESSIVE BULBAR PALSY Affects both UMN and LMN Limb involvement:  Most common  Upper limb weakness > Lower limb weakness  Wrist and foot drop  Fasciculations  Gait disturbances  Weakness of facial muscles  Dysphagia  Progressive dysarthria  Upper and lower limb weakness  Emotional lability

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management involves a multidisciplinary approach and includes drug therapy, positive pressure ventilation, nutritional support, pain management and end of life care planning.  The condition is associated with a poor prognosis, with less than a 20% 5-year survival rate. Epidemiology  The condition is rare with an incidence of around 2 cases in 100 000 population in the United Kingdom (UK).  Prevalence is 7 per 100 000 in the UK.  The condition can occur in all ages.  10% of patients present at the age of > 45 years while around 20% present at 70 years or greater.  Worldwide incidence is 1-3 per 100 000.  Male affected more than females; ratio 2 : 1. Aetiology  Structural lesions of the brain.  Infections like poliomyelitis, tetanus and Lyme disease.  Lead toxicity.  Paraneoplastic conditions.  Plasma cell dyscrasias.  Metabolic conditions, eg hypoglycaemia, vitamin deficiency and thyroid disorders.  Hyperlipidaemia.  Genetic disorders. Pathophysiology  Numerous modes of pathology have been suggested, including mitochondrial dysfunction leading to oxidative stress and may occur in the following pattern:  excessive stimulation of Glutamate receptors cause increased calcium influx leading to neuronal apoptosis and nitric acid formation  this leads to increased sensitivity to oxidation, accumulation of free oxygen radicals which can cause cell death.  Clinical Presentation PROGRESSIVE MUSCULAR ATROPHY PRIMARY LATERAL SCLEROSIS Affects only LMN  Muscle atrophy  Fasciculation  Muscle weakness  Poor prognosis  Progressive spastic weakness of the limbs  Spastic dysarthria  Dysphagia (when both corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts are involved)  Sensations are intact

JAM Bulbar involvement:  Slurred speech – usually the first sign  Dysphagia  Dysarthria Respiratory involvement:  Dyspnoea  Early morning headaches due to hypoventilation  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis include:  Guillain-Barré syndrome  Myasthenia Gravis  spinal cord tumours  cerebrovascular accident/stroke  gliomas  thyrotoxicosis with myopathy  diabetic neuropathy  post-radiation myeloplexopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations are carried out to help identify the underlying cause and include:  blood tests including vitamin levels, creatine kinase assay, anti-GM1 antibodies  EMG to look for fasciculation and fibrillations  nerve conduction studies  serum protein electrophoresis  muscle biopsy  CT/MRI of brain and spinal cord.  Management Non-pharmacological  Multidisciplinary team involvement involving home carers, dieticians and primary care nurses.  Physiotherapy and occupational therapy in view of respiratory and limb muscle weakness.  Speech therapy.  Adequate hydration and nutrition. Consider percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube or nasogastric (NG) tube insertion for feeding as the condition progresses.  Consideration for positive pressure ventilation – may improve quality and duration of life.

JAM Multiple Sclerosis Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune chronic inflammatory condition of the central nervous system that affects the brain, brain stem and spinal cord.  Overview Key Facts  Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune chronic inflammatory condition of the central nervous system (CNS) that affects the brain, brain stem and spinal cord.  Demyelination of the nerve fibres, gliosis and neuronal loss are the characteristic features of MS.  Types of MS:  relapsing-remitting type (90% of patients have RRMS)  secondary progressive type (following on from RRMS)  primary progressive type (10% of patients).  Optic neuritis with accompanying visual field loss is the initial presentation in the majority of cases.  MRI is the gold standard initial investigation for confirming areas of demyelination.  Treatment is divided into three categories:  treatment of acute attack  treatment using disease-modifying agents  symptomatic therapy. Epidemiology  MS is the most common cause of neurological disability (nontraumatic) in people younger than 40 years.  Worldwide occurrence: 1.1 to 2.5 million cases.  The prevalence rate of MS in the different parts of the United Kingdom (UK) is:  about 120/100 000 in England and Wales  about 170/100 000 in Northern Ireland  up to 190/100 000 in Scotland.  Women are affected 2–3 times more than men.  Mean age of onset is 30 years, although the mean onset of primary progressive MS is 50 years old. Aetiology The exact aetiology of MS is unclear although it is characterised by T cell attack on oligodendrocytes.  Associations include:  genetics:  strongest association is with HLA DRB 1 gene mutation  concordance rate in Monozygotic twins is 18%– 25% while in dizygotic twins is 5%.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Epstein Barr Virus Infection  vitamin D deficiency  smoking  relapses are seen in association with:  stress  the post-partum period  infection. Pathophysiology Blood-Brain Barrier  Tight junction function is compromised in infection. This leads to the blood-brain barrier being permeable to the immune cells which does not happen normally.  In the case of MS, a breach in the BBB allows entry of T cells into the nervous system.  Long-term loss of BBB function is thought to underly persistent passage of T cells into the CNS. Appearance With Changes Of NAWM Areas  Changes noticed in the normalappearing white matter (NAWM) are axonal injury without demyelination, low inflammation, including microglial and astrocytic activation  This is followed by the appearance of pre-active lesions with activated microglia. Inflammation  Interaction between the T cells attacking the myelin sheath leads to inflammation.  Cytokines and antibodies are stimulated  Myelin is destroyed in active lesions  A characteristic glial scar is formed once the attack resolves. Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  hearing loss.  Disease course  Relapsing-remitting type (RRMS):  most common type of MS  male : female ratio of 1 : 3  characterised by attacks of neurological dysfunction that evolve over days to weeks  complete recovery is seen in the initial phase but with continuous attacks, recovery becomes less evident.  Secondary progressive type (SPMS):  always begins with relapsing-remitting form and slowly the clinical course changes over a few months  produces a greater amount of fixed neurological disability than RRMS.  Primary progressive type (PPMS):  accounts for approximately 10% of the cases  no attacks but a steady decline in function from the onset  mean age of onset – 50 years  male : female ratio of 1 : 1.  Differential Diagnosis  Inflammatory conditions:  neuromyelitis optica  Sjögren’s syndrome  acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)  CNS lupus  sarcoidosis  Behçet’s disease  CNS vasculitis.  CNS infections:  CNS Syphilis  lyme disease  HIV.  Metabolic conditions:  vitamin B12 deficiency  copper deficiency  mitochondrial disease.  CNS lymphoma.  Paraneoplastic myelopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis of MS relies on proving the dissemination of disease activity in time (evidence of new and previous disease activity more than a month apart) and space (different areas of the central nervous system).

DR. JAM  Clinical history and examination can fulfil either dissemination in time or space (ie a previous episode of optic followed by a new myelopathy would fulfil both)  MRI – evidence of disseminated demyelinating lesions in two of the four key areas (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial and spinal chord) would provide dissemination in space. Contrast enhancement of one lesion, with others being non enhancing would provide evidence of dissemination in time  Unpaired oligoclonal bands in the CSF – indicate intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis and indicate dissemination in time. These are not specific to MS and occur in about 85% of cases  The Kurtzke Expanded Disability Status Score (EDSS) is a scoring system used to monitor disease status:  score 0 – no signs or symptoms during the assessment. Score 10 – death from MS.  Management Non-pharmacological  Lifestyle modifications:  exercise  Vitamin D supplementation can be considered  smoking cessation if applicable.  Multiple Sclerosis Society – provide advice and support to patients with MS.  Pharmacological Disease modifying treatments:  Disease modifying treatments are rapidly changing. In RRMS they are used inline with NICE recommendations, see external link . Broadly:  First line therapy includes subcutaneous injections of either interferon or glatiramer acetate for patients with mild active disease (1 relapses in the last two years)  Second line options include teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate (2 relapses in the last two years) and first line options  For rapidly evolving MS (2 disabling relapses in 1 year) additional options include natalizumab, alemtuzumab, ocrelizumab and cladribine  Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be used for patients with early highly active RRMS.  It is not known whether an escalation approach or selecting high efficacy treatment (with a greater risk of side effects) early in the disease course is most beneficial.  For the higher efficacy medications, they can be distinguished between immune sequestering (natalizumab) and lymphodepleting treatments (rituximab/ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab and cladribine)

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  For primary progressive MS, patients early in the disease course with mild to moderate disability can be prescribed ocrelizumab.  Secondary progressive MS patients with evidence of disease activity can be offered Siponimod  Interferon, glatiramer acetate and natalizumab (to 34 weeks gestation) can be used in pregnancy, the remaining DMTs should be avoided. Management of relapses:  Rule out a pseudo relapse (an exacerbation of pre-existing symptoms caused by an underlying stressor, for example infection)  Methylprednisolone 500mg orally for 5 days or 1g IV for 3 days if a hospital admission is required. Managing complications:  Spasticity can be treated with baclofen  Depression should be monitored for and treated as usual  Pain should be managed with neuropathic agents  Fatigue management  Bladder management with anti-cholinergics and, if needed, self catheterisation  Constipation can be treated with lifestyle advice (fibre), laxatives and potential manual evacuation methods  Prognosis  The natural history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) is unpredictable.  25% of people with RRMS developed SPMS within six years of disease onset, and about 50% by 15 years of disease onset.  Prognosis of RRMS tends to be more favourable in people who have less frequent initial relapses, in particular if there is more than 2–3 years between the first and second relapse and less favourable in people whose presentation (their first relapse) is severe or if they have a poor recovery from the first relapse.  Treatment of a relapse with steroids may shorten the length and severity of the relapse, but does not alter the overall course or prognosis of the disease.  Treatment with disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) may reduce the number and severity of relapses.  Other  d1.Effect on pregnancy:  pregnant patients may experience fewer attacks during gestation but a rebound may occur post partum

EDSS system in detail: Kurtzke expanded disability status scale 0.0 Normal neurologic examination 1.0 No disability, minimal signs in one FS 1.5 No disability, minimal signs in more than one FS 2.0 Minimal disability in one FS 2.5 Mild disability in one FS or minimal disability in two FS 3.0 Moderate disability in one FS, or mild disability in three or four FS. Fully ambulatory 3.5 Fully ambulatory but with moderate disability in one FS, and more than minimal disability in several others 4.0 Fully ambulatory without aid; up and about some 12 hours per day despite relatively severe disability; able to walk without aid or rest for about 500m 4.5 Fully ambulatory without aid; up and about much of the day; able to work a full day; may otherwise have some limitation of full activity or require minimal assistance; characterised by relatively severe disability; able to walk without aid or rest for about 300m 5.0 Ambulatory without aid or rest for about 200m; disability severe enough to impair full daily activities (eg work a full day without special provisions) 5.5 Ambulatory without aid or rest for about 100m; disability severe enough to preclude full daily activities 6.0 Intermittent or unilateral constant assistance (cane, crutch, brace) required to walk about 100m with or without resting 6.5 Constant bilateral assistance (canes, crutches, braces) required to walk about 20m without resting 7.0 Unable to walk beyond approximately 5m even with aid; essentially restricted to a wheelchair; wheels self in standard wheelchair and transfers alone; up and about in wheelchair some 12 h/day 7.5 Unable to take more than a few steps; restricted to a wheelchair; may need ain in transfer; wheels self but cannot carry on in standard wheelchair for a full day; may require motorised wheelchair 8.0 Essentially restricted to bed or chair or perambulated in a wheelchair, but may be out of bed itself much of the day; retains many selfcare functions; generally has effective use of arms

Muscular Dystrophy Muscular dystrophies are inherited conditions that result in the breakdown of muscle leading to weakness and loss of skeletal muscle mass.  Overview Key Facts  Muscular dystrophies (MDs) are inherited conditions that result in the breakdown of muscle leading to weakness and loss of skeletal muscle mass.  The most common type is Duchenne MD, followed by myotonic MD and facioscapulohumeral MD.  MD is a progressive disorder that may eventually become debilitating and life-threatening by affecting the cardiac and respiratory systems.  MD tends to present with muscle weakness that is progressive. The age at which it presents depends on the type of MD.  Most forms of MD tend to be inherited and are caused by genetic mutations.  The diagnosis is based on symptoms, physical examination, genetic testing, blood results (increased creatine phosphokinase, CPK3), electromyography or muscle biopsy.  There is no cure for MD with only supportive treatment available. Epidemiology  About 70 000 people have muscular dystrophy in the United Kingdom (UK).  The most common type is Duchenne MD:  half of all MD  100 boys with Duchenne are born every year  there are 2500 people in the UK with Duchenne MD at any time.  The second most common type is myotonic MD:

DR. JAM  1 in 8000 people.  The third most common type is facioscapulohumeral MD:  1 in 20 000 people. Aetiology  Genetic:  autosomal recessive:  some types of limb-girdle MD.  autosomal dominant:  myotonic dystrophy  facioscapulohumeral MD  oculopharyngeal MD  some types of limb-girdle MD.  X-linked:  affects males more often as they only have one X chromosome  Duchenne MD  Becker MD  Emery–Dreifuss MD.  Idiopathic gene mutation. Types of MD  Duchenne MD:  affects males predominantly  usually present with symptoms early (1–3 years old):  affects proximal lower limb muscles  difficulty with movement, standing up, climbing stairs  speech delay  behaviour or learning difficulties.  may progress to the point they need a wheelchair in early teenage years  may develop scoliosis  may develop respiratory and cardiac issues in mid-teens to 20s:  life-threatening.  life expectancy is shortened to around the 30s.  Myotonic MD:  progressive weakness and muscle wasting  affects smaller muscles first:  face, jaw, neck.  may also present with:  myotonia  cataract  sleepiness  dysphagia  behavioural and learning problems

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  bradyarrhythmia.  life expectancy is variable, but if developed early and severe, life expectancy is reduced  most deaths are related to cardiac or respiratory problems.  Facioscapulohumeral MD:  affects the upper girdle, leading to the reduced motion of the scapula and thoracic regions and winging of the scapula  facio = face:  more common in children  sleeping with eyes open  unable to shut eyes tightly  unable to purse lips.  scapula = shoulders  humeral = upper arms  more common in late teenage years and affects men more than women  50% of patients also have weakness in leg muscles  it may also affect the body asymmetrically  this form of MD does not tend to shorten life expectancy.  Becker MD:  similar to Duchenne but a milder form as patients have some functioning dystrophin  tend to live longer to 40–50 years.  Limb-girdle MD:  related to the upper and lower girdles:  shoulders and hips.  often affects the hip first then shoulders:  may cause problems with mobility and strength in lifting objects  there are different types of limb-girdle MD and progression depends on which type.  Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy:  usually presents later in the fifth decade  ocular = eyes  pharyngeal = throat  symptoms include dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, weakness around the shoulder and hip girdle  life expectancy is usually unaffected.  Emery–Dreifuss MD:  uncommon X-linked MD usually presents in teenage years  presents with contractures and cardiomyopathy:  shortened and tightened muscles and tendons, eg unable to straighten the elbow  reduced range of movement.  life expectancy is reduced because of the cardiorespiratory-associated problems

DR. JAM  commonly leads to death because of first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block. Pathophysiology  Duchenne MD and Becker MD involve the dystrophin gene mutation:  the dystrophin gene is important to form stability at the links between skeletal muscles  found on the short arm of the X chromosome, Xp21 region  mutations of the dystrophin gene cause instability at the cellular level which causes intracellular substance leakage and hence build-up of creatine phosphokinase (CPK) detected on blood tests  muscle unit gradually dies leading to the invasion of macrophages  class 1 HLA are found on the membrane of dystrophic muscles which makes the muscles more likely to have T-cell-mediated attacks  dead muscle units are replaced by fibrofatty infiltrates which lead to the pseudohypertrophy of muscles and weakness.  Other types of MD are not caused by the mutation of the dystrophin gene but mutations of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complexes:  these work by a different mechanism and based on their different locations; they affect other areas such as ocular and limb-girdle.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following signs and symptoms.  Progressive muscle weakening and wasting:  difficulty walking  limited range of movement  poor balance  waddling gait  calf deformation  muscle spasms  Gower’s sign:  weakness of proximal muscles of lower limbs  patients use their upper body to walk up from a squatting position  most commonly seen in Duchenne MD but also can present in other MDs.  Scoliosis.  Respiratory problems:  difficulty breathing.  Cardiomyopathy.  Gower’s sign:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  spinal muscle atrophy  peripheral neuropathy  myositis (polymyositis, dermatomyositis)  amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)  multiple sclerosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Muscular dystrophies can be investigated in a few ways.  History and physical examination:  most important to identify any family history and their current presentation.  Blood tests:  creatine phosphokinase (CPK) = most specific test:  not affected by haemolysis or liver dysfunction  specific to intracellular leakage from the muscle  three elevated levels 1 month apart = diagnostic  CPK levels may decrease with muscle mass atrophy.  Genetic testing.  Imaging:  electromyography  ultrasound.  Muscle biopsy:  definitive test.  Management Non-pharmacological  The main treatment is supportive treatment.  Support groups.

DR. JAM  Mobility:  physiotherapy:  muscle strengthening  flexibility.  physical aids:  wheelchair  walking aids  leg braces.  exercise:  low-impact.  occupational therapy. Pharmacological  Steroids:  strengthen muscle for six months to two years  slow down muscle weakening.  Ataluren:  for children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy above 5 years old who can still walk.  Creatine supplement:  improve muscle strength.  Cardiac medication:  ACE inhibitors  beta-blockers. Surgical  Surgical treatment is indicated for associated problems:  scoliosis surgery  weak shoulder blades – scapular fixation  loosen tight joints  pacemaker for cardiac problems  swallowing:  gastrostomy or PEG if dysphagia develops.  Prognosis  The prognosis depends on the specific type of MD that the patient has.  It may shorten life expectancy if it involves cardiac and respiratory function; however certain types of MD do not affect life expectancy.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Myasthenia Gravis Myasthenia gravis is an acquired autoimmune condition caused by autoantibodies against post-synaptic neuromuscular junction receptors.  Overview Key Facts  Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an acquired autoimmune condition caused by autoantibodies against post-synaptic neuromuscular junction receptors – commonly the nicotinic acetylcholine (Ach) receptor (90% of cases) or muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) receptor (10% of cases).  The clinical hallmark is painless, fatigable skeletal muscle weakness (showing increasing muscle weakness when carrying out a task, which improves with rest).  There is a bimodal pattern of onset, typically with younger onset in females and late onset in males.  Associations include autoimmune conditions and thymus abnormalities.  Abnormalities of the thymus are seen in almost 75% of patients (thymitis, thymoma or atrophy) - 10% of cases are associated with thymoma.  Diagnosis is mainly clinical; investigations to aid diagnosis include Anti-AChR radioimmunoassay – 85% positive, electromyography and imaging of the thymus.  Treatment include anticholinesterase inhibition, immunosuppression with plasmapheresis and intravenous (IV) Immunoglobulins for exacerbations.  Myasthenic crisis is a serious complication of MG (it can be the first presentation of the condition) that leads to lifethreatening weakness of the respiratory muscles.  IV immunoglobulins, plasmapheresis and intubation with ventilator support are the mainstays of treatment. Epidemiology  Prevalence of MG is approximately 15 : 100 000 in the United Kingdom (UK).  There is a bimodal pattern of onset, typically with a younger onset in females (< 40 years) and late onset in males.  Non-thymoma related cases have two peaks of incidence at 10–30 years in women and at 60–70 years of age in men; while those associated with thymoma have a peak incidence at 40–50 years of age.  Prevalence is slighter higher in women (3 : 2).  Myasthenic crises affect 10–15% of patients usually within 2– 3 years of diagnosis of MG. Aetiology Associations include:

DR. JAM  Autoimmune conditions (associated conditions includes systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis).  Genetic mutations in human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B8 and DR3 genes.  The HLA DR1 gene is specific for ocular myasthenia.  Abnormalities of the thymus are seen in almost 75% of patients – 10% of cases are associated with thymoma.  A myasthenic crisis can be triggered by:  non-compliance with medication  infection (especially respiratory)  electrolyte imbalance  anaemia  drugs (eg gentamycin, corticosteroids)  withdrawal of cholinesterase inhibitors  stress  surgery. Pathophysiology Diagrams of (A) normal and (B) myasthenic neuromuscular junctions:  Autoantibodies are directed towards ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction.  This leads to decreased numbers of ACh receptors at post synaptic membrane, for three reasons:  accelerated turnover by ACh receptors by cross linking and rapid endocytosis of the receptors  damage to postsynaptic muscle membrane by the antibody in collaboration with complement  blocking active.  This lead to flattening of post-synaptic folds and decreased neuromuscular transmission.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Note: there is normal ACh production but the small end plate potential produced fails to trigger muscle action potential, leading to weakness of muscle contraction.  This leads to presynaptic rundown (the amount of ACh released per impulse declines on repeated activity) and muscle weakness.  Clinical Presentation Signs of symptoms of MG include:  ophthalmoplegia (one of the earliest presentations in most cases):  ptosis  diplopia  weakness of eyelid closure.  muscle weakness, especially shoulder girdle muscles, face, neck, limbs and trunk is also commonly seen and may fluctuate  loss of facial expression/“myasthenic snarl”  dysarthria  dysphagia  slurred speech  dysphonia (voice fades on counting to 50)  breathing difficulty. Signs and symptoms of myasthenic crisis:  Episodes can be precipitated by acute infection and/or medications such as aminoglycoside antibiotics.  Early warning signs may include:  increasing muscle weakness  increasing double vision  quiet breath sounds with reduced chest expansion on chest examination  haemodynamic instability.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome  congenital myasthenic syndromes  motor neurone disease  multiple sclerosis  myopathies  polymyositis  cranial nerve palsy  hyperthyroidism  botulism.

DR. JAM  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis is based on history examination findings, response to treatment and the following tests:  ACh receptor and MuSK antibodies test  thyroid function tests (TFTs)  ice pack test – a bedside test done if the patient has ptosis. Application of ice (eg in a latex glove) over the ptosis causes temporary improvement due to neuromuscular junction defect (over 90% sensitivity). This is a clinical sign and not a diagnostic one.  single-fibre electromyography (EMG) – the gold standard, with a 97% sensitivity  computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) thorax – for thymoma; consider MRI brain for possible structural defects. Diagnosis of myasthenic crisis:  clinical signs and symptoms  ACh receptor antibodies test  pulmonary function tests eg forced vital capacity (FVC) – useful to predict impending respiratory failure  blood and urine cultures and chest X-ray if infection is suspected.  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoidance of triggers – adequate rest to avoid tiredness, avoidance of stress.  Severe weakness of ventilator muscles can lead to acute respiratory failure and requires intubation and mechanical ventilation. Pharmacological  Primary treatment is a cholinesterase inhibitor (pyridostigmine).  Immunosuppression with corticosteroids is also used initially.  Mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine cyclophosphamide, methotrexate and tacrolimus are typical steroid-sparing agents.  Plasmapheresis and IVIG are options to treat myasthenic crisis or severe exacerbations.  The monoclonal antibody rituximab and emerging options of targeted biological treatments, such as belimumab, show promise in treatment.  Several medications are contraindicated, including beta blockers and many antibiotics. All new medications should be checked in case they exacerbate myasthenia. Surgical  Thymectomy if indicated (thymoma), but can be also useful in patients without thymoma.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management of myasthenic crisis  Myasthenic crisis is a medical emergency which may require a combination of intubation and mechanical ventilation, plasmapheresis and IVIG.  The underlying cause should be identified and managed ie antibiotics for infection or removing causative drugs.  Prognosis  Prognosis has improved over the last 20–30 years due to the use of immunomodulating drugs, reducing mortality and improving quality of life.  20% of patients achieve sustained remission with treatment.  Because of its fluctuating course, myasthenia gravis usually progresses to maximum severity in approximately three years, after which the patient often stabilises or even improves.  Patients who have had only ocular disease for more than two years are unlikely to develop generalised MG.  Mortality is 1–2% and is most commonly due to myasthenic crisis, respiratory failure or arrest and pneumonia.

DR. JAM Myelopathy Myelopathy describes an injury to the spinal cord causing neurological symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Myelopathy describes an injury to the spinal cord causing neurological symptoms.  This may be due to trauma, inflammation congenital stenosis, degenerative disease or disc herniation (a major cause is central disc protrusion).  Myelopathy can be classed by the area affected, eg cervical myelopathy, thoracic myelopathy and lumbar myelopathy.  Common symptoms include:  numbness  clumsiness  pain of the legs, arms or back  weakness of legs/arms  difficulty in walking/balance  sensory impairment  poor bladder/bowel control.  Symptoms may present suddenly, gradually or with stepwise deterioration.  The condition is considered as an orthopaedic/neurosurgical emergency.  Urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is indicated for diagnosis.  Treatment is dependant on the underlying cause, but spinal decompression and microdiscectomy are common forms of surgical intervention. Epidemiology  Cervical spondylotic myelopathy is the most common disorder of the spinal cord in patients over 55. Aetiology  Causes include:  central disc protrusion  tumours  infections

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  trauma  inflammation  autoimmune conditions  ankylosing spondylitis  Paget’s disease. Pathophysiology  The underlying cause leads to narrowing of the spinal canal, therefore compressing the spinal cord and nerve roots.  The location of the myelopathy determines the symptoms.  Clinical Presentation Symptoms may present suddenly, gradually or with stepwise deterioration, such as:  numbness  clumsiness  weakness of legs  hand weakness in cervical spinal cord compression  difficulty in walking/balance  sensory impairment  difficulty in bladder/bowel control.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Orthopaedic/neurosurgical emergency.  Urgent consultation with the relevant specialists is required.  Urgent MRI is the investigation of choice. Compressive myelopathy:

DR. JAM  Management  Treatment to some extent is determined by underlying cause, however, definitive management is often surgical decompression. Non-pharmacological  For mild cases, physiotherapy and bracing may be helpful. Pharmacological:  Pharmacological management may be of use to help treat any underlying causes or slow progression in some cases. Surgical:  The aim of surgical spinal decompression is to relieve pressure on nerve roots, spinal cord or cauda equina.  Microdiscectomy – Gold standard approach for disc herniation causing compression.  Laminectomy.  Intradiscal extracanalicular approaches.  Foraminotomy.  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on underlying cause and time to diagnosis/intervention.  In cases of cervical spondylotic myelopathy, complete remission is rare. Myotonic Dystrophy Myotonic dystrophy is the second most common type of muscular dystrophy.  Overview Key Facts  Myotonic dystrophy is the second most common type of muscular dystrophy.  Myotonic dystrophy is normally inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and there are two main types:  type I (DM1, a mutation in DMPK gene)  type II (DM2, a mutation in CNBP gene).  Myotonic dystrophy tends to present in the mid-20–30s with progressive muscle weakness and may present with other symptoms such as cataracts, heart block and intellectual disability.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and genetic testing.  There is no cure for myotonic dystrophy, with only supportive treatment available.  Screening for complications should be performed. Epidemiology  About 70 000 people have a muscular dystrophy in the UK.  The second most common type of muscular dystrophy is myotonic muscular dystrophy:  1 in 8000 people. Aetiology  Autosomal-dominant genetic inheritance:  50% chance of being passed onto the next generation. Pathophysiology  Type I:  mutation in the DMPK gene:  the long arm of chromosome 19  DMPK is part of cell communication.  trinucleotide repeat expansions of the cytosine-thymineguanine (CTG) triplet:  5–37 repeats = normal  > 50 repeats = symptomatic.  altered messenger RNA affects normal protein production  anticipation:  symptoms come on earlier and more severe as it is passed onto the next generation.  congenital myotonic dystrophy type I:  inherited from the mother.  Type II:  mutation in the CNBP gene:  chromosome 3  regulates protein production and activities of other genes.  tetranucleotide repeat expansions of cytosine-cytosinethymine-guanosine (CCTG):  the number of repeats is not correlated with the severity of the disease or the age of onset.  Type I and type II are the main types but there are also other types of myotonic dystrophy.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following signs and symptoms in their second to third decade of life but can also present at any other time.

DR. JAM  The main presentation is progressive muscle weakness, tightness and wasting.  The severity is variable.  Type I:  affects the jaw, neck, shoulders, elbows and hips:  myotonia  weakness.  insulin resistance – type II diabetes  cataracts  cardiac problems  in men:  early balding  infertility.  may be congenital and present at birth.  Type II:  milder than type I  overlapping symptoms.  Differential Diagnosis  Duchenne muscular dystrophy.  Spinal muscle atrophy.  Peripheral neuropathy.  Myositis (polymyositis, dermatomyositis).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Myotonic dystrophy can be investigated in a few ways.  History and physical examination:  most important to identify any family history and their current presentation.  Genetic testing to detect DMPK or CNBP genes:  definitive test  chorionic villus sampling  amniocentesis.  Blood test:  creatine phosphokinase.  Imaging:  electromyography.  Management Non-pharmacological  The main treatment is supportive.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Support groups.  Mobility:  physiotherapy:  muscle strengthening  flexibility.  physical aids:  wheelchair  walking aids  leg braces.  exercise:  low impact.  occupational therapy.  Screening for complications:  ECG and/or echocardiogram  fasting glucose  ophthalmological examination  thyroid function tests  testosterone levels. Pharmacological  There is no medication available to reverse muscular weakness.  Pharmacological management aims to prevent and treat complications.  Analgesia.  Cardiac medication:  ACE inhibitors  beta-blockers.  Testosterone replacement therapy (if required). Surgical  Surgical treatment is indicated for associated problems:  cataract  pacemaker for cardiac problems.  Prognosis  The prognosis depends on the specific type of myotonic dystrophy.  It may shorten life expectancy if it involves cardiac and respiratory function.  Type II myotonic dystrophy is milder and people tend to have a normal lifespan.

DR. JAM Neurological And Ophthalmic Disease In Advanced HIV Neurological disease can be the first presentation of AIDS in 10% of patients with the condition and is associated with significant disability and mortality.  Overview Key Facts  Neurological disease can be the first presentation of AIDS in 10% of patients with the condition and is associated with significant disability and mortality.  Important presentations include hemiparesis and seizures (focal disorders) and confusion and drowsiness (generalised disorders).  Sub-clinical opportunistic CNS infection can also be unmasked after starting treatment with highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) due to immune reconstitution syndrome (IRIS).  Prolonged HIV infection also has direct neurotropic effects, notably HIV dementia.  Focal neurological disease in advanced HIV caused by toxoplasmosis and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (meningitis and abscesses) and carries a high mortality.  Reduced level of consciousness is seen in cryptococcal meningitis, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis.  AIDS may also affect any layer of the eye:  the most clinically significant causes of retinitis in patients with AIDS are CMV infection and toxoplasmosis. Epidemiology  HAART has significantly reduced the global incidence of opportunistic CNS infections over the last 10-20 years.  The most common CNS infections in advanced HIV are:  toxoplasmosis – accounts for 90% focal lesions in HIV and occurs in 10% AIDS patients. Key risk factor is exposure to infected cat faeces  cryptococcal meningitis – cause a subacute meningitic illness in 5-10% AIDS patients  PML  CMV encephalitis  aggressive and atypical neurosyphilis.  CMV retinitis occurs in up to a quarter of untreated patients with AIDS. Aetiology Focal neurological disease in AIDS:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  toxoplasmosis  TB meningitis. Generalised neurological disease in AIDS:  cryptococcal meningitis  PML – JC virus  CMV encephalitis. Pathophysiology  Low CD4 count causes defective T cell and humoral responses, and increases susceptibility to opportunistic infection.  HIV retrovirus also has direct effects on cognition and can cause progressive dementia.  Clinical Presentation  Fever, headache, neck stiffness and reduced level of consciousness (meningitis) are seen in cryptococcal, bacterial, viral and tuberculous meningitis. Distinguishing features include:  cryptococcal meningitis – subacute presentation over 1-2 weeks, often combined with encephalitic features of disorientation and confusion  tuberculous meningitis – subacute presentation over several weeks, with associated constitutional symptoms of weight loss, night sweats and fever.  Cognitive impairment may manifest as mild impairment of social functioning through to incapacitation.  Focal neurological disease commonly presents with dysphasia, hemiparesis and seizures.  fever is non-specific additional symptom  other constitutional symptoms eg weight loss/night sweats could point to tuberculous meningitis and primary CNS lymphoma.  Important ocular symptoms include progressive visual blurring and floaters:  CMV retinitis typically presents subacutely over 1-2 weeks  characteristic findings on ophthalmoscopy are ‘creamycoloured’ retinal discoloration and overlying haemorrhages – ‘pizza-pie’ appearance  retinal toxoplasmosis produces a similar picture.

DR. JAM  Patients with neurosyphilis can develop a highly aggressive and atypical form of disease characterised by myelopathy, retinitis and meningitis.  Differential Diagnosis  Reduced level of consciousness:  cryptococcal meningitis  CMV encephalitis  PML.  Cognitive impairment:  AIDS dementia  vascular dementia  alzheimer’s dementia  PML.  Focal neurology:  TB meningitis  cerebral toxoplasmosis  primary CNS lymphoma  stroke.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Useful investigations include:  full blood count (FBC) and CRP (acute inflammatory response)  renal and liver function tests prior to initiating treatment  viral load and CD4 count  lumbar puncture for CSF microscopy, serology, and viral PCR.  In high resource settings, CT and MRI imaging are also useful:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  cerebral toxoplasmosis manifests as solitary or multiple ring-enhancing lesions  MR imaging is more consistent than CT in PML, and typically shows consistent widespread small white matter lesions.  Cryptococcal meningitis can be confirmed by:  CSF staining with India ink - visualises yeast cells in 6080% patients  serology – serum cryptococcal antigen (CRAG) has a specificity and sensitivity > 99% in patients with HIV.  Besides neuroimaging, the investigation of choice for suspected toxoplasmosis infection is toxoplasma serology (positive in > 90% cases).  A typical CSF picture for tuberculous meningitis is low cell count (100-500) with lymphocytosis, low CSF glucose, and very high CSF protein:  AFB positive in around 70% of patients.  A definitive diagnosis of PML is made by brain biopsy, but this is rarely performed premortem. The investigations of choice are neuroimaging and CSF for JC virus DNA.  Investigations in patients with ophthalmic disease include:  CMV and toxoplasma IgG  CMV viral load.  The investigation of choice in patients with suspected neurosyphilis is serological testing (treponemal and nontreponemal tests).  Management Non-pharmacological  All patients with suspected opportunistic eye infection require same-day referral to an ophthalmologist for further assessment. Pharmacological  It is always important to consider the underlying diagnosis of advanced HIV and institute HAART at the earliest opportunity (while remembering the risk of IRIS).  The treatment of choice for toxoplasmosis is pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine:  co-prescribe folinic acid to prevent bone marrow suppression.  Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV+ patients is usually managed with combination antifungal therapy – amphotericin B, flucytosine and fluconazole.  TB meningitis is managed with:  prolonged (6-12 month) combination therapy – isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, with pyridoxine prophylaxis for peripheral neuropathy  a weaning dose of steroids to mitigate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome.

DR. JAM  Neurosyphilis is managed with a 17 day course of IM penicillin and oral probenecid.  PML has no specific treatment – early introduction of HAART helps to reverse infection.  Patients with severe sight-threatening CMV retinitis require intravitreal AND oral antiviral therapy with intravitreal ganciclovir and intravenous valganciclovir. Surgical  Patients with severe cerebral toxoplasmosis may develop secondary complications including CSF obstruction and hydrocephalus necessitating neurosurgical involvement.  This should be guided by neuroimaging.  Prognosis  HAART has significantly reduced the global incidence of opportunistic CNS infections over the last 10-20 years.  Focal neurological disease in advanced HIV caused by toxoplasmosis and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (meningitis and abscesses) and carries a high mortality.  10% of patients with cerebral toxoplasmosis will die.  25% will sustain enduring disability. Non-Epileptic Attack Disorder Non-epileptic attack disorder, also psychogenic non-epileptic seizures – characterised by changes in behaviour or movement that are not caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain (ie not caused by epilepsy).  Overview Key Facts  Non-epileptic attack disorder (NEAD), also psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) – characterised by changes in behaviour or movement that are not caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain (ie not caused by epilepsy).  Approximately 20% of patients assessed at epilepsy centres have non-epileptic seizures.  The clinical presentation can mimic any type of seizure, making NEAD difficult to distinguish from epilepsy.  Investigations include brain imaging (MRI), an electroencephalogram (EEG), laboratory investigations to exclude physical causes and serum prolactin.  There is no reliable treatment for NEAD; patient education is important. Psychological therapies (eg CBT) may be trialled.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Approximately 20% of patients assessed at epilepsy centres have non-epileptic seizures.  NEAD is more common in young women and in people who have other psychiatric conditions or have had previous injury or disease leading to stressful life events. Aetiology  Seizures are thought to be triggered by stressors and many patients have psychiatric co-morbidities. Pathophysiology  This is unknown in NEAD.  Clinical Presentation  Resembles seizures:  could mimic any type of seizure:  tonic-clonic  myoclonic  absence  partial seizures.  Features that make it more likely to be NEAD:  > 2 minutes  gradual onset  fluctuating course  head moving side to side  closed eyes  able to recall the episode  normal prolactin.  Features that make it more likely to be epilepsy:  tongue biting  incontinence  automatisms. DR.
