Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  psychiatric causes:  panic disorder  psychosis  dissociative convulsions.  absence seizures  complex partial seizures.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Any suspicion of a seizure should be further investigated.  Full history including description of the episode and family history.  Full assessment of epilepsy:  EEG and/or video telemetry  MRI brain.  Exclude physical causes:  hypoglycaemia  electrolyte imbalances  ECG  echocardiogram.  Psychiatric assessment.  Blood test:  prolactin may help to distinguish between true seizure and NEAD:  raised in 90% of patients after a tonic-clonic seizure  raised in 60% of patients after complex focal seizures.  Management Non-pharmacological  Patient education and explanation of the diagnosis is important.  Psychotherapy (eg CBT) – although there is a lack of evidence that these approaches are effective. Pharmacological  Antidepressants.  Anxiolytics. Surgical  There is no role for surgical treatment for NEAD.

DR. JAM  Prognosis  There is little evidence regarding the long-term outcomes for patients with NEAD. Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a neurological condition characterised by the buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain's ventricles, leading to symptoms like gait disturbances and urinary incontinence.  Overview Key Facts  More common in patients aged > 60 years.  Unclear but proposed mechanisms include abnormal absorption of CSF, compression of venous vasculature and a build-up of toxic metabolites in the CSF.  Vasculature in the brain becomes atheromatous and calcified resulting in decreased venous drainage.  Characterised by the symptoms and signs of hydrocephalus without significantly raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure.  Features include gait apraxia unresponsive to levodopa, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) scan shows ventriculomegaly without any obvious cause or brain atrophy.  Differential diagnosis include other causes of dementia and Parkinson’s disease.  Treatment includes ventriculoperitoneal shunting though this carries a high risk in many patients.  The most common complication of shunting is overdrainage and it presents as sustained or postural headaches, subdural effusions or hematoma. Epidemiology  More common in patients aged > 60 years.  Equally distributed in men and women. Aetiology  Unclear but proposed mechanisms include abnormal absorption of CSF, compression of venous vasculature and a build-up of toxic metabolites in the CSF  Secondary causes include:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  intraventricular or subarachnoid haemorrhage  meningitis  Paget disease  achondroplasia. Pathophysiology  Vascular disease is more common in ageing patients with preexisting risk factors.  Vasculature in the brain becomes atheromatous and calcified which causes an increase in pulse pressure due to the loss of elasticity.  Increase in pulse pressure transmitted to the arteries supplying blood to the brain which causes a mismatch between arterial supply to the brain and venous drainage away from the brain.  Insufficient perfusion of the brain results in ischaemia that is responsible for the characteristic signs and symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus.  Clinical Presentation  Insidious onset over months or years of:  gait disturbance – difficulty walking, loss of balance, slow, wide-based, magnetic gate  urinary disturbance – frequency, urgency, urge incontinence  cognitive impairment – attention difficulty, impairment of abstract thinking, memory impairment  upper motor neuron signs in lower extremities: lowerextremity spasticity, hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses.  Differential Diagnosis  Parkinson’s disease.  Parkinson’s plus syndromes.  Cerebrovascular parkinsonism.  Dementia.  Urinary outflow obstruction.  Cervical myelopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  First investigations:  CT head or MRI head – can be normal or show any mild to moderate enlargement of ventricles, periventricular leukomalacia, cerebral infarction, aqueduct flow void, reduced diameter of corpus callosum and decreased callosal angle  levodopa challenge – used to exclude Parkinson’s disease with no response to therapy in normal pressure hydrocephalus.

DR. JAM  Investigations to consider  lumbar puncture – normal or slightly elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure (7-25 mmHg)  lumbar puncture with large volume CSF/prolonged external lumbar drainage – improvement in gait symptoms after the procedure  CSF infusion procedure – elevated outflow resistance. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus versus atrophy  CT head (left) in normal pressure hydrocephalus – narrowing of CSF spaces and medial cisterns (red circle), acute callosal angle (blue lines) and leucoaraiosis (blue arrows)  MRI head (right) in normal pressure hydrocephalus – widening of CSF spaces (red circle) and medial cisterns (green arrow) consistent with brain atrophy, obtuse callosal angle (blue lines) and leucoaraiosis (blue arrows)  Management  If suitable for surgery - ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy  considered in patients with good response to CSF procedures.  Control of cardiovascular risk factors ie antihypertensive drugs, smoking cessation, cholesterol-lowering drugs.  Prognosis  Response to surgery can be variable but improvement in symptoms is less likely in patients with extensive radiological changes.  Many patients require shunt revision even after successful initial shunting.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Predictors of improvement after shunting for NPH Favourable Gait disorder ⇢ early appearance, most prominent symptom Shorter duration of symptoms (< 6 months) Identified aetiology of NPH CSF removal (tap test, lumbar drain) ⇢ clinical response Unfavourable Dementia ⇢ early appearance, moderate to severe, or ≥ 2 years Gait disorder absent or appearing after dementia Alcoholism MRI findings: marked white matter disease diffuse sulcal enlargement medial temporal atrophy  Other Complications of shunting  Shunt overdrainage: most common complication in the first year, presents as sustained or postural headaches, subdural effusions or hematoma  Intracranial infection  Seizures  Intracerebral haemorrhage from catheter placement  Mechanical shunt failures or blocked shunts  Abdominal injury in VP shunts: ascites, peritonitis, abdominal perforations, volvulus  Arrhythmias in ventriculoatrial shunts. Parkinsonism And Parkinson’s Disease Parkinsonism is a collective term for the clinical syndrome that includes bradykinesia along with at least one additional symptom.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Parkinsonism is a collective term for the clinical syndrome that includes bradykinesia along with at least one additional symptom of:  tremor  rigidity  gait disturbances.  Parkinson’s disease is the most common cause of parkinsonism.  Other causes of parkinsonism include:  drug-induced parkinsonism  cerebrovascular disease  dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)  multiple system atrophy  progressive supranuclear palsy.  Parkinson’s disease is defined as a chronic progressive neurodegenerative disease linked to decreased dopamine production in the substantia nigra.  Reduced dopamine levels lead to a movement disorder with classical parkinsonian features including:  bradykinesia  resting tremor  rigidity  shuffling gait.  Diagnosis is mainly clinical. However, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging may be helpful in confirming loss of dopaminergic neuronal function and ruling out alternative diagnoses.  Levodopa and dopamine agonists such as ropinirole are potential first-line treatment options.  Parkinson’s plus syndromes are a group of neurodegenerative diseases that consist of cardinal features of Parkinson’s disease (resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and shuffling gait) along with additional symptoms, which include reduced response to levodopa, dysarthria, autonomic dysfunction and supranuclear gaze palsy.  The syndromes include conditions such as:  multiple system dystrophy  dementia with Lewy bodies  progressive supranuclear palsy  corticobasal degeneration.  Diagnosis is usually clinical. However, MRI brain and Iiodobenzamide SPECT scanning may be of value.  A multi-disciplinary approach is essential for treatment, patients respond poorly to dopamine agonists or l-dopa.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  There were approximately 137 000 people living with Parkinson’s disease in the United Kingdom (UK) in 2017, based on a Parkinson’s UK report.  Each year, there are about 17 300 new diagnoses of Parkinson’s disease in people aged 45 years and above.  The prevalence of Parkinson's disease increases with age – the prevalence is 4–5 : 100 000 in those aged 30–39 years, compared with over 1 500 : 100 000 in those aged 80–84 years.  The prevalence is higher in men than in women.  By 2025, due to population growth and an increasingly ageing population, the estimated prevalence and yearly incidence of Parkinson’s disease is expected to increase by around 23%. Aetiology  The exact cause of Parkinson’s disease is unknown; however, around 20% of cases have a family history in a first-degree relative.  Early onset Parkinson’s disease is associated with the mutation of the PARK 1 gene, encoding protein Alpha synuclein, sat chromosome 4q, the main component of Lewy bodies. Other genes identified include PARK- Parkin, PARK, PINK 1, PARK DJ1.  Wilson’s disease, Huntington’s disease and spinocerebellar ataxia may all lead to symptoms of parkinsonism.  Medications known to cause parkinsonism include:  antipsychotic drugs  metoclopramide  prochlorperazine  tetrabenazine  sodium valproate  lithium.

DR. JAM Pathophysiology Genetic abnormalities:  lead to protein misfolding, resulting in impaired clearance and protein accumulation  this in turn leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and, ultimately, symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. Acquired aetiology:  destruction of dopamine producing neurones in the substantia nigra reduces availability of dopamine, which usually produces an inhibitory effect  this leads to increased excitatory effects, due to excess acetylcholine availability  excessive stimulation of neurons of basal ganglia causes increased muscle tone, rigidity and tremors.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons  loss of melanin containing neurons produce changes, including depigmentation leading to the formation of Lewy bodies.  Clinical Presentation CARDINAL FEATURES MOTOR FEATURES NON-MOTOR FEATURES bradykinesia (must be present) mask like facies depression ‘cogwheel’ rigidity reduced blink frequency fatigue resting tremor freezing sleep disturbances shuffling gait dysphasia cognitive impairment or dementia postural instability micrographia anosmia and other sensory disturbances eg pain hypophonia memory and thought processing dysfunction Signs and symptoms more consistent with a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease:  unilateral onset and persistent asymmetry  resting tremor  good response to levodopa  levodopa-induced dyskinesia  long disease course (> 10 years). Signs and symptoms more consistent of other diagnoses:  prominent early autonomic failure (postural hypotension, urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction) – consider multisystem atrophy (MSA) or DLB  cerebellar signs – consider MSA  prominent pyramidal signs – consider MSA  vascular parkinsonism – consider corticobasal syndrome (CBS)  vertical supranuclear gaze palsy – consider progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)

DR. JAM  early falls (within first year) – consider PSP and normal pressure hydrocephalus  neuroleptic use – consider drug-induced parkinsonism  poor levodopa response – consider MSA, PSP or CBS  early dementia – consider DLB, PSP or CBS.  Differential Diagnosis Differentials for parkinsonian symptoms include:  Parkinson’s disease  MSA  drug-induced parkinsonism  DLB  stroke/transient ischaemic attack (TIA)  PSA  liver failure  trauma  normal pressure hydrocephalus  tumour  infection  Wilson's disease  Huntington’s disease  prion diseases  Alzheimer’s disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is predominantly clinical.  If at least 2 of 4 cardinal signs are positive (including bradykinesia), then the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease should be considered.  Dopamine transporter SPECT imaging may be helpful. It shows reduced and asymmetrical uptake of striatal dopamine biomarkers, particularly in the posterior putamen with sparing of the caudate nucleus.  CT/MRI can be used to rule out alternative diagnoses.  Management Non-pharmacological  If Parkinson's disease is suspected, urgent neurology referral is required.  Look for and either reduce or stop any medications that could potentially cause parkinsonism, wherever possible.  If Parkinson's disease is confirmed:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  provide patient, family and/or carers with written information  provide information about local support groups and charity organisations, such as Parkinson’s UK  inform the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)  give lifestyle modification advice including – diet and exercise and avoidance of alcohol and smoking.  physiotherapy  speech and language therapy may be required in later stages. Pharmacological The first-line medication is levodopa, which is usually given with a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor, such as cobeneldopa or co-careldopa:  usually offered to people in the early stages of Parkinson's disease  typically provides more improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning  fewer adverse effects, such as excessive sleepiness, hallucinations and impulse control disorders, but may cause more motor complications than other drug classes. Oral dopamine agonists, such as pramipexole or ropinirole, or transdermal dopamine agonists, such as rotigotine:  typically provide less improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning when compared to levodopa but with fewer motor complications. Adverse effects include more risk of excessive sleepiness, hallucinations and impulse control disorders than other drug classes  Ergot-derived dopamine agonists, such as cabergoline and pergolide, should not be used as first-line treatment due to the risk of cardiac fibrosis with long-term use and need for additional monitoring. Adjuvant medications:  Oral monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline or safinamide):  do not cause an interaction after consumption of tyraminerich foods  typically provide less improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning, fewer motor complications and fewer adverse effects such as excessive sleepiness, hallucinations and impulse control disorders than other drug classes. Oral catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitors (such as entacapone):

DR. JAM  are given as part of the combination preparation of levodopa, carbidopa and entacapone to improve compliance  may be used as an adjunct to levodopa for people who have developed dyskinesia or motor fluctuations despite optimal levodopa therapy  typically provide more improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning, with more adverse effects such as excessive sleepiness and impulse control disorders, but a lower risk of hallucinations than other drug classes. Oral amantadine:  may be considered if dyskinesia is not adequately managed by modifying existing antiparkinsonian therapy. Subcutaneous apomorphine (dopamine agonist):  may be offered to people with advanced Parkinson's disease on optimal oral treatment, as intermittent subcutaneous bolus injections and/or continuous subcutaneous infusion. Surgical  Surgery involves the insertion of electrodes, usually bilaterally, into deep nuclei within the brain for deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus.  These are connected to a battery-powered generator via leads that are tunnelled beneath the skin.  A generator is usually implanted into the chest wall and it delivers an electric current to the electrodes placed in the targeted areas of the brain.  They may be considered for people with advanced Parkinson's disease with motor complications refractory to optimal medical treatment who are fit, levodopa-responsive and have no co-morbid mental health conditions.  Prognosis  Parkinson's disease is slowly progressive, but the rate of progression is variable.  The mortality rate for elderly people aged 70–89 years with Parkinson's disease is 2–5 times higher than age-matched control subjects without Parkinson’s.  The risk of dementia is 2–6 times higher in people with Parkinson's disease than in those without the disease.  Other Parkinson plus syndrome

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Progressive supranuclear palsy:  Chronic disorder with difficulty walking, abnormal eye movements, muscle stiffness, balance disturbances.  There are lesions in the area of the brain that controls eye movement hence blurred vision is an early characteristic feature.  Mood disorders are commonly seen.  Tremors are rare but the tendency to fall backwards is very common.  Do not respond to typical anti-Parkinson’s medication.  MSA:  A group of disorders that progressively affect the central and autonomic nervous systems.  Oligodendrocytes are damaged by abnormal accumulations of the protein alpha-synuclein.  There are two types of MSA:  MSA-P – characterised by Parkinson’s-like symptoms, such as slowness of movement, rigid muscles and lack of facial expression. MSP–P progresses much more rapidly than typical Parkinson's disease  MSA-C (cerebellar MSA) – characterised by lack of coordination and balance, tremor when reaching for an object, slurred speech and trouble swallowing.  Autonomic symptoms include:  orthostatic hypotension  constipation  increased sweating  sleep apnoea  sexual dysfunction.  DLB:  Presence of abnormal protein deposits of alpha synuclein (Lewy bodies) that are also seen in people with Parkinson's disease.  Second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer’s disease.  Characterised by:  cognitive impairment  visual hallucinations  inability to focus  inflexible thinking  paranoia.  A progressive disorder.  Symptomatic treatment is possible with cholinesterase inhibitors and atypical antipsychotics.  Corticobasal degeneration  Multiple areas of the brain sustain nerve cell loss and atrophy.

DR. JAM  Usually presents with symptoms beginning in the 6th–7th decade of life.  Initially affects only one side of the body, then proceeds to bilateral involvement.  Symptoms include common Parkinson’s symptoms along with behavioural and cognitive changes.  Only symptomatic treatment is possible. Phenytoin Toxicity Phenytoin is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker. It has a very narrow therapeutic window, which increases the risk of toxicity.  Overview Key Facts  Phenytoin is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker. It has a very narrow therapeutic window, which increases the risk of toxicity.  Toxicity may occur as a result of intentional overdose, inadequate monitoring, misinterpretation of phenytoin levels (especially in hypoalbuminaemia when less phenytoin will be bound to albumin) and drug interactions (particularly with cytochrome P450 inhibitors).  Symptoms of phenytoin toxicity are predominantly neurological and include ataxia, nystagmus, impaired coordination, dysarthria, coma, confusion, dyskinesia, seizures and hyperglycaemia.  It is thought that cardiac symptoms (hypotension, bradycardia and asystole) may be caused by the diluent used with intravenous (IV) preparations (propylene glycol).  Phenytoin has also rarely been known to cause DRESS syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens–Johnson syndrome.  Diagnosis is made on the basis of history, examination and serum phenytoin levels.  There is no antidote for phenytoin. Activated charcoal may be of benefit within one hour of ingestion and potentially later than this in large overdoses.  Management is centred around treating individual symptoms, such as cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, agitation, hypotension (may require ICU level care) delirium and electrolyte abnormalities.  Fatal cases are usually when a patient has taken another substance in combination with phenytoin.  10–20% may suffer from major morbidities, such as memory loss and cognitive defects.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Phenytoin is used for the prevention and treatment of seizures and as a second-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia under specialist supervision (unlicensed indication).  Phenytoin has a very narrow therapeutic window, which increases the risk of toxicity.  Older people are at greater risk of toxicity, as phenytoin clearance tends to decrease with age:  phenytoin clearance may be 20% less in patients > 70 years old compared with young adults. Aetiology  Phenytoin toxicity may occur in the following scenarios:  intentional overdose  inadequate monitoring after initiation or dose change  misinterpretation of phenytoin levels:  phenytoin is approximately 90% protein-bound in adults  in patients with hypoalbuminaemia, total phenytoin levels may be misleading as the percentage of unbound phenytoin (which is pharmacologically active) will be higher and may lead to toxicity in the context of seemingly normal total levels.  drug interactions:  phenytoin is metabolised by cytochrome P450, so levels may be increased by drugs or substances that inhibit cytochrome P450. Pathophysiology  Symptoms of phenytoin toxicity are predominantly neurological.  Phenytoin is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker and it targets neurones with high-frequency activity, prolonging the refractory period and preventing or reducing seizure activity.  It is also a class 1B antiarrhythmic acting on cardiac voltage-gated sodium channels:  cardiac effects are rare from oral ingestion and it is thought that they may be a side-effect of propylene glycol, the diluent used for IV administration  rapid infusions of propylene glycol can cause bradycardia, hypotension and asystole.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms are predominantly neurological and include:  ataxia  nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia  co-ordination impairment  dysarthria

DR. JAM  coma  confusion  dyskinesia  choreoathetosis  hyper-reflexia  seizures  hyperglycaemia.  Cardiovascular symptoms such as hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmias have also been reported and are usually associated with intravenous (IV) administration.  Phenytoin has also rarely been known to cause DRESS syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens–Johnson syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  History and examination.  Serum phenytoin levels:  the usual therapeutic range is 10–20 mg/l  > 20 mg/l is likely to be symptomatic  > 40 mg/l is associated with severe toxicity.  Management  ABCDE assessment.  Activated charcoal:  may be beneficial if the patient presents with one hour of ingestion of > 20 mg/kg phenytoin  in larger overdoses, activated charcoal may be beneficial > one hour  consider multiple-dose activated charcoal in symptomatic patients.  12-lead ECG:  may show QRS prolongation or VT  if QRS prolonged or the patient is hypotensive and not responsive to fluids, consider sodium bicarbonate infusion  treat bradyarrhythmias and tachyarrhythmias as required.  Check full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&Es), liver function tests (LFTs) and glucose and treat electrolyte abnormalities as necessary.  IV fluid resuscitation if hypotensive and referral to ICU if poorly responsive to fluids.  Treat agitation and delirium as per hospital protocol.  Treat seizures if frequent or prolonged (a brief convulsion will likely not require treatment).

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  The mean fatal dose for adults is thought to be 2–5 g and involve serum concentrations > 125 mg/l.  Fatal cases are usually when a patient has taken another substance in combination with phenytoin.  10–20% may suffer from major morbidities, such as memory loss and cognitive defects.  Other  Side Effects of Phenytoin Side effects of phenytoin include:  Gum hypertrophy (occurs in up to 50% of patients taking the drug)  Blood disorders (including megaloblastic anaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and aplastic anaemia  Fatigue  Skin and joint disorders. Polyneuropathies Polyneuropathy results in generalised nerve dysfunction affecting the same sides bilaterally.  Overview Key Facts  Polyneuropathy results in generalised nerve dysfunction affecting the same sides bilaterally.  Most polyneuropathies are chronic and usually develop over a number of months.  Neuropathy can reduce quality of life, impact activities of daily living and, in severe cases, can be fatal.  The condition can involve both sensory and motor fibres but sometimes purely sensory or motor neuropathy may occur.  They are classified on basis of the part of nerve affected:  distal axonopathy  myelinopathy  neuronopathy.  They are also classified by pattern into:  multiple mononeuropathy  acute symmetrical peripheral neuropathy (rare)  chronic symmetrical peripheral neuropathy (most common).

DR. JAM  Polyneuropathy can be caused by a wide range of underlying causes, the most common causes include diabetes and nutritional deficiencies.  Symptoms vary according to the type and severity of the neuropathic process; however, some common patterns are seen:  weakness  numbness  burning pain.  Electromyogram (EMG) and nerve conduction studies are potential investigations. Blood work is used to rule out a metabolic cause.  Treatment includes management of the underlying cause, and may also include analgesia and access to physiotherapy. Epidemiology  It is not possible to quantify the exact prevalence of polyneuropathy in the general population.  Some examples of condition-based prevalence are as below:  painful diabetic neuropathy: 16–26% of people with diabetes  post-herpetic neuralgia: 8–19% of people with herpes zoster when defined as pain at one month after rash onset, or 8% when defined as pain at three months after rash onset. Aetiology Group Aetiology Motor, sensory or mixed features Metabolic Diabetes Typically chronic, sensory predominant and length dependent Uraemia Vitamins B1, B6, B12 deficiency Hypothyroidism Mixed: may be acute and is relatively rare Infective Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) Distal sensory Often painful Lyme disease Variable presentation, including cranial neuropathies

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Group Aetiology Motor, sensory or mixed features Toxic Isoniazid Mixed: usually subacute Pyridoxine Sensory predominant Chemotherapeutics Mixed: may start and worsen even after chemotherapy has stopped (‘coasting’) Lead (and other metals) May be acute, in this case often motor predominant Immune Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) Mixed: may have a relapsing course; often non length dependent. Paraproteinaemic Mixed: patients may have monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or myeloma Connective tissue disease Mixed: consider: rheumatoid arthritis (RA) Sjőgren syndrome systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) sarcoidosis – may be mononeuropathy multiplex. Paraneoplastic Mixed: may be acute/subacute, lung carcinoma most implicated Guillain–Barre syndrome (GBS) Mixed: usually acute Genetic Charcot–Marie–Tooth (CMT) disease Mixed: numerous types exist CMT 1 is demyelinating

DR. JAM Group Aetiology Motor, sensory or mixed features while CMT 2 is axonal. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) Rare, acute and predominantly motor  Acute polyneuropathies suggest inflammatory, vasculitic or toxic causes.  Chronic neuropathic symptoms suggest genetic or metabolic causes. Pathophysiology  The pathophysiology of polyneuropathy depends upon the type and course of the underlying aetiology.  The most common pathology in metabolic and systemic disorders and toxicity is axonal degeneration – long-fibre, distal axonopathy.  Although axonal degeneration may also be present in demyelinating neuropathies, segmental demyelination with primary destruction of the myelin sheath, leaving the axon intact, is also seen.  Secondary segmental demyelination may be seen in axonal degeneration.  Sometimes, the cell bodies of axons, anterior horn cells or dorsal root ganglia are primarily affected.  These conditions are termed as neuronapathies.  Clinical Presentation  Several signs and symptoms are seen depending upon which group of nerves are affected.  In typical mixed sensory motor polyneuropathy, patients have distal symmetrical weakness affecting the lower limbs more than the upper limbs.  The most common signs symptoms exhibited are:  tingling and numbness  ‘pins and needles' sensation  muscle weakness and twitching  increased tendency to falls  skin and nail changes  lower limb ulcers  difficulty moving limbs  inability to sense pain and temperature changes  insomnia

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  involvement of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) presents with:  excessive sweating  hypertension  bowel and bladder incontinence  disturbance in digestion  breathing disturbances  high blood pressure.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  fibromyalgia  multiple sclerosis (MS)  vitamin deficiency  hepatitis C  renal disease  acromegaly  Friedreich’s ataxia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  History and general physical examination to check the pattern and course of the presentation.  First line investigations include:  full blood count (FBC)  vitamin B12  fasting blood glucose  urea and electrolytes (U&Es)  liver enzymes  thyroid function tests (TFTs)  serum immunoglobulins and electrophoresis.  Specific investigations include:  nerve conduction studies  electromyography (EMG).  Computed tomography (CT)/magenetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and nerve biopsy may be required to confirm the underlying cause.  Management Non-pharmacological  Lifestyle modification:  light daily activities with help of occupational therapist  weight loss if applicable

DR. JAM  vitamin-rich diet (may require dietician input)  avoidance of alcohol and smoking.  Use of devices such as a walking stick, splint, braces and/or a wheelchair may be required to prevent falls and other injuries.  Physiotherapy to help with muscle weakness and coordination. Pharmacological  Treat the underlying cause, for example:  control blood glucose in diabetes  treat hypothyroidism  Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) in multifocal motor neuropathy  IVIG, plasma exchange and possible ventilator support in GBS  IV methylprednisolone in CIDP.  Medical management for neurological pain:  analgesics such as amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin  capsaicin 0.075% cream for patients with localised pain or who cannot tolerate oral analgesics  tramadol can be prescribed if initial treatment fails and patient is awaiting review. Surgical  Surgical intervention may be required if symptoms are caused by a nerve being compressed by a tumour or a mass.  Prognosis  Prognosis depends upon the underlying cause.  Usually 40%–60% of patients receive only partial relief with treatment.  GBS is associated with a 5% mortality rate. Subdural Haematoma Intracranial haemorrhage is a collective term for numerous conditions that occur when a blood vessel within the skull ruptures or leaks leading to accumulation of blood within intracranial spaces.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Intracranial haemorrhage is a collective term for numerous conditions that occur when a blood vessel within the skull ruptures or leaks leading to accumulation of blood within intracranial spaces.  Intracranial haemorrhage can be classed by location (intra-axial or extra-axial haemorrhage) or underlying cause (trauma, vascular malformation, tumour-related haemorrhage, hypertension or cerebral venous thrombosis).  Intra-axial haemorrhage (intracerebral haemorrhage):  basal ganglia haemorrhage  lobar haemorrhage  pontine haemorrhage  cerebellar haemorrhage.  Extra-axial haemorrhage:  extradural haemorrhage (EDH)  intralaminar dural haemorrhage  subdural haemorrhage (SDH)  subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH)  intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)  subpial haemorrhage.  A subdural haematoma is a form of intracranial haemorrhage that leads to the formation of a clot over the surface of the brain in the subdural space.  The collection of blood lies between the dura and the arachnoid mater.  It usually occurs due to rupture of the bridging veins from shearing forces or laceration of the brain.  Both acute and chronic subdural haematomas present most commonly after mild-to-moderate head injury.  Spontaneous subdural haematoma is rare but can be caused by conditions such as clotting disorders, arteriovenous malformations and aneurysms.  Subdural haematomas are more likely to occur in older patients or patients with a significant alcohol history, as they are more likely to experience cerebral atrophy – there is a larger distance for bridging veins to cover, so they are at greater risk of being damaged.  The condition is also associated with a higher incidence in babies and very young children, adults with a history of alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy.  Acute subdural haematoma:  arises in approximately one-third of patients with a severe head injury  patients may initially have a lucid period with subsequent deterioration as the haematoma continues to form.

DR. JAM  Chronic subdural haematoma:  often due to traumatic brain injury that may be so mild that the patient may not recall the incident  patients present around 2–3 weeks after this incident  mild headache, confusion and coma are the symptoms of chronic subdural haematoma, with progressively worsening symptoms  less often, there may be a gradual onset of focal neurological signs  patients are often older and may also have a history of alcoholism or be on anticoagulation  these patients may present acutely if there is a large re-bleed into a pre-existing subdural haematoma.  Treatment depends on the size of the haematoma, the chronicity and clinical signs/focal neurology.  Small haematomas with no associated symptomatology may be managed conservatively with monitoring of the patient and serial CT scanning.  Burr hole drainage of the subdural space is the mainstay of surgical intervention. Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Subdural haematomas arise in approximately one-third of patients with a severe head injury.  The condition is most commonly found in babies, older people, those with alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy. Aetiology  Both acute and chronic subdural haematomas present most commonly after mild-to-moderate head injury.  Spontaneous subdural haematoma is rarer but can be caused by conditions such as clotting disorders, arteriovenous malformations and aneurysms.  Subdural haematomas are more likely to occur in older patients or patients with a significant alcohol history, as they are more likely to experience cerebral atrophy – there is a larger distance for bridging veins to cover, so they are at greater risk of being damaged.  The condition is also associated with a higher incidence in babies and very young children, adults with a history of alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy. Pathophysiology  The meninges are connective tissue membranes that line the skull and vertebral canal, covering the brain and spinal cord; they consist of three layers:  dura mater – outer layer  arachnoid mater – middle layer  pia mater – inner layer.  Epidural space describes the potential space between the vertebral column and the dura mater.  Subdural space describes the space between the dura and the arachnoid mater.

DR. JAM  Subarachnoid space describes the space between the arachnoid and the pia mater.  A subdural haematoma describes the collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid mater.  It usually occurs due to rupture of the bridging veins from shearing forces or laceration of the brain.  This is often caused by trauma.  Spontaneous subdural haematoma is rarer but can be caused by conditions such as clotting disorders, arteriovenous malformations and aneurysms. Types of brain haemorrhage:  Clinical Presentation  Acute subdural haematoma:  presents most commonly after mild-to-moderate head injury  more likely to occur in older patients or patients with a significant alcohol history, as they are more likely to experience cerebral atrophy  subdural haematoma arises in approximately one-third of patients with a severe head injury  the condition is also more commonly found in babies, adults with a history of alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy  patients may initially have a lucid period with subsequent deterioration as the haematoma continues to form  focal neurology may be present, depending on the area of the brain compressed.  Chronic subdural haematoma:  often due to traumatic brain injury that may be so mild that the patient may not recall the incident  patients present around 2–3 weeks after the incident

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  mild headache, confusion and coma are the symptoms of chronic subdural haematoma, with progressively worsening symptoms  less often, there may be a gradual onset of focal neurological signs  patients are often older and may also have a history of alcoholism or be on anticoagulation  these patients may present acutely if there is a large re-bleed into a pre-existing subdural haematoma.  Patients with subdural haematoma may also present with signs of raised intracranial pressure.  Raised intracranial pressure (ICP)  Normal ICP = 10 mmHg; abnormally raised ICP > 20 mmHg.  A haematoma within the constant volume of the skull will cause extrusion of an equal volume of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and venous blood initially (compensation) – ICP is maintained.  When the compensatory mechanisms reach their limit, the ICP will increase exponentially as the haematoma increases in volume.  Causes of raised ICP include:  haematoma  focal oedema – secondary to contusion or haematoma  diffuse cerebral oedema – secondary to ischaemia  obstruction to CSF flow (rarely seen in acute trauma)  obstruction to venous outflow (can occur as a result of a tight cervical collar).  The effects of raised ICP include:  temporal uncal herniation – cranial nerve III compression and pupil dilation  motor weakness (corticospinal tract compression)  compression of cardiorespiratory control centres if the brainstem herniates through the foramen magnum (coning)  Cushing’s response – respiratory rate (RR) decreases, heart rate (HR) decreases, systolic BP increases, pulse pressure increases.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for intracranial haemorrhage are as follows:  stroke  dementia  prion disease  subdural empyema  epilepsy of the temporal lobe  frontal lobe syndrome  encephalopathy

DR. JAM  hydrocephalus  other forms of traumatic brain injury.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A clinician with safeguarding training should be involved in the initial assessment of patients with head injuries and should follow local guidelines as appropriate.  ABCDE approach should be undertaken as soon as possible.  Basic observations (O2 saturations, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature) will help to assess the stability of the patient and the likelihood of injuries.  Establishing a patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is crucial in identifying the likelihood and severity of head injuries – GCS > 12 is associated with earlier recovery and minimal complications long term.  Also need to consistently assess pupil size and reactivity.  Patients may require invasive ICP monitoring.  Patients may have other associated injuries – important to assess all systems.  ECG if there are suspected cardiac events that may have led to the development of head injury.  Arterial and venous blood gas (ABG/VBG) will help in assessing the patient – look for acidosis (inadequate ventilation), electrolyte imbalances, etc.  Baseline blood tests: full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&Es), liver function tests (LFTs), clotting, group + save/crossmatch, troponin (if suspecting cardiac events leading to fall or head injury), etc.  C-spine investigation – X-ray or computed tomography (CT) of cervical spine within < 1 hour if C-spine thought to be at risk or patient has GCS < 13. CT head criteria  Adults who have sustained a head injury should receive a CT head scan within < 1 hour if they have any of the following risk factors:  GCS < 13 on initial assessment in Emergency Department (ED)  GCS < 15 at 2 hours after initial assessment in ED  suspected open or depressed skull fracture  any sign of basal skull fracture:  haemotympanum – bleeding in the middle ear cavity with an intact tympanic membrane  ‘panda eyes’ sign – bruising around both eyes  CSF leak from ear or nose  Battle's sign – bruising over the mastoid process posterior to the ear.  focal neurological deficit  post-traumatic seizure  > 1 episode of vomiting.  For children who have sustained a head injury – a CT head scan should be done within 1 hour if more than one of these risk factors are present:  loss of consciousness lasting > 5 minutes  abnormal drowsiness  three or more episodes of vomiting

DR. JAM  dangerous mechanism of injury (high-speed road traffic accident, fall from a height of >3 metres, other high-speed injuries)  amnesia (antegrade or retrograde) for > 5 minutes  children < 1 year with bruising, swelling, lacerations > 5 cm on the head.  If 0–1 of these risk factors are present, children should be observed for a minimum of four hours.  Adults and children without sufficient risk factors and who are having anticoagulant treatment – perform CT within 8 hours. Imaging For Subdural Haematoma  CT scan of the head is good for detecting acute subdural haematoma (SDH).  Subacute SDH may be more difficult to detect with plain CT, therefore MRI or CT with contrast is preferred.  Chronic SDH is usually detectable on non-contrast CT. Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management  Management depends on:  the size of the haematoma  presence of focal neurology  clinical signs  chronicity of the haematoma.  Patients with small haematomas with no associated symptomatology may be treated conservatively – observation and serial CT monitoring.  Any clotting defects should be corrected.  Generally, most haematomas > 5 cm require surgical excavation. Surgical treatment  Burr hole drainage.  Craniotomy.  Repeat surgery is required in 25% of cases.  General management of head injuries  Ensure patients airway, breathing and circulation are stable and being monitored.  Establish GCS early on – patients with GCS ≤ 8 require early involvement from the anaesthetics and critical care teams (may require intubation).  Establish the need for C-spine imaging and CT head with regards to the risk factors outlined above.  Adequate analgesia and pain management should be carried out (eg splinting fractured limbs and catheterising a full bladder) – pain can raise ICP.  Discuss patients with neurosurgery if there are:  new or abnormal changes seen on imaging  persisting coma (GCS ≤ 8) after initial resuscitation  unexplained confusion lasting > 4 hours  deterioration in GCS after admission  progressive focal neurological signs  seizure without full recovery  penetrating injuries  CSF leak.  Neurological observations should be carried out for GCS, pupil size or reactivity or limb movements. Major head injuries  The aim of management is to prevent secondary cerebral damage.  Adequate ventilation needs to be maintained with PaO2 >13 kPa and PaCO2 4–5 kPa:

DR. JAM  intubation may be required in patients with absent gag reflex, PaO2 <9 or PaCO2 >5.3  rule out potential pneumothoraces before considering ventilation.  Maintain adequate mean arterial pressure (MAP).  Mannitol: 0.5–1g/kg over 10–30 minutes to help reduce ICP.  Metabolic: correct any imbalances which may contribute to impaired consciousness, eg hypoglycaemia.  Prognosis  The prognosis of subarachnoid haematoma is variable and depends on the extent of the bleed as well as the development of complications.  Complications of subdural haematoma include:  raised intracranial pressure  cerebral oedema  seizures  permanent neurological or cognitive deficit including coma and persistent vegetative state  recurrence  death due to cerebellar herniation.  Mortality rates for acute subdural haematoma can be up to 50% if complicated by parenchymal brain injury.  Even uncomplicated cases are associated with mortality rates of up to 20%.  Chronic subdural haematoma with surgical intervention has a mortality rate of approximately 5%. Syphilis Syphilis infection is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.  Overview Key Facts  Syphilis infection is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.  Prevalence is increasing in the United Kingdom (UK).  Transmission is usually through direct contact with an active lesion.  Untreated syphilis can remain for many years and progress through several stages:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  early syphilis (< 2 years post-infection) - primary, secondary and early latent  late syphilis (> 2 years post-infection) - late-latent and tertiary.  Syphilis must be treated early to prevent progression to later stages of which symptoms may be irreversible.  Signs and symptoms depend on stage of the disease and may include a painless ulcer (chancre), maculopapular rash on palms/soles, condylomata lata (moist, wart-like lesions), snail-tract ulcers (oral mucosa) and unexplained neurological/ophthalmic symptoms.  Diagnosis should ideally take place in a genito-urinary medicine (GUM) clinic and will involve detailed history and examination, serology testing and dark-field microscopy tests of swabs taken from a suspected chancre.  All patients with suspected syphilis should be advised to avoid sexual contact/exposing others to active lesions until diagnosis excluded/fully treated.  Antibiotic therapy is primarily procaine penicillin (10 days if primary/secondary or 17 days in tertiary infection).  If left untreated, syphilis can cause several complications including:  neurological syphilis  cardiovascular complications  Gummatous disease  adverse outcomes in pregnancy  facilitation of other infections, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Epidemiology  Transmission rates of syphilis through sexual contact range from 10-60% - highest in primary and secondary syphilis.  Prevalence of syphilis in the UK greater than doubled from 20132018 to 7541 cases in 2018.  Most new diagnoses (75%) in men who have sex with men (MSM).  Risk factors for the condition include:  unprotected sex  multiple/anonymous sexual partners  transactional sex  substance use before sex  other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) previously/currently  social vulnerability (poverty, homelessness, migrant/refugee status)  needle-sharing contact with a known syphilis case.

DR. JAM Aetiology  Syphilis is an infectious disease caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.  Incubation period is around 21 days but can range from 9-90 days and is dependent on the infectious dose.  Most cases are sexually transmitted via direct contact with an infectious lesion.  Transmission may also occur via:  vertical transmission from mother to child in pregnancy  sharing needles in intravenous drug users (IVDUs)  blood products/organ transplants (screened for in UK). Pathophysiology  Untreated syphilis can persist for years and progress through several stages:  early syphilis (< 2 years of infection) = primary syphilis, secondary syphilis and early latent syphilis  late syphilis (> 2 years since infection) = late latent syphilis and tertiary syphilis.  Early syphilis:  primary syphilis is defined as a painless ulcer (chancre) at the site of infection + local lymphadenopathy  secondary syphilis is systemic involvement which may include: maculopapular rash (palms/soles), condylomata lata, patchy alopecia, snail-tract lesions (oral mucosa), generalised lymphadenopathy, low-grade fever, headache and malaise.  early latent - confirmed infection in absence of any current clinical features.  Late syphilis:  late latent is defined as confirmed infection in absence of current clinical features (infection > 2 years ago)  tertiary syphilis is rare, and may present with: cardiac disease, gummatous lesions or neurological disease.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms and signs can be varied and may include:  genital lesions – characteristic lesion of primary syphilis is a single, painless, indurated genital ulcer (also known as a chancre)  non-pruritic maculopapular rash (typically affecting palms and soles)  moist wart-like lesions (condylomata lata)  patchy lesions of the oral mucosa (snail-track ulcers)  generalised lymphadenopathy  unexplained neurological/ophthalmological symptoms.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis include:  genital herpes  balanitis  Behçet's syndrome  genital cancer  cervical erosion  chancroid lesions (haemophilus ducreyi).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full history – including symptoms of syphilis, risk factors (full sexual history) and past medical history (including treatment for previous STIs).  Examination – genital area, skin, eye, neurological and cardiovascular.  Referral to GUM clinic for full sexual health screen and diagnosis:  serology (usually positive from around 4 weeks but can take up to 3 months)  non-specific tests include venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) + rapid plasma reagin (RPR) (useful serial titres but high false + rate)  specific tests include treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA) and treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA)  dark-field microscopy – demonstrates T. Pallidum from swabs taken from primary lesion (high specificity but low sensitivity) – negative result doesn’t exclude syphilis.  All positive screening tests must be confirmed with a different serological test.  Negative serology tests should be repeated at 6 and 12 weeks postinfection or 2 weeks after possible chancre.  Management Non-pharmacological  All patients with suspected syphilis should be referred to genitourinary medicine (GUM) clinic for general advice, management and contact tracing.  Patients should receive advice regarding avoidance of any form of sexual contact and avoidance of exposing others to the active lesion until the diagnosis excluded or successful treatment completed.  Explain the condition, risk factors and potential complications.  Look-back periods for contact tracing will vary but as an idea:  primary syphilis - approximately 3 months  secondary syphilis - approximately 2 years

DR. JAM  tertiary syphilis - more than 2 years (back to the estimated time of infection).  People with suspected syphilis or a diagnosis of syphilis who decline testing/treatment should be advised that if they are found to have infected others with syphilis after knowing of their own infection, they may be subject to prosecution. Pharmacological Early syphilis  Procaine penicillin 750 mg IM OD for 10 days.  Or benzathine penicillin 2.4 mg IM for 1-2 doses, 1 week apart.  If penicillin allergic, doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days should be the preferred alternative. Late syphilis  Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mg IM for 3 doses, 1 week apart.  Or amoxicillin 2g PO TDS plus probenecid 500 mg QDS for 28 days.  If penicillin allergic, doxycycline 200 mg PO BD for 28 days.  Prognosis  If left untreated, around 1/3 of cases will progress to later stages of the disease and can lead to severe (and sometimes irreversible) complications including:  neuro-syphilis – neurological involvement which can occur at any stage of infection. Can affect: meninges, arteries, cranial nerves, eyes, brain and spinal cord  cardiovascular syphilis – aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, angina and heart failure  gummatous syphilis – granulomatous lesions with a necrotic centre, most commonly affects the skin and bones  adverse outcomes in pregnancy  facilitation of HIV transmission. Toxoplasmosis An intracellular obligate parasite Toxoplasma gondii causes toxoplasmosis.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  An intracellular obligate parasite Toxoplasma gondii (T. gondii) causes toxoplasmosis.  Rate of incidence is very high, yet many people remain asymptomatic (almost 90%).  Immunocompromised patients such as patients with HIV/AIDS suffer from the symptoms of toxoplasmosis.  Can also affect people on cancer chemotherapy or those on immunosuppressive drug treatment.  T. gondii can be found in the intestines of cats, which is the ultimate host of this parasite.  The symptoms are more like flu symptoms with fatigue, tiredness, fever and body aches. Symptoms can be from mild to severe depending upon the strength of the immune system of the affected person.  T. gondii can create cysts in the brain, muscles and heart.  The infection may pass from pregnant mothers to the fetus through the placenta and can cause a scale of complications ranging from mild eye infections to severe infections, causing serious eye disorders, seizures, mental disability, hearing loss or stillbirth.  The source of infection is raw uncooked or improperly cooked meat or cysts found in cat faeces or in goat's milk. Epidemiology  Prevalence is at its highest in tropical areas of the world such as South America, India and Malaysia, with a prevalence of around 60%. This is followed by southern European countries where there is a prevalence of around 54%.  Incidence in the United Kingdom (UK) is around 25%.  There are thee main strains of T. gondii.  T. gondii in Europe and North America – type I is the most virulent and type III the least; type II is the most common strain found in humans in Europe and North America. Aetiology  Pathogen – T. gondii, which is an obligate intracellular parasite.  Route of transmission is via oral or placental, or by blood transfusion or organ transplantation.  The cysts of T. gondii present in cat faeces are eaten by other animals such as goats or cows and enter the meat (either raw or improperly cooked), or they can gain entry to the human body by drinking unpasteurised goat's milk.  Most commonly acquired through undercooked meat (most commonly pork or lamb) which contain tissue cysts. It can also be acquired through drinking contaminated water.

DR. JAM  Risk factors identified are eating raw minced beef, raw oysters, clams, mussels, drinking unpasteurised goat’s milk and having three or more kittens. Pathophysiology  After the ingestion of T. gondii cysts, viable organisms are released which enter epithelial cells of the small gut where they multiply through asexual or sexual cell cycles and form oocysts (containing zygotes), which are released and then tachyzoite attach to the cell membrane of the host cell.  The attachment is augmented by the host cell’s protein.  After utilising the cellular matrix for its growth, the organism is then released into the blood circulation.  The response to the gut epithelial entry of the tachyzoite is the release of chemokines which bring macrophages and neutrophils to the site of damage.  An autoimmune pathway is then activated to recruit interleukin-12 (IL-12). This then stimulates interferongamma (IFN-gamma) synthesis by T lymphocytes and NK (natural killer) cells. (This is the most important step in controlling the infection of T. gondii.)  In immunocompromised patients these autoimmune pathways are not regulated which allows T. gondii to replicate unopposed and damage the epithelial cells, as well as cause cerebral toxoplasmosis.  The incubation period is 1–2 weeks.  It is transported to the gut via lymphatics and to the rest of the body via blood circulation.  Clinical Presentation  90% of patients are asymptomatic.  In immunocompromised patients, the symptoms are more like flu symptoms, including fever, body aches, chills, sore throat or pharyngitis, or maybe hepatosplenomegaly.  The level of suspicion should be high in patients with HIV/AIDS or patients who have undergone organ transplantation or multiple blood transfusions.  Neurological symptoms are evident in cerebral toxoplasmosis, including fever, seizures, confusion and severe headache with focal neurological deficit.  It can also cause chorioretinitis or pneumonitis in which the patient will present with vision disturbance or ocular pain, or breathing difficulty or cough, respectively.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  HIV infection  AIDS infection  CNS lymphoma or brain tumour  cerebral tuberculomas

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy  herpes viral encephalitis  human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5) or cytomegalovirus  brain abscess (bacterial or fungal).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Serological investigation by identifying IgM and IgG antibodies.  Detection of T. gondii by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).  Biopsy for definitive diagnosis is not routinely performed in toxoplasmosis; it is only indicated for patients who fail to respond to treatment to rule out differential diagnosis.  Radiological investigations:  CT scan of the brain for cerebral toxoplasmosis  MRI for differentiating brain lesions and cerebral tuberculosis (the preferred choice of investigation)  PET (positron emission tomography) scan has the highest specificity.  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoid uncooked/raw or improperly cooked food.  Keep the pets, especially cats, healthy.  Always drink pasteurised milk.  Thorough washing of fruits and vegetables.  Avoidance of stray cats. Pharmacological  Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine given for several weeks in combination is the first choice of treatment if the infection is not self-limiting.  Folinic acid (reduced folic acid) supplementation and weekly blood cell counts are required with the above treatment to avoid complications.  Alternative combinations can be considered as follows:  pyrimethamine – clindamycin  pyrimethamine – clarithromycin  pyrimethamine – azithromycin.  In immunocompromised symptomatic patients, long-term prophylaxis is also required with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole until the patient gains his/her immunity.  Spiramycin to avoid vertical transmission.

DR. JAM Surgical  Only attempted for ocular toxoplasmosis.  Antibiotic treatment is the mainstay of the treatment.  Prognosis  It is self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals.  Prognosis is good without any long-term side effects of the infection.  Timely diagnosis and detection and commencement of antibiotic treatment and antiviral treatment in patients with AIDS, improve the outcome many folds.  Other  Although the primary infection is self-limiting, the risk of latent reactivation is increased to 60% in immunocompromised patients.  Patient education is the key to its prevention, especially for patients with immunocompromised states.  The parasite T. gondii may change its behaviour, varying from host to host.  Toxoplasmosis is one of the causes of schizophrenia is also under study and research. Transient Ischaemic Attack Transient ischaemic attack is a transient neurological deficit caused by focal cerebral infarction without evidence of changes on the CT scan.  Overview Key Facts  Transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a transient neurological deficit caused by focal cerebral infarction without evidence of changes on the CT scan.  Symptoms in TIA last for less than 24 hours.  Symptoms are similar to those of a completed stroke.  Clinical symptoms depend on the area of the brain affected and may include:  limb weakness  facial weakness  slurred speech  cranial nerve deficits

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  gait disturbance  confusion  altered consciousness or loss of consciousness. Epidemiology  The incidence of the first episode of TIA is approximately 50 per 100 000 people in the United Kingdom (UK) annually. Aetiology  Conditions associated with increased risk of TIA include:  hypertension  diabetes mellitus  hypercholesterolaemia  permanent and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) – it has been estimated that AF causes more than 20% of ischaemic strokes  infective endocarditis  carotid artery disease – atheroma and stenosis of the carotid arteries are commonly associated with stroke and TIA  congestive heart failure  congenital or structural heart disease.  Other factors include:  age – the risk of having a stroke is doubled after the age of 55 years  genetics – family history of stroke in a first-degree relative  gender – the average age at presentation of stroke is lower for men versus women; in women, an increased risk of stroke is associated with current use of oral contraceptives, migraine with aura, the immediate postpartum period and pre-eclampsia  sickle cell disease – (microvascular disease and hypercoagulability)  antiphospholipid syndrome  chronic kidney disease (CKD).  Lifestyle factors that increase risk include:  smoking  excessive alcohol  physical inactivity  poor diet. Pathophysiology  Acute occlusion of an intracranial vessel occurs.  Blood flow reduced to the brain region supplied by the vessel.  This leads to decreased oxygen supply and infarction in that region.  Blood flow returns to normal within 24 hours, resulting in the resolution of symptoms.

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  The main differential diagnosis is a completed stroke (cerebrovascular accident) – this is confirmed by CT changes and/or symptoms lasting over 24 hours.  Other differentials include:  neurological conditions such as:  seizure  migraine with aura  peripheral neuropathies such as Bell’s palsy.  trauma  toxic/metabolic disturbance such as:  hypoglycaemia  drug and alcohol toxicity.  conditions which can cause dizziness or disturbed balance such as:  syncope  peripheral vestibular disturbance – vertigo or dizziness.  space-occupying lesions including:  tumour  subdural haematoma.  systemic or local infection including:  abscess  meningitis and encephalitis  encephalopathies such as hypertensive encephalopathy or Wernicke’s encephalopathy.  other conditions such as:  acute confusional state  dementia  vasculitis  somatoform or conversion disorder.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Take a detailed history from the patient and, if possible, a witness.  Follow up with a detailed clinical examination including ABC assessment, cardiovascular exam and detailed neurological exam.  The FAST test – Face (weakness or asymmetry), Arm (weakness), Speech (difficulty) test can be used for rapid assessment – one or more is classed as a positive result.  Suspect stroke if:  sudden onset, a focal neurological deficit that is ongoing or has persisted for longer than 24 hours without any other condition such as hypoglycaemia.  Suspect a TIA if:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  the patient presents with sudden onset, a focal neurological deficit that has completely resolved within 24 hours of onset  symptoms/signs cannot be explained by another condition such as hypoglycaemia  most TIAs tend to resolve within 1–2 hours but can persist for up to 24 hours.  Posterior circulation strokes may be difficult to diagnose and should be suspected if the person presents with:  symptoms of acute vestibular syndrome include acute continuous vertigo or dizziness with nystagmus, nausea or vomiting, head motion intolerance and new gait unsteadiness.  Investigations  Blood glucose levels.  Electrocardiogram (ECG).  Computed tomography (CT) head is the initial investigation of choice to exclude stroke.  Management  Initial management  Patients who have had more than one TIA in a week (crescendo TIA), have ongoing neurological symptoms, have severe cardiac stenosis or suspected cardio-embolic causes require urgent admission.  Patients who do not have anyone at home to contact emergency services if further symptoms occur may need urgent admission for observation.  Patients with a suspected TIA occurring within the last week (with symptoms that resolved within 24 hours) should receive aspirin as a 300 mg loading dose (and then continued for two weeks).  These patients must be seen by a specialist stroke physician within 24 hours:  a proton pump inhibitor can be added if required  if the patient has a history of a bleeding disorder or is on anticoagulation they must be admitted and reviewed urgently  if the patient is already taking aspirin, this dose should be continued  if aspirin is contraindicated, the patient should be discussed urgently with a specialist team.  If the patient had a TIA over a week ago, then a specialist review should be arranged within seven days.  Ongoing management  Continue aspirin for two weeks.  Change to clopidogrel 75 mg after two weeks.

DR. JAM  A statin, eg simvastatin 40 mg, should also be started immediately and continued long-term.  All patients with TIA and their carers or family members should be given advice regarding signs and symptoms of TIA and stroke and ask them to call 999 if symptoms recur.  Lifestyle modification advice should also be given, including:  cessation of smoking  reduction of alcohol consumption  increase in physical activity  diet modification.  The patient should also be advised not to drive until driving advice has been given by the specialist team.  Prognosis  TIAs are associated with a high risk of stroke in the following month and up to one year afterwards.  Estimates of risk of stroke following a TIA vary depending on the source and have been reported as:  3.9–5% within the first two days  5.5–8% within seven days  7.5–12% within 30 days  9.2–17% within 90 days. Trigeminal Neuralgia Trigeminal neuralgia describes severe, episodic facial pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal (V) cranial nerve.  Overview Key Facts  Trigeminal neuralgia describes severe, episodic facial pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal (V) cranial nerve.  Over 90% is due to vascular trigeminal nerve compression.  The condition is more common in women and is rare in patients under 40.  Symptoms include unilateral, episodic and recurrent facial pain.  Episodes may be infrequent, with long remissions (years) or occur hundreds of times a day.  'Atypical' or 'mixed' trigeminal neuralgia involves persistent discomfort between paroxysms or sensory loss and is more often refractory to treatment.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The diagnosis is clinical; neuroimaging, usually magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), is carried out to exclude structural causes.  Carbamazepine is the drug of choice for treatment.  Patients who are severely impacted by the condition warrant referral to neurology, as do those with atypical features or those whose symptoms suggest an underlying cause.  Prognosis is variable; some patients may achieve months or years of remission in between episodes, whereas others may continue to have frequent episodes in which activities of daily living can be impaired and lead to depression. Epidemiology  Annual incidence of 8 : 10 000 in the UK.  Overall prevalence of 0.7 : 100 000 people per year. Aetiology  The most common cause is the vascular compression of trigeminal nerve (90%).  Other rare causes include:  multiple sclerosis  arteriovenous (AV) malformations  tumours (posterior fossa tumours, cavernous sinus mass)  skull base abnormalities. Pathophysiology  Compression of trigeminal nerve leads to central demyelination of the nerve root entry zone and reinforced electrical excitability.  This causes impairment of the nociceptive system, leading to episodic and recurrent pain. Distribution of the trigeminal nerve branches:

DR. JAM  Clinical Presentation  Unilateral 'electric shock'-like or stabbing pain along the face in the distribution of the branches of trigeminal nerve.  Lasts a few seconds to minutes and stops abruptly.  Recurrent episodes that can be minutes, hours, days or even months apart.  There may be long periods of remission.  Triggers that may irritate the trigeminal nerve and start an episode include:  chewing  speaking  brushing and/or touching the face,  shaving  cold air.  Associated symptoms include:  depression and anxiety  weight loss  undernourishment.  Red flag symptoms and signs (suggesting more serious pathology) include:  age < 40  deafness  sensory loss  history of skin or oral lesions (perineural spread).  pain only in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (eye socket, forehead and nose)  bilateral signs and symptoms  optic neuritis  family history of multiple sclerosis.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  migraine  cluster headache  acoustic neuroma  trigeminal neuroma  meningioma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is usually clinical and involves a detailed history and thorough physical examination.  Neuroimaging includes CT or MRI and is to exclude serious underlying pathology or alternative diagnoses.  Management  The mainstay of treatment is carbamazepine:  the initial dose is 100 mg up to twice daily and can be titrated up every two weeks until symptoms are resolved  maximum dose is 1600 mg in divided does daily.  The patient should be advised to maintain a pain diary for followup and monitoring.  Specialist referral will be required in cases of uncontrolled pain despite optimal treatment or intolerance to carbamazepine.  Surgery is a treatment option where there is compression of the trigeminal nerve identified on MRI.  Prognosis  Prognosis is variable; longitudinal data on trigeminal neuralgia suggests remissions of at least six months are seen in 50% of patients following treatment.  Up to 10% do not respond to treatment and may have issues including:  weight loss (pain limits ability to eat)  depression  limitation of activities of daily living. Unconsciousness And Coma Coma is defined as a state of prolonged unconsciousness in which the patient is unresponsive to external stimuli or responds with only eye opening to pain and no eye tracking or fixation, as well as limb

DR. JAM withdrawal to a noxious stimulus at best (often with reflex motor movements).  Overview Key Facts  Coma is defined as a state of prolonged unconsciousness in which the patient is unresponsive to external stimuli or responds with only eye opening to pain and no eye tracking or fixation, as well as limb withdrawal to a noxious stimulus at best (often with reflex motor movements).  Brainstem reflexes can be partly absent or absent.  Coma is considered as an interruption of the ascending reticular activating system in the midbrain and pons projecting to the thalamus and cortex.  The principle causes of coma are:  lesions that damage the reticular activating system (RAS) at the level of midbrain or its projections  destructions to large surface of both cerebral hemispheres  suppression of reticulocerebral functions by metabolic disturbances, drugs or toxins.  The main diagnostic tool is the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), which measures the level of alertness.  Investigations include computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) along with metabolic studies to rule out the cause of coma.  Treatment depends upon the underlying cause. Aetiology Cause Features Trauma Epidural and subdural haematoma, intracerebral haemorrhage, skull fracture (depressed) Space-occupying lesions Neoplasms Neurological Epilepsy, raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus Uremia In patients with untreated, end stage renal disease Hypoglycaemia Prolonged, resulting in neuronal cell death

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Cause Features Infections Meningitis, encephalitis, malaria, toxploplasmosis etc Metabolic and endocrine disorders Addison’s disease, hypercalcaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia, hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, cyercapnia, hypoxia etc Anatomical and vascular causes Aneurysms Toxins affecting diffuse physiological brain functions Alcohol and/or drug intoxication, drug toxicity, poisoning, neuroleptic malignant syndrome or acute catatonia. Pathophysiology  Coma is related to one or more of the following aetiologies:  dysfunction of ascending RAS in the brainstem  extensive lesions in cortical and subcortical white matter in the brainstem  bilateral thalamic dysfunction.  Clinical Presentation The clinical presentations of different levels of consciousness:  Level 1 – Drowsy  easily arousable  light sleep  reflexes near normal  alert for brief period  other names – lethargy/semicoma.  Level 2 – Stupor  vigorous stimuli required to awaken  reduced motor activities due to abnormal muscle contraction  abnormal breathing  change in pupil size – may not react to light.  Level 3 – Coma  diminished brain stem reflexes  absent limb movements  reflexes present  absent pain stimulus or verbal command response  irregular breathing

DR. JAM  no spontaneous eye opening.  Level 4 – Persistent vegetative state  no awareness of self or environment  no response to any kind of stimuli  no language comprehension or expression  cranial nerves reflexes intact mostly  sleep wake cycle present – eyes usually open during the day  bowel and/or bladder incontinence  roving nystagmoid eye movements.  Level 5 – Minimal conscious state  Eye movement or head turn response to verbal commands  Ambulic emotionless state with eye tracking movements  Some intelligible verbalisation  May hold or use object when asked  May mouth words or fend off pain.  Level 6 – Locked-in syndrome  awake patient with voluntary vertical eye movement or lid elevation  inability to speak or perform movements  type of pseudocoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation A detailed history which includes:  the preceding symptoms such as confusion, fever, dizziness  history of medication use or substance abuse  past medical history. General examination:  temperature  blood pressure  respiratory rate  full body skin survey looking for skin discolouration, bruising, rash etc  fundoscopic examination. Neurological examination  Record Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score periodically – assessment of level of consciousness. Note: GCS of 8 or below requires intubation.  Assessment of brainstem reflexes – essential for localisation of lesion:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  the pupillary size, reaction to light, spontaneous and elicited eye movements, breathing pattern are assessed  pupils will be normal in lesions above the thalamus and below the pons  pinpoint pupils – opioid Intoxication or pontine lesion  fixed midpoint pupil – midbrain lesion or compression  dilated pupils – 3rd nerve or midbrain lesions, sympathomimetic drugs. Ocular Movements  Roving eye and/or conjugate lateral nystagmus implies an intact brainstem. Cause of coma – metabolic or bilateral hemisphere damage.  Skew deviation of eye – posterior fossa lesion.  Oculocephalic “doll's eye” reflex – if present, the coma is caused by a lesion or dysfunction in cerebral hemisphere. If absent, the damage is within the brainstem or due to drug intoxication.  Corneal reflex – useful test for pontine function. With an intact pons, the eyelids will close. If the pons and midbrain are intact, there will be upward movement of globe with eyelid closure (Bell’s phenomenon). Breathing pattern evaluation  Cheyne–Stokes breathing is the most common breathing pattern noticed in coma  deep breathing – acidosis  yawning or hiccups – brainstem lesions  regular shallow breathing – overdose. Investigations  full blood profile including full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&Es), liver function tests (LFTs), thyroid function tests (TFTS), glucose and arterial blood gas.  cardiac enzymes and electrocardiogram (ECG)  CT/ MRI head– to rule out a structural cause of coma  electroencephalogram (EEG)  infection screen – urine dip, chest X-ray, lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CFS) analysis  drug and alcohol levels.
