 Management Non-pharmacological  ABC assessment and subsequent appropriate management.  Supportive treatment:  IV fluids  Optimisation of electrolytes and acid–base balance  mechanical ventilation may be required (with GCS = 8, the patient may not be able to maintain their airway)  assess and manage feeding options  fall prevention while in the hospital  assess risk of pressure sores. Pharmacological  Treatment depends on the underlying cause:  3rd generation cephalosporins, vancomycin and/or ampicillin if there is a possibility of infection  IV thiamine if there is a suspicion of Wernicke’s encephalopathy or the diagnosis is unclear  give glucose if the patient is hypoglycaemic  trials of naloxone etc if overdose is suspected.  Prognosis  Prognosis is highly variable and is dependent on underlying conditions and duration of symptoms.  Overall, there is a poor prognosis associated with comatose patients which is not associated with head injury or overdose.  In patients with head injury, a GCS of > 6 confers a poor prognosis.  Other Brain death  Declared when brainstem reflexes, motor responses and respiratory drive are absent in a comatose patient.  Declared when there is an irreversible widespread brain lesion of known cause, along with satisfactory oxygenation, temperature,

DR. JAM absence of hypercapnia and pharmacological influences such as sedation. Viral Meningitis Inflammation of the meninges can be caused by a variety of viruses.  Overview Key Facts  Inflammation of the meninges can be caused by a variety of viruses.  Viral meningitis is usually self-limiting with no serious complications. However, it may be clinically indistinguishable from acute bacterial meningitis.  Can become complicated in infants, immunocompromised patients and patients infected with herpes or arboviruses.  Management involves supportive care and antiviral treatment (for confirmed HSV, varicella zoster or CMV).  Good prognosis with viral meningitis, with neurological damage being very uncommon. Epidemiology  Common infection of the CNS.  Estimated incidence of 2.73 per 100 000 people.  Affects all ages but is most common in children.  No differences between ethnicities.  Boys more commonly affected compared with girls. Aetiology  Commonly caused by human enteroviruses.  Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV2) is the most common cause of viral meningitis in the West. Pathophysiology  Enteroviruses replicate in the muscle, liver and respiratory and GI tracts and then spread to the CNS through the blood.  The viruses then penetrate the blood–brain barrier by infecting endothelial cells or by use of migrating leukocytes.  Viruses then spread through the subarachnoid space to cause meningitis.  The immune system responds to CNS infection by releasing inflammatory cytokines, eg IL-6, TNF and lymphocytes.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Presentation:  headache  nausea and vomiting  photophobia  neck stiffness  fever  rash.  Differential Diagnosis  May be clinically indistinguishable from bacterial meningitis.  Other differential diagnoses:  encephalitis  drug-induced meningitis  tuberculous meningitis  cryptococcal meningitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  CSF microscopy – WCC > 5 cells/mm3 (adult) and > 20 cells/mm3 (newborn)  CSF Gram stain – negative.  CSF bacterial culture - negative.  CSF protein – normal or elevated.  CSF glucose – may be low.  CT/MRI head scan – unremarkable.  Management  Supportive care – hydration, anti-pyretics, anti-emetics and analgesia.  Antiviral therapy – IV aciclovir or valaciclovir (for confirmed HSV, varicella zoster or CMV).  Prognosis  Good prognosis with viral meningitis, with neurological damage being very uncommon.  Headache and malaise may persist for several weeks.  Can recur with different serotypes.  Other  Neurodevelopmental deficits in infants.  Persistent headache and malaise.

DR. JAM Visual Field Defects Types of visual field loss include: central eg optic disc or nerve problem.  Overview Key Facts  Types of visual field loss include:  central eg optic disc or nerve problem  peripheral eg along the visual pathways from the optic chiasm back  scotoma (defect surrounded by a normal visual field, may begin as a gradual enlargement of the blind spot):  relative - low luminance objects cannot be seen, however bright or large objects can be seen  absolute - nothing can be seen within that area  hemianopia (binocular visual defect in each eyes hemifield):  bitemporal hemianopia - both temporal fields lost, creating tunnel vision  homonymous hemianopia - either the left or right visual field is lost  altitudinal hemianopia - dividing line between loss and sight is horizontal, with visual loss either above or below this line  sectoral defect - another term for incomplete hemianopia  quadrantanopia - a quarter of the visual field is lost.  Visual fields are assessed using confrontation and perimeter testing.  Treatment of the visual field loss depends upon the underlying cause. Aetiology There are many causes of visual field loss and they can lead to central or peripheral field loss. Central Field Loss Peripheral Field Loss Age-related macular degeneration Optic neuropathy Leber’s optic atrophy Macular holes Retinal artery occlusion Glaucoma Retinal detachment Retinitis pigmentosa Chorioretinitis Branch retinal occlusion Lesions at the level of the retina

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Retinal detachment Tends to be rapid in onset and may be preceded by floaters and flashes The patient notices a ‘curtain’ coming adown cross the visual field Central retinal artery occlusion Sudden and complete loss of vision in one eye If the occlusion is at the level of one of the 4 arteries to the retina, there will be loss of just one quadrant Affected area looks pale on fundoscopy Central retinal vein occlusion Presents in a similar way to arterial occlusion but the retina looks hyperaemic Dot and blot and flame-shaped haemorrhages are seen, alongside cotton wool spots Age-related macular degeneration Mainly affects the macular area, the periphery is only affected late on Drugs Tends to be bilateral eg chloroquine, vigabatrin Lesions before the chiasm:  These produce a visual field defect in the ipsilateral eye.  Optic nerve damage tends to lead to a defect that is central, asymmetrical, and unilateral.  Visual acuity is often affected.  Causes include:  optic neuritis  optic atrophy  glaucoma  trauma.  Lesions before the chiasm can also produce a small defect in the upper temporal field of the other eye, as the decussating fibres loop back into the optic nerve after crossing eg seen with a meningioma. Lesions at the chiasm:  Classically produce a bitemporal hemianopia.  If they spread up from below, the defect is worse in the upper field eg pituitary tumours.  If they spread down from above, then the defect is worse in the lower quadrants eg craniopharyngioma.

DR. JAM  Lesions may also show differing brightness between the two eyes eg a right hemianopia produces a left hemifield that is brighter than the right. Lesions after the chiasm:  Produce homonymous field defects, the distribution depends upon the location of the lesion:  right optic tract produces a left sided lesion  main optic radiation - complete homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing eg stroke, MCA lesions  Temporal radiation - upper quadrantic homonymous hemianopia, commonly with macula sparing eg tumours  Parietal radiation - inferior quadrantic homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing  Anterior visual cortex -contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing eg posterior cerebral artery occlusion  Macular cortex - homonymous macular defect eg blunt trauma to occiput  Intermediate visual cortex - homonymous arc scotoma, with sparing of both the macular and the periphery eg distal posterior cerebral artery occlusion. Occipital lobe lesions:  If both lobes are injured, then the patient has cortical visual impairment (cortical blindness).  Usually due to bilateral cortical infarcts and results in severe or complete loss of vision.  Lesions of the primary visual perception area of the right or left occipital lobe will produce a clear loss of the contralateral visual field, patients are usually aware of this, unlike in bilateral lesions.  Pupillary responses are preserved.  Other features may include:  subjective denial of vision loss (Anton syndrome)  macular sparing (tiny island of preserved central field, which may allow useful reading vision)  Charles-Bonnet syndrome (formed visual hallucinations).  Ventral stream damage does not tend to produce visual field defects. Cortical blindness:  Usually due to bilateral cortical infarcts and results in severe or complete loss of vision.  Pupillary responses are preserved.  Other features may include:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  subjective denial of vision loss (Anton syndrome)  macular sparing (tiny island of preserved central field, which may allow useful reading vision)  Charles-Bonnet syndrome (formed visual hallucinations). Optic pathway abnormalities and associated defects: image from p534 of ERN Pathophysiology  The optic nerve is formed from retinal nerve fibres which exit the eye and travel in the optic nerve to the optic chiasm.  Lesions of the retina and optic nerve produce field defects in the ipsilateral eye alone.  Lesions at the optic chiasm typically produce bitemporal hemianopia.  From the optic chiasm, the fibres run in the optic tract to the lateral geniculate nucleus in the thalamus.  Retrochiasmal lesions produce homonymous field defects, the more posterior the lesion, the greater the similarity between the two sides (congruity).  From the lateral geniculate nucleus, fibres pass in the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex (located in the occipital cortex).  The fibres from the lower and upper quadrants of the retina diverge, the upper fibres (from the lower half of the visual field) pass through the parietal lobe, and the lower fibres (from the upper half of the visual field) pass through the temporal lobes.  Temporal lobe lesions cause a superior homonymous quadrantanopia.  Parietal lobe lesions cause an inferior homonymous quadrantanopia.  The decussation of fibres at the optic chiasm means that the right visual field is represented in the left occipital cortex, and vice versa.  Right sided occipital lesion leads to a left sided visual field defect.

DR. JAM  Left sided occipital lesion leads to a right sided visual field defect.  Within the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe, the is a topographic representation of the visual field, with the more peripheral regions represented anteriorly, and the more central or foveal regions located more posteriorly.  At the very tip of the fovea is the vascular watershed, supplied by both the middle and posterior cerebral arteries.  A posterior cerebral artery stroke may be associated with sparing of this area because of the dual blood supply (macular sparing). Anatomy of visual pathway: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/The-main-parts-of-the-visualpathway_fig3_274318491 KDS444 [Public domain]  Diagnosis/Investigation  Examination of the fundus is carried out using ophthalmoscopy.  Pupillary reactions are also tested.  Visual fields are tested using confrontation.  An Amsler grid may also be used to identify any loss of visual fields (assesses the central 10° of the visual field, identifies central and paracentral scotomas, eg those seen in macular degeneration).  Perimetry testing can be used to assess the visual fields, this can be done in a variety of ways, however the Humphrey field test is commonly performed.  Imaging modalities may be required to assess for suspected lesions.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Wernickes Encephalopathy Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a severe and progressive encephalopathy secondary to thiamine deficiency, mostly seen in patients with alcohol dependence.  Overview Key Facts  Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a severe and progressive encephalopathy secondary to thiamine deficiency, mostly seen in patients with alcohol dependence.  Other causes include gastrointestinal malabsorption, starvation and hyperemesis.  10% present with a clinical triad of ataxia, confusion and eye signs (ACE).  Treatment – thiamine, support and management of underlying cause.  If untreated it develops into the permanent Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia and cognitive impairment).  Hospital alcohol withdrawal programmes include administration of IM/IV vitamin B preparations as a prevention.  Wernicke’s encephalopathy has a 20% mortality rate if untreated. Epidemiology  In Western countries, Wernicke’s is most likely due to alcohol dependence. In the United Kingdom (UK)  Less than one-third of hospital admissions are alcohol-related.  Approximately 10 million people drink more than the maximum recommended 14 units/week:  approximately 1 million of these are alcohol dependent.  Alcohol dependence (and thus Wernicke’s) is more common in men, but the sex ratio is reducing. Aetiology  Secondary to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.  In alcohol misuse, diet is often poor.  Common food sources of thiamine – whole grains, fish and meat. Cereals, breads and formula milk are often fortified.  Other possible causes:  stomach/duodenal/jejunal malabsorption (eg from GI cancer, bariatric surgery)  starvation  hyperemesis.

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Thiamine is an important factor in bodily carbohydrate metabolism; therefore, a deficiency can cause systemic difficulties.  Wernicke’s encephalopathy, the neuronal consequence, is important to diagnose and treat because it is a ‘warning sign’ prior to the development of permanent neurological damage (Korsakoff syndrome).  In alcohol dependence there are many factors causing thiamine deficiency:  increased thiamine requirement due to alcohol metabolism  poor dietary thiamine intake  low vitamin content in alcoholic drinks  decreased absorption  impaired hepatic storage  reduced hepatic phosphorylation (to the active thiamine pyrophosphate).  Post-mortems in those who have died with Wernicke’s show petechial haemorrhages mainly in the mammillary bodies.  Clinical Presentation  There should be a high index of suspicion, with a low threshold for action.  Symptoms – alcohol withdrawal, confusion, diplopia, difficulty moving.  Triad of signs, of which all three occur in approximately 10% of cases:  Possible signs:  oculomotor ophthalmoplegia  nystagmus  cerebellar dysfunction  ataxia  memory disturbance  peripheral neuropathy  reduced consciousness.  Likely patient history – alcohol dependence, GI carcinoma or starvation.  Features of alcohol withdrawal include alcohol cravings, anxiety, agitation, sweating, tremor, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, and hallucinations.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  acute alcohol intoxication  head injury

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  use of psychoactive substances  stroke  cerebral tumour  other encephalopathies (eg hepatic, infectious)  dementia  post-seizure  electrolyte disturbance  Korsakoff syndrome  hypo-/hyperglycaemia  sepsis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis  Diagnosis is made from clinical history, assessment of risk factors and examination.  A high index of suspicion in those with an alcohol misuse history.  Investigations  Full physical and neurological examination.  Electrocardiogram  Arterial blood gases (ABGs).  Blood cultures and/or lumbar puncture should also be considered.  Capillary bloods needed:  full blood count  clotting  liver function tests  glucose  urea and electrolytes  amylase  consider blood alcohol measurement.  Imaging considerations – computed tomography head/other brain imaging, ultrasound abdomen, chest X-ray.  Management  Most organisations have their own management pathway for alcohol withdrawal.  Treatment with thiamine should be initiated prior to awaiting other results and ‘ruling out’ of other differentials.

DR. JAM Non-pharmacological  Admission is essential as it is a medical emergency.  Close patient monitoring + regular symptom and neurology assessment.  If needed – patient care under the Mental Capacity Act/Mental Health Act.  Consider providing 1 : 1 staffing.  Referral to hepatology and in-patient alcohol services is advised. Pharmacological  Main treatment:  intravenous (IV)/intramuscular (IM) thiamine + other B vitamins:  eg pabrinex, IM administration reduces allergy risk  followed-up with oral B vitamins.  For those with Wernicke’s as a result of alcohol dependence, treatment protocols often include PO benzodiazepines (eg chlordiazepoxide) with dose and patient monitoring frequency dependent on symptom severity and the severity of alcohol withdrawal.  Oral thiamine prophylaxis for harmful/dependent drinkers if:  risk of or active malnourishment  decompensated liver disease  acute withdrawal  before/during medically assisted withdrawal  in medical services for any other reason. Prevention  Thiamine is given to all those with alcohol withdrawal in hospital.  Treatment of the other potential underlying cause (eg carcinoma).  Nutritionist advice.  Consider oral nutritional supplementation with thiamine in the community for alcoholics.  Prevention of drinking dependence recurrence includes engagement with alcohol services, good family/social support, management of any psychiatric comorbidities and possible pharmacological support (acamprosate, disulfiram). Surgical  In the treatment of non-alcohol-related Wernicke’s, surgery may be needed for gastrointestinal causes of thiamine malabsorption.

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Approximately 20% mortality rate if untreated.  Approximately 80% of untreated survivors develop permanent impairment, Korsakoff syndrome.  Other  Korsakoff syndrome is a permanent neurological consequence of thiamine deficiency characterised by confusion, confabulation, personality changes and memory impairment.  Current UK advice is for men and women not to drink more than 14 units of alcohol per week on a regular basis. Increased risk from drink  Alcohol dependence – a physiological, cognitive and behavioural need to drink combined with problems controlling its use.  Harmful drinking – drinking that causes physiological or psychological damage. Seen as > 35 units/week for women and > 50 units/week for men.  Hazardous drinking – drinking that causes physiological, psychological and social damage. Seen as between 14 and 35 units/week for women, and 14 and 50 units/week for men. The UK government has an educational resource for health professionals to reduce alcohol-related harm in patients. Wilson’s Disease Wilson’s disease is an inherited condition that is inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion.  Overview Key Facts  Wilson’s disease is an inherited condition that is inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion.  It is a rare inherited disorder, affecting 1 in 30 000 births.  The condition is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene which impairs copper incorporation into caeruloplasmina and copper excretion.  High levels of free copper, via oxidant damage, causes inflammation and cell injury resulting in hepatitis.  Continued exposure leads to fibrosis which can cause end-stage liver disease and hepatic failure.

DR. JAM  Copper can also accumulate in basal ganglia causing central nervous system (CNS) signs and symptoms, and the iris (manifesting as Kayser-Fleischer rings).  Management involves lifelong avoidance of copper containing foods, as well as copper chelation with lifelongs penacillamine. End stage hepatic disease requires transplantation.  Untreated, the condition is progressive and fatal.  Siblings should be screened for the condition once the diagnosis is confirmed. Aetiology  Autosomal-recessive disease caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene.  Copper is incorporated into caeruloplasmin in the liver.  The gene product of ATP7B is involved in excess copper excretion in the bile.  In Wilson’s disease, copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin and excretion of copper into bile is impaired. Pathophysiology  Excess copper is initially stored in the liver.  High levels of free copper, via oxidant damage, causes inflammation and cell injury resulting in hepatitis.  Continued exposure leads to fibrosis, which progresses to endstage liver disease and hepatic failure.  Copper can also accumulate in basal ganglia and iris.  Clinical Presentation  Children typically present with hepatic features  hepatitis  chirosis  liver failure.  Adults more often present with:  CNS signs:  tremor  dysarthria  dysphagia  dementia  parkinsonism  ataxia/clumsiness.  Mood symptoms:  depression/mania  loss of libido  personality change.  Cognition defects:

Neurology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  decreased memory.  slow to solve problems.  decreased IQ.  Kayser-Fleischer rings: Copper deposition in iris. Kayser-Fleischer ring:  Differential Diagnosis  Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency.  Hemochromatosis.  Viral hepatitis B.  Viral hepatitis C.  Autoimmune hepatitis.  Steatohepatitis.  Alcoholic cirrhosis.  Essential tremor.  Parkinson disease.  Psychiatric diseases.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Liver function tests.  24 hour urine copper - increased.  Slit-lamp exam – shows sunflower cataracts.  Blood ceruloplasmin - reduced.  Management  Avoid high copper containing foods eg liver, chocolate, nuts, mushrooms.  Lifelong penicillamine is the mainstay of treatment.  Liver transplantation may be indicated with severe hepatic disease.  Siblings should also be screened for the condition.

DR. JAM  Prognosis  Early, and then lifelong treatment has better prognosis.  Pre-cirrhotic liver disease is reversible.  Neurologic symptoms improve about 5-6 months’ post-treatment.  If untreated, Wilson’s is progressive and invariably fatal.

stem: A 38-year old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe right occipital headache and neck pain, which came on acutely while he was playing rugby for his local team. On examination, he has diminished sensation over the right side of his face, with ipsilateral facial weakness. He has diplopia on looking to the right. He has grade 4 power affecting his left arm and leg, with associated sensation loss. Coordination in his right hand is impaired. His blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular, and he is anxious. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Vertebral artery dissection Vertebral artery dissection typically presents with severe occipital headache and neck pain following head or neck injury. The trauma is generally from a trivial mechanism, but is associated with some degree of cervical distortion. Focal neurological signs attributable to ischaemia of the brainstem and cerebellum ultimately develop in 85% of patients, although there may be a latent period of up to 3

days between the onset of pain and the development of central nervous system sequelae. The commonest reported symptoms are attributable to lateral medullary dysfunction, including ipsilateral facial dysaesthesia, dysarthria or hoarseness, ipsilateral limb or trunk numbness, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, ipsilateral loss of taste, vertigo, dysphagia, diplopia and disequilibrium. Rarely patients may manifest symptoms of a medial medullary syndrome: contralateral weakness/paralysis (pyramidal tract) and contralateral numbness (medial lemniscus). Ipsilateral Horner syndrome occurs in as many as one-third of patients. Risk factors associated with vertebral artery dissection include spinal manipulation, yoga, ceiling painting, judo, nose blowing, minor neck trauma, ﬁbromuscular dysplasia, cystic medial necrosis, oral contaceptive pill use, chronic headache syndromes and female sex. E Basilar artery dissection Basilar artery dissection is very rare and is more likely to present with symptoms of a subarachnoid haemorrhage rather than the lateralising signs seen here. A Basilar artery aneurysm Basilar artery aneurysms are uncommon, and only rarely rupture; as they increase in size they may present with a 3rd nerve palsy. B Cervical vertebral fracture In cervical vertebral fracture, facial symptoms would not be expected. C Subarachnoid haemorrhage In subarachnoid haemorrhage, lateralising signs would be unusual unless there is an ischaemic event due to secondary vasospasm.

stem: You review a 26-year-old woman who presents with transient disturbances of vision and frequent headaches. She also reports dizziness and diplopia on a number of occasions. She has a body mass index (BMI) of 32. On examination there is bilateral papilloedema.
explanation: C Vitamin A excess Idiopathic intracranial hypertension has a female predominance, with estimates of the female to male sex ratio ranging between 2:1 and 10:1, presenting most commonly in the third decade. (The term ‘idiopathic’ is now preferred to ‘benign’, as the clinical course may have signiﬁcant morbidity). Incidence is increased in patients who have a markedly raised BMI. Drug causes include contraceptive hormones, vitamin A excess, dopamine agonists, antibiotics, phenytoin and a number of other agents. However, the underlying pathophysiology is poorly understood. Diagnosis is via CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans to rule out a space- occupying lesion, MR venography to exclude venous thrombosis and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement. Weight management is the cornerstone of treatment, coupled with withdrawal of any precipitating pharmacological agent. Diuretics (acetazolamide) may also be used to good effect and therapeutic lumbar puncture is also of value. E Vitamin C excess Unlike vitamin A, vitamin C is water soluble, which means that if you take more than your body can use, the excess is usually excreted without causing harm, although adverse reactions like diarrhoea, stomach cramps and nausea can occur. A Atenolol Atenolol, which is a beta blocker, is useful for treatment of angina and hypertension but has no role in idiopathic intracranial hypertension. B Bendroﬂumethiazide Acetazolamide, and not bendroﬂumethiazide, is useful for treatment of idiopathic intracranial hypertension. D Vitamin B excess People almost never get too much vitamin B from food, but taking high levels of certain B vitamins (such as B6) from supplements can cause severe peripheral neuropathy.
